(A) The dotted line corresponds to *a* = 1,*b* = 1, the gray line to *a* = 0.5,*b* = 0.5, and the red one to *a* = 3,*b* = 3. (B) The gray line corresponds to *a* = 2,*b* = 3, and the red one to *a* = 8,*b* = 4. For values *a* = *b*, the shape is symmetric around 1/2. For *a* < 1,*b* < 1, it is convex. For *a* > 1,*b* > 1, it is zero at *x* = 0 and *x* = 1. For *a* = 1 = *b*, it becomes the uniform distribution. If *a* < 1, *p*(*x*)⟶∞,*x*⟶0 and if *b* < 1, *p*(*x*)⟶∞,*x*⟶1.

#### The gamma distribution

A random variable follows the gamma distribution with positive parameters *a*, *b*<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si196.png), and we write *x* ∼ Gamma(*x*|*a*, *b*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>Gamma</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si214.png), if

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx019.jpg)(2.92) 

The mean and variance are given by

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack x\\rbrack = \\frac{a}{b},\\quad\\sigma\_{x}^{2} = \\frac{a}{b^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si215.png)(2.93) 

The gamma distribution also takes various shapes by varying the parameters. For *a* < 1<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si201.png), it is strictly decreasing and *p*(*x*) → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si216.png) as *x* → 0<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si212.png) and *p*(*x*) → 0<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si209.png) as *x* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si217.png). [Fig. 2.8](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0045) shows the resulting graphs for various values of the parameters.

Remarks 2.1

*   •  Setting in the gamma distribution *a* to be an integer (usually *a* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si218.png)), the *Erlang* distribution results. This distribution is used to model waiting times in queueing systems.
*   •  The *chi-squared* is also a special case of the gamma distribution, and it is obtained if we set *b* = 1/2<mml:math><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si219.png) and *a* = *ν*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ν</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si220.png). The chi-squared distribution results if we sum up *ν* squared normal variables.

![Figure 2.8 The PDF of the gamma distribution takes different shapes for the various values of the following parameters: a = 0.5,b = 1 (full line gray), a = 2,b = 0.5 (red), a = 1,b = 2 (dotted).](images/B9780443292385000081/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 2.8](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0470) The PDF of the gamma distribution takes different shapes for the various values of the following parameters: *a* = 0.5,*b* = 1 (full line gray), *a* = 2,*b* = 0.5 (red), *a* = 1,*b* = 2 (dotted).

#### The Dirichlet distribution

The Dirichlet distribution can be considered as the multivariate generalization of the beta distribution. Let **x** = \[*x*[1], …, *x*[*K*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si221.png) be a random vector, with components such as

$0 \\leq x\_{k} \\leq 1,\\quad k = 1,2,\\ldots,K,\\quad\\text{and}\\quad\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}x\_{k} = 1.$<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si222.png)(2.94) 

In other words, the random variables lie on (*K* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si223.png)\-dimensional *simplex*, [Fig. 2.9](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0050). We say that the random vector **x** follows a Dirichlet distribution with (positive) parameters **a** = \[*a*[1], …, *a*[*K*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si224.png), and we write **x** ∼ Dir(**x**|**a**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Dir</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si225.png), if

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx020.jpg)(2.95) 

where

$\\overline{a} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}a\_{k}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si226.png)(2.96) 

![Figure 2.9 The two-dimensional simplex in \\mathbb{R}^{3}Equation.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 2.9](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0475) The two-dimensional simplex in ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si227.png).

The mean, variance, and covariances of the involved random variables are given by (Problem [2.7](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0040)), i.e.,

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\mathbf{x}\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{\\overline{a}}\\mathbf{a},\\quad\\sigma\_{x\_{k}}^{2} = \\frac{a\_{k}(\\overline{a} - a\_{k})}{{\\overline{a}}^{2}(\\overline{a} + 1)},\\quad\\text{cov}(x\_{i},x\_{j}) = - \\frac{a\_{i}a\_{j}}{{\\overline{a}}^{2}(\\overline{a} + 1)},\\ i \\neq j.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo ## 2.4 Stochastic processes

The notion of a random variable has been introduced to describe the result of a random experiment whose outcome is a single value, such as “heads” or “tails” in a coin tossing experiment, or a value between one and six when throwing the die in a backgammon game.

In this section, the notion of a *stochastic process* is introduced to describe random experiments where the outcome of each experiment is a function or a sequence; in other words, the outcome of each experiment is an infinite number of values. In this book, we are only going to be concerned with stochastic processes associated with sequences. Thus, the result of a random experiment is a *sequence*, *u*[*n*]  (or sometimes denoted as  *u*(*n*)), *n* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>or sometimes denoted as</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si229.png), where ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si230.png) is the set of integers. Usually, *n* is interpreted as a time index, and *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si231.png) is called a *time series*, or in signal processing jargon, a *discrete-time signal*. In contrast, if the outcome is a function, *u*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si232.png), it is called a *continuous-time* signal. We are going to adopt the time interpretation of the free variable *n* for the rest of the chapter, without harming generality.

When discussing random variables, we used the notation x to denote the random variable, which assumes a value, *x*, from the sample space once an experiment is performed. Similarly, we are going to use *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si231.png) to denote the specific sequence resulting from a single experiment and the roman font, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png), to denote the corresponding *discrete-time* random process, that is, the rule that assigns a specific sequence as the outcome of an experiment. A stochastic process can be considered as a family or *ensemble* of sequences. The individual sequences are known as *sample sequences* or simply as *realizations*.

For our notational convention, in general, we are going to reserve different symbols for processes and random variables. We have already used the symbol u and not x; this is only for pedagogical reasons, just to make sure that the reader readily recognizes when the focus is on random variables and when it is on random processes. In signal processing jargon, a stochastic process is also known as a *random signal*. [Fig. 2.11](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0060) illustrates the fact that the outcome of an experiment involving a stochastic process is a sequence of values.

![Figure 2.11 The outcome of each experiment, associated with a discrete-time stochastic process, is a sequence of values. For each one of the realizations, the corresponding values obtained at any instant (e.g., n or m) comprise the outcomes of a corresponding random variable, un or um, respectively.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 2.11](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0490) The outcome of each experiment, associated with a *discrete-time* stochastic process, is a *sequence* of values. For each one of the realizations, the corresponding values obtained at any instant (e.g., *n* or *m*) comprise the outcomes of a corresponding random variable, u[*n*] or u[*m*], respectively.

Note that fixing the time to a specific value, *n* = *n*[0]<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si234.png), makes *u*[*n*[0]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si235.png) a random variable. Indeed, for each random experiment we perform, a single value results at time instant *n*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si236.png). From this perspective, a random process can be considered the collection of infinite random variables, {*u*[*n*], *n* ∈ ℤ}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si237.png). So, is there a need to study a stochastic process separate from random variables/vectors? The answer is yes, and the reason is that we are going to allow certain time dependencies among the random variables, corresponding to different time instants, and study the respective effect on the time evolution of the random process. Stochastic processes will be considered in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), where the underlying time dependencies will be exploited for computational simplifications, and in Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml) in the context of Gaussian processes.

### 2.4.1 First- and second-order statistics

For a stochastic process to be fully described, one must know the joint PDFs (PMFs for discrete-valued random variables)

*p*(*u*[*n*], *u*[*m*], …, *u*[*r*]; *n*, *m*, …, *r*),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si238.png)(2.98) 

for all possible combinations of random variables, *u*[*n*], *u*[*m*], …, *u*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si239.png). Note that, in order to emphasize it, we have explicitly denoted the dependence of the joint PDFs on the involved time instants. However, from now on, this will be suppressed for notational convenience. Most often, in practice, and certainly in this book, the emphasis is on computing first- and second-order statistics only, based on *p*(*u*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si240.png) and *p*(*u*[*n*], *u*[*m*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si241.png). To this end, the following quantities are of particular interest.

*Mean at time n*:

*μ*[*n*] :  = 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\] = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*u*[*n*]*p*(*u*[*n*])*d**u*[*n*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si242.png)(2.99) 

*Autocovariance at time instants* *n*, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si243.png):

cov(*n*, *m*) :  = 𝔼 \[(*u*[*n*]−𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\])(*u*[*m*]−𝔼\[*u*[*m*]\])\].<mml:math><mml:mtext>cov</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si244.png)(2.100) 

*Autocorrelation at time instants* *n*, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si243.png):

*r*(*n*, *m*) :  = 𝔼 \[*u*[*n*]*u*[*m*]\].<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si245.png)(2.101) 

Note that for notational simplicity, subscripts have been dropped from the respective symbols, e.g., *r*(*n*, *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si246.png) is used instead of the more formal notation, *r*[*u*](*n*, *m*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si247.png). We refer to these mean values as *ensemble* averages to stress that they convey statistical information over the ensemble of sequences that comprise the process.

The respective definitions for complex stochastic processes are

cov(*n*, *m*) = 𝔼 \[(*u*[*n*]−𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\])(*u*[*m*]−𝔼\[*u*[*m*]\])^(\*)\],<mml:math><mml:mtext>cov</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si248.png)(2.102) 

and

*r*(*n*, *m*) = 𝔼 \[*u*[*n*]*u*[*m*]^(\*)\].<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si249.png)(2.103) 

### 2.4.2 Stationarity and ergodicity

Definition 2.1

Strict-sense stationarity

A stochastic process *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) is said to be *strict-sense stationary* (SSS) if its statistical properties are invariant to a shift of the origin, or if ∀*k* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si250.png)

*p*(*u*[*n*], *u*[*m*], …, *u*[*r*]) = *p*(*u*[*n* − *k*], *u*[*m* − *k*], …, *u*[*r* − *k*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si251.png)(2.104) 

and for *any* possible combination of time instants, *n*, *m*, …, *r* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si252.png).

In other words, the stochastic processes *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) and *u*[*n* − *k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si253.png) are described by the same joint PDFs of all orders. A weaker version of stationarity is that of the *m*th-order stationarity, where joint PDFs involving up to *m* variables are invariant to the choice of the origin. For example, for a second-order (*m* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si254.png)) stationary process, we have *p*(*u*[*n*]) = *p*(*u*[*n* − *k*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si255.png) and *p*(*u*[*n*], *u*[*r*]) = *p*(*u*[*n* − *k*], *u*[*r* − *k*]), ∀*n*, *r*, *k* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si256.png).

Definition 2.2

Wide-sense stationarity

A stochastic process *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) is said to be *wide-sense stationary* (WSS) if the mean value is constant over all time instants and the autocorrelation/autocovariance sequences depend on the difference of the involved time indices, or

*μ*[*n*] = *μ*, and *r*(*n*, *n* − *k*) = *r*(*k*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si257.png)(2.105) 

Note that WSS is a weaker version of the second-order stationarity; in the latter case, all possible second-order statistics are independent of the time origin. In the former, we only require the autocorrelation (autocovariance) and the mean value to be independent of the time origin. The reason we focus on these two quantities (statistics) is that they are of major importance in the study of linear systems and in the mean-square estimation, as we will see in Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml).

Obviously, an SSS process is also WSS but, in general, not the other way around. For WSS processes, the autocorrelation becomes a *sequence* with a *single* time index as the free parameter; thus its value, which measures a relation of the random variables at two time instants, depends *solely on how much these time instants differ*, and not on their specific values.

From our basic statistics course, we know that given a random variable x, its mean value can be approximated by the sample mean. Carrying out *N* successive independent experiments, let *x*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si258.png), be the obtained values, known as *observations*. The *sample mean* is defined as

${\\widehat{\\mu}}\_{N}: = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}x\_{n}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si259.png)(2.106) 

For large enough values of *N*, we expect the sample mean to be close to the true mean value, 𝔼\[*x*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si260.png). In a more formal way, this is guaranteed by the fact that *μ̂*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si261.png) is associated with an *unbiased* and *consistent* estimator. We will discuss such issues in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml); however, we can refresh our memory at this point. Every time we repeat the *N* random experiments, different samples result and hence a different estimate *μ̂*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si261.png) is computed. Thus, the values of the estimates define a new random variable, *μ̂*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si263.png), known as the estimator. This is unbiased, because it can easily be shown that

𝔼\[*μ̂*[*N*]\] = 𝔼\[*x*\],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si264.png)(2.107) 

and it is consistent because its variance tends to zero as *N* →  + ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si265.png) (Problem [2.8](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0045)). These two properties guarantee that, with high probability, for large values of *N*, *μ̂*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si261.png) will be close to the true mean value.

To apply the concept of sample mean approximation to random processes, one must have at her/his disposal a number of *N* realizations, and compute the sample mean at different time instants “across the process,” using *different* realizations, representing the ensemble of sequences. Similarly, sample mean arguments can be used to approximate the autocovariance/autocorrelation sequences. However, this is a costly operation, since now each experiment results in an infinite number of values (a sequence of values). Moreover, it is common in practical applications that only one realization is available to the user.

To this end, we will now define a special type of stochastic processes, where the sample mean operation can be significantly simplified.

Definition 2.3

Ergodicity

A stochastic process is said to be *ergodic* if the complete statistics can be determined by any one of the realizations.

In other words, if a process is ergodic, every single realization carries identical statistical information and it can describe the entire random process. Since from a single sequence only one set of PDFs can be obtained, we conclude that *every ergodic process is necessarily stationary*. A nonstationary process has infinite sets of PDFs, depending upon the choice of the origin. For example, there is only one mean value that can result from a single realization and be obtained as a (time) average over the values of the sequence. Hence, the mean value of a stochastic process that is ergodic must be constant for all time instants, or independent of the time origin. The same is true for all higher-order statistics.

A special type of ergodicity is that of the *second-order* ergodicity. This means that only statistics up to a second order can be obtained from a single realization. Second-order ergodic processes are necessarily WSS. For second-order ergodic processes, the following are true:

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack u\_{n}\\rbrack = \\mu = \\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\widehat{\\mu}}\_{N},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si266.png)(2.108) 

where

${\\widehat{\\mu}}\_{N}: = \\frac{1}{2N + 1}\\sum\\limits\_{n = - N}^{N}u\_{n}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si267.png)

Also,

$\\text{cov}(k) = \\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac{1}{2N + 1}\\sum\\limits\_{n = - N}^{N}(u\_{n} - \\mu)(u\_{n - k} - \\mu),$<mml:math><mml:mtext>cov</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si268.png)(2.109) 

where both limits are meant in the mean-square sense. In other words, it is easily seen that the estimator *μ̂*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si263.png) is an unbiased one, then ergodicity demands that its variance in the limit tends to zero, i.e.,

$\\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack |{\\widehat{\\mu}}\_{N} - \\mu|^{2} \\right\\rbrack = 0,$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si270.png)

and similarly for the autocovariance. Note that often, ergodicity is only required to be assumed for the computation of the mean and covariance and not for all possible second-order statistics. In this case, we talk about *mean-ergodic* and *covariance-ergodic* processes.

*In summary, when ergodic processes are involved, ensemble averages “across the process” can be obtained as time averages “along the process”*; see [Fig. 2.12](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0065).

![Figure 2.12 For ergodic processes, the common mean value, for all time instants (ensemble averaging “across” the process), is computed as the time average “along” the process.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 2.12](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0500) For ergodic processes, the common mean value, for all time instants (ensemble averaging “across” the process), is computed as the time average “along” the process.

In practice, when only a finite number of samples from a realization are available, then the mean and covariance are approximated as the respective sample means.

An issue is to establish conditions under which a process is mean-ergodic or covariance-ergodic. Such conditions do exist, and the interested reader can find such information in more specialized books, e.g., \[6\]. It turns out that the condition for mean-ergodicity relies on second-order statistics and the condition for covariance-ergodicity on fourth-order statistics.

It is very common in statistics as well as in machine learning and signal processing to subtract the mean value from the data during the *preprocessing stage*. In such a case, we say that the data are *centered*. The resulting new process has now *zero mean* value, and the covariance and autocorrelation sequences coincide. From now on, we will assume that the mean is known (or computed as a sample mean) and then subtracted. Such a treatment simplifies the analysis without harming generality.

Example 2.2

The goal of this example is to construct a process that is WSS yet not ergodic. Let a WSS process, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png),

𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\] = *μ*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si271.png)

and

𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*u*[*n* − *k*]\] = *r*[*u*](*k*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si272.png)

Define the process

*v*[*n*] :  = *a**u*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">a</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si273.png)(2.110) 

where a is a random variable taking values in {0, 1}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si274.png), with probabilities *P*(0) = *P*(1) = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si275.png). Moreover, a and *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) are statistically independent. Then, we have

𝔼\[*v*[*n*]\] = 𝔼\[*a**u*[*n*]\] = 𝔼\[*a*\]𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\] = 0.5*μ*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">a</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si277.png)(2.111) 

and

𝔼\[*v*[*n*]*v*[*n* − *k*]\] = 𝔼\[*a*²\]𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*u*[*n* − *k*]\] = 0.5*r*[*u*](*k*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si278.png)(2.112) 

Thus, *v*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si279.png) is WSS. However, it is not ergodic. Indeed, some of the realizations will be equal to zero (when *a* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si280.png)), and the mean value and autocorrelation, which will result from them as time averages, will be zero, which is different from the ensemble averages.

### 2.4.3 Power spectral density

The Fourier transform is an indispensable tool for representing in a compact way, in the frequency domain, the variations that a function/sequence undergoes in terms of its free variable (e.g., time). Stochastic processes are inherently related to time. The question that is now raised is whether stochastic processes can be described in terms of a Fourier transform. The answer is in the affirmative, and the vehicle to achieve this is via the autocorrelation sequence for processes that are at least WSS. Prior to providing the necessary definitions, it is useful to summarize some common properties of the autocorrelation sequence.

#### Properties of the autocorrelation sequence

Let *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) be a WSS process. Its autocorrelation sequence has the following properties, which are given for the more general complex-valued case:

*   •  *Property I*.

*r*(*k*) = *r*^(\*)( − *k*), ∀*k* ∈ ℤ.<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si281.png)(2.113) 

*   This property is a direct consequence of the invariance with respect to the choice of the origin. Indeed,

*r*(*k*) = 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*u*[*n* − *k*]^(\*)\] = 𝔼\[*u*[*n* + *k*]*u*[*n*]^(\*)\] = *r*^(\*)( − *k*).<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si282.png)

*   
*   •  *Property II*.

*r*(0) = 𝔼\[|*u*[*n*]|²\].<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si283.png)(2.114) 

*   That is, the value of the autocorrelation at *k* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si284.png) is equal to the mean-square of the magnitude of the respective random variables. Interpreting the square of the magnitude of a variable as its energy, *r*(0)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si285.png) can be interpreted as the corresponding (average) power.
*   •  *Property III*.

*r*(0) ≥ |*r*(*k*)|, ∀*k* ≠ 0.<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si286.png)(2.115) 

*   The proof is provided in Problem [2.9](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0050). In other words, the correlation of the variables, corresponding to two different time instants, cannot be larger (in magnitude) than *r*(0)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si285.png). As we will see in Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml), interpreting the expectation as an inner product, this property is essentially the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the inner products (see also Appendix of Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)).
*   •  *Property IV*. The autocorrelation sequence of a stochastic process is *positive definite*. That is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx021.jpg)(2.116) 

*   
*   

Proof

The proof is easily obtained by the definition of the autocorrelation,

$0 \\leq \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\middle| \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}a\_{n}u\_{n}|^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{N}a\_{n}a\_{m}^{\\ast}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack u\_{n}u\_{m}^{\\ast} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" which proves the claim. Note that strictly speaking, we should say that it is positive semidefinite. However, the “positive definite” name is the one that has survived in the literature. This property will be useful when introducing *Gaussian processes* in Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml). □

*   
*   •  *Property V*. Let *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) and *v*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si279.png) be two WSS processes. Define the new process

*z*[*n*] = *u*[*n*] + *v*[*n*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si288.png)

*   Then,

*r*[*z*](*k*) = *r*[*u*](*k*) + *r*[*v*](*k*) + *r*[*u**v*](*k*) + *r*[*v**u*](*k*),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si289.png)(2.118) 

*   where the *cross-correlation* between two jointly WSS stochastic processes is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx022.jpg)(2.119) 

*   The proof is a direct consequence of the definition. Note that if the two processes are *uncorrelated*, as when *r*[*u**v*](*k*) = *r*[*v**u*](*k*) = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si290.png), then

*r*[*z*](*k*) = *r*[*u*](*k*) + *r*[*v*](*k*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si291.png)

*   Obviously, this is also true if the processes *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) and *v*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si279.png) are independent and of zero mean value, since then 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*v*[*n* − *k*]^(\*)\] = 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\]𝔼\[*v*[*n* − *k*]^(\*)\] = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si292.png). It should be stressed here that uncorrelatedness is a weaker condition and it *does not* necessarily imply independence; the opposite is true for zero mean values.
*   •  *Property VI*.

*r*[*u**v*](*k*) = *r*[*v**u*]^(\*)( − *k*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si293.png)(2.120) 

*   The proof is similar to that of Property I.
*   •  *Property VII*.

*r*[*u*](0)*r*[*v*](0) ≥ |*r*[*u**v*](*k*)|², ∀*k* ∈ ℤ.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si294.png)(2.121) 

*   The proof is also given in Problem [2.9](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0050).

#### Power spectral density

Definition 2.4

Given a WSS stochastic process *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png), its *power spectral density* (PSD) (or simply the *power spectrum*) is defined as the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation sequence,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx023.jpg)(2.122) 

Using the Fourier transform properties, we can recover the autocorrelation sequence via the *inverse Fourier transform* in the following manner:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx024.jpg)(2.123) 

Due to the properties of the autocorrelation sequence, the PSD has some interesting and useful properties, from a practical point of view.

*Properties of the PSD*

*   •  The PSD of a WSS stochastic process is a *real* and *nonnegative* function of *ω*. Indeed, we have

$S(\\omega) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}r(k)\\exp\\left( - j\\omega k \\right) = r(0) + \\sum\\limits\_{k = - \\infty}^{- 1}r(k)\\exp\\left( - j\\omega k \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}r(k)\\exp\\left( - j\\omega k \\right) = r(0) + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{+ \\infty}r^{\\ast}(k)\\exp\\left( j\\omega k \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{\\infty}r(k)\\exp\\left( - j\\omega k \\right) = r(0) + 2\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{+ \\infty}\\text{Real}\\left\\{ r(k)\\exp\\left( - j\\omega k \\right) \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo #### Transmission through a linear system

One of the most important tasks in signal processing and systems theory is the *linear filtering operation* on an *input* time series (*signal*) to generate another *output* sequence. The block diagram of the filtering operation is shown in [Fig. 2.13](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0070). From the linear system theory and signal processing basics, it is established that for a class of linear systems known as *linear time-invariant*, the input–output relation is given via the elegant *convolution* between the input sequence and the *impulse response* of the filter,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx025.jpg)(2.126) 

where …, *w*[0], *w*[1], *w*[2], …<mml:math><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si300.png) are the parameters comprising the impulse response describing the filter \[8\]. In case the impulse response is of finite duration, for example, *w*[0], *w*[1], …, *w*[*l* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si301.png), and the rest of the values are zero, then the convolution can be written as

$d\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{l - 1}w\_{i}^{\\ast}u\_{n - i} = \\mathbf{w}^{H}\\mathbf{u}\_{n},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si302.png)(2.127) 

where

**w** :  = \[*w*[0], *w*[1], …, *w*[*l* − 1]\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si303.png)(2.128) 

and

**u**[*n*] :  = \[*u*[*n*], *u*[*n* − 1], …, *u*[*n* − *l* + 1]\]^(*T*) ∈ ℝ^(*l*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si304.png)(2.129) 

The latter is known as the *input vector* of order *l* and at time *n*. It is interesting to note that this is a random vector. However, its elements are part of the stochastic process at *successive* time instants. This gives the respective autocorrelation matrix certain properties and a rich structure, which will be studied and exploited in Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml). As a matter of fact, this is a reason that we used different symbols to denote processes and general random vectors; thus, the reader can readily remember that when dealing with a process, the elements of the involved random vectors have this *extra structure*. Moreover, observe from Eq.
