[(2.126)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq146) that if the impulse response of the system is zero for negative values of the time index *n*, this guarantees *causality*. That is, the output depends only on the values of the input at the current and previous time instants, and there is no dependence on future values. As a matter of fact, this is also a necessary condition for causality; that is, if the system is causal, then its impulse response is zero for negative time instants \[8\].

![Figure 2.13 The linear system (filter) is excited by the input sequence (signal) un and provides the output sequence (signal) dn.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 2.13](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0530) The linear system (filter) is excited by the input sequence (signal) u[*n*] and provides the output sequence (signal) d[*n*].

Theorem 2.1

*The PSD of the output* *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si305.png) *of a linear time-invariant system, when it is excited by a WSS stochastic process* *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png)*, is given by*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx026.jpg)(2.130) 

*where*

$W(\\omega): = \\sum\\limits\_{n = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}w\_{n}\\exp\\left( - j\\omega n \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si307.png)(2.131) 

Proof

First, it is shown (Problem [2.10](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0055)) that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx027.jpg)(2.132) 

Then, taking the Fourier transform of both sides, we obtain Eq. [(2.130)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq150). To this end, we used the well-known properties of the Fourier transform,

*r*[*u*](*k*) \* *w*[*k*] ↦ *S*[*u*](*ω*)*W*(*ω*), and *w*[ − *k*]^(\*) ↦ *W*^(\*)(*ω*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si308.png)

 □

#### Physical interpretation of the PSD

We are now ready to justify why the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation sequence was given the specific name of “power spectral density.” We restrict our discussion to real processes, although similar arguments hold true for the more general complex case. [Fig. 2.14](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0075) shows the magnitude of the Fourier transform of the impulse response of a very special linear system. The Fourier transform is unity for any frequency in the range $|\\omega - \\omega\_{o}| \\leq \\frac{\\Delta\\omega}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si309.png) and zero otherwise. Such a system is known as *bandpass filter*. We assume that Δ*ω* is very small. Then, using Eq. [(2.130)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq150) and assuming that within the intervals $|\\omega - \\omega\_{o}| \\leq \\frac{\\Delta\\omega}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si309.png), *S*[*u*](*ω*) ≈ *S*[*u*](*ω*[*o*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si311.png), we have

$S\_{d}(\\omega) = \\begin{cases} {S\_{u}(\\omega\_{o}),\\;} & {\\text{if}\\ \\ |\\omega - \\omega\_{o}| \\leq \\frac{\\Delta\\omega}{2},} \\\\ {0,\\;} & {\\text{otherwise}.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>otherwise</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si312.png)(2.133) 

Hence,

$\\Delta P: = \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack |d\_{n}|^{2} \\right\\rbrack = r\_{d}(0) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\int\_{- \\pi}^{+ \\pi}S\_{d}(\\omega)d\\omega \\approx S\_{u}(\\omega\_{o})\\frac{\\Delta\\omega}{\\pi},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si313.png)(2.134) 

due to the symmetry of the PSD for real processes, *u*[*n*] ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si314.png) (*S*[*u*](*ω*) = *S*[*u*]( − *ω*))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si315.png). Hence,

$\\frac{1}{\\pi}S\_{u}(\\omega\_{o}) = \\frac{\\Delta P}{\\Delta\\omega}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si316.png)(2.135) 

In other words, the value *S*[*u*](*ω*[*o*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si317.png) can be interpreted as the power density (power per frequency interval) in the frequency (spectrum) domain.

![Figure 2.14 An ideal bandpass filter. The output contains frequencies only in the range |ω − ωo| ≤ Δω/2.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr014.jpg)

[Figure 2.14](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0560) An ideal bandpass filter. The output contains frequencies only in the range |*ω* − *ω*[*o*]| ≤ Δ*ω*/2.

Moreover, this also establishes what was said before that the PSD is a *nonnegative* real function for any value of *ω* ∈ \[ − *π*,  + *π*\]<mml:math><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si318.png) (the PSD, being the Fourier transform of a sequence, is periodic with period 2*π*, e.g., \[8\]).

Remarks 2.2

*   •  Note that for any WSS stochastic process, there is only one autocorrelation sequence that describes it. However, the converse is not true. A single autocorrelation sequence can correspond to more than one WSS process. Recall that the autocorrelation is the mean value of the product of random variables. However, many random variables can have the same mean value.
*   •  We have shown that the Fourier transform, *S*(*ω*)<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si298.png), of an autocorrelation sequence, *r*(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si319.png), is nonnegative. Moreover, if a sequence *r*(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si319.png) has a nonnegative Fourier transform, then it is positive definite and we can *always* construct a WSS process that has *r*(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si319.png) as its autocorrelation sequence (e.g., \[6, pages 410, 421\]). Thus, the *necessary and sufficient condition for a sequence to be an autocorrelation sequence is the nonnegativity of its Fourier transform.*

Example 2.3

White noise sequence

A stochastic process *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si320.png) is said to be *white noise* if the mean and its autocorrelation sequence satisfy

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx028.jpg)(2.136) 

where *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si321.png) is its variance. In other words, all variables at different time instants are uncorrelated. If, in addition, they are independent, we say that it is *strictly white noise*. It is readily seen that its PSD is given by

*S*[*η*](*ω*) = *σ*[*η*]².<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si322.png)(2.137) 

That is, it is constant, and this is the reason it is called white noise, analogous to white light, whose spectrum is equally spread over all wavelengths.

### 2.4.4 Autoregressive models

We have just seen an example of a stochastic process, namely, white noise. We now turn our attention to generating WSS processes via appropriate modeling. In this way, we will introduce controlled correlation among the variables, corresponding to the various time instants. We focus on the real data case, to simplify the discussion.

*Autoregressive* processes are among the most popular and widely used models. An autoregressive process of order *l*, denoted as AR(*l*), is defined via the following *difference equation*:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx029.jpg)(2.138) 

where *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si320.png) is a white noise process with variance *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si321.png).

As is always the case with any difference equation, one starts from some initial conditions and then generates samples recursively by plugging into the model the input sequence samples. The input samples here correspond to a white noise sequence and the initial conditions are set equal to zero, *u*[ − 1] = …*u*[ − *l*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si324.png).

There is no need to mobilize mathematics to see that such a process is not stationary. Indeed, time instant *n* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si325.png) is distinctly different from all the rest, since it is the time in which initial conditions are applied. However, the effects of the initial conditions tend asymptotically to zero if all the roots of the corresponding characteristic polynomial,

*z*^(*l*) + *a*[1]*z*^(*l* − 1) + ⋯ + *a*[*l*] = 0,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si326.png)

have magnitude *less than unity* (the solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, without input, tends to zero) \[7\]. Then, it can be shown that asymptotically, the AR(*l*) becomes WSS. This is the assumption that is usually adopted in practice, which will be the case for the rest of this section. Note that the mean value of the process is zero (try it).

The goal now becomes to compute the corresponding autocorrelation sequence, *r*(*k*), *k*∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si327.png). Multiplying both sides in Eq. [(2.138)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq159) with *u*[*n* − *k*], *k* > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si328.png), and taking the expectation, we obtain

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{l}a\_{i}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack u\_{n - i}u\_{n - k}\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\eta\_{n}u\_{n - k}\\rbrack,\\quad k > 0,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si329.png)

where *a*[0] :  = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si330.png), or

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{l}a\_{i}r(k - i) = 0.$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si331.png)(2.139) 

We have used the fact that 𝔼\[*η*[*n*]*u*[*n* − *k*]\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si332.png), *k* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si333.png), is zero. Indeed, *u*[*n* − *k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si253.png) depends recursively on *η*[*n* − *k*], *η*[*n* − *k* − 1]…<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si334.png), which are all uncorrelated to *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si320.png), since this is a white noise process. Note that Eq. [(2.139)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq162) is a difference equation, which can be solved provided we have the initial conditions. To this end, multiply Eq. [(2.138)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq159) by *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) and take expectations, which results in

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{l}a\_{i}r(i) = \\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2},$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si335.png)(2.140) 

since 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*η*[*n*]\] = *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si336.png). Note that *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si233.png) recursively depends on *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si320.png), which contributes the *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si321.png) term, and *η*[*n* − 1], *η*[*n* − 2]…<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si337.png), which are all uncorrelated to *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si320.png). Combining Eqs. [(2.140)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq163) and [(2.139)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq162) the following *linear* system of equations results:

$\\begin{bmatrix} {r(0)\\;} & {r(1)\\;} & {\\ldots\\;} & {r(l)} \\\\ {r(1)\\;} & {r(0)\\;} & {\\ldots\\;} & {r(l - 1)} \\\\ {\\vdots \\;} & {\\vdots \\;} & {\\vdots \\;} & \\vdots \\\\ {r(l)\\;} & {r(l - 1)\\;} & {\\ldots\\;} & {r(0)} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\\\ a\_{1} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ a\_{l} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix} \\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si339.png)(2.141) 

These are known as the *Yule–Walker equations*, whose solution results in the values *r*(0), …, *r*(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si340.png), which are then used as the initial conditions to solve the difference equation in [(2.139)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq162) and obtain *r*(*k*), ∀*k* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si341.png).

Observe the special structure of the matrix in the linear system. All elements along each diagonal of the matrix are the same. This type of matrices is known as *Toeplitz*, and this is the property that will be exploited to efficiently solve linear systems of equations that involve such matrices and which result when the autocorrelation sequence of a WSS process is involved; see Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml).

Besides the autoregressive models, other types of stochastic models have been suggested and used. The *autoregressive-moving average* (ARMA) model of order (*l*, *m*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si342.png) is defined by the difference equation

*u*[*n*] + *a*[1]*u*[*n* − 1] + … + *a*[*l*]*u*[*n* − *l*] = *b*[1]*η*[*n*] + … + *b*[*m*]*η*[*n* − *m*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si343.png)(2.142) 

and the *moving average* model of order *m*, denoted as MA(*m*), is defined as

*u*[*n*] = *b*[1]*η*[*n*] + ⋯ + *b*[*m*]*η*[*n* − *m*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si344.png)(2.143) 

Note that the AR(*l*) and the MA(*m*) models can be considered as special cases of the ARMA(*l*, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si345.png)). For a more theoretical treatment of the topic, see \[1\].

Example 2.4

Consider the AR(1) process,

*u*[*n*] + *a**u*[*n* − 1] = *η*[*n*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si346.png)

Following the general methodology explained before, we have

*r*(*k*) + *a**r*(*k* − 1) = 0, *k* = 1, 2, …*r*(0) + *a**r*(1) = *σ*[*η*]².<mml:math><mml:mi id="mmlbr0004">r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0004" linebreakstyle="after">…</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si347.png)

Taking the first equation for *k* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si348.png) together with the second one readily results in

$r(0) = \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{1 - a^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si349.png)

Plugging this value into the difference equation, we recursively obtain

$r(k) = {( - a)}^{|k|}\\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{1 - a^{2}},\\ k = 0, \\pm 1, \\pm 2,\\ldots,$<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si350.png)(2.144) 

where we used the property *r*(*k*) = *r*( − *k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si351.png). Observe that if |*a*| > 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si352.png), *r*(0) < 0<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si353.png), which is meaningless. Also, |*a*| < 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si354.png) guarantees that the magnitude of the root of the characteristic polynomial (*z*[\*] =  − *a*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si355.png)) is smaller than one. Moreover, |*a*| < 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si354.png) guarantees that *r*(*k*) → 0<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si356.png) as *k* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si357.png). This is in line with commonsense, since variables that are faraway must be uncorrelated.

[Fig. 2.15](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0080) shows the time evolution of two AR(1) processes (after the processes have converged to be stationary) together with the respective autocorrelation sequences, for two cases, corresponding to *a* =  − 0.9<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si358.png) and *a* =  − 0.4<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si359.png). Observe that the larger the magnitude of *a*, the smoother the realization becomes and time variations are *slower*. This is natural, since nearby samples are highly correlated and so, on average, they tend to have similar values. The opposite is true for small values of *a*. For comparison purposes, [Fig. 2.16](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0085)A is the case of *a* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si280.png), which corresponds to a white noise. [Fig. 2.16](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0085)B shows the PSDs in dBs $\\left( 10\\log\\frac{S(\\omega)}{S(0)} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si360.png) corresponding to the two cases of [Fig. 2.15](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0080). Observe that the faster the autocorrelation approaches zero, the more spread out the PSD is, and vice versa.

![Figure 2.15 (A) The time evolution of a realization of the AR(1) with a = −0.9 and (B) the respective autocorrelation sequence. (C) The time evolution of a realization of the AR(1) with a = −0.4 and (D) the corresponding autocorrelation sequence.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr015.jpg)

Figure 2.15 (A) The time evolution of a realization of the AR(1) with *a* = −0.9 and (B) the respective autocorrelation sequence. (C) The time evolution of a realization of the AR(1) with *a* = −0.4 and (D) the corresponding autocorrelation sequence.

![Figure 2.16 (A) The time evolution of a realization from a white noise process. (B) The PSDs in dBs, for the two AR(1) sequences of Fig. 2.15. The red one corresponds to a = −0.4 and the gray one to a = −0.9. The smaller the magnitude of a, the closer the process is to a white noise, and its PSD tends to increase the power with which high frequencies participate. Since the PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation sequence, observe that the broader a sequence is in time, the narrower its Fourier transform becomes, and vice versa.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr016.jpg)

Figure 2.16 (A) The time evolution of a realization from a white noise process. (B) The PSDs in dBs, for the two AR(1) sequences of [Fig. 2.15](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0080). The red one corresponds to *a* = −0.4 and the gray one to *a* = −0.9. The smaller the magnitude of *a*, the closer the process is to a white noise, and its PSD tends to increase the power with which high frequencies participate. Since the PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation sequence, observe that the broader a sequence is in time, the narrower its Fourier transform becomes, and vice versa.

## 2.5 Information theory

So far in this chapter, we have looked at some basic definitions and properties concerning probability theory and stochastic processes. In the same vein, we will now focus on the basic definitions and notions related to *information theory*. Although information theory was originally developed in the context of communications and coding disciplines, its application and use have now been adopted in a wide range of areas, including machine learning. Notions from information theory are used for establishing loss functions for optimization in parameter estimation problems, and concepts from information theory are employed to estimate unknown probability distributions in the context of constrained optimization tasks. We will discuss such methods later in this book.

The father of information theory is *Claude Elwood Shannon* (1916–2001), an American mathematician and electrical engineer. He founded information theory with the landmark paper “A mathematical theory of communication,” published in the Bell System Technical Journal in 1948. However, he is also credited with founding digital circuit design theory in 1937, when, as a 21-year-old Master's degree student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), he wrote his thesis demonstrating that electrical applications of Boolean algebra could construct and resolve any logical, numerical relationship. So he is also credited as a father of digital computers. Shannon, while working for the national defense during the Second World War, contributed to the field of cryptography, converting it from an art to a rigorous scientific field.

As is the case for probability, the notion of information is part of our everyday vocabulary. In this context, an event carries information if it is either unknown to us, or if the probability of its occurrence is very low and, in spite of that, it happens. For example, if one tells us that the sun shines bright during summer days in the Sahara desert, we could consider such a statement rather dull and useless. On the contrary, if somebody gives us news about snow in the Sahara during summer, that statement carries a lot of information and can possibly ignite a discussion concerning climate change.

Thus, trying to formalize the notion of information from a mathematical point of view, it is reasonable to define it in terms of the negative logarithm of the probability of an event. If the event is certain to occur, it carries zero information content; however, if its probability of occurrence is low, then its information content has a large positive value.

### 2.5.1 Discrete random variables

#### Information

Given a discrete random variable x, which takes values in the set 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si11.png), the *information* associated with any value *x* ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si361.png) is denoted as *I*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si362.png) and it is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx030.jpg)(2.145) 

Any base for the logarithm can be used. If the natural logarithm is chosen, information is measured in terms of *nats* (natural units). If the base 2 logarithm is employed, information is measured in terms of *bits* (binary digits). Employing the logarithmic function to define information is also in line with commonsense reasoning that the information content of two statistically independent events should be the sum of the information conveyed by each one of them individually; *I*(*x*, *y*) =  − log *P*(*x*, *y*) =  − log *P*(*x*) − log *P*(*y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si363.png).

Example 2.5

We are given a binary random variable *x* ∈ 𝒳 = {0, 1}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si364.png), and we assume that *P*(1) = *P*(0) = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si365.png). We can consider this random variable as a source that generates and emits two possible values. The information content of each one of the two equiprobable events is

*I*(0) = *I*(1) =  − log[2]0.5 = 1 bit.<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>bit</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si366.png)

Let us now consider another source of random events, which generates *code words* comprising *k* binary variables together. The output of this source can be seen as a random vector with binary-valued elements, **x** = \[*x*[1], …, *x*[*k*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si367.png). The corresponding probability space, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si11.png), comprises *K* = 2^(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si368.png) elements. If all possible values have the same probability, 1/*K*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si369.png), then the information content of each possible event is equal to

$I(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) = - \\log\_{2}\\frac{1}{K} = k\\ \\text{bits}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>bits</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si370.png)

We observe that in the case where the number of possible events is larger, the information content of each individual one (assuming equiprobable events) becomes larger. This is also in line with commonsense reasoning, since if the source can emit a large number of (equiprobable) events, then the occurrence of any one of them carries more information than a source that can only emit a few possible events.

#### Mutual and conditional information

Besides marginal probabilities, we have already been introduced to the concept of conditional probability. This leads to the definitions of mutual and conditional information.

Given two discrete random variables, *x* ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si371.png) and *y* ∈ 𝒴<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si372.png), the information content provided by the occurrence of the event *y* = *y*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si373.png) about the event *x* = *x*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si374.png) is measured by the *mutual information*, denoted as *I*(*x*; *y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si375.png) and defined by

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx031.jpg)(2.146) 

Note that if the two variables are statistically independent, then their mutual information is zero; this is most reasonable, since observing *y* says nothing about *x*. On the contrary, if by observing *y* it is certain that *x* will occur, as when *P*(*x*|*y*) = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si376.png), then the mutual information becomes *I*(*x*; *y*) = *I*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si377.png), which is again in line with common reasoning. Mobilizing our now familiar product rule, we can see that

*I*(*x*; *y*) = *I*(*y*; *x*).<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si378.png)

The *conditional information* of x given y is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx032.jpg)(2.147) 

It is straightforward to show that

*I*(*x*; *y*) = *I*(*x*) − *I*(*x*|*y*).<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si379.png)(2.148) 

Example 2.6

In a communications channel, the source transmits binary symbols, x, with probability *P*(0) = *P*(1) = 1/2<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si380.png). The channel is noisy, so the received symbols y may have changed polarity, due to noise, with the following probabilities:

*P*(*y* = 0|*x* = 0) = 1 − *p*, *P*(*y* = 1|*x* = 0) = *p*, *P*(*y* = 1|*x* = 1) = 1 − *q*, *P*(*y* = 0|*x* = 1) = *q*.<mml:math><mml:mi id="mmlbr0005">P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si381.png)

This example illustrates in its simplest form the effect of a *communications channel*. Transmitted bits are hit by noise and what the receiver receives is the noisy (possibly wrong) information. The task of the receiver is to decide, upon reception of a sequence of symbols, which was the originally transmitted one.

The goal of our example is to determine the mutual information about the occurrence of *x* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si382.png) and *x* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si383.png) once *y* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si384.png) has been observed. To this end, we first need to compute the marginal probabilities,

$P(y = 0) = P(y = 0|x = 0)P(x = 0) + P(y = 0|x = 1)P(x = 1) = \\frac{1}{2}(1 - p + q),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si385.png)

and similarly,

$P(y = 1) = \\frac{1}{2}(1 - q + p).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si386.png)

Thus, the mutual information is

$I(0;0) = \\log\_{2}\\frac{P(x = 0|y = 0)}{P(x = 0)} = \\log\_{2}\\frac{P(y = 0|x = 0)}{P(y = 0)} = \\log\_{2}\\frac{2(1 - p)}{1 - p + q},$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0006" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0006" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si387.png)

and

$I(1;0) = \\log\_{2}\\frac{2q}{1 - p + q}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si388.png)

Let us now consider that *p* = *q* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si389.png). Then *I*(0; 0) = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si390.png) bit, which is equal to *I*(*x* = 0)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si391.png), since the output specifies the input with certainty. If on the other hand *p* = *q* = 1/2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si392.png), then *I*(0; 0) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si393.png) bits, since the noise can randomly change polarity with equal probability. If now *p* = *q* = 1/4<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si394.png), then $I(0;0) = \\log\_{2}\\frac{3}{2} = 0.587$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.587</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si395.png) bits and *I*(1; 0) =  − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si396.png) bit. Observe that the mutual information can take negative values, too.

#### Entropy and average mutual information

Given a discrete random variable *x* ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si371.png), its *entropy* is defined as the average information over all possible outcomes,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx033.jpg)(2.149) 

Note that if *P*(*x*) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si397.png), *P*(*x*)log *P*(*x*) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si398.png), by taking into consideration that lim[*x* → 0]*x*log *x* = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si399.png).

In a similar way, the *average mutual information* between two random variables, *x*, *y*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si19.png), is defined as
