$I(x;y): = \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}}\\sum\\limits\_{y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}P(x,y)I(x;y) = \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}}\\sum\\limits\_{y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}P(x,y)\\log\\frac{P(x|y)}{P(x)} = \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}}\\sum\\limits\_{y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}P(x,y)\\log\\frac{P(x|y)P(y)}{P(x)P(y)}$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0007">:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0007" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0007" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si400.png)

or

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx034.jpg)(2.150) 

It can be shown that

*I*(*x*; *y*) ≥ 0,<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si401.png)

and it is zero if x and y are statistically independent (Problem [2.12](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0065)).

In comparison, the *conditional entropy* of x given y is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx035.jpg)(2.151) 

It is readily shown, by taking into account the probability product rule, that

*I*(*x*; *y*) = *H*(*x*) − *H*(*x*|*y*).<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si402.png)(2.152) 

Lemma 2.1

*The entropy of a random variable* *x* ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si371.png) *takes its maximum value if all possible values* *x* ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si361.png) *are equiprobable.*

Proof

The proof is given in Problem [2.14](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0075). □

In other words, the entropy can be considered as a measure of randomness of a source that emits symbols randomly. The maximum value is associated with the maximum uncertainty of what is going to be emitted, since the maximum value occurs if all symbols are equiprobable. The smallest value of the entropy is equal to zero, which corresponds to the case where all events have zero probability with the exception of one, whose probability to occur is equal to one.

Example 2.7

Consider a binary source that transmits the values 1 or 0 with probabilities *p* and 1 − *p*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si405.png), respectively. Then the entropy of the associated random variable is

*H*(*x*) =  − *p*log[2]*p* − (1 − *p*)log[2](1 − *p*).<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si406.png)

[Fig. 2.17](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#f0090) shows the graph for various values of *p* ∈ \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si407.png). Observe that the maximum value occurs for *p* = 1/2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si408.png).

![Figure 2.17 The maximum value of the entropy for a binary random variable occurs if the two possible events have equal probability, p = 1/2.](images/B9780443292385000081/gr017.jpg)

[Figure 2.17](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#cf0650) The maximum value of the entropy for a binary random variable occurs if the two possible events have equal probability, *p* = 1/2.

### 2.5.2 Continuous random variables

All the definitions given before can be generalized to the case of continuous random variables. However, this generalization must be made with caution. Recall that the probability of occurrence of any single value of a random variable that takes values in an interval in the real axis is zero. Hence, the corresponding information content is infinite.

To define the entropy of a continuous variable x, we first *discretize* it and form the corresponding discrete variable *x*[*Δ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si409.png), i.e.,

*x*[*Δ*] :  = *n**Δ*,  if  (*n* − 1)*Δ* < *x* ≤ *n**Δ*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si410.png)(2.153) 

where *Δ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si411.png). Then,

$P(x\_{\\Delta} = n\\Delta) = P(n\\Delta - \\Delta < x \\leq n\\Delta) = \\int\_{(n - 1)\\Delta}^{n\\Delta}p(x)\\ dx = \\Delta\\overline{p}(n\\Delta),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si412.png)(2.154) 

where $\\overline{p}(n\\Delta)$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si413.png) is a number between the maximum and the minimum value of *p*(*x*), *x* ∈ (*n**Δ* − *Δ*, *n**Δ*\]<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si414.png) (such a number exists by the mean value theorem of calculus). Then we can write

$H(x\_{\\Delta}) = - \\sum\\limits\_{n = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}\\Delta\\overline{p}(n\\Delta)\\log\\left( \\Delta\\overline{p}(n\\Delta) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si415.png)(2.155) 

and since

$\\sum\\limits\_{n = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}\\Delta\\overline{p}(n\\Delta) = \\int\_{- \\infty}^{+ \\infty}p(x)\\ dx = 1,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si416.png)

we obtain

$H(x\_{\\Delta}) = - \\log\\Delta - \\sum\\limits\_{n = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}\\Delta\\overline{p}(n\\Delta)\\log\\left( \\overline{p}(n\\Delta) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si417.png)(2.156) 

Note that *x*[*Δ*] → *x*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si418.png) as *Δ* → 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si419.png). However, if we take the limit in Eq. [(2.156)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq194), then  − log *Δ*<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si420.png) goes to infinity. This is the crucial difference compared to the discrete variables.

The entropy for a continuous random variable x is defined as the limit

$H(x): = \\lim\\limits\_{\\Delta\\rightarrow 0}\\left( H(x\_{\\Delta}) + \\log\\Delta \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si421.png)

or

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx036.jpg)(2.157) 

This is the reason that the entropy of a continuous variable is also called *differential entropy*.

Note that the entropy is still a measure of randomness (uncertainty) of the distribution describing x. This is demonstrated via the following example.

Example 2.8

We are given a random variable *x* ∈ \[*a*, *b*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si422.png). Of all the possible PDFs that can describe this variable, find the one that maximizes the entropy.

This task translates to the following constrained optimization task:

maximize with respect to *p* : *H* =  − ∫[*a*]^(*b*)*p*(*x*)ln *p*(*x*)*d**x*, subject to:∫[*a*]^(*b*)*p*(*x*)*d**x* = 1.<mml:math><mml:mtext id="mmlbr0008">maximize with respect to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0008" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>subject to:</mml:mtext><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si423.png)

The constraint guarantees that the function to result is indeed a PDF. Performing the above constrained optimization (Problem [2.15](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#o0080)), it turns out that

$p(x) = \\begin{cases} {\\frac{1}{b - a},\\;} & {\\text{if}\\ \\ x \\in \\lbrack a,b\\rbrack,} \\\\ {0,\\;} & {\\text{otherwise}.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>otherwise</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si424.png)

In other words, the result is the uniform distribution, which is indeed the most random one since it gives no preference to any particular subinterval of \[*a*, *b*\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si140.png).

We will come to this method of estimating PDFs in Section [12.8.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). This elegant method for estimating PDFs comes from Jaynes \[3,4\], and it is known as the *maximum entropy method*. In its more general form, more constraints are involved to fit the needs of the specific problem.

#### Average mutual information and conditional entropy

Given two continuous random variables, the average mutual information is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx037.jpg)(2.158) 

and the conditional entropy of x, given y,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx038.jpg)(2.159) 

Using standard arguments and the product rule, it is easy to show that

*I*(*x*; *y*) = *H*(*x*) − *H*(*x*|*y*) = *H*(*y*) − *H*(*y*|*x*).<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si425.png)(2.160) 

#### Relative entropy or Kullback–Leibler divergence

The *relative entropy* or *Kullback–Leibler divergence* is a quantity that has been developed within the context of information theory for measuring similarity between two PDFs. It is widely used in machine learning optimization tasks when PDFs are involved; see Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). Given two PDFs, *p* and *q*, their Kullback–Leibler divergence, denoted as KL(*p*||*q*)<mml:math><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si426.png), is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/fx039.jpg)(2.161) 

Note that

*I*(*x*; *y*) = KL(*p*(*x*,*y*)||*p*(*x*)*p*(*y*)).<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si427.png)

The Kullback–Leibler divergence is *not* symmetric, i.e., KL(*p*||*q*) ≠ KL(*q*||*p*)<mml:math><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si428.png), and it can be shown that it is a nonnegative quantity (the proof is similar to the proof that the mutual information is nonnegative; see Problem [12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) of Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)). Moreover, it is zero if and only if *p* = *q*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si429.png).

Note that all we have said concerning entropy and mutual information is readily generalized to the case of random vectors.

## 2.6 Stochastic convergence

We will close this memory refreshing tour of the theory of probability and related concepts with some definitions concerning convergence of sequences of random variables.

Consider a sequence of random variables

*x*[0], *x*[1], …, *x*[*n*]….<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si430.png)

We can consider this sequence as a discrete-time stochastic process. Due to the randomness, a realization of this process, as shown by

*x*[0], *x*[1], …, *x*[*n*]…,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si431.png)

may converge or may not. Thus, the notion of convergence of random variables has to be treated carefully, and different interpretations have been developed.

Recall from our basic calculus that a sequence of numbers, *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si432.png), converges to a value *x* if ∀*ϵ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si433.png) there exists a number *n*(*ϵ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si434.png) such that

|*x*[*n*] − *x*| < *ϵ*, ∀*n* ≥ *n*(*ϵ*).<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si435.png)(2.162) 

### Convergence everywhere

We say that a random sequence *converges everywhere* if every realization, *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si432.png), of the random process converges to a value *x*, according to the definition given in Eq. [(2.162)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml#deq206). Note that every realization converges to a different value, which itself can be considered as the outcome of a random variable x, and we write

$x\_{n}\\underset{n\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\rightarrow}x.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo>→</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si436.png)(2.163) 

It is common to denote a realization (outcome) of a random process as *x*[*n*](*ζ*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ζ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si437.png), where *ζ* denotes a specific experiment.

### Convergence almost everywhere

A weaker version of convergence, compared to the previous one, is the *convergence almost everywhere*. Consider the set of outcomes *ζ*, such that

lim *x*[*n*](*ζ*) = *x*(*ζ*), *n* → ∞.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ζ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ζ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si438.png)

We say that the sequence *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si439.png) converges almost everywhere if

*P*(*x*[*n*] → *x*) = 1, *n* → ∞.<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si440.png)(2.164) 

Note that {*x*[*n*] → *x*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si441.png) denotes the event comprising *all* the outcomes such that lim *x*[*n*](*ζ*) = *x*(*ζ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ζ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ζ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si442.png). The difference with the convergence everywhere is that now it is allowed to a finite or countably infinite number of realizations (that is, to a set of zero probability) not to converge. Often, this type of convergence is referred to as *almost sure* convergence or convergence *with probability 1*.

### Convergence in the mean-square sense

We say that a random sequence *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si439.png) converges to the random variable x in the *mean-square sense* if

𝔼 \[|*x*[*n*]−*x*|²\] → 0, *n* → ∞.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si443.png)(2.165) 

### Convergence in probability

Given a random sequence *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si439.png), a random variable x, and a nonnegative number *ϵ*, then {|*x*[*n*] − *x*| > *ϵ*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si444.png) is an event. We define the new sequence of numbers, *P*({|*x*[*n*]−*x*|>*ϵ*})<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si445.png). We say that *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si439.png) converges to x *in probability* if the constructed sequence of numbers tends to zero,

*P*({|*x*[*n*]−*x*|>*ϵ*}) → 0, *n* → ∞, ∀*ϵ* > 0.<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si446.png)(2.166) 

### Convergence in distribution

Given a random sequence *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si439.png) and a random variable x, let *F*[*n*](*x*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si447.png) and *F*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si448.png) be the CDFs, respectively. We say that *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si439.png) converges to x *in distribution* if

*F*[*n*](*x*) → *F*(*x*), *n* → ∞,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si449.png)(2.167) 

for *every* point *x* of continuity of *F*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si448.png).

It can be shown that if a random sequence converges either almost everywhere or in the mean-square sense, then it necessarily converges in probability, and if it converges in probability, then it necessarily converges in distribution. The converse arguments are not necessarily true. In other words, the weakest version of convergence is that of convergence in distribution.

## Problems

1.  2.1  Derive the mean and variance for the binomial distribution.
2.  2.2  Derive the mean and variance for the uniform distribution.
3.  2.3  Derive the mean and covariance matrix of the multivariate Gaussian.
4.  2.4  Show that the mean and variance of the beta distribution with parameters *a* and *b* are given by

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack x\\rbrack = \\frac{a}{a + b}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si450.png)

1.  and

$\\sigma\_{x}^{2} = \\frac{ab}{{(a + b)}^{2}(a + b + 1)}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000081/si451.png)

1.
