## 3.1 Introduction

Parametric modeling is a theme that runs across the spine of this book. A number of chapters focus on different aspects of this important problem. This chapter provides basic definitions and concepts related to the task of learning when parametric models are mobilized to describe the available data.

As has already been pointed out in the introductory chapter, a large class of machine learning problems ends up as being equivalent to a function estimation/approximation task. The function is “learned” during the learning/training phase by digging in the information that resides in the available training data set. This function relates the so-called input variables to the output variable(s). Once this functional relationship is established, one can in turn exploit it to *predict* the value(s) of the output(s), based on measurements from the respective input variables; these predictions can then be used to proceed to the decision-making phase.

In parametric modeling, the aforementioned functional dependence that relates the input to the output is defined via a set of parameters, whose number is *fixed* and a priori known. The values of the parameters are unknown and have to be estimated based on the available input–output observations. In contrast to the parametric, there are the so-called *nonparametric* methods. In such methods, parameters may still be involved to establish the input–output relationship, yet their number is *not* fixed; it depends on the size of the data set and it grows with the number of observations. Nonparametric methods will also be treated in this book (e.g., Chapters [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml)). However, the emphasis in the current chapter lies on parametric models.

There are two possible paths to deal with the uncertainty imposed by the unknown values of the involved parameters. According to the first one, parameters are treated as *deterministic* nonrandom variables. The task of learning is to obtain estimates of their unknown values. For each one of the parameters a single value estimate is obtained. The other approach has a stronger statistical flavor. The unknown parameters are treated as *random variables* and the task of learning is to *infer* the associated probability distributions. Once the distributions have been learned/inferred, one can use them to make predictions. Both approaches are introduced in the current chapter and are treated in more detail later on in various chapters of the book.

Two of the major machine learning tasks, namely, regression and classification, are presented and the main directions in dealing with these problems are exposed. Various issues that are related to the parameter estimation task, such as estimator efficiency, bias–variance dilemma, overfitting, and the curse of dimensionality, are introduced and discussed. The chapter can also be considered as a road map to the rest of the book. However, instead of just presenting the main ideas and directions in a rather “dry” way, we chose to deal and work with the involved tasks by adopting simple models and techniques, so that the reader gets a better feeling of the topic. An effort was made to pay more attention to the scientific notions than to algebraic manipulations and mathematical details, which will, unavoidably, be used to a larger extent while “embroidering” the chapters to follow.

The least-squares (LS), maximum likelihood (ML), regularization, and Bayesian inference techniques are presented and discussed. An effort has been made to assist the reader to grasp an informative view of the big picture conveyed by the book. Thus, this chapter could also be used as an overview introduction to the parametric modeling task in the realm of machine learning.

## 3.2 Parameter estimation: the deterministic point of view

The task of estimating the value of an unknown parameter vector, ***θ***, has been at the center of interest in a number of application areas. For example, in the early years at university, one of the very first subjects any student has to study is the so-called curve fitting problem. Given a set of data points, one must find a curve or a surface that “fits” the data. The usual path to follow is to *adopt* a functional form, such as a linear function or a quadratic one, and try to estimate the associated unknown parameters so that the graph of the function “passes through” the data and follows their deployment in space as close as possible. [Figs. 3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0010)A and B are two such examples. The data lie in the ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si1.png) space and are given to us as a set of points (*y*[*n*], *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si2.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png). The adopted functional form for the curve corresponding to [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0010)A is

*y* = *f*[**θ**](*x*) = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*,<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si4.png)(3.1) 

and for the case of [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0010)B it is

*y* = *f*[**θ**](*x*) = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x* + *θ*[2]*x*².<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si5.png)(3.2) 

The unknown parameter vectors are **θ** = \[*θ*[0], *θ*[1]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si6.png) and **θ** = \[*θ*[0], *θ*[1], *θ*[2]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si7.png), respectively. In both cases, the parameter values, which define the curves drawn by the red lines, provide a much better fit compared to the values associated with the black ones. In both cases, the task comprises two steps: (a) first adopt a specific *parametric functional* form which we reckon to be more appropriate for the data at hand and (b) estimate the values of the unknown parameters in order to obtain a “good” fit.

![Figure 3.1 (A) Fitting a linear function. (B) Fitting a quadratic function. The red lines are the optimized ones.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr001.jpg)

Figure 3.1 (A) Fitting a linear function. (B) Fitting a quadratic function. The red lines are the optimized ones.

In the more general and formal setting, the task can be defined as follows. Given a set of data points, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si8.png), *y*[*n*] ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si9.png), **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si10.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), and a parametric^([⁵](#fn5))

ℱ :  = {*f*[**θ**](⋅):  **θ**∈𝒜⊆ℝ^(*K*)},<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si13.png)(3.3) 

find a function in ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png), which will be denoted as *f*( ⋅ ) :  = *f*[**θ**[\*]]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si15.png), such that given a value of **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si16.png), *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si12.png) *best* approximates the corresponding value *y* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si18.png). The set 𝒜<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si19.png) is a constraint set in case we wish to constrain the unknown *K* parameters to lie within a specific region in ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si20.png). Constraining the parameters to be within a subset of the parameter space ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si20.png) is almost omnipresent in machine learning. We will deal with constrained optimization later on in this chapter (Section [3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0055)). We start our discussion by considering *y* to be a real variable, *y* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si18.png), and as we move on and understand better the various “secrets,” we will allow it to move to higher-dimensional spaces. The optimal parameter vector, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si21.png), is the one that results from a parameter estimation procedure. The values of **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si21.png) that define the red curves in [Figs. 3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0010)A and B are

**θ**[\*] = \[ − 0.5, 1\]^(*T*), **θ**[\*] = \[ − 3,  − 2, 1\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si22.png)(3.4) 

respectively.

To reach a decision with respect to the choice of ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png) is not an easy task. For the case of the data in [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0010), we were a bit “lucky.” First, the data live in the two-dimensional space, where we have the luxury of visualization. Second, the data were scattered along curves whose shape is pretty familiar to us; hence, a simple inspection suggested the proper family of functions, for each one of the two cases. Obviously, real life is hardly as generous as that and in the majority of practical applications, the data reside in high-dimensional spaces and/or the shape of the surface (hypersurface, for spaces of dimensionality higher than three) can be quite complex. Hence, the choice of ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png), which dictates the functional form (e.g., linear, quadratic, etc.), is not easy. In practice, one has to use as much a priori information as possible concerning the physical mechanism that underlies the generation of the data, and most often use different families of functions and finally keep the one that results in the best performance, according to a chosen criterion.

Having adopted a parametric family of functions, ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png), one has to get estimates for the set of the unknown parameters. To this end, a measure of fitness has to be adopted. The more classical approach is to adopt a *loss* function, which quantifies the deviation/error between the measured value of *y* and the predicted one using the corresponding measurements ***x***, as in *f*[**θ**](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si23.png). In a more formal way, we adopt a *nonnegative* (loss) function,

ℒ(⋅, ⋅ ) : ℝ × ℝ ↦ \[0, ∞),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si24.png)

and compute **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si21.png) so as to minimize the total loss, or as we say the *cost function*, over all the data points, or

$f( \\cdot ): = f\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}}( \\cdot ):\\ \\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} = \\text{arg}\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathcal{A}}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>arg</mml:mtext><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si25.png)(3.5) 

where

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}): = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}\\left( y\_{n},f\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si26.png)(3.6) 

assuming that a minimum exists. Note that, in general, there may be more than one optimal value **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si21.png), depending on the shape of *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si27.png).

As the book evolves, we are going to see different loss functions and different parametric families of functions. For the sake of simplicity, for the rest of this chapter we will adhere to the *squared error* loss function,

ℒ(*y*,*f*[**θ**](**x**)) = (*y*−*f*[**θ**](**x**))²,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si28.png)

and to the linear class of functions.

The squared error loss function is credited to the great mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who proposed the fundamentals of the least-squares (LS) method in 1795 at the age of 18. However, it was Adrien-Marie Legendre (1752–1833) who first published the method in 1805, working independently. Gauss published it in 1809. The strength of the method was demonstrated when it was used to predict the location of the asteroid Ceres. Since then, the squared error loss function has “haunted” all scientific fields, and even if it is not used directly, it is, most often, used as the standard against which the performance of more modern alternatives is compared. This success is due to some nice properties that this loss criterion has, which will be explored as we move on in this book.

The combined choice of linearity with the squared error loss function turns out to simplify the algebra and hence becomes very pedagogic for introducing the newcomer to the various “secrets” that underlie the area of parameter estimation. Moreover, understanding linearity is very important. Treating nonlinear tasks, often, turns out to finally resort to a linear problem. Take, for example, the nonlinear model in Eq. [(3.2)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq2) and consider the transformation

$\\mathbb{R} \\ni x\\longmapsto\\mathbf{\\phi}(x): = \\begin{bmatrix} x \\\\ x^{2} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>∋</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si29.png)(3.7) 

Then Eq. [(3.2)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq2) becomes

*y* = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*ϕ*[1](*x*) + *θ*[2]*ϕ*[2](*x*).<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si30.png)(3.8) 

That is, the model is now linear with respect to the components *ϕ*[*k*](*x*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si31.png), *k* = 1, 2<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si32.png), of the two-dimensional image **ϕ**(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si33.png) of *x*. As a matter of fact, this simple trick is at the heart of a number of nonlinear methods that will be treated later on in the book. No doubt, the procedure can be generalized to any number of functions *ϕ*[*k*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si34.png), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si35.png), and besides monomials, other types of nonlinear functions can be used, such as exponentials, splines, and wavelets. In spite of the nonlinear nature of the input–output dependence modeling, we still consider this model to be linear, because it retains its linearity with respect to the involved unknown parameters *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si36.png), *k* = 0, 1, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si37.png) (*K* parameters in total). Although for the rest of the chapter we will adhere to linear functions, in order to keep our discussion simple, everything that will be said applies, also, to this type of nonlinear models, which are known as *generalized linear models*. All that is needed is to replace ***x*** with **ϕ**(**x**) :  = \[*ϕ*[1](**x**), …, *ϕ*[*K* − 1](**x**)\]^(*T*) ∈ ℝ^(*K* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si38.png).

In the sequel, we will present two examples in order to demonstrate the use of parametric modeling. These examples are generic and can represent a wide class of problems.

## 3.3 Linear regression

In statistics, the term *regression* was coined to define the task of modeling a *dependent* random variable y, in terms of a set of random variables *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si39.png). The former is considered to be the response (output) of a system, which is activated by the latter set of (input) random variables. The input variables will be represented as the components of an equivalent random vector **x**.^([⁶](#fn6))

*y* = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*[1] + ⋯ + *θ*[*l*]*x*[*l*] + *η* = *θ*[0] + **θ**^(*T*)**x** + *η*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si40.png)(3.9) 

The parameter *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si363.png) is known as the *bias* or the *intercept*. Usually, this term is absorbed by the parameter vector ***θ*** with a simultaneous increase in the dimension of **x** by adding the constant 1 as its last element. Indeed, we can write

$\\theta\_{0} + \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{x} + \\eta = \\lbrack\\mathbf{\\theta}^{T},\\theta\_{0}\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{x} \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} + \\eta.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si42.png)

From now on, the regression model will be written as

*y* = **θ**^(*T*)**x** + *η*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si43.png)(3.10) 

and, unless otherwise stated, this notation means that the bias term has been absorbed by ***θ*** and **x** has been extended by adding 1 as an extra component. Because the noise variable is unobserved, we need a model to be able to *predict* the output value of y, given an observed value, ***x***, of the random vector **x**.

![Figure 3.2 Block diagram showing the input–output relation in a regression model.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr002.jpg)

[Figure 3.2](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#cf0200) Block diagram showing the input–output relation in a regression model.

In linear regression, given an estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si44.png) of ***θ***, we adopt the following prediction model:

$\\widehat{y} = {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{0} + {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{1}x\_{1} + \\cdots + {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{l}x\_{l}: = {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}^{T}\\mathbf{x}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si45.png)(3.11) 

Using the squared error loss function, the estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si44.png) is set equal to **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si21.png), which minimizes the square difference between *ŷ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si48.png) and *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si49.png) over the set of the available observations; that is, one minimizes, with respect to ***θ***, the cost function

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{n} \\right)^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si50.png)(3.12) 

We start our discussion by considering no constraints; hence, we set 𝒜 = ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si51.png), and we are going to search for solutions that lie anywhere in ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si20.png), where in the context of our current discussion, *K* = *l* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si52.png). Taking the derivative (gradient) of *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si27.png) with respect to ***θ*** (see Appendix A) and equating to the zero vector, **0**, we obtain (Problem [3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0010))

$\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T} \\right)\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si54.png)(3.13) 

Note that the sum on the left-hand side is an (*l* + 1) × (*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si55.png) matrix, being the sum of *N* outer vector products, i.e., **x**[*n*]**x**[*n*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si56.png). As we know from linear algebra, we need at least *N* = *l* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si57.png) observation vectors to guarantee that the matrix is invertible, assuming of course linear independence among the vectors (see, e.g., \[35\]).

For those who are not (yet) very familiar with working with vectors, note that Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16) is just a generalization of the scalar case. For example, in a “scalar” world, the input–output pairs would comprise scalars (*y*[*n*], *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si2.png) and the unknown parameter would also be a scalar, *θ*. The cost function would be $\\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}{(y\_{n} - \\theta x\_{n})}^{2}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si58.png). Taking the derivative and setting it equal to zero leads to

$\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}x\_{n}^{2} \\right)\\widehat{\\theta} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}x\_{n},\\ \\text{or}\\ \\widehat{\\theta} = \\frac{\\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}x\_{n}}{\\sum\_{n}^{N}x\_{n}^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>or</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si59.png)

A more popular way to write Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16) is via the so-called input matrix *X*, defined as the *N* × (*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si60.png) matrix, which has as rows the (extended) regressor vectors **x**[*n*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si61.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), expressed as

$X: = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{x}\_{1}^{T} \\\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{2}^{T} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{N}^{T} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix} {x\_{11}\\;} & {\\ldots\\;} & {x\_{1l}\\;} & 1 \\\\ {x\_{21}\\;} & {\\ldots\\;} & {x\_{2l}\\;} & 1 \\\\ {\\vdots \\;} & {\\ddots \\;} & {\\vdots \\;} & \\\\ {x\_{N1}\\;} & {\\ldots\\;} & {x\_{Nl}\\;} & 1 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.275em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si62.png)(3.14) 

Then it is straightforward to see that Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16) can be written as

$(X^{T}X)\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = X^{T}\\mathbf{y},$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si63.png)(3.15) 

where

**y** :  = \[*y*[1], *y*[2], …, *y*[*N*]\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si64.png)(3.16) 

Indeed,

$X^{T}X = \\lbrack\\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{x}\_{N}\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{x}\_{1}^{T} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{N}^{T} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si65.png)

and similarly,

$X^{T}\\mathbf{y} = \\lbrack\\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{x}\_{N}\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} y\_{1} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ y\_{N} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si66.png)

Thus, finally, the LS estimate is given by

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/fx001.jpg)(3.17) 

assuming, of course, that (*X*^(*T*)*X*)^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si67.png) exists. 

In other words, the obtained estimate of the parameter vector is given by a *linear set of equations*. This is a major advantage of the squared error loss function, when applied to a linear model. Moreover, this solution is *unique*, provided that the (*l* + 1) × (*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si55.png) matrix *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si69.png) is invertible. The uniqueness is due to the parabolic shape of the graph of the sum of squared errors cost function. This is illustrated in [Fig. 3.3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0020) for the two-dimensional space. It is readily observed that the graph has a unique minimum. This is a consequence of the fact that the sum of squared errors cost function is a strictly convex one. Issues related to convexity of loss functions will be treated in more detail in Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml).

![Figure 3.3 The squared error loss function has a unique minimum at the point θ⁎.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 3.3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#cf0230) The squared error loss function has a unique minimum at the point ***θ***[⁎].

Example 3.1

Consider the system that is described by the following model:

$y = \\theta\_{0} + \\theta\_{1}x\_{1} + \\theta\_{2}x\_{2} + \\eta: = \\lbrack 0.25, - 0.25,0.25\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} x\_{1} \\\\ x\_{2} \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} + \\eta,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.25</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.25</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.25</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si70.png)(3.18) 

where η is a Gaussian random variable of zero mean and variance *σ*² = 1<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si71.png). Observe that the generated data are spread, due to the noise, around the plane that is defined as

*y* = *f*(**x**) = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*[1] + *θ*[2]*x*[2],<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

in the three-dimensional space (see [Fig. 3.4](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0025)C).

The random variables *x*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si73.png) and *x*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si74.png) are assumed to be mutually independent and uniformly distributed over the interval \[0, 10\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si75.png). Furthermore, both variables are independent of the noise variable η. We generate *N* = 50<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>50</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si76.png) i.i.d. points^([⁷](#fn7))

*ŷ* = *θ̂*[0] + *θ̂*[1]*x*[1] + *θ̂*[2]*x*[2].<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si80.png)(3.20) 

Then we repeat the experiments with *σ*² = 10<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si81.png). Remarks 3.1

*   •  The set of points (*ŷ*[*n*], *x*[*n*1], …, *x*[*n**l*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si84.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), lie on a *hyperplane* in the ℝ^(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si85.png) space. Equivalently, they lie on a hyperplane that crosses the origin and, thus, it is a linear subspace in the extended space ℝ^(*l* + 2)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si86.png) when one absorbs *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si363.png) in ***θ***, as explained previously.
*   •  Note that the prediction model in Eq. [(3.11)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq14) could still be used, even if the true system structure does not obey the linear model in Eq. [(3.9)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq11). For example, the true dependence between y and **x** may be a nonlinear one. In such a case, the predictions of *y* based on the model in Eq. [(3.11)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq14) may, however, not be satisfactory. It all depends on the deviation of our adopted model from the true structure of the system that generates the data.
*   •  The prediction performance of the model also depends on the statistical properties of the noise variable. This is an important issue. We will see later on that, depending on the statistical properties of the noise variable, some loss functions and methods may be more suitable than others.
*   •  The two previous remarks suggest that in order to quantify the performance of an estimator some related criteria are necessary. In Section [3.9](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0065), we will present some theoretical touches that shed light on certain aspects related to the performance of an estimator.

## 3.4 Classification

*Classification* is the task of predicting the class to which an object, known as *pattern*, belongs. The pattern is assumed to belong to one and only one among a number of a priori known classes. Each pattern is *uniquely* represented by a set of values, known as *features*. One of the early stages in designing a classification system is to select an appropriate set of feature variables. These should “encode” as much class-discriminatory information so that, by measuring their value for a given pattern, we are able to predict, with high enough probability, the class of the pattern. Selecting the appropriate set of features for each problem is not an easy task, and it comprises one of the most important areas within the field of *pattern recognition* (see, e.g., \[12,37\]). Having selected, say, *l* feature (random) variables, *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si39.png), we stack them as the components of the so-called *feature vector* **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si88.png). The goal is to design a *classifier*, such as a function^([⁸](#fn8))

To formulate the task in mathematical terms, each class is represented by the *class label* variable y. For the simple two-class classification task, this can take either of two values, depending on the class (e.g., 1,  − 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si91.png) or 1, 0<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si92.png), etc.). Then, given the value of ***x***, corresponding to a specific pattern, its class label is predicted according to the rule

*ŷ* = *ϕ*(*f*(**x**)),<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si93.png)

where *ϕ*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si94.png) is a nonlinear function that indicates on which side of the decision surface *f*(**x**) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si89.png) lies ***x***. For example, if the class labels are ±1, the nonlinear function is chosen to be the sign function, or *ϕ*( ⋅ ) = *s**g**n*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si95.png). It is now clear that what we have said so far in the previous section can be transferred here and the task becomes that of estimating a function *f*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si11.png), based on a set of training points (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ *D* × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si96.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), where *D* denotes the discrete set in which *y* lies. Function *f*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si11.png) is selected so as to belong in a specific parametric class of functions, ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png), and the goal is, once more, to estimate the parameters so that the deviation between the true class labels, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si49.png), and the predicted ones, *ŷ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si48.png), is minimum according to a preselected criterion. So, is the classification any different from the regression task?

The answer to the previous question is that although they may share some similarities, they are different. Note that in a classification task, the dependent variables are of a *discrete* nature, in contrast to the regression, where they lie in an interval. This suggests that, in general, different techniques have to be adopted to optimize the parameters. For example, the most obvious choice for a criterion in a classification task is the probability of error. However, in a number of cases, one could attack both tasks using the same type of loss functions, as we will do in this section; even if such an approach is adopted, in spite of the similarities in their mathematical formalism, the goals of the two tasks remain different.

In the regression task, the function *f*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si11.png) has to “explain” the data generation mechanism. The corresponding surface in the (*y*, **x**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si97.png) space ℝ^(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si85.png) should develop so as to follow the spread of the data in the space as closely as possible. In contrast, in classification, the goal is to place the corresponding surface *f*(**x**) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si89.png) in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si90.png), so as to separate the data that belong to different classes as much as possible. The goal of a classifier is to *partition* the space where the feature vectors lie into regions and associate each region with a class. [Fig. 3.5](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0030) illustrates two cases of classification tasks. The first one is an example of two linearly separable classes, where a straight line can separate the two classes; the second case is an example of two nonlinearly separable classes, where the use of a linear classifier would have failed to separate the two classes.

![Figure 3.5 Examples of two-class classification tasks. (A) A linearly separable classification task. (B) A nonlinearly separable classification task. The goal of a classifier is to partition the space into regions and associate each region with a class.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr005.jpg)
