[Figure 3.5](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#cf0300) Examples of two-class classification tasks. (A) A linearly separable classification task. (B) A nonlinearly separable classification task. The goal of a classifier is to partition the space into regions and associate each region with a class.

Let us now make what we have said so far more concrete. We are given a set of training patterns, **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si10.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), that belong to either of two classes, say, *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si103.png) and *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si99.png). The goal is to design a hyperplane

*f*(**x**) = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*[1] + ⋯ + *θ*[*l*]*x*[*l*] = **θ**^(*T*)**x** = 0,<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0002" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si100.png)

where we have absorbed the bias *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si363.png) in ***θ*** and we have extended the dimension of ***x***, as explained before. Our aim is to place this hyperplane in between the two classes. Obviously, any point lying on this hyperplane scores a zero, *f*(**x**) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si89.png), and the points lying on either side of the hyperplane score either a positive (*f*(**x**) > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si101.png)) or a negative value (*f*(**x**) < 0<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si102.png)), depending on which side of the hyperplane they lie. We should therefore train our classifier so that the points from one class score a positive value and the points of the other a negative one. This can be done, for example, by labeling all points from class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si103.png) with *y*[*n*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si104.png), ∀*n* : **x**[*n*] ∈ *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si105.png), and all points from class *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si99.png) with *y*[*n*] =  − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si106.png), ∀*n* : **x**[*n*] ∈ *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si107.png). Then the squared error is mobilized to compute ***θ*** so as to minimize the cost, i.e.,

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{n} \\right)^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si108.png)

The solution is exactly the same as Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16). [Fig. 3.6](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0035) shows the resulting LS classifiers for two cases of data. Observe that in the case of [Fig. 3.6](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0035)B, the resulting classifier cannot classify correctly all the data points. Our desire to place all data which originate from one class on one side and the rest on the other cannot be satisfied. All that the LS classifier can do is to place the hyperplane so that the sum of squared errors between the desired (true) values of the labels *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si49.png) and the predicted outputs **θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si109.png) is minimal. It is mainly for cases such as overlapping classes, which are usually encountered in practice, where one has to look for an alternative to the squared error criteria and methods, in order to serve better the needs and the goals of the classification task. For example, a reasonable optimality criterion would be to minimize the probability of error, that is, the percentage of points for which the true labels, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si49.png), and the ones predicted by the classifier, *ŷ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si48.png), are different. Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml) presents methods and loss functions appropriate for the classification task. In Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), support vector machines are discussed and in Chapters [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml) and [19](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml) neural networks and deep learning methods are presented. These are currently among the most powerful techniques for classification problems.

![Figure 3.6 Design of a linear classifier, θ0 + θ1x1 + θ2x2 = 0, based on the squared error loss function. (A) The case of two linearly separable classes. (B) The case of nonseparable classes. In the latter case, the classifier cannot separate fully the two classes. All it can do is to place the separating (decision) line so as to minimize the deviation between the true labels and the predicted output values in the LS sense.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr006.jpg)

Figure 3.6 Design of a linear classifier, *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*[1] + *θ*[2]*x*[2] = 0, based on the squared error loss function. (A) The case of two linearly separable classes. (B) The case of nonseparable classes. In the latter case, the classifier cannot separate fully the two classes. All it can do is to place the separating (decision) line so as to minimize the deviation between the true labels and the predicted output values in the LS sense.

### Generative versus discriminative learning

The path that we have taken in order to introduce the classification task was to consider a functional dependence between the output variable (label) y and the input variables (features) **x**. The involved parameters were optimized with respect to a cost function. This path of modeling is also known as *discriminative learning*. We were not concerned with the statistical nature of the dependence that ties these two sets of variables together. In a more general setting, the term discriminative learning is also used to cover methods that model directly the posterior probability of a class, represented by its label *y*, given the feature vector ***x***, as in *P*(*y*|**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si110.png). The common characteristic of all these methods is that they bypass the need of modeling the input data distribution explicitly. From a statistical point of view, discriminative learning is justified as follows.

Using the product rule for probabilities, the joint distribution between the input data and their respective labels can be written as

*p*(*y*, **x**) = *P*(*y*|**x**)*p*(**x**).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si111.png)

In discriminative learning, only the first of the two terms in the product is considered; a functional form is adopted and parameterized appropriately as *P*(*y*|**x**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si112.png). Parameters are then estimated by optimizing a cost function. The distribution of the input data is ignored. Such an approach has the advantage that simpler models can be used, especially if the input data are described by a joint probability density function (PDF) of a complex form. The disadvantage is that the input data distribution is ignored, although it can carry important information, which could be exploited to the benefit of the overall performance.

In contrast, the alternative path, known as *generative learning*, exploits the input data distribution. Once more, employing the product rule, we have

*p*(*y*, **x**) = *p*(**x**|*y*)*P*(*y*),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si113.png)

where *P*(*y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si114.png) is the probability concerning the classes and *p*(**x**|*y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si115.png) is the distribution of the input given the class label. For such an approach, we end up with one distribution per class, which has to be learned. In parametric modeling, a set of parameters is associated with each one of these conditional distributions. Once the input–output joint distribution has been learned, the prediction of the class label of an unknown pattern, ***x***, is performed based on the a posteriori probability, i.e.,

$P(y|\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{p(y,\\mathbf{x})}{p(\\mathbf{x})} = \\frac{p(y,\\mathbf{x})}{\\sum\_{y}p(y,\\mathbf{x})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si116.png)

We will return to these issues in more detail in Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml).

## 3.5 Biased versus unbiased estimation

In supervised learning, we are given a set of training points, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si8.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), and we return an estimate of the unknown parameter vector, say, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si44.png). However, the training points themselves are random variables. If we are given another set of *N* observations of the *same* random variables, these are going to be different, and obviously the resulting estimate will also be different. In other words, by changing our training data, different estimates will result. Hence, we can assume that the resulting estimate, of a fixed yet unknown parameter, is itself a random variable. This, in turn, poses questions on how good an estimator is. Undoubtedly, each time the obtained estimate is optimal with respect to the adopted loss function *and* the specific training set used. However, who guarantees that the resulting estimates are “close” to the true value, assuming that there is one? In this section, we will try to address this task and to illuminate some related theoretical aspects. Note that we have already used the term *estimator* in place of the term *estimate*. Let us elaborate a bit on their difference, before presenting more details.

An estimate, such as $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si44.png), has a specific value, which is the result of a function acting on a set of observations on which our chosen estimate depends (see Eq. [(3.17)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq23)). In general, we could generalize Eq. [(3.17)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq23) and write

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = g(\\mathbf{y},X).$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si117.png)

However, once we allow the set of observations to change randomly, and the estimate becomes itself a random variable, we write the previous equation in terms of the corresponding random variables, i.e.,

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = g(\\mathbf{y},X),$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si118.png)

and we refer to this functional dependence as the *estimator* of the unknown vector ***θ***.

In order to simplify the analysis and focus on the insight behind the methods, we will assume that our parameter space is that of real numbers, ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si119.png). We will also assume that the model (i.e., the set of functions ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png)) which we have adopted for modeling our data is the correct one and that the (unknown to us) value of the associated true parameter is equal to^([⁹](#fn9))

MSE = 𝔼 \[(*θ̂*−*θ*[*o*])²\],<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si122.png)(3.21) 

where the mean 𝔼<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si123.png) is taken over *all* possible training data sets of size *N*. If the MSE is small, then we expect that, on average, the resulting estimates are close to the true value. Note that although *θ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si120.png) is not known, studying the way in which the MSE depends on various terms will still help us to learn how to proceed in practice and unravel possible paths that one can follow to obtain good estimators.

Indeed, this simple and “natural” looking criterion hides some interesting surprises for us. Let us insert the mean value 𝔼\[*θ̂*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si124.png) of *θ̂*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si121.png) in Eq. [(3.21)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq36). We get 

$\\text{MSE} = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\left\\{ \\left( \\widehat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\widehat{\\theta}\\rbrack \\right) + \\left( \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\widehat{\\theta}\\rbrack - \\theta\_{o} \\right) \\right\\}^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\underset{\\text{Variance}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\left( \\widehat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\widehat{\\theta}\\rbrack \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\text{Bias}^{2}}{\\underset{︸}{\\left( \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\widehat{\\theta}\\rbrack - \\theta\_{o} \\right)^{2}}},$<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo id="mmlbr0003" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0003" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Variance</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Bias</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si125.png)(3.22) 

where, for the second equality, we have taken into account that the mean value of the product of the two involved terms turns out to be zero, as can be readily seen. What Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37) suggests is that the MSE consists of two terms. The first one is the variance around the mean value and the second one is due to the bias, that is, the deviation of the mean value of the estimator from the true one.

### 3.5.1 Biased or unbiased estimators?

One may naively think that choosing an estimator that is *unbiased*, as is 𝔼\[*θ̂*\] = *θ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si126.png), such that the second term in Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37) becomes zero, is a reasonable choice. Adopting an unbiased estimator may also be appealing from the following point of view. Assume that we have *L* different training sets, each comprising *N* points. Let us denote each data set by 𝒟[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si127.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *L*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si128.png). For each one, an estimate *θ̂*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si129.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *L*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si128.png), will result. Then, we form a new estimator by taking the average value,

${\\widehat{\\theta}}^{(L)}: = \\frac{1}{L}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{L}{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si130.png)

This is also an unbiased estimator, because

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\widehat{\\theta}}^{(L)}\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{L}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{L}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{i}\\rbrack = \\theta\_{o}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si131.png)

Moreover, assuming that the involved estimators are mutually uncorrelated, i.e.,

𝔼 \[(*θ̂*[*i*]−*θ*[*o*])(*θ̂*[*j*]−*θ*[*o*])\] = 0,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si132.png)

and of the same variance, *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si133.png). The variance of the new estimator is now much smaller (Problem [3.2](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0015)), i.e.,

$\\sigma\_{{\\widehat{\\theta}}^{(L)}}^{2} = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\left( {\\widehat{\\theta}}^{(L)} - \\theta\_{o} \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\frac{\\sigma^{2}}{L}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si134.png)

Hence, by averaging a large number of such unbiased estimators, we expect to get an estimate close to the true value. However, in practice, data are a commodity that is not always abundant. As a matter of fact, very often the opposite is true and one has to be very careful about how to exploit them. In such cases, where one cannot afford to obtain and average a large number of estimators, an unbiased estimator may not necessarily be the best choice. Going back to Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37), there is no reason to suggest that by making the second term equal to zero, the MSE (which, after all, is the quantity of interest to us) becomes minimal. Indeed, let us look at Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37) from a slightly different point of view. Instead of computing the MSE for a given estimator, let us replace *θ̂*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si121.png) with θ in Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37) and compute an estimator that will minimize the MSE with respect to θ directly. In this case, focusing on unbiased estimators, or 𝔼\[*θ*\] = *θ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si135.png), introduces a constraint to the task of minimizing the MSE, and it is well known that an unconstrained minimization problem always results in loss function values that are less than or equal to any value generated by a constrained counterpart, i.e.,

$\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\text{MSE}(\\theta) \\leqslant \\min\\limits\_{\\theta:\\ \\ \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\theta\\rbrack = \\theta\_{o}}\\text{MSE}(\\theta),$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si136.png)(3.23) 

where the dependence of the MSE on the estimator θ in Eq. [(3.23)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq42) is explicitly denoted.

Let us denote by *θ̂*[MVU]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si137.png) a solution of the task min[*θ*:  𝔼\[*θ*\] = *θ*[*o*]]MSE(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si138.png). It can be readily verified by Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37) that *θ̂*[MVU]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si137.png) is an unbiased estimator of minimum variance. Such an estimator is known as the *minimum variance unbiased* (MVU) estimator and we assume that such an estimator exists. An MVU does not always exist (see \[20\], Problem [3.3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0020)). Moreover, if it exists it is unique (Problem [3.4](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0025)). Motivated by Eq. [(3.23)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq42), our next goal is to search for a *biased* estimator, which results, hopefully, in a smaller MSE. Let us denote this estimator as *θ̂*[*b*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si139.png). For the sake of illustration, and in order to limit our search for *θ̂*[*b*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si139.png), we consider here *θ̂*[*b*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si139.png) to be a scalar multiple of *θ̂*[MVU]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si137.png), such that

*θ̂*[*b*] = (1 + *α*)*θ̂*[MVU],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si140.png)(3.24) 

where *α* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si141.png) is a free parameter. Note that 𝔼\[*θ̂*[*b*]\] = (1 + *α*)*θ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si142.png). By substituting Eq. [(3.24)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq43) into Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37) and after some simple algebra we obtain

MSE(*θ̂*[*b*]) = (1 + *α*)²MSE(*θ̂*[MVU]) + *α*²*θ*[*o*]².<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si143.png)(3.25) 

In order to get MSE(*θ̂*[*b*]) < MSE(*θ̂*[MVU])<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si144.png), *α* must be in the range (Problem [3.5](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0030)) of

$- \\frac{2\\text{MSE}({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}})}{\\text{MSE}({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}}) + \\theta\_{o}^{2}} < \\alpha < 0.$<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si145.png)(3.26) 

It is easy to verify that this range implies that |1 + *α*| < 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si146.png). Hence, |*θ̂*[*b*]| = |(1 + *α*)*θ̂*[MVU]| < |*θ̂*[MVU]|<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si147.png). We can go a step further and try to compute the optimum value of *α*, which corresponds to the minimum MSE. By taking the derivative of MSE(*θ̂*[*b*])<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si148.png) in Eq. [(3.25)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq44) with respect to *α*, it turns out (Problem [3.6](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0035)) that this occurs for

$\\alpha\_{\\ast} = - \\frac{\\text{MSE}({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}})}{\\text{MSE}({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}}) + \\theta\_{o}^{2}} = - \\frac{1}{1 + \\frac{\\theta\_{o}^{2}}{\\text{MSE}({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}})}}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si149.png)(3.27) 

Therefore, we have found a way to obtain the optimum estimator among those in the set {*θ̂*[*b*] = (1 + *α*)*θ̂*[MVU] : *α* ∈ ℝ}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si150.png), which results in the minimum MSE. This is true, but as many nice things in life, this is not, in general, realizable. The optimal value for *α* is given in terms of the unknown *θ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si120.png)! However, Eq. [(3.27)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq46) is useful in a number of other ways. First, there are cases where the MSE is proportional to *θ*[*o*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si151.png); hence, this formula can be used. Also, for certain cases, it can be used to provide useful bounds \[19\]. Moreover, as far as we are concerned in this book, it says something very important. If we want to do better than the MVU, then, looking at the text following Eq. [(3.26)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq45), a possible way is to *shrink* the norm of the MVU estimator. Shrinking the norm is a way of introducing bias into an estimator. We will discuss ways to achieve this in Section [3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0055) and later on in Chapters [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml) and [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml).

Note that what we have said so far is readily generalized to parameter vectors. An unbiased parameter vector estimator satisfies

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}\\rbrack = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si152.png)

and the MSE around the true value **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si153.png) is defined as

$\\text{MSE} = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack {(\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o})}^{T}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}) \\right\\rbrack = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack {({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{i} - \\theta\_{oi})}^{2} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si154.png)

Looking carefully at the previous definition reveals that the MSE for a parameter vector is the sum of the MSEs of the components *θ̂*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si155.png), around the corresponding true values *θ*[*o**i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si156.png).

## 3.6 The Cramér–Rao lower bound

In the previous sections, we saw how one can improve the performance of the MVU estimator, provided that this exists and it is known. However, how can one know that an unbiased estimator that has been obtained is also of minimum variance? The goal of this section is to introduce a criterion that can provide such information.

The *Cramér–Rao lower bound* \[9,31\] is an elegant theorem and one of the most well-known techniques used in statistics. It provides a lower bound on the variance of *any* unbiased estimator. This is very important because (a) it offers the means to assert whether an unbiased estimator has minimum variance, which, of course, in this case coincides with the corresponding MSE in Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37), (b) if this is not the case, it can be used to indicate how far away the performance of an unbiased estimator is from the optimal one, and finally (c) it provides the designer with a tool to know the best possible performance that can be achieved by an unbiased estimator. Because our main purpose here is to focus on the insight and physical interpretation of the method, we will deal with the simple case where our unknown parameter is a real number. The general form of the theorem, involving vectors, is given in Appendix B.

We are looking for a bound of the variance of an unbiased estimator, whose randomness is due to the randomness of the training data, as we change from one set to another. Thus, it does not come as a surprise that the bound involves the joint PDF of the data, parameterized in terms of the unknown parameter *θ*. Let 𝒳 = {**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si157.png) denote the set of *N* observations, corresponding to a random vector^([^(10)](#fn10))

Theorem 3.1

*It is assumed that the joint PDF satisfies the following* regularity *condition:*

$\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\partial\\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\theta)}{\\partial\\theta} \\right\\rbrack = 0,\\quad\\forall\\theta.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si159.png)(3.28) 

*This regularity condition is a weak one and holds for most of the cases in practice (Problem* [3.7](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0040)*). Then, the variance of any unbiased estimator,* *θ̂*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si121.png)*, must satisfy the following inequality:*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/fx002.jpg)(3.29) 

*where*

$I(\\theta): = - \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\partial^{2}\\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\theta)}{\\partial\\theta^{2}} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si161.png)(3.30) 

*Moreover, the necessary and sufficient condition for obtaining an unbiased estimator that achieves the bound is the existence of a function* *g*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si162.png) *such that for all possible values of θ,*

$\\frac{\\partial\\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\theta)}{\\partial\\theta} = I(\\theta)\\left( g(\\mathcal{X}) - \\theta \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si163.png)(3.31) 

*The MVU estimate is then given by*

*θ̂* = *g*(𝒳) :  = *g*(**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]),<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si164.png)(3.32) 

*and the variance of the respective estimator is equal to* 1/*I*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si165.png)*.*

When an MVU estimator attains the Cramér–Rao bound, we say that it is *efficient*. All the expectations before are taken with respect to *p*(𝒳; *θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si158.png). The interested reader may find more on the topic in more specialized books on statistics \[20,27,36\].

Example 3.2

Let us consider the simplified version of the linear regression model in Eq. [(3.10)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq13), where the regressor is real-valued and the bias term is zero,

*y*[*n*] = *θ**x* + *η*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si166.png)(3.33) 

where we have explicitly denoted the dependence on *n*, which runs over the number of available observations. Note that in order to further simplify the discussion, we have assumed that our *N* observations are the result of different realizations of the noise variable only, and that we have kept the value of the input, *x*, constant, which can be considered to be equal to one, without harming generality; that is, our task is reduced to that of estimating a parameter from its noisy measurements. Thus, for this case, the observations are the scalar outputs *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si49.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), which we consider to be the components of a vector **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si167.png). We further assume that *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si168.png) are samples of a white Gaussian noise (Section [2.4](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)) with zero mean and variance equal to *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si169.png); that is, successive samples are i.i.d. drawn and, hence, they are mutually uncorrelated (𝔼\[*η*[*i*]*η*[*j*]\] = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si170.png), *i* ≠ *j*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si171.png)). Then, the joint PDF of the output observations is given by

$p(\\mathbf{y};\\theta) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{{(y\_{n} - \\theta)}^{2}}{2\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si172.png)(3.34) 

or

$\\ln p(\\mathbf{y};\\theta) = - \\frac{N}{2}\\ln(2\\pi\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}) - \\frac{1}{2\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}{(y\_{n} - \\theta)}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si173.png)(3.35) 

We will derive the corresponding Cramér–Rao bound. Taking the derivative of the logarithm with respect to *θ* we have

$\\frac{\\partial\\ln p(\\mathbf{y};\\theta)}{\\partial\\theta} = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}(y\_{n} - \\theta) = \\frac{N}{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}(\\overline{y} - \\theta),$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si174.png)(3.36) 

where
