$\\overline{y}: = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si175.png)

that is, the sample mean of the observations. The second derivative, as required by the theorem, is given by

$\\frac{\\partial^{2}\\ln p(\\mathbf{y};\\theta)}{\\partial\\theta^{2}} = - \\frac{N}{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}},$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si176.png)

and hence,

$I(\\theta) = \\frac{N}{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si177.png)(3.37) 

Eq. [(3.36)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq57) is in the form of Eq. [(3.31)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq52), with $g(\\mathbf{y}) = \\overline{y}$<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si178.png); thus, an efficient estimator can be obtained and the lower bound of the variance of any unbiased estimator, for our data model of Eq. [(3.33)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq54), is

$\\sigma\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}^{2} \\geq \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{N}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si179.png)(3.38) 

We can easily verify that the corresponding estimator $\\overline{y}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si180.png) is indeed an unbiased one under the adopted model of Eq. [(3.33)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq54),

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\overline{y}\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack y\_{n}\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\theta + \\eta\_{n}\\rbrack = \\theta.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si181.png)

Moreover, the previous formula, combined with Eq. [(3.36)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq57), also establishes the regularity condition, as required by the Cramér–Rao theorem.

The bound in Eq. [(3.38)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq61) is a very natural result. The Cramér–Rao lower bound depends on the variance of the noise source. The higher this is, and therefore the higher the uncertainty of each observation with respect to the value of the true parameter is, the higher the minimum variance of an estimator is expected to be. On the other hand, as the number of observations increases and more “information” is disclosed to us, the uncertainty decreases and we expect the variance of our estimator to decrease.

Having obtained the lower bound for our task, let us return our attention to the LS estimator for the specific regression model of Eq. [(3.33)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq54). This results from Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16) by setting *x*[*n*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si182.png), and a simple inspection shows that the LS estimate is nothing but the sample mean, $\\overline{y}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si183.png), of the observations. Furthermore, the variance of the corresponding estimator is given by

$\\sigma\_{\\overline{y}}^{2} = \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack {(\\overline{y} - \\theta)}^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{N^{2}}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}(y\_{n} - \\theta) \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{N^{2}}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\left( \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\eta\_{n} \\right)^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{N^{2}}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\eta\_{i}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}\\eta\_{j} \\right\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{N^{2}}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\eta\_{i}\\eta\_{j}\\rbrack = \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{N},$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si184.png)

 which coincides with our previous finding via the use of the Cramér–Rao theorem. In other words, for this particular task and having assumed that the noise is white Gaussian, the LS estimator $\\overline{y}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si180.png) is an MVU estimator and it attains the Cramér–Rao bound. However, if the input is not fixed, but it also varies from experiment to experiment and the training data become (*y*[*n*], *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si2.png), then the LS estimator attains the Cramér–Rao bound only asymptotically, for large values of *N* (Problem [3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0045)). Moreover, it has to be pointed out that if the assumptions for the noise being Gaussian *and* white are not valid, then the LS estimator is not efficient anymore.

It turns out that this result, which has been obtained for the real axis case, is also true for the general regression model given in Eq. [(3.10)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq13) (Problem [3.9](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0050)). We will return to the properties of the LS estimator in more detail in Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml).

Remarks 3.2

*   •  The Cramér–Rao bound is not the only one that is available in the literature. For example, the Bhattacharyya bound makes use of higher-order derivatives of the PDF. It turns out that in cases where an efficient estimator does not exist, the Bhattacharyya bound is tighter compared to the Cramér–Rao one with respect to the variance of the MVU estimator \[27\]. Other bounds also exist \[21\]; however, the Cramér–Rao bound is the easiest to determine.

## 3.7 Sufficient statistic

If an efficient estimator does not exist, this does not necessarily mean that the MVU estimator cannot be determined. It may exist, but it will not be an efficient one, in the sense that it does not satisfy the Cramér–Rao bound. In such cases, the notion of *sufficient statistic* and the Rao–Blackwell theorem come into the picture.^([^(11)](#fn11))

The notion of sufficient statistic is due to Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher (1890–1962). Fisher was an English statistician and biologist who made a number of fundamental contributions that laid out many of the foundations of modern statistics. Besides statistics, he made important contributions in genetics.

In short, given a random vector **x**, whose distribution depends on a parameter *θ*, a sufficient statistic for the unknown parameter is a function,

*T*(𝒳) :  = *T*(**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si186.png)

of the respective observations, which contains *all* information about *θ*. From a mathematical point of view, a statistic *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) is said to be sufficient for the parameter *θ* if the conditional joint PDF

*p*(𝒳|*T*(𝒳);*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si188.png)

*does not* depend on *θ*. In such a case, it becomes apparent that *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) must provide *all* information about *θ*, which is contained in the set 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si189.png). Once *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) is known, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si189.png) is no longer needed, because no further information can be extracted from it; this justifies the name of “sufficient statistic.” The concept of sufficient statistic is also generalized to parameter vectors ***θ***. In such a case, the sufficient statistic may be a *set* of functions, called a *jointly sufficient statistic*. Typically, there are as many functions as there are parameters; in a slight abuse of notation, we will still write *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) to denote this set of (vector of) functions.

A very important theorem, which facilitates the search for a sufficient statistic in practice, is the following \[27\].

Theorem 3.2

Factorization theorem

*A statistic* *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) *is sufficient if and only if the respective joint PDF can be factored as*

*p*(𝒳; **θ**) = *h*(𝒳)*g*(*T*(𝒳),**θ**).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si192.png)

*That is, the joint PDF is factored into two parts: one part that depends only on the statistic and the parameters and a second part that is independent of the parameters. The theorem is also known as the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem.*

Once a sufficient statistic has been found and under certain conditions related to the statistic, the Rao–Blackwell theorem determines the MVU estimator by taking the expectation conditioned on *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png). A by-product of this theorem is that if an unbiased estimator is expressed *solely* in terms of the sufficient statistic, then it is necessarily the unique MVU estimator \[23\]. The interested reader can obtain more on these issues from \[20,21,27\].

Example 3.3

Let x be a Gaussian random variable, 𝒩(*μ*, *σ*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si193.png), and let the set of i.i.d. observations be 𝒳 = {*x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si194.png). Assume the mean value, *μ*, to be the unknown parameter. Show that

$S\_{\\mu} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}x\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si195.png)

is a sufficient statistic for the parameter *μ*.

The joint PDF is given by

$p(\\mathcal{X};\\mu) = \\frac{1}{{(2\\pi\\sigma^{2})}^{\\frac{N}{2}}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2\\sigma^{2}}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}{(x\_{n} - \\mu)}^{2} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

$S\_{\\sigma^{2}} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}{(x\_{n} - S\_{\\mu})}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si201.png)

In other words, in this case, all information concerning the unknown set of parameters that can be possibly extracted from the available *N* observations can be fully recovered by considering only the sum of the observations and the sum of their squares.

## 3.8 Regularization

We have already seen that the LS estimator is an MVU estimator, under the assumptions of linearity of the regression model and in the presence of a Gaussian white noise source. We also know that one can improve the performance by shrinking the norm of the MVU estimator. There are various ways to achieve this goal, and they will be discussed later on in this book. In this section, we focus on one possibility. Moreover, we will see that trying to keep the norm of the solution small serves important needs in the context of machine learning.

*Regularization* is a mathematical tool to impose a priori information on the structure of the solution, which comes as the outcome of an optimization task. Regularization was first suggested by the great Russian mathematician Andrey Nikolayevich Tychonoff (sometimes spelled Tikhonov) for the solution of integral equations. Sometimes it is also referred as Tychonoff–Phillips regularization, to honor David Phillips as well, who developed the method independently \[29,39\].

In the context of our task and in order to shrink the norm of the parameter vector estimate, we can reformulate the sum of squared errors minimization task, given in Eq. [(3.12)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq15), as

$\\text{minimize}\\qquad\\ \\ J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{n} \\right)^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>minimize</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si202.png)(3.39) 

subject to   ∥**θ**∥² ≤ *ρ*,<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>subject to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si203.png)(3.40) 

where ∥⋅∥<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si204.png) stands for the Euclidean norm of a vector. In this way, we do not allow the LS criterion to be completely “free” to reach a solution, but we *limit* the space in which we search for it. Obviously, using different values of *ρ*, we can achieve different levels of shrinkage. As we have already discussed, the optimal value of *ρ* cannot be analytically obtained, and one has to experiment in order to select an estimator that results in a good performance. For the squared error loss function and the constraint used before, the optimization task can equivalently be written as \[6,8\]

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/fx003.jpg)(3.41) 

It turns out that for specific choices of *λ* ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si205.png) and *ρ*, the two tasks are equivalent. Note that this new cost function, *L*(**θ**, *λ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si206.png), involves one term that measures the model *misfit* and a second one that quantifies the *size* of the norm of the parameter vector. It is straightforward to see that taking the gradient of *L* in Eq. [(3.41)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq74) with respect to ***θ*** and equating to zero, we obtain the *regularized version* of the LS solution for the linear regression task of Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16),

$\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T} + \\lambda I \\right)\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si207.png)(3.42) 

where *I* is the identity matrix of appropriate dimensions. The presence of *λ* biases the new solution away from that which would have been obtained from the unregularized LS formulation. The task is also known as *ridge regression*. Ridge regression attempts to reduce the norm of the estimated vector and *at the same time* tries to keep the sum of squared errors small; in order to achieve this *combined* goal, the vector components, *θ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si208.png), are modified in such a way so that the contribution in the misfit measuring term, from the less informative directions in the input space, is minimized. In other words, those of the components that are associated with less informative directions will be pushed to smaller values to keep the norm small and at the same time have minimum influence on the misfit measuring term. We will return to this in more detail in Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml). Ridge regression was first introduced in \[18\].

It has to be emphasized that in practice, the bias parameter *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si363.png) is left out from the norm in the regularization term; penalization of the bias would make the procedure dependent on the origin chosen for *y*. Indeed, it is easily checked that adding a constant term to each one of the output values, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si49.png), in the cost function would not result in just a shift of the predictions by the same constant, if the bias term is included in the norm. Hence, usually, ridge regression is formulated as

$\\text{minimize}\\quad L(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\lambda) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - \\theta\_{0} - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\theta\_{i}x\_{ni} \\right)^{2} + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}|\\theta\_{i}|^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>minimize</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si209.png)(3.43) 

It turns out (Problem [3.11](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0060)) that minimizing Eq. [(3.43)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq76) with respect to *θ*[*i*], *i* = 0, 1, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si210.png), is equivalent to minimizing Eq. [(3.41)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq74) using *centered* data and neglecting the intercept. That is, one solves the task

$\\text{minimize}\\quad L(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\lambda) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( (y\_{n} - \\overline{y}) - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\theta\_{i}(x\_{ni} - {\\overline{x}}\_{i}) \\right)^{2} + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}|\\theta\_{i}|^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mtext>minimize</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si211.png)(3.44) 

and the estimate of *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si363.png) in Eq. [(3.43)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq76) is given in terms of the obtained estimates *θ̂*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si129.png), i.e.,

${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{0} = \\overline{y} - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{i}{\\overline{x}}\_{i},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si212.png)

where

$\\overline{y} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}\\quad\\text{and}\\quad{\\overline{x}}\_{i} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}x\_{ni},\\ \\ i = 1,2,\\ldots,l.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si213.png)

In other words, *θ̂*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si214.png) compensates for the differences between the sample means of the output and input variables. Note that similar arguments hold true if the Euclidean norm, used in Eq. [(3.42)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq75) as a regularizer, is replaced by other norms, such as ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si215.png) or in general ℓ[*p*], *p* > 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si216.png), norms (Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)).

From a different viewpoint, reducing the norm can be considered as an attempt to “simplify” the structure of the estimator, because a smaller number of components of the regressor now have an important say. This viewpoint becomes more clear if one considers nonlinear models, as discussed in Section [3.2](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0015). In this case, the existence of the norm of the respective parameter vector in Eq. [(3.41)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq74) forces the model to get rid of the less important terms in the nonlinear expansion, $\\sum\_{k = 1}^{K - 1}\\theta\_{k}\\phi\_{k}(\\mathbf{x})$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si217.png), and effectively pushes *K* to lower values.

Although in the current context the complexity issue emerges in a rather disguised form, one can make it a major player in the game by choosing to use different functions and norms for the regularization term; as we will see next, there are many reasons that justify such choices.

### Inverse problems: ill-conditioning and overfitting

Most tasks in machine learning belong to the so-called *inverse problems*. The latter term encompasses all the problems where one has to infer/predict/estimate the values of a model based on a set of available output/input observations (training data). In a less mathematical terminology, in inverse problems one has to unravel unknown causes from known effects, or in other words, to reverse the cause–effect relations. Inverse problems are typically *ill-posed*, as opposed to the *well-posed* ones. Well-posed problems are characterized by (a) the existence of a solution, (b) the uniqueness of the solution, and (c) the stability of the solution. The latter condition is usually violated in machine learning problems. This means that the obtained solution may be very sensitive to changes of the training set. *Ill-conditioning* is another term used to describe this sensitivity. The reason for this behavior is that the model used to describe the data can be complex, in the sense that the number of the unknown free parameters is large with respect to the number of data points. The “face” with which manifests itself in machine learning is known as *overfitting*. This means that during training, the estimated parameters of the unknown model learn too much about the idiosyncrasies of the specific training data set, and the model performs badly when it deals with data sets other than that used for training. As a matter of fact, the MSE criterion discussed in Section [3.5](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0035) attempts to quantify exactly this data dependence of the task, that is, the mean deviation of the obtained estimates from the true value, by changing the training sets.

When the number of training samples is small with respect to the number of unknown parameters, the available information is not enough to “reveal” a sufficiently good model that fits the data, and it can be misleading due to the presence of the noise and possible outliers. Regularization is an elegant and efficient tool to cope with the complexity of the model, that is, to make it less complex, more smooth. There are different ways to achieve this. One way is by constraining the norm of the unknown vector, as ridge regression does. When dealing with more complex, compared to linear, models, one can use constraints on the smoothness of the involved nonlinear function, for example, by involving derivatives of the model function in the regularization term. Also, regularization can help when the adopted model and the number of training points are such that no solution is possible. For example, in the LS linear regression task of Eq. [(3.13)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq16), if the number *N* of training points is less than the dimension of the regressors **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si79.png), then the (*l* + 1) × (*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si55.png) matrix, $\\overline{\\Sigma} = \\sum\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si218.png), is not invertible. Indeed, each term in the summation is the outer product of a vector with itself and hence it is a matrix of rank one. Thus, as we know from linear algebra, we need at least *l* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si219.png) linearly independent terms of such matrices to guarantee that the sum is of full rank, and hence invertible. However, in ridge regression, this can be bypassed, because the presence of *λI* in Eq. [(3.42)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq75) guarantees that the left-hand side matrix is invertible. Furthermore, the presence of *λI* can also help when $\\overline{\\Sigma}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si220.png) is invertible but it is ill-conditioned. Usually in such cases, the resulting LS solution has a very large norm and, thus, it is meaningless. Regularization helps to replace the original ill-conditioned problem with a “nearby” one, which is well conditioned and whose solution approximates the target one.

Another example where regularization can help to obtain a solution is when the model's order is large compared to the number of data, although we know that it is sparse. That is, only a very small percentage of the model's parameters is nonzero. For such a task, regularizing the sum of squared errors cost function using the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si215.png) norm of the parameter vector promotes sparse solutions, by assigning zero values to the least significant parameters; the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si215.png) norm of a vector comprises the sum of the absolute values of its components. This problem will be considered in Chapters [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml).

Regularization is closely related to the task of using priors in Bayesian learning, as we will discuss in Section [3.11](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0090). Finally, note that regularization is not a panacea for facing the problem of overfitting. As a matter of fact, selecting the right set of functions ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si14.png) in Eq. [(3.3)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq3) is the first crucial step. The issue of the complexity of an estimator and the consequences on its “average” performance, as measured over all possible data sets, is discussed in Section [3.9](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0065).

Example 3.4

The goal of this example is to demonstrate that the estimator obtained via ridge regression can score a better MSE performance compared to the unconstrained LS solution. Let us consider, once again, the scalar model exposed in [Example 3.2](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#enun0025), and assume that the data are generated according to

*y*[*n*] = *θ*[*o*] + *η*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si221.png)

where, for simplicity, we have assumed that the regressors *x*[*n*] ≡ 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≡</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si222.png) and *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si168.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), are i.i.d. zero mean Gaussian noise samples of variance *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si169.png).

We have already seen in [Example 3.2](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#enun0025) that the solution to the LS parameter estimation task is the sample mean ${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si224.png). We have also shown that this solution scores an MSE of *σ*[*η*]²/*N*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si225.png) and under the previous Gaussian assumption for the noise it achieves the Cramér–Rao bound. The question now is whether a biased estimator, *θ̂*[*b*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si139.png), which corresponds to the solution of the associated ridge regression task, can achieve an MSE lower than MSE(*θ̂*[MVU])<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si226.png).

It can be readily verified that Eq. [(3.42)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq75), adapted to the needs of the current linear regression scenario, results in

${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{b}(\\lambda) = \\frac{1}{N + \\lambda}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}y\_{n} = \\frac{N}{N + \\lambda}{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si227.png)

where we have explicitly expressed the dependence of the estimate *θ̂*[*b*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si228.png) on the regularization parameter *λ*. Note that for the associated estimator we have $\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{b}(\\lambda)\\rbrack = \\frac{N}{N + \\lambda}\\theta\_{o}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si229.png).

A simple inspection of the previous relation takes us back to the discussion related to Eq. [(3.24)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq43). Indeed, by following a sequence of steps similar to those in Section [3.5.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0040), one can verify (see Problem [3.12](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0065)) that the minimum value of MSE(*θ̂*[*b*])<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si148.png) is

$\\text{MSE}\\left( {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{b}(\\lambda\_{\\ast}) \\right) = \\frac{\\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{N}}{1 + \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{N\\theta\_{o}^{2}}} < \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{N} = \\text{MSE}\\left( {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{MVU}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si230.png)(3.45) 

attained at *λ*[\*] = *σ*[*η*]²/*θ*[*o*]²<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si231.png). The answer to the question whether the ridge regression estimator offers an improvement to the MSE performance is therefore positive in the current context. As a matter of fact, there *always* exists a *λ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si232.png) such that the ridge regression estimator, which solves the general task of Eq. [(3.41)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq74), achieves an MSE lower than the one corresponding to the MVU estimator \[5, Section 8.4\].

We will now demonstrate the previous theoretical findings via some simulations. To this end, the true value of the model was chosen to be *θ*[*o*] = 10^( − 2)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si235.png). The noise was Gaussian of zero mean value and variance *σ*[*η*]² = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si236.png). The number of i.i.d. generated samples was *N* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si237.png). Note that this is quite large, compared to the single parameter we have to estimate. The previous values imply that *θ*[*o*]² < *σ*[*η*]²/*N*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si238.png). Then it can be shown that for any value of *λ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si232.png), we can obtain a value for MSE(*θ̂*[*b*](*λ*))<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si240.png) which is smaller than that of MSE(*θ̂*[MVU])<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si226.png) (see Problem [3.12](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0065)). This is verified by the values shown in [Table 3.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#t0010). To compute the MSE values in the table, the expectation operation in the definition in Eq. [(3.21)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq36) was approximated by the respective sample mean. To this end, the experiment was repeated *L* times and the MSE was computed as

$\\text{MSE} \\approx \\frac{1}{L}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{L}{({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{i} - \\theta\_{o})}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si241.png)

To get accurate results, we perform *L* = 10⁶<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si242.png) trials. The corresponding MSE value for the unconstrained LS task is equal to MSE(*θ̂*[MVU]) = 1.00108 × 10^( − 3)<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.00108</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si234.png). Observe that substantial improvements can be attained when using regularization, in spite of the relatively large number of training data.

However, the percentage of performance improvement depends heavily on the specific values that define the model, as Eq. [(3.45)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq82) suggests. For example, if *θ*[*o*] = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si244.png), the obtained values from the experiments were MSE(*θ̂*[MVU]) = 1.00061 × 10^( − 3)<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MVU</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.00061</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si245.png) and MSE(*θ̂*[*b*](*λ*[\*])) = 9.99578 × 10^( − 4)<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>9.99578</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si246.png). The theoretical ones, as computed from Eq. [(3.45)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq82), are 1 × 10^( − 3)<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si247.png) and 9.99001 × 10^( − 4)<mml:math><mml:mn>9.99001</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si248.png), respectively. The improvement obtained by using the ridge regression is now rather insignificant.

## 3.9 The bias–variance dilemma

This section goes one step beyond Section [3.5](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0035). There, the MSE criterion was used to quantify the performance with respect to the unknown parameter. Such a setting was useful to help us understand some trends and also better digest the notions of “biased” versus “unbiased” estimation. Here, although the criterion will be the same, it will be used in a more general setting. To this end, we shift our interest from the unknown parameter to the dependent variable and our goal becomes obtaining an estimator of the value y, given a measurement of the regressor vector, **x** = **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si249.png). Let us first consider the more general form of regression,

*y* = *g*(**x**) + *η*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si250.png)(3.46) 

where, for simplicity and without loss of generality, once more we have assumed that the dependent variable takes values in the real axis, *y* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si251.png). The first question to be addressed is whether there exists an estimator that guarantees minimum MSE performance.

### 3.9.1 Mean-square error estimation

Our goal is estimating an unknown (nonlinear in general) function *g*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si252.png). This problem can be cast in the context of the more general estimation task setting.

Consider the *jointly distributed* random variables *y*, **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si253.png). Then, given any observation, **x** = **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si254.png), the task is to obtain a function *ŷ* :  = *ĝ*(**x**) ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si255.png), such that

*ĝ*(**x**) = *a**r**g* *m**i**n*[*f* : ℝ^(*l*) → ℝ] 𝔼 \[(*y*−*f*(**x**))²\],<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si256.png)(3.47) 

where the expectation is taken with respect to the conditional probability of y given the value of ***x***, or in other words, *p*(*y*|**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si257.png).

We will show that the optimal estimator is the mean value of y, or

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/fx004.jpg)(3.48) 

Proof

We have

𝔼 \[(*y*−*f*(**x**))²\] = 𝔼 \[(*y*−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]+𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]−*f*(**x**))²\] = 𝔼 \[(*y*−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\])²\] + 𝔼 \[(𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]−*f*(**x**))²\] + 2𝔼 \[(*y*−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\])(𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]−*f*(**x**))\],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo id="mmlbr0005" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak"
