indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="before">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si258.png)

where the dependence of the expectation on ***x*** has been omitted for notational convenience. It is readily seen that the last (product) term on the right-hand side is zero, hence, we are left with the following:

𝔼 \[(*y*−*f*(**x**))²\] = 𝔼 \[(*y*−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\])²\] + (𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]−*f*(**x**))²,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si259.png)(3.49) 

where we have taken into account that, for fixed ***x***, the terms 𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si260.png) and *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si12.png) are not random variables. From Eq. [(3.49)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq88) we finally obtain our claim,

𝔼 \[(*y*−*f*(**x**))²\] ≥ 𝔼 \[(*y*−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\])²\].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si261.png)(3.50) 

 □

Note that this is a very elegant result. The optimal estimate, in the MSE sense, of the value of the unknown function at a point ***x*** is given as *ĝ*(**x**) = 𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si262.png). Sometimes, the latter is also known as the *regression of* y *conditioned on* **x** = **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si249.png). This is, in general, a nonlinear function. It can be shown that if (*y*, **x**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si263.png) take values in ℝ × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si264.png) and are jointly Gaussian, then the optimal MSE estimator 𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si265.png) is a linear (affine) function of ***x***.

The previous results generalize to the case where **y** is a random vector that takes values in ℝ^(*k*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si266.png). The optimal MSE estimate, given the values of **x** = **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si249.png), is equal to

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{g}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si267.png)

where now $\\widehat{\\mathbf{g}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^{k}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si268.png) (Problem [3.15](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0080)). Moreover, if (**y**, **x**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si269.png) are jointly Gaussian random vectors, the MSE optimal estimator is also an affine function of ***x*** (Problem [3.16](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0085)).

The findings of this subsection can be fully justified by physical reasoning. Assume, for simplicity, that the noise source in Eq. [(3.46)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq84) is of zero mean. Then, for a fixed value **x** = **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si249.png), we have 𝔼\[*y*|**x**\] = *g*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si270.png) and the respective MSE is equal to

MSE = 𝔼\[(*y*−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\])²\] = *σ*[*η*]².<mml:math><mml:mtext>MSE</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si271.png)(3.51) 

No other function of ***x*** can do better, because the optimal one achieves an MSE equal to the noise variance, which is irreducible; it represents the intrinsic uncertainty of the system. As Eq. [(3.49)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq88) suggests, any other function *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si12.png) will result in an MSE larger by the quantity (𝔼\[*y*|**x**\] − *f*(**x**))²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si272.png), which corresponds to the deviation from the optimal one.

### 3.9.2 Bias–variance tradeoff

We have just seen that the optimal estimator, in the MSE sense, of the dependent variable in a regression task is given by the conditional expectation 𝔼\[*y*|**x**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si265.png). In practice, any estimator is computed based on a specific training data set, say, 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png). Let us make the dependence on the training set explicit and express the estimator as a function of ***x*** parameterized on 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png), or *f*(**x**; 𝒟)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si274.png). A reasonable measure to quantify the performance of an estimator is its mean-square deviation from the optimal one, expressed by 𝔼[𝒟]\[(*f*(**x**;𝒟)−𝔼\[*y*|**x**\])²\]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si275.png), where the mean is taken with respect to all possible training sets, because each one results in a different estimator. Following a similar path as for Eq. [(3.22)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq37), we obtain

![](images/B9780443292385000093/fx005.jpg)

As was the case for the MSE parameter estimation task when changing from one training set to another, the mean-square deviation from the optimal estimator comprises two terms. The first one is the variance of the estimator around its own mean value and the second one is the squared difference of the mean from the optimal one, that is, the bias. It turns out that one *cannot* make *both* terms small simultaneously. For a fixed number of training points *N* in the data sets 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png), trying to minimize the variance term results in an increase of the bias term and vice versa. This is because in order to reduce the bias term, one has to increase the complexity (more free parameters) of the adopted estimator *f*(⋅;𝒟)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si276.png). This, in turn, results in higher variance as we change the training sets. This is a manifestation of the overfitting issue that we have already discussed. The only way to reduce both terms simultaneously is to increase the number of the training data points *N*, and at the same time increase the complexity of the model *carefully*, so as to achieve the aforementioned goal. If one increases the number of training points and at the same time increases the model complexity excessively, the overall MSE may increase. This is known as the *bias–variance dilemma* or *tradeoff*. This is an issue that is omnipresent in any estimation task. Usually, we refer to it as *Occam's razor* rule.

Occam was a logician and a nominalist scholastic medieval philosopher who expressed the following law of parsimony: “Plurality must never be posited without necessity.” The great physicist Paul Dirac (1902–1984) expressed the same statement from an esthetics point of view, which underlies mathematical theories: “A theory with a mathematical beauty is more likely to be correct than an ugly one that fits the data.” In our context of model selection, it is understood that one has to select the simplest model that can “explain” the data. Although this is not a scientifically proven result, it underlies the rationale behind a number of developed model selection techniques \[1,32,33,40\] and \[37, Chapter 5\], which trade off complexity with accuracy.

Let us now try to find the MSE, given ***x***, by considering all possible sets 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png). To this end, note that the left-hand side of Eq. (3.52) is the mean with respect to 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png) of the second term in Eq. [(3.49)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq88), if 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png) is brought explicitly in the notation. It is easy to see that, by reconsidering Eq. [(3.49)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq88) and taking the expectation on both y and 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png), given the value of **x** = **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si249.png), the resulting MSE becomes (try it, following similar arguments as for Eq. (3.52))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si277.png)(3.53) 

where Eq. [(3.51)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq91) has been used and the product rule, as stated in Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml), has been exploited. In the sequel, one can take the mean over ***x***. In other words, this is the prediction MSE over all possible inputs, averaged over all possible training sets. The resulting MSE is also known as the *test* or *generalization error* and it is a measure of the performance of the respective adopted model. Note that the generalization error in Eq. [(3.53)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq92) involves averaging over (theoretically) all possible training data sets of certain size *N*. In contrast, the so-called *training error* is computed over a single data set, the one used for the training, and this results in an overoptimistic estimate of the error. We will come back to this important issue in Section [3.13](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0105).

Example 3.5

Let us consider a simplistic, yet pedagogic, example that demonstrates this tradeoff between bias and variance. We are given a set of training points that are generated according to a regression model of the form

*y* = *g*(*x*) + *η*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si279.png)(3.54) 

The graph of *g*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si280.png) is shown in [Fig. 3.7](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0045). The function *g*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si280.png) is a fifth-order polynomial. Training sets are generated as follows. For each set, the *x*\-axis is sampled at *N* equidistant points *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si281.png), *n* = 1, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si282.png), in the interval \[ − 1, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si283.png). Then, each training set 𝒟[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si127.png) is created as

𝒟[*i*] = {(*x*[*n*],*g*(*x*[*n*])+*η*[*n*, *i*]):*n*\=1,2,…,*N*}, *i* = 1, 2, …,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si284.png)

where *η*[*n*, *i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si285.png) denotes different noise samples, drawn i.i.d. from a white noise process. In other words, all training points have the same *x*\-coordinate but different *y*\-coordinates due to the different values of the noise. The gray dots in the (*x*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si286.png)\-plane in [Fig. 3.7](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0045) correspond to one realization of a training set, for the case of *N* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si287.png). For comparison, the set of noiseless points, (*x*[*n*], *g*(*x*[*n*]))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si288.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, 10<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si289.png), is shown as red dots on the graph of *g*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si280.png).

On the other hand, the variance of the “estimator” will be zero. In contrast, fitting a high-degree polynomial f\_{2}(x;\\mathcal{D})Equation results in low bias, because the corresponding curve goes through all the data points; however, the respective variance will be high.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr007.jpg)

Figure 3.7 The observed data are denoted as gray dots. These are the result of adding noise to the red points, which lie on the red curve associated with the unknown *g*(⋅). Fitting the data by the fixed polynomial *f*[1](*x*) results in high bias; observe that most of the data points lie outside the straight line. On the other hand, the variance of the “estimator” will be zero. In contrast, fitting a high-degree polynomial *f*[2](*x*; 𝒟)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si278.png) results in low bias, because the corresponding curve goes through all the data points; however, the respective variance will be high.

First, we are going to be very naive, and choose a fixed linear model to fit the data,

*ŷ* = *f*[1](*x*) = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*,<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si290.png)

where the values *θ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si291.png) and *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si363.png) have been chosen arbitrarily, irrespective of the training data. The graph of this straight line is shown in [Fig. 3.7](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0045). Because no training was involved and the model parameters are fixed, there is no variation as one changes the training sets and 𝔼[𝒟]\[*f*[1](*x*)\] = *f*[1](*x*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si292.png), with the variance term being equal to zero. On the other hand, the square of the bias, which is equal to (*f*[1](*x*) − 𝔼\[*y*|*x*\])²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si293.png), is expected to be large because the choice of the model was arbitrary, without paying attention to the training data.

In the sequel, we go to the other “extreme.” We choose a relatively complex class of functions, such as a high-order (10th-order) polynomial *f*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si294.png). The dependence of the resulting estimates on the respective set 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si273.png), which is used for training, is explicitly denoted as *f*[2](⋅;𝒟)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si295.png). Note that for each one of the sets, the corresponding graph of the resulting optimal model is expected to go through the training points, i.e.,

*f*[2](*x*[*n*]; 𝒟[*i*]) = *g*(*x*[*n*]) + *η*[*n*, *i*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si296.png)

This is shown in [Fig. 3.7](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0045) for one curve. Note that, in general, this is always the case if the order of the polynomial (model) is large and the number of parameters to be estimated is larger than the number of training points. For the example shown in the figure, we are given 10 training points and 11 parameters have to be estimated, for a 10th-order polynomial (including the bias). One can obtain a perfect fit on the training points by solving a linear system comprising 10 equations (*N* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si287.png)) with 11 unknowns. This is the reason that when the order of the model is large, a *zero* (or very small, in practice) error can be achieved on the training data set. We will come back to this issue in Section [3.13](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#s0105).

For this high-order polynomial fitting setup of the experiment, the following reasoning holds true. The bias term at each point *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si281.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), is zero, because

𝔼[𝒟]\[*f*[2](*x*[*n*];𝒟)\] = 𝔼[𝒟]\[*g*(*x*[*n*])+*η*\] = *g*(*x*[*n*]) = 𝔼[𝒟]\[*y*|*x*[*n*]\].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si297.png)

On the other hand, the variance term at the points *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si281.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si3.png), is expected to be large, because

𝔼[𝒟] \[(*f*[2](*x*[*n*];𝒟)−*g*(*x*[*n*]))²\] = 𝔼[𝒟] \[(*g*(*x*[*n*])+*η*−*g*(*x*[*n*]))²\] = *σ*[*η*]².<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si298.png)

Assuming that the functions *f*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si294.png) and *g* are continuous and smooth enough and the points *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si281.png) are sampled densely enough to cover the interval of interest in the real axis, we expect similar behavior at all points *x* ≠ *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si299.png).

Example 3.6

This is a more realistic example that builds upon the previous one. The data are generated as before, via the regression model in Eq. [(3.54)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#deq93) using the fifth-order polynomial for *g*. The number of training points is equal to *N* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si287.png) and 1000 training sets 𝒟[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si127.png), *i* = 1, 2…, 1000<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si300.png), are generated. Two sets of experiments have been run.

The first one attempts to fit in the noisy data a high-order polynomial of degree equal to 10 (as in the previous example) and the second one adopts a second-order polynomial. For each one of the two setups, the experiment is repeated 1000 times, each time with a different data set 𝒟[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si127.png). [Figs. 3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0050)A and C show 10 (for visibility reasons) out of the 1000 resulting curves for the high- and low-order polynomials, respectively. The substantially higher variance for the case of the high-order polynomial is readily noticed. [Figs. 3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0050)B and D show the corresponding curves which result from averaging over the 1000 performed experiments, together with the graph of the “unknown” (original *g*) function. The high-order polynomial results in an excellent fit of very low bias. The opposite is true for the case of the second-order polynomial.

![Figure 3.8 (A) Ten of the resulting curves from fitting a 10th-order polynomial. (B) The corresponding average over 1000 different experiments. The red curve represents the unknown polynomial. The dots indicate the points that give birth to the training data, as described in the text. (C), (D) The results from fitting a second-order polynomial. Observe the bias–variance tradeoff as a function of the complexity of the fitted model.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr008.jpg)

Figure 3.8 (A) Ten of the resulting curves from fitting a 10th-order polynomial. (B) The corresponding average over 1000 different experiments. The red curve represents the unknown polynomial. The dots indicate the points that give birth to the training data, as described in the text. (C), (D) The results from fitting a second-order polynomial. Observe the bias–variance tradeoff as a function of the complexity of the fitted model.

Thus, in summary, for a fixed number of training points, the more complex the prediction model is (larger number of parameters), the larger the variance becomes, as we change from one training set to another. On the other hand, the more complex the model is, the smaller the bias gets; that is, the average model by training over different data sets gets closer to the optimal MSE one. The reader may find more information on the bias–variance dilemma task in \[16\]. 

## 3.10 Maximum likelihood method

So far, we have approached the estimation problem as an optimization task around a set of training examples, without paying any attention to the underlying statistics that generates these points. We only used statistics in order to check under which conditions the estimators were efficient. However, the optimization step did not involve any statistical information. For the rest of the chapter, we are going to involve statistics more and more. In this section, the *maximum likelihood* (ML) method is introduced. It is not an exaggeration to say that ML and LS are two of the major pillars on which parameter estimation is based and new methods are inspired from. The ML method was suggested by Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher.

Once more, we will first formulate the method in a general setting, independent of the regression/classification tasks. We are given a set of, say, *N* observations, 𝒳 = {**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si157.png), drawn from a probability distribution. We assume that the joint PDF of these *N* observations is of a known parametric functional type, denoted as *p*(𝒳; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si301.png), where the parameter vector **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si302.png) is unknown and the task is to estimate its value. This joint PDF is known as the *likelihood function* of ***θ*** with respect to the given set of observations 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si189.png). According to the ML method, the estimate is provided by

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/fx006.jpg)(3.55) 

For simplicity, we will assume that the constraint set, 𝒜<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si19.png), coincides with ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si20.png), i.e., 𝒜 = ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si51.png), and that the parameterized family {*p*(𝒳; **θ**) : **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*K*)}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si303.png) enjoys a unique minimizer with respect to the parameter ***θ***. This is illustrated in [Fig. 3.9](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#f0055). In other words, given the set of observations 𝒳 = {**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si157.png), one selects the unknown parameter vector so as to make this joint event the most likely one to happen.

![Figure 3.9 According to the maximum likelihood method, we assume that, given the set of observations, the estimate of the unknown parameter is the value that maximizes the corresponding likelihood function.](images/B9780443292385000093/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 3.9](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#cf0810) According to the maximum likelihood method, we assume that, given the set of observations, the estimate of the unknown parameter is the value that maximizes the corresponding likelihood function.

Because the logarithmic function ln ( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si305.png) is monotone and increasing, one can instead search for the maximum of the *log-likelihood function*,

$\\left. \\frac{\\partial\\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\theta})}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right|\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} = {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{ML}}} = 0.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>ML</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si306.png)(3.56) 

Assuming the observations to be i.i.d., the ML estimator has some very attractive properties, namely:

*   •  The ML estimator is asymptotically unbiased; that is, assuming that the model of the PDF, which we have adopted, is correct and there exists a true parameter **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si153.png), we have

$\\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{ML}} \\right\\rbrack = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>ML</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si308.png)(3.57) 

*   
*   •  The ML estimator is asymptotically *consistent* so that given any value of *ϵ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si309.png),

$\\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}{Prob}\\ \\left\\{ \\left| {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{ML}} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o} \\right| > \\epsilon \\right\\} = 0,$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prob</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>ML</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si310.png)(3.58) 

*   that is, for large values of *N*, we expect the ML estimate to be very close to the true value with high probability.
*   •  The ML estimator is asymptotically efficient; that is, it achieves the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
*   •  If there exists a sufficient statistic *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) for an unknown parameter, then only *T*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si187.png) suffices to express the respective ML estimate (Problem [3.20](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0105)).
*   •  Moreover, assuming that an efficient estimator does exist, this estimator is optimal in the ML sense (Problem [3.21](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml#o0110)).

Example 3.7

Let **x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000093/si311.png) be the observation vectors stemming from a multivariate normal distribution with known covariance matrix and unknown mean (Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)), that is,

$p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\mu}) = \\frac{1}{{(2\\pi)}^{l/2}|\\Sigma|^{1/2}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}{(\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\mu})}^{T}\\Sigma^{- 1}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\mu}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" Assume that the observations are mutually independent. Obtain the ML estimate of the unknown mean vector.

For the *N* statistically independent observations, the joint log-likelihood function is given by

$L(\\mathbf{\\mu}) = \\ln\\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\mu}) = - \\frac{N}{2}\\ln\\left( {(2\\pi)}^{l}|\\Sigma| \\right) - \\frac{1}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}{(\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\mu})}^{T}\\Sigma^{- 1}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\mu}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi \\frac{\\partial L}{\\partial\\mu\_{l}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\Sigma^{- 1}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n} -
