mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si19.png)(4.9) 

is the minimum achieved at the optimal solution. From Eqs. [(4.8)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq11) and [(4.9)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq12), the following remarks can be made.

Remarks 4.1

*   •  The cost at the optimal value **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si18.png) is always less than the variance 𝔼\[*y*²\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si20.png) of the output variable. This is guaranteed by the positive definite nature of *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si15.png) or *Σ*[*x*]^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si21.png), which makes the second term on the right-hand side in Eq. [(4.9)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq12) always positive, unless **p** = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si22.png); however, the cross-correlation vector will only be zero if **x** and y are uncorrelated. Well, in this case, one cannot say anything (make any prediction) about y by observing samples of **x**, at least as far as the MSE criterion is concerned, which turns out to involve information residing up to the second-order statistics. In this case, the variance of the error, which coincides with *J*(**θ**[\*])<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si23.png), will be equal to the variance *σ*[*y*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si24.png); the latter is a measure of the “intrinsic” uncertainty of y around its (zero) mean value. On the contrary, if the input–output variables are correlated, then observing **x** removes part of the uncertainty associated with y.
*   •  For any value ***θ*** other than the optimal **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si18.png), the error variance increases as Eq. [(4.8)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq11) suggests, due to the positive definite nature of *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si15.png). [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0010) shows the cost function (MSE) surface defined by *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si10.png) in Eq. [(4.8)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq11). The corresponding isovalue contours are shown in [Fig. 4.2](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0015). In general, they are ellipses, whose axes are determined by the eigenstructure of *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si15.png). For *Σ*[*x*] = *σ*²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si26.png), where all eigenvalues are equal to *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si27.png), the contours are circles (Problem [4.3](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0020)).

![Figure 4.1 The MSE cost function has the form of a (hyper)paraboloid.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr001.jpg)

Figure 4.1 The MSE cost function has the form of a (hyper)paraboloid.

![Figure 4.2 The isovalue contours for the cost function surface corresponding to Fig. 4.1. They are ellipses; the major and the minor axes of each ellipse are determined by the maximum and minimum eigenvalues, λmax and λmin, of the covariance matrix, Σ, of the input random variables. The largest the ratio \\frac{\\lambda\_{\\text{max}}}{\\lambda\_{\\text{min}}}Equation is, the more elongated the ellipses are. The ellipses become circles if the covariance matrix has the special form of σ2I. That is, all variables are mutually uncorrelated and they have the same variance. By varying Σ, different shapes of the ellipses and different orientations result.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr002.jpg)

[Figure 4.2](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#cf0215) The isovalue contours for the cost function surface corresponding to [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0010). They are ellipses; the major and the minor axes of each ellipse are determined by the maximum and minimum eigenvalues, *λ*[max] and *λ*[min], of the covariance matrix, *Σ*, of the input random variables. The largest the ratio $\\frac{\\lambda\_{\\text{max}}}{\\lambda\_{\\text{min}}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si28.png) is, the more elongated the ellipses are. The ellipses become circles if the covariance matrix has the special form of *σ*²*I*. That is, all variables are mutually uncorrelated and they have the same variance. By varying *Σ*, different shapes of the ellipses and different orientations result.

*   

## 4.3 A geometric viewpoint: orthogonality condition

A very intuitive view of what we have said so far comes from the geometric interpretation of the random variables. The reader can easily check out that the set of random variables is a *linear space* over the field of real (and complex) numbers. Indeed, if x and y are any two random variables then *x* + *y*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si29.png), as well as *α**x*<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si30.png), are also random variables for every *α* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si31.png).^([^(18)](#fn18))

*   •  𝔼\[*x**y*\] = 𝔼\[*y**x*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">xy</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">yx</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si32.png),
*   •  𝔼\[(*α*[1]*x*[1] + *α*[2]*x*[2])*y*\] = *α*[1]𝔼\[*x*[1]*y*\] + *α*[2]𝔼\[*x*[2]*y*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si33.png),
*   •  𝔼\[*x*²\] ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si34.png), with equality if and only if *x* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si35.png).

Thus, the norm induced by this inner product,

$\\| x\\|: = \\sqrt{\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack x^{2}\\rbrack},$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si36.png)

coincides with the respective standard deviation (assuming 𝔼\[*x*\] = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si37.png)). From now on, given two uncorrelated random variables *x*, *y*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si38.png), or 𝔼\[*x**y*\] = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">xy</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si39.png), we can call them *orthogonal*, because their inner product is zero. We are now free to apply to our task of interest the orthogonality theorem, which is known to us from our familiar finite-dimensional (Euclidean) linear (vector) spaces.

Let us now rewrite Eq. [(4.1)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq2) as

*ŷ* = *θ*[1]*x*[1] + ⋯ + *θ*[*l*]*x*[*l*].<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si40.png)

Thus, the random variable, *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si41.png), which is now interpreted as a point in a vector space, results as a linear combination of *l* elements in this space. Thus, the variable *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si41.png) will necessarily lie in the subspace spanned by these points. In contrast, the true variable, y, will not lie, in general, in this subspace. Because our goal is to obtain a *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si41.png) that is a good approximation of y, we have to seek the specific linear combination that makes the norm of the error, *e* = *y* − *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si42.png), minimum. This specific linear combination corresponds to the *orthogonal* projection of y onto the subspace spanned by the points *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si43.png). This is equivalent to requiring

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx003.jpg)(4.10) 

The error variable being orthogonal to every point *x*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si44.png), will be orthogonal to the respective subspace. This is illustrated in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0020). Such a choice guarantees that the resulting error will have the minimum norm; by the definition of the norm, this corresponds to the minimum MSE, i.e., to the minimum 𝔼\[*e*²\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si45.png).

![Figure 4.3 Projecting y on the subspace spanned by x1,x2 (shaded plane) guarantees that the deviation between y and \\widehat{y}Equation corresponds to the minimum MSE.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 4.3](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#cf0240) Projecting y on the subspace spanned by x[1],x[2] (shaded plane) guarantees that the deviation between y and *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si41.png) corresponds to the minimum MSE.

The set of equations in [(4.10)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq15) can now be written as

$\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\left( y - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\theta\_{i}x\_{i} \\right)x\_{k} \\right\\rbrack = 0,\\quad k = 1,2,\\ldots,l,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si46.png)

or

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack x\_{i}x\_{k}\\rbrack\\theta\_{i} = \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack x\_{k}y\\rbrack,\\quad k = 1,2,\\ldots,l,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si47.png)(4.11) 

which leads to Eq. [(4.5)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq7).

This is the reason that this elegant set of equations is known as *normal equations*. Another name is *Wiener–Hopf equations*. Strictly speaking, the Wiener–Hopf equations were first derived for continuous-time processes in the context of the causal estimation task \[49,50\]; for a discussion see \[16,44\].

Nobert Wiener (1894–1964) was a mathematician and philosopher. He was awarded a PhD at Harvard at the age of 17 in mathematical logic. During the Second World War, he laid the foundations of linear estimation theory in a classified work, independently of Kolmogorov. Later on, Wiener was involved in pioneering work embracing automation, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science. Being a pacifist, he was regarded with suspicion during the Cold War years.

The other pillar on which linear estimation theory is based is the pioneering work of Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov (1903–1987) \[24\], who developed his theory independent of Wiener. Kolmogorov's contributions cover a wide range of topics in mathematics, including probability, computational complexity, and topology. He is the father of the modern axiomatic foundation of the notion of probability (see Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)).

Remarks 4.2

*   •  So far, in our theoretical findings, we have assumed that **x** and y are jointly distributed (correlated) variables. If, in addition, we assume that they are linearly related according to the linear regression model,

*y* = **θ**[*o*]^(*T*)**x** + *η*, **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(*k*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si48.png)(4.12) 

*   where η is a zero mean noise variable independent of **x**, then, if the dimension *k* of the true system **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si49.png) is equal to the number of parameters, *l*, adopted for the model, so that *k* = *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si50.png), then it turns out that (Problem [4.4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0025))

**θ**[\*] = **θ**[*o*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si51.png)

*   and the optimal MSE is equal to the variance of the noise, *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si506.png).
*   •  *Undermodeling*. If *k* > *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si53.png), then the order of the model is less than that of the true system, which relates y and **x** in Eq. [(4.12)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq18); this is known as *undermodeling*. It is easy to show that if the variables comprising **x** are uncorrelated, then (Problem [4.5](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0030))

**θ**[\*] = **θ**[*o*]¹,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si54.png)

*   where

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}: = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}^{1} \\\\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}^{2} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},\\quad\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}^{1} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l},\\quad\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}^{2} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{k - l}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si55.png)

*   In other words, the MSE-optimal estimator identifies the first *l* components of **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si56.png).

## 4.4 Extension to complex-valued variables

Everything that has been said so far can be extended to complex-valued variables. However, there are a few subtle points involved, and this is the reason that we chose to treat this case separately. Complex-valued variables are very common in a number of applications, as for example in communications, e.g., \[41\].

Given two real-valued variables, (*x*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si57.png), one can either consider them as a vector quantity in the two-dimensional space, \[*x*, *y*\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si58.png), or describe them as a complex variable, *z* = *x* + *j**y*<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si59.png), where *j*² :  =  − 1<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si60.png). Adopting the latter approach offers the luxury of exploiting the operations available in the field ℂ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si61.png) of complex numbers, i.e., multiplication and division. The existence of such operations greatly facilitates the algebraic manipulations. Recall that such operations are not defined in vector spaces.^([^(19)](#fn19))

Let us assume that we are given a complex-valued (output) random variable

*y* :  = *y*[*r*] + *j**y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si63.png)(4.13) 

and a complex-valued (input) random vector

**x** = **x**[*r*] + *j***x**[*i*].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si64.png)(4.14) 

The quantities *y*[*r*], *y*[*i*], **x**[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si65.png), and **x**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si66.png) are real-valued random variables/vectors. The goal is to compute a linear estimator defined by a complex-valued parameter vector **θ** = **θ**[*r*] + *j***θ**[*i*] ∈ ℂ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si67.png), so as to minimize the respective MSE,

𝔼 \[|*e*|²\] :  = 𝔼 \[*e**e*^(\*)\] = 𝔼 \[|*y*−**θ**^(*H*)**x**|²\].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si68.png)(4.15) 

Looking at Eq. [(4.15)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq24), it is readily observed that in the case of complex variables the inner product operation between two complex-valued random variables should be defined as 𝔼\[*x**y*^(\*)\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si69.png), so as to guarantee that the implied norm by the inner product, $\\| x\\| = \\sqrt{\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack xx^{\\ast}\\rbrack}$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si70.png), is a valid quantity. Applying the orthogonality condition as before, we rederive the normal equations as in Eq. [(4.11)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq17),

*Σ*[*x*]**θ**[\*] = **p**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si71.png)(4.16) 

where now the covariance matrix and cross-correlation vector are given by

*Σ*[*x*] = 𝔼 \[**x****x**^(*H*)\],<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si72.png)(4.17) 

**p** = 𝔼 \[**x***y*^(\*)\].<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si73.png)(4.18) 

Note that Eqs. [(4.16)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq25)–[(4.18)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq27) can alternatively be obtained by minimizing Eq. [(4.15)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq24) (Problem [4.6](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0035)). Moreover, the counterpart of Eq. [(4.9)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq12) is given by

*J*(**θ**[\*]) = *σ*[*y*]² − **p**^(*H*)*Σ*[*x*]^( − 1)**p** = *σ*[*y*]² − **p**^(*H*)**θ**[\*].<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si74.png)(4.19) 

Using the definitions in Eqs. [(4.13)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq22) and [(4.14)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq23), the cost in Eq. [(4.15)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq24) is written as

*J*(**θ**) = 𝔼\[|*e*|²\] = 𝔼\[|*y* − *ŷ*|²\] = 𝔼\[|*y*[*r*] − *ŷ*[*r*]|²\] + 𝔼\[|*y*[*i*] − *ŷ*[*i*]|²\],<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0002" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi or

*ŷ* = (**θ**[*r*]^(*T*) − *j***θ**[*i*]^(*T*))(**x**[*r*] + *j***x**[*i*]) = (**θ**[*r*]^(*T*)**x**[*r*] + **θ**[*i*]^(*T*)**x**[*i*]) + *j*(**θ**[*r*]^(*T*)**x**[*i*] − **θ**[*i*]^(*T*)**x**[*r*]).<mml:math><mml:mover Eq. [(4.22)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq31) reveals the true flavor behind the complex notation; that is, its *multichannel* nature. In multichannel estimation, we are given more than one set of input variables, namely, **x**[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si77.png) and **x**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si66.png), and we want to generate, jointly, more than one output variable, namely, *ŷ*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si78.png) and *ŷ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si79.png). Eq. [(4.22)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq31) can equivalently be written as

$\\begin{bmatrix} {\\widehat{y}}\_{r} \\\\ {\\widehat{y}}\_{i} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\Theta\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{x}\_{r} \\\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{i} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si80.png)(4.23) 

where

$\\Theta: = \\begin{bmatrix} {\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{r}^{T}\\ } & \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{T} \\\\ {- \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{T}\\ } & \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{r}^{T} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si81.png)(4.24) 

Multichannel estimation can be generalized to more than two outputs and to more than two input sets of variables. We will come back to the more general multichannel estimation task toward the end of this chapter.

Looking at Eqs. [(4.23)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq32) and [(4.24)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq33), we observe that starting from the direct generalization of the linear estimation task for real-valued signals, which led to the adoption of *ŷ* = **θ**^(*H*)**x**<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si82.png), resulted in a matrix, Θ, of a *very special structure*.

### 4.4.1 Widely linear complex-valued estimation

Let us define the linear two-channel estimation task starting from the definition of a linear operation in vector spaces. The task is to generate a vector output, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = {\\lbrack{\\widehat{y}}\_{r},{\\widehat{y}}\_{i}\\rbrack}^{T} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" Minimizing Eq. [(4.27)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq36) is equivalent to minimizing the two terms individually; in other words, treating each channel separately (Problem [4.7](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0040)). Thus, the task can be tackled by solving two sets of normal equations, namely,

$\\Sigma\_{\\varepsilon}\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{11} \\\\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{12} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\mathbf{p}\_{r},\\quad\\Sigma\_{\\varepsilon}\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{21} \\\\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{22} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\mathbf{p}\_{i},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ε</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ε</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>21</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

$\\mathbf{p}\_{r}: = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\begin{bmatrix} {\\mathbf{x}\_{r}y\_{r}} \\\\ {\\mathbf{x}\_{i}y\_{r}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},\\quad\\mathbf{p}\_{i}: = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\begin{bmatrix} linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si92.png)(4.30) 

The obvious question that is now raised is whether we can tackle this more general task of the two-channel linear estimation task by employing complex-valued arithmetic. The answer is in the affirmative. Let us define

**θ** :  = **θ**[*r*] + *j***θ**[*i*], **v** :  = **v**[*r*] + *j***v**[*i*],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si93.png)(4.31) 

and

**x** = **x**[*r*] + *j***x**[*i*].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si64.png)

Then we define

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{r}: = \\frac{1}{2}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{11} + \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{22}),\\quad\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}: = \\frac{1}{2}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{12} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{21})$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>21</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si95.png)(4.32) 

and

$\\mathbf{v}\_{r}: = \\frac{1}{2}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{11} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{22}),\\quad\\mathbf{v}\_{i}: = - \\frac{1}{2}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{12} + \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{21}).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>21</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si96.png)(4.33) 

Under the previous definitions, it is a matter of simple algebra (Problem [4.8](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0045)) to prove that the set of equations in [(4.25)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq34) is equivalent to

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx005.jpg)(4.34) 

To distinguish from Eq. [(4.21)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq30), this is known as *widely linear* complex-valued estimator. Note that in Eq. [(4.34)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq46), **x** and its complex conjugate **x**^(\*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si97.png) are *simultaneously* used in order to cover all possible solutions, as those are dictated by the vector space description, which led to the formulation in Eq. [(4.25)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq34).

#### Circularity conditions

We now turn our attention to investigating conditions under which the widely linear formulation in Eq. [(4.34)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq46) breaks down to Eq. [(4.21)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq30); that is, the conditions for which the optimal widely linear estimator turns out to have **v** = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si98.png).

Let

$\\mathbf{\\varphi}: = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\theta} \\\\ \\mathbf{v} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}\\quad{and}\\quad\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}: = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{x} \\\\ \\mathbf{x}^{\\ast} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">and</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si99.png)(4.35) 

Then the widely linear estimator is written as

$\\widehat{y} = \\mathbf{\\varphi}^{H}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si100.png)

Adopting the orthogonality condition in its complex formulation

$\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}e^{\\ast} \\right\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}\\left( y - \\widehat{y} \\right)^{\\ast} \\right\\rbrack = 0,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si101.png)

we obtain the following set of normal equations for the optimal **φ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si102.png)

$\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}^{H} \\right\\rbrack\\mathbf{\\varphi}\_{\\ast} = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}^{H} \\right\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\\\ \\mathbf{v}\_{\\ast} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\begin{bmatrix} {\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\mathbf{x}y^{\\ast}\\rbrack} \\\\ {\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast}y^{\\ast}\\rbrack} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:mi The matrix *P*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si106.png) is known as the *pseudocovariance/autocorrelation* matrix of **x**. Note that Eq. [(4.36)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq51) is the equivalent of Eq. [(4.28)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq39); to obtain the widely linear estimator, one needs to solve one set of complex-valued equations whose number is double compared to that of the linear (complex) formulation.

Assume now that

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx006.jpg)(4.38) 

We say that in this case, the input–output variables are *jointly circular* and the input variables in **x** obey the (second-order) *circular* condition. It is readily observed that under the previous circularity assumptions, Eq. [(4.36)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq51) leads to **v**[\*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si107.png) and the optimal **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si18.png) is given by the set of normal equations given in Eqs. [(4.16)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq25)–[(4.18)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq27), which govern the more restricted linear case. Thus, adopting the linear formulation leads to optimality only under certain conditions, which do not always hold true in practice; typical examples of such variables, which do not respect circularity, are met in fMRI imaging (see \[1\] and the references therein). It can be shown that the MSE achieved by a widely linear estimator is always less than or equal to that obtained via a linear one (Problem [4.9](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0050)).

The notions of circularity and of the widely linear estimation were treated in a series of fundamental papers \[35,36\]. A stronger condition for circularity is based on the PDF of a complex random variable: A random variable x is circular (or strictly circular) if x and *x**e*^(*j**ϕ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si108.png) are distributed according to the same PDF; that is, the PDF is *rotationally invariant* \[35\]. [Fig. 4.4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0025)A shows the scatter plot of points generated by a circularly distributed variable, and [Fig. 4.4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0025)B corresponds to a noncircular one. Strict circularity implies the second-order circularity, but the converse is not always true. For more on complex random variables, the interested reader may consult \[3,37\]. In \[28\], it is pointed out that the full second-order statistics of the error, without doubling the dimension, can be achieved if instead of the MSE one employs the Gaussian entropy criterion.

![Figure 4.4 Scatter plots of points corresponding to (A) a circular process and (B) a noncircular one, in the two-dimensional space.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr004.jpg)

Figure 4.4 Scatter plots of points corresponding to (A) a circular process and (B) a noncircular one, in the two-dimensional space.

### 4.4.2 Optimizing with respect to complex-valued variables: Wirtinger calculus

So far, in order to derive the estimates of the parameters, for both the linear as well as the widely linear estimators, the orthogonality condition was mobilized. For the complex linear estimation case, the normal equations were derived in Problem [4.6](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0035), by direct minimization of the cost function in Eq. [(4.20)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq29). Those who got involved with solving the problem have experienced a procedure that was more cumbersome compared to the real-valued linear estimation. This is because one has to use the real and imaginary parts of all the involved complex variables and express the cost function in terms of the equivalent real-valued quantities *only*; then the required gradients for the optimization have to be performed. Recall that any complex function *f* : ℂ → ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si112.png) is not differentiable with respect to its complex argument, because the Cauchy–Riemann conditions are violated (Problem [4.11](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0060)). The previously stated procedure of splitting the involved variables into their real and imaginary parts can become cumbersome with respect to algebraic manipulations. Wirtinger calculus provides an equivalent formulation that is based on simple rules and principles, which bear a great resemblance to the rules of standard complex differentiation.

Let *f* : ℂ ↦ ℂ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si113.png) be a complex function defined on ℂ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si61.png). Obviously, such a function can be regarded as either defined on ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si114.png) or ℂ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si61.png) (i.e., *f*(*z*) = *f*(*x* + *j**y*) = *f*(*x*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si115.png)). Furthermore, it may be regarded as either complex-valued, *f*(*x*, *y*) = *f*[*r*](*x*, *y*) + *j**f*[*i*](*x*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si116.png), or as vector-valued *f*(*x*, *y*) = (*f*[*r*](*x*,*y*),*f*[*i*](*x*,*y*))<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si117.png). We say that *f* is *differentiable in the real sense* if both *f*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si118.png) and *f*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si119.png) are differentiable. Wirtinger's calculus considers the complex structure of *f* and the real derivatives are described using an equivalent formulation that greatly simplifies calculations; moreover, this formulation bears a surprising similarity to the complex derivatives.

Definition 4.1

The *Wirtinger derivative* or *W-derivative* of a complex function *f* at a point *z*[0] ∈ ℂ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si120.png) is defined as

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx007.jpg)

The *conjugate Wirtinger's derivative* or *CW-derivative* of *f* at *z*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si121.png) is defined as

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx008.jpg)

For some of the properties and the related proofs regarding Wirtinger's derivatives, see Appendix A.3. An important property for us is that if *f* is real-valued (i.e., ℂ ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si122.png)) and *z*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si121.png) is a (local) optimal point of *f*, it turns out that

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx009.jpg)(4.40) 

In order to apply Wirtinger's derivatives, the following simple *tricks* are adopted:

*   •  express function *f* in terms of *z and* *z*^(\*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si123.png);
*   •  to compute the W-derivative apply the usual differentiation rule, treating *z*^(\*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si123.png) as a constant;
*   •  to compute the CW-derivative apply the usual differentiation rule, treating *z* as a constant.

It should be emphasized that all these statements must be regarded as useful computational tricks rather than rigorous mathematical rules. Analogous definitions and properties carry on for complex vectors ***z***, and the W-gradient and CW-gradients

∇[**z**] *f*(**z**[0]), ∇[**z**^(\*)] *f*(**z**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si124.png)

result from the respective definitions if partial derivatives are replaced by partial gradients, ∇[**x**], ∇[**y**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si125.png).

Although Wirtinger's calculus has been known since 1927 \[51\], its use in applications has a rather recent history \[7\]. Its revival was ignited by the widely linear filtering concept \[27\]. The interested reader may obtain more on this issue from \[2,25,30\]. Extensions of Wirtinger's derivative to general Hilbert (infinite-dimensional) spaces was done more recently in \[6\] and to the subgradient notion in \[46\].

*Application in linear estimation*. The cost function in this case is

*J*(**θ**, **θ**^(\*)) = 𝔼 \[|*y*−**θ**^(*H*)**x**|²\] = 𝔼 \[(*y*−**θ**^(*H*)**x**)(*y*^(\*)−**θ**^(*T*)**x**^(\*))\].<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si126.png)

Thus, treating ***θ*** as a constant, the optimal occurs at

∇[**θ**^(\*)]*J* = 𝔼\[**x***e*^(\*)\] = 0,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si127.png)

which is the orthogonality condition leading to the normal equations [(4.16)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq25)–[(4.18)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq27).

*Application in widely linear estimation*. The cost function is now (see notation in Eq. [(4.35)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq47))
