$J(\\mathbf{\\varphi},\\mathbf{\\varphi}^{\\ast}) = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\left( y - \\mathbf{\\varphi}^{H}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}} \\right)\\left( y^{\\ast} - \\mathbf{\\varphi}^{T}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}^{\\ast} \\right) \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si128.png)

and treating ***φ*** as a constant,

$\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\varphi}^{\\ast}}J = \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}e^{\\ast} \\right\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\begin{bmatrix} {\\mathbf{x}e^{\\ast}} \\\\ {\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast}e^{\\ast}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = 0,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si129.png)

which leads to Eq. [(4.36)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq51).

Wirtinger's calculus will prove very useful in subsequent chapters for deriving gradient operations in the context of online/adaptive estimation in Euclidean as well as in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.

## 4.5 Linear filtering

Linear statistical filtering is an instance of the general estimation task, when the notion of time evolution needs to be taken into consideration and estimates are obtained at each time instant. There are three major types of problems that emerge:

*   •  *Filtering*, where the estimate at time instant *n* is based on all previously received (measured) input information *up to and including* the current time index, *n*.
*   •  *Smoothing*, where data over a discrete time set, {0, 1, …, *N*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si130.png) are first collected and an estimate is obtained at each time instant *n* ≤ *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si131.png), using *all* the available information corresponding to the time index set {0, 1, …, *N*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si130.png).
*   •  *Prediction*, where estimates at times *n* + *τ*, *τ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si132.png), are to be obtained based on the information up to and including time instant *n*.

To fit in the above definitions more with what has been said so far in the chapter, take for example a time-varying case, where the output variable at time instant *n* is *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png) and its value depends on observations included in the corresponding input vector **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si134.png). In filtering, the latter can include observations received only at time instants *n*, *n* − 1, …, 0<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si135.png). This restriction in the index set is directly related to *causality*. In contrast, in smoothing, future time instants are included in addition to the past, i.e., …, *n* + 2, *n* + 1, *n*, *n* − 1, …<mml:math><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si136.png).

Most of the effort in this book will be spent on filtering whenever time information enters into the picture. The reason is that this is the most commonly encountered task and, also, the techniques used for smoothing and prediction are similar in nature to that of filtering, with usually minor modifications.

In signal processing, the term filtering is usually used in a more specific context, and it refers to the operation of a *filter*, which acts on an input random process/signal (*u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png)), to transform it into another one (*d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png)); see Section [2.4.3](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml). Note that we have switched into the notation, introduced in Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml), used to denote random processes. We prefer to keep different notation for processes and random variables, because in the case of random processes, the filtering task obtains a special structure and properties, as we will soon see. Moreover, although the mathematical formulation of the involved equations, for both cases, may end up to be the same, we feel that it is good for the reader to keep in mind that there is a different underlying mechanism for generating the data.

The task in statistical linear filtering is to compute the coefficients (impulse response) of the filter so that the output process of the filter, *d̂*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si139.png), when the filter is excited by the input random process, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png), is as close as possible to a (target) *desired* response process, *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png). In other words, the goal is to minimize, in some sense, the corresponding error process (see [Fig. 4.5](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0030)).  Assuming that the unknown filter is of a finite impulse response (FIR) (see Section [2.4.3](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml) for related definitions), denoted as *w*[0], *w*[1], …, *w*[*l* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si141.png), the output *d̂*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si139.png) of the filter is given as

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx010.jpg)(4.41) 

where

**w** = \[*w*[0], *w*[1], …, *w*[*l* − 1]\]^(*T*) and **u**[*n*] = \[*u*[*n*], *u*[*n* − 1], …, *u*[*n* − *l* + 1]\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si143.png)(4.42) 

![Figure 4.5 In statistical filtering, the impulse response coefficients are estimated so as to minimize the error between the output and the desired response processes. In MSE linear filtering, the cost function is \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack e\_{n}^{2}\\rbrackEquation.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 4.5](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#cf0565) In statistical filtering, the impulse response coefficients are estimated so as to minimize the error between the output and the desired response processes. In MSE linear filtering, the cost function is 𝔼\[*e*[*n*]²\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si140.png).

[Fig. 4.6](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0035) illustrates the convolution operation of the linear filter, when its input is excited by a realization *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si144.png) of the input process to provide in the output the signal/sequence *d̂*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si145.png).

![Figure 4.6 The linear filter is excited by a realization of an input process. The output signal is the convolution between the input sequence and the filter's impulse response.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 4.6](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#cf0570) The linear filter is excited by a realization of an input process. The output signal is the convolution between the input sequence and the filter's impulse response.

Alternatively, Eq. [(4.41)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq63) can be viewed as a *linear* estimator function; given the jointly distributed variables, at time instant *n*, (*d*[*n*], **u**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si146.png), Eq. [(4.41)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq63) provides the estimator, *d̂*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si139.png), given the values of **u**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si147.png). In order to obtain the coefficients, ***w***, the MSE criterion will be adopted. Furthermore, we will assume that:

*   •  The processes *u*[*n*], *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si148.png) are *wide-sense stationary* real random processes (Section [2.4](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)).
*   •  Their mean values are equal to zero, in other words, 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]\] = 𝔼\[*d*[*n*]\] = 0, ∀*n*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si149.png). If this is not the case, we can subtract the respective mean values from the processes, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png) and *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png), during a preprocessing stage. Due to this assumption, the autocorrelation and covariance matrices of **u**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si147.png) coincide, so that

*R*[*u*] = *Σ*[*u*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si151.png)

*   

The normal equations in [(4.5)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq7) now take the form

*Σ*[*u*]**w** = **p**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si152.png)

where

**p** = \[𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*d*[*n*]\],…,𝔼\[*u*[*n* − *l* + 1]*d*[*n*]\]\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si153.png)

and the respective covariance/autocorrelation matrix, of order *l*, of the input process is given by

$\\Sigma\_{u}: = \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{u}\_{n}\\mathbf{u}\_{n}^{T} \\right\\rbrack = \\begin{bmatrix} {r(0)} & {r(1)} & \\ldots & {r(l - 1)} \\\\ {r(1)} & {r(0)} & \\ldots & {r(l - 2)} \\\\ \\vdots & & \\ddots & \\\\ {r(l - 1)} & {r(l - 2)} & \\ldots & {r(0)} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋱</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si154.png)(4.43) 

where *r*(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si155.png) is the autocorrelation sequence of the input process. Because we have assumed that the involved processes are wide-sense stationary, we have

*r*(*n*, *n* − *k*) :  = 𝔼\[*u*[*n*]*u*[*n* − *k*]\] = *r*(*k*).<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si156.png)

Also, recall that, for real wide-sense stationary processes, the autocorrelation sequence is symmetric, or *r*(*k*) = *r*( − *k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si157.png) (Section [2.4.3](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)). Observe that in this case, where the input vector results from a random process, the covariance matrix has a special structure, which will be exploited later on to derive efficient schemes for the solution of the normal equations.

For the complex linear filtering case, the only differences are:

*   •  the output is given as *d̂*[*n*] = **w**^(*H*)**u**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si158.png),
*   •  **p** = 𝔼\[**u**[*n*]*d*[*n*]^(\*)\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si159.png),
*   •  *Σ*[*u*] = 𝔼\[**u**[*n*]**u**[*n*]^(*H*)\]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si160.png),
*   •  *r*( − *k*) = *r*^(\*)(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si161.png).

## 4.6 MSE linear filtering: a frequency domain point of view

Let us now turn our attention to the more general case, and assume that our filter is of *infinite impulse response* (IIR). Then Eq. [(4.41)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq63) becomes

${\\widehat{d}}\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}w\_{i}u\_{n - i}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si162.png)(4.44) 

Moreover, we have allowed the filter to be *noncausal*.^([^(20)](#fn20))

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx011.jpg)(4.45) 

Observe that this is a generalization (involving an infinite number of terms) of the orthogonality condition stated in Eq. [(4.10)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq15). A rearrangement of the terms in Eq. [(4.45)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq71) results in

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}w\_{i}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack u\_{n - i}u\_{n - j}\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack d\_{n}u\_{n - j}\\rbrack,\\ j \\in \\mathbb{Z},$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si166.png)(4.46) 

and finally to

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}w\_{i}r(j - i) = r\_{du}(j),\\ j \\in \\mathbb{Z},$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si167.png)(4.47) 

where *r*[*d**u*](*j*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si168.png) denotes the cross-correlation sequence between the processes *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png) and *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png). Eq. [(4.47)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq73) can be considered as the generalization of Eq. [(4.5)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq7) to the case of random processes. The problem now is how one can solve Eq. [(4.47)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq73) that involves infinite many parameters. The way out is to cross into the frequency domain. The left-hand side of Eq. [(4.47)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq73) can be seen as the convolution of the unknown sequence with the autocorrelation sequence of the input process, which gives rise to the cross-correlation sequence on its right-hand side. However, we know that convolution of two sequences corresponds to the product of the respective Fourier transforms (e.g., \[42\] and Section [2.4.3](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml). Thus, we can now write that

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx012.jpg)(4.48) 

where *W*(*ω*)<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si169.png) is the Fourier transform of the sequence of the unknown parameters and *S*[*u*](*ω*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si170.png) is the *power spectral density* of the input process, defined in Section [2.4.3](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml). In analogy, the Fourier transform *S*[*d**u*](*ω*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si171.png) of the cross-correlation sequence is known as the *cross-spectral density*. Once *W*(*ω*)<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si169.png) has been computed, the unknown parameters can be obtained via the inverse Fourier transform.

### Deconvolution: image deblurring

We will now consider an important application in order to demonstrate the power of MSE linear estimation. Image deblurring is a typical *deconvolution* task. An image is degraded due to its transmission via a nonideal system; the task of deconvolution is to optimally recover (in the MSE sense in our case) the original undegraded image. [Fig. 4.7](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0040)A shows the original image and [4.7](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0040)B a blurred version (e.g., taken by a nonsteady camera) with some small additive noise.

![Figure 4.7 (A) The original image and (B) its blurred and noisy version.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr007.jpg)

Figure 4.7 (A) The original image and (B) its blurred and noisy version.

At this point, it is interesting to recall that deconvolution is a process that our human brain performs all the time. The human (and not only) vision system is one of the most complex and highly developed biological systems that has been formed over millions years of a continuous evolution process. Any raw image that falls on the retina of the eye is *severely blurred*. Thus, one of the main early processing activities of our visual system is to deblur it (see, e.g., \[29\] and the references therein for a related discussion).

Before we proceed any further, the following assumptions are adopted:

*   •  The image is a *wide-sense stationary* two-dimensional random process. Two-dimensional random processes are also known as *random fields* (see Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml)).
*   •  The image is of an infinite extent; this can be justified for the case of large images. This assumption will grant us the “permission” to use Eq. [(4.48)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq74). The fact that an image is a two-dimensional process does not change anything in the theoretical analysis; the only difference is that now the Fourier transform involves two frequency variables, *ω*[1], *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si172.png), one for each of the two dimensions.

A gray image is represented as a two-dimensional array. To stay close to the notation used so far, let *d*(*n*, *m*), *n*, *m* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si173.png), be the original undegraded image (which for us is now the desired response), and *u*(*n*, *m*), *n*, *m* ∈ ℤ<mml:math><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si174.png), be the degraded one, obtained as

$u(n,m) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}\\sum\\limits\_{j = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}h(i,j)d(n - i,m - j) + \\eta(n,m),$<mml:math><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si175.png)(4.49) 

where *η*(*n*, *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si176.png) is the realization of a noise field, which is assumed to be zero mean and independent of the input (undegraded) image. The sequence *h*(*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si177.png) is the *point spread sequence* (impulse response) of the system (e.g., camera). We will assume that this is known and it has, somehow, been measured.^([^(21)](#fn21))

Our task now is to estimate a two-dimensional filter, *w*(*n*, *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si178.png), which is applied to the degraded image to optimally reconstruct (in the MSE sense) the original undegraded one. In the current context, Eq. [(4.48)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq74) is written as

*W*(*ω*[1], *ω*[2])*S*[*u*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2]) = *S*[*d**u*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2]).<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si179.png)

Following similar arguments as those used to derive Eq. [(2.130)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml) of Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml), it is shown that (Problem [4.13](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0070))

*S*[*d**u*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2]) = *H*^(\*)(*ω*[1], *ω*[2])*S*[*d*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si180.png)(4.50) 

and

*S*[*u*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2]) = |*H*(*ω*[1], *ω*[2])|²*S*[*d*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2]) + *S*[*η*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2]),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si181.png)(4.51) 

where “\*” denotes complex conjugation and *S*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si182.png) is the power spectral density of the noise field. Thus, we finally obtain

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/fx013.jpg)(4.52) 

Once *W*(*ω*[1], *ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si183.png) has been computed, the unknown parameters could be obtained via an inverse (two-dimensional) Fourier transform. The deblurred image then results as

$\\widehat{d}(n,m) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}\\sum\\limits\_{j = - \\infty}^{+ \\infty}w(i,j)u(n - i,m - j).$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si184.png)(4.53) 

In practice, because we are not really interested in obtaining the weights of the deconvolution filter, we implement Eq. [(4.53)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq80) in the frequency domain

*D̂*(*ω*[1], *ω*[2]) = *W*(*ω*[1], *ω*[2])*U*(*ω*[1], *ω*[2]),<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si185.png)

and then obtain the inverse Fourier transform. Thus all processing is efficiently performed in the frequency domain. Software packages to perform Fourier transforms (via the fast Fourier transform (FFT)) of an image array are “omnipresent” on the internet.

Another important issue is that in practice we do not know *S*[*d*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si186.png). An approximation which is usually adopted and renders sensible results can be made by assuming that $\\frac{S\_{\\eta}(\\omega\_{1},\\omega\_{2})}{S\_{d}(\\omega\_{1},\\omega\_{2})}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si187.png) is a constant, *C*, and trying different values of it. [Fig. 4.8](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0045) shows the deblurred image for *C* = 2.3 × 10^( − 6)<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si188.png). The quality of the end result depends a lot on the choice of this value (computer exercise [4.25](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#o0130)). Other, more advanced, techniques have also been proposed. For example, one can get a better estimate of *S*[*d*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si186.png) by using information from *S*[*η*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si190.png) and *S*[*u*](*ω*[1], *ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si191.png). The interested reader can obtain more on the image deconvolution/restoration task from, e.g., \[14,34\].

![Figure 4.8 (A) The original image and (B) the deblurred one for C = 2.3 × 10−6. Observe that in spite of the simplicity of the method, the reconstruction is pretty good. The differences become more obvious to the eye when the images are enlarged.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 4.8](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#cf0680) (A) The original image and (B) the deblurred one for *C* = 2.3 × 10^(−6). Observe that in spite of the simplicity of the method, the reconstruction is pretty good. The differences become more obvious to the eye when the images are enlarged.

## 4.7 Some typical applications

Optimal linear estimation/filtering has been applied in a wide range of diverse applications of statistical learning, such as regression modeling, communications, control, biomedical signal processing, seismic signal processing, and image processing. In the sequel, we present some typical applications in order for the reader to grasp the main rationale of how the previously stated theory can find its way in solving practical problems. In all cases, wide-sense stationarity of the involved random processes is assumed.

### 4.7.1 Interference cancellation

In interference cancellation, we have access to a mixture of two signals expressed as *d*[*n*] = *y*[*n*] + *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si192.png). Ideally, we would like to remove one of them, say, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si193.png). We will consider them as realizations of respective random processes/signals, or *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png), *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png), and *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si194.png). To achieve this goal, the only available information is another signal, say, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png), that is statistically related to the unwanted signal, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png). For example, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png) may be a filtered version of *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png). This is illustrated in [Fig. 4.9](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0050), where the corresponding realizations of the involved random processes are shown.

![Figure 4.9 A basic block diagram illustrating the interference cancellation task.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr009.jpg)

Figure 4.9 A basic block diagram illustrating the interference cancellation task.

Process *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png) is the output of an unknown system *H*, whose input is excited by *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png). The task is to model *H* by obtaining estimates of its impulse response (assuming that it is linear time-invariant and of known order). Then the output of the model will be an approximation of *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png) when this is activated by the same input, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png). We will use *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png) as the target/desired response process. The optimal estimates of *w*[0], …, *w*[*l* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si195.png) (assuming the order of the unknown system *H* to be *l*) are provided by the normal equations

*Σ*[*u*]**w**[\*] = **p**.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si196.png)

However,

**p** = 𝔼 \[**u**[*n*]*d*[*n*]\] = 𝔼 \[**u**[*n*](*y*[*n*]+*s*[*n*])\] = 𝔼 \[**u**[*n*]*y*[*n*]\],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo id="mmlbr0005" linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si197.png)(4.54) 

because the respective input vector **u**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si147.png) and *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si194.png) are considered statistically independent. That is, the previous formulation of the problem leads to the same normal equations as when the desired response was the signal *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png), which we want to remove! Hence, the output of our model will be an approximation (in the MSE sense), *ŷ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si199.png), of *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png), and if subtracted from *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si138.png) the resulting (error) signal *e*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si200.png) will be an approximation to *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si194.png). How good this approximation is depends on whether *l* is a good “estimate” of the true order of *H*. The cross-correlation in the right-hand side of Eq. [(4.54)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#deq83) can be approximated by computing the respective sample mean values, in particular over periods where *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si194.png) is absent. In practical systems, online/adaptive versions of this implementation are usually employed, as we will see in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml).

Interference cancellation schemes have been widely used in many systems such as noise cancellation, echo cancellation in telephone networks, and video conferencing, and in biomedical applications, for example, in order to cancel the maternal interference in a fetal electrocardiograph.

[Fig. 4.10](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0055) illustrates the echo cancellation task in a video conference application. The same setup applies to the hands-free telephone service in a car. The *far-end* speech signal is considered to be a realization *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si144.png) of a random process *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si137.png); through the loudspeakers, it is broadcasted in room A (car) and it is reflected in the interior of the room. Part of it is absorbed and part of it enters the microphone; this is denoted as *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si193.png). The equivalent response of the room (reflections) on *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si144.png) can be represented by a filter, *H*, as in [Fig. 4.9](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0050). Signal *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si193.png) returns back and the speaker in location B listens to her or his own voice, together with the *near-end* speech signal, *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si203.png), of the speaker in A. In certain cases, this feedback path from the loudspeakers to the microphone can cause instabilities, giving rise to a “howling” sound effect. The goal of the echo canceller is to optimally remove *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si193.png).

![Figure 4.10 The echo canceller is optimally designed to remove the part of the far-end signal, un, that interferes with the near-end signal, sn.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr010.jpg)

[Figure 4.10](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#cf0700) The echo canceller is optimally designed to remove the part of the far-end signal, *u*[*n*], that interferes with the near-end signal, *s*[*n*].

### 4.7.2 System identification

System identification is similar in nature to the interference cancellation task. Note that in [Fig. 4.9](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0050), one basically models the unknown system. However, the focus there was on replicating the output *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si133.png) and not on the system's impulse response.

In system identification, the aim is to model the impulse response of an unknown plant. To this end, we have access to its input signal as well as to a *noisy* version of its output. The task is to design a model whose impulse response approximates that of the unknown plant. To achieve this, we optimally design a linear filter whose input is the same signal as the one that activates the plant and its desired response is the noisy output of the plant (see [Fig. 4.11](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0060)). The associated normal equations are

*Σ*[*u*]**w**[\*] = 𝔼\[**u**[*n*]*d*[*n*]\] = 𝔼\[**u**[*n*]*y*[*n*]\] + 0,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si204.png)

assuming the noise *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si205.png) is statistically independent of **u**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si147.png). Thus, once more, the resulting normal equations are as if we had provided the model with a desired response equal to the noiseless output of the unknown plant, expressed as *d*[*n*] = *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si206.png). Hence, the impulse response of the model is estimated so that its output is close, in the MSE sense, to the true (noiseless) output of the unknown plant. System identification is of major importance in a number of applications. In control, it is used for driving the associated controllers. In data communications, it is used for estimating the transmission channel in order to build up maximum likelihood estimators of the transmitted data. In many practical systems, online versions of the system identification scheme are implemented, as we will discuss in following chapters.

![Figure 4.11 In system identification, the impulse response of the model is optimally estimated so that the output is close, in the MSE sense, to that of the unknown plant. The red line indicates that the error is used for the optimal estimation of the unknown parameters of the filter.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr011.jpg)

Figure 4.11 In system identification, the impulse response of the model is optimally estimated so that the output is close, in the MSE sense, to that of the unknown plant. The red line indicates that the error is used for the optimal estimation of the unknown parameters of the filter.

### 4.7.3 Deconvolution: channel equalization

Note that in the cancellation task the goal was to “remove” the (filtered version of the) input signal (*u*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si207.png) to the unknown system *H*. In system identification, the focus was on the (unknown) system itself. In *deconvolution*, the emphasis is on the input of the unknown system. That is, our goal now is to recover, in the MSE-optimal sense, a (delayed) input signal, *d*[*n*] = *s*[*n* − *L*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si208.png), where *L* is the delay in units of the sampling period *T*. The task is also called *inverse system identification*. The term *equalization* or *channel equalization* is used in communications. The deconvolution task was introduced in the context of image deblurring in Section [4.6](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#s0055). There, the required information about the *unknown* input process was obtained via an approximation. In the current framework, this can be approached via the transmission of a training sequence.

The goal of an *equalizer* is to recover the transmitted information symbols by mitigating the so-called *intersymbol interference* (ISI) that any (imperfect) dispersive communication channel imposes on the transmitted signal; besides ISI, additive noise is also present in the transmitted information bits (see [Example 4.2](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#enun0030)). Equalizers are “omnipresent” in these days; in our mobile phones, in our modems, etc. [Fig. 4.12](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0065) presents the basic scheme for an equalizer. The equalizer is trained so that its output is as close as possible to the transmitted data bits delayed by some time lag *L*; the delay is used in order to account for the overall delay imposed by the channel-equalizer system. Deconvolution/channel equalization is at the heart of a number of applications besides communications, such as acoustics, optics, seismic signal processing, and control. The channel equalization task will also be discussed in the next chapter in the context of online learning via the decision feedback equalization mode of operation.

![Figure 4.12 The task of an equalizer is to optimally recover the originally transmitted information sequence sn, delayed by L time lags.](images/B978044329238500010X/gr012.jpg)

Figure 4.12 The task of an equalizer is to optimally recover the originally transmitted information sequence *s*[*n*], delayed by *L* time lags.

Example 4.1

Noise cancellation

The noise cancellation application is illustrated in [Fig. 4.13](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml#f0070). The signal of interest is a realization of a process *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si194.png), which is contaminated by the noise process *v*[1](*n*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500010X/si209.png).
