## 5.1 Introduction

In Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml), we introduced the notion of mean-square error (MSE) optimal linear estimation and stated the normal equations for computing the parameters/coefficients of the optimal estimator/filter. A prerequisite for the normal equations is the knowledge of the second-order statistics of the involved processes/variables, so that the covariance matrix of the input and the input–output cross-correlation vector can be obtained. However, most often in practice, all the designer has at her/his disposal is a set of training samples; thus, the covariance matrix and the cross-correlation vector have to be estimated somehow. More importantly, in a number of practical applications, the underlying statistics may be time-varying. We discussed this scenario while introducing Kalman filtering. The path taken there was to adopt a state-space representation and assume that the time dynamics of the model were known. However, although Kalman filtering is an elegant tool, it does not scale well in high-dimensional spaces due to the involved matrix operations and inversions.

The focus of this chapter is to introduce *online learning* techniques for estimating the unknown parameter vector. These are time-iterative schemes, which update the available estimate every time a measurement set (input–output pair of observations) is acquired. Thus, in contrast to the so-called *batch processing* methods, which process the whole block of data as a single entity, online algorithms operate on a single data point at a time; therefore, such schemes do not require the training data set to be known and stored in advance. Online algorithmic schemes learn the underlying statistics from the data in a *time-iterative* fashion. Hence, one does not have to provide further statistical information. Another characteristic of the algorithmic family, to be developed and studied in this chapter, is its computational simplicity. The required complexity for updating the estimate of the unknown parameter vector is linear with respect to the number of the unknown parameters. This is one of the major reasons that have made such schemes very popular in a number of practical applications; besides complexity, we will discuss other reasons that have contributed to their popularity. A discussion concerning batch versus online algorithms is provided in Section [8.12](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml).

The fact that such learning algorithms work in a time-iterative mode gives them the agility to learn and *track* slow time variations of the statistics of the involved processes/variables; this is the reason these algorithms are also called *time-adaptive* or simply *adaptive*, because they can adapt to the needs of a changing environment. Online/time-adaptive algorithms have been used extensively since the early 1960s in a wide range of applications, including signal processing, control, and communications. More recently, the philosophy behind such schemes has been gaining in popularity in the context of applications where data reside in large datasets, with a massive number of samples; for such tasks, storing all the data points in the memory may not be possible, and they have to be considered one at a time. Moreover, the complexity of batch processing techniques can amount to prohibitive levels for today's technology. The current trend is to refer to such applications as *big data* problems.

In this chapter, we focus on a very popular class of online/adaptive algorithms that springs from the classical gradient descent method for optimization. Although our emphasis will be on the squared error loss function, the same rationale can also be adopted for other (differentiable) loss functions. The case of nondifferentiable loss functions will be treated in Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml).

The gradient descent concept is presented and the notion of stochastic approximation is introduced. Besides treating some classical members of this algorithmic family, such as the LMS, the APA, the NLMS, and the transform-domain LMS, the important issues related to convergence analysis and tracking performance of online algorithms in time-varying environments are also considered. Finally, the more recent trend of online distributed learning in graphs is introduced and some representative algorithms are presented. A case study related to the target localization task is considered at the end of the chapter. A number of algorithmic variants of the stochastic gradient family, in the context of deep neural networks, are given in Chapter [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml). The online processing rationale will be a recurrent theme in this book.

## 5.2 The steepest descent method

Our starting point is the method of *gradient descent*, one of the most widely used methods for iterative minimization of a differentiable cost function, *J*(**θ**), **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si1.png). As does any other iterative technique, the method starts from an initial estimate, **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si2.png), and generates a sequence, **θ**^((*i*)), *i* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si3.png), such that

**θ**^((*i*)) = **θ**^((*i* − 1)) + *μ*[*i*]*Δ***θ**^((*i*)), *i* > 0,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si4.png)(5.1) 

where *μ*[*i*] > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si5.png). All the schemes for the iterative minimization of a cost function, which we will deal with in this book, have the general form of Eq. [(5.1)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq1). Their differences are in the way that *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si6.png) and *Δ***θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si7.png) are selected; the latter vector is known as the *update direction* or the *search direction*. The sequence *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si6.png) is known as the *step size* or the *step length* at the *i*th iteration; note that the values of *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si6.png) may either be constant or change at each iteration. In the gradient descent method, the choice of *Δ***θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si7.png) is made to guarantee that

*J*(**θ**^((*i*))) < *J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1))),<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si9.png)

except at a minimizer, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si10.png).

Assume that at the (*i* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si11.png))th iteration step the value **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si12.png) has been obtained. Then, for sufficiently small *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si6.png) and mobilizing a first-order Taylor expansion around **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si12.png), we can write

*J*(**θ**^((*i*))) = *J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1))+*μ*[*i*]*Δ***θ**^((*i*))) ≈ *J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1))) + *μ*[*i*]∇*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))^(*T*)*Δ***θ**^((*i*)).<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo Looking carefully at the above approximation, what we basically do is to *linearize* locally the cost function with respect to *Δ***θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si7.png). Selecting the search direction so that

∇*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))^(*T*)*Δ***θ**^((*i*)) < 0,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si15.png)(5.2) 

this guarantees that *J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1))+*μ*[*i*]*Δ***θ**^((*i*))) < *J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si16.png).  For such a choice, *Δ***θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si7.png) and ∇*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si17.png) must form an *obtuse* angle. [Fig. 5.1](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0010) shows the graph of a cost function in the two-dimensional case, **θ**∈ ℝ²<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si18.png), and [Fig. 5.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0015) shows the respective isovalue contours in the two-dimensional plane. Note that, in general, the contours can have any shape and are not necessarily ellipses; it all depends on the functional form of *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si19.png). However, because *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si19.png) has been assumed differentiable, the contours must be smooth and accept at any point a (unique) tangent plane, as this is defined by the respective gradient. Furthermore, recall from basic calculus that the gradient vector, ∇*J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si21.png), is perpendicular to the plane (line) tangent to the corresponding isovalue contour at the point ***θ*** (Problem [5.1](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#o0010)).  The geometry is illustrated in [Fig. 5.3](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0020); to facilitate the drawing and unclutter notation, we have removed the iteration index *i*. Note that selecting the search direction which forms an obtuse angle with the gradient, it places **θ**^((*i* − 1)) + *μ*[*i*]*Δ***θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si22.png) at a point on a contour which corresponds to a lower value of *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si19.png). Two issues are now raised: (a) to choose the best search direction along which to move and (b) to compute how far along this direction one can go. Even without much mathematics, it is obvious from [Fig. 5.3](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0020) that if *μ*[*i*]||*Δ***θ**^((*i*))||<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si23.png) is too large, then the new point can be placed on a contour corresponding to a larger value than that of the current one; after all, the first-order Taylor expansion holds approximately true for small deviations from **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si12.png).

![Figure 5.1 A cost function in the two-dimensional parameter space.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr001.jpg)

Figure 5.1 A cost function in the two-dimensional parameter space.

![Figure 5.2 The corresponding isovalue curves of the cost function in Fig. 5.1, in the two-dimensional plane. All the points θ lying on the same (isovalue) ellipse score the same value for the cost J(θ). Note that as we move away from the optimal value, θ⁎, the values of c increase.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr002.jpg)

[Figure 5.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0235) The corresponding isovalue curves of the cost function in [Fig. 5.1](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0010), in the two-dimensional plane. All the points ***θ*** lying on the same (isovalue) ellipse score the same value for the cost *J*(***θ***). Note that as we move away from the optimal value, ***θ***[⁎], the values of *c* increase.

![Figure 5.3 The gradient vector at a point θ is perpendicular to the tangent plane (dotted line) at the isovalue curve crossing θ. The descent direction forms an obtuse angle, ϕ, with the gradient vector.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr003.jpg)

Figure 5.3 The gradient vector at a point ***θ*** is perpendicular to the tangent plane (dotted line) at the isovalue curve crossing ***θ***. The descent direction forms an obtuse angle, *ϕ*, with the gradient vector.

To address the first of the two issues, let us assume *μ*[*i*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si25.png) and search for all vectors, ***z***, with unit Euclidean norm and having their origin at **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si12.png). Then it does not take long to see that for all possible directions, the one that gives the most negative value of the inner product, ∇*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))^(*T*)**z**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si27.png), is that of the negative gradient

$\\mathbf{z} = - \\frac{\\nabla J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\left\\| \\nabla J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right) \\right\\|}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si28.png)

This is illustrated in [Fig. 5.4](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0025). Center the unit Euclidean norm ball at **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si12.png). Then from all the unit norm vectors having their origin at **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si12.png), choose the one pointing to the negative gradient direction. Thus, for all unit Euclidean norm vectors, the steepest descent direction coincides with the (negative) *gradient descent* direction, and the corresponding update recursion becomes

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx001.jpg)(5.3) 

Note that we still have to address the second point, concerning the choice of *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si6.png). The choice must be made in such a way to guarantee convergence of the minimizing sequence. We will come to this issue soon.

![Figure 5.4 From all the descent directions of unit Euclidean norm (dotted circle centered at θ(i−1), which for notational simplicity is shown as θ), the negative gradient one leads to the maximum decrease of the cost function.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 5.4](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0255) From all the descent directions of unit Euclidean norm (dotted circle centered at ***θ***^((*i*−1)), which for notational simplicity is shown as ***θ***), the negative gradient one leads to the maximum decrease of the cost function.

Iteration in Eq. [(5.3)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq6) is illustrated in [Fig. 5.5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0030) for the one-dimensional case. If at the current iteration the algorithm has “landed” at *θ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si29.png), then the derivative of *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si19.png) at this point is positive (the tangent of an acute angle, *ϕ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si30.png)), and this will force the update to move to the left toward the minimum. The scenario is different if the current estimate was *θ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si31.png). The derivative is negative (the tangent of an obtuse angle, *ϕ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si32.png)) and this will push the update to the right, toward, again, the minimum. Note, however, that it is important how far to the left or to the right one has to move. A large move from, say, *θ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si29.png) to the left may land the update on the other side of the optimal value. In such a case, the algorithm may oscillate around the minimum and never converge. A major effort in this chapter will be devoted in providing theoretical frameworks for establishing bounds for the values of the step size that guarantee convergence.

![Figure 5.5 Once the algorithm is at θ1, the gradient descent will move the point to the left, toward the minimum. The opposite is true for point θ2.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 5.5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0265) Once the algorithm is at *θ*[1], the gradient descent will move the point to the left, toward the minimum. The opposite is true for point *θ*[2].

The gradient descent method exhibits approximately *linear convergence*; that is, the error between **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si33.png) and the minimum converges to zero asymptotically in the form of a *geometric series*. However, the convergence rate depends heavily on the eigenvalue spread of the Hessian matrix of *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si19.png). The dependence of the convergence rate on the eigenvalues will be unraveled in Section [5.3](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#s0020). For large eigenvalue spreads, the rate of convergence can become extremely low. On the other hand, the great advantage of the method lies in its low computational requirements.

Finally, it has to be pointed out that we arrived at the scheme in Eq. [(5.3)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq6) by searching all directions via the unit Euclidean norm. However, there is nothing “sacred” around Euclidean norms. One can employ other norms, such as the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si34.png) and the *P*\-weighted, (**z**^(*T*)*P***z**)^(1/2)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si35.png), norms, where *P* is a positive definite matrix. Under such choices, one will end up with alternative update iterations (see, e.g., \[23\]). We will return to this point in Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml), when dealing with Newton's iterative and coordinate descent minimization schemes.

## 5.3 Application to the mean-square error cost function

Let us apply the gradient descent scheme to derive an iterative algorithm to minimize our familiar cost function

*J*(**θ**) = 𝔼 \[(*y*−**θ**^(*T*)**x**)²\] = *σ*[*y*]² − 2**θ**^(*T*)**p** + **θ**^(*T*)*Σ*[*x*]**θ**,<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0001" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0001" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si36.png)(5.4) 

where *Σ*[*x*] = 𝔼\[**x****x**^(*T*)\]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si37.png) is the input covariance matrix and **p** = 𝔼\[**x***y*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si38.png) is the input–output cross-correlation vector (Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml)). The respective cost function gradient with respect to ***θ*** is easily seen to be (e.g., Appendix A)

∇*J*(**θ**) = 2*Σ*[*x*]**θ** − 2**p**.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si39.png)(5.5) 

In this chapter, we will also adhere to zero mean jointly distributed input–output random variables, except if otherwise stated. Thus, the covariance and correlation matrices coincide. If this is not the case, the covariance in Eq. [(5.5)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq8) is replaced by the correlation matrix. The treatment is focused on real data and we will point out differences with the complex-valued data case whenever needed.

Employing Eq. [(5.5)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq8), the update recursion in Eq. [(5.3)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq6) becomes

**θ**^((*i*)) = **θ**^((*i* − 1)) − *μ*(*Σ*[*x*]**θ**^((*i* − 1))−**p**) = **θ**^((*i* − 1)) + *μ*(**p**−*Σ*[*x*]**θ**^((*i* − 1))),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo id="mmlbr0002" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si40.png)(5.6) 

where the step size has been considered constant and it has also absorbed the factor 2. The more general case of iteration-dependent values of the step size will be discussed soon after. Our goal now becomes that of searching for all values of *μ* that guarantee convergence. To this end, define

**c**^((*i*)) :  = **θ**^((*i*)) − **θ**[\*],<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si41.png)(5.7) 

where **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si10.png) is the (unique) optimal MSE solution that results by solving the respective normal equations (Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml)),

*Σ*[*x*]**θ**[\*] = **p**.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si42.png)(5.8) 

Subtracting **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si10.png) from both sides of Eq. [(5.6)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq9) and plugging in Eq. [(5.7)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq10), we obtain

**c**^((*i*)) = **c**^((*i* − 1)) + *μ*(**p**−*Σ*[*x*]**c**^((*i* − 1))−*Σ*[*x*]**θ**[\*]) = **c**^((*i* − 1)) − *μ**Σ*[*x*]**c**^((*i* − 1)) = (*I*−*μ**Σ*[*x*])**c**^((*i* − 1)).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo id="mmlbr0003" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0003" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si43.png)(5.9) 

Recall that *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si44.png) is a symmetric positive definite matrix (Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)); hence all its eigenvalues are positive, and moreover (Appendix A.2) it can be written as

*Σ*[*x*] = *Q**Λ**Q*^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si45.png)(5.10) 

where

*Λ* :  = diag{*λ*[1], …, *λ*[*l*]} and *Q* :  = \[**q**[1], **q**[2], …, **q**[*l*]\],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>diag</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si46.png)

with *λ*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si47.png), **q**[*j*], *j* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si48.png), being the eigenvalues and the respective normalized (*orthogonal*) eigenvectors of the covariance matrix,^([^(26)](#fn26))

**q**[*k*]^(*T*)**q**[*j*] = *δ*[*k**j*], *k*, *j* = 1, 2, …, *l* ⇒ *Q*^(*T*) = *Q*^( − 1).<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟹</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si49.png)

That is, the matrix *Q* is orthogonal. Plugging the factorization of *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si44.png) into Eq. [(5.9)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq12), we obtain

**c**^((*i*)) = *Q*(*I*−*μ**Λ*)*Q*^(*T*)**c**^((*i* − 1)),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si50.png)

or

**v**^((*i*)) = (*I*−*μ**Λ*)**v**^((*i* − 1)),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si51.png)(5.11) 

where

**v**^((*i*)) :  = *Q*^(*T*)**c**^((*i*)), *i* = 1, 2, ….<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si52.png)(5.12) 

The previously used “trick” is a standard one and its aim is to “decouple” the various components of **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si33.png) in Eq. [(5.6)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq9). Indeed, each one of the components *v*^((*i*))(*j*), *j* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si54.png), of **v**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si55.png) follows an iteration path, which is independent of the rest of the components; in other words,

*v*^((*i*))(*j*) = (1 − *μ**λ*[*j*])*v*^((*i* − 1))(*j*) = (1 − *μ**λ*[*j*])²*v*^((*i* − 2))(*j*) = ⋯ = (1 − *μ**λ*[*j*])^(*i*)*v*^((0))(*j*),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

where *v*^((0))(*j*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si57.png) is the *j*th component of **v**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si58.png), corresponding to the initial vector. It is readily seen that if

|1 − *μ**λ*[*j*]| < 1 ⇔  − 1 < 1 − *μ**λ*[*j*] < 1, *j* = 1, 2, …, *l*,<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟺</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si59.png)(5.14) 

the geometric series tends to zero and

**v**^((*i*)) → 0 ⇒ *Q*^(*T*)(**θ**^((*i*)) − **θ**[\*]) → 0 ⇒ **θ**^((*i*)) → **θ**[\*].<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟹</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟹</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si60.png)(5.15) 

Note that [(5.14)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq20) is equivalent to

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx002.jpg)(5.16) 

where *λ*[max]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si61.png) denotes the maximum eigenvalue of *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si44.png).

*Time constant*: [Fig. 5.6](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0035) shows a typical sketch of the evolution of *v*^((*i*))(*j*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si62.png) as a function of the iteration steps for the case 0 < 1 − *μ**λ*[*j*] < 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si63.png). Assume that the envelope, denoted by the red line, is (approximately) of an exponential form, *f*(*t*) = exp ( − *t*/*τ*[*j*])<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si64.png). Plug into *f*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si65.png), as the values corresponding at the time instants *t* = *i**T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si66.png) and *t* = (*i* − 1)*T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si67.png), the values of *v*^((*i*))(*j*), *v*^((*i* − 1))(*j*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si68.png) from [(5.13)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq19); then the *time constant* results as

$\\tau\_{j} = \\frac{- 1}{\\ln(1 - \\mu\\lambda\_{j})},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si69.png)

assuming that the sampling time between two successive iterations is *T* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si70.png). For small values of *μ*, we can write

$\\tau\_{j} \\approx \\frac{1}{\\mu\\lambda\_{j}},\\quad\\text{for}\\ \\mu \\ll 1.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>for</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si71.png)

That is, the lowest rate of convergence is associated with the component that corresponds to the smallest eigenvalue. However, this is only true for small enough values of *μ*. For the more general case, this may not be true. Recall that the rate of convergence depends on the value of the term 1 − *μ**λ*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si72.png). This is also known as the *j*th *mode*. Its value depends not only on *λ*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si47.png) but also on *μ*. Let us consider as an example the case of *μ* taking a value very close to the maximum allowable one, *μ* ≈ 2/*λ*[max]<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si73.png). Then the mode corresponding to the maximum eigenvalue will have an absolute value very close to one. On the other hand, the time constant of the mode corresponding to the minimum eigenvalue will be controlled by the value of |1 − 2*λ*[min]/*λ*[max]|<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si74.png), which can be much smaller than one. In such a case, the mode corresponding to the maximum eigenvalue exhibits slower convergence.

![Figure 5.6 Convergence curve for one of the components of the transformed error vector. Note that the curve is of an approximate exponentially decreasing type.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 5.6](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0330) Convergence curve for one of the components of the transformed error vector. Note that the curve is of an approximate exponentially decreasing type.

To obtain the optimum value for the step size, one has to select its value in such a way that the resulting maximum absolute mode value is minimized. This is a min/max task,

$\\begin{array}{l} {\\mu\_{o} = \\ \\ \\ \\text{arg}\\min\_{\\mu}\\max\_{j}|1 - \\mu\\lambda\_{j}|,} \\\\ {\\text{s.t.}\\quad\\quad|1 - \\mu\\lambda\_{j}| < 1,\\ j = 1,2,\\ldots,l.} \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>arg</mml:mtext><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si75.png)

The task can be solved easily graphically. [Fig. 5.7](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0040) shows the absolute values of the modes (corresponding to the maximum, minimum, and an intermediate eigenvalue). The (absolute) values of the modes initially decrease as *μ* increases, and then they start increasing. Observe that the optimal value results at the point where the curves for the maximum and minimum eigenvalues intersect. Indeed, this corresponds to the minimum-maximum value. Moving *μ* away from *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si76.png), the maximum mode value increases; increasing *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si76.png), the mode corresponding to the maximum eigenvalue becomes larger, and decreasing it, the mode corresponding to the minimum eigenvalue is increased. At the intersection we have

1 − *μ*[*o*]*λ*[min] =  − (1 − *μ*[*o*]*λ*[max]),<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si77.png)

which results in

$\\mu\_{\\textit{o}} = \\frac{2}{\\lambda\_{\\text{max}} + \\lambda\_{\\text{min}}}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si78.png)(5.17) 

At the optimal value, *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si76.png), there are two slowest modes; one corresponding to *λ*[min]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si79.png) (i.e., 1 − *μ*[*o*]*λ*[min]<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si80.png)) and another one corresponding to *λ*[max]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si61.png) (i.e., 1 − *μ*[*o*]*λ*[max]<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si82.png)). They have equal magnitudes but opposite signs, and they are given by

$\\pm \\frac{\\rho - 1}{\\rho + 1},$<mml:math><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si83.png)

where

$\\rho: = \\frac{\\lambda\_{\\text{max}}}{\\lambda\_{\\text{min}}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si84.png)

In other words, the *convergence rate depends on the eigenvalues spread of the covariance matrix*.

![Figure 5.7 For each mode, increasing the value of the step size, the time constant starts decreasing and then after a point starts increasing. The full black line corresponds to the maximum eigenvalue, the red one to the minimum, and the dotted curve to an intermediate eigenvalue. The overall optimal, \\mu\_{\\textit{o}}Equation, corresponds to the value where the red and full black curves intersect.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 5.7](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0340) For each mode, increasing the value of the step size, the time constant starts decreasing and then after a point starts increasing. The full black line corresponds to the maximum eigenvalue, the red one to the minimum, and the dotted curve to an intermediate eigenvalue. The overall optimal, *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si76.png), corresponds to the value where the red and full black curves intersect.

*Parameter error vector convergence*: From the definitions in Eqs. [(5.7)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq10) and [(5.12)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq18), we get 

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} + Q\\mathbf{v}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} + \\lbrack\\mathbf{q}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{q}\_{l}\\rbrack{\\lbrack v^{(i)}(1),\\ldots,v^{(i)}(l)\\rbrack}^{T} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{l}\\mathbf{q}\_{k}v^{(i)}(k),$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo id="mmlbr0005" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo or

$\\theta^{(i)}(j) = \\theta\_{\\ast}(j) + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{l}q\_{k}(j)v^{(0)}(k){(1 - \\mu\\lambda\_{k})}^{i},\\ j = 1,2,\\ldots,l.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo
