linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si86.png)(5.19) 

In other words, the components of **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si33.png) converge to the respective components of the optimum vector **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si10.png) as a weighted average of powers of 1 − *μ**λ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si88.png), i.e., (1 − *μ**λ*[*k*])^(*i*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si89.png). Computing the respective time constant in closed form is not possible; however, we can state lower and upper bounds. The lower bound corresponds to the time constant of the fastest converging mode and the upper bound to the slowest of the modes. For small values of *μ* ≪ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si90.png), we can write

$\\frac{1}{\\mu\\lambda\_{\\text{max}}} \\leq \\tau \\leq \\frac{1}{\\mu\\lambda\_{\\text{min}}}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si91.png)(5.20) 

*The learning curve*: We now turn our focus to the mean-square error (MSE). Recall from Eq. [(4.8)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml) that

*J*(**θ**^((*i*))) = *J*(**θ**[\*]) + (**θ**^((*i*))−**θ**[\*])^(*T*)*Σ*[*x*](**θ**^((*i*))−**θ**[\*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

or, mobilizing Eqs. [(5.18)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq30) and [(5.10)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq13) and taking into consideration the orthonormality of the eigenvectors, we obtain

$J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} \\right) = J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{l}\\lambda\_{j}|v^{(i)}(j)|^{2}\\ \\Longrightarrow J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} \\right) = J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{l}\\lambda\_{j}{(1 - \\mu\\lambda\_{j})}^{2i}|v^{(0)}(j)|^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mi id="mmlbr0006">J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

which converges to the minimum value *J*(**θ**[\*])<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si94.png) asymptotically. Moreover, observe that this convergence is monotonic, because *λ*[*j*](1 − *μ**λ*[*j*])²<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si95.png) is positive. Following similar arguments as before, the respective time constants for each one of the modes are now

$\\tau\_{j}^{\\text{mse}} = \\frac{- 1}{2\\ln(1 - \\mu\\lambda\_{j})} \\approx \\frac{1}{2\\mu\\lambda\_{j}}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>mse</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si96.png)(5.23) 

Example 5.1

The aim of the example is to demonstrate what we have said so far, concerning the convergence issues of the gradient descent scheme in Eq. [(5.6)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq9). The cross-correlation vector was chosen to be

**p** = \[0.05, 0.03\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.03</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si97.png)

and we consider two different covariance matrices,

$\\Sigma\_{1} = \\begin{bmatrix} {1\\ } & 0 \\\\ {0\\ } & 0.1 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},\\quad\\Sigma\_{2} = \\begin{bmatrix} {1\\ } & 0 \\\\ {0\\ } & 1 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si613.png)

Note that for the case of *Σ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si99.png), both eigenvalues are equal to 1, and for *Σ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si100.png) they are *λ*[1] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si101.png) and *λ*[2] = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si102.png) (for diagonal matrices the eigenvalues are equal to the diagonal elements of the matrix).

[Fig. 5.8](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0045) shows the error curves for two values of *μ* for the case of *Σ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si100.png); the gray one corresponds to the optimum value (*μ*[*o*] = 1.81<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.81</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si105.png)) and the red one to *μ* = *μ*[*o*]/2 = 0.9<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si106.png). Observe the faster convergence toward zero that is achieved by the optimal value. Note that it may happen, as is the case in [Fig. 5.8](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0045), that initially the convergence for some *μ* ≠ *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si107.png) will be faster compared to *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si76.png). What the theory guarantees is that, eventually, the curve corresponding to the optimal will tend to zero faster than for any other value of *μ*. [Fig. 5.9](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0050) shows the respective trajectories of the successive estimates in the two-dimensional space, together with the isovalue curves; the latter are ellipses, as we can readily deduce if we look carefully at the form of the quadratic cost function written as in Eq. [(5.21)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq33). Compare the zig-zag path, which corresponds to the larger value of *μ* = 1.81<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.81</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si108.png), with the smoother one, obtained for the smaller step size *μ* = 0.9<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si109.png).

![Figure 5.8 The black curve corresponds to the optimal value \\mu = \\mu\_{\\textit{o}}Equation and the gray one to \\mu = \\mu\_{\\textit{o}}/2Equation, for the case of an input covariance matrix with unequal eigenvalues.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr008.jpg)

Figure 5.8 The black curve corresponds to the optimal value *μ* = *μ*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si103.png) and the gray one to *μ* = *μ*[*o*]/2<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si104.png), for the case of an input covariance matrix with unequal eigenvalues.

![Figure 5.9 The trajectories of the successive estimates (dots) obtained by the gradient descent algorithm for (A) the larger value of μ = 1.81 and (B) the smaller value of μ = 0.9. In (B), the trajectory toward the minimum is smooth. In contrast, in (A), the trajectory consists of zig-zags.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 5.9](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0380) The trajectories of the successive estimates (dots) obtained by the gradient descent algorithm for (A) the larger value of *μ* = 1.81 and (B) the smaller value of *μ* = 0.9. In (B), the trajectory toward the minimum is smooth. In contrast, in (A), the trajectory consists of zig-zags.

For comparison reasons, to demonstrate the dependence of the convergence speed on the eigenvalues spread, [Fig. 5.10](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0055) shows the error curves using the same step size, *μ* = 1.81<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.81</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si108.png), for both cases, *Σ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si100.png) and *Σ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si99.png). Observe that large eigenvalues spread of the input covariance matrix slows down the convergence. Note that if the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix are equal to, say, *λ*, the isovalue curves are circles; the optimal step size in this case is *μ* = 1/*λ*<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si110.png) and convergence is achieved in only one step ([Fig. 5.11](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0060)).

![Figure 5.10 For the same value of μ = 1.81, the error curves for the case of unequal eigenvalues (λ1 = 1 and λ2 = 0.1) (gray) and for equal eigenvalues (λ1 = λ2 = 1). For the latter case, the isovalue curves are circles; if the optimal value \\mu\_{\\textit{o}} = 1Equation is used, the algorithm converges in one step. This is demonstrated in Fig. 5.11.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr010.jpg)

[Figure 5.10](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#cf0390) For the same value of *μ* = 1.81, the error curves for the case of unequal eigenvalues (*λ*[1] = 1 and *λ*[2] = 0.1) (gray) and for equal eigenvalues (*λ*[1] = *λ*[2] = 1). For the latter case, the isovalue curves are circles; if the optimal value *μ*[*o*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si111.png) is used, the algorithm converges in one step. This is demonstrated in [Fig. 5.11](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#f0060).

![Figure 5.11 When the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix are all equal to a value, λ, the use of the optimal \\mu\_{\\textit{o}} = 1/\\lambdaEquation achieves convergence in one step.](images/B9780443292385000111/gr011.jpg)

Figure 5.11 When the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix are all equal to a value, *λ*, the use of the optimal *μ*[*o*] = 1/*λ*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">o</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si112.png) achieves convergence in one step.

### Time-varying step sizes

The previous analysis cannot be carried out for the case of an iteration-dependent step size. It can be shown (Problem [5.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#o0015)) that in this case, the gradient descent algorithm converges if

*   •  *μ*[*i*] → 0, as *i* → ∞<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>as</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si113.png),
*   •  $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{\\infty}\\mu\_{i} = \\infty$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si114.png).

A typical example of sequences which comply with both conditions is those that satisfy the following:

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{\\infty}\\mu\_{i}^{2} < \\infty,\\quad\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{\\infty}\\mu\_{i} = \\infty,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si115.png)(5.24) 

as, for example, the sequence

$\\mu\_{i} = \\frac{1}{i}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si116.png)

Note that the two (sufficient) conditions require that the sequence tends to zero, yet its infinite sum diverges. We will meet this pair of conditions in various parts of this book. The previous conditions state that the step size has to become smaller and smaller as iterations progress, but this should not take place in a very aggressive manner, so that the algorithm is left to be active for a sufficient number of iterations to learn the solution. If the step size tends to zero very fast, then updates are practically frozen after a few iterations, without the algorithm having acquired enough information to get close to the solution.

### 5.3.1 The complex-valued case

In Section [4.4.2](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml) we stated that a function *f* : ℂ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si117.png) is not differentiable with respect to its complex argument. To deal with such cases, the Wirtinger calculus was introduced. In this section, we use this mathematically convenient tool to derive the corresponding steepest descent direction.

To this end, we again employ a first-order Taylor series approximation \[22\]. Let

**θ** = **θ**[*r*] + *j***θ**[*i*].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si118.png)

Then the cost function

*J*(**θ**) : ℂ^(*l*) ↦ \[0,  + ∞)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si119.png)

is approximated as

*J*(**θ** + *Δ***θ**) = *J*(**θ**[*r*] + *Δ***θ**[*r*], **θ**[*i*] + *Δ***θ**[*i*]) = *J*(**θ**[*r*], **θ**[*i*]) + *Δ***θ**[*r*]^(*T*)∇[*r*]*J*(**θ**[*r*], **θ**[*i*]) + *Δ***θ**[*i*]^(*T*)∇[*i*]*J*(**θ**[*r*], **θ**[*i*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0007" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0007" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si120.png)(5.25) 

where ∇[*r*] (∇[*i*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si121.png) denotes the gradient with respect to **θ**[*r*] (**θ**[*i*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si122.png). Taking into account that

$\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{r} = \\frac{\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta} + \\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{\\ast}}{2},\\quad\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i} = \\frac{\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta} - \\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{\\ast}}{2j},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si123.png)

it is easy to show (Problem [5.3](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#o0020)) that

*J*(**θ** + *Δ***θ**) = *J*(**θ**) + Re{*Δ***θ**^(*H*)∇[**θ**^(\*)]*J*(**θ**)},<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Re</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si124.png)(5.26) 

where ∇[**θ**^(\*)]*J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si125.png) is the CW-derivative, defined in Section [4.4.2](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml) as

$\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}^{\\ast}}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\frac{1}{2}\\left( \\nabla\_{r}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) + j\\nabla\_{i}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si126.png)

Looking carefully at Eq. [(5.26)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq44), it is straightforward to observe that the direction

*Δ***θ** =  − *μ*∇[**θ**^(\*)]*J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si127.png)

makes the updated cost equal to

*J*(**θ** + *Δ***θ**) = *J*(**θ**) − *μ*∥∇[**θ**^(\*)]*J*(**θ**)∥²,<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si128.png)

which guarantees that *J*(**θ** + *Δ***θ**) < *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si129.png); it is straightforward to see, by taking into account the definition of an inner product, that the above search direction is the one of the largest decrease. Thus, the counterpart of Eq. [(5.3)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq6) becomes

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx003.jpg)(5.27) 

For the MSE cost function and for the linear estimation model, we get

*J*(**θ**) = 𝔼 \[(*y*−**θ**^(*H*)**x**)(*y*−**θ**^(*H*)**x**)^(\*)\] = *σ*[*y*]² + **θ**^(*H*)*Σ*[*x*]**θ** − **θ**^(*H*)**p** − **p**^(*H*)**θ**,<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0008" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0008" linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si130.png)

and taking the gradient with respect to **θ**^(\*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si131.png), by treating ***θ*** as a constant (Section [4.4.2](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml)), we obtain

∇[**θ**^(\*)]*J*(**θ**) = *Σ*[*x*]**θ** − **p**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si132.png)

and the respective gradient descent iteration is the same as in Eq. [(5.6)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq9).

## 5.4 Stochastic approximation

Solving for the normal equations (Eq. [(5.8)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq11)) as well as using the gradient descent iterative scheme (for the case of the MSE), one has to have access to the second-order statistics of the involved variables. However, in most of the cases, this is not known and it has to be approximated using a set of observations. In this section, we turn our attention to algorithms that can learn the statistics iteratively via the training set. The origins of such techniques are traced back to 1951, when Robbins and Monro introduced the method of *stochastic approximation* \[79\], or the *Robbins–Monro algorithm*.

Let us consider the case of a function that is defined in terms of the expected value of another one, namely,

*f*(**θ**) = 𝔼\[*ϕ*(**θ**,**η**)\], **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si133.png)

where **η** is a random vector of unknown distribution. The goal is to compute a root of *f*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si134.png). If the distribution was known, the expectation could be computed, at least in principle, and one could use any root-finding algorithm to compute the roots. The problem emerges when the statistics are unknown; hence the exact form of *f*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si134.png) is not known. All one has at her/his disposal is a sequence of i.i.d. observations **η**[0], **η**[1], …<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si135.png). Robbins and Monro proved that the following algorithm,^([^(27)](#fn27))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx004.jpg)(5.28) 

starting from an arbitrary initial condition, **θ**[ − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si136.png), converges^([^(28)](#fn28))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx005.jpg)(5.29) 

In other words, in the iteration [(5.28)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq52), we get rid of the expectation operation and use the value of *ϕ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si137.png), which is computed using the current observations and the currently available estimate. That is, the algorithm learns both the statistics as well as the root; two in one! The same comments made for the convergence conditions, met in the iteration-dependent step size case in Section [5.3](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#s0020), are valid here as well.

In the context of optimizing a general differentiable cost function of the form

*J*(**θ**) = 𝔼 \[ℒ(**θ**,*y*,**x**)\],<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si138.png)(5.30) 

the Robbins–Monro scheme can be mobilized to find a root of the respective gradient, i.e.,

∇*J*(**θ**) = 𝔼 \[∇ℒ(**θ**,*y*,**x**)\],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si139.png)

where the expectation is with respect to the pair (*y*, **x**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si140.png). As we have seen in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), such cost functions are also known as the *expected risk* or the *expected loss* in machine learning terminology. Given the sequence of observations (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 0, 1, …<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si141.png), the recursion in Eq. [(5.28)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq52) now becomes

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx006.jpg)(5.31) 

Let us now assume, for simplicity, that the expected risk has a unique minimum, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si10.png). Then, according to the Robbins–Monro theorem and using an appropriate sequence *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si142.png), **θ**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si143.png) will converge to **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si10.png). However, although this information is important, it is not by itself enough. In practice, one has to cease iterations after a *finite* number of steps. Hence, one has to know something more concerning the rate of convergence of such a scheme. To this end, two quantities are of interest, namely, the mean and the covariance matrix of the estimator at iteration *n*, i.e.,

𝔼 \[**θ**[*n*]\], Cov(**θ**[*n*]).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>Cov</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si144.png)

It can be shown (see \[67\]) that if *μ*[*n*] = 𝒪(1/*n*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si145.png) and assuming that iterations have brought the estimate close to the optimal value, then^([^(29)](#fn29))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx007.jpg)(5.32) 

and

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/fx008.jpg)(5.33) 

where ***c*** and *V* are constants that depend on the form of the expected risk. The above formulas have also been derived under some further assumptions concerning the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix of the expected risk.^([^(30)](#fn30))

The previously reported fluctuation depends on the choice of the sequence *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si142.png), being smaller for smaller values of the step size sequence. However, *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si142.png) cannot be made to decrease very fast due to the two convergence conditions, as discussed before. This is the price one pays for using the *noisy version of the gradient* and it is the reason that such schemes suffer from relatively low convergence rates. However, this does not mean that such schemes are, necessarily, the poor relatives of other more “elaborate” algorithms. As we will discuss in Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml), their low complexity requirements make this algorithmic family to be the preferred choice in a number of practical applications.

### Application to the MSE linear estimation

Let us apply the Robbins–Monro algorithm to solve for the optimal MSE linear estimator if the covariance matrix and the cross-correlation vector are unknown. We know that the solution corresponds to the root of the gradient of the cost function, which can be written in the form (recall the orthogonality theorem from Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) and Eq. [(5.8)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq11))

*Σ*[*x*]**θ** − **p** = 𝔼 \[**x**(**x**^(*T*)**θ**−*y*)\] = 0.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si150.png)

Given the training sequence of observations, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si151.png), which are assumed to be i.i.d. drawn from the joint distribution of (*y*, **x**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si140.png), the Robbins–Monro algorithm becomes

**θ**[*n*] = **θ**[*n* − 1] + *μ*[*n*]**x**[*n*](*y*[*n*]−**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*n* − 1]),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si153.png)(5.34) 

which converges to the optimal MSE solution provided that the two conditions in [(5.29)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq53) are satisfied. Compare Eq. [(5.34)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq61) with Eq. [(5.6)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq9). Taking into account the definitions, *Σ*[*x*] = 𝔼\[**x****x**^(*T*)\], **p** = 𝔼\[**x***y*\]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si154.png), the former equation results from the latter one by dropping out the expectation operations and using an iteration-dependent step size. Observe that the iterations in Eq. [(5.34)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq61) coincide with *time updates*; time has now explicitly entered into the scene. This prompts us to start thinking about modifying such schemes appropriately to track time-varying environments. Algorithms such as the one in Eq. [(5.34)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq61), which result from the generic gradient descent formulation by replacing the expectation by the respective instantaneous observations, are also known as *stochastic gradient descent schemes*.

Remarks 5.1

*   •  All the algorithms to be derived next can also be applied to nonlinear estimation/filtering tasks of the form

$\\widehat{y} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{l}\\theta\_{k}\\phi\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{\\phi},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si155.png)

*   and the place of **x** is taken by **ϕ**, where

**ϕ** = \[*ϕ*[1](**x**), …, *ϕ*[*l*](**x**)\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si156.png)

*   

Example 5.2

The aim of this example is to demonstrate the pair of Eqs. [(5.32)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq58) and [(5.33)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq59), which characterize the convergence properties of the stochastic gradient scheme.

Data samples were first generated according to the regression model

*y*[*n*] = **θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*] + *η*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si157.png)

where **θ** ∈ ℝ²<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si158.png) was randomly chosen and then fixed. The elements of **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si159.png) were i.i.d. generated via a normal distribution 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si160.png) and *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si161.png) are samples of a white noise sequence with variance equal to *σ*² = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si162.png). Then the observations (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si151.png) were used in the recursive scheme in Eq. [(5.34)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq61) to obtain an estimate of ***θ***. The experiment was repeated 200 times and the mean and variance of the obtained estimates were computed for each iteration step. Observe that the mean values of the estimates tend to the true value, corresponding to the red line, and the standard deviation keeps decreasing as *n* grows. ## 5.5 The least-mean-squares adaptive algorithm

The stochastic gradient descent algorithm in Eq. [(5.34)](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#deq61) converges to the optimal MSE solution provided that *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si142.png) satisfies the two convergence conditions. Once the algorithm has converged, it “locks” at the obtained solution. In a case where the statistics of the involved variables/processes and/or the unknown parameters start changing, the algorithm cannot track the changes. Note that if such changes occur, the error term

*e*[*n*] = *y*[*n*] − **θ**[*n* − 1]^(*T*)**x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si164.png)

will attain larger values; however, because *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si142.png) is very small, the increased value of the error will not lead to corresponding changes of the estimate at time *n*. This can be overcome if one sets the value of *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si142.png) to a preselected *fixed* value, *μ*. The resulting algorithm is the celebrated least-mean-squares (LMS) algorithm \[102\].

Algorithm 5.1

**The LMS algorithm**

*   •  Initialize 
    1.  –  **θ**[ − 1] = 0 ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si165.png); other values can also be used.
    2.  –  Select the value of *μ*.
*   •  **For** *n* = 0, 1, …<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si166.png), **Do** 
    1.  –  *e*[*n*] = *y*[*n*] − **θ**[*n* − 1]^(*T*)**x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si167.png)
    2.  –  **θ**[*n*] = **θ**[*n* − 1] + *μ**e*[*n*]**x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000111/si168.png)
*   •  **End For**

In case the input is a time series,^([^(31)](#fn31))

Let us now comment on this simple structure. Assume that the algorithm has converged close to the solution; then the error term is expected to take small values and thus the updates will remain close to the solution. If the statistics and/or the system parameters now start changing, the error values are expected to increase. Given that *μ* has a constant value, the algorithm has now the “agility” to update the estimates in an attempt to “push” the error to lower values. This small variation of the iterative scheme has important implications. The resulting algorithm is no more a member of the Robbins–Monro stochastic approximation family. Thus, one has to study its convergence conditions as well as its performance properties. Moreover, since the algorithm now has the potential to track changes in the values of the underlying parameters, as well as the statistics of the involved processes/variables, one has to study its performance in nonstationary environments; this is associated to what is known as the *tracking* performance of the algorithm, and it will be treated at the end of the chapter.

### 5.5.1 Convergence and steady-state performance of the LMS in stationary environments

The goal of this subsection is to study the performance of the LMS in stationary environments, that is, to answer the following questions. (a) Does the scheme converge and under which conditions? And if it converges, where does it converge? Although we introduced the scheme having in mind nonstationary environments, we still have to know how it behaves under stationarity; after all, the environment can change very slowly, and it can be considered “locally” stationary.

The convergence properties of the LMS, as well as of any other online/adaptive algorithm, are related to its *transient* characteristics; that is, the period from the initial estimate until the algorithm reaches a “steady-state” mode of operation. In general, analyzing the transient performance of an online algorithm is a formidable task indeed. This is also true even for the very simple structure of the LMS summarized in [Algorithm 5.1](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#enun0025). The LMS update recursions are equivalent to a time-varying, nonlinear (Problem [5.5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml#o0030)), and stochastic in nature estimator. Many papers, some of them of high scientific insight and mathematical skill, have been produced. However, with the exception of a few rare and special cases, the analysis involves approximations. Our goal in this book is not to treat this topic in detail. Our focus will be restricted to the most “primitive” of the techniques, which are easier for the reader to follow compared with more advanced and mathematically elegant theories; after all, even this primitive approach provides results that turn out to be in agreement with what one experiences in practice.
