mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si303.png)

where ⁎ denotes any value of the element. Without going into detail, the low partition can relate the Kalman gain of order *l* and time *n* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si191.png) to the Kalman gain of order *l* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si304.png) and time *n* (step up). Then the upper partition can be used to obtain the time update Kalman gain at order *l* and time *n* (step down). Such a procedure bypasses the need for matrix operations leading to 𝒪(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si305.png) RLS-type algorithms \[7,9\] with complexity 7*l* per time update. However, these versions turned out to be numerically unstable. Numerically stabilized versions, at only a small extra computational cost, were proposed in \[5,58\]. All the aforementioned schemes have also been developed for solving the (regularized) exponentially weighted LS cost function.

Besides this line, variants that obtain approximate solutions have been derived in an attempt to reduce complexity; these schemes use an approximation of the covariance or inverse covariance matrix \[14,38\]. The *fast Newton transversal filter* (FNTF) algorithm \[45\] approximates the inverse covariance matrix by a banded matrix of width *p*. Such a modeling has a specific physical interpretation. A banded inverse covariance matrix corresponds to an AR process of order *p*. Hence, if the input signal can sufficiently be modeled by an AR model, FNTF obtains a least-squares performance. Moreover, this performance is obtained at 𝒪(*p*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si306.png) instead of 𝒪(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si305.png) computational cost. This can be very effective in applications where *p* ≪ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si307.png). This is the case, for example, in audio conferencing, where the input signal is speech. Speech can efficiently be modeled by an AR of the order of 15, yet the filter order can be of a few hundred taps \[49\]. FNTF bridges the gap between LMS (*p* = 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si308.png) and (fast) RLS (*p* = *l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si309.png). Moreover, FNTF builds upon the structure of the stabilized fast RLS. More recently, the banded inverse covariance matrix approximation has been successfully applied in spectral analysis \[21\]. More on efficient LS schemes can be found in \[15,17,20,24,29,57\].

## 6.11 The coordinate and cyclic coordinate descent methods

So far, we have discussed the gradient descent and Newton's method for optimization. We will conclude the discussion with a third method, which can also be seen as a member of the steepest descent family of methods. Instead of the Euclidean and *P*\-weighted norms, let us consider the following minimization task for obtaining the normalized descent direction:

$\\mathbf{v} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{z}}\\mathbf{z}^{T}\\nabla J,$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si310.png)(6.60) 

s.t. ||**z**||[1] = 1,<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si311.png)(6.61) 

where || ⋅ ||[1]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si312.png) denotes the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si313.png) norm, defined as

$||\\mathbf{z}||\_{1}: = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}|z\_{i}|.$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si314.png)

Most of Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) is dedicated to this norm and its properties. Observe that this is not differentiable. Solving the minimization task (Problem [6.17](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#o0090)) results in

**v** =  − *s**g**n*((∇*J*)[*k*])**e**[*k*],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si315.png)

where **e**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si316.png) is the direction of the coordinate corresponding to the component (∇*J*)[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si317.png) with the largest absolute value, i.e.,

|(∇*J*)[*k*]| > |(∇*J*)[*j*]|, *j* ≠ *k*,<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si318.png)

and *s**g**n*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si319.png) is the sign function. The geometry is illustrated in [Fig. 6.7](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#f0045). In other words, the descent direction is along a single basis vector; that is, each time only a *single component* of ***θ*** is updated. It is the component that corresponds to the directional derivative, (∇*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1))))[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si321.png), with the largest increase and the update rule becomes

![](images/B9780443292385000123/fx020.jpg)

Because only one component is updated at each iteration, this greatly simplifies the update mechanism. The method is known as *coordinate descent*.

![Figure 6.7 The unit norm || ⋅ ||1 ball centered at θ(i−1) is a rhombus (in \\mathbb{R}^{2}Equation). The direction e1 is the one corresponding to the largest component of ∇J. Recall that the components of the vector ∇J are the respective directional derivatives.](images/B9780443292385000123/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 6.7](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#cf0625) The unit norm || ⋅ ||[1] ball centered at ***θ***^((*i*−1)) is a rhombus (in ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si320.png)). The direction ***e***[1] is the one corresponding to the largest component of ∇*J*. Recall that the components of the vector ∇*J* are the respective directional derivatives.

Based on this rationale, a number of variants of the basic coordinate descent have been proposed. The *cyclic coordinate descent* (CCD) method in its simplest form entails a *cyclic* update with respect to one coordinate per iteration cycle; that is, at the *i*th iteration the following minimization is solved:

$\\theta\_{k}^{(i)}: = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}J(\\theta\_{1}^{(i)},\\ldots,\\theta\_{k - 1}^{(i)},\\theta,\\theta\_{k + 1}^{(i - 1)},\\ldots,\\theta\_{l}^{(i - 1)}).$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si322.png)

In words, all components but *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si323.png) are assumed constant; those components *θ*[*j*], *j* < *k*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si324.png), are fixed to their updated values, *θ*[*j*]^((*i*)), *j* = 1, 2, …, *k* − 1<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si325.png), and the rest, *θ*[*j*], *j* = *k* + 1, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si326.png), to the available estimates, *θ*[*j*]^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si327.png), from the previous iteration. The nice feature of such a technique is that a simple closed form solution for the minimizer may be obtained. A revival of such techniques has happened in the context of sparse learning models (Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml)) \[18,67\]. Convergence issues of CCD have been considered in \[36,62\]. CCD algorithms for the LS task have also been considered in \[66\] and the references therein. Besides the basic CCD scheme, variants are also available, using different scenarios for the choice of the direction to be updated each time, in order to improve convergence, ranging from a random choice to a change of the coordinate systems, which is known as *adaptive coordinate descent* scheme \[35\].

## 6.12 Simulation examples

In this section, simulation examples are presented concerning the convergence and tracking performance of the RLS compared to algorithms of the gradient descent family, which have been discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml).

Example 6.1

The goal of this example is to demonstrate the comparative performance, with respect to the convergence rates of the RLS, NLMS, and APA algorithms, which have been discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). To this end, we generate data according to the regression model

*y*[*n*] = **θ**[*o*]^(*T*)**x**[*n*] + *η*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si328.png)

where **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(200)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>200</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si329.png). Its elements are generated randomly according to the normalized Gaussian. The noise samples are i.i.d. generated via the zero mean Gaussian with variance equal to *σ*[*η*]² = 0.01<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si330.png). The elements of the input vector are also i.i.d. generated via the normalized Gaussian. Using the generated samples (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 0, 1, …<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si331.png), as the training sequence for all three previously stated algorithms, the convergence curves of [Fig. 6.8](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#f0055) are obtained. The curves show the squared error in dBs (10log[10](*e*[*n*]²)<mml:math><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si332.png)), averaged over 100 different realizations of the experiments, as a function of the time index *n*. The following parameters were used for the involved algorithms. (a) For the NLMS, we used *μ* = 1.2<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si333.png) and *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si334.png); (b) for the APA, we used *μ* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si335.png), *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si334.png), and *q* = 30<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>30</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si336.png); and (c) for the RLS, we used *β* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si179.png) and *λ* = 0.1<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si337.png). The parameters for the NLMS algorithm and the APA were chosen so that both algorithms converge to the same error floor. The improved performance of the APA concerning the convergence rate compared to the NLMS is readily seen. However, both algorithms fall short when compared to the RLS. Note that the RLS converges to lower error floor, because no forgetting factor was used. To be consistent, a forgetting factor *β* < 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si204.png) should have been used in order for this algorithm to settle at the same error floor as the other two algorithms; this would have a beneficial effect on the convergence rate. However, having chosen *β* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si179.png), it is demonstrated that the RLS can converge really fast, even to lower error floors. On the other hand, this improved performance is obtained at substantial higher complexity. In case the input vector is part of a random process, and the special time shift structure can be exploited, as discussed in Section [6.10](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#s0105), the lower-complexity versions are at the disposal of the designer. A further comparative performance example, including another family of online algorithms, will be given in Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml).

![Figure 6.8 MSE curves as a function of the number of iterations for NLMS, APA, and RLS. The RLS converges faster and at lower error floor.](images/B9780443292385000123/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 6.8](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#cf0640) MSE curves as a function of the number of iterations for NLMS, APA, and RLS. The RLS converges faster and at lower error floor.

However, it has to be stressed that this notable advantage (between RLS- and LMS-type schemes) in convergence speed from the initial conditions to steady state may not be the case concerning the tracking performance, when the algorithms have to track time-varying environments. This is demonstrated next.

Example 6.2

This example focuses on the comparative tracking performance of the RLS and NLMS. Our goal is to demonstrate some cases where the RLS fails to do as well as the NLMS. Of course, it must be kept in mind that according to the theory, the comparative performance is very much dependent on the specific application.

For the needs of our example, let us mobilize the time-varying model of the parameters given in Eq. [(6.55)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq110) in a more practical version and generate the data according to the following linear system:

*y*[*n*] = **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*o*, *n* − 1] + *η*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si338.png)(6.64) 

where

**θ**[*o*, *n*] = *α***θ**[*o*, *n* − 1] + **ω**[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si339.png)

with **θ**[*o*, *n*] ∈ ℝ⁵<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si340.png). It turns out that such a time-varying model is closely related (for the right choice of the involved parameters) to what is known in communications as a Rayleigh fading channel, if the parameters comprising **θ**[*o*, *n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si341.png) are thought to represent the impulse response of such a channel \[57\]. Rayleigh fading channels are very common and can adequately model a number of transmission channels in wireless communications. Playing with the parameter *α* and the variance of the corresponding noise source, **ω**, one can achieve fast or slow time-varying scenarios. In our case, we chose *α* = 0.97<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.97</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si342.png) and the noise followed a Gaussian distribution of zero mean and covariance matrix *Σ*[*ω*] = 0.1*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si343.png).

Concerning the data generation, the input samples were generated i.i.d. from a Gaussian 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png), and the noise was also Gaussian of zero mean value and variance equal to *σ*[*η*]² = 0.01<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si330.png). Initialization of the time-varying model (**θ**[*o*, 0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si345.png)) was randomly done by drawing samples from 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png).

[Fig. 6.9](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#f0060) shows the obtained MSE curve as a function of the iterations for the NLMS and the RLS. For the RLS, the forgetting factor was set equal to *β* = 0.995<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.995</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si346.png) and for the NLMS, *μ* = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si347.png) and *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si334.png). Such a choice resulted in the best performance, for both algorithms, after extensive experimentation. The curves are the result of averaging out 200 independent runs.

![Figure 6.9 For a fast time-varying parameter model, the RLS (gray) fails to track it, in spite of its very fast initial convergence, compared to the NLMS (red).](images/B9780443292385000123/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 6.9](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#cf0660) For a fast time-varying parameter model, the RLS (gray) fails to track it, in spite of its very fast initial convergence, compared to the NLMS (red).

[Fig. 6.10](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#f0065) shows the resulting curves for medium and slow time-varying channels, corresponding to *Σ*[*ω*] = 0.01*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si348.png) and *Σ*[*ω*] = 0.001*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si349.png), respectively. 

![Figure 6.10 MSE curves as a function of iteration for (A) a medium and (B) a slow time-varying parameter model. The red curve corresponds to the NLMS and the gray one to the RLS.](images/B9780443292385000123/gr010.jpg)

## 6.13 Total least-squares

In this section, the LS task will be formulated from a different perspective. Assume zero mean (centered) data and our familiar linear regression model, employing the observed samples,

**y** = *X***θ** + **η**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si350.png)

as in Section [6.2](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#s0015). We have seen that the LS task is equivalent to (orthogonally) projecting ***y*** onto the span{**x**[1]^(*c*), …, **x**[*l*]^(*c*)}<mml:math><mml:mtext>span</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si19.png) of the columns of *X*, hence making the error

$\\mathbf{e} = \\mathbf{y} - \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si352.png)

orthogonal to the column space of *X*. Equivalently, this can be written as,

minimize ∥**e**∥², s.t. **y** − **e** ∈ ℛ(*X*),<mml:math><mml:mtext id="mmlbr0014">minimize</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0014" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si353.png)(6.65) 

where ℛ(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si130.png) is the range space of *X* (see Remarks [6.1](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#enun0015) for the respective definition). Moreover, once ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{LS}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">LS</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si355.png) has been obtained, we can write

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = X{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{LS} = \\mathbf{y} - \\mathbf{e},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">LS</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si356.png)

or

$\\lbrack X\\ \\vdots \\ \\mathbf{y} - \\mathbf{e}\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{LS} \\\\ {- 1} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = 0,$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">LS</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si357.png)(6.66) 

where \[*X* ⋮ **y** − **e**\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si358.png) is the matrix that results after extending *X* by an extra column, **y** − **e**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si359.png). Thus, all the points (*y*[*n*] − *e*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ^(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si360.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si361.png), lie on the same hyperplane, crossing the origin, as shown in Fig. [6.11](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#f0070). In other words, in order to fit a hyperplane to the data, the LS method applies a correction *e*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si192.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si361.png), to the *output samples*. Thus, we have silently assumed that the regressors have been obtained via exact measurements and that the noise affects *only* the output observations.

![Figure 6.11 According to the LS method, only the output points yn are corrected to yn − en, so that the pairs (yn − en,xn) lie on a hyperplane, crossing the origin for centered data. If the data are not centered, it crosses the centroid, (\\overline{y},\\overline{x})Equation.](images/B9780443292385000123/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 6.11](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#cf0680) According to the LS method, *only* the output points *y*[*n*] are corrected to *y*[*n*] − *e*[*n*], so that the pairs (*y*[*n*] − *e*[*n*],*x*[*n*]) lie on a hyperplane, crossing the origin for centered data. If the data are not centered, it crosses the centroid, $(\\overline{y},\\overline{x})$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si363.png).

In this section, the more general case will be considered, where we allow both the input (regressors) and the output variables to be perturbed by (unobserved) noise samples. Such a treatment has a long history, dating back to the 19th century \[1\]. The method remained in obscurity until it was revived 50 years later for two-dimensional models by Deming \[13\]; it is sometimes known as *Deming regression* (see, e.g., \[19\] for a historical overview). Such models are also known as *errors-in-variables* regression models.

Our kick-off point is the formulation in Eq. [(6.65)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq148). Let ***e*** be the correction vector to be applied on ***y*** and *E* the correction matrix to be applied on *X*. The method of *total least-squares* (TLS) computes the unknown parameter vector by solving the following optimization task:

minimize ∥\[*E* ⋮ **e**\]∥[*F*], s.t. **y** − **e** ∈ ℛ(*X* − *E*).<mml:math><mml:mtext id="mmlbr0015">minimize</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0015" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si364.png)(6.67) 

Recall ([Remarks 6.1](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#enun0015)) that the Frobenius norm of a matrix is defined as the square root of the sum of the squares of all its entries, and it is the direct generalization of the Euclidean norm defined for vectors. Also, note that the set of constraints in [(6.67)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq151) can equivalently be written as

(*X* − *E*)**θ** = **y** − **e**.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si365.png)(6.68) 

It turns out that the solution to the constrained task in [(6.67)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq151) is given by,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/fx021.jpg)(6.69) 

where ${\\overline{\\sigma}}\_{l + 1}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si366.png) is the smallest (nonzero) singular value of \[*X*⋮**y**\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si367.png). Under some general assumptions this solution is unique. See the chapter's Additional Material part for a detailed proof and related comments.

### Geometric interpretation of the total least-squares method

Inserting the solution obtained from Eq. [(6.69)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq153) into Eq. [(6.68)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq152), the latter can be rewritten as,

${(\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{e}\_{n})}^{T}{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{TLS} - (y\_{n} - e\_{n}) = 0,\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="bold">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">TLS</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si368.png)(6.70) 

In words, both the regressors **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si5.png) and the outputs *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si369.png) are corrected in order for the points (*y*[*n*] − *e*[*n*], **x**[*n*] − **e**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si370.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si361.png), to lie on a hyperplane in ℝ^(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si371.png). Also, once such a hyperplane is computed and it is unique, it has an interesting interpretation. It is the hyperplane that *minimizes the total squared distance* of all the training points (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si372.png)) from it. Moreover, the corrected points (*y*[*n*] − *e*[*n*], **x**[*n*] − **e**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si373.png), are the *orthogonal projections* of the respective (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si374.png) training examples onto this hyperplane (see Additional Material part). This is illustrated in [Fig. 6.12](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#f0075).

![Figure 6.12 The total least-squares method corrects both the values of the output variable as well as the input vector so that the points, after the correction, lie on a hyperplane. The corrected points are the orthogonal projections of (yn, xn) on the respective hyperplane; for centered data, this crosses the origin. For noncentered data, it crosses the centroid (\\overline{y},\\overline{\\mathbf{x}})Equation.](images/B9780443292385000123/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 6.12](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#cf0730) The total least-squares method corrects both the values of the output variable as well as the input vector so that the points, after the correction, lie on a hyperplane. The corrected points are the orthogonal projections of (*y*[*n*], ***x***[*n*]) on the respective hyperplane; for centered data, this crosses the origin. For noncentered data, it crosses the centroid $(\\overline{y},\\overline{\\mathbf{x}})$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si375.png).

The Total Least-Squares method has been used in a number of applications, such as computer vision \[47\], system identification \[59\], speech and image processing \[25,51\], and spectral analysis \[63\]. A distributed algorithm for solving the TLS task in ad hoc sensor networks has been proposed in \[4\]. A recursive scheme for the efficient solution of the TLS task has appeared in \[12\]. For further reading, the interested reader can look at \[37,64\] and the references therein.

Example 6.3

To demonstrate the potential of the TLS to improve upon the performance of the LS estimator, in this example, we use noise in the output as well as in the input samples. To this end, we generate randomly an input matrix, *X* ∈ ℝ^(150 × 90)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>150</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si376.png), filling it with elements according to the normalized Gaussian, 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png). In the sequel, we generate the vector **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(90)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si377.png) by randomly drawing samples also from the normalized Gaussian. The output vector is formed as

**y** = *X***θ**[*o*].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si378.png)

Then we generate a noise vector **η** ∈ ℝ^(150)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>150</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si379.png), filling it with elements randomly drawn from 𝒩(0, 0.01)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si380.png), and form

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y} + \\mathbf{\\eta}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si381.png)

A noisy version of the input matrix is obtained as

*X̃* = *X* + *E*,<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si382.png)

where *E* is filled randomly with elements by drawing samples from 𝒩(0, 0.2)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si383.png).

Using the generated $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},X,\\widetilde{X}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si384.png) and pretending that we do not know **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si33.png), the following three estimates are obtained for its value.

*   •  Using the LS estimator Eq. [(6.5)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq12) together with *X* and $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si385.png), the average (over 10 different realizations) Euclidean distance of the obtained estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si386.png) from the true one is equal to $\\|\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}\\| = 0.0125$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0125</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si387.png).
*   •  Using the LS estimator Eq. [(6.5)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq12) together with *X̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si388.png) and $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si385.png), the average (over 10 different realizations) Euclidean distance of the obtained estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si386.png) from the true one is equal to $\\|\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}\\| = 0.4272$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.4272</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si389.png).
*   •  Using the TLS estimator Eq. [(6.69)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq153) together with *X̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si388.png) and $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si385.png), the average (over 10 different realizations) Euclidean distance of the obtained estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si386.png) from the true one is equal to $\\|\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}\\| = 0.2652$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2652</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si390.png).

Observe that using noisy input data, the LS estimator resulted in higher error compared to the TLS one. Note, however, that the successful application of the TLS presupposes that the assumptions that led to the TLS estimator are valid.

## Problems

1.  6.1  Show that if *A* ∈ ℂ^(*m* × *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si391.png) is positive semidefinite, its trace is nonnegative.
2.  6.2  Show that under (a) the independence assumption of successive observation vectors and (b) the presence of white noise independent of the input, the LS estimator is asymptotically distributed according to the normal distribution, i.e.,
