### Computer exercises

1.  6.20  Consider the regression model

*y*[*n*] = **θ**[*o*]^(*T*)**x**[*n*] + *η*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si328.png)

1.  where **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(200)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>200</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si329.png) (*l* = 200<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>200</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si429.png)) and the coefficients of the unknown vector are obtained randomly via the Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png). The noise samples are also i.i.d., according to a Gaussian of zero mean and variance *σ*[*η*]² = 0.01<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si330.png). The input sequence is a white noise one, i.i.d. generated via the Gaussian 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png).
2.  Using as training data the samples (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^(200), *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>200</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si431.png), run the APA ([Algorithm 5.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)), the NLMS algorithm ([Algorithm 5.3](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)), and the RLS algorithm ([Algorithm 6.1](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#enun0020)) to estimate the unknown **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si33.png).
3.  For the APA, choose *μ* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si335.png), *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si334.png), and *q* = 30<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>30</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si336.png). Furthermore, in the NLMS set *μ* = 1.2<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si333.png) and *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si334.png). Finally, for the RLS set the forgetting factor *β* equal to 1. Run 100 independent experiments and plot the average error per iteration in dBs, i.e., 10log[10](*e*[*n*]²)<mml:math><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si332.png), where *e*[*n*]² = (*y*[*n*] − **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*n* − 1])²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si432.png). Compare the performance of the algorithms.
4.  Keep playing with different parameters and study their effect on the convergence speed and the error floor in which the algorithms converge.
5.  6.21  Consider the linear system

*y*[*n*] = **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*o*, *n* − 1] + *η*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si338.png)(6.74) 

1.  where *l* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si434.png) and the unknown vector is time-varying. Generate the unknown vector with respect to the following model:

**θ**[*o*, *n*] = *α***θ**[*o*, *n* − 1] + **ω**[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si339.png)

1.  where *α* = 0.97<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.97</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si342.png) and the coefficients of **ω**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si435.png) are i.i.d. drawn from the Gaussian distribution, with zero mean and variance equal to 0.1. Generate the initial value **θ**[*o*, 0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si345.png) with respect to 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png).
2.  The noise samples are i.i.d., having zero mean and variance equal to 0.001. Furthermore, generate the input samples so that they follow the Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png). Compare the performance of the NLMS and RLS algorithms. For the NLMS, set *μ* = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si347.png) and *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si334.png). For the RLS, set the forgetting factor *β* equal to 0.995. Run 200 independent experiments and plot the average error per iteration in dBs, i.e., 10log[10](*e*[*n*]²)<mml:math><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si332.png), with *e*[*n*]² = (*y*[*n*] − **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*n* − 1])²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si432.png). Compare the performance of the algorithms.
3.  Keep the same parameters, but set the variance associated with **ω**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si437.png) equal to 0.01, 0.001<mml:math><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si438.png). Play with different values of the parameters and the variance of the noise **ω**.
4.  6.22  Generate a 150 × 90<mml:math><mml:mn>150</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si439.png) matrix *X*, the entries of which follow the Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png). Generate the vector **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(90)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si377.png). The components of this vector are i.i.d. obtained, also, via the Gaussian 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si344.png). Compute the vector **y** = *X***θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si441.png). Add a 90 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>90</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si442.png) noise vector, ***η***, to ***y*** in order to generate $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y} + \\mathbf{\\eta}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si443.png). The elements of ***η*** are generated via the Gaussian 𝒩(0, 0.01)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si380.png). In the sequel, add a 150 × 90<mml:math><mml:mn>150</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si439.png) noise matrix, *E*, so as to produce *X̃* = *X* + *E*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si444.png); the elements of *E* are generated according to the Gaussian 𝒩(0, 0.2)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si383.png). Compute the LS estimate via Eq. [(6.5)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq12) by employing (a) the true input matrix *X* and the noisy output $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si385.png); and (b) the noisy input matrix *X̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si388.png) and the noisy output $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si385.png).
5.  In the sequel, compute the TLS estimate via Eq. [(6.69)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml#deq153) using the noisy input matrix *X̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si388.png) and the noisy output $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si385.png).
6.  Repeat the experiments a number of times and compute the average Euclidean distances between the obtained estimates for the previous three cases and the true parameter vector **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000123/si33.png).
7.  Play with different noise levels and comment on the results.

## 7.1 Introduction

The classification task was introduced in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). There, it was pointed out that, in principle, one could employ the same loss functions as those used for regression in order to optimize the design of a classifier; however, for most cases in practice, this is not the most reasonable way to attack such problems. This is because in classification the output random variable, y, is of a *discrete nature*; hence, different measures than those used for the regression task are more appropriate for quantifying performance quality.

The goal of this chapter is to present a number of widely used loss functions and methods. Most of the techniques covered are conceptually simple and constitute the basic pillars on which classification is built. Besides their pedagogical importance, these techniques are still in use in a number of practical applications and often form the basis for the development of more advanced methods, to be covered later in the book.

The classical Bayesian classification rule, the notion of minimum distance classifiers, the logistic regression loss function, Fisher's linear discriminant, classification trees, and the method of combining classifiers, including the powerful technique of boosting, are discussed. The perceptron rule, although it boasts to be among the most basic classification rules, will be treated in Chapter [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml) and it will be used as the starting point for introducing neural networks and deep learning techniques. Support vector machines are treated in the framework of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml).

In a nutshell, this chapter can be considered a beginner's tour of the task of designing classifiers.

## 7.2 Bayesian classification

In Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), a linear classifier was designed via the least-squares (LS) method. However, the squared error criterion cannot serve well the needs of the classification task. In Chapters [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) and [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml), we have proved that the LS estimator is an efficient one only if the conditional distribution of the output variable y, given the feature values ***x***, follows a Gaussian one of a special type. However, in classification, the dependent variable is discrete, hence it is not Gaussian; thus, the use of the squared error criterion cannot be justified, in general. We will return to this issue in Section [7.10](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#s0105) ([Remarks 7.7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#enun0065)), where the squared error is discussed against other loss functions used in classification.

In this section, the classification task will be approached via a different path, inspired by the *Bayesian decision theory*. In spite of its conceptual simplicity, which ties very well with common sense, Bayesian classification possesses a strong optimality flavor with respect to the probability of error, that is, the probability of wrong decisions/class predictions that a classifier commits.

*Bayesian classification rule*: Given a set of *M* classes, *ω*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si1.png), and the respective *posterior probabilities* *P*(*ω*[*i*]|**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si2.png), classify a feature vector, ***x***, according to the following rule:^([^(44)](#fn44))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/fx001.jpg)(7.1) 

In words, the pattern represented by ***x*** is assigned to the class for which the posterior probability becomes maximum. Sometimes, we refer to this rule, also, as the *Bayes classifier*.

Note that prior to receiving any observation, our uncertainty concerning the classes is expressed via the prior class probabilities, denoted by *P*(*ω*[*i*]), *i* = 1, 2, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si3.png). Once the feature vector, ***x***, has been obtained, this extra information removes part of our original uncertainty, and the related statistical information is now provided by the posterior probabilities, which are then used for the classification.

Employing in [(7.1)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#deq1) the Bayes theorem,

$P(\\omega\_{j}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{j})P(\\omega\_{j})}{p(\\mathbf{x})},\\quad j = 1,2,\\ldots,M,$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si4.png)(7.2) 

where *p*(**x**|*ω*[*j*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si5.png) are the respective conditional PDFs, the Bayesian classification rule becomes

$\\text{Assign}\\ \\mathbf{x}\\ \\text{to}\\ \\omega\_{i} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\omega\_{j}}p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{j})P(\\omega\_{j}),\\quad j = 1,2\\ldots,M.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>Assign</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si6.png)(7.3) 

Note that the probability density function (PDF) of the data, *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si7.png), in the denominator of Eq. [(7.2)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#deq2), does not enter in the maximization task, because it is a positive quantity independent of the classes *ω*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si8.png); hence, it does not affect the maximization. In other words, the classifier depends on the a priori class probabilities and the respective conditional PDFs. Also, recall that

*p*(**x**|*ω*[*j*])*P*(*ω*[*j*]) = *p*(*ω*[*j*], **x**) :  = *p*(*y*, **x**),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si9.png)

where in the current context, the output variable, *y*, denotes the label associated with the corresponding class *ω*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si10.png). The last equation verifies what was said in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml); that is, the Bayesian classifier is a generative modeling technique.

We now turn our attention to how one can obtain estimates of the involved quantities. Recall that in practice, all one has at one's disposal is a set of training data, from which estimates of the prior probabilities as well as the conditional PDFs must be obtained. Let us assume that we are given a set of training points, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ *D* × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si11.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si12.png), where *D* is the discrete set of class labels, and consider the general task comprising *M* classes. Assume that each class *ω*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si1.png), is represented by *N*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si13.png) points in the training set, with $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{M}N\_{i} = N$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si14.png). Then the a priori probabilities can be approximated by

$P(\\omega\_{i}) \\approx \\frac{N\_{i}}{N},\\quad i = 1,2,\\ldots,M.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si15.png)(7.4) 

For the conditional PDFs, *p*(**x**|*ω*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si16.png), *i* = 1, 2…, *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si17.png), any method for estimating PDFs can be mobilized. For example, one can assume a known parametric form for each one of the conditionals and adopt the maximum likelihood (ML) method, discussed in Section [3.10](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), or the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, discussed in Section [3.11.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), in order to obtain estimates of the parameters using the training data from each one of the classes. Another alternative is to resort to nonparametric histogram-like techniques, such as Parzen windows and the *k*\-nearest neighbor density estimation techniques, as discussed in Section [3.15](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). Other methods for PDF estimation can also be employed, such as mixture modeling, to be discussed in Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). The interested reader may also consult \[38,39\].

### The Bayesian classifier minimizes the misclassification error

In Section [3.4](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), it was pointed out that the goal of designing a classifier is to partition the space in which the feature vectors lie into regions, and associate each one of the regions to one and only one class. For a two-class task (the generalization to more classes is straightforward), let ℛ[1], ℛ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si18.png) be the two regions in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si19.png), where we decide in favor of class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si20.png) and *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si21.png), respectively. The probability of classification error is given by

*P*[*e*] = *P*(**x** ∈ ℛ[1], **x** ∈ *ω*[2]) + *P*(**x** ∈ ℛ[2], **x** ∈ *ω*[1]).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si22.png)(7.5) 

That is, it is equal to the probability of the feature vector to belong to class *ω*[1] (*ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si23.png) *and* to lie in the “wrong” region ℛ[2] (ℛ[1])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si24.png) in the feature space.

Eq. [(7.5)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#deq6) can be written as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/fx002.jpg)(7.6) 

It turns out that the Bayesian classifier, as defined in [(7.3)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#deq3), minimizes *P*[*e*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si25.png) with respect to ℛ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si26.png) and ℛ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si27.png) \[11,38\]. This is also true for the general case of *M* classes (Problem [7.1](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#o0010)).

[Fig. 7.1](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#f0010)A demonstrates geometrically the optimality of the Bayesian classifier for the two-class one-dimensional case and assuming equiprobable classes (*P*(*ω*[1]) = *P*(*ω*[2]) = 1/2<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si113.png)). The region ℛ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si26.png), to the left of the threshold value *x*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si30.png), corresponds to *p*(*x*|*ω*[1]) > *p*(*x*|*ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si31.png), and the opposite is true for region ℛ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si27.png). The probability of error is equal to the area of the shaded region, which is equal to the sum of the two integrals in Eq. [(7.6)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#deq7). In [Fig. 7.1](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml#f0010)B, the threshold has been moved away from the optimal Bayesian value, and as a result the probability of error, given by the total area of the corresponding shaded region, increases.

(B) Moving the threshold value away from the value corresponding to the optimal Bayes rule increases the probability of error, as is indicated by the increase of the area of the corresponding shaded region.

### 7.2.1 Average risk

Because in classification the dependent variable (label), y, is of a discrete nature, the classification error probability may seem like the most natural cost function to be optimized. However, this is not always true. In certain applications, not all errors are of the same importance. For example, in a medical diagnosis system, committing an error by predicting the class of a finding in an X-ray image as being “malignant” while its true class is “normal” is less significant than an error the other way around. In the former case, the wrong diagnosis will be revealed in the next set of medical tests. However, the opposite may have unwanted consequences. For such cases, one uses an alternative to the probability of error cost function that puts relative weights on the errors according to their importance. This cost function is known as the *average risk* and it results in a rule that resembles that of the Bayesian classifier, yet it is slightly modified due to the presence of the weights.

Let us start from the simpler two-class case. The *risk* or *loss* associated with each one of the two classes is defined as

$r\_{1} = \\lambda\_{11}\\int\_{\\mathcal{R}\_{1}}p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{1})d\\mathbf{x} + \\lambda\_{12}\\underset{\\text{error}}{\\underset{︸}{\\int\_{\\mathcal{R}\_{2}}p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{1})d\\mathbf{x}}},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>error</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si32.png)(7.7) 

$r\_{2} = \\lambda\_{21}\\underset{\\text{error}}{\\underset{︸}{\\int\_{\\mathcal{R}\_{1}}p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{2})d\\mathbf{x}}} + \\lambda\_{22}\\int\_{\\mathcal{R}\_{2}}p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{2})d\\mathbf{x}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>21</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>error</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si33.png)(7.8) 

Typically, *λ*[11] = *λ*[22] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si34.png), since they correspond to correct decisions. The *average* risk, to be minimized, is given by

*r* = *P*(*ω*[1])*r*[1] + *P*(*ω*[2])*r*[2].<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/si35.png)

Then, following similar arguments as before for the optimal Bayes classifier, the optimal average risk classifier rule becomes

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000135/fx003.jpg)(7.9)

$\\text{Assign}\\ \\mathbf{x}\\ \\text{to}\\ \\omega\_{1}\\ (\\omega\_{2})\\ \\text{if}:\\underset{P^{\\prime}(\\omega\_{1})}{\\underset{︸}{\\lambda\_{12}P(\\omega\_{1})}}p(\\mathbf{x}|\\omega\_{1}) > stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace
