## 8.1 Introduction

The theory of convex sets and functions has a rich history and has been the focus of intense study for over a century in mathematics. In the terrain of applied sciences and engineering, the revival of interest in convex functions and optimization is traced back to the early 1980s. In addition to the increased processing power that became available via the use of computers, certain theoretical developments were catalytic in demonstrating the power of such techniques. For example, the advent of the so-called interior point methods opened a new path in solving the classical linear programming task. Moreover, it was increasingly realized that, despite its advantages, the least-squares (LS) method also has a number of drawbacks, particularly in the presence of non-Gaussian noise and the presence of outliers. It has been demonstrated that the use of alternative loss functions, which may not even be differentiable, can alleviate a number of problems that are associated with the LS methods. Furthermore, the increased interest in robust learning methods brought into the scene the need for nontrivial constraints, which the optimized solution has to respect. In the machine learning community, the discovery of support vector machines, to be treated in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), played an important role in popularizing convex optimization techniques.

The goal of this chapter is to present some basic notions and definitions related to convex analysis and optimization in the context of machine learning and signal processing. Convex optimization is a discipline in itself, and it cannot be summarized in one chapter. The emphasis here is on computationally light techniques with a focus on online versions, which are gaining in importance in the context of big data applications. A related discussion is also part of this chapter.

The material revolves around two families of algorithms. One goes back to the classical work of Von Neumann on projections on convex sets, which is reviewed together with its more recent online versions. The notions of projection and related properties are treated in some detail. The method of projections, in the context of constrained optimization, has gained in popularity over the recent years.

The other family of algorithms that is considered builds around the notion of subgradient for optimizing nondifferentiable convex functions and generalizations of the gradient descent family, discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). Furthermore, a powerful tool for analyzing the performance of online algorithms for convex optimization, known as regret analysis, is discussed and a related case study is presented. Finally, some current trends in convex optimization involving proximal and mirror descent methods are introduced.

## 8.2 Convex sets and functions

Although most of the algorithms we will discuss in this chapter refer to vector variables in Euclidean spaces, which is in line with what we have done so far in this book, the definitions and some of the fundamental theorems will be stated in the context of the more general case of Hilbert spaces.^([^(49)](#fn49))

### 8.2.1 Convex sets

Definition 8.1

A nonempty subset *C* of a Hilbert space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png), *C* ⊆ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si2.png), is called *convex* if ∀ **x**[1], **x**[2] ∈ *C*<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si3.png) and ∀*λ* ∈ \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si4.png) the following holds true:^([^(50)](#fn50))

**x** :  = *λ***x**[1] + (1 − *λ*)**x**[2] ∈ *C*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si5.png)(8.1) 

Note that if *λ* = 1, **x** = **x**[1]<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si6.png), and if *λ* = 0, **x** = **x**[2]<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si7.png). For any other value of *λ* in \[0, 1\], **x**<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si8.png) lies in the line segment joining **x**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si9.png) and **x**[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si10.png). Indeed, from Eq. [(8.1)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq1) we can write

**x** − **x**[2] = *λ*(**x**[1] − **x**[2]), 0 ≤ *λ* ≤ 1.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si11.png)

[Fig. 8.1](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0010) shows two examples of convex sets, in the two-dimensional Euclidean space, ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si12.png). In [Fig. 8.1](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0010)A, the set comprises all points whose Euclidean (ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si13.png)) norm is less than or equal to one,

$C\_{2} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x}:\\sqrt{x\_{1}^{2} + x\_{2}^{2}} \\leq 1 \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si14.png)

Sometimes we refer to *C*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si15.png) as the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si13.png)\-*ball* of radius equal to one. Note that the set includes all the points *on and inside the circle*. The set in [Fig. 8.1](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0010)B comprises all the points *on and inside the rhombus* defined by

*C*[1] = {**x**:|*x*[1]|+|*x*[2]|≤1}.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si16.png)

Because the sum of the absolute values of the components of a vector defines the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) norm, that is, ∥**x**∥[1] :  = |*x*[1]| + |*x*[2]|<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si18.png), in analogy to *C*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si15.png) we call the set *C*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si19.png) as the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) ball of radius equal to one. In contrast, the sets whose ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si13.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) norms are equal to one, or in other words

${\\overline{C}}\_{2} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x}:x\_{1}^{2} + x\_{2}^{2} = 1 \\right\\},{\\overline{C}}\_{1} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x}:|x\_{1}| + |x\_{2}| = 1 \\right\\}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si20.png)

are not convex (Problem [8.2](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0040)). [Fig. 8.2](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0015) shows two examples of nonconvex sets.

### 8.2.2 Convex functions

Definition 8.2

A function

*f*: 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si21.png)

is called *convex* if 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si22.png) is convex and if ∀ **x**[1], **x**[2] ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si23.png) the following holds true:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx001.jpg)(8.2) 

The function is called *strictly convex* if Eq. [(8.2)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq7) holds true with strict inequality when *λ* ∈ (0, 1), **x**[1] ≠ **x**[2]<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si24.png). The geometric interpretation of Eq. [(8.2)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq7) is that the line segment joining the points (**x**[1], *f*(**x**[1]))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si25.png) and (**x**[2], *f*(**x**[2]))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si26.png) lies above the graph of *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si27.png), as shown in [Fig. 8.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0020). We say that a function is *concave* (*strictly concave*) if the negative, −*f*, is convex (strictly convex). Next, we state three important theorems.

Theorem 8.1

First-order convexity condition

*Let* 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si28.png) *be a convex set and let*

*f* : 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si29.png)

*be a differentiable function. Then f is convex if and only if* ∀ **x**, **y** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si30.png)*,*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx002.jpg)(8.3) 

The proof of the theorem is given in Problem [8.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0045). The theorem generalizes to nondifferentiable convex functions; it will be discussed in this context in Section [8.10](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0090).

![Figure 8.3 The line segment joining the points (x1,f(x1)) and (x2,f(x2)) lies above the graph of f(x). The shaded region corresponds to the epigraph of the function.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr003.jpg)

Figure 8.3 The line segment joining the points (*x*[1],*f*(*x*[1])) and (*x*[2],*f*(*x*[2])) lies above the graph of *f*(*x*). The shaded region corresponds to the epigraph of the function.

[Fig. 8.4](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0025) illustrates the geometric interpretation of this theorem. It means that the graph of the convex function is located above the graph of the affine function

*g* : **y** ↦ ∇^(*T*)*f*(**x**)(**y** − **x**) + *f*(**x**),<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si31.png)

which defines the tangent hyperplane of the graph at the point (**x**,*f*(**x**))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si32.png).

![Figure 8.4 The graph of a convex function is above the tangent plane at any point of the respective graph.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 8.4](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0260) The graph of a convex function is above the tangent plane at any point of the respective graph.

Theorem 8.2

Second-order convexity condition

*Let* 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si28.png) *be a convex set. Then a twice differentiable function* *f* : 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si33.png) *is convex (strictly convex) if and only if the Hessian matrix is positive semidefinite (positive definite).*

The proof of the theorem is given in Problem [8.5](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0055). Recall that in previous chapters, when we dealt with the squared error loss function, we commented that it is a convex one. Now we are ready to justify this argument. Consider the quadratic function,

$f(\\mathbf{x}): = \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{x}^{T}Q\\mathbf{x} + \\mathbf{b}^{T}\\mathbf{x} + c,$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si34.png)

where *Q* is a positive definite matrix. Taking the gradient, we have

∇*f*(**x**) = *Q***x** + **b**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si35.png)

and the Hessian matrix is equal to *Q*, which by assumption is positive definite, hence *f* is a (strictly) convex function.

In the sequel, two very important notions in convex analysis and optimization are defined.

Definition 8.3

The *epigraph* of a function *f* is defined as the set of points

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx003.jpg)(8.4) 

From a geometric point of view, the epigraph is the set of all points in ℝ^(*l*) × ℝ<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si36.png) that lie on and above the graph of *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si27.png), as indicated by the gray shaded region in [Fig. 8.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0020). It is important to note that a function is convex *if and only if* its epigraph is a convex set (Problem [8.6](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0060)).

Definition 8.4

Given a real number *ξ*, the *lower level set* of a function *f* : 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si298.png) at *height ξ* is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx004.jpg)(8.5) 

In words, it is the set of all points at which the function takes a value less than or equal to *ξ*. The geometric interpretation of the level set is shown in [Fig. 8.5](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0030). It can easily be shown (Problem [8.7](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0065)) that if a function *f* is convex, then its lower level set is convex for any *ξ* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si38.png). The converse is not true. We can easily check that the function *f*(*x*) =  − exp (*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si39.png) is not convex (as a matter of fact it is concave) and all its lower level sets are convex.

Theorem 8.3

Local and global minimizers

*Let a convex function* *f* : 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si33.png)*. Then if a point* **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si40.png) *is a local minimizer, it is also a global one, and the set of all minimizers is convex. Further, if the function is strictly convex, the minimizer is unique.*

Proof

Inasmuch as the function is convex we know that ∀ **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si41.png),

*f*(**x**) ≥ *f*(**x**[\*]) + ∇^(*T*)*f*(**x**[\*])(**x** − **x**[\*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si42.png)

and because at the minimizer the gradient is zero, we get

*f*(**x**) ≥ *f*(**x**[\*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si43.png)(8.6) 

which proves the claim. Let us now denote

$f\_{\\ast} = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}}f(\\mathbf{x}).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si44.png)(8.7) 

Note that the set of all minimizers coincides with the level set at height *f*[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si45.png). Then, because the function is convex, we know that the level set lev[*f*[\*]](*f*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>lev</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si46.png) is convex, which verifies the convexity of the set of minimizers. Finally, for strictly convex functions, the inequality in [(8.6)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq16) is a strict one, which proves the uniqueness of the (global) minimizer. The theorem is also true even if the function is not differentiable (Problem [8.10](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0080)). □

![Figure 8.5 The level set at height ξ comprises all the points in the interval denoted as the “red” segment on the x-axis.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 8.5](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0280) The level set at height *ξ* comprises all the points in the interval denoted as the “red” segment on the *x*\-axis.

## 8.3 Projections onto convex sets

The projection onto a hyperplane in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces was discussed and used in the context of the affine projection algorithm (APA) in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). The notion of projection will now be generalized to include any closed convex set and also in the framework of general (infinite-dimensional) Hilbert spaces.

The concept of projection is among the most fundamental concepts in mathematics, and everyone who has attended classes in basic geometry has used and studied it. What one may not have realized is that while performing a projection, for example, drawing a line segment from a point to a line or a plane, basically he or she solves an *optimization* task. The point **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si40.png) in [Fig. 8.6](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0035), that is, the projection of ***x*** onto the plane *H* in the three-dimensional space, is that point, among all the points lying on the plane, whose (Euclidean) distance from **x** = \[*x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[3]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si48.png) is minimum; in other words,

$\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast} = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in H}\\left( {(x\_{1} - y\_{1})}^{2} + {(x\_{2} - y\_{2})}^{2} + {(x\_{3} - y\_{3})}^{2} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si49.png)(8.8) 

 As a matter of fact, what we have learned to do in our early days at school is to solve a *constrained optimization* task. Indeed, Eq. [(8.8)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq18) can equivalently be written as

$\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y}}||\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{y}||^{2},\\text{s.t.}\\quad\\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{y} + \\theta\_{0} = 0,$<mml:math><mml:msub id="mmlbr0001"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0001" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si50.png)

where the constraint is the equation describing the specific plane. Our goal herein focuses on generalizing the notion of projection, to employ it to attack more general and complex tasks.

Theorem 8.4

*Let C be a nonempty closed*^([^(51)](#fn51))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx005.jpg)

*The term* *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si54.png) *is called the (metric) projection of* ***x*** *onto C. Note that if* **x** ∈ *C*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si55.png)*, then* *P*[*C*](**x**) = **x**<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si56.png)*, since this makes the norm* ∥**x** − *P*[*C*](**x**)∥ = 0<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si57.png)*.*

![Figure 8.6 The projection x⁎ of x onto the plane minimizes the distance of x from all the points lying on the plane.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 8.6](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0300) The projection ***x***[⁎] of ***x*** onto the plane minimizes the distance of ***x*** from all the points lying on the plane.

Proof

The proof comprises two paths. One is to establish *uniqueness* and the other to establish *existence*. Uniqueness is easier, and the proof will be given here. Existence is slightly more technical, and its proof is provided in Problem [8.11](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0085).

To show *uniqueness*, assume that there are two points, **x**[\*,1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si58.png) and **x**[\*,2], **x**[\*,1] ≠ **x**[\*,2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si59.png), such that

$\\|\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,1}\\| = \\|\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,2}\\| = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in C}\\|\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{y}\\|.$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si60.png)(8.9) 

1.  **(a)**  If **x** ∈ *C*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si55.png), then *P*[*C*](**x**) = **x**<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si56.png) is unique, since any other point in *C* would make ∥**x** − *P*[*C*](**x**)∥ > 0<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si63.png).
2.  **(b)**  Let **x** ∉ *C*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si64.png). [(8.9)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq21) and the fact that ∥**x**[\*,1] − **x**[\*,2]∥ > 0<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si67.png), we have

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{x} - \\left( \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,1} + \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,2} \\right) \\right\\|^{2} < {\\|\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,1}\\|}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si68.png)(8.10) 

1.  However, due to the convexity of *C*, the point $\\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,1} + \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast ,2}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si69.png) lies in *C*. Also, by the definition of projection, **x**[\*,1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si58.png) is the point with the smallest distance, and hence the inequality in [(8.10)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq24) cannot be valid. □

For the existence, one has to use the property of closeness (every sequence in *C* has its limit in *C*) as well as the property of completeness of Hilbert spaces, which guarantees that every Cauchy sequence in ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) has a limit (see chapter's appendix). The proof is given in Problem [8.11](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0085).

Remarks 8.1

*   •  Note that if **x** ∉ *C* ⊆ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si70.png), then its projection onto *C* lies on the *boundary* of *C* (Problem [8.12](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0090)).

Example 8.1

Derive analytical expressions for the projections of a point **x** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si52.png), where ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) is a real Hilbert space, onto (a) a hyperplane, (b) a halfspace, and (c) the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si13.png) ball of radius *δ*.

1.  **(a)**  A hyperplane *H* is defined as

*H* :  = {**y**:⟨**θ**,**y**⟩+*θ*[0]\=0},<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

If ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) breaks down to a Euclidean space, the projection is readily available by simple geometric arguments, and it is given by
