Remarks 8.2

*   •  In the context of sparsity-aware learning, which is dealt with in Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml), a key point is the projection of a point in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si86.png) (ℂ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si87.png)) onto the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) ball. There it is shown that, given the size of the ball, this projection corresponds to the so-called soft thresholding operation (see, also, [Example 8.10](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#enun0260) for a definition).
*   It should be stressed that a linear space equipped with the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) norm is no more Euclidean (Hilbert), inasmuch as this norm *is not induced* by an inner product operation; moreover, uniqueness of the projection with respect to this norm is not guaranteed (Problem [8.15](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0105)). 

### 8.3.1 Properties of projections

In this section, we summarize some basic properties of the projections. These properties are used to prove a number of theorems and convergence results associated with algorithms that are developed around the notion of projection.

Readers who are interested only in the algorithms can bypass this subsection.

Proposition 8.1

*Let* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) *be a Hilbert space,* *C* ⫅ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>⫅</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si89.png) *be a closed convex set, and* **x** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si52.png)*. Then the projection* *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si54.png) *satisfies the following two properties:*^([^(52)](#fn52))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx009.jpg)(8.14) 

*and*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx010.jpg)(8.15) 

The proof of the proposition is provided in Problem [8.16](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0110). The geometric interpretation of [(8.15)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq30) for the case of real Euclidean space is shown in [Fig. 8.10](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0060). Note that for a real Hilbert space, the first property becomes

⟨**x** − *P*[*C*](**x**), **y** − *P*[*C*](**x**)⟩ ≤ 0, ∀**y** ∈ *C*.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si90.png)(8.16) 

From the geometric point of view, [(8.17)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq32) means that the angle formed by the two vectors **x** − *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si91.png) and **y** − *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si92.png) is *obtuse*. The hyperplane that crosses *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si54.png) and is orthogonal to **x** − *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si91.png) is known as *supporting* hyperplane and it leaves all points in *C* on one side and ***x*** on the other. It can be shown that if *C* is closed and convex and **x** ∉ *C*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si64.png), there is always such a hyperplane (see, for example, \[30\]).

Lemma 8.1

*Let S be a closed subspace* *S* ⊆ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si94.png) *in a Hilbert space* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png)*. Then* ∀ **x**, **y** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si100.png)*, the following properties hold true:*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx011.jpg)(8.17) 

*and*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx012.jpg)(8.18) 

*where a and b are arbitrary scalars. In other words, the projection operation on a closed subspace is a linear one (Problem* [8.17](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0115)*). Recall that in a Euclidean space all subspaces are closed, and hence the linearity is always valid.*

![Figure 8.10 The vectors y − PC(x) and x − PC(x) form an obtuse angle, ϕ.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr010.jpg)

[Figure 8.10](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0395) The vectors ***y*** − *P*[*C*](***x***) and ***x*** − *P*[*C*](***x***) form an obtuse angle, *ϕ*.

It can be shown (Problem [8.18](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0120)) that if *S* is a closed subspace in a Hilbert space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png), its orthogonal complement, *S*^⊥<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si96.png), is also a closed subspace, such that *S* ∩ *S*^⊥ = {0}<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>∩</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si637.png); by definition, the orthogonal compliment *S*^⊥<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si96.png) is the set whose elements are orthogonal to each element of *S*. Moreover, ℍ = *S* ⊕ *S*^⊥<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊕</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si98.png); that is, each element **x** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si52.png) can be *uniquely* decomposed as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx013.jpg)(8.19) 

as demonstrated in [Fig. 8.11](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0065).

Definition 8.5

Let a mapping

*T* : ℍ ↦ ℍ.<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si99.png)

*T* is called *nonexpansive* if ∀ **x**, **y** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si100.png)

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx014.jpg)(8.20) 

![Figure 8.11 Every point in a Hilbert space \\mathbb{H}Equation can be uniquely decomposed into the sum of its projections on any closed subspace S and its orthogonal complement S⊥.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 8.11](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0420) Every point in a Hilbert space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) can be uniquely decomposed into the sum of its projections on any *closed* subspace *S* and its orthogonal complement *S*^⊥.

Proposition 8.2

*Let C be a closed convex set in a Hilbert space* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png)*. Then the associated projection operator*

*P*[*C*] : ℍ ↦ *C*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si101.png)

*is nonexpansive.* 

Proof

Let **x**, **y** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si102.png). Recall property [(8.16)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq31), that is,

∥*P*[*C*](**x**) − *P*[*C*](**y**)∥² ≤ Real{⟨**x**−**y**,*P*[*C*](**x**)−*P*[*C*](**y**)⟩}.<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Real</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si103.png)(8.21) 

Moreover, by employing the Schwarz inequality (Eq. (8.149) of chapter's appendix), we get

|⟨**x** − **y**, *P*[*C*](**x**) − *P*[*C*](**y**)⟩| ≤ ∥**x** − **y**∥∥*P*[*C*](**x**) − *P*[*C*](**y**)∥.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si104.png)(8.22) 

Combining the inequalities in [(8.22)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq39) and [(8.23)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq40), we readily obtain

∥*P*[*C*](**x**) − *P*[*C*](**y**)∥ ≤ ∥**x** − **y**∥.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si105.png)(8.23) 

 □

[Fig. 8.12](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0070) provides a geometric interpretation of [(8.24)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq41). The property of nonexpansiveness, as well as a number of its variants (for example, \[6,7,30,81,82\]), is of paramount importance in convex set theory and learning. It is the property that guarantees the convergence of an algorithm, which comprises a sequence of successive projections (mappings), to the so-called *fixed point set*, that is, to the set whose elements are left unaffected by the respective mapping *T*, i.e.,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx015.jpg)

In the case of a projection operator on a closed convex set, we know that the respective fixed point set is the set *C* itself, since *P*[*C*](**x**) = **x**, ∀**x** ∈ *C*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si106.png).

Definition 8.6

Let *C* be a closed convex set *C* in a Hilbert space. An operator

*T*[*C*] : ℍ ↦ *C*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si107.png)

is called *relaxed projection* if

*T*[*C*] :  = *I* + *μ*(*P*[*C*] − *I*), *μ* ∈ (0, 2),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si108.png)

or in other words, ∀ **x** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si109.png),

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx016.jpg)

![Figure 8.12 The nonexpansiveness property of the projection operator, PC(⋅), guarantees that the distance between two points can never be smaller than the distance between their respective projections on a closed convex set.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 8.12](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0440) The nonexpansiveness property of the projection operator, *P*[*C*](⋅), guarantees that the distance between two points can never be smaller than the distance between their respective projections on a closed convex set.

We readily see that for *μ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si110.png), *T*[*C*](**x**) = *P*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si111.png). [Fig. 8.13](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0075) shows the geometric illustration of the relaxed projection. Observe that for different values of *μ* ∈ (0, 2)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si112.png), the relaxed projection traces all points in the line segment joining the points ***x*** and **x** + 2(*P*[*C*](**x**)−**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si113.png). Note that

*T*[*C*](**x**) = **x**, ∀**x** ∈ *C*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si114.png)

that is, Fix(*T*[*C*]) = *C*<mml:math><mml:mtext>Fix</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si115.png). Moreover, it can be shown that the relaxed projection operator is also nonexpansive, that is (Problem [8.19](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0125)),

∥*T*[*C*](**x**) − *T*[*C*](**y**)∥ ≤ ∥**x** − **y**∥, ∀*μ* ∈ (0, 2).<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si116.png)

A final property of the relaxed projection, which can also be easily shown (Problem [8.20](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0130)), is the following:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx017.jpg)(8.24) 

Such mappings are known as *η*\-*nonexpansive* or *strongly attracting* mappings; it is guaranteed that the distance ∥*T*[*C*](**x**) − **y**∥<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si117.png) is *smaller* than ∥**x** − **y**∥<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si118.png) at least by the positive quantity *η*∥*T*[*C*](**x**) − **x**∥²<mml:math><mml:mi>η</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si119.png); that is, the fixed point set Fix(*T*[*C*]) = *C*<mml:math><mml:mtext>Fix</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si115.png) *strongly attracts* ***x***. The geometric interpretation is given in [Fig. 8.14](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0080).

![Figure 8.13 Geometric illustration of the relaxed projection operator.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 8.13](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0450) Geometric illustration of the relaxed projection operator.

![Figure 8.14 The relaxed projection is a strongly attracting mapping; TC(x) is closer to any point y ∈ C = Fix(TC) than the point x is.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr014.jpg)

[Figure 8.14](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0465) The relaxed projection is a strongly attracting mapping; *T*[*C*](***x***) is closer to any point ***y*** ∈ *C* = Fix(*T*[*C*]) than the point ***x*** is.

## 8.4 Fundamental theorem of projections onto convex sets

In this section, one of the most celebrated theorems in the theory of convex sets is stated: the fundamental theorem of projections onto convex sets (POCS). This theorem is at the heart of a number of powerful algorithms and methods, some of which are described in this book. The origin of the theorem is traced back to Von Neumann \[98\], who proposed the theorem for the case of two subspaces.

John von Neumann (1903–1957) was a Hungarian-born American of Jewish descent. He was a child prodigy who earned his PhD at age 22. It is difficult to summarize his numerous significant contributions, which range from pure mathematics to economics (he is considered the founder of the game theory) and from quantum mechanics (he laid the foundations of the mathematical framework in quantum mechanics) to computer science (he was involved in the development of ENIAC, the first general purpose electronic computer). He was heavily involved in the Manhattan project for the development of the hydrogen bomb.

Let *C*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si120.png), be a *finite* number of *closed* convex sets in a Hilbert space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png), and assume that they share a *nonempty* intersection,

$C = \\bigcap\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}C\_{k} \\neq \\varnothing.$<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">⋂</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si121.png)

Let *T*[*C*[*k*]], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si122.png), be the respective relaxed projection mappings

*T*[*C*[*k*]] = *I* + *μ*[*k*](*P*[*C*[*k*]] − *I*), *μ*[*k*] ∈ (0, 2), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si123.png)

Form the concatenation of these relaxed projections,

*T* :  = *T*[*C*[*k*]]*T*[*C*[*k* − 1]]⋯*T*[*C*[1]],<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si124.png)

where the specific order is not important. In words, *T* comprises a sequence of relaxed projections, starting from *C*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si19.png). In the sequel, the obtained point is projected onto *C*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si15.png), and so on.

Theorem 8.5

*Let* *C*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si125.png)*, be closed convex sets in a Hilbert space* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png)*, with nonempty intersection. Then for any* **x**[0] ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si126.png)*, the sequence* (*T*^(*n*)(**x**[0])), *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si127.png)*, converges weakly to a point in* $C = \\bigcap\_{k = 1}^{K}C\_{k}$<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si128.png)*.*

The theorem \[17,42\] states the notion of *weak convergence*. When ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) becomes a Euclidean (finite-dimensional) space, the notion of weak convergence coincides with the familiar “standard” definition of (strong) convergence. Weak convergence is a weaker version of strong convergence, and it is met in infinite-dimensional spaces. A sequence **x**[*n*] ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si129.png) is said to converge weakly to a point **x**[\*] ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si130.png) if, ∀ **y** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si131.png),

$\\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{y}\\rangle\\underset{n\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\rightarrow}\\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast},\\mathbf{y}\\rangle,$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo>→</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si132.png)

and we write

$\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\underset{n\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\overset{w}{\\rightarrow}}\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>→</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si133.png)

As already said, in Euclidean spaces, weak convergence implies strong convergence. This is not necessarily true for general Hilbert spaces. On the other hand, strong convergence always implies weak convergence (for example, \[87\]) (Problem [8.21](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0135)).  [Fig. 8.15](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0085) gives the geometric illustration of the theorem.

![Figure 8.15 Geometric illustration of the fundamental theorem of projections onto convex sets (POCS), for T\_{C\_{i}} = P\_{C\_{i}}Equation, i = 1,2\\ (\\mu\_{C\_{i}} = 1)Equation. The closed convex sets are the two straight lines in \\mathbb{R}^{2}Equation, that is, Ci = Hi, i = 1,2. Observe that the sequence of projections tends to the intersection of H1,H2.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr015.jpg)

[Figure 8.15](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0485) Geometric illustration of the fundamental theorem of projections onto convex sets (POCS), for *T*[*C*[*i*]] = *P*[*C*[*i*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si134.png), *i* = 1, 2 (*μ*[*C*[*i*]] = 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si135.png). The closed convex sets are the two straight lines in ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si12.png), that is, *C*[*i*] = *H*[*i*], *i* = 1,2. Observe that the sequence of projections tends to the intersection of *H*[1],*H*[2].

The proof of the theorem is a bit technical for the general case (for example, \[87\]). However, it can be simplified for the case where the involved convex sets are closed subspaces (Problem [8.23](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0145)). At the heart of the proof lie (a) the nonexpansiveness property of *T*[*C*[*k*]], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si137.png), which is retained by *T*, and (b) the fact that the fixed point set of *T* is $\\text{Fix}(T) = \\bigcap\_{k = 1}^{K}C\_{k}$<mml:math><mml:mtext>Fix</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si138.png).

Remarks 8.3

*   •  In the special case where all *C*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si125.png), are closed subspaces, we have

*T*^(*n*)(**x**[0]) → *P*[*C*](**x**[0]).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si140.png)

*   In other words, the sequence of relaxed projections converges *strongly* to the projection of **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si141.png) on *C*. Recall that if each *C*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si125.png), is a closed subspace of ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png), it can easily be shown that their intersection is also a closed subspace. As said before, in a Euclidean space ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si86.png), all subspaces are closed.
*   •  The previous statement is also true for *linear varieties*. A linear variety is the translation of a subspace by a constant vector ***a***. That is, if *S* is a subspace and **a** ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si142.png), then the set of points

*S*[**a**] = {**y** : **y** = **a** + **x**, **x** ∈ *S*}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si143.png)

*   is a linear variety. Hyperplanes are linear varieties (see, for example, [Fig. 8.16](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0090)).

![Figure 8.16 A hyperplane (not crossing the origin) is a linear variety; P\_{S\_{\\mathbf{a}}}Equation and PS are the projections of x onto Sa and S, respectively.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr016.jpg)

[Figure 8.16](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0500) A hyperplane (not crossing the origin) is a linear variety; *P*[*S*[**a**]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si136.png) and *P*[*S*] are the projections of ***x*** onto *S*[***a***] and *S*, respectively.

*   
*   •  The scheme resulting from the POCS theorem, employing the relaxed projection operator, is summarized in [Algorithm 8.1](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#enun0115).

Algorithm 8.1

**The POCS algorithm**

1.  –  Initialization. 
    1.  ⁎  Select **x**[0] ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si126.png).
    2.  ⁎  Select *μ*[*k*] ∈ (0, 2), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si145.png)
2.  –  **For** *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si146.png), **Do**
    
    1.  ⁎  ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{0,n} = \\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si147.png)
    2.  ⁎  **For** *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si148.png), **Do**
    
    ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{k,n} = {\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{k - 1,n} + \\mu\_{k}\\left( P\_{C\_{k}}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{k - 1,n}) - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{k - 1,n} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" ## 8.5 A parallel version of POCS

In \[68\], a parallel version of the POCS algorithm was stated. In addition to its computational advantages (when parallel processing can be exploited), this scheme will be our vehicle for generalizations to the online processing, where one can cope with the case where the number of convex sets becomes infinite (or very large in practice). The proof for the parallel POCS is slightly technical and relies heavily on the results stated in the previous section. The concept behind the proof is to construct appropriate product spaces, and this is the reason that the algorithm is also referred to as POCS in *product spaces*. For the detailed proof, the interested reader may consult \[68\].

Theorem 8.6

*Let* *C*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si125.png)*, be closed convex sets in a Hilbert space* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png)*. Then, for any* **x**[0] ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si126.png)*, the sequence* **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si152.png)*, defined as*

$\\mathbf{x}\_{n} = \\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1} + \\mu\_{n}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\omega\_{k}P\_{C\_{k}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}) - \\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si153.png)(8.26) 

*weakly converges to a point in* $\\bigcap\_{k = 1}^{K}C\_{k}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si154.png)*, if*

0 < *μ*[*n*] ≤ *M*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si155.png)

*and*

$M\_{n}: = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\frac{\\omega\_{k}{\\| P\_{C\_{k}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}) - \\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}\\|}^{2}}{\\left\\| \\sum\_{k = 1}^{K}\\omega\_{k}P\_{C\_{k}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}) - \\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1} \\right\\|^{2}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" *where* *ω*[*k*] > 0, *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si157.png)*, such that*

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\omega\_{k} = 1.$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si158.png)

The update recursion Eq. [(8.27)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq57) says that at each iteration, all projections on the convex sets take place *concurrently*, and then they are *convexly* combined. The extrapolation parameter *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si159.png) is chosen in interval (0, *M*[*n*]\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si160.png), where *M*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si161.png) is recursively computed in Eq. [(8.28)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq59), so that convergence is guaranteed. [Fig. 8.17](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0095) illustrates the updating process.

![Figure 8.17 The parallel POCS algorithm for the case of two (hyperplanes) lines in \\mathbb{R}^{2}Equation. At each step, the projections on H1 and H2 are carried out in parallel and then they are convexly combined.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr017.jpg)

[Figure 8.17](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0530) The parallel POCS algorithm for the case of two (hyperplanes) lines in ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si12.png). At each step, the projections on *H*[1] and *H*[2] are carried out in parallel and then they are convexly combined.

## 8.6 From convex sets to parameter estimation and machine learning

Let us now see how this elegant theory can be turned into a useful tool for parameter estimation in machine learning. We will demonstrate the procedure using two examples.

### 8.6.1 Regression

Consider the regression model, relating input–output observation points,

*y*[*n*] = **θ**[*o*]^(*T*)**x**[*n*] + *η*[*n*], (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^(*l*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si162.png)(8.28) 

where **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png) is the unknown parameter vector. Assume that *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si164.png) is a bounded noise sequence, that is,

|*η*[*n*]| ≤ *ϵ*.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si165.png)(8.29) 

Then Eq. [(8.29)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq61) and [(8.30)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq62) guarantee that

|*y*[*n*] − **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*o*]| ≤ *ϵ*.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si166.png)(8.30) 

 Consider now the following set of points:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx018.jpg)(8.31) 

This set is known as a *hyperslab*, and it is geometrically illustrated in [Fig. 8.18](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0100). The definition is generalized for any ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si1.png) by replacing the inner product notation as ⟨**x**[*n*], **θ**⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si167.png). The set comprises all the points that lie in the region formed by the two hyperplanes

**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** − *y*[*n*] = *ϵ*, **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** − *y*[*n*] =  − *ϵ*.<mml:math><mml:msubsup id="mmlbr0002"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si168.png)

This region is trivially shown to be a *closed convex* set. Note that *every pair* of training points, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si169.png), defines a hyperslab of different orientation (depending on **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si152.png)) and position in space (determined by *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si171.png)). Moreover, [(8.31)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq63) guarantees that the unknown, **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png), lies within all these hyperslabs; hence, **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png) lies in their *intersection*. All we need to do now is derive the projection operator onto hyperslabs (we will do it soon) and use one of the POCS schemes to find a point in the intersection. Assuming that enough training points are available and that the intersection is “small” enough, any point in this intersection will be “close” to **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png). Note that such a procedure is not based on optimization arguments. Recall, however, that even in optimization techniques, iterative algorithms have to be used, and in practice, iterations have to stop after a finite number of steps. Thus, one can only approximately reach the optimal value. More on these issues and related convergence properties will be discussed later in this chapter.

![Figure 8.18 Each pair of training points, (yn,xn), defines a hyperslab in the parameters' space.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr018.jpg)

[Figure 8.18](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0545) Each pair of training points, (*y*[*n*],***x***[*n*]), defines a hyperslab in the parameters' space.

The obvious question now is what happens if the noise is not bounded. There are two answers to this point. First, in any practical application where measurements are involved, the noise has to be bounded. Otherwise, the circuits will be burned out. So, at least conceptually, this assumption does not conflict with what happens in practice. It is a matter of selecting the right value for *ϵ*. The second answer is that one can choose *ϵ* to be a few times the standard deviation of the assumed noise model. Then **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png) will lie in these hyperslabs with high probability. We will discuss strategies for selecting *ϵ*, but our goal in this section is to discuss the main rationale in using the theory in practical applications. Needless to say, there is nothing divine around hyperslabs. Other closed convex sets can also be used if the nature of the noise in a specific application suggests a different type of convex sets.

It is now interesting to look at the set where the solution lies, in this case at the hyperslab, from a different perspective. Consider the loss function

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx019.jpg)(8.32) 

which is illustrated in [Fig. 8.19](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0105) for the case *θ* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si173.png). This is known as linear *ϵ*\-insensitive loss function, and it has been popularized in the context of support vector regression (Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml)). For all ***θ***s which lie within the hyperslab defined in Eq. [(8.32)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq64), the loss function scores a zero. For points outside the hyperslab, there is a linear increase of its value. Thus, the hyperslab is the *zero level set* of the linear *ϵ*\-insensitive loss function, defined *locally* according to the point (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si174.png). Thus, although no optimization concept is associated with POCS, the choice of the closed convex sets can be made to minimize “locally,” at each point, a convex loss function by selecting its zero level set.

![Figure 8.19 The linear ϵ-insensitive loss function τ = y − θTx. Its value is zero if |τ| < ϵ, and it increases linearly for |τ| ≥ ϵ.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr019.jpg)

[Figure 8.19](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0555) The linear *ϵ*\-insensitive loss function *τ* = *y* − ***θ***^(*T*)***x***. Its value is zero if |*τ*| < *ϵ*, and it increases linearly for |*τ*| ≥ *ϵ*.

We conclude our discussion by providing the projection operator onto a hyperslab, *S*[*ϵ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si175.png). It is trivially shown that, given ***θ***, its projection onto *S*[*ϵ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si175.png) (defined by (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*], *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si176.png))) is given by

*P*[*S*[*ϵ*]] = **θ** + *β*[**θ**](*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])**x**[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si177.png)(8.33) 

where

$\\beta\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ \\frac{y\_{n} - \\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{\\theta}\\rangle - \\epsilon}{{\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\|}^{2}},} & {\\text{~if~}\\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{\\theta}\\rangle - y\_{n} < - \\epsilon,} \\\\ {\\ \\ 0,} & {\\text{~if~}|\\langle\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{\\theta}\\rangle - y\_{n}| \\leq \\epsilon,} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\frac{y\_{n} - \\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{\\theta}\\rangle + \\epsilon}{{\\| x\_{n}\\|}^{2}},} & {\\text{~if~}\\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{\\theta}\\rangle - y\_{n} > \\epsilon.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext> if </mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mo
