mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext> if </mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si178.png)(8.34) 

That is, if the point lies within the hyperslab, it coincides with its projection. Otherwise, the projection is on one of the two hyperplanes (depending on which side of the hyperslab the point lies on), which define *S*[*ϵ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si175.png). Recall that the projection of a point that does not belong to the set lies on the boundary of the corresponding closed convex set.

### 8.6.2 Classification

Let us consider the two-class classification task, and assume that we are given the set of training points (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si179.png).

Our goal now will be to design a linear classifier so as to score

**θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*] ≥ *ρ*,  if *y*[*n*] =  + 1,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mtext> if </mml:mtext><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si180.png)

and

**θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*] ≤  − *ρ*,  if *y*[*n*] =  − 1.<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mtext> if </mml:mtext><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si181.png)

This requirement can be expressed as follows. Given (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ { − 1, 1} × ℝ^(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si182.png), design a linear classifier,^([^(53)](#fn53))

*y*[*n*]**θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*] ≥ *ρ* > 0.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si184.png)(8.35) 

Note that, given *y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si185.png), and *ρ*, [(8.36)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq71) defines a *halfspace* ([Example 8.1](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#enun0065)); this is the reason that we used “≥*ρ*” rather than a strict inequality. In other words, all ***θ***s which satisfy the desired inequality in [(8.36)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq71) lie in this halfspace. Since each pair (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si169.png), defines a single halfspace, our goal now becomes that of trying to find a point at the intersection of all these halfspaces. This intersection is guaranteed to be nonempty if the classes are linearly separable. [Fig. 8.20](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0110) illustrates the concept. The more realistic case of nonlinearly separable classes will be treated in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), where a mapping in a high-dimensional (kernel) space makes the probability of two classes being linearly separable to tend to 1 as the dimensionality of the kernel space goes to infinity.

![Figure 8.20 Each training point (yn,xn) defines a halfspace in the parameters θ-space, and the linear classifier will be searched in the intersection of all these halfspaces.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr020.jpg)

[Figure 8.20](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0585) Each training point (*y*[*n*],***x***[*n*]) defines a halfspace in the parameters ***θ***\-space, and the linear classifier will be searched in the intersection of all these halfspaces.

The halfspace associated with a training pair (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si174.png) can be seen as the level set of height zero of the so-called *hinge loss* function, defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx020.jpg)(8.36) 

whose graph is shown in [Fig. 8.21](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0115). Thus, choosing the halfspace as the closed convex set to represent (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si174.png) is equivalent to selecting the zero level set of the hinge loss, “adjusted” for the point (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si174.png).

Remarks 8.4

*   •  In addition to the two applications typical of the machine learning point of view, POCS has been applied in a number of other applications; see, for example, \[7,24,87,89\] for further reading.
*   •  If the involved sets do not intersect, that is, $\\bigcap\_{k = 1}^{K}C\_{k} = \\varnothing$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si188.png), then it has been shown \[25\] that the parallel version of POCS in Eq. [(8.27)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq57) converges to a point whose weighted squared distance from each one of the convex sets (defined as the distance of the point from its respective projection) is minimized.
*   •  Attempts to generalize the theory to nonconvex sets have also been made (for example, \[87\] and more recently in the context of sparse modeling in \[83\]).
*   •  When $C: = \\bigcap\_{k = 1}^{K}C\_{K} \\neq \\varnothing$<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si189.png), we say that the problem is *feasible* and the intersection *C* is known as the *feasibility* set. The closed convex sets *C*[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si120.png), are sometimes called the *property* sets, for obvious reasons. In both previous examples, namely, regression and classification, we commented that the involved property sets resulted as the 0-level sets of a corresponding loss function ℒ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si191.png). Hence, assuming that the problem is feasible (the cases of bounded noise in regression and linearly separable classes in classification), any solution in the feasible set *C* will also be a *minimizer* of the respective loss functions in Eqs. [(8.33)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq66) and [(8.37)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq72), respectively. Thus, although optimization did not enter into our discussion, there can be an optimizing flavor in the POCS method. Moreover, note that in this case, the loss functions need *not* be differentiable and the techniques we discussed in the previous chapters are not applicable. We will return to this issue in Section [8.10](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0090). 

![Figure 8.21 The hinge loss function. For the classification task τ = yθTx, its value is zero if τ ≥ ρ, and it increases linearly for τ < ρ.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr021.jpg)

[Figure 8.21](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0590) The hinge loss function. For the classification task *τ* = *y**θ***^(*T*)***x***, its value is zero if *τ* ≥ *ρ*, and it increases linearly for *τ* < *ρ*.

## 8.7 Infinitely many closed convex sets: the online learning case

In our discussion so far, we have assumed a finite number, *K*, of closed convex (property) sets. To land at their intersection (feasibility set) one has to cyclically project onto all of them or to perform the projections in parallel. Such a strategy is not appealing for the online processing scenario. At every time instant, a new pair of observations becomes available, which defines a new property set. Hence, in this case, the number of the available convex sets increases. Visiting all the available sets makes the complexity time-dependent and after some time the required computational resources will become unmanageable.

An alternative viewpoint was suggested in \[101–103\], and later on extended in \[76,104,105\]. The main idea here is that at each time instant *n*, a pair of output–input training samples is received and a (property) closed convex set, *C*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si192.png), is constructed. The time index, *n*, is left to grow unbounded. However, at each time instant, *q* (a user-defined parameter) most recently constructed property sets are considered. In other words, the parameter *q* defines a *sliding window* in time. At each time instant, projections/relaxed projections are performed within this time window. The rationale is illustrated in [Fig. 8.22](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0120). Thus, the number of sets onto which projections are performed does not grow with time, their number remains finite, and it is fixed by the user. The developed algorithm is an offspring of the parallel version of POCS and it is known as *adaptive projected subgradient method* (APSM). The scheme can be considered as the online version of the classical POCS framework. We will describe the algorithm in the context of regression. Following the discussion in Section [8.6](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0050), as each pair (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si193.png) becomes available, a hyperslab *S*[*ϵ*, *n*], *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si194.png), is constructed and the goal is to find a **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si195.png) that lies in the intersection of all these property sets, starting from an arbitrary value, **θ**[0] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si196.png).

![Figure 8.22 At time n, the property sets Cn−q+1,…,Cn are used, while at time n + 1, the sets Cn−q+2,…,Cn+1 are considered. Thus, the required number of projections does not grow with time.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr022.jpg)

[Figure 8.22](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0630) At time *n*, the property sets *C*[*n*−*q*+1],…,*C*[*n*] are used, while at time *n* + 1, the sets *C*[*n*−*q*+2],…,*C*[*n*+1] are considered. Thus, the required number of projections does not grow with time.

Algorithm 8.2

**The APSM algorithm**

*   •  Initialization 
    1.  –  Choose **θ**[0] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si196.png).
    2.  –  Choose *q*; The number of property sets to be processed at each time instant.
*   •  **For** *n* = 1, 2, …, *q* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si197.png), **Do**; Initial period, that is, *n* < *q*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si198.png).
    
    1.  –  Choose $\\omega\_{1},\\ldots,\\omega\_{n}:\\quad\\sum\_{k = 1}^{n}\\omega\_{k} = 1,\\omega\_{k} \\geq 0$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si199.png)
    2.  –  Select *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si159.png)
    
    $\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} + \\mu\_{n}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\omega\_{k}P\_{S\_{\\epsilon,k}}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}) - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

The extrapolation parameter can now be chosen in the interval (0, 2*M*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si205.png) in order for convergence to be guaranteed. For the case of Eq. [(8.39)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq74)

$M\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = n - q + 1}^{n}\\frac{\\omega\_{k}{\\| P\_{S\_{\\epsilon,k}}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}) - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}\\|}^{2}}{\\left\\| \\sum\_{k = n - q + ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si206.png)(8.39) 

Note that this interval differs from that reported in the case of a finite number of sets in Eq. [(8.27)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq57). For the first iteration steps associated with Eq. [(8.38)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq73), the summations in the above formula start from *k* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si207.png) instead of *k* = *n* − *q* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si208.png).

Recall that *P*[*S*[*ϵ*, *k*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si209.png) is the projection operation given in Eqs. [(8.34)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq67)–[(8.35)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq68). Note that this is a generic scheme and can be applied with different property sets. All that is needed is to change the projection operator. For example, if classification is considered, all we have to do is to replace *S*[*ϵ*, *n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si210.png) by the halfspace *H*[*n*]^+<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si211.png), defined by the pair (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ { − 1, 1} × ℝ^(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si182.png), as explained in Section [8.6.2](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0060), and use the projection from Eq. [(8.13)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq28) (see \[78,79\]). At this point, it must be emphasized that the original APSM form (e.g., \[103,104\]) is more general and can cover a wide range of convex sets and functions.

[Fig. 8.23](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0125) illustrates geometrically the APSM algorithm. We have assumed that the number of hyperslabs that are considered for projection at each time instant is *q* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si213.png). Each iteration comprises:

*   •  *q* projections, which can be carried out in parallel,
*   •  their convex combination, and
*   •  the update step.

![Figure 8.23 At time n, q = 2 hyperslabs are processed, namely, Sϵ,n,Sϵ,n−1; θn−1 is concurrently projected onto both of them and the projections are convexly combined. The new estimate is θn. Next, Sϵ,n+1 “arrives” and the process is repeated. Note that at every time, the estimate gets closer to the intersection; the latter will become smaller and smaller as more hyperslabs arrive.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr023.jpg)

[Figure 8.23](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0675) At time *n*, *q* = 2 hyperslabs are processed, namely, *S*[*ϵ*,*n*],*S*[*ϵ*,*n*−1]; ***θ***[*n*−1] is *concurrently* projected onto both of them and the projections are convexly combined. The new estimate is ***θ***[*n*]. Next, *S*[*ϵ*,*n*+1] “arrives” and the process is repeated. Note that at every time, the estimate gets closer to the intersection; the latter will become smaller and smaller as more hyperslabs arrive.

### 8.7.1 Convergence of APSM

The proof of the convergence of the APSM is a bit technical and the interested reader can consult the related references. Here, we can be content with a geometric illustration that intuitively justifies the convergence, under certain assumptions. This geometric interpretation is at the heart of a stochastic approach to the APSM convergence, which was presented in \[23\].

Assume the noise to be bounded and that there is a true **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png) that generates the data, that is,

*y*[*n*] = **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*o*] + *η*[*n*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si215.png)(8.40) 

By assumption,

|*η*[*n*]| ≤ *ϵ*.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si165.png)

Hence,

|**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**[*o*] − *y*[*n*]| ≤ *ϵ*.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si217.png)

Thus, **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png) does lie in the intersection of all the hyperslabs of the form

|**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** − *y*[*n*]| ≤ *ϵ*,<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si218.png)

and in this case the problem is feasible. The question that is raised is how close one can go, even asymptotically as *n* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si219.png), to **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png). For example, if the volume of the intersection is large, even if the algorithm converges to a point in the boundary of this intersection this does not necessarily say much about how close the solution is to the true value **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png). The proof in \[23\] establishes that the algorithm brings the estimate *arbitrarily close* to **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png), under some general assumptions concerning the sequence of observations, and given that the noise is bounded.

To understand what is behind the technicalities of the proof, recall that there are two main geometric issues concerning a hyperslab: (a) its orientation, which is determined by **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si152.png), and (b) its width. In finite-dimensional spaces, it is a matter of simple geometry to show that the width of a hyperslab is equal to

$d = \\frac{2\\epsilon}{\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\|}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si220.png)(8.41) 

This is a direct consequence of the fact that the distance^([^(54)](#fn54))

**x**^(*T*)**θ** − *y* = 0,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si223.png)

is equal to

$\\frac{|\\mathbf{x}^{T}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}} - y|}{\\|\\mathbf{x}\\|}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si224.png)

Indeed, let $\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si225.png) be a point on one of the two boundary hyperplanes (e.g., **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** − *y*[*n*] = *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si226.png)) which define the hyperslab and consider its distance from the other one (**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** − *y*[*n*] =  − *ϵ*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si227.png); then Eq. [(8.42)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq80) is readily obtained.

[Fig. 8.24](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0130) shows four hyperslabs in two different directions (one for the full lines and one for the dotted lines). The red hyperslabs are narrower than the black ones. Moreover, all four necessarily include **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png). If **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si152.png) is left to vary randomly so that any orientation will occur, with high probability and for any orientation, the norm can also take small as well as arbitrarily large values, and then intuition says that the volume of the intersection around **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si163.png) will become arbitrarily small. Further results concerning the APSM algorithm can be found in, e.g., \[82,89,103,104\].

![Figure 8.24 For each direction, the width of a hyperslab varies inversely proportional to ‖xn‖. In this figure, ||xn|| < ||xm|| although both vectors point to the same direction. The intersection of hyperslabs of different directions and widths renders the volume of their intersection arbitrarily small around θo.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr024.jpg)

[Figure 8.24](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0700) For each direction, the width of a hyperslab varies inversely proportional to ‖***x***[*n*]‖. In this figure, ||***x***[*n*]|| < ||***x***[*m*]|| although both vectors point to the same direction. The intersection of hyperslabs of different directions and widths renders the volume of their intersection arbitrarily small around ***θ***[*o*].

#### Some practical hints

The APSM algorithm needs the setting of three parameters, namely, *ϵ*, *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si228.png), and *q*. It turns out that the algorithm is not particularly sensitive to their choice:

*   •  The choice of the parameter *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si159.png) is similar in concept to the choice of the step size in the LMS algorithm. In particular, the larger *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si159.png), the faster the convergence, at the expense of a higher steady-state error floor. In practice, a step size approximately equal to 0.5*M*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si229.png) will lead to a low steady-state error, although the convergence speed will be relatively low. On the contrary, if one selects a larger step size, 1.5*M*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si230.png) approximately, then the algorithm enjoys a faster convergence, although the steady-state error after convergence is increased.
*   •  Regarding the parameter *ϵ*, a typical choice is to set $\\epsilon \\approx \\sqrt{2}\\sigma$<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si231.png), where *σ* is the standard deviation of the noise. In practice (see, e.g., \[47\]), it has been shown that the algorithm is rather insensitive to this parameter. Hence, one needs only a *rough* estimate of the noise standard deviation.
*   •  Concerning the choice of *q*, this is analogous to the *q* used for the APA in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). The larger the *q* is, the faster the convergence becomes; however, large values of *q* increase complexity as well as the error floor after convergence. In practice, relatively small values of *q*, for example, a small fraction of *l*, can significantly improve the convergence speed compared to the normalized least-mean-squares (NLMS) algorithm. Sometimes one can start with a relatively large value of *q*, and once the error decreases, *q* can be given smaller values to achieve lower error floors.
*   It is important to note that the past data reuse within the sliding window of length *q* in the APA is implemented via the inversion of a *q* × *q*<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si232.png) matrix. In the APSM, this is achieved via a sequence of *q* projections, leading to a complexity of linear dependence on *q*; moreover, these projections can be performed in parallel. Furthermore, the APA tends to be more sensitive to the presence of noise, since the projections are carried out on hyperplanes. In contrast, for the APSM case, projections are performed on hyperslabs, which implicitly care for the noise (for example, \[102\]).

Remarks 8.5

*   •  If the hyperslabs collapse to hyperplanes (*ϵ* = 0)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si233.png) and *q* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si234.png), the algorithm becomes the NLMS. Indeed, for this case the projection in Eq. [(8.39)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq74) becomes the projection on the hyperplane, *H*, defined by (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si174.png), that is,

**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** = *y*[*n*],<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si235.png)

*   and from Eq. [(8.11)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq26), after making the appropriate notational adjustments, we have

$P\_{H}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}) = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} - \\frac{\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} - y\_{n}}{{\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\|}^{2}}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si236.png)(8.42) 

*   Plugging Eq. [(8.43)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq84) into Eq. [(8.39)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq74), we get

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} + \\frac{\\mu\_{n}}{{\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\|}^{2}}e\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n},e\_{n} = y\_{n} - \\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - *   •  Closely related to the APSM algorithmic family are the *set-membership* algorithms (for example, \[29,32–34,61\]). This family can be seen as a special case of the APSM philosophy, where only special types of convex sets are used, for example, hyperslabs. Also, at each iteration step, a single projection is performed onto the set associated with the most recent pair of observations. For example in \[34,99\], the update recursion of a set-membership APA is given by

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n} = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} + X\_{n}{(X\_{n}^{T}X\_{n})}^{- 1}(\\mathbf{e}\_{n} - \\mathbf{y}\_{n}),} & {\\text{if}\\ |e\_{n}| > \\epsilon,} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1},} & {\\text{otherwise},} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi Example 8.2

The goal of this example is to demonstrate the comparative convergence performance of the NLMS, APA, APSM, and recursive least-squares (RLS) algorithms. The experiments were performed in two different noise settings, one for low and one for high noise levels, to demonstrate the sensitivity of the APA compared to the APSM. Data were generated according to our familiar model

*y*[*n*] = **θ**[*o*]^(*T*)**x**[*n*] + *η*[*n*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si243.png)

The parameters **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(200)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>200</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si244.png) were randomly generated from 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si245.png) and then fixed. The input vectors were formed by a white noise sequence with samples i.i.d. drawn from 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si245.png).

In the first experiment, the white noise sequence was selected to have variance *σ*² = 0.01<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si246.png). The parameters for the three algorithms were chosen as *μ* = 1.2<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si247.png) and *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si248.png) for the NLMS, *q* = 30, *μ* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>30</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si249.png), and *δ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si248.png) for the APA, and $\\epsilon = \\sqrt{2}\\sigma,\\ q = 30$<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>30</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si250.png), and *μ*[*n*] = 0.5*M*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si251.png) for the APSM. These parameters lead the algorithms to settle at the same error floor. [Fig. 8.25](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0135) shows the obtained squared error, averaged over 100 realizations, in dBs (10log[10](*e*[*n*]²)<mml:math><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si252.png)). For comparison, the RLS convergence curve is given for *β* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si253.png), which converges faster and at the same time settles at a lower error floor. If *β* is modified to a smaller value so that the RLS settles at the same error floor as the other algorithms, then its convergence gets even faster. However, this improved performance of the RLS is achieved at higher complexity, which becomes a problem for large values of *l*. Observe the faster convergence achieved by the APA and APSM, compared to the NLMS.

![Figure 8.25 Mean-square error in dBs as a function of iterations. The data reuse (q = 30), associated with the APA and APSM, offers a significant improvement in convergence speed compared to the NLMS. The curves for the APA and APSM almost coincide in this low-noise scenario.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr025.jpg)

Figure 8.25 Mean-square error in dBs as a function of iterations. The data reuse (*q* = 30), associated with the APA and APSM, offers a significant improvement in convergence speed compared to the NLMS. The curves for the APA and APSM almost coincide in this low-noise scenario.

For the high-level noise, the corresponding variance was increased to 0.3. The obtained MSE curves are shown in [Fig. 8.26](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0140). Observe that now the APA shows an inferior performance compared to APSM in spite of its higher complexity, due to the involved matrix inversion.

![Figure 8.26 Mean-square error in dBs as a function of iterations for a high-noise scenario. Compared to Fig. 8.25, all curves settled at higher noise levels. Moreover, note that now the APA settles at higher error floor than the corresponding APSM algorithm, for the same convergence rate.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr026.jpg)

[Figure 8.26](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0745) Mean-square error in dBs as a function of iterations for a high-noise scenario. Compared to [Fig. 8.25](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0135), all curves settled at higher noise levels. Moreover, note that now the APA settles at higher error floor than the corresponding APSM algorithm, for the same convergence rate.

## 8.8 Constrained learning

Learning under a set of constraints is of significant importance in signal processing and machine learning, in general. We have already discussed a number of such learning tasks. Beamforming, discussed in Chapters [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) and [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml), is a typical one. In Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), while introducing the concept of overfitting, we discussed the notion of regularization, which is another form of constraining the norm of the unknown parameter vector. In some other cases, we have available a priori information concerning the unknown parameters; this extra information can be given in the form of a set of constraints.

For example, if one is interested in obtaining estimates of the pixels in an image, then the values must be nonnegative. More recently, the unknown parameter vector may be known to be sparse; that is, only a few of its components are nonzero. In this case, constraining the respective ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) norm can significantly improve the accuracy as well as the convergence speed of an iterative scheme toward the solution. Schemes that explicitly take into consideration the underlying sparsity are known as *sparsity promoting* algorithms. They will be considered in more detail in Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml).

Algorithms that spring from the POCS theory are particularly suited to treat constraints in an elegant, robust, and rather straightforward way. Note that the goal of each constraint is to define a region in the solution space, where the required estimate is “forced” to lie. For the rest of this section, we will assume that the required estimate must satisfy *M* constraints, each one defining a *convex* set of points, *C*[*m*], *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si254.png). Moreover,

$\\bigcap\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}C\_{m} \\neq \\varnothing,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">⋂</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si255.png)

which means that the constraints are consistent (there are also methods where this condition can be relaxed). Then it can be shown that the mapping *T*, defined as

*T* :  = *P*[*C*[*m*]]…*P*[*C*[1]],<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si256.png)

is a *strongly attracting nonexpansive* mapping, [(8.25)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq48) (for example, \[6,7\]). Note that the same holds true if instead of the concatenation of the projection operators, one could convexly combine them.

In the presence of a set of constraints, the only difference in the APSM in [Algorithm 8.2](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#enun0130) is that the update recursion Eq. [(8.39)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq74) is now replaced by 

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n} = T\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} + \\mu\_{n}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{k = n - q + 1}^{n}\\omega\_{k}P\_{S\_{\\epsilon,k}}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}) - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} \\right) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si257.png)(8.44) 

In other words, for *M* constraints, *M* extra projection operations have to be performed. The same applies to Eq. [(8.38)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq73) with the difference being in the summation term in the brackets.

Remarks 8.6

*   •  The constrained form of the APSM has been successfully applied in the beamforming task, and in particular in treating nontrivial constraints, as required in the robust beamforming case \[77,80,103,104\]. It has also been efficiently used for sparsity-aware learning (for example, \[47,83\]; see also Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml)). A more detailed review of related techniques is presented in \[89\].

## 8.9 The distributed APSM

Distributed algorithms were discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). In Section [5.13.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), two versions of the diffusion LMS were introduced, namely, the adapt-then-combine and combine-then-adapt schemes. Diffusion versions of the APSM algorithm have also appeared in both configurations \[20,22\]. For the APSM case, both schemes result in very similar performances.

Following the discussion in Section [5.13.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), let the most recently received data pair at node *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si148.png) be (*y*[*k*](*n*), **x**[*k*](*n*)) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si258.png). For the regression task, a corresponding hyperslab is constructed, that is,

*S*[*ϵ*, *n*]^((*k*)) = {**θ**:|*y*[*k*](*n*)−**x**[*k*]^(*T*)(*n*)**θ**|≤*ϵ*[*k*]}.<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si259.png)

The goal is the computation of a point that lies in the intersection of all these sets, for *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si146.png). Following similar arguments as those employed for the diffusion LMS, the combine-then-adapt version of the APSM, given in [Algorithm 8.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#enun0150), is obtained.

Algorithm 8.3

**The combine-then-adapt diffusion APSM**

*   •  Initialization 
    1.  –  **For** *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si148.png), **Do** 
        1.  ⁎  **θ**[*k*](0) = 0 ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si260.png); or any other value.
    2.  –  **End For**
    3.  –  Select *A*: *A*^(*T*)1 = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si261.png)
    4.  –  Select *q*; The number of property sets to be processed at each time instant.
*   •  **For** *n* = 1, 2, …, *q* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si197.png), **Do**; Initial period, that is, *n* < *q*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si198.png). 
    1.  –  **For** *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si148.png), **Do** 
        1.  ⁎  **ψ**[*k*](*n* − 1) = ∑[*m* ∈ 𝒩[*k*]]*a*[*m**k*]**θ**[*m*](*n* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si262.png); 𝒩[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si263.png) the neighborhood of node *k*.
    2.  –  **End For**
    3.  –  **For** *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si148.png), **Do** 
        1.  ⁎  Choose *ω*[1], …, *ω*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si264.png): $\\quad\\sum\_{j = 1}^{n}\\omega\_{j} = 1,\\ \\ \\omega\_{j} > 0$<mml:math><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si265.png)
        2.  ⁎  Select *μ*[*k*](*n*) ∈ (0, 2*M*[*k*](*n*))<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si266.png).

- \\mathbf{\\psi}\_{k}(n - 1) \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo
