Remarks 8.7

*   •  An important theoretical property of the APSM-based diffusion algorithms is that they enjoy *asymptotic consensus*. In other words, the nodes converge asymptotically to the *same* estimate. This asymptotic consensus is not in the mean, as is the case with the diffusion LMS. This is interesting, since no explicit consensus constraints are employed.
*   •  In \[22\], an extra projection step is used after the combination and prior to the adaptation step. The goal of this extra step is to “harmonize” the local information, which comprises the input/output observations, with the information coming from the neighborhood, that is, the estimates obtained from the neighboring nodes. This speeds up convergence, at the cost of only one extra projection.
*   •  A scenario in which some of the nodes are damaged and the associated observations are very noisy is also treated in \[22\]. To deal with such a scenario, instead of the hyperslab, the APSM algorithm is rephrased around the Huber loss function, developed in the context of robust statistics, to deal with cases where outliers are present (see also Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml)).

Example 8.3

The goal of this example is to demonstrate the comparative performance of the diffusion LMS and APSM. A network of *K* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si274.png) nodes is considered, and there are 32 connections among the nodes. In each node, data are generated according to a regression model, using the same vector **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(60)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>60</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si275.png). The latter was randomly generated via a normal 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si245.png). The input vectors were i.i.d. generated according to the normal 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si245.png). The noise level at each node varied between 20 and 25 dBs. The parameters for the algorithms were chosen for optimized performance (after experimentation) and for similar convergence rate. For the LMS, *μ* = 0.035<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.035</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si276.png), and for the APSM, $\\epsilon = \\sqrt{2}\\sigma,\\ q = 20,\\ \\mu\_{k}(n) = 0.2M\_{k}(n)$<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si277.png). The combination weights were chosen according to the Metropolis rule (see [Remarks 5.4](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)) and the data combination matrix was the identity one (no observations are exchanged). [Fig. 8.27](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0145) shows the benefits of the data reuse offered by the APSM. The curves show the mean-square deviation (MSD $= \\frac{1}{K}\\sum\_{k = 1}^{K}||\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k}(n) - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}||^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si278.png)) as a function of the number of iterations.

![Figure 8.27 The MSD as a function of the number of iterations. The improved performance due to the data reuse offered by the diffusion ASPM is readily observed. Moreover, observe the significant performance improvement offered by all cooperation schemes, compared to the noncooperative LMS; for the latter, only one node is used.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr027.jpg)

[Figure 8.27](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0790) The MSD as a function of the number of iterations. The improved performance due to the data reuse offered by the diffusion ASPM is readily observed. Moreover, observe the significant performance improvement offered by all cooperation schemes, compared to the noncooperative LMS; for the latter, only one node is used.

## 8.10 Optimizing nonsmooth convex loss functions

Estimating parameters via the use of convex loss functions in the presence of a set of constraints is an established and well-researched field in optimization, with numerous applications in a wide range of disciplines. The mainstream methods follow either the Lagrange multiplier philosophy \[11,15\] or the rationale behind the so-called *interior point* methods \[15,90\]. In this section, we will focus on an alternative path and consider iterative schemes, which can be considered as the generalization of the gradient descent method, discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). The reason is that such techniques give rise to variants that scale well with the dimensionality and have inspired a number of algorithms, which have been suggested for online learning within the machine learning community. Later on, we will move to more advanced techniques that build on the so-called *operator/mapping* and *fixed point* theoretic framework.

Although the stage of our discussion will be that of Euclidean spaces, ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si86.png), everything that will be said can be generalized to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; we will consider such cases in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml).

### 8.10.1 Subgradients and subdifferentials

We have already met the first-order convexity condition in [(8.3)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq9) and it was shown that this is a sufficient and necessary condition for convexity, provided, of course, that the gradient exists. The condition basically states that the graph of the convex function lies above the hyperplanes which are tangent at any point (**x**, *f*(**x**))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si279.png) that lies on this graph.

Let us now move a step forward and assume a function

*f* : 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si280.png)

to be convex and continuous, but *nonsmooth*. This means that there are points where the gradient is not defined. Our goal now becomes that of generalizing the notion of gradient for the case of convex functions.

Definition 8.7

A vector **g** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si281.png) is said to be the *subgradient* of a convex function *f* at a point **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si282.png) if the following is true:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx021.jpg)(8.45) 

It turns out that this vector is *not* unique. All the subgradients of a (convex) function at a point comprise a set.

Definition 8.8

The *subdifferential* of a convex function *f* at **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si282.png), denoted as ∂*f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si284.png), is defined as the *set*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx022.jpg)(8.46) 

If *f* is differentiable at a point ***x***, then ∂*f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si284.png) becomes a singleton, that is,

∂*f*(**x**) = {∇*f*(**x**)}.<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si285.png)

Note that if *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si27.png) is convex, then the set ∂*f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si284.png) is *nonempty and convex*. Moreover, *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si27.png) is differentiable at a point ***x*** *if and only if* it has a unique subgradient \[11\]. From now on, we will also denote a subgradient of *f* at a point ***x*** as *f*^′(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si286.png).

[Fig. 8.28](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0150) gives a geometric interpretation of the notion of the subgradient. Each one of the subgradients at the point **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si141.png) defines a hyperplane that *supports* the graph of *f*. At **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si141.png), there is an infinity of subgradients, which comprise the subdifferential (set) at **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si141.png). At **x**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si9.png), the function is differentiable and there is a *unique* subgradient that coincides with the gradient at **x**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si9.png).

Example 8.4

Let *x* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si287.png) and

*f*(*x*) = |*x*|.<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si288.png)

Show that

$\\partial f(x) = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ {sgn}(x),} & {\\text{if}\\ x \\neq 0,} \\\\ {\\ \\ g:\\ g \\in \\lbrack - 1,1\\rbrack,} & {\\text{if}\\ x = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si289.png)

where *s**g**n*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si290.png) is the sign function, being equal to 1 if its argument is positive and −1 if the argument is negative.

Indeed, if *x* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si291.png), then

$g = \\frac{dx}{dx} = 1,$<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si292.png)

and similarly *g* =  − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si293.png), if *x* < 0<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si294.png). For *x* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si295.png), any *g* ∈ \[ − 1, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si296.png) satisfies

*g*(*y* − 0) + 0 = *g**y* ≤ |*y*|,<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si297.png)

and it is a subgradient. This is illustrated in [Fig. 8.29](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#f0155).

![Figure 8.28 At x0, there is an infinity of subgradients, each one defining a hyperplane in the extended (x,f(x)) space. All these hyperplanes pass through the point (x0,f(x0)) and support the graph of f(⋅). At the point x1, there is a unique subgradient that coincides with the gradient and defines the unique tangent hyperplane at the respective point of the graph.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr028.jpg)

[Figure 8.28](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0805) At ***x***[0], there is an infinity of subgradients, each one defining a hyperplane in the extended (***x***,*f*(***x***)) space. All these hyperplanes pass through the point (***x***[0],*f*(***x***[0])) and support the graph of *f*(⋅). At the point ***x***[1], there is a unique subgradient that coincides with the gradient and defines the unique tangent hyperplane at the respective point of the graph.

![Figure 8.29 All lines with slope in \[−1,1\] comprise the subdifferential at x = 0.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr029.jpg)

[Figure 8.29](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf0810) All lines with slope in \[−1,1\] comprise the subdifferential at *x* = 0.

Lemma 8.2

*Given a convex function* *f* : 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si298.png)*, a point* **x**[\*] ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si299.png) *is a minimizer of f if and only if the zero vector belongs to its subdifferential set, that is,*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx023.jpg)(8.47) 

Proof

The proof is straightforward from the definition of a subgradient. Indeed, assume that 0 ∈ ∂*f*(**x**[\*])<mml:math><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si300.png). Then the following is valid:

*f*(**y**) ≥ *f*(**x**[\*]) + 0^(*T*)(**y** − **x**[\*]), ∀**y** ∈ 𝒳,<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si301.png)

and **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si40.png) is a minimizer. If now **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si40.png) is a minimizer, then we have

*f*(**y**) ≥ *f*(**x**[\*]) = *f*(**x**[\*]) + 0^(*T*)(**y** − **x**[\*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si302.png)

and hence 0 ∈ ∂*f*(**x**[\*])<mml:math><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si300.png).  □

Example 8.5

Let the metric *distance* function

$d\_{C}(\\mathbf{x}): = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in C}\\|\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{y}\\|.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

\\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi where

*N*[*C*](**x**) :  = {**g**∈ℝ^(*l*):**g**^(*T*)(**y**−**x**)≤0,∀**y**∈*C*},<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si305.png)

and

*B*\[0, 1\] :  = {**x**∈ℝ^(*l*):∥**x**∥≤1}.<mml:math><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si306.png)

Moreover, if ***x*** is an *interior* point of *C*, then

∂*d*[*C*](**x**) = {0}.<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si307.png)

Observe that for all points **x** ∉ *C*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si64.png) as well as for all interior points of *C*, the subgradient is a singleton, which means that *d*[*C*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si308.png) is differentiable. Recall that the function *d*[*C*]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si309.png) is nonnegative, convex, and continuous \[44\]. Note that Eq. [(8.49)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq105) is also generalized to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. 

### 8.10.2 Minimizing nonsmooth continuous convex loss functions: the batch learning case

Let *J* be a cost function^([^(55)](#fn55))

*J* : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ \[0,  + ∞),<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si310.png)

and let *C* be a closed convex set, *C* ⊆ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si311.png). Our task is to compute a minimizer with respect to an unknown parameter vector, that is,

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}),\\text{s.t.}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\mathbf{\\theta} \\in C,$<mml:math><mml:msub id="mmlbr0004"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0004" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si312.png)(8.49) 

and we will assume that the set of solutions is *nonempty*; *J* is assumed to be convex, continuous, but not necessarily differentiable at all points. We have already seen examples of such loss function, such as the *ϵ*\-insensitive linear function in Eq. [(8.33)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq66) and the hinge one Eq. [(8.37)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq72). The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) norm function is another example, and it will be treated in Chapters [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml).

#### The subgradient method

Our starting point is the simplest of the cases, where *C* = ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si313.png); that is, the minimizing task is unconstrained. The first thought that comes into mind is to consider the generalization of the gradient descent method, which was introduced in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), and replace the gradient by the subgradient operation. The resulting scheme is known as the *subgradient algorithm* \[74,75\].

Starting from an arbitrary estimate, **θ**^((0)) ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si314.png), the update recursions become

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx024.jpg)(8.50) 

where *J*^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si315.png) denotes *any* subgradient of the cost function, and *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si316.png) is a step size sequence judicially chosen so that convergence is guaranteed. In spite of the similarity in the appearance with our familiar gradient descent scheme, there are some major differences. The reader may have noticed that the new algorithm was not called subgradient “descent.” This is because the update in Eq. [(8.51)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq111) is not necessarily performed in the descent direction. Thus, during the operation of the algorithm, the value of the cost function may increase. Recall that in the gradient descent methods, the value of the cost function is guaranteed to decrease with each iteration step, which also led to a linear convergence rate, as we have pointed out in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml).

In contrast here, concerning the subgradient method, such comments cannot be made. To establish convergence, a different route has to be adopted. To this end, let us define

*J*[\*]^((*i*)) :  = min {*J*(**θ**^((*i*))),*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1))),…,*J*(**θ**^((0)))},<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si317.png)(8.51) 

which can also be recursively obtained by

*J*[\*]^((*i*)) = min {*J*[\*]^((*i* − 1)),*J*(**θ**^((*i*)))}.<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si318.png)

Then the following holds true.

Proposition 8.3

*Let J be a convex cost function. Assume that the subgradients at all points are bounded, that is,*

||*J*^′(**x**)|| ≤ *G*, ∀**x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*).<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si319.png)

*Let us also assume that the step size sequence is a diminishing one, such that*

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{\\infty}\\mu\_{i} = \\infty,\\quad\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{\\infty}\\mu\_{i}^{2} < \\infty.$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si320.png)

*Then*

$\\lim\\limits\_{i\\longrightarrow\\infty}J\_{\\ast}^{(i)} = J(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}),$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si321.png)

*where* **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png) *is a minimizer, assuming that the set of minimizers is not empty.*
