Setting $\\mu\_{n} = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{n}}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si420.png), using the obvious bound

$\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{n}} \\leq 1 + \\int\_{1}^{N}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{t}}\\ dt = 2\\sqrt{N} - 1,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si429.png)(8.89) 

and dividing both sides of [(8.89)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq170) by *N*, the proposition is proved for any ***h***. Hence, it will also be true for **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png). □

The previous proof follows the one given in \[113\]; this was the first paper to adopt the notion of “regret” for the analysis of convex online algorithms. Proofs given later for more complex algorithms have borrowed, in one way or another, the arguments used there.

Remarks 8.8

*   •  Tighter regret bounds can be derived when the loss function is strongly convex \[43\]. A function *f* : 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si298.png) is said to be *σ*\-*strongly convex* if, ∀ **y**, **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si431.png),

$f(\\mathbf{y}) \\geq f(\\mathbf{x}) + \\mathbf{g}^{T}(\\mathbf{y} - \\mathbf{x}) + \\frac{\\sigma}{2}||\\mathbf{y} - \\mathbf{x}||^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si432.png)(8.90) 

*   for any subgradient ***g*** at ***x***. It also turns out that a function *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si27.png) is strongly convex if $f(\\mathbf{x}) - \\frac{\\sigma}{2}||\\mathbf{x}||^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si433.png) is convex (Problem [8.30](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0180)).
*   For *σ*\-strongly convex loss functions, if the step size of the subgradient algorithm is diminishing at a rate $\\mathcal{O}(\\frac{1}{\\sigma n})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si434.png), then the average cumulative loss is approaching the average loss of the optimal predictor at a rate $\\mathcal{O}(\\frac{\\ln N}{N})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si435.png) (Problem [8.31](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0185)). This is the case, for example, for the PEGASOS algorithm, discussed in Section [8.10.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0125).
*   •  In \[4,5\], 𝒪(1/*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si436.png) convergence rates are derived for a set of non-strongly convex smooth loss functions (e.g., squared error and logistic regression) even for the case of constant step sizes. The analysis method follows statistical arguments.

## 8.12 Online learning and big data applications: a discussion

Online learning algorithms have been treated in Chapters [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml), [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), and [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml). The purpose of this section is to first summarize some of the findings and at the same time present a discussion related to the performance of online schemes compared to their batch relatives.

Recall that the ultimate goal in obtaining a parametric predictor,

*ŷ* = *f*[**θ**](**x**),<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si437.png)

is to select ***θ*** so that to optimize the *expected loss/risk* function in Eq. [(8.65)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq139). For practical reasons, the corresponding empirical formulation in Eq. [(8.66)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq140) is most often adopted instead. From the learning theory's point of view, this is justified provided the respective class of functions is sufficiently restrictive \[94\]. The available literature is quite rich in obtaining performance bounds that measure how close the optimal value obtained via the expected loss is to that obtained via the empirical one, as a function of the number of points *N*. Note that as *N* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si421.png), and recalling well-known arguments from probability theory and statistics, the empirical risk tends to the expected loss (under general assumptions). Thus, for very large training data sets, adopting the empirical risk may not be that different from using the expected loss. However, for data sets of shorter lengths, a number of issues occur. Besides the value of *N*, another critical factor enters the scene; this is the *complexity* of the family of the functions in which we search a solution. In other words, the generalization performance critically depends not only on *N* but also on how large or small this set of functions is. A related discussion for the specific case of the MSE was presented in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), in the context of the bias–variance tradeoff. The roots of the more general theory go back to the pioneering work of Vapnik–Chervonenkis; see \[31,95,96\], and \[88\] for a less mathematical summary of the major points.

In the sequel, some results tailored to the needs of our current discussion will be discussed.

### Approximation, estimation, and optimization errors

Recall that all we are given in a machine learning task is the available training set of examples. To set up the “game,” the designer has to decide on the selection of (a) the loss function, ℒ(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si439.png), which measures the deviation (error) between predicted and target values, and (b) the set ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si405.png) of (parametric) functions,

ℱ = {*f*[**θ**]: **θ**∈ℝ^(*K*)}.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si441.png)

Based on the choice of ℒ(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si439.png), the *benchmark* function, denoted as *f*[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si45.png), is the one that minimizes the expected loss (see also Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)), that is,^([^(57)](#fn57))

$f\_{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{f}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\mathcal{L}\\left( y,f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si442.png)

or equivalently

$f\_{\\ast}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\widehat{y}}\\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\mathcal{L}\\left( y,\\widehat{y} \\right) \\middle| \\mathbf{x} \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si443.png)(8.91) 

Let also *f*[**θ**[\*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si444.png) denote the optimal function that results by minimizing the expected loss constrained within the parametric family ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si405.png), that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx031.jpg)(8.92) 

However, instead of *f*[**θ**[\*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si444.png), we obtain another function, denoted as *f*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si445.png), by minimizing the empirical risk, *J*[*N*](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si446.png),

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx032.jpg)(8.93) 

Once *f*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si445.png) has been obtained, we are interested in evaluating its generalization performance; that is, to compute the value of the expected loss at *f*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si445.png), 𝔼\[ℒ(*y*,*f*[*N*](**x**))\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si447.png). The excess error with respect to the optimal value can then be decomposed as \[13\]

ℰ = 𝔼 \[ℒ(*y*,*f*[*N*](**x**))\] − 𝔼 \[ℒ(*y*,*f*[\*](**x**))\] = ℰ[appr] + ℰ[est],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>appr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si448.png)(8.94) 

where

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx033.jpg)

and

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx034.jpg)

where ℰ[appr]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>appr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si449.png) is known as the *approximation* error and ℰ[est]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si450.png) is known as the *estimation* error. The former measures how well the adopted family of functions can perform compared to the optimal/benchmark value and the latter measures the performance loss within the family ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si405.png), due to the fact that optimization is performed via the empirical risk function. Large (small) families of functions lead to low (high) approximation error but higher (lower) estimation error. A way to improve upon the estimation error, while keeping the approximation error small, is to increase *N*. The size/complexity of the family ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si405.png) is measured by its *capacity*, which may depend on the number of parameters, but this is not always the whole story; see, for example, \[88,95\]. For example, the use of regularization, while minimizing the empirical risk, can have a decisive effect on the approximation–estimation error tradeoff.

In practice, while optimizing the (regularized) empirical risk, one has to adopt an iterative minimization or an online algorithm, which leads to an approximate solution, denoted as *f̃*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si451.png). Then the excess error, ℰ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si452.png), in Eq. [(8.95)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq179) involves a third term \[13,14\],

ℰ = ℰ[appr] + ℰ[est] + ℰ[opt],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>appr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>opt</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si453.png)(8.95) 

where

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx035.jpg)

The literature is rich in studies deriving bounds concerning the excess error. More detailed treatment is beyond the scope of this book. As a case study, we will follow the treatment given in \[14\].

Let the computation of *f̃*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si451.png) be associated with a predefined accuracy,

𝔼 \[ℒ(*y*,*f̃*[*N*](**x**))\] < 𝔼 \[ℒ(*y*,*f*[*N*](**x**))\] + *ρ*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si454.png)

Then, for a class of functions that are often met in practice, for example, under strong convexity of the loss function \[51\] or under certain assumptions on the data distribution \[92\], the following equivalence relation can be established:

$\\mathcal{E}\_{\\text{appr}} + \\mathcal{E}\_{\\text{est}} + \\mathcal{E}\_{\\text{opt}} \\sim \\mathcal{E}\_{\\text{appr}} + \\left( \\frac{\\ln N}{N} \\right)^{a} + \\rho,\\quad a \\in \\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{2},1 \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>appr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>opt</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>appr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si455.png)(8.96) 

which verifies the fact that as *N* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si421.png) the estimation error decreases and provides a rule for the respective convergence rate. The excess error ℰ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">E</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si452.png), besides the approximation component, on which we have no access to control (given the family of functions, ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si405.png)), it depends on (a) the number of data and (b) the accuracy, *ρ*, associated with the algorithm used. How one can control these parameters depends on the type of learning task at hand.

*   •  *Small-scale tasks*: These types of tasks are constrained by the number of training points, *N*. In this case, one can reduce the optimization error, since computational load is not a problem, and achieve the minimum possible estimation error, as this is allowed by the number of available training points. In this case, one achieves the approximation–estimation tradeoff.
*   •  *Large-scale/big data tasks*: These types of tasks are constrained by the computational resources. Thus, a computationally cheap and less accurate algorithm may end up with lower excess error, since it has the luxury of exploiting more data, compared to a more accurate yet computationally more complex algorithm, given the maximum allowed computational load.

### Batch versus online learning

Our interest in this subsection lies in investigating whether there is a performance loss if in place of a batch algorithm an online one is used. There is a very subtle issue involved here, which turns out to be very important from a practical point of view. We will restrict our discussion to differentiable convex loss functions.

Two major factors associated with the performance of an algorithm (in a stationary environment) are its convergence rate and its accuracy after convergence. The general form of a batch algorithm in minimizing Eq. [(8.66)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq140) is written as

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu\_{i}\\Phi\_{i}\\nabla J\_{N}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right) = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\frac{\\mu\_{i}}{N}\\Phi\_{i}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}^{\\prime}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)},y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo id="mmlbr0011" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0011" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si457.png)(8.97) 

For gradient descent, *Φ*[*i*] = *I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si458.png), and for Newton-type recursions, *Φ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si459.png) is the inverse Hessian matrix of the loss function (Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)).

Note that these are not the only possible choices for matrix Φ. For example, in the Levenberg–Marquardt method, the square Jacobian is employed, that is,

*Φ*[*i*] = \[∇*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))∇^(*T*)*J*(**θ**^((*i* − 1)))+*λ**I*\]^( − 1),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si460.png)

where *λ* is a regularization parameter. In \[3\], the *natural gradient* is proposed, which is based on the Fisher information matrix associated with the noisy distribution implied by the adopted prediction model, *f*[**θ**](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si461.png). In both cases, the involved matrices asymptotically behave like the Hessian, yet they may provide improved performance during the initial convergence phase. For a further discussion, the interested reader may consult \[49,56\].

As already mentioned in Chapters [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) and [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml) (Section [6.7](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)), the convergence rate to the respective optimal value of the simple gradient descent method (for the mean-square error case) is *linear*, that is,

$\\ln\\frac{1}{\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}(N) \\right\\|} \\propto i,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si462.png)

and the corresponding rate for a Newton-type algorithm is (approximately) quadratic, that is,

$\\ln\\ln\\frac{1}{\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}(N) \\right\\|} \\propto i.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si463.png)

In contrast, the online version of Eq. [(8.98)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq186), that is,

**θ**[*n*] = **θ**[*n* − 1] − *μ*[*n*]*Φ*[*n*]ℒ^′(**θ**[*n* − 1], *y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si464.png)(8.98) 

is based on a *noisy* estimation of the gradient, using the current sample point, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si174.png), only. The effect of this is to slow down convergence, in particular when the algorithm gets close to the solution. Moreover, the estimate of the parameter vector fluctuates around the optimal value. We have extensively studied this phenomenon in the case of the LMS, when *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si159.png) is assigned a constant value. This is the reason that in the stochastic gradient rationale, *μ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si159.png) must be a decreasing sequence. However, it *must not* decrease very fast, which is guaranteed by the condition ∑[*n*]*μ*[*n*] → ∞<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si465.png) (Section [5.4](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)). Furthermore, recall from our discussion there that the rate of convergence toward **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png) is, on average, 𝒪(1/*n*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si466.png), that is *sublinear* (e.g., Eq. [(6.53)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)). This result also covers the more general case of online algorithms given in Eq. [(8.99)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq190) (see, for example, \[56\]). Note, however, that all these results have been derived under a number of assumptions, for example, that the algorithm is close enough to a solution.

Our major interest now turns to comparing the rate at which a batch and a corresponding online algorithm converge to **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png), that is, the value that minimizes the expected loss, which is the ultimate goal of our learning task. Since the aim is to compare performances, given the same number of training samples, let us use the same number, both for *n* for the online and for *N* for the batch. Following \[12\] and applying a second-order Taylor expansion on *J*[*n*](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si468.png), it can be shown (Problem [8.32](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0190)) that

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}(n) = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}(n - 1) - \\frac{1}{n}\\Psi\_{n}^{- 1}\\mathcal{L}^{\\prime}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}(n - 1),y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si469.png)(8.99) 

where

$\\Psi\_{n} = \\left( \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\nabla^{2}\\mathcal{L}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}(n - 1),y\_{k},\\mathbf{x}\_{k} \\right) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si470.png)

Note that Eq. [(8.100)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq191) is similar in structure to Eq. [(8.99)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq190). Also, as *n* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si219.png), *Ψ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si471.png) converges to the Hessian matrix, *H*, of the expected loss function. Hence, for appropriate choices of the involved weighting matrices and setting *μ*[*n*] = 1/*n*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si472.png), Eqs. [(8.99)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq190) and [(8.100)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq191) can converge to **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png) at similar rates; thus, in both cases, the critical factor that determines how close to the optimal **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png) the resulting estimates are is the number of data points used. It can be shown \[12,56,93\] that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx036.jpg)

where *C* is a term depending on the specific form of the associated expected loss function used. *Thus, batch algorithms and their online versions can be made to converge at similar rates to* **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png)*, after appropriate fine-tuning of the involved parameters.* Once more, since the critical factor in big data applications is not data but computational resources, a cheap online algorithm can achieve enhanced performance (lower excess error) compared to a batch, yet being a computationally more thirsty scheme. This is because for a given computational load, the online algorithm can process more data points (Problem [8.33](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0195)). More importantly, an online algorithm needs not to store the data, which can be processed on the fly as they arrive. For a more detailed treatment of the topic, the interested reader may consult \[14\].

In \[14\], two forms of batch linear support vector machines (Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml)) were tested against their online stochastic gradient counterparts. The tests were carried out on the RCV1 data set \[53\], and the training set comprised 781.265 documents represented by (relatively) sparse feature vectors consisting of 47.152 feature values. The stochastic gradient online versions, appropriately tuned with a diminishing step size, achieved comparable error rates at substantially lower computational times (less than one tenth) compared to their batch processing relatives.

Remarks 8.9

*   •  Most of our discussion on the online versions has been focused on the simplest version, given in Eq. [(8.99)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq190) for *Φ*[*n*] = *I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si473.png). However, the topic of stochastic gradient descent schemes, especially in the context of smooth loss functions, has a very rich history of over 60 years, and many algorithmic variants have been “born.” In Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), a number of variations of the basic LMS scheme were discussed. Some more notable examples which are still popular are the following.
*   *Stochastic gradient descent with momentum*: The basic iteration of this variant is

**θ**[*n*] = **θ**[*n* − 1] − *μ*[*n*]ℒ[*n*]^′(**θ**[*n* − 1]) + *β*[*n*](**θ**[*n* − 1] − **θ**[*n* − 2]).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si474.png)(8.100) 

*   Very often, *β*[*n*] = *β*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si475.png) is chosen to be a constant (see, for example, \[91\]).
*   *Gradient averaging*: Another widely used version results if the place of the single gradient is taken by an average estimate, that is,

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1} - \\frac{\\mu\_{n}}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{n}\\mathcal{L}\_{k}^{\\prime}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si476.png)(8.101) 

*   Variants with different averaging scenarios (e.g., random selection instead of using all previously points) are also around. Such an averaging has a smoothing effect on the convergence of the algorithm. We have already seen this rationale in the context of the PEGASOS algorithm (Section [8.10.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0125)). The general trend of all the variants of the basic stochastic gradient scheme is to improve with respect to the involved constants, but the convergence rate still remains 𝒪(1/*n*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si466.png).
*   In \[50\], the online learning rationale was used in the context of data sets of fixed size, *N*. Instead of using the gradient descent scheme in Eq. [(8.98)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq186), the following version is proposed:

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\frac{\\mu\_{i}}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{g}\_{k}^{(i)},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si478.png)(8.102) 

*   where

$\\mathbf{g}\_{k}^{(i)} = \\begin{cases} {\\mathcal{L}\_{k}^{\\prime}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right),\\ } & {\\text{if}\\ k = i\_{k},} \\\\ {\\mathbf{g}\_{k}^{(i - 1)},\\ } & {\\text{otherwise}.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>otherwise</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si479.png)(8.103) 

*   The index *i*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si480.png) is randomly chosen every time from {1, 2, …, *N*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si481.png). Thus, in each iteration only one gradient is computed and the rest are drawn from the memory. It turns out that for strongly convex smooth loss functions, the algorithm exhibits linear convergence to the solution of the empirical risk in Eq. [(8.56)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq122). Of course, compared to the basic online schemes, an 𝒪(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si482.png) memory is required for keeping track of the gradient computations.
*   •  The literature on deriving performance bounds concerning online algorithms is very rich, both in studies and in ideas. For example, another line of research involves bounds for *arbitrary* online algorithms (see \[1,19,69\] and references therein). 

## 8.13 Proximal operators

So far in the chapter, we have dealt with the notion of the projection operator. In this section, we go one step further and we will introduce an elegant generalization of the notion of projection. Note that when we refer to an operator, we mean a mapping from ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si483.png), in contrast to a function, which is a mapping ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si484.png).

Definition 8.9

Let

*f* : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si485.png)

be a convex function and *λ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si486.png). The corresponding *proximal* or *proximity* operator of index *λ* \[60,71\],

*P**r**o**x*[*λ**f*] : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ^(*l*),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si487.png)(8.104) 

is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx037.jpg)(8.105) 

We stress that the proximal operator is a point in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si86.png). The definition can also be extended to include functions defined as *f* : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ ∪ { + ∞}<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si488.png). A closely related notion to the proximal operator is the following.

Definition 8.10

Let *f* be a convex function as before. We call the *Moreau* envelope of *f* the function

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx038.jpg)(8.106) 

Note that the Moreau envelope \[59\] is a *function* related to the proximal *operator* as

$e\_{\\lambda f}(\\mathbf{x}) = f\\left( \\text{Prox}\_{\\lambda f}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) + \\frac{1}{2\\lambda}||\\mathbf{x} - \\text{Prox}\_{\\lambda f}(\\mathbf{x})||^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Prox</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Prox</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si489.png)(8.107) 

The Moreau envelope can also be thought of as a regularized minimization, and it is also known as the *Moreau–Yosida regularization* \[109\]. Moreover, it can be shown that it is differentiable (e.g., \[7\]).

A first point to clarify is whether the minimum in Eq. [(8.106)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq200) exists. Note that the two terms in the brackets are both convex; namely, *f*(**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si490.png) and the quadratic term ||**x** − **v**||²<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si491.png). Hence, as can easily be shown by recalling the definition of convexity, their sum is also convex. Moreover, the latter of the two terms is strictly convex, hence their sum is also strictly convex, which guarantees a *unique* minimum.

Example 8.9

Let us calculate Prox[*λ**ι*[*C*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Prox</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ι</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si492.png), where *ι*[*C*] : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ ∪ { + ∞}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ι</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si493.png) stands for the indicator function of a nonempty closed convex subset *C* ⊂ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si494.png), defined as

$\\iota\_{C}(\\mathbf{x}): = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ 0,} & {\\text{if}\\ \\mathbf{x} \\in C,} \\\\ {\\ + \\infty,} & {\\text{if}\\ \\mathbf{x} \\notin C.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ι</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si495.png)

It is not difficult to verify that 

${Prox}\_{\\lambda\\iota\_{C}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\arg\\ \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{v} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ \\iota\_{C}(\\mathbf{v}) + \\frac{1}{2\\lambda}\\left\\| \\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{v} \\right\\|^{2} \\right\\} = \\arg\\ \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{v} \\in C}\\left\\| \\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{v} \\right\\|^{2} = P\_{C}(\\mathbf{x}),\\quad\\forall\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l},\\ \\forall\\lambda > 0,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi Moreover,

$e\_{\\lambda\\iota\_{C}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{v} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ \\iota\_{C}(\\mathbf{v}) + \\frac{1}{2\\lambda}\\left\\| \\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{v} \\right\\|^{2} Thus, as said in the beginning of this section, the proximal operator can be considered as the generalization of the projection one.

Example 8.10

${Prox}\_{\\lambda{\\| \\cdot \\|}\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})|\_{i} = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ x\_{i} - {sgn}(x\_{i})\\lambda,} & {\\text{if}\\ |x\_{i}| > \\lambda,} \\\\ {\\ \\ 0,} & {\\text{if}\\ |x\_{i}| \\leqslant \\lambda} \\\\ \\end{cases} = {sgn}(x\_{i})\\max\\{ 0,|x\_{i}| - \\lambda\\}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi For the time being, the proof is left as an exercise. The same task is treated in detail in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), and the proof is provided in Section [9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). The operation in Eq. [(8.110)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq208) is also known as *soft thresholding*. In other words, it sets to zero all values with magnitude less than a threshold value (*λ*) and adds a constant bias (depending on the sign) to the rest. To provoke the unfamiliar reader a bit, this is a way to impose sparsity on a parameter vector.

Having calculated *P**r**o**x*[*λ*∥ ⋅ ∥[1]](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si504.png), the Moreau envelope of ∥⋅∥[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si505.png) can be directly obtained by

$e\_{\\lambda{\\| \\cdot \\|}\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\left( \\frac{1}{2\\lambda}\\left( x\_{i} - {Prox}\_{\\lambda{\\| \\cdot \\|}\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})|\_{i} \\right)^{2} + \\left| {Prox}\_{\\lambda{\\| \\cdot \\|}\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})|\_{i} \\right| \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\left( \\chi\_{\\lbrack 0,\\lambda\\rbrack}(|x\_{i}|)\\frac{x\_{i}^{2}}{2\\lambda} + \\chi\_{(\\lambda, + \\infty)}(|x\_{i}|)\\left( |x\_{i} - {sgn}(x\_{i})\\lambda| + \\frac{\\lambda}{2} \\right) \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\left( \\chi\_{\\lbrack 0,\\lambda\\rbrack}(|x\_{i}|)\\frac{x\_{i}^{2}}{2\\lambda} + \\chi\_{(\\lambda, + \\infty)}(|x\_{i}|)\\left( |x\_{i}| - \\frac{\\lambda}{2} \\right) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0015" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" It is worth noting here that *e*[*λ*| ⋅ |]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si512.png) is a scaled version, more accurately 1/*λ*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si513.png) times, of the celebrated Huber function; a loss function vastly used against outliers in robust statistics, which will be discussed in more detail in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml). Note that the Moreau envelope is a “blown-up” smoothed version of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si17.png) norm function and although the original function is not differentiable, its Moreau envelope is continuously differentiable; moreover, *they both share the same minimum*. This is most interesting, and we will come back to this very soon.

![Figure 8.30 The |x| function (black solid line), its Moreau envelope eλ|⋅|(x) (red solid line), and x2/2 (black dotted line), for x \\in \\mathbb{R}Equation. Even if | ⋅ | is nondifferentiable at 0, eλ|⋅|(x) is everywhere differentiable. Note also that although x2/2 and eλ|⋅|(x) behave exactly the same for small values of x, eλ|⋅|(x) is more conservative than x2/2 in penalizing large values of x; this is the reason for the extensive usability of the Huber function, a scaled-down version of eλ|⋅|(x), as a robust tool against outliers in robust statistics.](images/B9780443292385000147/gr030.jpg)

[Figure 8.30](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#cf1300) The |*x*| function (black solid line), its Moreau envelope *e*[*λ*|⋅|](*x*) (red solid line), and *x*²/2 (black dotted line), for *x* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si287.png). Even if | ⋅ | is nondifferentiable at 0, *e*[*λ*|⋅|](*x*) is everywhere differentiable. Note also that although *x*²/2 and *e*[*λ*|⋅|](*x*) behave exactly the same for small values of *x*, *e*[*λ*|⋅|](*x*) is more conservative than *x*²/2 in penalizing large values of *x*; this is the reason for the extensive usability of the Huber function, a scaled-down version of *e*[*λ*|⋅|](*x*), as a robust tool against outliers in robust statistics.

### 8.13.1 Properties of the proximal operator

We now focus on some basic properties of the proximal operator, which will soon be used to give birth to a new class of algorithms for the minimization of nonsmooth convex loss functions.

Proposition 8.5

*Consider a convex function*

*f* : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ ∪ { + ∞},<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si514.png)

*and let* *P**r**o**x*[*λ**f*]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si515.png) *be its corresponding proximal operator of index λ. Then*

**p** :  = *P**r**o**x*[*λ**f*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si516.png)

*if and only if*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx039.jpg)(8.110) 

*Another necessary condition is*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx040.jpg)(8.111) 

The proofs of [(8.111)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq213) and [(8.112)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq214) are given in Problems [8.34](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0200) and [8.35](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#o0205), respectively.
