$\\psi(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\frac{1}{2}||\\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1}||^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si597.png)

and in place of the average gradient consider the most recent value, ℒ[*n* − 1]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si598.png). Then Eq. [(8.140)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq257) becomes equivalent to

0 ∈ ℒ[*n* − 1]^′ + ∂*ϕ*(**θ**) + *μ*[*n*](**θ** − **θ**[*n* − 1]).<mml:math><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si599.png)(8.140) 

This is the same relation that would result from Eq. [(8.131)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq244) if we set

$f\\rightarrow\\phi,\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{k}\\rightarrow\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n},\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{k - 1}\\rightarrow\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n - 1},\\ g\\rightarrow\\mathcal{L},\\ \\lambda\_{k}\\rightarrow\\frac{1}{\\mu}\_{n}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si600.png)(8.141) 

As a matter of fact, using these substitutions and setting *ϕ*( ⋅ ) = || ⋅ ||[1]<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si601.png), the FOBOS algorithm results \[36\]. However, in the case of Eq. [(8.140)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq257) one has the luxury of using other functions in place of the squared Euclidean distance from **θ**[*n* − 1]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si392.png).

A popular auxiliary function that has been exploited is the *Bregman divergence*. The Bregman divergence with respect to a function, say, *ψ*, between two points **x**, **y**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si603.png) is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/fx044.jpg)(8.142) 

It is left as a simple exercise to verify that the Euclidean distance results as the Bregman divergence if *ψ*(**x**) = ||**x**||²<mml:math><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si604.png).

Another algorithmic variant is the so-called *composite mirror descent*, which employs the currently available estimate of the subgradient, instead of the average, combined with the Bregman divergence; that is, ${\\overline{\\mathcal{L}}}^{\\prime}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si605.png) is replaced by ℒ[*n* − 1]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si598.png) and *ψ*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si606.png) by *B*[*ψ*](**θ**, **θ**[*n* − 1])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si607.png) for some function *ψ* \[37\]. In \[38\], a time-varying *ψ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si608.png) is involved by using a weighted average of the Euclidean norm. Note that in these modifications, although they may look simple, the analysis of the respective algorithms can be quite hard and substantial differences can be obtained in the performance.

In proximal-type algorithms the base operation is solving a small optimization problem at each iteration. In general, these subproblems can be solved with standard methods and, often, they admit a closed form solution. Proximal algorithms are well suited for big data application involving high dimensional datasets, e.g., \[67\].

## 8.15 Distributed optimization: some highlights

Distributed optimization (e.g., \[86\]) has already been discussed in the context of the stochastic gradient descent with an emphasis on LMS and diffusion-type algorithms in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) and also in Section [8.9](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#s0085). At the heart of distributed or decentralized optimization lies a cost function,

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}J\_{k}(\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si609.png)

which is defined over a connected network of *K* nodes (agents). Each *J*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si610.png), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si148.png), is fed with the *k*th node's data and quantifies the contribution of the corresponding agent to the overall cost. The goal is to compute a *common*, to all nodes, optimizer, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png). Moreover, each node communicates its updates, in the context of an iterative algorithm, *only* to its neighbors, instead of a common fusion center.

The *i*th step of the general iterative scheme of the so-called consensus algorithms (Section [5.13.4](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)) is of the form

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k}^{(i)} = \\sum\\limits\_{m \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{k}}a\_{mk}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m}^{(i - 1)} + \\mu\_{i}\\nabla J\_{k}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k}^{(i - 1)} \\right),\\ k = 1,2,\\ldots,K,$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si612.png)(8.143) 

where 𝒩[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si263.png) is the set of indices corresponding to the neighbors of the *k*th agent, that is, the nodes with which the *k*th node shares links in the corresponding graph (see Section [5.13](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)). Matrix *A* = \[*a*[*m**k*]\], *m*, *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si613.png), is a mixing matrix, which has to satisfy certain properties, e.g., to be left or doubly stochastic (Section [5.13.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)).

In the above framework, a number of algorithms have been suggested based on a diminishing step size sequence that converge to a solution **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si322.png), i.e.,

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si614.png)

For example in \[39\], under the assumption of bounded gradients and a step size of $\\mu\_{i} = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{i}}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si615.png), a convergence rate of $\\mathcal{O}(\\frac{\\ln i}{\\sqrt{i}})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si616.png) is attained. Similar results hold for the so-called *push* method that is implemented on a dynamic graph \[62\]. Improved rates are obtained under the assumption of strong convexity \[63\].

In \[85\], a modification known as the EXTRA version of the basic iterative scheme, given in Eq. [(8.144)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#deq264), is introduced, which adopts a constant step size, *μ*[*i*] = *μ*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si351.png), and it can achieve a convergence rate of $\\mathcal{O}(\\frac{1}{i})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si617.png) and a linear convergence rate under the strong convexity assumption for the cost function. In \[110,111\], a relation for diffusion-type algorithms is developed, which also relaxes some of the assumptions, concerning matrix *A*, compared to the original EXTRA algorithm.

Distributed optimization is a topic with ongoing intense research at the time the third edition of the book is compiled. Our goal in this section was not to present and summarize the related literature but more to make the reader alert of some key contributions and directions in the field.

6.  8.39  Create an ad hoc network having 10 nodes and a total number of 32 connections. Generate at each node the data which adhere to the following model:

*y*[*k*](*n*) = **θ**[*o*]^(*T*)**x**[*k*](*n*) + *η*[*k*](*n*),  *k* = 1, …, 10.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si668.png)

1.  The unknown vector **θ**[*o*] ∈ ℝ^(60)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>60</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si275.png) and its components are generated randomly via the Gaussian 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si245.png). The input vectors are i.i.d. and follow an 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si245.png). Moreover, the noise samples are i.i.d. generated from zero mean Gaussians with variances corresponding to different signal-to-noise levels, varying randomly from 20 to 25 dBs from node to node.
2.  For the unknown vector estimation employ the combine-then-adapt diffusion APSM ([Algorithm 8.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml#enun0150)), adapt-then-combine LMS ([Algorithm 5.7](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)), combine-then-adapt LMS ([Algorithm 5.8](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)), and noncooperative LMS ([Algorithm 5.1](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)) algorithms. For the combine-then-adapt APSM, set *μ*[*n*] = 0.5 × *M*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si669.png), $\\epsilon\_{k} = \\sqrt{2}\\sigma\_{k}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si670.png), and *q* = 20<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si671.png). For the adapt-then-combine, combine-then-adapt, and noncooperative LMS, set the step size equal to 0.03. Finally, choose the combination weights *a*[*m**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000147/si672.png) with respect to the Metropolis rule ([Remarks 5.4](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)).
3.  Run 100 independent experiments and plot the average MSD per iteration in dBs, that is,

${MSD}(n) = 10\\log\_{10}\\left( \\frac{1}{K}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}{\\|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k}(n) - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o}\\|}^{2} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MSD</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

1.  Compare the performance of the combine-then-adapt APSM with the performance of the LMS-based algorithms. 
2.  Keep playing with different values of the parameters for the involved algorithms and observe their influence on the obtained performance.

## 9.1 Introduction

In Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), the notion of regularization was introduced as a tool to address a number of problems that are usually encountered in machine learning. Improving the performance of an estimator by shrinking the norm of the minimum variance unbiased (MVU) estimator, guarding against overfitting, coping with ill-conditioning, and providing a solution to an underdetermined set of equations are some notable examples where regularization has provided successful answers. Some of the advantages were demonstrated via the ridge regression concept, where the sum of squared errors cost function was combined, in a tradeoff rationale, with the squared Euclidean norm of the desired solution.

In this and the next chapter, our interest will be on alternatives in the Euclidean norm, and in particular the focus will revolve around the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm; this is the sum of the absolute values of the components comprising a vector. Although seeking a solution to a problem via the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm regularization of a cost function has been known and used since the 1970s, it took almost thirty years to become the focus of attention of a massive volume of research in the context of compressed sensing. At the heart of this problem lies an underdetermined set of linear equations, which, in general, accepts an infinite number of solutions. However, in a number of cases, an extra piece of information is available: the true model, whose estimate we want to obtain, is sparse; that is, only a few of its coordinates are nonzero. It turns out that a large number of commonly used applications can be cast under such a scenario and can benefit by sparse modeling.

Besides its practical significance, sparsity-aware learning has offered to the scientific community novel theoretical tools and solutions to problems that only a few years ago seemed intractable. This is also a reason that this is an interdisciplinary field of research encompassing scientists from, for example, mathematics, statistics, machine learning, and signal processing. Moreover, it has already been applied in many areas, ranging from biomedicine to communications and astronomy. In this and the following chapters, I made an effort to present in a unifying way the basic notions and ideas that run across this field. The goal is to provide the reader with an overview of the major contributions that have taken place in the theoretical and algorithmic fronts and have been consolidated as a distinct scientific area.

In the current chapter, the focus is on presenting the main concepts and theoretical foundations related to sparsity-aware learning techniques. We start by reviewing various norms. Then we move on to establish conditions on the recovery of sparse vectors, or vectors that are sparse in a transform domain, using less observations than the dimension of the corresponding space. Geometry plays an important part in our approach. Finally, some theoretical advances that tie sparsity and sampling theory are presented. At the end of the chapter, a case study concerning image denoising is discussed.

## 9.2 Searching for a norm

Mathematicians have been very imaginative in proposing various norms in order to equip linear spaces. Among the most popular norms used in functional analysis are the ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norms. To tailor things to our needs, given a vector **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si345.png), its ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norm is defined as

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{p}: = \\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}|\\theta\_{i}|^{p} \\right)^{1/p}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si5.png)(9.1) 

For *p* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si6.png), the Euclidean or ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm is obtained, and for *p* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si8.png), Eq. [(9.1)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq1) results in the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm, that is,

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}|\\theta\_{i}|.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si9.png)(9.2)

One can show that all the ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norms are true norms for *p* ≥ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si15.png); that is, satisfy all four requirements that a function ℝ^(*l*) ↦ \[0, ∞)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si16.png) must respect in order to be called a norm, that is,

2.  **2.**  ∥**θ**∥[*p*] = 0 ⇔ **θ** = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">⇔</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si18.png),
3.  **3.**  ∥*α***θ**∥[*p*] = |*α*|∥**θ**∥[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si19.png), ∀*α* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si20.png),
4.  **4.**  ∥**θ**[1]+**θ**[2]∥[*p*] ≤ ∥**θ**[1]∥[*p*] + ∥**θ**[2]∥[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si21.png).

The third condition enforces the norm function to be (*positively*) *homogeneous* and the fourth one is the *triangle inequality*. These properties also guarantee that any function that is a norm is also a convex one (Problem [9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0040)). Though strictly speaking, if we allow *p* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si22.png) to take values less than one in Eq. [(9.1)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq1), the resulting function is not a true norm (Problem [9.8](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0065)), we may still call them norms, although we know that this is an abuse of the definition of a norm. An interesting case, which will be used extensively in this chapter, is the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm, which can be obtained as the limit, for *p* → 0<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si23.png), of

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{0}: = \\lim\\limits\_{p\\rightarrow 0}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{p}^{p} = \\lim\\limits\_{p\\rightarrow 0}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}|\\theta\_{i}|^{p} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\chi\_{(0,\\infty)}(|\\theta\_{i}|),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si24.png)(9.4) 

where *χ*[𝒜]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si25.png) is the characteristic function with respect to a set 𝒜<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si26.png), defined as

$\\chi\_{\\mathcal{A}}(\\tau): = \\begin{cases} {1,} & {\\text{if}\\ \\tau \\in \\mathcal{A},} \\\\ {0,} & {\\text{if}\\ \\tau \\notin \\mathcal{A}.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si27.png)

That is, the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm is equal to the number of nonzero components of the respective vector. It is very easy to check that this function is not a true norm. Indeed, this is not homogeneous, that is, ∥*α***θ**∥[0] ≠ |*α*|∥**θ**∥[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si28.png), ∀ |*α*| ≠ 1<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si29.png). [Fig. 9.1](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0010) shows the isovalue curves, in the two-dimensional space, that correspond to ∥**θ**∥[*p*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si30.png), for *p* = 0, 0.5, 1, 2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si31.png), and ∞. Observe that for the Euclidean norm the isovalue curve has the shape of a circle and for the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm the shape of a rhombus. We refer to them as the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) and the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) balls, respectively, by slightly “abusing” the meaning of a ball.^([^(61)](#fn61))

![Figure 9.1 The isovalue curves for \\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{p} = 1Equation and for various values of p, in the two-dimensional space. Observe that for the ℓ0 norm, the respective values cover the two axes with the exception of the point (0,0). For the ℓ1 norm, the isovalue curve is a rhombus, and for the ℓ2 (Euclidean) norm, it is a circle.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 9.1](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#cf0175) The isovalue curves for ∥**θ**∥[*p*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si30.png) and for various values of *p*, in the two-dimensional space. Observe that for the *ℓ*[0] norm, the respective values cover the two axes with the exception of the point (0,0). For the *ℓ*[1] norm, the isovalue curve is a rhombus, and for the *ℓ*[2] (Euclidean) norm, it is a circle.

[Fig. 9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0015) shows the graph of |*θ*|^(*p*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si35.png), which is the individual contribution of each component of a vector to the ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norm, for different values of *p*. Observe that (a) for *p* < 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si36.png), the region that is formed above the graph (epigraph, see Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)) is not a convex one, which verifies what we have already said, that is, the respective function is not a true norm; and (b) for values of the argument |*θ*| > 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si37.png), the larger the value of *p* ≥ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si15.png) and the larger the value of |*θ*|<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si38.png), the higher the contribution of the respective component to the norm. Hence, if ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norms, *p* ≥ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si15.png), are used in the regularization method, components with large values become the dominant ones and the optimization algorithm will concentrate on these by penalizing them to get smaller so that the overall cost can be reduced. The opposite is true for values |*θ*| < 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si39.png); ℓ[*p*], *p* > 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si40.png), norms tend to push the contribution of such components to zero. The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm is the only one (among *p* ≥ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si15.png)) that retains relatively large values even for small values of |*θ*| < 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si39.png) and, hence, components with small values can still have a say in the optimization process and can be penalized by being pushed to smaller values. Hence, if the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm is used to replace the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) one in Eq. [(3.41)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), *only those components of the parameter vector that are really significant in reducing the model misfit measuring term in the regularized cost function will be kept, and the rest will be forced to zero*. The same tendency, yet more aggressive, is true for 0 ≤ *p* < 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si41.png). The extreme case is when one considers the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm. Even a small increase of a component from zero makes its contribution to the norm large, so the optimizing algorithm has to be very “cautious” in making an element nonzero.

![Figure 9.2 Observe that the epigraph, that is, the region above the graph, is nonconvex for values p < 1, indicating the nonconvexity of the respective |θ|p function. The value p = 1 is the smallest one for which convexity is retained. Also note that, for large values of p > 1, the contribution of small values of |θ| < 1 to the respective norm becomes insignificant.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr002.jpg)

[Figure 9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#cf0185) Observe that the epigraph, that is, the region above the graph, is nonconvex for values *p* < 1, indicating the nonconvexity of the respective |*θ*|^(*p*) function. The value *p* = 1 is the smallest one for which convexity is retained. Also note that, for large values of *p* > 1, the contribution of small values of |*θ*| < 1 to the respective norm becomes insignificant.

In a nutshell, from all the true norms (*p* ≥ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si15.png)), the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) is the only one that shows respect to small values. The rest of the ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norms, *p* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si42.png), just squeeze them to make their values even smaller, and care mainly for the large values. We will return to this point very soon.

## 9.3 The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)

In Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), we discussed some of the benefits in adopting the regularization method for enhancing the performance of an estimator. In this chapter, we will see and study more reasons that justify the use of regularization. The first one refers to what is known as the *interpretation* power of an estimator. For example, in the regression task, we want to select those components *θ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si43.png) of ***θ*** that have the most important say in the formation of the output variable. This is very important if the number of parameters, *l*, is large and we want to concentrate on the most important of them. In a classification task, not all features are informative, hence one would like to keep the most informative of them and make the less informative ones equal to zero. Another related problem refers to those cases where we know, a priori, that a number of the components of a parameter vector are zero, but we do not know which ones. Now, the discussion at the end of the previous section becomes more meaningful. Can we use, while regularizing, an appropriate norm that can assist the optimization process (a) in unveiling such zeros or (b) to put more emphasis on the most significant of its components, those that play a decisive role in reducing the misfit measuring term in the regularized cost function, and set the rest of them equal to zero? Although the ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png) norms, with *p* < 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si36.png), seem to be the natural choice for such a regularization, the fact that they are not convex makes the optimization process hard. The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm is the one that is “closest” to them, yet it retains the computationally attractive property of convexity.

The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm has been used for such problems for a long time. In the 1970s, it was used in seismology \[27,86\], where the reflected signal that indicates changes in the various earth substrates is a sparse one, that is, very few values are relatively large and the rest are small and insignificant. Since then, it has been used to tackle similar problems in different applications (e.g., \[40,80\]). However, one can trace two papers that were catalytic in providing the spark for the strong interest around the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm. One came from statistics \[89\], which addressed the LASSO task (first formulated, to our knowledge, in \[80\]), to be discussed next, and the other came from the signal analysis community \[26\], which formulated the *basis pursuit*, to be discussed in a later section.

We first address our familiar regression task

**y** = *X***θ** + **η**, **y**, **η** ∈ ℝ^(*N*), **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *N* ≥ *l*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si44.png)

and obtain the estimate of the unknown parameter vector ***θ*** via the sum of squared errors cost, regularized by the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm, that is, for *λ* ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si45.png), 

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}: = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ L(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\lambda)$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si46.png)(9.5) 

$: = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\left( \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - \\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)^{2} + \\lambda\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} \\right) = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\left( \\left( \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)^{T}\\left( \\mathbf{y} - If this is not the case, the data can be centered by subtracting their respective sample means.

It turns out that the task in Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq8) can be equivalently written in the following two formulations:

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}:\\ \\ \\ \\ \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left( \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)^{T}\\left( \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right) \\leq \\epsilon,$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true" id="mmlbr0003"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0003" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si49.png)(9.8) 

given the user-defined parameters *ρ*, *ϵ* ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si50.png). The formulation in [(9.7)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq9) is known as the LASSO and the one in [(9.8)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq10) as the *basis pursuit denoising* (BPDN) (e.g., \[15\]). All three formulations are equivalent for specific choices of *λ*, *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si51.png), and *ρ* (see, e.g., \[14\]). Observe that the minimized cost function in Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq8) corresponds to the Lagrangian of the formulation in [(9.7)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq9). However, this functional dependence among *λ*, *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si51.png), and *ρ* is hard to compute, unless the columns of *X* are mutually orthogonal. Moreover, this equivalence does not necessarily imply that all three formulations are equally easy or difficult to solve. As we will see later in this chapter, algorithms have been developed along each one of the previous formulations. From now on, we will refer to all three formulations as the LASSO task, in a slight abuse of the standard terminology, and the specific formulation will be apparent from the context, if not stated explicitly.

We know that ridge regression admits a closed form solution, that is,

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{R} = \\left( X^{T}X + \\lambda I \\right)^{- 1}X^{T}\\mathbf{y}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si52.png)

In contrast, this is not the case for LASSO, and its solution requires iterative techniques. It is straightforward to see that LASSO can be formulated as a standard convex quadratic problem with linear inequalities. Indeed, we can rewrite Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq8) as

$\\min\\limits\_{{\\{\\theta\_{i},u\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{l}}\\quad\\left( \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)^{T}\\left( \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right) + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}u\_{i},\\ \\ \\ \\ \\text{s.t.}\\qquad\\left\\{ \\begin{aligned} & {- u\_{i} \\leq \\theta\_{i} \\leq u\_{i},} \\\\ & {u\_{i} \\geq 0,} \\\\ \\end{aligned}\\quad i = 1,2,\\ldots,l, \\right.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0004"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0004" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable displaystyle="true" columnspacing="0.2em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"/><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"/><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si53.png)

which can be solved by any standard convex optimization method (e.g., \[14,101\]). The reason that developing algorithms for the LASSO task has been at the center of an intense research activity is due to the emphasis on obtaining *efficient* algorithms by exploiting the specific nature of this task, especially for cases where *l* is very large, as is often the case in practice.

In order to get better insight into the nature of the solution that is obtained by LASSO, let us assume that the regressors are mutually orthogonal and of unit norm, hence *X*^(*T*)*X* = *I*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si54.png). Orthogonality of the input matrix helps to decouple the coordinates and results to *l* one-dimensional problems that can be solved analytically. For this case, the LS estimate becomes

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{LS}} = {(X^{T}X)}^{- 1}X^{T}\\mathbf{y} = X^{T}\\mathbf{y},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si55.png)

and the ridge regression gives

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{R} = \\frac{1}{1 + \\lambda}{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{LS}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si56.png)(9.9) 

that is, every component of the LS estimate is simply shrunk by the *same* factor, $\\frac{1}{1 + \\lambda}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si57.png); see, also, Section [6.5](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml).

In the case of ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) regularization, the minimized Lagrangian function is no more differentiable, due to the presence of the absolute values in the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm. So, in this case, we have to consider the notion of the subdifferential. It is known (Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)) that if the zero vector belongs to the subdifferential set of a convex function at a point, this means that this point corresponds to a minimum of the function. Taking the subdifferential of the Lagrangian defined in Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq8) and recalling that the subdifferential set of a differentiable function includes as its *single* element the respective gradient, the estimate ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{1}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si58.png), resulting from the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) regularized task, must satisfy

0 ∈  − 2*X*^(*T*)**y** + 2*X*^(*T*)*X***θ** + *λ*∂∥**θ**∥[1],<mml:math><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si59.png)

where ∂ stands for the subdifferential set (Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)). If *X* has orthonormal columns, the previous equation can be written component-wise as follows:

$0 \\in - {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{LS},i} + {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{1,i} + \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\partial\\left| {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{1,i} \\right|,\\quad\\forall i,$<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si60.png)(9.10) 

where the subdifferential of the function | ⋅ |<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si61.png), derived in [Example 8.4](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml) (Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)), is given as

$\\partial|\\theta| = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ \\{ 1\\},} & {\\text{if}\\ \\theta > 0,} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\{ - 1\\},} & {\\text{if}\\ \\theta < 0,} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\lbrack - 1,1\\rbrack,} & {\\text{if}\\ \\theta = 0.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si62.png)

Thus, we can now write for each component of the LASSO optimal estimate

![](images/B9780443292385000159/gr003.jpg)

Note that Eq. (9.11) can only be true if ${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{LS},i} > \\frac{\\lambda}{2}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si63.png), and Eq. (9.12) only if ${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{LS},i} < - \\frac{\\lambda}{2}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si64.png).
