Moreover, in the case where *θ̂*[1, *i*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si65.png), [(9.10)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq16) and the subdifferential of | ⋅ |<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si61.png) suggest that necessarily $\\left| \\widehat{\\theta}{}\_{\\text{LS},i} \\middle| \\leqslant \\frac{\\lambda}{2} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msub><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si66.png). Concluding, we can write in a more compact way that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/fx001.jpg)(9.13) 

where ( ⋅ )[+]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si67.png) denotes the “positive part” of the respective argument; it is equal to the argument if this is nonnegative, and zero otherwise. This is very interesting indeed. In contrast to the ridge regression which shrinks all coordinates of the unregularized LS solution by the same factor, LASSO forces all coordinates, whose absolute value is less than or equal to *λ*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si68.png), to zero, and the rest of the coordinates are reduced, in absolute value, by the same amount *λ*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si68.png). This is known as *soft thresholding*, to distinguish it from the *hard thresholding* operation; the latter is defined as $\\theta \\cdot \\chi\_{(0,\\infty)}\\left( |\\theta| - \\frac{\\lambda}{2} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si69.png), *θ* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si70.png), where *χ*[(0, ∞)]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si71.png) stands for the characteristic function with respect to the set (0, ∞)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si72.png). [Fig. 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0025) shows the graphs illustrating the effect that the ridge regression, LASSO, and hard thresholding have on the unregularized LS solution, as a function of its value (horizontal axis). Note that our discussion here, simplified via the orthonormal input matrix case, has quantified what we said before about the tendency of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm to push small values to become *exactly zero*. This will be further strengthened, via a more rigorous mathematical formulation, in Section [9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0030).

![Figure 9.3 Curves relating the output (vertical) to the input (horizontal) for the hard thresholding and the soft thresholding operators shown together with the linear operator that is associated with the ridge regression, for the same value of λ = 1.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr004.jpg)

Figure 9.3 Curves relating the output (vertical) to the input (horizontal) for the hard thresholding and the soft thresholding operators shown together with the linear operator that is associated with the ridge regression, for the same value of *λ* = 1.

Example 9.1

Assume that the unregularized LS solution, for a given regression task, **y** = *X***θ** + **η**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si73.png), is given by

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{LS}} = {\\lbrack 0.2, - 0.7,0.8, - 0.1,1.0\\rbrack}^{T}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.8</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si74.png)

Derive the solutions for the corresponding ridge regression and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm regularization tasks. Assume that the input matrix *X* has orthonormal columns and that the regularization parameter is *λ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si75.png). Also, what is the result of hard thresholding the vector ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{LS}}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si76.png) with threshold equal to 0.5?

We know that the corresponding solution for the ridge regression is

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{R} = \\frac{1}{1 + \\lambda}{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{LS}} = {\\lbrack 0.1, - 0.35,0.4, - 0.05,0.5\\rbrack}^{T}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>LS</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.35</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.4</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si77.png)

The solution for the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm regularization is given by soft thresholding, with threshold equal to *λ*/2 = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si78.png), and hence the corresponding vector is

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{1} = {\\lbrack 0, - 0.2,0.3,0,0.5\\rbrack}^{T}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si79.png)

The result of the hard thresholding operation is the vector \[0,  − 0.7, 0.8, 0, 1.0\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.8</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si80.png).

Remarks 9.1

*   •  The hard and soft thresholding rules are only two possibilities out of a larger number of alternatives. Note that the hard thresholding operation is defined via a discontinuous function, and this makes this rule unstable in the sense of being very sensitive to small changes of the input. Moreover, this shrinking rule tends to exhibit large variance in the resulting estimates. The soft thresholding rule is a continuous function, but, as readily seen from the graph in [Fig. 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0025), it introduces bias even for the large values of the input argument. In order to ameliorate such shortcomings, a number of alternative thresholding operators have been introduced and studied both theoretically and experimentally. Although these are not within the mainstream of our interest, we provide two popular examples for the sake of completeness—the *smoothly clipped absolute deviation* (SCAD) thresholding rule,

${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{SCAD}} = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ {sgn}(\\theta)\\left( |\\theta| - \\lambda\_{\\text{SCAD}} \\right)\_{+},} & {|\\theta| \\leq 2\\lambda\_{\\text{SCAD}},} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\frac{(\\alpha - 1)\\theta - \\alpha\\lambda\_{\\text{SCAD}}{sgn}(\\theta)}{\\alpha - 2},} & {2\\lambda\_{\\text{SCAD}} < |\\theta| \\leqslant \\alpha\\lambda\_{\\text{SCAD}},} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\theta,} & {|\\theta| > \\alpha\\lambda\_{\\text{SCAD}},} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>SCAD</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si81.png)

*   and the *nonnegative garrote* thresholding rule,

${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\text{garr}} = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ 0,} & {|\\theta| \\leq \\lambda\_{\\text{garr}},} \\\\ {\\ \\ \\theta - \\frac{\\lambda\_{\\text{garr}}^{2}}{\\theta},} & {|\\theta| > \\lambda\_{\\text{garr}}.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>garr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>garr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>garr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>&gt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>garr</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si82.png)

*   [Fig. 9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0030) shows the respective graphs. Observe that in both cases, an effort has been made to remove the discontinuity (associated with the hard thresholding) and to remove/reduce the bias for large values of the input argument. The parameter *α* > 2<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si83.png) is a user-defined one. For a more detailed related discussion, the interested reader can refer, for example, to \[2\]. In \[83\], a generalized thresholding rule is suggested that encompasses all previously mentioned ones as special cases. Moreover, the proposed framework is general enough to provide means for designing novel thresholding rules and/or incorporating a priori information associated with the sparsity level, i.e., the number of nonzero components, of the sparse vector to be recovered.

![Figure 9.4 Output (vertical)–input (horizontal) graph for the SCAD and nonnegative garrote rules with parameters α = 3.7 and λSCAD = λgarr = 1. Observe that both rules smoothen out the discontinuity associated with the hard thresholding rule. Note, also, that the SCAD rule removes the bias associated with the soft thresholding rule for large values of the input variable. On the contrary, the garrote thresholding rule allows some bias for large input values, which diminishes as λgarr gets smaller and smaller.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#cf0270) Output (vertical)–input (horizontal) graph for the SCAD and nonnegative garrote rules with parameters *α* = 3.7 and *λ*[SCAD] = *λ*[garr] = 1. Observe that both rules smoothen out the discontinuity associated with the hard thresholding rule. Note, also, that the SCAD rule removes the bias associated with the soft thresholding rule for large values of the input variable. On the contrary, the garrote thresholding rule allows some bias for large input values, which diminishes as *λ*[garr] gets smaller and smaller.

*   

## 9.4 Sparse signal representation

In the previous section, we brought into our discussion the need to take special care for zeros. Sparsity is an attribute that is met in a plethora of natural signals, because nature tends to be parsimonious. The notion of and need for parsimonious models was also discussed in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), in the context of inverse problems in machine learning tasks. In this section, we will briefly present a number of application cases where the existence of zeros in a mathematical expansion is of paramount importance; hence, it justifies our search for and development of related analysis tools.

In Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml), we discussed the task of echo cancellation. In a number of cases, the echo path, represented by a vector comprising the values of the impulse response samples/coefficients, is a sparse one. This is the case, for example, in internet telephony and in acoustic and network environments (e.g., \[3,10,73\]). [Fig. 9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0035) shows the impulse response of such an echo path. The impulse response of the echo path is of short duration; however, the delay with which it appears is not known. So, in order to model it, one has to use a long impulse response, yet only a relatively small number of the coefficients will be significant and the rest will be close to zero. Of course, one could ask, why not use an LMS or an RLS, and eventually the significant coefficients will be identified? The answer is that this turns out not to be the most efficient way to tackle such problems, because the convergence of the algorithm can be very slow. In contrast, if one embeds, somehow, into the problem the a priori information concerning the existence of (almost) zero coefficients, then the convergence speed can be significantly increased and also better error floors can be attained.

![Figure 9.5 The impulse response function of an echo path in a telephone network. Observe that although it is of relatively short duration, it is not a priori known where exactly in time it will occur.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#cf0285) The impulse response function of an echo path in a telephone network. Observe that although it is of relatively short duration, it is not a priori known where exactly in time it will occur.

A similar situation occurs in wireless communication systems, which involve multipath channels. A typical application is in high-definition television (HDTV) systems, where the involved communication channels consist of a *few* nonnegligible coefficients, some of which may have quite large time delays with respect to the main signal (see, e.g., \[4,32,52,77\]). If the information signal is transmitted at high symbol rates through such a dispersive channel, then the introduced intersymbol interference (ISI) has a span of several tens up to hundreds of symbol intervals. This in turn implies that quite long channel estimators are required at the receiver's end in order to reduce effectively the ISI component of the received signal, although only a small part of it has values substantially different from zero. The situation is even more demanding when the channel-frequency response exhibits deep nulls. More recently, sparsity has been exploited in channel estimation for multicarrier systems, both for single-antenna as well as for multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) systems \[46,47\]. A thorough, in-depth treatment related to sparsity in multipath communication systems is provided in \[5\].

Another example, which might be more widely known, is that of signal compression. It turns out that if the signal modalities with which we communicate (e.g., speech) and also sense the world (e.g., images, audio) are transformed into a suitably chosen domain, then they are sparsely represented; only a relatively small number of the signal components in this domain are large, and the rest are close to zero. As an example, [Fig. 9.6](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0040)A shows an image and [Fig. 9.6](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0040)B shows the plot of the magnitude of the obtained discrete cosine transform (DCT) components, which are computed by writing the corresponding image array as a vector in lexicographic order. Note that more than 95% of the total energy is contributed by only 5% of the largest components. This is at the heart of any compression technique. Only the large coefficients are chosen to be coded and the rest are considered to be zero. Hence, significant gains are obtained in memory/bandwidth requirements while storing/transmitting such signals, without much perceptual loss. Depending on the modality, different transforms are used. For example, in JPEG-2000, an image array, represented in terms of a vector that contains the intensity of the gray levels of the image pixels, is transformed via the discrete wavelet transform (DWT), resulting in a transformed vector that comprises only a few large components.

![Figure 9.6 (A) A 512 × 512 pixel image and (B) the magnitude of its DCT components in descending order and logarithmic scale. Note that more than 95% of the total energy is contributed by only 5% of the largest components.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr007.jpg)

Figure 9.6 (A) A 512 × 512 pixel image and (B) the magnitude of its DCT components in descending order and logarithmic scale. Note that more than 95% of the total energy is contributed by only 5% of the largest components.

Let

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}} = \\Phi^{H}\\mathbf{s},\\ \\mathbf{s},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}} \\in \\mathbb{C}^{l},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si84.png)(9.14) 

where ***s*** is the vector of the “raw” signal samples, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si85.png) is the (complex-valued) vector of the transformed ones, and Φ is the *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si86.png) transformation matrix. Often, this is an orthonormal/unitary matrix, *Φ*^(*H*)*Φ* = *I*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si87.png). Basically, a transform is nothing more than a projection of a vector on a new set of coordinate axes, which comprise the columns of the transformation matrix Φ. Celebrated examples of such transforms are the wavelet, the discrete Fourier (DFT), and the discrete cosine (DCT) transforms (e.g., \[87\]). In such cases, where the transformation matrix is orthonormal, one can write

$\\mathbf{s} = \\Psi\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si88.png)(9.15) 

where *Ψ* = *Φ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si89.png). Eq. [(9.14)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq24) is known as the *analysis* and Eq. [(9.15)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq25) as the *synthesis* equation.

Compression via such transforms exploits the fact that many signals in nature, which are rich in context, can be *compactly* represented in an appropriately chosen basis, depending on the modality of the signal. Very often, the construction of such bases tries to “imitate” the sensory systems that the human brain has developed in order to sense these signals; and we know that nature (in contrast to modern humans) does not like to waste resources. A standard compression task comprises the following stages: (a) obtain the *l* components of $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si85.png) via the analysis step Eq. [(9.14)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq24); (b) keep the *k* most significant of them; (c) code these values, as well as their respective locations in the transformed vector $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si85.png); and (d) obtain the (approximate) original signal ***s*** when needed (after storage or transmission), via the synthesis equation (Eq. [(9.15)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq25)), where in place of $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si85.png) only its *k* most significant components are used, which are the ones that were coded, while the rest are set equal to zero. However, there is something unorthodox in this process of compression as it has been practiced until fairly recently. One processes (transforms) large signal vectors of *l* coordinates, where *l* in practice can be quite large, and then uses only a small percentage of the transformed coefficients, while the rest are simply ignored. Moreover, one has to store/transmit the location of the respective large coefficients that are finally coded.

A natural question that is raised is the following: Because $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si85.png) in the synthesis equation is (approximately) sparse, can one compute it via an alternative path to the analysis model in Eq. [(9.14)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq24)? The issue here is to investigate whether one could use a more informative way of sampling the available raw data so that fewer than *l* samples/observations are sufficient to recover all the necessary information. The ideal case would be to recover it via a set of *k* such samples, because this is the number of the significant free parameters. On the other hand, if this sounds a bit extreme, can one obtain *N* (*k* < *N* ≪ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si90.png)) such signal-related measurements, from which ***s*** can eventually be retrieved? It turns out that such an approach is possible and it leads to the solution of an *underdetermined* system of linear equations, under the constraint that the unknown target vector is a sparse one in some domain.

The importance of such techniques becomes even more apparent when, instead of an orthonormal basis, as discussed before, a more general type of expansion is adopted, in terms of what is known as *overcomplete dictionaries*. A dictionary \[65\] is a collection of parameterized waveforms, which are discrete-time signal samples, represented as vectors **ψ**[*i*] ∈ ℂ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si91.png), *i* ∈ ℐ<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si92.png), where ℐ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si93.png) is an integer index set. For example, the columns of a DFT or a discrete wavelet (DWT) matrix comprise a dictionary. These are two examples of what are known as *complete* dictionaries, which consist of *l* (orthonormal) vectors, that is, a number equal to the length of the signal vector. However, in many cases in practice, using such dictionaries is very restrictive. Let us take, for example, a segment of audio signal, from a news media or a video, that needs to be processed. This consists, in general, of different types of signals, namely, speech, music, and environmental sounds. For each type of these signals, different signal vectors may be more appropriate in the expansion for the analysis. For example, music signals are characterized by a strong harmonic content and the use of sinusoids seems to be best for compression, while for speech signals a Gabor-type signal expansion (sinusoids of various frequencies weighted by sufficiently narrow pulses at different locations in time \[31,87\]) may be a better choice. The same applies when one deals with an image. Different parts of an image, such as parts that are smooth or contain sharp edges, may demand a different expansion vector set for obtaining the best overall performance. The more recent tendency, in order to satisfy such needs, is to use *overcomplete* dictionaries. Such dictionaries can be obtained, for example, by concatenating different dictionaries together, for example, a DFT and a DWT matrix to result in a combined *l* × 2*l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si94.png) transformation matrix. Alternatively, a dictionary can be “trained” in order to effectively represent a set of available signal exemplars, a task that is often referred to as dictionary learning \[75,78,90,100\]. While using such overcomplete dictionaries, the synthesis equation takes the form

$\\mathbf{s} = \\sum\\limits\_{i \\in \\mathcal{I}}\\theta\_{i}\\mathbf{\\psi}\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si95.png)(9.16) 

Note that, now, the analysis is an ill-posed problem, because the elements {**ψ**[*i*]}[*i* ∈ ℐ]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si96.png) (usually called *atoms*) of the dictionary are not linearly independent, and there is not a unique set of parameters {*θ*[*i*]}[*i* ∈ ℐ]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si97.png) that generates ***s***. Moreover, we expect most of these parameters to be (nearly) zero. Note that in such cases, the cardinality of ℐ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si93.png) is larger than *l*. This necessarily leads to underdetermined systems of equations with infinitely many solutions. The question that is now raised is whether we can exploit the fact that most of these parameters are known to be zero, in order to come up with a unique solution. If yes, under which conditions is such a solution possible? We will return to the task of learning dictionaries in Chapter [20](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml).

Besides the previous examples, there are a number of cases where an underdetermined system of equations is the result of our inability to obtain a sufficiently large number of measurements, due to physical and technical constraints. This is the case in MRI imaging, which will be presented in more detail in Section [10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml).

## 9.5 In search of the sparsest solution

Inspired by the discussion in the previous section, we now turn our attention to the task of solving underdetermined systems of equations by imposing the sparsity constraint on the solution. We will develop the theoretical setup in the context of regression, and we will adhere to the notation that has been adopted for this task. Moreover, we will focus on the real-valued data case in order to simplify the presentation. The theory can be readily extended to the more general complex-valued data case (see, e.g., \[64,99\]). We assume that we are given a set of observations/measurements, **y** :  = \[*y*[1], *y*[2], …, *y*[*N*]\]^(*T*) ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si98.png), according to the linear model

**y** = *X***θ**, **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*), **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *l* > *N*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si99.png)(9.17) 

where *X* is the *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) input matrix, which is assumed to be of full row rank, that is, *r**a**n**k*(*X*) = *N*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">rank</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si101.png). Our starting point is the noiseless case. The linear system of equations in [(9.17)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq27) is an underdetermined one and accepts an infinite number of solutions. The set of possible solutions lies in the intersection of the *N* hyperplanes^([^(62)](#fn62))

{**θ**∈ℝ^(*l*):*y*[*n*]\=**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**}, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si104.png)

We know from geometry that the intersection of *N* nonparallel hyperplanes (which in our case is guaranteed by the fact that *X* has been assumed to be full row rank, hence **x**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si105.png), are linearly independent) is a plane of dimensionality *l* − *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si106.png). For example, the intersection of two (nonparallel) (hyper)planes in the three-dimensional space is a straight line, that is, a plane of dimensionality equal to one. In a more formal way, the set of all possible solutions, to be denoted as Θ, is an *affine* set. An affine set is the translation of a linear subspace by a constant vector. Let us pursue this a bit further, because we will need it later on.

Let the null space of *X* be denoted as *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si107.png) (sometimes denoted as 𝒩(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si108.png)), and it is defined as the linear subspace

*n**u**l**l*(*X*) = {**z**∈ℝ^(*l*):*X***z**\=0}.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si109.png)

Obviously, if **θ**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si110.png) is a solution to Eq. [(9.17)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq27), that is, **θ**[0] ∈ *Θ*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si111.png), then it is easy to verify that ∀**θ** ∈ *Θ*<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si112.png), *X*(**θ** − **θ**[0]) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si113.png), or **θ** − **θ**[0] ∈ *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si114.png). As a result,

*Θ* = **θ**[0] + *n**u**l**l*(*X*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si115.png)

and Θ is an affine set. We also know from linear algebra basics (and it is easy to show it; see Problem [9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0070)) that the null space of a full row rank matrix, *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png), *l* > *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si116.png), is a subspace of dimensionality *l* − *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si106.png). [Fig. 9.7](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0045) illustrates the case for one observation in the two-dimensional space, *l* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si117.png) and *N* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si118.png). The set of solutions Θ is a straight line, which is the translation of the linear subspace crossing the origin (the *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si107.png)). Therefore, if one wants to select a *single* point among all the points that lie in the affine set of solutions, Θ, then an extra constraint/a priori knowledge has to be imposed.

![Figure 9.7 The set of solutions Θ is an affine set (gray line), which is a translation of the null(X) subspace (red line). (A) The ℓ2 norm minimizer: The dotted circle corresponds to the smallest ℓ2 ball that intersects the set Θ. As such, the intersection point, \\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}Equation, is the ℓ2 norm minimizer of the task in (9.18). Note that the vector \\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}Equation contains no zero component. (B) The ℓ1 norm minimizer: The dotted rhombus corresponds to the smallest ℓ1 ball that intersects Θ. Hence, the intersection point, \\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}Equation, is the solution of the constrained ℓ1 minimization task of (9.21). Note that the obtained estimate \\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = (0,1)Equation contains a zero.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr008.jpg)

Figure 9.7 The set of solutions Θ is an affine set (gray line), which is a translation of the null(*X*) subspace (red line). (A) The *ℓ*[2] norm minimizer: The dotted circle corresponds to the smallest *ℓ*[2] ball that intersects the set Θ. As such, the intersection point, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si119.png), is the *ℓ*[2] norm minimizer of the task in [(9.18)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq31). Note that the vector $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si119.png) contains no zero component. (B) The *ℓ*[1] norm minimizer: The dotted rhombus corresponds to the smallest *ℓ*[1] ball that intersects Θ. Hence, the intersection point, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si119.png), is the solution of the constrained *ℓ*[1] minimization task of [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq34). Note that the obtained estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = (0,1)$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si120.png) contains a zero.

In the sequel, three such possibilities are examined.

### The ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm minimizer

Our goal now becomes to pick a point in (the affine set) Θ that corresponds to the minimum ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm. This is equivalent to solving the following constrained task:

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\quad\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\quad\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta} = y\_{n},\\quad n = 1,2,\\ldots,N.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0005"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si121.png)(9.18) 

We already know from Section [6.4](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml) (and one can rederive it by employing Lagrange multipliers; see Problem [9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0075)) that the previous optimization task accepts a *unique* solution given in closed form as

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = X^{T}\\left( XX^{T} \\right)^{- 1}\\mathbf{y}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si122.png)(9.19) 

The geometric interpretation of this solution is provided in [Fig. 9.7](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0045)A, for the case of *l* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si117.png) and *N* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si118.png). The radius of the Euclidean norm ball keeps increasing, until it touches the plane that contains the solutions. This point is the one with the minimum ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm or, equivalently, the point that lies closest to the origin. Equivalently, the point $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si119.png) can be seen as the (metric) projection of **0** onto Θ.

Minimizing the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm in order to solve a linear set of underdetermined equations has been used in various applications. The closest to us is in the context of determining the unknown parameters in an expansion using an overcomplete dictionary of functions (vectors) \[35\]. A main drawback of this method is that it is not sparsity preserving. There is no guarantee that the solution in Eq. [(9.19)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq32) will give zeros even if the true model vector ***θ*** has zeros. Moreover, the method is *resolution-limited* \[26\]. This means that even if there may be a sharp contribution of specific atoms in the dictionary, this is not portrayed in the obtained solution. This is a consequence of the fact that the information provided by *X**X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si124.png) is a global one, containing all atoms of the dictionary in an “averaging” fashion, and the final result tends to smoothen out the individual contributions, especially when the dictionary is overcomplete.

### The ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm minimizer

Now we turn our attention to the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm (once more, it is pointed out that this is an abuse of the definition of the norm), and we make sparsity our new flag under which a solution will be obtained. The task now becomes

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\quad\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{0},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\quad\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta} = y\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N,$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0006"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0006" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si125.png)(9.20) 

that is, from all the points that lie on the plane of all possible solutions, find the *sparsest* one, that is, the one with the lowest number of nonzero elements. As a matter of fact, such an approach is within the spirit of *Occam's razor* rule—it corresponds to the smallest number of parameters that can explain the obtained observations. The points that are now raised are:

*   •  Is a solution to this problem unique, and under which conditions?
*   •  Can a solution be obtained with low enough complexity in realistic time?

We postpone the answer to the first question until later. As for the second one, the news is not good. Minimizing the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm under a set of linear constraints is a task of combinatorial nature, and as a matter of fact, the problem is, in general, NP-hard \[72\]. The way to approach the problem is to consider all possible combinations of zeros in ***θ***, removing the respective columns of *X* in Eq. [(9.17)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq27), and check whether the system of equations is satisfied; keep as solutions the ones with the smallest number of nonzero elements. Such a searching technique exhibits complexity of an exponential dependence on *l*. [Fig. 9.7](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0045)A illustrates the two points ((1.5, 0)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si126.png) and (0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si127.png)) that comprise the solution set of minimizing the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm for the single observation (constraint) case.

### The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm minimizer

The current task is now given by

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\quad\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\quad\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta} = y\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0007"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0007" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si128.png)(9.21) 

[Fig. 9.7](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0045)B illustrates the geometry. The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) ball is increased until it touches the affine set of the possible solutions. For this specific geometry, the solution is the point (0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si127.png), which is a sparse solution. In our discussion in Section [9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0015), we saw that the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm is the one, out of all ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png), *p* ≥ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si15.png) norms, that bears some similarity with the sparsity promoting (nonconvex) ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si3.png), *p* < 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si36.png) “norms.” Also, we have commented that the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm encourages zeros when the respective values are small. In the sequel, we will state one lemma that establishes this zero favoring property in a more formal way. The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm minimization task is also known as *basis pursuit* and it was suggested for decomposing a vector signal in terms of the atoms of an overcomplete dictionary \[26\].

The ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimizer can be brought into the standard linear programming (LP) form and then can be solved by recalling any related method; the simplex method and the more recent interior point method are two possibilities (see, e.g., \[14,33\]). Indeed, consider the LP task

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\quad\\mathbf{c}^{T}\\mathbf{x},\\text{s.t.}\\quad A\\mathbf{x} = \\mathbf{b},\\quad\\mathbf{x} \\geq 0.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0008"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em" id="mmlbr0009"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0008" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0009" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si129.png)

To verify that our ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimizer can be cast in the previous form, note first that any *l*\-dimensional vector ***θ*** can be decomposed as

**θ** = **u** − **v**, **u** ≥ 0, **v** ≥ 0.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si130.png)

Indeed, this holds true if, for example,

**u** :  = **θ**[+], **v** :  = ( − **θ**)[+],<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si131.png)

where **x**[+]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si132.png) stands for the vector obtained after keeping the positive components of ***x*** and setting the rest equal to zero. Moreover, note that

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} = \\lbrack 1,1,\\ldots,1\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{+} \\\\ {( - \\mathbf{\\theta})}\_{+} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\lbrack 1,1,\\ldots,1\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{u} \\\\ \\mathbf{v} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si133.png)

Hence, our ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimization task can be recast in the LP form if

**c** :  = \[1, 1, …, 1\]^(*T*), **x** :  = \[**u**^(*T*), **v**^(*T*)\]^(*T*), *A* :  = \[*X*,  − *X*\], **b** :  = **y**.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic" id="mmlbr0010">c</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0010" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si134.png)

### Characterization of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm minimizer

Lemma 9.1

*An element* ***θ*** *in the affine set* Θ *of the solutions of the underdetermined linear system in Eq.* [(9.17)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq27) *has minimal* ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) *norm if and only if the following condition is satisfied:*

$\\left| \\sum\\limits\_{i:\\ \\theta\_{i} \\neq 0}{sgn}(\\theta\_{i})z\_{i} \\middle| \\leq \\sum\\limits\_{i:\\ \\theta\_{i} = 0}|z\_{i}|,\\quad\\forall\\mathbf{z} \\in {null}(X). \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="6.6ex" minsize="6.6ex">|</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="6.6ex" minsize="6.6ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si136.png)(9.22) 

*Moreover, the* ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) *minimizer is unique if and only if the inequality in* [(9.22)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq40) *is a strict one for all* **z** ≠ 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si137.png) *(see, e.g.,* \[74\] *and Problem* [9.11](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0080)*).*

Remarks 9.2

*   •  The previous lemma has a very interesting and important consequence. If $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si119.png) is the *unique* minimizer of [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq34), then

*c**a**r**d*{*i*:*θ̂*[*i*]\=0} ≥ dim (*n**u**l**l*(*X*)),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">card</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">dim</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si138.png)(9.23) 

*   where *c**a**r**d*{ ⋅ }<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">card</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si139.png) denotes the cardinality of a set. In words, the number of zero components of the unique minimizer cannot be smaller than the dimension of the null space of *X*. Indeed, if this is not the case, then the unique minimizer could have fewer zeros than the dimensionality of *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si107.png).
