This means that one can always find a **z** ∈ *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si140.png), which has zeros in the same locations where the components of the unique minimizer are zero, and at the same time it is not identically zero, that is, **z** ≠ 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si137.png) (Problem [9.12](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0085)). However, this would violate [(9.22)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq40), which in the case of uniqueness holds as a strict inequality.

Definition 9.1

A vector ***θ*** is called *k*\-sparse if it has *at most k* nonzero components. 

Remarks 9.3

*   •  If the minimizer of [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq34) is *unique*, then it is a *k*\-sparse vector with

*k* ≤ *N*.<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si142.png)

*   This is a direct consequence of [Remarks 9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0025), and the fact that for the matrix *X*,

dim (*n**u**l**l*(*X*)) = *l* − *r**a**n**k*(*X*) = *l* − *N*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">dim</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">rank</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si143.png)

*   Hence, the number of the nonzero elements of the unique minimizer must be at most equal to *N*. If one resorts to geometry, all the previously stated results become crystal clear.

### Geometric interpretation

Assume that our target solution resides in the three-dimensional space and we are given one observation

*y*[1] = **x**[1]^(*T*)**θ** = *x*[11]*θ*[1] + *x*[12]*θ*[2] + *x*[13]*θ*[3].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>13</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si144.png)

Then the solution lies in the two-dimensional (hyper)plane, which is described by the previous equation. To get the minimal ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) solution we keep increasing the size of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) ball^([^(63)](#fn63))

![Figure 9.8 (A) The ℓ1 ball intersecting with a plane. The only possible scenario, for the existence of a unique common intersecting point of the ℓ1 ball with a plane in the Euclidean \\mathbb{R}^{3}Equation space, is for the point to be located at one of the vertices of the ℓ1 ball, that is, to be a 1-sparse vector. (B) The ℓ1 ball intersecting with lines. In this case, the sparsity level of the unique intersecting point is relaxed; it could be a 1- or a 2-sparse vector.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr009.jpg)

Figure 9.8 (A) The *ℓ*[1] ball intersecting with a plane. The only possible scenario, for the existence of a unique common intersecting point of the *ℓ*[1] ball with a plane in the Euclidean ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si145.png) space, is for the point to be located at one of the vertices of the *ℓ*[1] ball, that is, to be a 1-sparse vector. (B) The *ℓ*[1] ball intersecting with lines. In this case, the sparsity level of the unique intersecting point is relaxed; it could be a 1- or a 2-sparse vector.

Let us now assume that we are given an extra observation,

*y*[2] = *x*[21]*θ*[1] + *x*[22]*θ*[2] + *x*[23]*θ*[3].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>21</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>22</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>23</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si146.png)

The solution now lies in the intersection of the two previous planes, which is a straight line. However, now, we have more alternatives for a unique solution. A line, for example, *Θ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si147.png), can either touch the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) ball at a vertex (1-sparse solution) or, as shown in [Fig. 9.8](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0050)B, touch the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) ball at one of its edges, for example, *Θ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si148.png). The latter case corresponds to a solution that lies on a two-dimensional subspace; hence it will be a 2-sparse vector. This also complies with the findings stated in [Remarks 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0035), because in this case we have *N* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si149.png), *l* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si150.png), and the sparsity level for a unique solution can be either 1 or 2.

Note that uniqueness is associated with the particular geometry and orientation of the affine set, which is the set of all possible solutions of the underdetermined system of equations. For the case of the squared ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm, the solution is always unique. This is a consequence of the (hyper)spherical shape formed by the Euclidean norm. From a mathematical point of view, the squared ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm is a strictly convex function. This is not the case for the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm, which is convex, albeit not a strictly convex function (Problem [9.13](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0090)).

Example 9.2

Consider a sparse vector parameter \[0, 1\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si151.png), which we assume to be unknown. We will use one observation to *sense* it. Based on this single observation, we will use the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimizer of [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq34) to recover its true value. Let us see what happens.

We will consider three different values of the “sensing” (input) vector ***x*** in order to obtain the observation *y* = **x**^(*T*)**θ**<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si152.png): (a) $\\mathbf{x} = {\\lbrack\\frac{1}{2},1\\rbrack}^{T}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si153.png), (b) **x** = \[1, 1\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si154.png), and (c) **x** = \[2, 1\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si155.png). The resulting observation, after sensing ***θ*** by ***x***, is *y* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si156.png) for all three previous cases.

Case a: The solution will lie on the straight line

$\\Theta = \\left\\{ {\\lbrack\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}\\rbrack}^{T} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{2}:\\frac{1}{2}\\theta\_{1} + \\theta\_{2} = 1 \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si157.png)

which is shown in [Fig. 9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0055)A. For this setting, expanding the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) ball, this will touch the straight line (our solution's affine set) at the vertex \[0, 1\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si151.png). This is a unique solution, hence it is sparse, and it coincides with the true value.

![Figure 9.9 (A) Sensing with x = \[\\frac{1}{2}Equation,1\]T. (B) Sensing with x = \[1, 1\]T. (C) Sensing with x = \[2, 1\]T. The choice of the sensing vector x is crucial to unveiling the true sparse solution (0,1). Only the sensing vector x = {\\lbrack\\frac{1}{2},1\\rbrack}^{T}Equation identifies uniquely the desired (0,1).](images/B9780443292385000159/gr010.jpg)

Figure 9.9 (A) Sensing with ***x*** = \[$\\frac{1}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si158.png),1\]^(*T*). (B) Sensing with ***x*** = \[1, 1\]^(*T*). (C) Sensing with ***x*** = \[2, 1\]^(*T*). The choice of the sensing vector ***x*** is crucial to unveiling the true sparse solution (0,1). Only the sensing vector ***x*** = ${\\lbrack\\frac{1}{2},1\\rbrack}^{T}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si159.png) identifies uniquely the desired (0,1).

Case b: The solution lies on the straight line

*Θ* = {\[*θ*[1], *θ*[2]\]^(*T*)∈ℝ²:*θ*[1]+*θ*[2]\=1},<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si160.png)

which is shown in [Fig. 9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0055)B. For this setup, there is an infinite number of solutions, including two sparse ones.

Case c: The affine set of solutions is described by

*Θ* = {\[*θ*[1], *θ*[2]\]^(*T*)∈ℝ²:2*θ*[1]+*θ*[2]\=1},<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si161.png)

which is sketched in [Fig. 9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0055)C. The solution in this case is sparse, but it is not the correct one.

This example is quite informative. *If we sense (observe/measure) the unknown parameter vector with appropriate sensing (input) data, the use of the* *ℓ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) *norm can unveil the true value of the parameter vector, even if the system of equations is underdetermined, provided that the true parameter is sparse*. This becomes our new goal, to investigate whether what we have just said can be generalized, and under which conditions it holds true. In such a case, the choice of the regressors (which we called sensing vectors) and hence the input matrix (which we will refer to more and more frequently as the sensing matrix) acquire extra significance. It is not enough for the designer to care only for the rank of the matrix, that is, the linear independence of the sensing vectors. One has to make sure that the corresponding affine set of the solutions has such an orientation so that the touch with the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) ball (as this increases from zero to meet this plane) is a “gentle” one; that is, they meet at a single point, and more importantly, at the correct one, which is the point that represents the true value of the sparse parameter vector.

Remarks 9.4

*   •  Often in practice, the columns of the input matrix, *X*, are normalized to unit ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm. Although ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm is insensitive to the values of the nonzero components of ***θ***, this is not the case with the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) and ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norms. Hence, while trying to minimize the respective norms and at the same time fulfill the constraints, components that correspond to columns of *X* with high energy (norm) are favored over the rest. Hence, the latter become more popular candidates to be pushed to zero. In order to avoid such situations, the columns of *X* are normalized to unity by dividing each element of the column vector by the respective (Euclidean) norm.

## 9.6 Uniqueness of the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizer

Our first goal is to derive *sufficient* conditions that guarantee uniqueness of the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizer, which has been defined in Section [9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0030).

Definition 9.2

The *spark* of a full row rank *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) (*l* ≥ *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si162.png)) matrix, *X*, denoted as *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si163.png), is the *smallest* number of its linearly *dependent* columns.

According to the previous definition, *any* *m* < *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si164.png) columns of *X* are necessarily *linearly independent*. The spark of a square, *N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si165.png), full rank matrix is equal to *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si166.png).

Remarks 9.5

*   •  In contrast to the rank of a matrix, which can be easily determined, its spark can only be obtained by resorting to a combinatorial search over all possible combinations of the columns of the respective matrix (see, e.g., \[15,37\]). The notion of the spark was used in the context of sparse representation, under the name *uniqueness representation property*, in \[53\]. The name “spark” was coined in \[37\]. An interesting discussion relating this matrix index with indices used in other disciplines is given in \[15\].
*   •  Note that the notion of “spark” is related to the notion of the minimum Hamming weight of a linear code in coding theory (e.g., \[60\]).

} & {1\\ } & {0\\ } & 0 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si167.png)

The matrix has rank equal to 4 and spark equal to 3. Indeed, any pair of columns is linearly independent. On the other hand, the first, second, and fifth columns are linearly dependent. The same is also true for the combination of the second, third, and sixth columns. Also, the maximum number of linearly independent columns is four.

Lemma 9.2

*If* *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si107.png) *is the null space of X, then*

∥**θ**∥[0] ≥ *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*), ∀**θ** ∈ *n**u**l**l*(*X*), **θ** ≠ 0.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si169.png)

Proof

To derive a contradiction, assume that there exists a **θ** ∈ *n**u**l**l*(*X*), **θ** ≠ 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si170.png), such that ∥**θ**∥[0] < *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si171.png). Because by definition *X***θ** = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si172.png), there exists a number of ∥**θ**∥[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si173.png) columns of *X* that are linearly dependent. However, this contradicts the minimality of *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si163.png), and the claim of [Lemma 9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0065) is established.  

Lemma 9.3

*If a linear system of equations,* *X***θ** = **y**<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si174.png)*, has a solution that satisfies*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/fx002.jpg)

*then this is the sparsest possible solution. In other words, this is necessarily the unique solution of the* ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) *minimizer.*

Proof

Consider any other solution **h** ≠ **θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si176.png). Then **θ** − **h** ∈ *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si177.png), that is,

*X*(**θ** − **h**) = 0.<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si178.png)

Thus, according to [Lemma 9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0065),

*s**p**a**r**k*(*X*) ≤ ∥**θ**−**h**∥[0] ≤ ∥**θ**∥[0] + ∥**h**∥[0].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si179.png)(9.24) 

Observe that although the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) “norm” is not a true norm, it can be readily verified by simple inspection and reasoning that the triangular property is satisfied. Indeed, by adding two vectors together, the resulting number of nonzero elements will always be at most equal to the total number of nonzero elements of the two vectors. Therefore, if $\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{0} < \\frac{1}{2}{spark}(X)$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si180.png), then [(9.24)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq53) suggests that

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{h} \\right\\|\_{0} > \\frac{1}{2}{spark}(X) > \\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{0}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si181.png)

 

Remarks 9.6

*   •  [Lemma 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0075) is a very interesting result. We have a sufficient condition to check whether a solution is the unique optimal in a generally NP-hard problem. Of course, although this is nice from a theoretical point of view, it is not of much use by itself, because the related bound (the spark) can only be obtained after a combinatorial search. In the next section, we will see that we can relax the bound by involving another index in place of the spark, which is easier to be computed.
*   •  An obvious consequence of the previous lemma is that if the unknown parameter vector is a sparse one with *k* nonzero elements, then if matrix *X* is chosen in order to have *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*) > 2*k*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si182.png), the true parameter vector is necessarily the sparsest one that satisfies the set of equations, and the (unique) solution to the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizer.
*   •  In practice, the goal is to sense the unknown parameter vector by a matrix that has a spark as high as possible, so that the previously stated sufficiency condition covers a wide range of cases. For example, if the spark of the input matrix is equal to three, then one can check for optimal sparse solutions up to a sparsity level of *k* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si183.png). From the respective definition, it is easily seen that the values of the spark are in the range 1 < spark(*X*) ≤ *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mtext>spark</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si184.png).
*   •  Constructing an *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) matrix *X* in a random manner, by generating i.i.d. entries, guarantees with high probability that *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*) = *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si185.png); that is, any *N* columns of the matrix are linearly independent. 

### 9.6.1 Mutual coherence

Because the spark of a matrix is a number that is difficult to compute, our interest shifts to another index, which can be derived more easily and at the same time offers a useful bound on the spark. The *mutual coherence* of an *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) matrix *X* \[65\], denoted as *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si186.png), is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/fx003.jpg)(9.25) 

where **x**[*i*]^(*c*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si187.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si188.png), denote the columns of *X* (note the difference in notation between a row **x**[*i*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si189.png) and a column **x**[*i*]^(*c*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si187.png) of the matrix *X*). This number reminds us of the correlation coefficient between two random variables. Mutual coherence is bounded as 0 ≤ *μ*(*X*) ≤ 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si190.png). For a square orthogonal matrix *X*, *μ*(*X*) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si191.png). For general matrices with *l* > *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si116.png), *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si186.png) satisfies

$\\sqrt{\\frac{l - N}{N(l - 1)}} \\leq \\mu(X) \\leq 1,$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si192.png)

which is known as the *Welch bound* \[98\] (Problem [9.15](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0100)). For large values of *l*, the lower bound becomes approximately $\\mu(X) \\geq \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}}$<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si193.png). Common sense reasoning guides us to construct input (sensing) matrices of mutual coherence as small as possible. Indeed, the purpose of the sensing matrix is to “measure” the components of the unknown vector and “store” this information in the vector of observations, ***y***. Thus, this should be done in such a way that ***y*** retains as much information about the components of ***θ*** as possible. This can be achieved if the columns of the sensing matrix *X* are as “independent” as possible. Indeed, ***y*** is the result of a combination of the columns of *X*, each one weighted by a different component of ***θ***. Thus, if the columns are as “independent” as possible, then the information regarding each component of ***θ*** is contributed by a different direction, making its recovery easier. This is easier understood if *X* is a square orthogonal matrix. In the more general case of a nonsquare matrix, the columns should be made as “orthogonal” as possible.

Example 9.4

Assume that *X* is an *N* × 2*N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si194.png) matrix, formed by concatenating two orthonormal bases together,

*X* = \[*I*, *W*\],<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si195.png)

where *I* is the identity matrix, having as columns the vectors **e**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si196.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si197.png), with elements equal to

$\\delta\_{ir} = \\begin{cases} {\\ \\ 1,} & {\\text{if}\\ i = r,} \\\\ {\\ \\ 0,} & {\\text{if}\\ i \\neq r,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si198.png)

for *r* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si199.png). The matrix *W* is the orthonormal DFT matrix, defined as

$W = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}}\\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & \\ldots & 1 \\\\ 1 & W\_{N} & \\ldots & W\_{N}^{N - 1} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ 1 & W\_{N}^{N - 1} & \\ldots & W\_{N}^{(N - 1)(N - 1)} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si201.png)

For example, such an overcomplete dictionary could be used in the expansion in Eq. [(9.16)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq26) to represent signal vectors, which comprise the sum of sinusoids with spiky-like signal pulses. The inner products between any two columns of *I* and between any two columns of *W* are zero, due to orthogonality. On the other hand, it is easy to see that the inner product between any column of *I* and any column of *W* has absolute value equal to $\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si202.png). Hence, the mutual coherence of this matrix is $\\mu(X) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}}$<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si203.png). Moreover, observe that the spark of this matrix is *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*) = *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si185.png).

Lemma 9.4

*For any* *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) *matrix X, the following inequality holds:*

${spark}(X) \\geq 1 + \\frac{1}{\\mu(X)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si205.png)(9.26) 

The proof is given in \[37\] and it is based on arguments that stem from matrix theory applied on the Gram matrix, *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si206.png), of *X* (Problem [9.16](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0105)). A “superficial” look at the previous bound is that for very small values of *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si186.png) the spark can be larger (!) than *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si166.png). Looking at the proof, it is seen that in such cases the spark of the matrix attains its maximum value *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si166.png).

The result complies with commonsense reasoning. The smaller the value of *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si186.png), the more independent the columns of *X*, hence the higher the value of its spark is expected to be. Based on this lemma, we can now state the following theorem, first given in \[37\]. Combining [Lemma 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0075) and [(9.26)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq61), we come to the following important theorem.

Theorem 9.1

*If the linear system of equations in Eq.* [(9.17)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq27) *has a solution that satisfies the condition*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/fx004.jpg)(9.27) 

*then this solution is the sparsest one.*

Remarks 9.7

*   •  The bound in [(9.27)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq62) is “psychologically” important. It provides an easily computed bound to check whether the solution to an NP-hard task is the optimal one. However, it is not a particularly good bound and it restricts the range of values in which it can be applied. As it was discussed in [Example 9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0090), while the maximum possible value of the spark of a matrix was equal to *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si166.png), the minimum possible value of the mutual coherence was $\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si202.png). Therefore, the bound based on the mutual coherence restricts the range of sparsity, that is, ∥**θ**∥[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si173.png), where one can check optimality, to around $\\frac{1}{2}\\sqrt{N}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si207.png). Moreover, as the previously stated Welch bound suggests, this $\\mathcal{O}(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si208.png) dependence of the mutual coherence seems to be a more general trend and not only the case for [Example 9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0090) (see, e.g., \[36\]). On the other hand, as we have already stated in [Remarks 9.6](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0085), one can construct random matrices with spark equal to *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si166.png); hence, using the bound based on the spark, one could expand the range of sparse vectors up to $\\frac{1}{2}N$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si209.png). 

## 9.7 Equivalence of ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimizers: sufficiency conditions

We have now come to the crucial point where we will establish the conditions that guarantee the equivalence between the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) and ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizers. Hence, under such conditions, a problem that is in general an NP-hard one *can be solved via a tractable convex optimization task*. Under these conditions, the zero value encouraging nature of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm, which has already been discussed, obtains a much higher stature; it provides the sparsest solution.

### 9.7.1 Condition implied by the mutual coherence number

Theorem 9.2

*Consider the underdetermined system of equations*

**y** = *X***θ**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si210.png)

*where X is an* *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) (*N* < *l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si211.png) *full row rank matrix. If a solution exists and satisfies the condition*

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{0} < \\frac{1}{2}\\left( 1 + \\frac{1}{\\mu(X)} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si212.png)(9.28) 

*then this is the unique solution of both the* ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) *and* ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) *minimizers.*

This is a very important theorem, and it was shown independently in \[37,54\]. Earlier versions of the theorem addressed the special case of a dictionary comprising two orthonormal bases \[36,48\]. A proof is also summarized in \[15\] (Problem [9.17](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0110)). This theorem established, for the first time, what was until then empirically known: often, the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) and ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizers result in the same solution.

Remarks 9.8

*   •  The theory that we have presented so far is very satisfying, because it offers the theoretical framework and conditions that guarantee uniqueness of a sparse solution to an underdetermined system of equations. Now we know that under certain conditions, the solution which we obtain by solving the convex ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimization task is the (unique) sparsest one. However, from a practical point of view, the theory, which is based on mutual coherence, does not tell the whole story and falls short in predicting what happens in practice. Experimental evidence suggests that the range of sparsity levels, for which the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) tasks give the same solution, is much wider than the range guaranteed by the mutual coherence bound. Hence, there was a lot of theoretical happening in order to improve this bound. A detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this book. In the next subsection, we will present one of these bounds, because it is the one that has dominated the scene. For more details and a related discussion, the interested reader may consult, for example, \[39,49,50\].

### 9.7.2 The restricted isometry property (RIP)

Definition 9.3

For each integer *k* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si213.png), define the *isometry constant* *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si214.png) of an *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) matrix *X* as the *smallest* number such that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/fx005.jpg)(9.29) 

holds true for *all k*\-sparse vectors ***θ***. 

This definition was introduced in \[19\]. We loosely say that matrix *X* obeys the RIP of order *k* if *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si214.png) is not too close to one. When this property holds true, it implies that the Euclidean norm of ***θ*** is approximately *preserved* after projecting it onto the rows of *X*. Obviously, if matrix *X* was orthonormal, we would have *δ*[*k*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si215.png). Of course, because we are dealing with nonsquare matrices, this is not possible. However, the closer *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si214.png) is to zero, the closer to orthonormal *all* subsets of *k* columns of *X* are. Another viewpoint of the condition in [(9.29)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq65) is that *X* preserves Euclidean distances between *k*\-sparse vectors. Let us consider two *k*\-sparse vectors, **θ**[1], **θ**[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si216.png), and apply [(9.29)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq65) to their difference, **θ**[1] − **θ**[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si217.png), which, in general, is a 2*k*\-sparse vector. Then we obtain

(1 − *δ*[2*k*])∥**θ**[1]−**θ**[2]∥[2]² ≤ ∥*X*(**θ**[1]−**θ**[2])∥[2]² ≤ (1 + *δ*[2*k*])∥**θ**[1]−**θ**[2]∥[2]².<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si218.png)(9.30) 

Thus, when *δ*[2*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si219.png) is small enough, the Euclidean distance is preserved after projection in the lower-dimensional observations' space. In words, if the RIP holds true, this means that searching for a sparse vector in the lower-dimensional subspace, ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si220.png), formed by the observations, and not in the original *l*\-dimensional space, one can still recover the vector since distances are preserved and the target vector is not “confused” with others. After projection onto the rows of *X*, the discriminatory power of the method is retained. It is interesting to point out that the RIP is also related to the condition number of the Grammian matrix. In \[6,19\], it is pointed out that if *X*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si221.png) denotes the matrix that results by considering only *r* of the columns of *X*, then the RIP in [(9.29)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq65) is equivalent to requiring the respective Grammian, *X*[*r*]^(*T*)*X*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si222.png), *r* ≤ *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si223.png), to have its eigenvalues within the interval \[1 − *δ*[*k*], 1 + *δ*[*k*]\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si224.png). Hence, the more well-conditioned the matrix is, the better we dig out the information hidden in the lower-dimensional space.

Theorem 9.3

*Assume that for some k,* $\\delta\_{2k} < \\sqrt{2} - 1$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si225.png)*. Then the solution to the* ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) *minimizer of* [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq34)*, denoted as* **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si226.png)*, satisfies the following two conditions:*

∥**θ**−**θ**[\*]∥[1] ≤ *C*[0]∥**θ**−**θ**[*k*]∥[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si227.png)(9.31) 

*and*

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\right\\|\_{2} \\leq C\_{0}k^{- \\frac{1}{2}}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k} \\right\\|\_{1},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si228.png)(9.32) 

*for some constant* *C*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si229.png)*. In the previously stated formulas,* ***θ*** *is the true (target) vector that generates the observations in* [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq34) *and* **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si230.png) *is the vector that results from* ***θ*** *if we keep its k largest components and set the rest equal to zero* \[18,19,22,23\]*.*

Hence, if the true vector is a sparse one, that is, **θ** = **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si231.png), then the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) minimizer recovers the (unique) exact value. On the other hand, if the true vector is not a sparse one, then the minimizer results in a solution whose accuracy is dictated by a genie-aided procedure that knew in advance the locations of the *k* largest components of ***θ***. This is a groundbreaking result. Moreover, it is deterministic; it is always true, not with high probability. Note that the isometry property of order 2*k* is used, because at the heart of the method lies our desire to preserve the norm of the differences between vectors.

Let us now focus on the case where there is a *k*\-sparse vector that generates the observations, that is, **θ** = **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si231.png). Then it is shown in \[18\] that the condition *δ*[2*k*] < 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si233.png) guarantees that the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizer has a unique *k*\-sparse solution. In other words, in order to get the equivalence between the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) and ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) minimizers, the range of values for *δ*[2*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si219.png) has to be decreased to $\\delta\_{2k} < \\sqrt{2} - 1$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si225.png), according to [Theorem 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0125). This sounds reasonable. If we relax the criterion and use ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) instead of ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png), then the sensing matrix has to be more carefully constructed. Although we will not provide the proofs of these theorems here, because their formulation is well beyond the scope of this book, it is interesting to follow what happens if *δ*[2*k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si235.png). This will give us a flavor of the essence behind the proofs. If *δ*[2*k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si235.png), the left-hand side term in [(9.30)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq66) becomes zero. In this case, there may exist two *k*\-sparse vectors **θ**[1], **θ**[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si216.png) such that *X*(**θ**[1] − **θ**[2]) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si237.png), or *X***θ**[1] = *X***θ**[2]<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si238.png). Thus, it is not possible to recover all *k*\-sparse vectors, after projecting them in the observations space, by any method.

The previous argument also establishes a connection between RIP and the spark of a matrix. Indeed, if *δ*[2*k*] < 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si233.png), this guarantees that any number of columns of *X* up to 2*k* are linearly independent, because for any 2*k*\-sparse ***θ***, [(9.29)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq65) guarantees that ∥*X***θ**∥[2] > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si239.png). This implies that *s**p**a**r**k*(*X*) > 2*k*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">spark</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si182.png). A connection between RIP and the coherence is established in \[16\], where it is shown that if *X* has coherence *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si186.png), and unit norm columns, then *X* satisfies the RIP of order *k* with *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si214.png), where *δ*[*k*] ≤ (*k* − 1)*μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si240.png).

#### Constructing matrices that obey the RIP of order *k*

It is apparent from our previous discussion that the higher the value of *k*, for which the RIP property of a matrix *X* holds true, the better, since a larger range of sparsity levels can be handled.
