Hence, a main goal toward this direction is to construct such matrices. It turns out that verifying the RIP for a matrix of a general structure is a difficult task. This reminds us of the spark of the matrix, which is also a difficult task to compute. However, it turns out that for a certain class of random matrices, the RIP can be established in an affordable way. Thus, constructing such sensing matrices has dominated the scene of related research. We will present a few examples of such matrices, which are also very popular in practice, without going into details of the proofs, because this is beyond the scope of this book. The interested reader may find this information in the related references.

Perhaps the most well-known example of a random matrix is the Gaussian one, where the entries *X*(*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si241.png) of the sensing matrix are i.i.d. realizations from a Gaussian PDF $\\mathcal{N}(0,\\frac{1}{N})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si242.png). Another popular example of such matrices is constructed by sampling i.i.d. entries from Bernoulli, or related, distributions

$X(i,j) = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{rlr} & {\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}},} & {\\quad\\text{with\\ probability}\\ \\frac{1}{2},} \\\\ - & {\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}},} & {\\quad\\text{with\\ probability}\\ \\frac{1}{2},} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable displaystyle="true" columnspacing="0.1em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"/><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>with probability</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>with probability</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si243.png)

or

$X(i,j) = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{rlr} {+ \\sqrt{\\frac{3}{N}}} & , & {\\quad\\text{with\\ probability}\\ \\frac{1}{6},} \\\\ 0 & , & {\\quad\\text{with\\ probability}\\ \\frac{2}{3},} \\\\ {- \\sqrt{\\frac{3}{N}}} & , & {\\quad\\text{with\\ probability}\\ \\frac{1}{6}.} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable displaystyle="true" columnspacing="0.1em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>with probability</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>with probability</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>with probability</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si244.png)

Finally, one can adopt the uniform distribution and construct the columns of *X* by sampling uniformly at random on the unit sphere in ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si220.png). It turns out that such matrices obey the RIP of order *k* with overwhelming probability, provided that the number of observations, *N*, satisfies the inequality

*N* ≥ *C**k*ln (*l*/*k*),<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si245.png)(9.33) 

where *C* is some constant which depends on the isometry constant *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si214.png). In words, having such a matrix at our disposal, one can recover a *k*\-sparse vector from *N* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si246.png) observations, where *N* is larger than the sparsity level by an amount controlled by the inequality in [(9.33)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq71). More on these issues can be obtained from, for example, \[6,67\].

Besides random matrices, one can construct other matrices that obey the RIP. One such example includes the partial Fourier matrices, which are formed by selecting uniformly at random *N* rows drawn from the *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si86.png) DFT matrix. Although the required number of samples for the RIP to be satisfied may be larger than the bound in [(9.33)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq71) (see \[79\]), Fourier-based sensing matrices offer certain computational advantages when it comes to storage (𝒪(*N*ln *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si247.png)) and matrix-vector products (𝒪(*l*ln *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si248.png)) \[20\]. In \[56\], the case of random Toeplitz sensing matrices containing statistical dependencies across rows is considered, and it is shown that they can also satisfy the RIP with high probability. This is of particular importance in signal processing and communications applications, where it is very common for a system to be excited in its input via a time series, and hence independence between successive input rows cannot be assumed. In \[44,76\], the case of separable matrices is considered where the sensing matrix is the result of a Kronecker product of matrices, which satisfy the RIP individually. Such matrices are of interest for multidimensional signals, in order to exploit the sparsity structure along each one of the involved dimensions. For example, such signals may occur while trying to “encode” information associated with an event whose activity spreads across the temporal, spectral, spatial, and other domains.

In spite of their theoretical elegance, the derived bounds that determine the number of the required observations for certain sparsity levels fall short of the experimental evidence (e.g., \[39\]). In practice, a rule of thumb is to use *N* of the order of 3*k*–5*k* \[18\]. For large values of *l*, compared to the sparsity level, the analysis in \[38\] suggests that we can recover most sparse signals when *N* ≳ 2*k*ln (*l*/*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>≳</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si249.png). In an effort to overcome the shortcomings associated with the RIP, a number of other techniques have been proposed (e.g., \[11,30,39,85\]). Furthermore, in specific applications, the use of an empirical study may be a more appropriate path.

Note that, in principle, the minimum number of observations that are required to recover a *k*\-sparse vector from *N* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si246.png) observations is *N* ≥ 2*k*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si250.png). Indeed, in the spirit of the discussion after [Theorem 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0125), the main requirement that a sensing matrix must fulfill is not to map two different *k*\-sparse vectors to the same vector of observations, ***y***. Otherwise, one can never recover both vectors from their (common) observations. If we have 2*k* observations and a sensing matrix that guarantees that any 2*k* columns are linearly independent, then the previously stated requirement is satisfied. However, the bounds on the number of observations set in order for the respective matrices to satisfy the RIP are larger. This is because RIP accounts also for the stability of the recovery process. We will come to this issue in Section [9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0095), where we talk about *stable* embeddings.

## 9.8 Robust sparse signal recovery from noisy measurements

In the previous section, our focus was on recovering a sparse solution from an underdetermined system of equations. In the formulation of the problem, we assumed that there is no noise in the obtained observations. Having acquired some experience and insight from a simpler scenario, we now turn our attention to the more realistic task, where uncertainties come into the scene. One type of uncertainty may be due to the presence of noise, and our observations' model comes back to the standard regression form

**y** = *X***θ** + **η**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si251.png)(9.34) 

where *X* is our familiar nonsquare *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) matrix. A sparsity-aware formulation for recovering ***θ*** from Eq. [(9.34)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq72) can be cast as

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\leq \\epsilon,$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0011"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0011" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si252.png)(9.35) 

which coincides with the LASSO task given in [(9.8)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq10). Such a formulation implicitly assumes that the noise is bounded and the respective range of values is controlled by *ϵ*. One can consider a number of different variants. For example, one possibility would be to minimize the ∥⋅∥[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si253.png) norm instead of the ∥⋅∥[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si254.png), albeit losing the computational elegance of the latter. An alternative route would be to replace the Euclidean norm in the constraints with another one.

Besides the presence of noise, one could see the previous formulation from a different perspective. The unknown parameter vector, ***θ***, may not be exactly sparse, but it may consist of a few large components, while the rest are small and close to, yet not necessarily equal to, zero. Such a model misfit can be accommodated by allowing a deviation of ***y*** from *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si255.png).

In this relaxed setting of a sparse solution recovery, the notions of uniqueness and equivalence concerning the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) solutions no longer apply. Instead, the issue that now gains importance is that of *stability* of the solution. To this end, we focus on the computationally attractive ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) task. The counterpart of [Theorem 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0125) is now expressed as follows.

Theorem 9.4

*Assume that the sensing matrix, X, obeys the RIP with* $\\delta\_{2k} < \\sqrt{2} - 1$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si225.png)*, for some k. Then the solution* **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si226.png) *of* [(9.35)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq73) *satisfies the following (*\[22,23\]*):*

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\right\\|\_{2} \\leq C\_{0}k^{- \\frac{1}{2}}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k} \\right\\|\_{1} + C\_{1}\\sqrt{\\epsilon},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si257.png)(9.36) 

*for some constants* *C*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si258.png)*,* *C*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si229.png)*, and* **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si230.png) *as defined in* [Theorem 9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#enun0125)*.*

This is also an elegant result. If the model is exact and *ϵ* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si260.png), we obtain [(9.32)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq68). If not, the higher the uncertainty (noise) term in the model is, the higher our ambiguity about the solution becomes. Note, also, that the ambiguity about the solution depends on how far the true model is from **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si230.png). If the true model is *k*\-sparse, the first term on the right-hand side of the inequality is zero. The values of *C*[1], *C*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si262.png) depend on *δ*[2*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si219.png) but they are small, for example, close to five or six \[23\].

The important conclusion here is that *adopting the* *ℓ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) *norm and the associated LASSO optimization for solving inverse problems (which in general, as we noted in Chapter* [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)*, tend to be ill-conditioned) is a stable one and the noise is not amplified excessively during the recovery process*.

## 9.9 Compressed sensing: the glory of randomness

The way in which this chapter was deployed followed, more or less, the sequence of developments that took place during the evolution of the sparsity-aware parameter estimation field. We intentionally made an effort to follow such a path, because this is also indicative of how science evolves in most cases. The starting point had a rather strong mathematical flavor: to develop conditions for the solution of an underdetermined linear system of equations, under the sparsity constraint and in a mathematically tractable way, that is, using convex optimization. In the end, the accumulation of a sequence of individual contributions revealed that the solution can be (uniquely) recovered if the unknown quantity is sensed via randomly chosen data samples. This development has, in turn, given birth to a new field with strong theoretical interest as well as with an enormous impact on practical applications. This new emerged area is known as *compressed sensing* or *compressive sampling* (CS), and it has changed our view on how to sense and process signals efficiently.

### Compressed sensing

In CS, the goal is to directly acquire as few samples as possible that encode the minimum information needed to obtain a compressed signal representation. In order to demonstrate this, let us return to the data compression example discussed in Section [9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0025). There, it was commented that the “classical” approach to compression was rather unorthodox, in the sense that first all (i.e., a number of *l*) samples of the signal are used, and then they are processed to obtain *l* transformed values, from which only a small subset is used for coding. In the CS setting, the procedure changes to the following one.

Let *X* be an *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) sensing matrix, which is applied to the (unknown) signal vector, ***s***, in order to obtain the observations, ***y***, and let Ψ be the dictionary matrix that describes the domain where the signal ***s*** accepts a sparse representation, that is,

**s** = *Ψ***θ**, **y** = *X***s**.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic" id="mmlbr0012">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0012" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si264.png)(9.37) 

Assuming that at most *k* of the components of ***θ*** are nonzero, this can be obtained by the following optimization task:

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\mathbf{y} = X\\Psi\\mathbf{\\theta},$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0013"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0013" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si265.png)(9.38) 

*provided that the combined matrix X*Ψ *complies* with the RIP, and the number of observations, *N*, is large enough, as dictated by the bound in [(9.33)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq71). Note that ***s*** needs not be stored and can be obtained any time, once ***θ*** is known. Moreover, as we will soon discuss, there are techniques that allow observations, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si266.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si267.png), to be acquired directly from an analog signal *s*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si268.png), prior to obtaining its sample (vector) version, ***s***! Thus, from such a perspective, CS fuses the data acquisition and the compression steps together.

There are different ways to obtain a sensing matrix, *X*, that lead to a product *X*Ψ, which satisfies the RIP. It can be shown (Problem [9.19](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0120)) that if Ψ is orthonormal and *X* is a random matrix, which is constructed as discussed at the end of Section [9.7.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0080), then the product *X*Ψ obeys the RIP, provided that [(9.33)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq71) is satisfied. An alternative way to obtain a combined matrix that respects the RIP is to consider another orthonormal matrix Φ, whose columns have low coherence with the columns of Ψ (coherence between two matrices is defined in Eq. [(9.25)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq55), where now the place of **x**[*i*]^(*c*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si187.png) is taken by a column of Φ and that of **x**[*j*]^(*c*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si269.png) by a column of Ψ). For example, Φ could be the DFT matrix and *Ψ* = *I*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si270.png), or vice versa. Then choose *N* rows of Φ uniformly at random to form *X* in Eq. [(9.37)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq75). In other words, for such a case, the sensing matrix can be written as *R*Φ, where *R* is an *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si100.png) matrix that extracts *N* rows uniformly at random. The notion of incoherence (low coherence) between the sensing and the basis matrices is closely related to RIP. The more incoherent the two matrices, the lower the number of the required observations for the RIP to hold (e.g., \[21,79\]). Another way to view incoherence is that the rows of Φ cannot be sparsely represented in terms of the columns of Ψ. It turns out that if the sensing matrix *X* is a random one, formed as described in Section [9.7.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0080), then the RIP and the incoherence with any Ψ are satisfied with high probability.

It gets even better when we say that all the previously stated philosophy can be extended to the more general type of signals, which are not necessarily sparse or sparsely represented in terms of the atoms of a dictionary, and they are known as *compressible*. A signal vector is said to be compressible if its expansion in terms of a basis consists of just a few large parameters *θ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si43.png) and the rest are small. In other words, the signal vector is *approximately* sparse in some basis. Obviously, this is the most interesting case in practice, where exact sparsity is scarcely (if ever) met. Reformulating the arguments used in Section [9.8](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0090), the CS task for this case can be cast as

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\Psi\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\leq \\epsilon,$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0014"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0014" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si271.png)(9.39) 

and everything that has been said in Section [9.8](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0090) is also valid for this case, if in place of *X* we consider the product *X*Ψ.

Remarks 9.9

*   •  An important property in CS is that the sensing matrix, which provides the observations, may be chosen independently of the matrix Ψ, that is, the basis/dictionary in which the signal is sparsely represented. In other words, the sensing matrix can be “universal” and can be used to provide the observations for reconstructing any sparse or sparsely represented signal in any dictionary, provided the RIP is not violated.
*   •  Each observation, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si266.png), is the result of an inner product of the signal vector with a row **x**[*n*]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si272.png) of the sensing matrix *X*. Assuming that the signal vector ***s*** is the result of a sampling process on an analog signal, *s*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si268.png), *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si266.png) can be directly obtained, to a good approximation, by taking the inner product (integral) of *s*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si268.png) with a sensing waveform, *x*[*n*](*t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si273.png), that corresponds to **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si274.png). For example, if *X* is formed by ±1, as described in Section [9.7.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0080), then the configuration shown in [Fig. 9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0060) results in *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si266.png). An important aspect of this approach, besides avoiding computing and storing the *l* components of ***s***, is that multiplying by ±1 is a relatively easy operation. It is equivalent to changing the polarity of the signal and it can be implemented by employing inverters and mixers. It is a process that can be performed, in practice, at much higher rates than sampling. The sampling system shown in [Fig. 9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0060) is referred to as *random demodulator* \[58,91\]. It is one among the popular analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion architectures, which exploit the CS rationale in order to sample at rates much lower than those required for classical sampling. We will come back to this soon.

![Figure 9.10 Sampling an analog signal s(t) in order to generate the sample/observation yn at time instant n. The sampling period Ts is larger than that required by the Nyquist sampling.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr011.jpg)

Figure 9.10 Sampling an analog signal *s*(*t*) in order to generate the sample/observation *y*[*n*] at time instant *n*. The sampling period *T*[*s*] is larger than that required by the Nyquist sampling.

*   One of the very first CS-based acquisition systems was an imaging system called the *one-pixel camera* \[84\], which followed an approach resembling the conventional digital CS. According to this, light of an image of interest is projected onto a random base generated by a micromirror device. A sequence of projected images is collected by a *single photodiode* and used for the reconstruction of the full image using conventional CS techniques. This was among the most catalytic examples that spread the rumor about the practical power of CS. CS is an example of common wisdom: “There is nothing more practical than a good theory!”

### 9.9.1 Dimensionality reduction and stable embeddings

We will now shed light on what we have said so far in this chapter from a different point of view. In both cases, either when the unknown quantity was a *k*\-sparse vector in a high-dimensional space, ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si102.png), or when the signal ***s*** was (approximately) sparsely represented in some dictionary (**s** = *Ψ***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si275.png)), we chose to work in a lower-dimensional space (ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si220.png)), that is, the space of the observations, ***y***. This is a typical task of dimensionality reduction (see Chapter [20](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml)). The main task in any (linear) dimensionality reduction technique is to choose the proper matrix *X*, which dictates the projection to the lower-dimensional space. In general, there is always a loss of information by projecting from ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si102.png) to ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si220.png), with *N* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si246.png), in the sense that we cannot recover any vector **θ**[*l*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si276.png) from its projection **θ**[*N*] ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si277.png). Indeed, take any vector **θ**[*l* − *N*] ∈ *n**u**l**l*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">null</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si278.png) that lies in the (*l* − *N*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si279.png)\-dimensional null space of the (full row rank) *X* (see Section [9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0030)). Then all vectors **θ**[*l*] + **θ**[*l* − *N*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si280.png) share the same projection in ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si220.png). However, what we have discovered in this chapter is that if the original vector is sparse, then we can recover it exactly. This is because all the *k*\-sparse vectors do not lie anywhere in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si102.png), but rather in a subset of it, that is, in a *union of subspaces*, each one having dimensionality *k*. If the signal ***s*** is sparse in some dictionary Ψ, then one has to search for it in the union of all possible *k*\-dimensional subspaces of ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si102.png), which are spanned by *k*\-column vectors from Ψ \[8,62\]. Of course, even in this case, where sparse vectors are involved, no projection can guarantee unique recovery. The guarantee is provided if the projection in the lower-dimensional space is a *stable embedding*. A stable embedding in a lower-dimensional space must guarantee that if **θ**[1] ≠ **θ**[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si281.png), then their projections also remain different. Yet this is not enough. A stable embedding must guarantee that distances are (approximately) preserved; that is, vectors that lie far apart in the high-dimensional space have projections that also lie far apart. Such a property guarantees robustness to noise. The sufficient conditions, which have been derived and discussed throughout this chapter, and guarantee the recovery of a sparse vector lying in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si102.png) from its projections in ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si220.png), are conditions that guarantee stable embeddings. The RIP and the associated bound on *N* provide a condition on *X* that leads to stable embeddings. We commented on this norm preserving property of RIP in the related section. The interesting fact that came from the theory is that we can achieve such stable embeddings via random projection matrices.

Random projections for dimensionality reduction are not new and have extensively been used in pattern recognition, clustering, and data mining (see, e.g., \[1,13,34,82,87\]). The advent of the big data era resparked the interest in random projection-aided data analysis algorithms (e.g., \[55,81\]) for two major reasons. The first is that data processing is computationally lighter in the lower-dimensional space, because it involves operations with matrices or vectors represented with fewer parameters. Moreover, the projection of the data to lower-dimensional spaces can be realized via well-structured matrices at a computational cost significantly lower compared to that implied by general matrix-vector multiplications \[29,42\]. The reduced computational power required by these methods renders them appealing when dealing with excessively large data volumes. The second reason is that there exist randomized algorithms which access the data matrix a (usually fixed) number of times that is much smaller than the number of accesses performed by ordinary methods \[28,55\]. This is very important whenever the full amount of data does not fit in fast memory and has to be accessed in parts from slow memory devices, such as hard discs. In such cases, the computational time is often dominated by the cost of memory access.

The spirit underlying CS has been exploited in the context of pattern recognition too. In this application, one need not return to the original high-dimensional space after the information digging activity in the low-dimensional subspace. Since the focus in pattern recognition is to identify the class of an object/pattern, this can be performed in the observations subspace, provided that there is no class-related information loss. In \[17\], it is shown, using compressed sensing arguments, that if the data are approximately linearly separable in the original high-dimensional space and the data have a sparse representation, even in an unknown basis, then projecting randomly in the observations subspace retains the structure of linear separability.

*Manifold learning* is another area where random projections have also been applied. A manifold is, in general, a nonlinear *k*\-dimensional surface, embedded in a higher-dimensional (ambient) space. For example, the surface of a sphere is a two-dimensional manifold in a three-dimensional space. In \[7,96\], the compressed sensing rationale is extended to signal vectors that live along a *k*\-dimensional submanifold of the space ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si102.png). It is shown that if choosing a matrix *X* to project and a sufficient number *N* of observations, then the corresponding submanifold has a stable embedding in the observations subspace, under the projection matrix *X*; that is, pair-wise Euclidean and geodesic distances are approximately preserved after the projection mapping. More on these issues can be found in the given references and in, for example, \[8\]. We will come to the manifold learning task in Chapter [20](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml).

### 9.9.2 Sub-Nyquist sampling: analog-to-information conversion

In our discussion in the remarks presented before, we touched on a very important issue—that of going from the analog domain to the discrete one. The topic of A/D conversion has been at the forefront of research and technology since the seminal works of Shannon, Nyquist, Whittaker, and Kotelnikof were published; see, for example, \[92\] for a thorough related review. We all know that if the highest frequency of an analog signal *s*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si268.png) is less than *F*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si282.png), then Shannon's theorem suggests that no loss of information is achieved if the signal is sampled, at least, at the Nyquist rate of *F* = 1/*T*<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si283.png), where *T* is the corresponding sampling period, and the signal can be perfectly recovered by its samples

$s(t) = \\sum\\limits\_{n}s(nT){sinc}(Ft - n),$<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si284.png)

where sinc is the sampling function

${sinc}(t) = \\frac{\\sin(\\pi t)}{\\pi t}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si285.png)

While this has been the driving force behind the development of signal acquisition devices, the increasing complexity of emerging applications demands increasingly higher sampling rates that cannot be accommodated by today's hardware technology. This is the case, for example, in wideband communications, where conversion speeds, as dictated by Shannon's bound, have become more and more difficult to obtain. Consequently, alternatives to high-rate sampling are attracting strong interest, with the goal of reducing the sampling rate by exploiting the *underlying structure* of the signals at hand. For example, in many applications, the signal comprises a few frequencies or bands; see [Fig. 9.11](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0065) for an illustration. In such cases, sampling at the Nyquist rate is inefficient. This is an old problem investigated by a number of authors, leading to techniques that allow low-rate sampling whenever the locations of the nonzero bands in the frequency spectrum are known (see, e.g., \[61,93,94\]). CS theory has inspired research to study cases where the locations (carrier frequencies) of the bands are not known a priori. A typical application of this kind, of high practical interest, lies within the field of cognitive radio (e.g., \[68,88,103\]).

![Figure 9.11 The Fourier transform of an analog signal, s(t), which is sparse in the frequency domain; only a limited number of frequency bands contribute to its spectrum content S(Ω), where Ω stands for the angular frequency. Nyquist's theory guarantees that sampling at a frequency larger than or equal to twice the maximum Ωmax is sufficient to recover the original analog signal. However, this theory does not exploit information related to the sparse structure of the signal in the frequency domain.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr012.jpg)

Figure 9.11 The Fourier transform of an analog signal, *s*(*t*), which is sparse in the frequency domain; only a limited number of frequency bands contribute to its spectrum content *S*(Ω), where Ω stands for the angular frequency. Nyquist's theory guarantees that sampling at a frequency larger than or equal to twice the maximum Ω[max] is sufficient to recover the original analog signal. However, this theory does not exploit information related to the sparse structure of the signal in the frequency domain.

The process of sampling an analog signal with a rate lower than the Nyquist one is referred to as *analog-to-information* sampling or *sub-Nyquist* sampling. Let us focus on two among the most popular CS-based A/D converters. The first is the *random demodulator* (RD), which was first presented in \[58\] and later improved and theoretically developed in \[91\]. RD in its basic configuration is shown in [Fig. 9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0060), and it is designed for acquiring at sub-Nyquist rates sparse multitone signals, that is, signals having a sparse DFT. This implies that the signal comprises a few frequency components, but these components are constrained to correspond to integral frequencies. This limitation was pointed out in \[91\], and potential solutions have been sought according to the general framework proposed in \[24\] and/or the heuristic approach described in \[45\]. Moreover, more elaborate RD designs, such as the *random-modulation preintegrator* (RMPI) \[102\], have the potential to deal with signals that are sparse in any domain.

Another CS-based sub-Nyquist sampling strategy that has received much attention is the *modulated wideband converter* (MWC) \[68,69,71\]. The MWC is very efficient in acquiring multiband signals such as the one depicted in [Fig. 9.11](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0065). This concept has also been extended to accommodate signals with different characteristics, such as signals consisting of short pulses \[66\]. An in-depth investigation which sheds light on the similarities and differences between the RD and MWC sampling architectures can be found in \[59\].

Note that both RD and MWC sample the signal uniformly in time. In \[97\], a different approach is adopted, leading to much easier implementations. In particular, the preprocessing stage is avoided and nonuniformly spread in time samples is acquired directly from the raw signal. In total, fewer samples are obtained compared to Nyquist sampling. Then CS-based reconstruction is mobilized in order to recover the signal under consideration based on the values of the samples and the time information. Like in the basic RD case, the nonuniform sampling approach is suitable for signals sparse in the DFT basis. From a practical point of view, there are still a number of hardware implementation-related issues that more or less concern all the approaches above and need to be solved (see, e.g., \[9,25,63\]).

An alternative path to sub-Nyquist sampling embraces a different class of analog signals, known as *multipulse* signals, that is, signals that consist of a stream of short pulses. Sparsity now refers to the time domain, and such signals may not even be bandlimited. Signals of this type can be met in a number of applications, such as radar, ultrasound, bioimaging, and neuronal signal processing (see, e.g., \[41\]). An approach known as *finite rate of innovation sampling* passes an analog signal having *k* degrees of freedom per second through a linear time-invariant filter, and then samples at a rate of 2*k* samples per second. Reconstruction is performed via rooting a high-order polynomial (see, e.g., \[12,95\] and the references therein). In \[66\], the task of sub-Nyquist sampling is treated using CS theory arguments and an expansion in terms of Gabor functions; the signal is assumed to consist of a sum of a few pulses of finite duration, yet of unknown shape and time positions. More on this topic can be obtained in \[43,51,70\] and the references therein.

Example 9.5

We are given a set of *N* = 20<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si286.png) observations stacked in the **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si287.png) vector. These were taken by applying a sensing matrix *X* on an “unknown” vector in ℝ^(50)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>50</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si288.png), which is known to be sparse with *k* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si289.png) nonzero components; the location of these nonzero components in the unknown vector is not known. The sensing matrix was a random one with elements drawn from a normal distribution 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si290.png), and then the columns were normalized to unit norm. There are two scenarios for the observations. In the first one, we are given their exact values while in the second one, white Gaussian noise of variance *σ*² = 0.025<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.025</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si291.png) was added.

In order to recover the unknown sparse vector, the CS matching pursuit (CoSaMP, Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml)) algorithm was used for both scenarios.

The results are shown in [Fig. 9.12](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0070)A and B for the noiseless and noisy scenarios, respectively. The values of the true unknown vector ***θ*** are represented with black stems topped with open circles. Note that all but five of them are zero. In [Fig. 9.12](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0070)A, exact recovery of the unknown values is achieved; the estimated values of *θ*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2…, 50<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>50</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si292.png), are indicated with squares in red color. In the noisy case of [Fig. 9.12](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0070)B, the resulting estimates, which are denoted with squares, deviate from the correct values. Note that estimated values very close to zero (|*θ*| ≤ 0.01<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si293.png)) have been omitted from the figure in order to facilitate visualization. In both figures, the stemmed gray-filled circles correspond to the minimum ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) norm LS solution. The advantages of adopting a sparsity promoting approach to recover the solution are obvious. The CoSaMP algorithm was provided with the exact number of sparsity. The reader is advised to reproduce the example and play with different values of the parameters and see how results are affected.

An exact recovery of the signal has been obtained. The stems topped with gray-filled circles correspond to the minimum Euclidean norm LS solution. ## 9.10 A case study: image denoising

We have already discussed CS as a notable application of sparsity-aware learning. Besides CS that has acquired a lot of fame, a number of classical signal processing and machine learning tasks lend themselves to efficient modeling via sparsity-related arguments. Two typical examples are the following:

*   •  *Denoising*: The problem in signal denoising is that instead of the actual signal samples, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si294.png), a noisy version of the corresponding observations, ***y***, is available; that is, $\\mathbf{y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + \\mathbf{\\eta}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si295.png), where ***η*** is the vector of noise samples. Under the sparse modeling framework, the unknown signal $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si294.png) is modeled as a sparse representation in terms of a specific known dictionary Ψ, that is, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\Psi\\mathbf{\\theta}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si296.png). Moreover, the dictionary is allowed to be redundant (overcomplete). Then the denoising procedure is realized in two steps.
*   First, an estimate of the sparse representation vector, ***θ***, is obtained via the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si1.png) norm minimizer or via any LASSO formulation, for example,

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si297.png)(9.40) 

*   

s.t.    ∥**y**−*Ψ***θ**∥[2]² ≤ *ϵ*.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si298.png)(9.41) 

*   Second, the estimate of the true signal is computed as $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\Psi\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si299.png). In Chapter [20](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml), we will study the case where the dictionary is not fixed and known, but is estimated from the data.
*   •  *Linear inverse problems*: Such problems, which come under the more general umbrella of what is known as *signal restoration*, go one step beyond denoising. Now, the available observations are *distorted* as well as noisy versions of the true signal samples; that is, $\\mathbf{y} = H\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + \\mathbf{\\eta}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si300.png), where *H* is a known linear operator. For example, *H* may correspond to the blurring point spread function of an image, as discussed in Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml). Then, similar to the denoising example, assuming that the original signal samples can be efficiently represented in terms of an overcomplete dictionary, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si119.png) is estimated, via any sparsity promoting method, using *H*Ψ in place of Ψ in [(9.41)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq81), and the estimate of the true signal is obtained as $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\Psi\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si299.png).
*   Besides deblurring, other applications that fall under this formulation include image inpainting, if *H* represents the corresponding sampling mask; inverse-Radon transform in tomography, if *H* comprises the set of parallel projections, and so on. See, for example, \[49\] for more details on this topic.

In this case study, the image denoising task, based on the sparse and redundant formulation as discussed above, is explored. Our starting point is the 256 × 256<mml:math><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si302.png) image shown in [Fig. 9.13](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0075)A. In the sequel, the image is corrupted by zero mean Gaussian noise, leading to the noisy version of [Fig. 9.13](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0075)B, corresponding to a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) equal to 22 dB, which is defined as

${PSNR} = 20\\log\_{10}\\left( \\frac{m\_{I}}{\\sqrt{MSE}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">PSNR</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">log</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MSE</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si303.png)(9.42) 

where *m*[*I*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si304.png) is the maximum pixel value of the image and ${MSE} = \\frac{1}{N\_{p}}\\left\\| I - \\widetilde{I} \\right\\|\_{F}^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MSE</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si305.png), where *I* and *Ĩ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si306.png) are the noisy and original image matrices, *N*[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si307.png) is equal to the total number of pixels, and the Frobenius norm for matrices has been employed.

![Figure 9.13 Denoising based on sparse and redundant representations.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr014.jpg)

Figure 9.13 Denoising based on sparse and redundant representations.

Denoising could be applied to the full image at once. However, a more efficient practice with respect to memory consumption is to split the image to patches of size much smaller than that of the image; for our case, we chose 12 × 12<mml:math><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si308.png) patches. Then denoising is performed to each patch separately as follows: The *i*th patch image is reshaped in lexicographic order forming a one-dimensional vector, **y**[*i*] ∈ ℝ^(144)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>144</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si309.png). We assume that each one of the patches can be reproduced in terms of an overcomplete dictionary, as discussed before; hence, the denoising task is equivalently formulated around [(9.40)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq80)–[(9.41)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq81). Denote by $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}\_{i}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si310.png) the *i*th patch of the noise-free image. What is left is to choose a dictionary Ψ, which sparsely represents $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}\_{i}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si310.png), and then solve for sparse ***θ*** according to [(9.40)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq80)–[(9.41)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#deq81).

It is known that images often exhibit sparse DCT transforms, so an appropriate choice for the dictionary is to fill the columns of Ψ with atoms of a redundant 2D-DCT reshaped in lexicographic order \[49\]. Here, 196 such atoms were used. There is a standard way to develop such a dictionary given the dimensionality of the image, described in Exercise [9.22](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#o0135). The *same* dictionary is used for *all* patches. The atoms of the dictionary, reshaped to form 12 × 12<mml:math><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si308.png) blocks, are depicted in [Fig. 9.14](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0080).

![Figure 9.14 2D-DCT dictionary atoms, corresponding to 12 × 12 patch size.](images/B9780443292385000159/gr015.jpg)

[Figure 9.14](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#cf1010) 2D-DCT dictionary atoms, corresponding to 12 × 12 patch size.

A question that naturally arises is how many patches to use. A straightforward approach is to tile the patches side by side in order to cover the whole extent of the image. This is feasible; however, it is likely to result in blocking effects at the edges of several patches. A better practice is to let the patches overlap. During the reconstruction phase ($\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\Psi\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si299.png)), because each pixel is covered by more than one patch, the final value of each pixel is taken as the average of the corresponding predicted values from all the involved patches. The results of this method, for our case, are shown in [Fig. 9.13](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#f0075)C. The attained PSNR is higher than 28 dB.

## Problems

1.  9.1  If *x*[*i*], *y*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si312.png), are real numbers, then prove the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

$\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}x\_{i}y\_{i} \\right)^{2} \\leq \\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}x\_{i}^{2} \\right)\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}y\_{i}^{2} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si313.png)

1.  
2.  9.2  Prove that the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si7.png) (Euclidean) norm is a true norm, that is, it satisfies the four conditions that define a norm.
3.  *Hint*: To prove the triangle inequality, use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
4.  9.3  Prove that any function that is a norm is also a convex function.
5.  9.4  Show Young's inequality for nonnegative real numbers *a* and *b*,

$ab \\leq \\frac{a^{p}}{p} + \\frac{b^{q}}{q},$<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>
