2.  9.12  Prove that if the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm minimizer is unique, then the number of its components, which are identically zero, must be at least as large as the dimensionality of the null space of the corresponding input matrix.
3.  9.13  Show that the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si135.png) norm is a convex function (as all norms), yet it is not strictly convex. In contrast, the squared Euclidean norm is a strictly convex function.

width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"/><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>with probability</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si349.png)
    
    1.  for *p* equal to 1, 9, 25, 36, 64 (make sure that each row and each column of *X* has at least one nonzero component). Give an explanation why the probability of reconstruction falls as *p* increases (observe that both the sensing matrix and the unknown vector are sparse). 
    2.  9.22  This exercise reproduces the denoising results of the case study in Section [9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml#s0115), where the image depicting the boat can be downloaded from the book website. First, extract from the image all the possible sliding patches of size 12 × 12<mml:math><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si308.png) using the im2col.m MATLAB® function. Confirm that (256 − 12 + 1)² = 60, 025<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>60</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>025</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si350.png) patches in total are obtained. Next, a dictionary in which all the patches are sparsely represented needs to be designed. 
    3.  Specifically, the dictionary atoms are going to be those corresponding to the two-dimensional redundant DCT transform, and are obtained as follows \[49\]: 
        
        1.  **a)**  Consider vectors **d**[*i*] = \[*d*[*i*, 1], *d*[*i*, 2], …, *d*[*i*, 12]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si351.png), *i* = 0, …, 13<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>13</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si352.png), being the sampled sinusoids of the form
        
        $d\_{i,t + 1} = \\cos\\left( \\frac{t\\pi i}{14} \\right),\\quad t = 0,\\ldots,11.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>11</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>
        
        ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si353.png)
        
        1.  Then make a (12 × 14)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si354.png) matrix $\\overline{D}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si355.png), having as columns the vectors **d**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si356.png) normalized to unit norm; *D* resembles a redundant DCT matrix. 
        2.  **b)**  Construct the (12² × 14²)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si357.png) dictionary Ψ according to *Ψ* = *D*⨂*D*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>⨂</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si358.png), where ⨂ denotes Kronecker product. Built in this way, the resulting atoms correspond to atoms related to the overcomplete 2D-DCT transform \[49\]. 
        3.  As a next step, denoise each image patch separately. In particular, assuming that **y**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000159/si359.png) is the *i*th patch reshaped in column vector, use the function “solvelasso.m,”^([^(65)](#fn65))

## 10.1 Introduction

This chapter is the follow-up to the previous one concerning sparsity-aware learning. The emphasis now is on the algorithmic front. Following the theoretical advances concerning sparse modeling, a true scientific happening occurred in trying to derive algorithms tailored for the efficient solution of the related constrained optimization tasks. Our goal is to present the main directions that have been followed and to provide in a more explicit form some of the most popular algorithms. We will discuss batch as well as online algorithms. This chapter can also be considered as a complement to Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml), where some aspects of convex optimization were introduced; a number of algorithms discussed there are also appropriate for tasks involving sparsity-related constraints/regularization.

Besides describing various algorithmic families, some variants of the basic sparsity promoting ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) and ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si2.png) norms are discussed. Furthermore, some typical examples are considered and a case study concerning time-frequency analysis is presented. Finally, a discussion concerning the issue “synthesis versus analysis” models is provided.

## 10.2 Sparsity promoting algorithms

In the previous chapter, our emphasis was on highlighting some of the most important aspects underlying the theory of sparse signal/parameter vector recovery from an underdetermined set of linear equations. We now turn our attention to the algorithmic aspects of the problem (e.g., \[52,54\]). The issue now becomes that of discussing *efficient* algorithmic schemes, which can achieve the recovery of the unknown set of parameters. In Sections [9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and [9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), we saw that the constrained ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm minimization (basis pursuit) can be solved via linear programming techniques and the LASSO task via convex optimization schemes. However, such general purpose techniques tend to be inefficient, because they often require many iterations to converge, and the respective computational resources can be excessive for practical applications, especially in high-dimensional spaces ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si3.png). As a consequence, a huge research effort has been invested for the goal of developing efficient algorithms that are tailored to these specific tasks. Our aim here is to provide the reader with some general trends and philosophies that characterize the related activity. We will focus on the most commonly used and cited algorithms, which at the same time are structurally simple, so the reader can follow them, without deeper knowledge of optimization. Moreover, these algorithms involve, in one way or another, arguments that are directly related to notions we have already used while presenting the theory; thus, they can also be exploited from a pedagogical point of view in order to strengthen the reader's understanding of the topic. We start our review with the class of batch algorithms, where all data are assumed to be available prior to the application of the algorithm, and then we will move on to online/time-adaptive schemes. Furthermore, our emphasis is on algorithms that are appropriate for any sensing matrix. This is stated in order to point out that in the literature, efficient algorithms have also been developed for specific forms of highly structured sensing matrices, and exploiting their particular structure can lead to reduced computational demands \[61,93\].

There are three rough types of families along which this algorithmic activity has grown: (a) greedy algorithms, (b) iterative shrinkage schemes, and (c) convex optimization techniques. We have used the word rough because in some cases, it may be difficult to assign an algorithm to a specific family.

### 10.2.1 Greedy algorithms

Greedy algorithms have a long history; see, for example, \[114\] for a comprehensive list of references. In the context of dictionary learning, a greedy algorithm known as *matching pursuit* was introduced in \[88\]. A greedy algorithm is built upon a series of *locally* optimal *single-term* updates. In our context, the goals are (a) to unveil the “active” columns of the sensing matrix *X*, that is, those columns that correspond to the nonzero locations of the unknown parameters, and (b) to estimate the respective sparse parameter vector. The set of indices that correspond to the nonzero vector components is also known as the *support*. To this end, the set of active columns of *X* (and the support) is increased by one at each iteration step. In the sequel, an updated estimate of the unknown sparse vector is obtained. Let us assume that at the (*i* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si4.png)th iteration step, the algorithm has selected the columns denoted as Let also the current estimate of the solution be **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si11.png), which is a (*i* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si4.png)\-sparse vector, with zeros at all locations with index outside the support. The *orthogonal matching pursuit* (OMP) scheme given in [Algorithm 10.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#enun0010) builds up recursively a sparse solution.

Algorithm 10.1

**The OMP algorithm**

The algorithm is initialized with **θ**^((0)) :  = 0<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si12.png), **e**^((0)) :  = **y**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si13.png), and *S*^((0)) = ⌀<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si14.png). At iteration step *i*, the following computational steps are performed:

1.  1\.  Select the column **x**[*j*[*i*]]^(*c*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si15.png) of *X*, which is *maximally* correlated to (forms the smallest angle with) the respective error vector, **e**^((*i* − 1)) :  = **y** − *X***θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si16.png), that is,

$\\mathbf{x}\_{j\_{i}}^{c}:\\ j\_{i}: = {arg\\, max}\_{j = 1,2,\\ldots,l}\\ \\frac{\\left| {\\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c}}^{T}\\mathbf{e}^{(i - 1)} \\right|}{\\left\\| \\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c} \\right\\|\_{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si17.png)

1.  
2.  2\.  Update the support and the corresponding set of active columns, *S*^((*i*)) = *S*^((*i* − 1)) ∪ {*j*[*i*]}<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si18.png) and *X*^((*i*)) = \[*X*^((*i* − 1)), **x**[*j*[*i*]]^(*c*)\]<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si19.png).
3.  3\.  Update the estimate of the parameter vector: Solve the least-squares (LS) problem that minimizes the norm of the error, using the active columns of *X* only, that is,

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}: = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{z} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{i}}\\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X^{(i)}\\mathbf{z} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si20.png)

1.  Obtain **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si21.png) by inserting the elements of $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si22.png) in the respective locations (*j*[1], *j*[2], …, *j*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si23.png), which comprise the support (the rest of the elements of **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si21.png) retain their zero values).
2.  4\.  Update the error vector

**e**^((*i*)) :  = **y** − *X***θ**^((*i*)).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si24.png)

1.  

The algorithm terminates if the norm of the error becomes less than a preselected user-defined constant, *ϵ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si25.png). The following observations are in order.

Remarks 10.1

*   •  Because **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si21.png), in Step 3, is the result of an LS task, we know from Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml) that the error vector is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by the active columns involved, that is,

**e**^((*i*))⊥*s**p**a**n*{**x**[*j*[1]]^(*c*),…,**x**[*j*[*i*]]^(*c*)}.<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">span</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si26.png)

*   This guarantees that in the next step, taking the correlation of the columns of *X* with **e**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si27.png), none of the previously selected columns will be reselected; they result to zero correlation, being orthogonal to **e**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si27.png) (see [Fig. 10.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0010)).

![Figure 10.1 The error vector at the ith iteration is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by the currently available set of active columns. Here is an illustration for the case of the three-dimensional Euclidean space \\mathbb{R}^{3}Equation, and for i = 2.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 10.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#cf0170) The error vector at the *i*th iteration is orthogonal to the subspace spanned by the currently available set of active columns. Here is an illustration for the case of the three-dimensional Euclidean space ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si31.png), and for *i* = 2.

*   
*   •  The column which has maximal correlation (maximum absolute value of the inner product) with the currently available error vector is the one that maximally reduces (compared to any other column) the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) norm of the error, when ***y*** is approximated by linearly combining the currently available active columns. This is the point where the heart of the greedy strategy beats. This minimization is with respect to a *single term*, keeping the rest fixed, as they have been obtained from the previous iteration steps (Problem [10.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#o0230)).
*   •  Starting with all the components being zero, if the algorithm stops after *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png) iteration steps, the result will be a *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png)\-sparse solution.
*   •  Note that there is no optimality in this searching strategy. The only guarantee is that the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) norm of the error vector is decreased at every iteration step. In general, there is no guarantee that the algorithm can obtain a solution close to the true one (see, for example, \[38\]). However, under certain constraints on the structure of *X*, performance bounds can be obtained (see, for example, \[37,115,123\]).
*   •  The complexity of the algorithm amounts to 𝒪(*k*[0]*l**N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si30.png) operations, which are contributed by the computations of the correlations, plus the demands raised by the solution of the LS task in step 3, whose complexity depends on the specific algorithm used. The *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png) is the sparsity level of the delivered solution and, hence, the total number of iteration steps that are performed.

Another more qualitative argument that justifies the selection of the columns based on their correlation with the error vector is the following. Assume that the matrix *X* is orthonormal. Let **y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png). Then ***y*** lies in the subspace spanned by the active columns of *X*, that is, those that correspond to the nonzero components of ***θ***. Hence, the rest of the columns are orthogonal to ***y***, because *X* is assumed to be orthonormal. Taking the correlation of ***y***, at the first iteration step, with all the columns, it is certain that one among the active columns will be selected. The inactive columns result in zero correlation. A similar argument holds true for all subsequent steps, because all activity takes place in a subspace that is orthogonal to all the inactive columns of *X*. In the more general case, where *X* is not orthonormal, we can still use the correlation as a measure that quantifies geometric similarity. The smaller the correlation/magnitude of the inner product is, the more orthogonal the two vectors are. This brings us back to the notion of mutual coherence, which is a measure of the maximum correlation (smallest angle) among the columns of *X*.

#### OMP can recover optimal sparse solutions: sufficiency condition

We have already stated that, in general, there are no guarantees that OMP will recover optimal solutions. However, when the unknown vector is sufficiently sparse, with respect to the structure of the sensing matrix *X*, OMP can exactly solve the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si2.png) minimization task in [(9.20)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and recover the solution in *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png) steps, where *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png) is the sparsest solution that satisfies the associated linear set of equations.

Theorem 10.1

*Let the mutual coherence (Section* [9.6.1](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)*) of the sensing matrix X be* *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si33.png)*. Assume, also, that the linear system* **y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png) *accepts a solution such that*

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{0} < \\frac{1}{2}\\left( 1 + \\frac{1}{\\mu(X)} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si35.png)(10.1) 

*Then OMP guarantees recovery of the sparsest solution in* *k*[0] = ∥**θ**∥[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si36.png) *steps.*

We know from Section [9.6.1](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) that under the previous condition, any other solution will be necessarily less sparse. Hence, there is a unique way to represent ***y*** in terms of *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png) columns of *X*. Without harming generality, let us assume that the true support corresponds to the first *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png) columns of *X*, that is,

$\\mathbf{y} = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{k\_{0}}\\theta\_{j}\\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c},\\quad\\theta\_{j} \\neq 0,\\quad\\forall j \\in \\{ 1,\\ldots,k\_{0}\\}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si37.png)

The theorem is a direct consequence of the following proposition.

Proposition 10.1

*If the condition* [(10.1)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq5) *holds true, then the OMP algorithm will never select a column with index outside the true support (see, for example,* \[115\] *and Problem* [10.2](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#o0235)*). In a more formal way, this is expressed as*

$j\_{i} = {arg\\, max}\_{j = 1,2,\\ldots,l}\\ \\frac{\\left| {\\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c}}^{T}\\mathbf{e}^{(i - 1)} \\right|}{\\left\\| \\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c} \\right\\|\_{2}} \\in \\{ 1,\\ldots,k\_{0}\\}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si38.png)

A geometric interpretation of this proposition is the following. If the angles formed between all the possible pairs among the columns of *X* are close to 90^∘<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∘</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si39.png) (columns almost orthogonal) in the ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si3.png) space, which guarantees that *μ*(*X*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si33.png) is small enough, then ***y*** will lean more (form a smaller angle) toward any one of the active columns that contribute to its formation, compared to the rest that are inactive and do not participate in the linear combination that generates ***y***. [Fig. 10.2](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0015) illustrates the geometry, for the extreme case of mutually orthogonal vectors ([Fig. 10.2](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0015)A), and for the more general case where the vectors are not orthogonal, yet the angle between any pair of columns is close enough to 90^∘<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>90</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∘</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si39.png) ([Fig. 10.2](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0015)B).

![Figure 10.2 (A) In the case of an orthogonal matrix, the observations vector y will be orthogonal to any inactive column, here, \\mathbf{x}\_{3}^{c}Equation. (B) In the more general case, it is expected to “lean” closer (form smaller angles) to the active than to the inactive columns.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr002.jpg)

Figure 10.2 (A) In the case of an orthogonal matrix, the observations vector ***y*** will be orthogonal to any inactive column, here, **x**[3]^(*c*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si41.png). (B) In the more general case, it is expected to “lean” closer (form smaller angles) to the active than to the inactive columns.

In a nutshell, the previous proposition guarantees that during the first iteration, a column corresponding to the true support will be selected. In a similar way, this is also true for all subsequent iterations. In the second step, another column, different from the previously selected one (as has already been stated) will be chosen. At step *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si29.png), the last remaining active column corresponding to the true support is selected, and this necessarily results in zero error. To this end, it suffices to set *ϵ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si25.png) equal to zero.

#### The LARS algorithm

The least-angle regression (LARS) algorithm \[48\] shares the first two steps with OMP. It selects *j*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si42.png) to be an index outside the currently available active set in order to maximize the correlation with the residual vector. However, instead of performing an LS fit to compute the nonzero components of **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si21.png), these are computed so that the residual will be equicorrelated with all the columns in the active set, that is,

|**x**[*j*]^(*c*)^(*T*)(**y**−*X***θ**^((*i*)))|=constant, ∀*j*∈*S*^((*i*)),<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>constant</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si43.png)

where we have assumed that the columns of *X* are normalized, as is common in practice (recall, also, [Remarks 9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)). In other words, in contrast to the OMP, where the error vector is forced to be orthogonal to the active columns, LARS demands this error to form equal angles with each one of them. Like OMP, it can be shown that, provided the target vector is sufficiently sparse and under incoherence of the columns of *X*, LARS can exactly recover the sparsest solution \[116\].

A further small modification leads to the LARS-LASSO algorithm. According to this version, a previously selected index in the active set can be removed at a later stage. This gives the algorithm the potential to “recover” from a previously bad decision. Hence, this modification departs from the strict rationale that defines the greedy algorithms. It turns out that this version solves the LASSO optimization task. This algorithm is the same as the one suggested in \[99\] and it is known as a *homotopy* algorithm. Homotopy methods are based on a continuous transformation from one optimization task to another. The solutions to this sequence of tasks lie along a continuous parameterized path. The idea is that while the optimization tasks may be difficult to solve by themselves, one can trace this path of solutions by slowly varying the parameters. For the LASSO task, it is the *λ* parameter that is varying (see, for example, \[4,86,104\]). Take as an example the LASSO task in its regularized version in [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). For *λ* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si44.png), the task minimizes the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) error norm and for *λ* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si45.png) the task minimizes the parameter vector's ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm, and for this case the solution tends to zero. It turns out that the solution path, as *λ* changes from large to small values, is polygonal. Vertices on this solution path correspond to vectors having nonzero elements only on a subset of entries. This subset remains unchanged until *λ* reaches the next critical value, which corresponds to a new vertex of the polygonal path and to a new subset of potential nonzero values. Thus, the solution is obtained via this sequence of steps along this polygonal path.

#### Compressed sensing matching pursuit (CSMP) algorithms

Strictly speaking, the algorithms to be discussed here are not greedy, yet as stated in \[93\], they are at heart greedy algorithms. Instead of performing a single term optimization per iteration step, in order to increase the support by one, as is the case with OMP, these algorithms attempt to obtain first an estimate of the support and then use this information to compute an LS estimate of the target vector, constrained on the respective active columns. The quintessence of the method lies in the near-orthogonal nature of the sensing matrix, assuming that this obeys the RIP condition.

Assume that *X* obeys the RIP for some small enough value *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si46.png) and sparsity level *k* of the unknown vector. Let, also, the observations be exact, that is, **y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png). Then *X*^(*T*)**y** = *X*^(*T*)*X***θ** ≈ **θ**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si48.png), due to the near-orthogonal nature of *X*. Therefore, intuition indicates that it is not unreasonable to select, in the first iteration step, the *t* (a user-defined parameter) largest in magnitude components of *X*^(*T*)**y**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si49.png) as indicative of the nonzero positions of the sparse target vector. This reasoning carries on for all subsequent steps, where, at the *i*th iteration, the place of ***y*** is taken by the residual **e**^((*i* − 1)) :  = **y** − *X***θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si16.png), where **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si11.png) indicates the estimate of the target vector at the (*i* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si4.png)th iteration. Basically, this could be considered as a generalization of the OMP. However, as we will soon see, the difference between the two mechanisms is more substantial.

Algorithm 10.2

**The CSMP scheme**

1.  **1.**  Select the value of *t*.
2.  **2.**  Initialize the algorithm: **θ**^((0)) = 0<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si52.png), **e**^((0)) = **y**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si53.png).
3.  **3.**  For *i* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si54.png), execute the following;
    
    1.  **(a)**  Obtain the current support:
    
    $S^{(i)}: = {supp}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right) \\cup \\left\\{ \\frac{\\text{indices\\ of\\ the}\\ t\\ \\text{largest\\ in\\ magnitude}}{\\text{components\\ of}\\ X^{T}\\mathbf{e}^{(i - 1)}} \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">supp</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mfrac linethickness="0"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>indices of the</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>largest in magnitude</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>components of</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si55.png)
    
    1.  
    2.  **(b)**  Select the active columns: Construct *X*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si56.png) to comprise the active columns of *X* in accordance to *S*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si57.png). Obviously, *X*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si56.png) is an *N* × *r*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si58.png) matrix, where *r* denotes the cardinality of the support set *S*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si57.png).
    3.  **(c)**  Update the estimate of the parameter vector: solve the LS task
    
    $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}: = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{z} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{r}}\\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X^{(i)}\\mathbf{z} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si59.png)
    
    1.  Obtain ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}^{(i)} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si60.png) having the *r* elements of $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si22.png) in the respective locations, as indicated by the support, and the rest of the elements being zero.
    2.  **(d)**  $\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)}: = H\_{k}\\left( {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}^{(i)} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si61.png). The mapping *H*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si62.png) denotes the *hard thresholding* function; that is, it returns a vector with the *k* largest in magnitude components of the argument, and the rest are forced to zero.
    3.  **(e)**  Update the error vector: **e**^((*i*)) = **y** − *X***θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si63.png).

The algorithm requires as input the sparsity level *k*. Iterations carry on until a halting criterion is met. The value of *t*, which determines the largest in magnitude values in steps 1 and 3a, depends on the specific algorithm. In the compressive sampling matching pursuit (CoSaMP) \[93\], *t* = 2*k*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si64.png) (Problem [10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#o0240)), and in the subspace pursuit (SP) \[33\], *t* = *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si65.png).

Having stated the general scheme, a major difference with OMP becomes readily apparent. In OMP, only one column is selected per iteration step. Moreover, this remains in the active set for all subsequent steps. If, for some reason, this was not a good choice, the scheme cannot recover from such a bad decision. In contrast, the support and, hence, the active columns of *X* are continuously updated in CSMP, and the algorithm has the ability to correct a previously bad decision, as more information is accumulated and iterations progress. In \[33\], it is shown that if the observations are exact (**y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png)), then SP can recover the *k*\-sparse true vector in a finite number of iteration steps, provided that *X* satisfies the RIP with *δ*[3*k*] < 0.205<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.205</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si67.png). If the observations are noisy, performance bounds have been derived, which hold true for *δ*[3*k*] < 0.083<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.083</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si68.png). For the CoSaMP, performance bounds have been derived for *δ*[4*k*] < 0.1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si69.png).

### 10.2.2 Iterative shrinkage/thresholding (IST) algorithms

This family of algorithms also has a long history (see, for example, \[44,69,70,73\]). However, in the “early” days, most of the developed algorithms had some sense of heuristic flavor, without establishing a clear bridge with optimizing a cost function. Later attempts were substantiated by sound theoretical arguments concerning issues such as convergence and convergence rate \[31,34,50,56\].

The general form of this algorithmic family has a striking resemblance to the classical linear algebra iterative schemes for approximating the solution of large linear systems of equations, known as *stationary iterative* or *iterative relaxation* methods. The classical Gauss–Seidel and Jacobi algorithms (e.g., \[65\]) in numerical analysis can be considered members of this family. Given a linear system of *l* equations with *l* unknowns, **z** = *A***x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si70.png), the basic iteration at step *i* has the following form:

**x**^((*i*)) = (*I*−*Q**A*)**x**^((*i* − 1)) + *Q***z** = **x**^((*i* − 1)) + *Q***e**^((*i* − 1)),  **e**^((*i* − 1)) :  = **z** − *A***x**^((*i* − 1)),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo id="mmlbr0001" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0001" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="2em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si71.png)

which does not come as a surprise. It is of the same form as most of the iterative schemes for numerical solutions! The matrix *Q* is chosen in order to guarantee convergence, and different choices lead to different algorithms with their pros and cons. It turns out that this algorithmic form can also be applied to underdetermined systems of equations, **y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png), with a “minor” modification, which is imposed by the sparsity constraint of the target vector. This leads to the following general form of iterative computation:

**θ**^((*i*)) = *T*[*i*](**θ**^((*i* − 1))+*Q***e**^((*i* − 1))),  **e**^((*i* − 1)) = **y** − *X***θ**^((*i* − 1)),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="2em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo
