linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si72.png)

starting from an initial guess of **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si73.png) (usually **θ**^((0)) = 0<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si52.png), **e**^((0)) = **y**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si53.png)). In certain cases, *Q* can be made to be iteration dependent. The function *T*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si74.png) is a nonlinear thresholding that is applied *entry-wise*, that is, *component-wise*. Depending on the specific scheme, this can be either the hard thresholding function, denoted as *H*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si62.png), or the soft thresholding function, denoted as *S*[*α*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si75.png). Hard thresholding, as we already know, keeps the *k* largest components of a vector unaltered and sets the rest equal to zero. Soft thresholding was introduced in Section [9.3](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). All components with magnitude less than a threshold value *α* are forced to zero and the rest are reduced in magnitude by *α*; that is, the *j*th component of a vector ***θ***, after soft thresholding, becomes

(*S*[*α*](**θ**))[*j*] = *s**g**n*(*θ*[*j*])(|*θ*[*j*]|−*α*)[+].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sgn</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si76.png)

Depending on (a) the choice of *T*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si74.png), (b) the specific value of the parameter *k* or *α*, and (c) the matrix *Q*, different instances occur. The most common choice for *Q* is *μ**X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si77.png), and the generic form of the main iteration becomes

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/fx001.jpg)(10.2) 

where *μ* is a relaxation (user-defined) parameter, which can also be left to vary with each iteration step. The choice of *X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si78.png) is intuitively justified, once more, by the near-orthogonal nature of *X*. For the first iteration step and for a linear system of the form **y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png), starting from a zero initial guess, we have *X*^(*T*)**y** = *X*^(*T*)*X***θ** ≈ **θ**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si48.png) and we are close to the solution.

Although intuition is most important in scientific research, it is not enough, by itself, to justify decisions and actions. The generic scheme in Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14) has been reached from different paths, following different perspectives that lead to different choices of the involved parameters. Let us spend some more time on that, with the aim of making the reader more familiar with techniques that address optimization tasks of nondifferentiable loss functions. The term in parentheses in Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14) coincides with the gradient descent iteration step if the cost function is the unregularized sum of squared errors cost (LS), that is,

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si79.png)

In this case, the gradient descent rationale leads to

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu\\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu X^{T}\\left( X\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mathbf{y} \\right) = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} + \\mu X^{T}\\mathbf{e}^{(i - 1)}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo id="mmlbr0002" linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si80.png)

The gradient descent can alternatively be viewed as the result of minimizing a regularized version of the linearized cost function (verify it),

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right) + \\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)^{T}\\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} + \\frac{1}{2\\mu}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub id="mmlbr0003"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0003" linebreakstyle="before">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si81.png)(10.3) 

One can adopt this view of the gradient descent philosophy as a kick-off point to minimize iteratively the following LASSO task:

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ L(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\lambda) = \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} + \\lambda\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} = J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) + \\lambda\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si82.png)

The difference now is that the loss function comprises two terms: one that is smooth (differentiable) and a nonsmooth one. Let the current estimate be **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si11.png). The updated estimate is obtained by

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right) + \\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)^{T}\\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} + \\frac{1}{2\\mu}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} + \\lambda\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo which, after ignoring constants, is equivalently written as

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} + \\lambda\\mu\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

where

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}: = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu\\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si85.png)(10.5) 

Following exactly the same steps as those that led to the derivation of Eq. [(9.13)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) from Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) (after replacing ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{LS}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si86.png) with $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si22.png)), we obtain

\\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si87.png)(10.6) 

 = *S*[*λ**μ*](**θ**^((*i* − 1))+*μ**X*^(*T*)**e**^((*i* − 1))).<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si88.png)(10.7) 

This is very interesting and practically useful. The only effect of the presence of the nonsmooth ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm in the loss function is an extra simple thresholding operation, which as we know is an operation performed *individually* on each component. It can be shown (e.g., \[11,95\]) that this algorithm converges to a minimizer **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si89.png) of the LASSO [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), provided that *μ* ∈ (0, 1/*λ*[max](*X*^(*T*)*X*))<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si90.png), where *λ*[max]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si91.png) denotes the maximum eigenvalue of *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si92.png). The convergence rate is dictated by the rule

*L*(**θ**^((*i*)), *λ*) − *L*(**θ**[\*], *λ*) ∝ *O*(1/*i*),<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si93.png)

which is known as *sublinear* (Eq. [(6.53)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)) global rate of convergence. Moreover, it can be shown that

$L(\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)},\\lambda) - L(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast},\\lambda) \\leq \\frac{C\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(0)} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}}{2i}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si94.png)

The latter result indicates that if one wants to achieve an accuracy of *ϵ*, then this can be obtained by at most $\\left\\lfloor \\frac{C\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(0)} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}}{2\\epsilon} \\right\\rfloor$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">⌊</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">⌋</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si95.png) iterations, where ⌊ ⋅ ⌋<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">⌊</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⌋</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si96.png) denotes the floor function.

In \[34\], Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14) was obtained from a nearby corner, building upon arguments from the classical *proximal point* methods in optimization theory (e.g., \[105\]). The original LASSO regularized cost function is modified to the *surrogate objective*,

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}) = \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} + \\lambda\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} + \\frac{1}{2}d(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si97.png)

where

$d(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}): = c\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} - \\left\\| X\\mathbf{\\theta} - X\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si98.png)

If *c* is appropriately chosen (larger than the largest eigenvalue of *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si92.png)), the surrogate objective is guaranteed to be strictly convex. Then it can be shown (Problem [10.4](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#o0245)) that the minimizer of the surrogate objective is given by

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = S\_{\\lambda/c}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}} + \\frac{1}{c}X^{T}(\\mathbf{y} - X\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si99.png)(10.8) 

In the iterative formulation, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si22.png) is selected to be the previously obtained estimate; in this way, one tries to keep the new estimate close to the previous one. The procedure readily results in our generic scheme in Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14), using soft thresholding with parameter *λ*/*c*<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si100.png). It can be shown that such a strategy converges to a minimizer of the original LASSO problem. The same algorithm was reached in \[56\], using *majorization-minimization* techniques from optimization theory. So, from this perspective, the IST family has strong ties with algorithms that belong to the convex optimization category.

In \[118\], the *sparse reconstruction by separable approximation* (SpaRSA) algorithm is proposed, which is a modification of the standard IST scheme. The starting point is Eq. [(10.3)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq17); however, the multiplying factor, $\\frac{1}{2\\mu}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si101.png), instead of being constant, is now allowed to change from iteration to iteration according to a rule. This results in a speedup in the convergence of the algorithm. Moreover, inspired by the homotopy family of algorithms, where *λ* is allowed to vary, SpaRSA can be extended to solve a sequence of problems that are associated with a corresponding sequence of values of *λ*. Once a solution has been obtained for a particular value of *λ*, it can be used as a “warm start” for a nearby value. Solutions can therefore be computed for a range of values, at a small extra computational cost, compared to solving for a single value from a “cold start.” This technique abides by the *continuation strategy*, which has been used in the context of other algorithms as well (e.g., \[66\]). Continuation has been shown to be a very successful tool to increase the speed of convergence.

An interesting variation of the basic IST scheme has been proposed in \[11\], which improves the convergence rate to *O*(1/*i*²)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si102.png), by only a simple modification with almost no extra computational burden. The scheme is known as *fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm* (FISTA). This scheme is an evolution of \[96\], which introduced the basic idea for the case of differentiable costs, and consists of the following steps:

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = S\_{\\lambda\\mu}\\left( \\mathbf{z}^{(i)} + \\mu X^{T}\\left( \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{z}^{(i)} \\right) \\right),\\mathbf{z}^{(i + 1)}: = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} + \\frac{t\_{i} - 1}{t\_{i + 1}}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msup id="mmlbr0005"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si103.png)

where

$t\_{i + 1}: = \\frac{1 + \\sqrt{1 + 4t\_{i}^{2}}}{2},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si104.png)

with initial points *t*[1] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si105.png) and **z**^((1)) = **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si106.png). In words, in the thresholding operation, **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si11.png) is replaced by **z**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si107.png), which is a specific linear combination of two successive updates of ***θ***. Hence, at a marginal increase of the computational cost, a substantial increase in convergence speed is achieved.

In \[17\] the hard thresholding version has been used, with *μ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si108.png), and the thresholding function *H*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si62.png) uses the sparsity level *k* of the target solution, which is assumed to be known. In a later version, \[19\], the relaxation parameter is left to change so that, at each iteration step, the error is maximally reduced. It has been shown that the algorithm converges to a local minimum of the cost function ∥**y**−*X***θ**∥[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si109.png), under the constraint that ***θ*** is a *k*\-sparse vector. Moreover, the latter version is a stable one and it results in a near-optimal solution if a form of RIP is fulfilled.

A modified version of the generic scheme given in Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14), which evolves along the lines of \[84\], obtains the updates component-wise, one vector component at a time. Thus, a “full” iteration consists of *l* steps. The algorithm is known as *coordinate descent* and its basic iteration has the form (Problem [10.5](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#o0250))

$\\theta\_{j}^{(i)} = S\_{\\lambda/{\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c}\\|}\_{2}^{2}}\\left( \\theta\_{j}^{(i - 1)} + \\frac{{\\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c}}^{T}\\mathbf{e}^{(i - 1)}}{\\left\\| \\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{c} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2}} \\right),\\quad j = 1,2,\\ldots,l.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si110.png)(10.9) 

This algorithm replaces the constant *c* in the previously reported soft thresholding algorithm with the norm of the respective column of *X*, if the columns of *X* are not normalized to unit norm. It has been shown that the parallel coordinate descent algorithm also converges to a LASSO minimizer of [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) \[50\]. Improvements of the algorithm, using line search techniques to determine the steepest descent direction for each iteration, have also been proposed (see \[124\]).

The main contribution to the complexity for the iterative shrinkage algorithmic family comes from the two matrix-vector products, which amounts to 𝒪(*N**l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si111.png), unless *X* has a special structure (e.g., DFT) that can be exploited to reduce the load.

In \[85\], the two-stage thresholding (TST) scheme is presented, which brings together arguments from the iterative shrinkage family and the OMP. This algorithmic scheme involves two stages of thresholding. The first step is exactly the same as in Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14). However, this is now used only for determining “significant” nonzero locations, just as in CSMP algorithms, presented in the previous subsection. Then, an LS problem is solved to provide the updated estimate, under the constraint of the available support. This is followed by a second step of thresholding. The thresholding operations in the two stages can be different. In hard thresholding, *H*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si62.png) is used in both steps; this results in the algorithm proposed in \[58\]. For this latter scheme, convergence and performance bounds are derived if the RIP holds for *δ*[3*k*] < 0.58<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.58</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si112.png). In other words, the basic difference between the TST and CSMP approaches is that, in the latter case, the most significant nonzero coefficients are obtained by looking at the correlation term *X*^(*T*)**e**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si113.png), and in the TST family by looking at **θ**^((*i* − 1)) + *μ**X*^(*T*)**e**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si114.png). The differences between different approaches can be minor and the crossing lines between the different algorithmic categories are not necessarily crispy and clear. However, from a practical point of view, sometimes small differences may lead to substantially improved performance.

In \[41\], the IST algorithmic framework was treated as a *message passing* algorithm in the context of graphical models (Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml)), and the following modified recursion was obtained:

**θ**^((*i*)) = *T*[*i*](**θ**^((*i* − 1))+*X*^(*T*)**z**^((*i* − 1))),<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si115.png)(10.10) 

$\\mathbf{z}^{(i - 1)} = \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} + \\frac{1}{\\alpha}\\mathbf{z}^{(i - 2)}\\bar{T\_{i}^{\\prime}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i-2)}+X^{T}\\mathbf{z}^{(i-2)} \\right)},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" where $\\alpha = \\frac{N}{l}$<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si117.png), the overbar denotes the average over all the components of the corresponding vector, and *T*[*i*]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si118.png) denotes the respective derivative of the component-wise thresholding rule. The extra term on the right-hand side in Eq. [(10.11)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq33) which now appears turns out to provide a performance improvement of the algorithm, compared to the IST family, with respect to the undersampling–sparsity tradeoff (Section [10.2.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0045)). Note that *T*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si74.png) is iteration dependent and it is controlled via the definition of certain parameters. A parameterless version of it has been proposed in \[91\]. A detailed treatment on the message passing algorithms can be found in \[2\].

Remarks 10.2

*   •  The iteration in Eq. [(10.6)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq22) bridges the IST algorithmic family with another powerful tool in convex optimization, which builds upon the notion of *proximal mapping* or *Moreau envelopes* (see Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml) and, e.g., \[32,105\]). Given a convex function *h* : ℝ^(*l*) → ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si119.png) and a *μ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si120.png), the proximal mapping, *P**r**o**x*[*μ**h*] : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si121.png), with respect to *h* and of index *μ*, is defined as the (unique) minimizer

${Prox}\_{\\mu h}(\\mathbf{x}): = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{v} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\{ h(\\mathbf{v}) + \\frac{1}{2\\mu}\\left\\| \\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{v} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\right\\},\\quad\\forall\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si122.png)(10.12) 

*   Let us now assume that we want to minimize a convex function, which is given as the sum

*f*(**θ**) = *J*(**θ**) + *h*(**θ**),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si123.png)

*   where *J* is convex and differentiable, and *h* is also convex, but not necessarily smooth. Then it can be shown (Section [8.14](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)) that the following iterations converge to a minimizer of *f*,

$\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = {Prox}\_{\\mu h}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu\\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si124.png)(10.13) 

*   where *μ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si120.png), and it can also be made iteration dependent, that is, *μ*[*i*] > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si125.png). If we now use this scheme to minimize our familiar cost,

*J*(**θ**) + *λ*∥**θ**∥[1],<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si126.png)

*   we obtain Eq. [(10.6)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq22); this is so because the proximal operator of *h*(**θ**) :  = *λ*∥**θ**∥[1]<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si127.png) is shown (see \[31,32\] and Section [8.13](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)) to be identical to the soft thresholding operator, that is,

*P**r**o**x*[*h*](**θ**) = *S*[*λ*](**θ**).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prox</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si128.png)

*   In order to feel more comfortable with this operator, note that if *h*(**x**) ≡ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≡</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si129.png), its proximal operator is equal to ***x***, and in this case Eq. [(10.13)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq36) becomes our familiar gradient descent algorithm.
*   •  All the nongreedy algorithms that have been discussed so far have been developed to solve the task defined in the formulation [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). This is mainly because this is an easier task to solve; once *λ* has been fixed, it is an unconstrained optimization task. However, there are algorithms that have been developed to solve the alternative formulations.
*   The NESTA algorithm has been proposed in \[12\] and solves the task in its [(9.8)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) formulation. Adopting this path can have an advantage because *ϵ* may be given as an estimate of the uncertainty associated with the noise, which can readily be obtained in a number of practical applications. In contrast, selecting a priori the value for *λ* is more intricate. In \[28\], the value $\\lambda = \\sigma\_{\\eta}\\sqrt{2\\ln l}$<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si130.png), where *σ*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si131.png) is the noise standard deviation, is argued to have certain optimality properties; however, this argument hinges on the assumption of the orthogonality of *X*. NESTA relies heavily on Nesterov's generic scheme \[96\], hence its name. The original Nesterov algorithm performs a constrained minimization of a smooth convex function *f*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si132.png), i.e.,

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in Q}f(\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si133.png)

*   where *Q* is a convex set, and in our case this is associated with the quadratic constraint in [(9.8)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). The algorithm consists of three basic steps. The first one involves an auxiliary variable, and is similar to the step in Eq. [(10.3)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq17), i.e.,

$\\mathbf{w}^{(i)} = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in Q}\\left\\{ \\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)^{T}\\frac{\\partial f\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} + \\frac{L}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si134.png)(10.14) 

*   where *L* is an upper bound on the Lipschitz coefficient, which the gradient of *f* has to satisfy. The difference with Eq. [(10.3)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq17) is that the minimization is now a constrained one. However, Nesterov has also added a second step, involving another auxiliary variable, **z**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si107.png), which is computed in a similar way as **w**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si135.png), but in place of the square Euclidean norm it involves a proxy-function for *Q*, and the linearized term is now replaced by a weighted cumulative gradient,

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{i - 1}\\alpha\_{k}\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(k)} \\right)^{T}\\frac{\\partial f\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(k)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}.$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si136.png)

*   The effect of this term is to smooth out the “zig-zagging” of the path toward the solution, whose effect is to increase the convergence speed significantly. The final step of the scheme involves an averaging of the previously obtained variables,

**θ**^((*i*)) = *t*[*i*]**z**^((*i*)) + (1 − *t*[*i*])**w**^((*i*)).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si137.png)

*   The values of the parameters *α*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si138.png), *k* = 0, …, *i* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si139.png), and *t*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si140.png) result from the theory so that convergence is guaranteed. As was the case with its close relative FISTA, the algorithm enjoys an *O*(1/*i*²)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si102.png) convergence rate. In our case, where the function to be minimized, ∥**θ**∥[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si141.png), is not smooth, NESTA uses a smoothed prox-function of it. Moreover, it turns out that closed form updates are obtained for **z**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si107.png) and **w**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si135.png). If *X* is chosen in order to have orthonormal rows, the complexity per iteration is *O*(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si142.png) plus the computations needed for performing the product *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si92.png), which is the most computationally thirsty part. However, this complexity can substantially be reduced if the sensing matrix is chosen to be a submatrix of a unitary transform which admits fast matrix-vector product computations (e.g., a subsampled DFT matrix). For example, for the case of a subsampled DFT matrix, the complexity amounts to *O*(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si142.png) plus the load to perform the two fast Fourier transforms (FFTs). Moreover, the continuation strategy can also be employed to accelerate convergence. In \[12\], it is demonstrated that NESTA exhibits good accuracy results, while retaining a complexity that is competitive with algorithms developed around the [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) formulation and scales in an affordable way for large-size problems. Furthermore, NESTA and, in general, Nesterov's scheme enjoy a generality that allows their use for other optimization tasks as well.
*   •  The task in [(9.7)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) has been considered in \[14\] and \[99\]. In the former, the algorithm comprises a projection on the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) ball ∥**θ**∥[1] ≤ *ρ*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si143.png) (see also Section [10.4.4](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0075)) per iteration step. The most computationally dominant part of the algorithm consists of matrix-vector products. In \[99\], a homotopy algorithm is derived for the same task, where now the bound *ρ* becomes the homotopy parameter that is left to vary. This algorithm is also referred to as the LARS-LASSO, as has already been reported.

### 10.2.3 Which algorithm? Some practical hints

We have already discussed a number of algorithmic alternatives to obtain solutions to the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si2.png) or ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm minimization tasks. Our focus was on schemes whose computational demands are rather low and that scale well to very large problem sizes. We have not touched more expensive methods such as interior point methods for solving the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) convex optimization task. A review of such methods is provided in \[72\]. Interior point methods evolve along the Newton-type recursion, and their complexity per iteration step is at least of the order 𝒪(*l*³)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si144.png). As is most often the case, there is a tradeoff. Schemes of higher complexity tend to result in enhanced performance. However, such schemes become impractical in problems of large size. Some examples of other algorithms that were not discussed can be found in \[14,35,118,121\]. Talking about complexity, it has to be pointed out that what really matters at the end is not so much the complexity per iteration step, but the overall required resources in computer time/memory for the algorithm to converge to a solution within a specified accuracy. For example, an algorithm may be of low complexity per iteration step, but it may need an excessive number of iterations to converge.
