Computational load is only one among a number of indices that characterize the performance of an algorithm. Throughout the book so far, we have considered a number of other performance measures, such as convergence rate, tracking speed (for the adaptive algorithms), and stability with respect to the presence of noise and/or finite word length computations. No doubt, all these performance measures are of interest here as well. However, there is an additional aspect that is of particular importance when quantifying performance of sparsity promoting algorithms. This is related to the *undersampling–sparsity tradeoff* or the *phase transition curve*.

One of the major issues on which we focused in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) was to derive and present the conditions that guarantee uniqueness of the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si2.png) minimization and its equivalence to the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) minimization task, under an underdetermined set of observations, **y** = *X***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si32.png), for the recovery of sparse enough signals/vectors. While discussing the various algorithms in this section, we reported a number of different RIP-related conditions that some of the algorithms have to satisfy in order to recover the target sparse vector. As a matter of fact, it has to be admitted that this was quite confusing, because each algorithm had to satisfy its own conditions. In addition, in practice, these conditions are not easy to be verified. Although such results are undoubtedly important to establish convergence, make us more confident, and help us better understand why and how an algorithm works, one needs further experimental evidence in order to establish good performance bounds for an algorithm. Moreover, all the conditions we have dealt with, including coherence and RIP, are sufficient conditions. In practice, it turns out that sparse signal recovery is possible with sparsity levels much higher than those predicted by the theory, for given *N* and *l*. Hence, proposing a new algorithm or selecting an algorithm from an available palette, one has to demonstrate experimentally the range of sparsity levels that can be recovered by the algorithm, as a percentage of the number of observations and the dimensionality. Thus, in order to select an algorithm, one should cast her/his vote for the algorithm that, for given *l* and *N*, has the potential to recover *k*\-sparse vectors with *k* being as high as possible for most of the cases, that is, with *high probability*.

[Fig. 10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0020) illustrates the type of curve that is expected to result in practice. The vertical axis is the probability of exact recovery of a target *k*\-sparse vector, and the horizontal axis shows the ratio *k*/*N*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si145.png), for a given number of observations, *N*, and the dimensionality of the ambient space, *l*. Three curves are shown. The red ones correspond to the same algorithm, for two different values of the dimensionality *l*, and the gray one corresponds to another algorithm. Curves of this shape are expected to result from experiments of the following setup. Assume that we are given a sparse vector **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si146.png), with *k* nonzero components in the *l*\-dimensional space. Using a sensing matrix *X*, we generate *N* samples/observations **y** = *X***θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si147.png). The experiment is repeated a number of *M* times, each time using a different realization of the sensing matrix and a different *k*\-sparse vector. For each instance, the algorithm is run to recover the target sparse vector. This is not always possible. We count the number, *m*, of successful recoveries, and compute the corresponding percentage of successful recovery (probability), *m*/*M*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si148.png), which is plotted on the vertical axis of [Fig. 10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0020). The procedure is repeated for a different value of *k*, 1 ≤ *k* ≤ *N*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si149.png). A number of issues now jump onto the stage: (a) how does one select the ensemble of sensing matrices, and (b) how does one select the ensemble of sparse vectors? There are different scenarios, and some typical examples are described next.

1.  **1.**  The *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si150.png) sensing matrices *X* are formed by: 
    1.  **(a)**  different i.i.d. realizations with elements drawn from a Gaussian 𝒩(0, 1/*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si151.png),
    2.  **(b)**  different i.i.d. realizations from the uniform distribution on the unit sphere in ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si152.png), which is also known as the uniform spherical ensemble,
    3.  **(c)**  different i.i.d. realizations with elements drawn from Bernoulli-type distributions,
    4.  **(d)**  different i.i.d. realizations of partial Fourier matrices, each time using a different set of *N* rows.
2.  **2.**  The *k*\-sparse target vector **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si146.png) is formed by selecting the locations of (at most) *k* nonzero elements randomly, with probability *p* = *k*/*l*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si153.png), and filling the values of the nonzero elements according to a statistical distribution (e.g., Gaussian, uniform, double exponential, Cauchy).

![Figure 10.3 For any algorithm, the transition between the regions of 100% success and complete failure is very sharp. For the algorithm corresponding to the red curve, this transition occurs at higher sparsity values and, from this point of view, it is a better algorithm than the one associated with the gray curve. Also, given an algorithm, the higher the dimensionality, the higher the sparsity level where this transition occurs, as indicated by the two red curves.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr003.jpg)

Figure 10.3 For any algorithm, the transition between the regions of 100% success and complete failure is very sharp. For the algorithm corresponding to the red curve, this transition occurs at higher sparsity values and, from this point of view, it is a better algorithm than the one associated with the gray curve. Also, given an algorithm, the higher the dimensionality, the higher the sparsity level where this transition occurs, as indicated by the two red curves.

Other scenarios are also possible. Some authors set all nonzero values to one \[16\], or to ±1, with the randomness imposed on the choice of the sign. It must be stressed that the performance of an algorithm may vary significantly under different experimental scenarios, and this may be indicative of the stability of an algorithm. In practice, a user may be interested in a specific scenario that is more representative of the available data.

Looking at [Fig. 10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0020), the following conclusions are in order. In all curves, there is a sharp transition between two levels, from the 100% success to the 0% success. Moreover, the higher the dimensionality, the sharper the transition. This has also been shown theoretically in \[40\]. For the algorithm corresponding to the red curves, this transition occurs at higher values of *k*, compared to the algorithm that generates the curve drawn in gray. Provided that the computational complexity of the “red” algorithm can be accommodated by the resources that are available for a specific application, this seems to be the more sensible choice between the two algorithms. However, if the resources are limited, concessions are unavoidable.

Another way to “interrogate” and demonstrate the performance of an algorithm, with respect to its robustness to the range of values of sparsity levels that can be successfully recovered, is via the *phase transition curve*. To this end, define:

*   •  $\\alpha: = \\frac{N}{l}$<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si154.png), which is a normalized measure of the problem indeterminacy,
*   •  $\\beta: = \\frac{k}{N}$<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si155.png), which is a normalized measure of sparsity.

In the sequel, plot a graph having *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si156.png) in the horizontal axis and *β* ∈ \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si157.png) in the vertical one. For each point (*α*, *β*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si158.png) in the \[0, 1\] × \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si159.png) region, compute the probability of the algorithm to recover a *k*\-sparse target vector. In order to compute the probability, one has to adopt one of the previously stated scenarios. In practice, one has to form a grid of points that cover densely enough the region \[0, 1\] × \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si159.png) in the graph. Use a varying intensity level scale to color the corresponding (*α*, *β*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si158.png) point. Black corresponds to probability one and red to probability zero. [Fig. 10.4](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0025) illustrates the type of graph that is expected to be recovered in practice for large values of *l*; that is, the transition from the region (phase) of “success” (black) to that of “fail” (red) is very sharp. As a matter of fact, there is a curve that separates the two regions. The theoretical aspects of this curve have been studied in the context of combinatorial geometry in \[40\] for the asymptotic case, *l* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si161.png), and in \[42\] for finite values of *l*. Observe that the larger the value of *α* (larger percentage of observations), the larger the value of *β* at which the transition occurs. This is in line with what we have said so far in this chapter, and the problem gets increasingly difficult as one moves up and to the left in the graph. In practice, for smaller values of *l*, the transition region from red to black is smoother, and it gets narrower as *l* increases. In such cases, one can draw an approximate curve that separates the “success” and “fail” regions using regression techniques (see, e.g., \[85\]).

![Figure 10.4 Typical phase transition behavior of a sparsity promoting algorithm. Black corresponds to 100% success of recovering the sparsest solution, and red to 0%. For high-dimensional spaces, the transition is very sharp, as is the case in the figure. For lower dimensionality values, the transition from black to red is smoother and involves a region of varying color intensity.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr004.jpg)

Figure 10.4 Typical phase transition behavior of a sparsity promoting algorithm. Black corresponds to 100% success of recovering the sparsest solution, and red to 0%. For high-dimensional spaces, the transition is very sharp, as is the case in the figure. For lower dimensionality values, the transition from black to red is smoother and involves a region of varying color intensity.

The reader may already be aware of the fact that, so far, we have avoided talking about the performance of individual algorithms. We have just discussed some “typical” behavior that algorithms tend to exhibit in practice. What the reader might have expected is a discussion of comparative performance tests and related conclusions. The reason is that at the time the current edition is being compiled there are not definite answers. Most authors compare their newly suggested algorithm with a few other algorithms, usually within a certain algorithmic family, and, more importantly, under some specific scenarios, where the advantages of the newly suggested algorithm are documented. However, the performance of an algorithm can change significantly by changing the experimental scenario under which the tests are carried out. A comprehensive comparative performance study is reported in \[85\]. However, even in this work, the scenario of exact observations has been considered and there are no experiments concerning the robustness of individual algorithms to the presence of noise. It is important to say that this study involved a huge effort of computation. We will comment on some of the findings from this study, which will also reveal to the reader that different experimental scenarios can significantly affect the performance of an algorithm.

[Fig. 10.5](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0030)A shows the obtained phase transition curves for (a) the iterative hard thresholding (IHT); (b) the iterative soft thresholding (IST) scheme of Eq. [(10.2)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq14); (c) the two-stage thresholding (TST) scheme, as discussed earlier; (d) the LARS algorithm; and (e) the OMP algorithm, together with the theoretically obtained one using ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) minimization. All algorithms were tuned with the optimal values, with respect to the required user-defined parameters, after extensive experimentation. The results in the figure correspond to the uniform spherical scenario for the generation of the sensing matrices. Sparse vectors were generated according to the ±1 scenario for the nonzero coefficients. The interesting observation is that, although the curves deviate from each other as they move to larger values of *β*, for smaller values, the differences in their performance become less and less. This is also true for computationally simple schemes such as the IHT one. The performance of LARS is close to the optimal one. However, this comes at the cost of computational increase. The required computational time for achieving the same accuracy, as reported in \[85\], favors the TST algorithm. In some cases, LARS required excessively longer time to reach the same accuracy, in particular when the sensing matrix was the partial Fourier one and fast schemes to perform matrix vector products can be exploited. For such matrices, the thresholding schemes (IHT, IST, TST) exhibited a performance that scales very well to large-size problems.

![Figure 10.5 (A) The obtained phase transition curves for different algorithms under the same experimental scenario, together with the theoretical one. (B) Phase transition curve for the IST algorithm under different experimental scenarios for generating the target sparse vector. (C) The phase transition for the IST algorithms under different experimental scenarios for generating the sensing matrix X.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr005.jpg)

Figure 10.5 (A) The obtained phase transition curves for different algorithms under the same experimental scenario, together with the theoretical one. (B) Phase transition curve for the IST algorithm under different experimental scenarios for generating the target sparse vector. (C) The phase transition for the IST algorithms under different experimental scenarios for generating the sensing matrix *X*.

[Fig. 10.5](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0030)B indicates the phase transition curve for one of the algorithms (IST) as we change the scenarios for generating the sparse (target) vectors, using different distributions: (a) ±1, with equiprobable selection of signs (constant amplitude random selection \[CARS\]); (b) double exponential (power); (c) Cauchy; and (d) uniform in \[ − 1, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si162.png). This is indicative and typical for other algorithms as well, with some of them being more sensitive than others. Finally, [Fig. 10.5](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0030)C shows the transition curves for the IST algorithm by changing the sensing matrix generation scenario. Three curves are shown corresponding to (a) uniform spherical ensemble (USE); (b) random sign ensemble (RSE), where the elements are ±1 with signs uniformly distributed; and (c) the uniform random projection (URP) ensemble. Once more, one can observe the possible variations that are expected due to the use of different matrix ensembles. Moreover, changing ensembles affects each algorithm in a different way.

Concluding this section, it must be emphasized that algorithmic development is still an ongoing research field, and it is early to come up with definite and concrete comparative performance conclusions. Moreover, besides the algorithmic front, existing theories often fall short in predicting what is observed in practice, with respect to their phase transition performance. For a related discussion, see, for example, \[43\].

## 10.3 Variations on the sparsity-aware theme

In our tour so far, we have touched a number of aspects of sparsity-aware learning that come from mainstream theoretical developments. However, a number of variants have appeared and have been developed with the goal of addressing problems of a more special structure and/or proposing alternatives, which can be beneficial in boosting the performance in practice by serving the needs of specific applications. These variants focus on the regularization term in Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), and/or on the misfit measuring term. Once more, research activity in this direction has been dense, and our purpose is to simply highlight possible alternatives and make the reader aware of the various possibilities that spring forth from the basic theory.

In a number of tasks, it is a priori known that the nonzero parameters in the target signal/vector occur in groups and they are not randomly spread in all possible positions. A typical example is the echo path in internet telephony, where the nonzero coefficients of the impulse response tend to cluster together (see [Fig. 9.5](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)). Other examples of “structured” sparsity can be traced in DNA microarrays, MIMO channel equalization, source localization in sensor networks, magnetoencephalography, and neuroscience problems (e.g., \[1,9,10,60,101\]). As is always the case in machine learning, being able to incorporate a priori information into the optimization can only be of benefit for improving performance, because the estimation task is externally assisted in its effort to search for the optimal solution.

The *group LASSO* \[8,59,97,98,117,122\] addresses the task where it is a priori known that the nonzero components occur in groups. The unknown vector ***θ*** is divided into *L* groups, that is,

**θ**^(*T*) = \[**θ**[1]^(*T*),…,**θ**[*L*]^(*T*)\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si163.png)

each of them of a predetermined size, *s*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *L*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si164.png), with $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{L}s\_{i} = l$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si165.png). The regression model can then be written as

$\\mathbf{y} = X\\mathbf{\\theta} + \\mathbf{\\eta} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{L}X\_{i}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i} + \\mathbf{\\eta},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si166.png)

where each *X*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si167.png) is a submatrix of *X* comprising the corresponding *s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si168.png) columns. The solution of the group LASSO is given by the following regularized task:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/fx002.jpg)(10.15) 

where ∥**θ**[*i*]∥[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si169.png) is the Euclidean norm (not the squared one) of **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si170.png), that is,

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i} \\right\\|\_{2} = \\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{s\_{i}}|\\theta\_{i,j}|^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si171.png)

In other words, the individual components of ***θ***, which contribute to the formation of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm in the standard LASSO formulation, are now replaced by the square root of the energy of each individual block. In this setting, it is not the individual components but *blocks* of them that are forced to zero, when their contribution to the LS misfit measuring term is not significant. Sometimes, this type of regularization is coined as the ℓ[1]/ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si172.png) regularization. An example of an ℓ[1]/ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si172.png) ball for **θ** ∈ ℝ³<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si173.png) can be seen in [Fig. 10.6](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0035)B in comparison with the corresponding ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) ball depicted in [Fig. 10.6](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0035)A.

![Figure 10.6 Representation of balls of \\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{3}Equation corresponding to: (A) the ℓ1 norm; (B) an ℓ1/ℓ2 with nonoverlapping groups (one group comprises {θ1,θ2} and the other one {θ3}); and (C) the ℓ1/ℓ2 with overlapping groups comprising {θ1,θ2,θ3}, {θ1}, and {θ3} \[6\].](images/B9780443292385000160/gr006.jpg)

Figure 10.6 Representation of balls of **θ** ∈ ℝ³<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si173.png) corresponding to: (A) the *ℓ*[1] norm; (B) an *ℓ*[1]/*ℓ*[2] with nonoverlapping groups (one group comprises {*θ*[1],*θ*[2]} and the other one {*θ*[3]}); and (C) the *ℓ*[1]/*ℓ*[2] with overlapping groups comprising {*θ*[1],*θ*[2],*θ*[3]}, {*θ*[1]}, and {*θ*[3]} \[6\].

Beyond the conventional group LASSO, often referred to as *block sparsity*, research effort has been dedicated to the development of learning strategies incorporating more elaborate *structured sparse* models. There are two major reasons for such directions. First, in a number of applications the unknown set of parameters, ***θ***, exhibit a structure that cannot be captured by the block sparse model. Second, even for cases where ***θ*** is block sparse, standard grouped ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norms require information about the partitioning of ***θ***. This can be rather restrictive in practice. The adoption of overlapping groups has been proposed as a possible solution. Assuming that every parameter belongs to at least one group, such models lead to optimization tasks that, in many cases, are not hard to solve, for example, by resorting to proximal methods \[6,7\]. Moreover, by using properly defined overlapping groups \[71\], the allowed sparsity patterns can be constrained to form *hierarchical* structures, such as connected and rooted trees and subtrees that are met, for example, in multiscale (wavelet) decompositions. In [Fig. 10.6](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0035)C, an example of an ℓ[1]/ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si172.png) ball for overlapping groups is shown.

Besides the previously stated directions, extensions of the compressed sensing principles to cope with structured sparsity led to the *model-based* compressed sensing \[10,26\]. The (*k*, *C*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si174.png) model allows the significant parameters of a *k*\-sparse signal to appear in at most *C* clusters, whose size is unknown. In Section [9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), it was commented that searching for a *k*\-sparse solution takes place in a union of subspaces, each one of dimensionality *k*. Imposing a certain structure on the target solution restricts the searching in a subset of these subspaces and leaves a number of these out of the game. This obviously facilitates the optimization task. In \[27\], structured sparsity is considered in terms of graphical models, and in \[110\] the C-HiLasso group sparsity model was introduced, which allows each block to have a sparse structure itself. Theoretical results that extend the RIP to the block RIP have been developed and reported (see, for example, \[18,83\]) and in the algorithmic front, proper modifications of greedy algorithms have been proposed in order to provide structured sparse solutions \[53\].

In \[24\], it is suggested to replace the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm by a weighted version of it. To justify such a choice, let us recall [Example 9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and the case where the “unknown” system was sensed using **x** = \[2, 1\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si175.png). We have seen that by “blowing up” the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) ball, the wrong sparse solution was obtained. Let us now replace the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm in [(9.21)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) with its weighted version,

∥**θ**∥[1, *w*] :  = *w*[1]|*θ*[1]| + *w*[2]|*θ*[2]|, *w*[1], *w*[2] > 0,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si176.png)

and set *w*[1] = 4<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si177.png) and *w*[2] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si178.png). [Fig. 10.7](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0040)A shows the isovalue curve ∥**θ**∥[1, *w*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si179.png), together with that resulting from the standard ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm. The weighted one is sharply “pinched” around the vertical axis, and the larger the value of *w*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si180.png), compared to that of *w*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si181.png), the sharper the corresponding ball will be. [Fig. 10.7](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0040)B shows what happens when “blowing up” the weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) ball. It will first touch the point (0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si182.png), which is the true solution. Basically, what we have done is “squeeze” the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) ball to be aligned more to the axis that contains the (sparse) solution. For the case of our example, any weight *w*[1] > 2<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si183.png) would do the job.

![Figure 10.7 (A) The isovalue curves for the ℓ1 and the weighted ℓ1 norms for the same value. The weighted ℓ1 is sharply pinched around one of the axes, depending on the weights. (B) Adopting to minimize the weighted ℓ1 norm for the setup of Fig. 9.9C, the correct sparse solution is obtained.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr007.jpg)

Figure 10.7 (A) The isovalue curves for the *ℓ*[1] and the weighted *ℓ*[1] norms for the same value. The weighted *ℓ*[1] is sharply pinched around one of the axes, depending on the weights. (B) Adopting to minimize the weighted *ℓ*[1] norm for the setup of [Fig. 9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)C, the correct sparse solution is obtained.

Consider now the general case of a weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/fx003.jpg)(10.16) 

The ideal choice of the weights would be

$w\_{j} = \\begin{cases} {\\frac{1}{|\\theta\_{o,j}|},} & {\\theta\_{o,j} \\neq 0,} \\\\ {\\infty,} & {\\theta\_{o,j} = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si185.png)

where **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si146.png) is the target true vector, and where we have tacitly assumed that 0 ⋅ ∞ = 0<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si186.png). In other words, the smaller a parameter is, the larger the respective weight becomes. This is justified, because large weighting will force respective parameters toward zero during the minimization process. Of course, in practice the values of the true vector are not known, so it is suggested to use their estimates during each iteration of the minimization procedure. The resulting scheme is of the following form.

Algorithm 10.3

1.  **1.**  Initialize weights to unity, *w*[*j*]^((0)) = 1<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si187.png), *j* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si188.png).
2.  **2.**  Minimize the weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm,

**θ**^((*i*)) = *a**r**g* *m**i**n*[**θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)] ∥**θ**∥[1, *w*]s.t.     **y** = *X***θ**.<mml:math><mml:msup id="mmlbr0006"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace linebreak="newline"/><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si189.png)

1.  
2.  **3.**  Update the weights

$w\_{j}^{(i + 1)} = \\frac{1}{\\left| \\theta\_{j}^{(i)} \\middle| + \\epsilon \\right.},\\quad j = 1,2,\\ldots,l.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si190.png)

1.  
2.  **4.**  Terminate when a stopping criterion is met, otherwise return to step 2.

The constant *ϵ* is a small user-defined parameter to guarantee stability when the estimates of the coefficients take very small values. Note that if the weights have constant preselected values, the task retains its convex nature; this is no longer true when the weights are changing. It is interesting to point out that this intuitively motivated weighting scheme can result if the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm is replaced by $\\sum\_{j = 1}^{l}\\ln\\left( |\\theta\_{j}| + \\epsilon \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si191.png) as the regularizing term of Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). [Fig. 10.8](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0045) shows the respective graph in the one-dimensional space together with that of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm. The graph of the logarithmic function reminds us of the ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si192.png), 0 < *p* < 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si193.png), “norms” and the comments made in Section [9.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). This is no longer a convex function, and the iterative scheme given before is the result of a majorization-minimization procedure in order to solve the resulting nonconvex task \[24\] (Problem [10.6](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#o0255)).

![Figure 10.8 One-dimensional graphs of the ℓ1 norm and the logarithmic regularizer \\ln\\left( \\frac{|\\theta|}{\\epsilon} + 1 \\right) = \\ln\\left( |\\theta| + \\epsilon \\right) - \\ln\\epsilonEquation, with ϵ = 0.1. The term \\ln\\epsilonEquation was subtracted for illustration purposes only and does not affect the optimization. Note the nonconvex nature of the logarithmic regularizer.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 10.8](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#cf0600) One-dimensional graphs of the *ℓ*[1] norm and the logarithmic regularizer $\\ln\\left( \\frac{|\\theta|}{\\epsilon} + 1 \\right) = \\ln\\left( |\\theta| + \\epsilon \\right) - \\ln\\epsilon$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si194.png), with *ϵ* = 0.1. The term ln *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si195.png) was subtracted for illustration purposes only and does not affect the optimization. Note the nonconvex nature of the logarithmic regularizer.

The concept of iterative weighting, as used before, has also been applied in the context of the *iterative reweighted LS algorithm*. Observe that the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm can be written as

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1} = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{l}|\\theta\_{j}| = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathcal{W}\_{\\theta}\\mathbf{\\theta},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si196.png)

where

$\\mathcal{W}\_{\\theta} = \\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{1}{|\\theta\_{1}|} & 0 & \\cdots & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\frac{1}{|\\theta\_{2}|} & \\cdots & 0 \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\ 0 & 0 & \\cdots & \\frac{1}{|\\theta\_{l}|} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋱</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si197.png)

and where in the case of *θ*[*i*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si198.png), for some *i* ∈ {1, 2, …, *l*}<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si199.png), the respective coefficient of 𝒲[*θ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si200.png) is defined to be 1. If 𝒲[*θ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si200.png) were a constant weighting matrix, that is, 𝒲[*θ*] :  = 𝒲[*θ̃*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si201.png), for some fixed $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si22.png), then obtaining the minimum 

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} + \\lambda\\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathcal{W}\_{\\widetilde{\\theta}}\\mathbf{\\theta},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si202.png)

would be straightforward and similar to the ridge regression. In the iterative reweighted scheme, 𝒲[*θ̃*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si203.png) is replaced by 𝒲[*θ*^((*i*))]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si204.png), formed by using the respective estimates of the parameters, which have been obtained from the previous iteration, that is, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}: = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si205.png), as we did before. In the sequel, each iteration solves a weighted ridge regression task.

The *focal underdetermined system solver* (FOCUSS) algorithm \[64\] was the first one to use the concept of *iterative-reweighted-least-squares* to represent ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si192.png), *p* ≤ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si206.png), as a weighted ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) norm in order to find a sparse solution to an underdetermined system of equations. This algorithm is also of historical importance, because it is among the very first ones to emphasize the importance of sparsity; moreover, it provides comprehensive convergence analysis as well as a characterization of the stationary points of the algorithm. Variants of this basic iterative weighting scheme have also been proposed (see, e.g., \[35\] and the references therein).

In \[126\], the *elastic net* regularization penalty was introduced, which combines the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) concepts together in a tradeoff fashion, that is,

$\\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\left( \\alpha\\theta\_{i}^{2} + (1 - \\alpha)|\\theta\_{i}| \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si207.png)

where *α* is a user-defined parameter controlling the influence of each individual term. The idea behind the elastic net is to combine the advantages of the LASSO and the ridge regression. In problems where there is a group of variables in ***x*** that are highly correlated, LASSO tends to select one of the corresponding parameters in ***θ***, and set the rest to zero in a rather arbitrary fashion. This can be understood by looking carefully at how the greedy algorithms work. When sparsity is used to select the most important of the variables in ***x*** (feature selection), it is better to select all the relevant components in the group. If one knew which of the variables are correlated, he/she could form a group and then use the group LASSO. However, if this is not known, involving the ridge regression offers a remedy to the problem. This is because the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) penalty in ridge regression tends to shrink the parameters associated with correlated variables toward each other (e.g., \[68\]). In such cases, it would be better to work with the elastic net rationale that involves LASSO and ridge regression in a combined fashion.

In \[23\], the LASSO task is modified by replacing the squared error term with one involving correlations, and the minimization task becomes

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}:\\ \\ \\ \\ \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\ \\ \\ \\left\\| X^{T}(\\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\|\_{\\infty} \\leq \\epsilon,$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true" id="mmlbr0007"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0007" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si208.png)

where *ϵ* is related to *l* and the noise variance. This task is known as the *Dantzig selector*. That is, instead of constraining the energy of the error, the constraint now imposes an upper limit to the correlation of the error vector with any of the columns of *X*. In \[5,15\], it is shown that under certain conditions, the LASSO estimator and the Dantzig selector become identical.

*Total variation* (TV) \[107\] is a closely related to ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) sparsity promoting notion that has been widely used in image processing. Most of the grayscale image arrays, *I* ∈ ℝ^(*l* × *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si209.png), consist of slowly varying pixel intensities except at the edges. As a consequence, the discrete gradient of an image array will be approximately sparse (compressible). The discrete directional derivatives of an image array are defined pixel-wise as

∇[*x*](*I*)(*i*, *j*) :  = *I*(*i* + 1, *j*) − *I*(*i*, *j*), ∀*i* ∈ {1, 2, …, *l* − 1},<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si210.png)(10.17) 

∇[*y*](*I*)(*i*, *j*) :  = *I*(*i*, *j* + 1) − *I*(*i*, *j*), ∀*j* ∈ {1, 2, …, *l* − 1},<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si211.png)(10.18) 

and

∇[*x*](*I*)(*l*, *j*) :  = ∇[*y*](*I*)(*i*, *l*) :  = 0, ∀*i*, *j* ∈ {1, 2, …, *l* − 1}.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si212.png)(10.19) 

The *discrete gradient transform*

∇ : ℝ^(*l* × *l*) → ℝ^(*l* × 2*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si213.png)

is defined in terms of a matrix form as

∇(*I*)(*i*, *j*) :  = \[∇[*x*](*i*, *j*), ∇[*y*](*i*, *j*)\], ∀*i*, *j* ∈ {1, 2, …*l*}.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si214.png)(10.20) 

The total variation of the image array is defined as the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm of the *magnitudes* of the elements of the discrete gradient transform, that is,

$\\left\\| I \\right\\|\_{\\text{TV}}: = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{l}\\left\\| \\nabla(I)(i,j) \\right\\|\_{2} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{l}\\sqrt{\\left( \\nabla\_{x}(I)(i,j) \\right)^{2} + \\left( \\nabla\_{y}(I)(i,j) \\right)^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo
