Note that this is a mixture of ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si28.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norms. The sparsity promoting optimization around the total variation is defined as

$I\_{\\ast} \\in \\text{arg}\\min\\limits\_{I}\\left\\| I \\right\\|\_{TV},\\text{s.t.}\\ \\ \\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - \\mathcal{F}(I) \\right\\|\_{2} \\leq \\epsilon,$<mml:math><mml:msub id="mmlbr0008"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>arg</mml:mtext><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0008" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si216.png)(10.22) 

where **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si217.png) is the observations vector and ℱ(*I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si218.png) denotes the result in vectorized form of the application of a linear operator on *I*. For example, this could be the result of the action of a partial two-dimensional DFT on the image. Subsampling of the DFT matrix as a means of forming sensing matrices has already been discussed in Section [9.7.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). The task in [(10.22)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq63) retains its convex nature and it basically expresses our desire to reconstruct an image that is as smooth as possible, given the available observations. The NESTA algorithm can be used for solving the total variation minimization task; besides NESTA, other efficient algorithms for this task can be found in, for example, \[63,120\].

It has been shown in \[22\] for the exact observations case (*ϵ* = 0)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si219.png), and in \[94\] for the erroneous observations case, that conditions and bounds that guarantee recovery of an image array from the task in [(10.22)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq63) can be derived and are very similar to those we have discussed for the case of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm.

Example 10.1

(*Magnetic resonance imaging* (MRI)). In contrast to ordinary imaging systems, which directly acquire pixel samples, MRI scanners sense the image in an encoded form. Specifically, MRI scanners sample components in the spatial frequency domain, known as “*k*\-space” in the MRI nomenclature. If all the components in this transform domain were available, one could apply the inverse 2D-DFT to recover the exact MR image in the pixel domain. Sampling in the *k*\-space is realized along particular trajectories in a number of successive acquisitions. This process is time consuming, merely due to physical constraints. As a result, techniques for efficient image recovery from a *limited number of observations* are of high importance, because they can reduce the required acquisition time for performing the measurements. Long acquisition times are not only inconvenient but even impossible, because the patients have to stay still for long time intervals. Thus, MRI was among the very first applications where compressed sensing found its way to offering its elegant solutions.

[Fig. 10.9](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0050)A shows the “famous” Shepp–Logan phantom, and the goal is to recover it via a limited number of samples (observations) in its frequency domain. The observed MRI samples are taken along 17 radial lines in the spatial frequency domain, as shown in [Fig. 10.9](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0050)B. A “naive” approach to recovering the image from this limited number of samples would be to adopt a zero-filling rationale for the missing components. The recovered image according to this technique is shown in [Fig. 10.9](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0050)C. [Fig. 10.9](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0050)D shows the recovered image using the approach of minimizing the total variation, as explained before. Observe that the results for this case are astonishingly good. The original image is almost perfectly recovered. The constrained minimization was performed via the NESTA algorithm. Note that if the minimization of the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm of the image array were used in place of the total variation, the results would not be as good; the phantom image is sparse in the discrete gradient domain, because it contains large sections that share constant intensities.

![Figure 10.9 (A) The original Shepp–Logan image phantom. (B) The white lines indicate the directions along which the sampling in the spatial Fourier transform were obtained. (C) The recovered image after applying the inverse DFT, having first filled with zeros the missing values in the DFT transform. (D) The recovered image using the total variation minimization approach.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr009.jpg)

Figure 10.9 (A) The original Shepp–Logan image phantom. (B) The white lines indicate the directions along which the sampling in the spatial Fourier transform were obtained. (C) The recovered image after applying the inverse DFT, having first filled with zeros the missing values in the DFT transform. (D) The recovered image using the total variation minimization approach.

## 10.4 Online sparsity promoting algorithms

In this section, online schemes for sparsity-aware learning are presented. There are a number of reasons why one has to resort to such schemes. As has already been noted in previous chapters, in various signal processing tasks the data arrive sequentially. Under such a scenario, using batch processing techniques to obtain an estimate of an unknown target parameter vector would be highly inefficient, because the number of training points keeps increasing. Such an approach is prohibited for real-time applications. Moreover, time-recursive schemes can easily incorporate the notion of adaptivity, when the learning environment is not stationary but undergoes changes as time evolves. Besides signal processing, there are an increasing number of other machine learning application areas where online processing is of paramount importance, such as bioinformatics, hyperspectral imaging, and data mining. In such disciplines, the number of training points easily amounts to a few thousand up to hundreds of thousands of points. Concerning the dimensionality of the ambient (feature) space, one can claim numbers that lie in similar ranges. For example, in \[82\], the task is to search for sparse solutions in feature spaces with dimensionality as high as 10⁹ having access to data sets as large as 10⁷ points. Using batch techniques on a single computer is out of the question with today's technology.

The setting that we have adopted for this section is the same as that used in previous chapters (e.g., Chapters [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) and [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)). We assume that there is an unknown parameter vector that generates data according to the linear regression model

*y*[*n*] = **x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** + *η*[*n*], ∀*n*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si220.png)

and the training samples are received sequentially (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si221.png), *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si222.png). In the case of a stationary environment, we would expect our algorithm to converge asymptotically, as *n* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si223.png), to or “nearly to” the true parameter vector that gives birth to the observations, *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si224.png), when it is sensed by **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si225.png). For time-varying environments, the algorithms should be able to track the underlying changes as time goes by. Before we proceed, a comment is important. Because the time index, *n*, is left to grow, all we have said in the previous sections with respect to underdetermined systems of equations loses its meaning. Sooner or later we are going to have more observations than the dimension of the space in which the data reside. Our major concern here becomes the issue of asymptotic convergence for the case of stationary environments. The obvious question that is now raised is, why not use a standard algorithm (e.g., LMS, RLS, or APSM), as we know that these algorithms converge to, or nearly enough in some sense, the solution (i.e., the algorithm will identify the zeros asymptotically)? The answer is that if such algorithms are modified to be aware of the underlying sparsity, convergence is significantly sped up; in real-life applications, one does not have the “luxury” of waiting a long time for the solution. In practice, a good algorithm should be able to provide a good enough solution, and in the case of sparse solutions to *obtain the support*, after a relatively small number of iteration steps.

In Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), we commented on attempts to modify classical online schemes (for example, the proportionate LMS) in order to consider sparsity. However, these algorithms were of a rather ad hoc nature. In this section, the powerful theory around the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm regularization will be used to obtain sparsity promoting time-adaptive schemes.

### 10.4.1 LASSO: asymptotic performance

When presenting the basic principles of parameter estimation in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), the notions of bias, variance, and consistency, which are related to the performance of an estimator, were introduced. In a number of cases, such performance measures were derived asymptotically. For example, we have seen that the maximum likelihood estimator is asymptotically unbiased and consistent. In Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml), we saw that the LS estimator is also asymptotically consistent in the presence of i.i.d. white noise samples. Moreover, under the latter assumption, the LS estimator, ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si226.png), based on *n* observations, is itself a random vector that satisfies the $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png)\-estimation consistency, that is,

$\\sqrt{n}\\left( {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o} \\right)\\longrightarrow\\mathcal{N}\\left( 0,\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}\\Sigma^{- 1} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si228.png)

where **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si146.png) is the true vector that generates the observations, *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si229.png) denotes the variance of the noise source, and *Σ* is the covariance matrix 𝔼\[**x****x**^(*T*)\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si230.png) of the input sequence, which has been assumed to be zero mean and the limit denotes convergence in distribution.

The LASSO in its Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) formulation is the task of minimizing the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png)\-norm regularized version of the sum of squared errors cost function. However, nothing has been said so far about the statistical properties of this estimator. The only performance measure that we referred to was the error norm bound given in [(9.36)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). However, this bound, although important in the context for which it was proposed, does not provide much statistical information. Since the introduction of the LASSO estimator, a number of papers have addressed problems related to its statistical performance (see, e.g., \[45,55,74,127\]).

When dealing with sparsity promoting estimators such as the LASSO, two crucial issues emerge: (a) whether the estimator, even asymptotically, can obtain the support, if the true parameter vector is a sparse one; and (b) to quantify the performance of the estimator with respect to the estimates of the nonzero components that is, those components whose index belongs to the support. Especially for LASSO, the latter issue becomes to study whether LASSO behaves as well as the unregularized LS with respect to these nonzero components. This task was addressed for the first time and in a more general setting in \[55\]. Let the support of the true, yet unknown, *k*\-sparse parameter vector **θ**[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si146.png) be denoted as *S*. Let also *Σ*[|*S*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si231.png) be the *k* × *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si232.png) covariance matrix 𝔼\[**x**[|*S*]**x**[|*S*]^(*T*)\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si233.png), where **x**[|*S*] ∈ ℝ^(*k*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si234.png) is the random vector that contains only the *k* components of **x**, with indices in the support *S*. Then we say that an estimator satisfies asymptotically the *oracle properties* if:

*   •  $\\lim\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}{Prob}\\left\\{ S\_{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{n}} = S \\right\\} = 1$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prob</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si235.png); this is known as *support consistency*;
*   •  $\\sqrt{n}\\left( {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{n|S} - \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o|S} \\right)\\longrightarrow\\mathcal{N}\\left( 0,\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}\\Sigma\_{|S}^{- 1} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si236.png); this is the $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png)\-*estimation consistency*.

We denote as **θ**[*o*|*S*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si238.png) and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{n|S}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si239.png) the *k*\-dimensional vectors that result from $\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{o},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si240.png), respectively, if we keep the components whose indices lie in the support *S*, and the limit is meant in distribution. In other words, according to the oracle properties, a good sparsity promoting estimator should be able to predict, asymptotically, the true support, and its performance with respect to the nonzero components should be as good as that of a genie-aided LS estimator, which is informed in advance of the positions of the nonzero coefficients.

Unfortunately, the LASSO estimator *cannot* satisfy simultaneously both conditions. It has been shown \[55,74,127\] that:

*   •  For support consistency, the regularization parameter *λ* :  = *λ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si241.png) should be time-varying, such that

$\\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac{\\lambda\_{n}}{\\sqrt{n}} = \\infty,\\quad\\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac{\\lambda\_{n}}{n} = 0.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si242.png)

*   That is, *λ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si243.png) must grow faster than $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png), but slower than *n*.
*   •  For $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png)\-consistency, *λ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si243.png) must grow as

$\\lim\\limits\_{n\\rightarrow\\infty}\\frac{\\lambda\_{n}}{\\sqrt{n}} = 0,$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si244.png)

*   that is, it grows slower than $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png).

The previous two conditions are conflicting and the LASSO estimator cannot comply with the two oracle conditions simultaneously. The respective proofs are somewhat technical and are not given here. The interested reader can obtain them from the previously given references. However, before we proceed, it is instructive to see why the regularization parameter has to grow more slowly than *n*, in any case. Without being too rigorous mathematically, recall that the LASSO solution comes from Eq. [(9.6)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). This can be written as

$0 \\in - \\frac{2}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{i}y\_{i} + \\frac{2}{n}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{i}\\mathbf{x}\_{i}^{T} \\right)\\mathbf{\\theta} + \\frac{\\lambda\_{n}}{n}\\partial\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|\_{1},$<mml:math><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si245.png)(10.23) 

where we have divided both sides by *n*. Taking the limit as *n* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si223.png), if *λ*[*n*]/*n* → 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si246.png), then we are left with the first two terms; this is exactly what we would have if the unregularized sum of squared errors had been chosen as the cost function. Recall from Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml) that in this case, the solution asymptotically converges^([^(66)](#fn66))

### 10.4.2 The adaptive norm-weighted LASSO

There are two ways to get out of the previously stated conflict. One is to replace the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm with a nonconvex function, which can lead to an estimator that satisfies the oracle properties simultaneously \[55\]. The other is to modify the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm by replacing it with a *weighted* version. Recall that the weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm was discussed in Section [10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0050) as a means to assist the optimization procedure to unveil the sparse solution. Here the notion of the weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm comes as a necessity imposed by our desire to satisfy the oracle properties. This gives rise to the *adaptive time-and-norm-weighted LASSO* (TNWL) estimate, defined as

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = {arg\\, min}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\ \\left\\{ \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n}\\beta^{n - j}\\left( y\_{j} - \\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)^{2} + \\lambda\_{n}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}w\_{i,n}|\\theta\_{i}| \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si247.png)(10.24) 

where *β* ≤ 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si248.png) is used as the forgetting factor to allow for tracking slow variations. The time-varying weighting sequences are denoted as *w*[*i*, *n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si249.png). There are different options. In \[127\] and under a stationary environment with *β* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si250.png), it is shown that if

$w\_{i,n} = \\frac{1}{|\\theta\_{i}^{\\text{est}}|^{\\gamma}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si251.png)

where *θ*[*i*]^(est)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si252.png) is the estimate of the *i*th component obtained by *any* $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png)\-consistent estimator, such as the unregularized LS, then for specific choices of *λ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si243.png) and *γ* the corresponding estimator satisfies the oracle properties simultaneously. The main reasoning behind the weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm is that as time goes by, and the $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png)\-consistent estimator provides better and better estimates, the weights corresponding to indices outside the true support (zero values) are inflated and those corresponding to the true support converge to a finite value. This helps the algorithm simultaneously to locate the support and obtain unbiased (asymptotically) estimates of the large coefficients.

Another choice for the weighting sequence is related to the *smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD)* \[55,128\]. This is defined as

$w\_{i,n} = \\chi\_{(0,\\mu\_{n})}(|\\theta\_{i}^{\\text{est}}|) + \\frac{\\left( \\alpha\\mu\_{n} - |\\theta\_{i}^{\\text{est}}| \\right)\_{+}}{(\\alpha - 1)\\mu\_{n}}\\chi\_{(\\mu\_{n},\\infty)}(|\\theta\_{i}^{\\text{est}}|),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>est</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si253.png)

where *χ*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si254.png) stands for the characteristic function, *μ*[*n*] = *λ*[*n*]/*n*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si255.png), and *α* > 2<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si256.png). Basically, this corresponds to a quadratic spline function. It turns out \[128\] that if *λ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si243.png) is chosen to grow faster than $\\sqrt{n}$<mml:math><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si227.png) and slower than *n*, the adaptive LASSO with *β* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si250.png) satisfies both oracle conditions simultaneously.

A time-adaptive scheme for solving the TNWL LASSO was presented in \[3\]. The cost function of the adaptive LASSO in Eq. [(10.24)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq69) can be written as

*J*(**θ**) = **θ**^(*T*)*R*[*n*]**θ** − **r**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ** + *λ*[*n*]∥**θ**∥[1, *w*[*n*]],<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si257.png)

where

$R\_{n}: = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n}\\beta^{n - j}\\mathbf{x}\_{j}\\mathbf{x}\_{j}^{T},\\quad\\mathbf{r}\_{n}: = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n}\\beta^{n - j}y\_{j}\\mathbf{x}\_{j},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si258.png)

and ∥**θ**∥[1, **w**[*n*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si259.png) is the weighted ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm. We know from Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml), and it is straightforward to see, that

*R*[*n*] = *β**R*[*n* − 1] + **x**[*n*]**x**[*n*]^(*T*), **r**[*n*] = *β***r**[*n* − 1] + *y*[*n*]**x**[*n*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si260.png)

The complexity for both of the previous updates, for matrices of a general structure, amounts to 𝒪(*l*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si261.png) multiplication/addition operations. One alternative is to update *R*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si262.png) and **r**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si263.png) and then solve a convex optimization task for each time instant, *n*, using any standard algorithm. However, this is not appropriate for real-time applications, due to its excessive computational cost. In \[3\], a time-recursive version of a coordinate descent algorithm has been developed. As we saw in Section [10.2.2](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0040), coordinate descent algorithms update one component at each iteration step. In \[3\], iteration steps are associated with time updates, as is always the case with the online algorithms. As each new training pair (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si221.png) is received, a single component of the unknown vector is updated. Hence, at each time instant, a scalar optimization task has to be solved, and its solution is given in closed form, which results in a simple soft thresholding operation. One of the drawbacks of the coordinate techniques is that each coefficient is updated every *l* time instants, which, for large values of *l*, can slow down convergence. Variants of the basic scheme that cope with this drawback are also addressed in \[3\], referred to as online cyclic coordinate descent time-weighted LASSO (OCCD-TWL). The complexity of the scheme is of the order of 𝒪(*l*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si261.png). Computational savings are possible if the input sequence is a time series and fast schemes for the updates of *R*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si262.png) and the RLS can then be exploited. However, if an RLS-type algorithm is used in parallel, the convergence of the overall scheme may be slowed down, because the RLS-type algorithm has to converge first in order to provide reliable estimates for the weights, as pointed out before.

### 10.4.3 Adaptive CoSaMP algorithm

In \[90\], an online version of the CoSaMP algorithm, whose steps are summarized in [Algorithm 10.2](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#enun0030), was proposed. Iteration steps *i* now coincide with time updates *n*, and the LS solver in step 3c of the general CSMP scheme is replaced by an LMS one.

Let us focus first on the quantity *X*^(*T*)**e**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si113.png) in step 3a of the CSMP scheme, which is used to compute the support at iteration *i*. In the online setting and at (iteration) time *n*, this quantity is now “rephrased” as

$X^{T}\\mathbf{e}\_{n - 1} = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n - 1}\\mathbf{x}\_{j}e\_{j}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si264.png)

In order to make the algorithm flexible to adapt to variations of the environment as the time index *n* increases, the previous correlation sum is modified to

$\\mathbf{p}\_{n}: = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{n - 1}\\beta^{n - 1 - j}\\mathbf{x}\_{j}e\_{j} = \\beta\\mathbf{p}\_{n - 1} + \\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}e\_{n - 1}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si265.png)

The LS task, constrained on the active columns that correspond to the indices in the support *S* in step 3c, is performed in an online rationale by involving the basic LMS recursions, that is,^([^(67)](#fn67))

${\\widetilde{e}}\_{n}: = y\_{n} - \\mathbf{x}\_{n|S}^{T}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}(n - 1),{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}(n): = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}(n - 1) + \\mu\\mathbf{x}\_{n|S}{\\widetilde{e}}\_{n},$<mml:math><mml:msub id="mmlbr0009"><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si266.png)

where ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}( \\cdot )$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si267.png) and **x**[*n*|*S*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si268.png) denote the respective subvectors corresponding to the indices in the support *S*. The resulting algorithm is summarized as follows.

Algorithm 10.4

**The AdCoSaMP scheme**

1.  **1.**  Select the value of *t* = 2*k*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si64.png).
2.  **2.**  Initialize the algorithm: **θ**(1) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si269.png), $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(1) = 0$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si270.png), **p**[1] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si271.png), *e*[1] = *y*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si272.png).
3.  **3.**  Choose *μ* and *β*.
4.  **4.**  For *n* = 2, 3, …<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si273.png), execute the following steps:
    
    1.  **(a)**  **p**[*n*] = *β***p**[*n* − 1] + **x**[*n* − 1]*e*[*n* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si274.png).
    2.  **(b)**  Obtain the current support:
    
    $S = {supp}\\{\\mathbf{\\theta}(n - 1)\\} \\cup \\left\\{ \\frac{\\text{indices\\ of\\ the}\\ t\\ \\text{largest\\ in}}{\\text{magnitude\\ components\\ of}\\ \\mathbf{p}\_{n}} \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">supp</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mfrac linethickness="0"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>indices of the</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>largest in</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>magnitude components of</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si275.png)
    
    1.  
    2.  **(c)**  Perform the LMS update:
    
    ${\\widetilde{e}}\_{n} = y\_{n} - \\mathbf{x}\_{n|S}^{T}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}(n - 1),{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}(n) = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{|S}(n - 1) + mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover
