The vertical axis shows the log[10] of the mean-squared error, that is, $\\text{log}\_{10}\\frac{1}{2}||\\mathbf{s} - \\Psi\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n}||^{2}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>log</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si332.png), and the horizontal axis shows the time index. At time *n* = 1500, the system undergoes a sudden change.

## 10.5 Learning sparse analysis models

Our discussion so far has been spent in the terrain of signals that are either sparse themselves or that can be sparsely represented in terms of the atoms of a dictionary in a synthesis model, as introduced in Eq. [(9.16)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), that is,

$\\mathbf{s} = \\sum\\limits\_{i \\in \\mathcal{I}}\\theta\_{i}\\mathbf{\\psi}\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si348.png)

As a matter of fact, most of the research activity has been focused on the synthesis model. This may be partly due to the fact that the synthesis modeling path may provide a more intuitively appealing structure to describe the generation of the signal in terms of the elements (atoms) of a dictionary. Recall from Section [9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) that the sparsity assumption was imposed on ***θ*** in the synthesis model and the corresponding optimization task was formulated in [(9.38)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and [(9.39)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) for the exact and noisy cases, respectively.

However, this is not the only way to approach the task of sparse modeling. Very early in this chapter, in Section [9.4](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), we referred to the analysis model

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}} = \\Phi^{H}\\mathbf{s}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si349.png)

and pointed out that in a number of real-life applications, the resulting transform $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si350.png) is sparse. To be fair, the most orthodox way to deal with the underlying model sparsity would be to consider ∥*Φ*^(*H*)**s**∥[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si351.png). Thus, if one wants to estimate ***s***, a very natural way would be to cast the related optimization task as

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{s}}\\quad\\left\\| \\Phi^{H}\\mathbf{s} \\right\\|\_{0},\\text{s.t.}\\quad\\mathbf{y} = X\\mathbf{s},\\ \\text{or}\\ \\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{s} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\leq \\epsilon,$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0011"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0011" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>or</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si352.png)(10.28) 

depending on whether the observations via a sensing matrix *X* are exact or noisy. Strictly speaking, the total variation minimization approach, which was used in [Example 10.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#enun0045), falls under this analysis model formulation umbrella, because what is minimized is the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) norm of the gradient transform of the image.

The optimization tasks in either of the two formulations given in [(10.28)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq89) build around the assumption that the signal of interest has *sparse analysis representation*. The obvious question that is now raised is whether the optimization tasks in [(10.28)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq89) and their counterparts in [(9.38)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) or [(9.39)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) are any different. One of the first efforts to shed light on this problem was in \[51\]. There, it was pointed out that the two tasks, though related, are in general different. Moreover, their comparative performance depends on the specific problem at hand. Let us consider, for example, the case where the involved dictionary corresponds to an orthonormal transformation matrix (e.g., DFT). In this case, we already know that the analysis and synthesis matrices are related as

*Φ* = *Ψ* = *Ψ*^( − *H*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si353.png)

which leads to an equivalence between the two previously stated formulations. Indeed, for such a transform we have

$\\underset{\\text{Analysis}}{\\underset{︸}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}} = \\Phi^{H}\\mathbf{s}}}\\quad\\Leftrightarrow\\quad\\underset{\\text{Synthesis}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbf{s} = \\Phi\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}}}.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Analysis</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">⇔</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Synthesis</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si354.png)

Using the last formula in [(10.28)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq89), the tasks in [(9.38)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) or [(9.39)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) are readily obtained by replacing ***θ*** by ***s***. However, this reasoning cannot be extended to the case of overcomplete dictionaries; in these cases, the two optimization tasks may lead to different solutions.

The previous discussion concerning the comparative performance between the synthesis or analysis-based sparse representations is not only of “philosophical” value. It turns out that often in practice, the nature of certain overcomplete dictionaries does not permit the use of the synthesis-based formulation. These are the cases where the columns of the overcomplete dictionary exhibit a high degree of dependence; that is, the coherence of the matrix, as defined in Section [9.6.1](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), has large values. Typical examples of such overcomplete dictionaries are the Gabor frames, the curvelet frames, and the oversampled DFT. The use of such dictionaries leads to enhanced performance in a number of applications (e.g., \[111,112\]). Take as an example the case of our familiar DFT transform. This transform provides a representation of our signal samples in terms of sampled exponential sinusoids, whose integral frequencies are multiples of $\\frac{2\\pi}{l}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si355.png), that is,

$\\mathbf{s}: = \\begin{bmatrix} s\_{1} \\\\ s\_{2} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ s\_{l - 1} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{l - 1}{\\widetilde{s}}\_{i}\\mathbf{\\psi}\_{i},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si356.png)(10.29) 

where, now, *s̃*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si357.png) are the DFT coefficients and **ψ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si358.png) is the sampled sinusoid with frequency equal to $\\frac{2\\pi}{l}i$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si359.png), that is,

$\\mathbf{\\psi}\_{i} = \\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\\\ {\\exp\\left( - j\\frac{2\\pi}{l}i \\right)} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ {\\exp\\left( - j\\frac{2\\pi}{l}i(l - 1) \\right)} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si360.png)(10.30) 

However, this is not necessarily the most efficient representation. For example, it is highly unlikely that a signal comprises only integral frequencies and only such signals can result in a sparse representation using the DFT basis. Most probably, in general, there will be frequencies lying in between the frequency samples of the DFT basis that result in nonsparse representations. Using these extra frequencies, a much better representation of the frequency content of the signal can be obtained. However, in such a dictionary, the atoms are no longer linearly independent, and the coherence of the respective (dictionary) matrix increases.

Once a dictionary exhibits high coherence, then there is no way of finding a sensing matrix *X* so that *X*Ψ obeys the RIP. Recall that at the heart of sparsity-aware learning lies the concept of stable embedding, which allows the recovery of a vector/signal after projecting it onto a lower-dimensional space, which is what all the available conditions (e.g., RIP) guarantee. However, no stable embedding is possible with highly coherent dictionaries. Take as an extreme example the case where the first and second atoms are identical. Then no sensing matrix *X* can achieve a signal recovery that distinguishes the vector \[1, 0, …, 0\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si361.png) from \[0, 1, 0, …, 0\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si362.png). Can one then conclude that for highly coherent overcomplete dictionaries, compressed sensing techniques are not possible? Fortunately, the answer to this is negative. After all, our goal in compressed sensing has always been the recovery of the signal **s** = *Ψ***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si333.png) and not the identification of the sparse vector ***θ*** in the synthesis model representation. The latter was just a means to an end. While the unique recovery of ***θ*** cannot be guaranteed for highly coherent dictionaries, this does not necessarily cause any problems for the recovery of ***s***, using a small set of measurement samples. The escape route will come by considering the analysis model formulation.

### 10.5.1 Compressed sensing for sparse signal representation in coherent dictionaries

Our goal in this subsection is to establish conditions that guarantee recovery of a signal vector, which accepts a sparse representation in a redundant and coherent dictionary, using a small number of signal-related measurements. Let the dictionary at hand be a tight frame Ψ (see appendix of the chapter, which can be downloaded from the book's website). Then our signal vector is written as

**s** = *Ψ***θ**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si363.png)(10.31) 

where ***θ*** is assumed to be *k*\-sparse. Recalling the properties of a tight frame, as they are summarized in the appendix, the parameters in the expansion in Eq. [(10.31)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq94) can be written as ⟨**ψ**[*i*],**s**⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si364.png), and the respective vector as

**θ** = *Ψ*^(*T*)**s**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si365.png)

because a tight frame is self-dual. Then the analysis counterpart of the synthesis formulation in [(9.39)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) can be cast as

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{s}}\\quad\\left\\| \\Psi^{T}\\mathbf{s} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\quad\\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{s} \\right\\|\_{2}^{2} \\leq \\epsilon.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0012"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0012" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si366.png)(10.32) 

The goal now is to investigate the accuracy of the recovered solution to this convex optimization task. It turns out that similar strong theorems are also valid for this problem, as with the case of the synthesis formulation, which was studied in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml).

Definition 10.1

Let *Σ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si367.png) be the union of all subspaces spanned by all subsets of *k* columns of Ψ. A sensing matrix *X* obeys the restricted isometry property adapted to Ψ (Ψ-RIP) with *δ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si46.png), if

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/fx006.jpg)(10.33) 

for all **s** ∈ *Σ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si368.png).

The union of subspaces, *Σ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si367.png), is the image under Ψ of all *k*\-sparse vectors. This is the difference with the RIP definition given in Section [9.7.2](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). All the random matrices discussed earlier in this chapter can be shown to satisfy this form of RIP, with overwhelming probability, provided the number of observations, *N*, is at least of the order of *k*ln (*l*/*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si369.png). We are now ready to establish the main theorem concerning our ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) minimization task.

Theorem 10.2

*Let* Ψ *be an arbitrary tight frame and X a sensing matrix that satisfies the* Ψ*\-RIP with* *δ*[2*k*] ≤ 0.08<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.08</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si370.png)*, for some positive k. Then the solution,* **s**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si371.png)*, of the minimization task in* [(10.32)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq96) *satisfies the property*

$\\left\\| \\mathbf{s} - \\mathbf{s}\_{\\ast} \\right\\|\_{2} \\leq C\_{0}k^{- \\frac{1}{2}}\\left\\| \\Psi^{T}\\mathbf{s} - {(\\Psi^{T}\\mathbf{s})}\_{k} \\right\\|\_{1} + C\_{1}\\sqrt{\\epsilon},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si372.png)(10.34) 

*where* *C*[0], *C*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si373.png) *are constants depending on* *δ*[2*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si374.png) *and* (*Ψ*^(*T*)**s**)[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si375.png) *denotes the best k-sparse approximation of* *Ψ*^(*T*)**s**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si376.png)*, which results by setting all but the k largest in magnitude components of* *Ψ*^(*T*)**s**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si376.png) *equal to zero.*

The bound in [(10.34)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq98) is the counterpart of that given in [(9.36)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). In other words, the previous theorem states that if *Ψ*^(*T*)**s**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si376.png) decays rapidly, then ***s*** can be reconstructed from just a few (compared to the signal length *l*) observations. The theorem was first given in \[25\] and it is the first time that such a theorem provides results for the sparse analysis model formulation in a general context.

### 10.5.2 Cosparsity

In the sparse synthesis formulation, one searches for a solution in a union of subspaces that are formed by all possible combinations of *k* columns of the dictionary, Ψ. The signal vector lies in one of these subspaces—the one that is spanned by the columns of Ψ whose indices lie in the support set (Section [10.2.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0020)). In the sparse analysis approach, things get different. The kick-off point is the sparsity of our original transform $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}: = \\Phi^{T}\\mathbf{s}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si378.png), where Φ defines the transformation matrix or analysis operator. Because $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si350.png) is assumed to be sparse, there exists an index set ℐ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si379.png) such that ∀*i* ∈ ℐ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si380.png), *s̃*[*i*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si381.png). In other words, ∀*i* ∈ ℐ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si380.png), **ϕ**[*i*]^(*T*)**s** :  = ⟨**ϕ**[*i*],**s**⟩ = 0<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">〉</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si383.png), where **ϕ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si384.png) stands for the *i*th column of Φ. Hence, the subspace in which ***s*** resides is the orthogonal complement of the subspace formed by those columns of Φ that correspond to a zero in the transform vector $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si350.png). Assume, now, that *c**a**r**d*(ℐ) = *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">card</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si385.png). The signal, ***s***, can be identified by searching on the *orthogonal complements* of the subspaces formed by all possible combinations of *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si386.png) columns of Φ, that is,

⟨**ϕ**[*i*],**s**⟩ = 0, ∀*i* ∈ ℐ.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">〉</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si387.png)

The difference between the synthesis and analysis problems is illustrated in [Fig. 10.12](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0065). To facilitate the theoretical treatment of this new setting, the notion of *cosparsity* was introduced in \[92\].

![Figure 10.12 Searching for a sparse vector s. (A) In the synthesis model, the sparse vector lies in subspaces formed by combinations of k (in this case k = 2) columns of the dictionary Ψ. (B) In the analysis model, the sparse vector lies in the orthogonal complement of the subspace formed by Co (in this case Co = 2) columns of the transformation matrix Φ.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 10.12](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#cf0900) Searching for a sparse vector ***s***. (A) In the synthesis model, the sparse vector lies in subspaces formed by combinations of *k* (in this case *k* = 2) columns of the dictionary Ψ. (B) In the analysis model, the sparse vector lies in the orthogonal complement of the subspace formed by *C*[*o*] (in this case *C*[*o*] = 2) columns of the transformation matrix Φ.

Definition 10.2

The cosparsity of a signal **s** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si388.png) with respect to a *p* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si389.png) matrix *Φ*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si390.png) is defined as

*C*[*o*] :  = *p* − ∥*Φ*^(*T*)**s**∥[0].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si391.png)(10.35) 

In words, the cosparsity is the number of zeros in the obtained transform vector $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{s}} = \\Phi^{T}\\mathbf{s}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si392.png); in contrast, the sparsity measures the number of the nonzero elements of the respective sparse vector. If one assumes that Φ has “full spark,”^([^(68)](#fn68))

Let now the cosparsity of our signal with respect to a matrix *Φ*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si390.png) be *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si386.png). Then, in order to dig out the signal from the subspace in which it is hidden, one must form all possible combinations of *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si386.png) columns of Φ and search in their orthogonal complements. In the case that Φ is full rank, we have seen previously that *C*[*o*] < *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si398.png), and, hence, any set of *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si386.png) columns of Φ are linearly independent. In other words, the dimension of the span of those columns is *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si386.png). As a result, the dimensionality of the orthogonal complement, into which we search for ***s***, is *l* − *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si399.png).

We have by now accumulated enough information to elaborate a bit more on the statement made before concerning the different nature of the synthesis and analysis tasks. Let us consider a synthesis task using an *l* × *p*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si394.png) dictionary, and let *k* be the sparsity level in the corresponding expansion of a signal in terms of this dictionary. The dimensionality of the subspaces in which the solution is sought is *k* (*k* is assumed to be less than the spark of the respective matrix). Let us keep the same dimensionality for the subspaces in which we are going to search for a solution in an analysis task. Hence, in this case *C*[*o*] = *l* − *k*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si400.png) (assuming a full spark matrix). Also, for the sake of comparison, assume that the analysis matrix is *p* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si389.png). Solving the synthesis task, one has to search $\\begin{pmatrix} p \\\\ k \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}$<mml:math><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si401.png) subspaces, while solving the analysis task one has to search $\\begin{pmatrix} p \\\\ {C\_{o} = l - k} \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}$<mml:math><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si402.png) subspaces. These are two different numbers; assuming that *k* ≪ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si403.png) and also that *l* < *p*/2<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si404.png), which are natural assumptions for overcomplete dictionaries, then the latter of the two numbers is much larger than the former (use your computer to play with some typical values). In other words, there are many more analysis than synthesis low-dimensional subspaces for which to search. The large number of low-dimensional subspaces makes the algorithmic recovery of a solution from the analysis model a tougher task \[92\]. However, it might reveal a much stronger descriptive power of the analysis model compared to the synthesis one.

Another interesting aspect that highlights the difference between the two approaches is the following. Assume that the synthesis and analysis matrices are related as *Φ* = *Ψ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si405.png), as was the case for tight frames. Under this assumption, *Φ*^(*T*)**s**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si406.png) provides a set of parameters for the synthesis expansion in terms of the atoms of *Φ* = *Ψ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ψ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si405.png). Moreover, if ∥*Φ*^(*T*)**s**∥[0] = *k*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si407.png), then *Φ*^(*T*)**s**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si406.png) is a possible *k*\-sparse solution for the synthesis model. However, there is no guarantee that this is the sparsest one.

It is now time to investigate whether conditions that guarantee uniqueness of the solution for the sparse analysis formulation can be derived. The answer is in the affirmative, and it has been established in \[92\] for the case of exact observations.

Lemma 10.1

*Let* Φ *be a transformation matrix of full spark. Then, for almost all* *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si150.png) *sensing matrices and for* *N* > 2(*l* − *C*[*o*])<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si409.png)*, the equation*

**y** = *X***s**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si410.png)

*has at most one solution with cosparsity at least* *C*[*o*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si386.png)*.*

The above lemma guarantees the uniqueness of the solution, if one exists, of the optimization

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{s}}\\quad\\left\\| \\Phi^{T}\\mathbf{s} \\right\\|\_{0},\\text{s.t.}\\quad\\mathbf{y} = X\\mathbf{s}.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0013"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0013" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si412.png)(10.36) 

However, solving the previous ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si2.png) minimization task is a difficult one, and we know that its synthesis counterpart has been shown to be NP-hard, in general. Its relaxed convex relative is the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) minimization

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{s}}\\quad\\left\\| \\Phi^{T}\\mathbf{s} \\right\\|\_{1},\\text{s.t.}\\quad\\mathbf{y} = X\\mathbf{s}.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0014"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0014" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si413.png)(10.37) 

In \[92\], conditions are derived that guarantee the equivalence of the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si2.png) and ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) tasks, in [(10.36)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq102) and [(10.37)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq103), respectively; this is done in a way similar to that for the sparse synthesis modeling. Also, in \[92\], a greedy algorithm inspired by the orthogonal matching pursuit, discussed in Section [10.2.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0020), has been derived. A thorough study on greedy-like algorithms applicable to the cosparse model can be found in \[62\]. In \[103\] an iterative analysis thresholding is proposed and theoretically investigated. Other algorithms that solve the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) optimization in the analysis modeling framework can be found in, for example, \[21,49,108\]. NESTA can also be used for the analysis formulation. Moreover, a critical aspect affecting the performance of algorithms obeying the cosparse analysis model is the choice of the analysis matrix Φ. It turns out that it is not always the best practice to use fixed and predefined matrices. As a promising alternative, problem-tailored analysis matrices can be learned using the available data (e.g., \[106,119\]).

## 10.6 A case study: time-frequency analysis

The goal of this section is to demonstrate how all the previously stated theoretical findings can be exploited in the context of a real application. Sparse modeling has been applied to almost everything. So picking up a typical application would not be easy. We preferred to focus on a less “publicized” application, i.e., that of analyzing echolocation signals emitted by bats. However, the analysis will take place within the framework of time-frequency representation, which is one of the research areas that significantly inspired the evolution of compressed sensing theory. Time-frequency analysis of signals has been a field of intense research for a number of decades, and it is one of the most powerful signal processing tools. Typical applications include speech processing, sonar sounding, communications, biological signals, and EEG processing, to name but a few (see, e.g., \[13,20,57\]). The time-frequency analysis is extensively used to transform time sequences to two-dimensional image arrays (time-frequency) that subsequently feed, e.g., convolutional deep neural networks or transformers (Chapters [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml) and [19](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml)), to perform various classification tasks.

### Gabor transform and frames

It is not our intention to present the theory behind the Gabor transform. Our goal is to outline some basic related notions and use them as a vehicle for the less familiar reader to better understand how redundant dictionaries are used and to get better acquainted with their potential performance benefits.

The Gabor transform was introduced in the mid-1940s by Dennis Gabor (1900–1979), a Hungarian-British engineer. His most notable scientific achievement was the invention of holography, for which he won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1971.

The discrete version of the Gabor transform can be seen as a special case of the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) (e.g., \[57,87\]). In the standard DFT transform, the full length of a time sequence, comprising *l* samples, is used all in “one go” in order to compute the corresponding frequency content. However, the latter can be time-varying, so the DFT will provide an average information, which cannot be of much use. The Gabor transform (and the STFT in general) introduces time localization via the use of a window function, which slides along the signal segment in time, and at each time instant focuses on a different part of the signal. This is a way that allows one to follow the slow time variations which take place in the frequency domain. The time localization in the context of the Gabor transform is achieved via a Gaussian window function, that is,

$g(n): = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi\\sigma^{2}}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{n^{2}}{2\\sigma^{2}} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si414.png)(10.38) 

[Fig. 10.13](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0070)A shows the Gaussian window, *g*(*n* − *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si415.png), centered at time instant *m*. The choice of the window spreading factor, *σ*, will be discussed later on.

![Figure 10.13 (A) The Gaussian window with spreading factor σ centered at time instant m. (B) Pulses obtained by windowing three different sinusoids with Gaussian windows of different spread and applied at different time instants.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr013.jpg)

Figure 10.13 (A) The Gaussian window with spreading factor *σ* centered at time instant *m*. (B) Pulses obtained by windowing three different sinusoids with Gaussian windows of different spread and applied at different time instants.

Let us now construct the atoms of the Gabor dictionary. Recall that in the case of the signal representation in terms of the DFT in Eq. [(10.29)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq92), each frequency is represented only once, by the corresponding sampled sinusoid, Eq. [(10.30)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq93). In the Gabor transform, each frequency appears *l* times; the corresponding sampled sinusoid is multiplied by the Gaussian window sequence, each time shifted by one sample. Thus, at the *i*th frequency bin, we have *l* atoms, **g**^((*m*, *i*)), *m* = 0, 1, …, *l* − 1<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si416.png), with elements given by

*g*^((*m*, *i*))(*n*) = *g*(*n* − *m*)*ψ*[*i*](*n*), *n*, *m*, *i* = 0, 1, …, *l* − 1,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si417.png)(10.39) 

where *ψ*[*i*](*n*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si418.png) is the *n*th element of the vector **ψ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si358.png) in Eq. [(10.30)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq93). This results in an overcomplete dictionary comprising *l*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si420.png) atoms in the *l*\-dimensional space. [Fig. 10.13](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0070)B illustrates the effect of multiplying different sinusoids with Gaussian pulses of different spread and at different time delays. [Fig. 10.14](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0075) is a graphical interpretation of the atoms involved in the Gabor dictionary. Each node (*m*, *i*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si421.png) in this time-frequency plot corresponds to an atom of frequency equal to $\\frac{2\\pi}{l}i$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si359.png) and delay equal to *m*.

![Figure 10.14 Each atom of the Gabor dictionary corresponds to a node in the time-frequency grid. That is, it is a sampled windowed sinusoid whose frequency and location in time are given by the coordinates of the respective node. In practice, this grid may be subsampled by factors α and β for the two axes, respectively, in order to reduce the number of the involved atoms.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr014.jpg)

Figure 10.14 Each atom of the Gabor dictionary corresponds to a node in the time-frequency grid. That is, it is a sampled windowed sinusoid whose frequency and location in time are given by the coordinates of the respective node. In practice, this grid may be subsampled by factors *α* and *β* for the two axes, respectively, in order to reduce the number of the involved atoms.

Note that the windowing of a signal of finite duration inevitably introduces boundary effects, especially when the delay *m* gets close to the time segment edges, 0 and *l* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si422.png). A solution that facilitates the theoretical analysis is to use a modulo *l* arithmetic to wrap around at the edge points (this is equivalent to extending the signal periodically); see, for example, \[113\].

Once the atoms have been defined, they can be stacked one next to the other to form the columns of the *l* × *l*²<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si423.png) Gabor dictionary, *G*. It can be shown that the Gabor dictionary is a tight frame \[125\].

### Time-frequency resolution

By definition of the Gabor dictionary, it is readily understood that the choice of the window spread, as measured by *σ*, must be a critical factor, since it controls the localization in time. As known from our Fourier transform basics, when the pulse becomes short, in order to increase the time resolution, its corresponding frequency content spreads out, and vice versa. From Heisenberg's principle, we know that we can never achieve high time and frequency resolution simultaneously; one is gained at the expense of the other. It is here where the Gaussian shape in the Gabor transform is justified. It can be shown that the Gaussian window gives the optimal tradeoff between time and frequency resolution \[57,87\]. The time-frequency resolution tradeoff is demonstrated in [Fig. 10.15](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0080), where three sinusoids are shown windowed with different pulse durations. The diagram shows the corresponding spread in the time-frequency plot. The value of *σ*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si424.png) indicates the time spread and *σ*[*f*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si425.png) the spread of the respective frequency content around the basic frequency of each sinusoid.

![Figure 10.15 The shorter the width of the pulsed (windowed) sinusoid is in time, the wider the spread of its frequency content around the frequency of the sinusoid. The Gaussian-like curves along the frequency axis indicate the energy spread in frequency of the respective pulses. The values of σt and σf indicate the spread in time and frequency, respectively.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr015.jpg)

[Figure 10.15](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#cf1000) The shorter the width of the pulsed (windowed) sinusoid is in time, the wider the spread of its frequency content around the frequency of the sinusoid. The Gaussian-like curves along the frequency axis indicate the energy spread in frequency of the respective pulses. The values of *σ*[*t*] and *σ*[*f*] indicate the spread in time and frequency, respectively.

### Gabor frames

In practice, *l*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si420.png) can take large values, and it is desirable to see whether one can reduce the number of the involved atoms without sacrificing the frame-related properties. This can be achieved by an appropriate subsampling, as illustrated in [Fig. 10.14](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0075). We only keep the atoms that correspond to the red nodes. That is, we subsample by keeping every *α* nodes in time and every *β* nodes in frequency in order to form the dictionary, that is,

$G\_{(\\alpha,\\beta)} = \\{\\mathbf{g}^{(m\\alpha,i\\beta)}\\},\\quad m = 0,1,\\ldots,\\frac{l}{\\alpha} - 1,\\ i = 0,1,\\ldots,\\frac{l}{\\beta} - 1,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si426.png)

where *α* and *β* are divisors of *l*. Then it can be shown (e.g., \[57\]) that if *α**β* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si427.png) the resulting dictionary retains its frame properties. Once *G*[(*α*, *β*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si428.png) is obtained, the canonical dual frame is readily available via Eq. (10.46) (adjusted for complex data) of the appendix associated with the chapter (which can be downloaded from the book's website), from which the corresponding set of expansion coefficients, ***θ***, results.

### Time-frequency analysis of echolocation signals emitted by bats

Bats use echolocation for navigation (flying around at night), for prey detection (small insects), and for prey approaching and catching; each bat adaptively changes the shape and frequency content of its calls in order to better serve the previous tasks. Echolocation is used in a similar way for sonars. Bats emit calls as they fly, and “listen” to the returning echoes in order to build up a sonic map of their surroundings. In this way, bats can infer the distance and the size of obstacles as well as of other flying creatures/insects. Moreover, all bats emit special types of calls, called social calls, which are used for socializing, flirting, and so on. The fundamental characteristics of the echolocation calls, for example, the frequency range and average time duration, differ from species to species because, thanks to evolution, bats have adapted their calls in order to become better suited to the environment in which a species operates.

Time-frequency analysis of echolocation calls provides information about the species (species identification) as well as the specific task and behavior of the bats in certain environments. Moreover, the bat biosonar system is studied in order for humans to learn more about nature and get inspired for subsequent advances in applications such as sonar navigation systems, radars, and medical ultrasonic devices.

[Fig. 10.16](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0085) shows a case of a recorded echolocation signal from bats. Zooming at two different parts of the signal, we can observe that the frequency is changing with time. In [Fig. 10.17](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0090), the DFT of the signal is shown, but there is not much information that can be drawn from it except that the signal is compressible in the frequency domain; most of the activity takes place within a short range of frequencies. The echolocation signal was a recording of total length *T* = 21.845 ms<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>21.845</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mtext>ms</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si429.png) \[75\]. Samples were taken at the sampling frequency *f*[*s*] = 750<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>750</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si430.png) kHz, which results in a total of *l*\= 16,384 samples. Although the signal itself is not sparse in the time domain, we will take advantage of the fact that it is sparse in a transformed domain. We will assume that the signal is sparse in its expansion in terms of the Gabor dictionary.

![Figure 10.16 The recorded echolocation signal. The frequency of the signal is time-varying, which is indicated by focusing on two different parts of the signal.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr016.jpg)

[Figure 10.16](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#cf1015) The recorded echolocation signal. The frequency of the signal is time-varying, which is indicated by focusing on two different parts of the signal.

![Figure 10.17 Plot of the energy of the DFT transform coefficients, Si. Observe that most of the frequency activity takes place within a short frequency range.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr017.jpg)

[Figure 10.17](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#cf1020) Plot of the energy of the DFT transform coefficients, *S*[*i*]. Observe that most of the frequency activity takes place within a short frequency range.

Our goal in this example is to demonstrate that one does not really need all 16,384 samples to perform time-frequency analysis; all the processing can be carried out using a reduced number of observations, by exploiting the theory of compressed sensing. To form the observations vector, ***y***, the number of observations was chosen to be *N* = 2048<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2048</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si431.png). This amounts to a reduction of eight times with respect to the number of available samples. The observations vector was formed as

**y** = *X***s**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si432.png)

where *X* is an *N* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si150.png) sensing matrix comprising ±1 generated in a random way. This means that once we obtain ***y***, we do not need to store the original samples anymore, leading to a saving in memory requirements. Ideally, one could have obtained the reduced number of observations by sampling directly the analog signal at sub-Nyquist rates, as has already been discussed at the end of Section [9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). Another goal is to use both the analysis and synthesis models and demonstrate their difference.

Three different spectrograms were computed. Two of them, shown in [Fig. 10.18](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0095)B and C, correspond to the reconstructed signals obtained by the analysis [(10.37)](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#deq103) and the synthesis [(9.37)](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) formulations, respectively. In both cases, the NESTA algorithm was used and the *G*[(128, 64)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>64</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si433.png) frame was employed. Note that the latter dictionary is redundant by a factor of 2. The spectrograms are the result of plotting the time-frequency grid and coloring each node (*t*, *i*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si434.png) according to the energy |*θ*|²<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si435.png) of the parameter associated with the respective atom in the Gabor dictionary. The full Gabor transform was applied to the reconstructed signals to obtain the spectrograms, in order to get better coverage of the time-frequency grid. The scale is logarithmic and the darker areas correspond to larger values. The spectrogram of the original signal obtained via the full Gabor transform is shown in [Fig. 10.18](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0095)D. It is evident that the analysis model resulted in a more clear spectrogram, which resembles the original one better. When the frame *G*[(64, 32)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>64</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si436.png) is employed, which is a highly redundant Gabor dictionary comprising 8*l* atoms, then the analysis model results in a recovered signal whose spectrogram is visually indistinguishable from the original one in [Fig. 10.18](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0095)D.

![Figure 10.18 (A) Plot of the magnitude of the coefficients, sorted in decreasing order, in the expansion in terms of the G(128,64) Gabor frame. The results correspond to the analysis and synthesis model formulations. The third curve corresponds to the case of analyzing the original vector signal directly, by projecting it on the dual frame. (B) The spectrogram from the analysis and (C) the spectrogram from the synthesis formulations. (D) The spectrogram corresponding to the G(64,32) frame using the analysis formulation. For all cases, the number of observations used was one-eighth of the total number of signal samples. A, B, and C indicate different parts of the signal, as explained in the text.](images/B9780443292385000160/gr018.jpg)

Figure 10.18 (A) Plot of the magnitude of the coefficients, sorted in decreasing order, in the expansion in terms of the *G*[(128,64)] Gabor frame. The results correspond to the analysis and synthesis model formulations. The third curve corresponds to the case of analyzing the original vector signal directly, by projecting it on the dual frame. (B) The spectrogram from the analysis and (C) the spectrogram from the synthesis formulations. (D) The spectrogram corresponding to the *G*[(64,32)] frame using the analysis formulation. [Fig. 10.18](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0095)A is the plot of the magnitude of the corresponding Gabor transform coefficients, sorted in decreasing values. The synthesis model provides a sparser representation in the sense that the coefficients decrease much faster. The third curve is the one that results if we multiply the dual frame matrix *G̃*[(128, 64)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>64</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si437.png) directly with the vector of the original signal samples, and it is shown for comparison reasons.

To conclude, the curious reader may wonder what these curves in [Fig. 10.18](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0095)D mean after all. The call denoted by (A) belongs to a *Pipistrellus pipistrellus* (!) and the call denoted by (B) is either a social call or belongs to a different species. The signal (C) is the return echo from the signal (A). The large spread in time of (C) indicates a highly reflective environment \[75\].
