(a) Plot this signal in the time and in the frequency domain (use the “fft.m” MATLAB® function to compute the Fourier transform). (b) Build a sensing matrix 30 × 2⁸<mml:math><mml:mn>30</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si453.png) with entries drawn from a normal distribution, $\\mathcal{N}(0,\\frac{1}{N})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si454.png), and recover ***θ*** based on these observations by ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) minimization using, for example, “solvelasso.m” (see MATLAB® exercise [9.21](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)). (c) Build a sensing matrix 30 × 2⁸<mml:math><mml:mn>30</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si453.png), where each of its rows contains only a single nonzero component taking the value 1. Moreover, each column has at most one nonzero component. Observe that the multiplication of this sensing matrix with ***θ*** just picks certain components of ***θ*** (those that correspond to the position of the nonzero value of each row of the sampling matrix). Show by solving the corresponding ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si1.png) minimization task, as in question (b), that ***θ*** can be recovered exactly using such a sparse sensing matrix (containing only 30 nonzero components!). Observe that the unknown ***θ*** is sparse in the frequency domain and give an explanation why the recovery is successful with the specific sparse sensing matrix.
2.  **10.12**  Implement the OMP algorithm (see Section [10.2.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0020)) as well as the CSMP (see Section [10.2.1](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#s0020)) with *t* = 2*k*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si64.png). Assume a compressed sensing system using a normally distributed sensing matrix. (a) Compare the two algorithms in the case where $\\alpha = \\frac{N}{l} = 0.2$<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si455.png) for $\\beta = \\frac{k}{N}$<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si456.png) taking values in the set {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, ⋯, 1}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si457.png) (choose yourself a signal and a sensing matrix in order to comply with the recommendations above). (b) Repeat the same test when *α* = 0.8<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.8</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si458.png). Observe that this experiment, if it is performed for many different *α* values, 0 ≤ *α* ≤ 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000160/si459.png), can be used for the estimation of phase transition diagrams such as the one depicted in [Fig. 10.4](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0025). (c) Repeat (a) and (b) with the obtained observations now contaminated with noise corresponding to 20 dB SNR.
3.  **10.13**  Reproduce the MRI reconstruction experiment of [Fig. 10.9](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0050) by running the MATLAB® script “MRIcs.m,” which is available from the website of the book.
4.  **10.14**  Reproduce the bat echolocation time-frequency analysis experiment of [Fig. 10.18](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml#f0095) by running the MATLAB® script “BATcs.m,” which is available from the website of the book.

## 11.1 Introduction

Our emphasis in this chapter will be on learning nonlinear models. The necessity of adopting nonlinear models has already been discussed in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), in the context of the classification as well as the regression tasks. For example, recall that given two jointly distributed random vectors (**y**, **x**) ∈ ℝ^(*k*) × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si1.png), we know that the optimal estimate of **y** given **x** = **x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si2.png) in the mean-square error (MSE) sense is the corresponding conditional mean, that is, 𝔼\[**y**|**x**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si3.png), which in general is a nonlinear function of ***x***.

There are different ways of dealing with nonlinear modeling tasks. Our emphasis in this chapter will be on a path through the so-called reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). The technique consists of mapping the input variables to a new space, such that the originally nonlinear task is transformed into a linear one. From a practical point of view, the beauty behind these spaces is that their rich structure allows us to perform inner product operations in a very efficient way, with complexity independent of the dimensionality of the respective RKHS. Moreover, note that the dimension of such spaces can even be infinite.

We start the chapter by reviewing some more “traditional” techniques concerning Volterra series expansions, and then we move slowly to exploring the RKHS concept. Cover's theorem, the basic properties of RKHSs, and their defining kernels are discussed. Kernel ridge regression and the support vector machine (SVM) framework is presented. Approximation techniques concerning the kernel function and the kernel matrix, such as random Fourier features (RFFs) and the Nyström method, and their implication to online and distributed learning in RKHS are discussed. Finally, some more advanced concepts related to sparsity and multikernel representations are presented. A case study in the context of text mining is presented at the end of the chapter.

## 11.2 Generalized linear models

Given (*y*, **x**) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si4.png), a generalized linear estimator *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si5.png) of y has the form

$\\widehat{y} = f(\\mathbf{x}): = \\theta\_{0} + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\theta\_{k}\\phi\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}),$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si6.png)(11.1) 

where *ϕ*[1], …, *ϕ*[*K*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si7.png) are *preselected* (nonlinear) functions. A popular family of functions is the polynomial one, for example,

$\\widehat{y} = \\theta\_{0} + \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\theta\_{i}x\_{i} + \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l - 1}\\sum\\limits\_{m = i + 1}^{l}\\theta\_{im}x\_{i}x\_{m} + \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\theta\_{ii}x\_{i}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si15.png), *ϕ*[5](**x**) = *x*[2]²<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si16.png). The generalization of Eq. [(11.2)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq2) to *r*th-order polynomials is readily obtained and it will contain products of the form xx2p21p1⋯xlpl<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mmultiscripts><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mprescripts/><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mmultiscripts><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si17.png), with *p*[1] + *p*[2] + ⋯ + *p*[*l*] ≤ *r*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si18.png). It turns out that the number of free parameters, *K*, for an *r*th-order polynomial is equal to

$K = \\frac{(l + r)!}{r!l!}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>!</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si19.png)

Just to get a feeling for *l* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si20.png) and *r* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si21.png), *K* = 286<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>286</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si22.png). The use of polynomial expansions is justified by the Weierstrass theorem, stating that every continuous function defined on a compact (closed and bounded) subset *S* ⊂ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si23.png) can be uniformly approximated as closely as desired, with an arbitrarily small error, *ϵ*, by a polynomial function (for example, \[95\]). Of course, in order to achieve a good enough approximation, one may have to use a large value of *r*. Besides polynomial functions, other types of functions can also be used, such as splines and trigonometric functions.

A common characteristic of this type of models is that the basis functions in the expansion are *preselected* and they are fixed and independent of the data. The advantage of such a path is that the associated models are linear with respect to the unknown set of free parameters, and they can be estimated by following any one of the methods described for linear models, presented in Chapters [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml)–[8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml). However, one has to pay a price for that. As shown in \[7\], for an expansion involving *K* fixed functions, the squared approximation error *cannot* be made smaller than order $\\left( \\frac{1}{K} \\right)^{\\frac{2}{l}}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si24.png). In other words, for high-dimensional spaces and in order to get a small enough error, one has to use large values of *K*. This is another face of the curse of dimensionality problem. In contrast, one can get rid of the dependence of the approximation error on the input space dimensionality, *l*, if the expansion involves data dependent functions, which are optimized with respect to the specific data set. This is, for example, the case for a class of neural networks, to be discussed in Chapter [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml). In this case, the price one pays is that the dependence on the free parameters is now nonlinear, making the optimization with regard to the unknown parameters a harder task.

## 11.3 Volterra, Wiener, and Hammerstein models

Let us start with the case of modeling nonlinear systems, where the involved input–output entities are time series/discrete-time signals denoted as (*u*[*n*], *d*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si25.png)), respectively. The counterpart of polynomial modeling in Eq. [(11.2)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq2) is now known as the Volterra series expansion.

These types of models will not be pursued any more in this book, and they are briefly discussed here in order to put the nonlinear modeling task in a more general context as well as for historical reasons. *Thus, this section can be bypassed in a first reading*.

Vito Volterra (1860–1940) was an Italian mathematician who made major contributions to mathematics as well as physics and biology. One of his landmark theories is the development of Volterra series, which is used to solve integral and integro-differential equations. He was one of the Italian professors who refused to take an oath of loyalty to the fascist regime of Mussolini, and he was obliged to resign from his university post.

[Fig. 11.1](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0010) shows an unknown nonlinear system/filter with the respective input–output signals. The output of a discrete-time Volterra model can be written as

$d\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{r}\\sum\\limits\_{i\_{1} = 0}^{M}\\sum\\limits\_{i\_{2} = 0}^{M}\\cdots\\sum\\limits\_{i\_{k} = 0}^{M}w\_{k}(i\_{1},i\_{2},\\ldots,i\_{k})\\prod\\limits\_{j = 1}^{k}u\_{n - i\_{j}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si26.png)(11.3) 

where *w*[*k*](⋅,…,  ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si27.png) denotes the *k*th-order *Volterra kernel*; in general, *r* can be infinite. For example, for *r* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si28.png) and *M* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si29.png), the input–output relation involves the linear combination of the terms

*u*[*n*], *u*[*n* − 1], *u*[*n*]², *u*[*n* − 1]², *u*[*n*]*u*[*n* − 1].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si30.png)

Special cases of the Volterra expansion are the *Wiener*, *Hammerstein*, and *Wiener–Hammerstein* models. These models are shown in [Fig. 11.2](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0015). The systems *h*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si31.png) and *g*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si32.png) are linear systems with memory, that is,

$s\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{M\_{1}}h\_{n}u\_{n - i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si33.png)

and

$d\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{M\_{2}}g\_{n}x\_{n - i}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si34.png)

The central box corresponds to a memoryless nonlinear system, which can be approximated by a polynomial of degree *r*. Hence,

$x\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{r}c\_{k}{(s\_{n})}^{k}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si35.png)

In other words, a Wiener model is a linear time-invariant (LTI) system followed by the memoryless nonlinearity and the Hammerstein model is the combination of a memoryless nonlinearity followed by an LTI system. The Wiener–Hammerstein model is the combination of the two. Note that that such models are nonlinear with respect to the involved free parameters. In contrast, the equivalent Volterra model is linear with regard to the involved parameters; however, the number of the resulting free parameters is significantly increased with the order of the polynomial and the filter memory taps (*M*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si36.png) and *M*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si37.png)). The interesting feature is that the equivalent to a Hammerstein model Volterra expansion consists only of the diagonal elements of the associated Volterra kernels. In other words, the output is expressed in terms of *u*[*n*], *u*[*n* − 1], *u*[*n* − 2], …<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si38.png) and their powers; there are no cross-product terms \[60\].

Remarks 11.1

*   •  The Volterra series expansion was first introduced as a generalization of the Taylor series expansion. Following \[101\], assume a memoryless nonlinear system. Then its input–output relationship is given by

*d*(*t*) = *f*(*u*(*t*)),<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si39.png)

*   and adopting the Taylor expansion, for a particular time *t* ∈ ( − ∞,  + ∞)<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si40.png), we can write

$d(t) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 0}^{+ \\infty}c\_{n}{(u(t))}^{n},$<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si41.png)(11.4) 

*   assuming that the series converges. The Volterra series is the extension of Eq. [(11.4)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq10) to systems with memory, and we can write

*d*(*t*) = *w*[0] + ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*w*[1](*τ*[1])*u*(*t* − *τ*[1])*d**τ*[1] + ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*w*[2](*τ*[1], *τ*[2])*u*(*t* − *τ*[1])*u*(*t* − *τ*[2])*d**τ*[1]*d**τ*[2] + ….<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si42.png)(11.5) 

*   In other words, the Volterra series is a power series with memory. The problem of convergence of the Volterra series is similar to that of the Taylor series. In analogy to the Weierstrass approximation theorem, it turns out that the output of a nonlinear system can be approximated arbitrarily close using a sufficient number of terms in the Volterra series expansion \[44\].
*   A major difficulty in the Volterra series is the computation of the Volterra kernels. Wiener was the first to realize the potential of the Volterra series for nonlinear system modeling. In order to compute the involved Volterra kernels, he used the method of orthogonal functionals. The method resembles the method of using a set of orthogonal polynomials, when one tries to approximate a function via a polynomial expansion \[129\]. More on the Volterra modeling and related models can be obtained in, for example, \[57,70,102\]. Volterra models have been extensively used in a number of applications, including communications (e.g., \[11\]), biomedical engineering (e.g., \[72\]), and automatic control (e.g., \[32\]).

![Figure 11.2 The Wiener model comprises a linear filter followed by a memoryless polynomial nonlinearity. The Hammerstein model consists of a memoryless nonlinearity followed by a linear filter. The Wiener–Hammerstein model is the combination of the two.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr002.jpg)

The Hammerstein model consists of a memoryless nonlinearity followed by a linear filter. The Wiener–Hammerstein model is the combination of the two.

## 11.4 Cover's theorem: capacity of a space in linear dichotomies

We have already justified the method of expanding an unknown nonlinear function in terms of a fixed set of nonlinear ones, by mobilizing arguments from the approximation theory. Although this framework fits perfectly to the regression task, where the output takes values in an interval in ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si43.png), such arguments are not well suited for the classification. In the latter case, the output value is of a discrete nature. For example, in a binary classification task, *y* ∈ {1,  − 1}<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si44.png), and as long as the sign of the predicted value, *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si45.png), is correct, we do not care how close *y* and *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si45.png) are. In this section, we will present an elegant and powerful theorem that justifies the expansion of a classifier, *f*, in the form of Eq. [(11.1)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq1). It suffices to look at Eq. [(11.1)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq1) from a different angle.

Let us consider *N* points, **x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si46.png). We can say that these points are *in general position* if *there is no* subset of *l* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si47.png) of them lying on an (*l* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si48.png)\-dimensional hyperplane. For example, in the two-dimensional space, any three of these points are not permitted to lie on a straight line.

Theorem 11.1

Cover's theorem

*The number of groupings, denoted as* 𝒪(*N*, *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si49.png)*, that can be formed by* (*l* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si48.png)*\-dimensional hyperplanes to separate the N points in two classes, exploiting all possible combinations, is given by (see* \[31\] *and Problem* [11.1](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#o0030)*)*

$\\mathcal{O}(N,l) = 2\\sum\\limits\_{i = 0}^{l}\\begin{pmatrix} {N - 1} \\\\ i \\\\ \\end{pmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si51.png)

*where*

$\\begin{pmatrix} {N - 1} \\\\ i \\\\ \\end{pmatrix} = \\frac{(N - 1)!}{(N - 1 - i)!i!}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>!</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>!</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si52.png)

Each one of these groupings in two classes is also known as a (linear) *dichotomy*. [Fig. 11.3](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0020) illustrates the theorem for the case of *N* = 4<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si54.png) points in the two-dimensional space. Observe that the possible groupings are \[(ABCD)\], \[A, (BCD)\], \[B, (ACD)\], \[C, (ABD)\], \[D, (ABC)\], \[(AB), (CD)\], and \[(AC), (BD)\]. Each grouping is counted twice, as it can belong to either *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si55.png) or *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si56.png) class. Hence, the total number of groupings is 14, which is equal to 𝒪(4, 2)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si57.png). Note that the number of all possible combinations of *N* points in two groups is 2^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si58.png), which is 16 in our case. The grouping that is not counted in 𝒪(4, 2)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si57.png), as it cannot be linearly separated, is \[(BC),(AD)\]. Note that if *N* ≤ *l* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si59.png), then 𝒪(*N*, *l*) = 2^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si60.png). That is, all possible combinations in groups of two are linearly separable; verify it for the case of *N* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si61.png) in the two-dimensional space.

![Figure 11.3 The possible number of linearly separable groupings of two, for four points in the two-dimensional space is \\mathcal{O}(4,2) = 14 = 2 \\times 7Equation.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 11.3](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#cf0320) The possible number of linearly separable groupings of two, for four points in the two-dimensional space is 𝒪(4, 2) = 14 = 2 × 7<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si53.png).

Based on the previous theorem, given *N* points in the *l*\-dimensional space, the probability of grouping these points in two *linearly* separable classes is

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx001.jpg)(11.6) 

To visualize this finding, let us write *N* = *r*(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si62.png), and express the probability *P*[*N*]^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si63.png) in terms of *r*, for a fixed value of *l*. The resulting graph is shown in [Fig. 11.4](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0025). Observe that there are two distinct regions. One to the left of the point *r* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si28.png) and one to the right. At the point *r* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si28.png), that is, *N* = 2(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si64.png), the probability is always $\\frac{1}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si65.png), because 𝒪(2*l* + 2, *l*) = 2^(2*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si66.png) (Problem [11.2](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#o0035)). Note that the larger the value of *l* is, the sharper the transition from one region to the other becomes. Thus, for high-dimensional spaces and as long as *N* < 2(*l* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si67.png), the probability of any grouping of the points in two classes to be *linearly separable* tends to unity.

![Figure 11.4 For N > 2(l + 1) the probability of linear separability becomes small. For large values of l, and provided N < 2(l + 1), the probability of any grouping of the data into two classes to be linearly separable tends to unity. Also, if N ≤ (l + 1), all possible groupings in two classes are linearly separable.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 11.4](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#cf0325) For *N* > 2(*l* + 1) the probability of linear separability becomes small. For large values of *l*, and provided *N* < 2(*l* + 1), the probability of any grouping of the data into two classes to be linearly separable tends to unity. Also, if *N* ≤ (*l* + 1), all possible groupings in two classes are linearly separable.

The way the previous theorem is exploited in practice is the following. Given *N* feature vectors **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si68.png), a mapping

**ϕ** : ℝ^(*l*) ∋ **x**[*n*] ↦ **ϕ**(**x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ^(*K*), *K* ≫ *l*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∋</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>≫</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si69.png)

is performed. Then according to the theorem, the higher the value of *K* is, the higher the probability becomes for the images of the mapping, **ϕ**(**x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ^(*K*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si70.png), to be linearly separable in the space ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si71.png). Note that the expansion of a nonlinear classifier (that predicts the label in a binary classification task) is equivalent to using a linear one on the images of the original points after the mapping. Indeed,

$f(\\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\theta\_{k}\\phi\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\theta\_{0} = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\begin{bmatrix} {\\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x})} \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si72.png)(11.7) 

with

**ϕ**(**x**) :  = \[*ϕ*[1](**x**), *ϕ*[2](**x**), …, *ϕ*[*K*](**x**)\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si73.png)

Provided that *K* is large enough, our task is *linearly separable* in the new space, ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si71.png), with high probability, which justifies the use of a linear classifier, ***θ***, in Eq. [(11.7)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq16). The procedure is illustrated in [Fig. 11.5](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0030). The points in the two-dimensional space are not linearly separable. However, after the following mapping in the three-dimensional space,

\[*x*[1], *x*[2]\]^(*T*) ↦ **ϕ**(**x**) = \[*x*[1], *x*[2], *f*(*x*[1], *x*[2])\]^(*T*),  *f*(*x*[1], *x*[2]) = 4exp (−(*x*[1]²+*x*[2]²)/3) + 5,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="2em"/><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si74.png)

the points in the two classes become linearly separable. Note, however, that after the mapping, the points lie on the surface of a paraboloid. This surface is fully described in terms of two free variables. Loosely speaking, we can think of the two-dimensional plane, on which the data lie originally, to be folded/transformed to form the surface of the paraboloid. This is basically the idea behind the more general problem. After the mapping from the original *l*\-dimensional space to the new *K*\-dimensional one, the images of the points **ϕ**(**x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si75.png), lie on an *l*\-dimensional surface (*manifold*) in ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si71.png) \[19\]. We cannot fool nature. Because *l* variables were originally chosen to describe each pattern (dimensionality, number of free parameters), the same number of free parameters will be required to describe the same objects after the mapping in ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si71.png). In other words, after the mapping, we embed an *l*\-dimensional manifold in a *K*\-dimensional space in such a way that the data in the two classes become linearly separable.

![Figure 11.5 The points (red in one class and black for the other) that are not linearly separable in the original two-dimensional plane become linearly separable after the nonlinear mapping in the three-dimensional space; one can draw a plane that separates the “black” from the “red” points.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 11.5](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#cf0340) The points (red in one class and black for the other) that are not linearly separable in the original two-dimensional plane become linearly separable after the nonlinear mapping in the three-dimensional space; one can draw a plane that separates the “black” from the “red” points.

We have by now fully justified the need for mapping the task from the original low-dimensional space to a higher-dimensional one, via a set of nonlinear functions. However, life is not easy to work in high-dimensional spaces. A large number of parameters are needed; this in turn poses computational complexity problems, and raises issues related to the generalization and overfitting performance of the designed predictors. In the sequel, we will address the former of the two problems by making a “careful” mapping to a higher-dimensional space of a specific structure. The latter problem will be addressed via regularization, as has already been discussed in various parts in previous chapters.

## 11.5 Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces

Consider a linear space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) of real-valued functions defined on a set^([^(69)](#fn69))

Definition 11.1

A Hilbert space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) is called *reproducing kernel Hilbert space* (RKHS) if there exists a *kernel* function

*κ* : 𝒳 × 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si80.png)

with the following properties:

*   •  for every **x** ∈ 𝒳, *κ*(⋅,**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si81.png) belongs to ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png);
*   •  *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png) has the so-called *reproducing property*, that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx002.jpg)(11.8) 

*   

In words, the kernel function is a function of two arguments. Fixing the value of one of them to, say, **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si83.png), then the kernel becomes a function of single argument (associated with the dot ⋅) and this function belongs to ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png). The reproducing property means that the value of any function *f* ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si175.png), at any **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si83.png), is equal to the respective inner product, performed in ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png), between *f* and *κ*(⋅,**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si85.png).

A direct consequence of the reproducing property, if we set *f*( ⋅ ) = *κ*(⋅,**y**), **y** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si86.png), is that

⟨*κ*(⋅,**y**), *κ*(⋅,**x**)⟩ = *κ*(**x**, **y**) = *κ*(**y**, **x**).<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si87.png)(11.9) 

Definition 11.2

Let ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) be an RKHS, associated with a kernel function *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png), and 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png) a set of elements. Then the mapping

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx003.jpg)

is known as *feature map* and the space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) as the *feature space*.

In other words, if 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png) is the set of our observation vectors, the feature mapping maps each vector to the RKHS ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png). Note that, in general, ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) can be of infinite dimension and its elements are functions. That is, each training point is mapped to a function. In special cases, where ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) is of a finite dimension, *K*, the image can be represented as an equivalent vector **ϕ**(**x**) ∈ ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si89.png). From now on, the general infinite-dimensional case will be treated and the images will be denoted as functions, *ϕ*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si90.png).

Let us now see what we have gained by choosing to perform the feature mapping from the original space to a high-dimensional RKHS one. Let **x**, **y** ∈ 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si91.png). Then the inner product of the respective mapping images is written as

⟨*ϕ*(**x**), *ϕ*(**y**)⟩ = ⟨*κ*(⋅,**x**), *κ*(⋅,**y**)⟩,<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si92.png)

or

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx004.jpg)

In other words, employing this type of mapping to our problem, we can perform inner product operations in ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) in a very efficient way; that is, via a function evaluation performed in the original low-dimensional space! This property is also known as the *kernel trick*, and it facilitates significantly the computations. As will become apparent soon, the way this property is exploited in practice involves the following steps:

1.  **1.**  Map (implicitly) the input training data to an RKHS

**x**[*n*] ↦ *ϕ*(**x**[*n*]) ∈ ℍ, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si93.png)

1.  
2.  **2.**  Solve a *linear* estimation task in ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png), involving the images *ϕ*(**x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si94.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si247.png).
3.  **3.**  Cast the algorithm that solves for the unknown parameters in terms of inner product operations in the form

⟨*ϕ*(**x**[*i*]),*ϕ*(**x**[*j*])⟩, *i*, *j* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">〉</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si96.png)

1.  
2.  **4.**  Replace each inner product by a kernel evaluation, that is,

⟨*ϕ*(**x**[*i*]),*ϕ*(**x**[*j*])⟩ = *κ*(**x**[*i*], **x**[*j*]).<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">〉</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si97.png)

1.  

It is apparent that one does not need to perform any explicit mapping of the data. All is needed is to perform the kernel operations at the final step. Note that the specific form of *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png) does not concern the analysis. Once the algorithm for the prediction, *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si45.png), has been derived, one can use different choices for *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png). As we will see, different choices for *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png) correspond to different types of nonlinearity. [Fig. 11.6](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0035) illustrates the rationale behind the procedure. In practice, the four steps listed above are equivalent to (a) work in the original (low-dimensional Euclidean space) and express all operations in terms of inner products and (b) at the final step substitute the inner products with kernel evaluations.

Example 11.1

The goal of this example is to demonstrate that one can map the input space into another of higher dimension (finite-dimensional for this case),^([^(70)](#fn70))

$\\mathbb{R}^{2} \\ni \\mathbf{x}\\longmapsto\\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\lbrack x\_{1}^{2},\\ \\sqrt{2}x\_{1}x\_{2},\\ x\_{2}^{2}\\rbrack \\in \\mathbb{R}^{3}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∋</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si98.png)

Then, given two vectors **x** = \[*x*[1], *x*[2]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si99.png) and **y** = \[*y*[1], *y*[2]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si100.png), it is straightforward to see that

**ϕ**^(*T*)(**x**)**ϕ**(**y**) = (**x**^(*T*)**y**)².<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si101.png)

That is, the inner product in the three-dimensional space, after the mapping, is given in terms of a function of the variables in the original space.

![Figure 11.6 The nonlinear task in the original low-dimensional space is mapped to a linear one in the high-dimensional RKHS \\mathbb{H}Equation. Using feature mapping, inner product operations in \\mathbb{H}Equation are efficiently performed via kernel evaluations in the original low-dimensional space.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 11.6](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#cf0360) The nonlinear task in the original low-dimensional space is mapped to a linear one in the high-dimensional RKHS ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png). Using feature mapping, inner product operations in ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) are efficiently performed via kernel evaluations in the original low-dimensional space.

### 11.5.1 Some properties and theoretical highlights

The reader who has no “mathematical anxieties” can bypass this subsection during a first reading.

Let 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png) be a set of points.
