Typically 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png) is a compact (closed and bounded) subset of ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si102.png). Consider a function

*κ* : 𝒳 × 𝒳 ↦ ℝ.<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si103.png)

Definition 11.3

The function *κ* is called a *positive definite kernel* if

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx005.jpg)(11.10) 

for any real numbers, *a*[*n*], *a*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si104.png), any points **x**[*n*], **x**[*m*] ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si105.png), and any *N* ∈ ℕ<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si106.png).

Note that [(11.10)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq31) can be written in an equivalent form. Define the so-called *kernel matrix*, 𝒦<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si107.png), of order *N*,

$\\mathcal{K}: = \\begin{bmatrix} {\\kappa(\\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{1})} & \\cdots & {\\kappa(\\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{N})} \\\\ \\vdots & \\vdots & \\vdots \\\\ {\\kappa(\\mathbf{x}\_{N},\\mathbf{x}\_{1})} & \\cdots & {\\kappa(\\mathbf{x}\_{N},\\mathbf{x}\_{N})} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si108.png)(11.11) 

Then [(11.10)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq31) is written as

**a**^(*T*)𝒦**a** ≥ 0,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si109.png)(11.12) 

where

**a** = \[*a*[1], …, *a*[*N*]\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si110.png)

Because [(11.10)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq31) is true for any **a** ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si111.png), [(11.12)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq33) suggests that for a kernel to be positive definite, it suffices for the corresponding kernel matrix to be positive semidefinite.^([^(71)](#fn71))

Lemma 11.1

*The reproducing kernel associated with an RKHS* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) *is a positive definite kernel.*

The proof of the lemma is given in Problem [11.3](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#o0040). Note that the opposite is also true. It can be shown \[82,106\] that if *κ* : 𝒳 × 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si113.png) is a positive definite kernel, then there exists an RKHS ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) of functions on 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png) such that *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png) is a reproducing kernel of ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png). This establishes the equivalence between reproducing and positive definite kernels. Historically, the theory of positive definite kernels was developed first in the context of integral equations by Mercer \[76\], and the connection to RKHS was developed later on (see, for example, \[3\]).

Lemma 11.2

*Let* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) *be an RKHS on the set* 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png) *with reproducing kernel* *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png)*. Then the linear span of the function* *κ*(⋅,**x**), **x** ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si116.png)*, is dense in* ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png)*, that is,*

$\\mathbb{H} = \\bar{\\textit{span}\\left\\{ \\kappa(\\cdot,\\mathbf{x}),\\mathbf{x}\\in\\mathcal{X} \\right\\}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">span</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>‾</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si117.png)(11.13) 

The proof of the lemma is given in Problem [11.4](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#o0045). The overbar denotes the closure of a set. In other words, ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) can be constructed by *all* possible linear combinations of the kernel function computed in 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si114.png), as well as the *limit points* of sequences of such combinations. Simply stated, ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) can be *fully generated from the knowledge* of *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si115.png).

The interested reader can obtain more theoretical results concerning RKHSs from, for example, \[64,83,87,103,106,112\].

### 11.5.2 Examples of kernel functions

In this subsection, we present some typical examples of kernel functions, which are commonly used in various applications.

*   •  The *Gaussian* kernel is among the most popular ones, and it is given by our familiar form

$\\kappa(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) = \\exp\\left( - \\frac{{\\|\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{y}\\|}^{2}}{2\\sigma^{2}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si119.png)

*   with *σ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si120.png) being a parameter. [Fig. 11.7](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0040)A shows the Gaussian kernel as a function of *x*, *y* ∈ 𝒳 = ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si121.png) and *σ* = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si122.png). [Fig. 11.7](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0040)B shows the graphs of the resulting functions if we set one of the kernel's arguments to 0, i.e., *κ*(⋅,0)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si123.png), for various values of *σ*.

![Figure 11.7 (A) The Gaussian kernel for \\mathcal{X} = \\mathbb{R},\\ \\sigma = 0.5Equation. (B) The function κ(⋅,0) for different values of σ.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr007.jpg)

Figure 11.7 (A) The Gaussian kernel for 𝒳 = ℝ, *σ* = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si118.png). (B) The function *κ*(⋅,0) for different values of *σ*.

*   The dimension of the RKHS generated by the Gaussian kernel is *infinite*. A proof that the Gaussian kernel satisfies the required properties can be obtained, for example, from \[112\].
*   •  The *homogeneous polynomial* kernel has the form

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = (**x**^(*T*)**y**)^(*r*),<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si124.png)

*   where *r* is a parameter.
*   •  The *inhomogeneous* polynomial kernel is given by

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = (**x**^(*T*)**y** + *c*)^(*r*),<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si126.png)

*   where *c* ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si127.png) and *r* > 0, *r* ∈ ℕ<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si128.png), are parameters. The graph of the kernel is given in [Fig. 11.8](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0045)A. In [Fig. 11.8](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0045)B the graphs of the function *ϕ*(⋅,*x*[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si129.png) are shown for different values of *x*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si130.png). The dimensionality of the RKHS associated with polynomial kernels is finite.

![Figure 11.8 (A) The inhomogeneous polynomial kernel for \\mathcal{X} = \\mathbb{R}Equation, r = 2. (B) The graphs of κ(⋅,x0) for different values of x0.](images/B9780443292385000172/gr008.jpg)

Figure 11.8 (A) The inhomogeneous polynomial kernel for 𝒳 = ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si125.png), *r* = 2. (B) The graphs of *κ*(⋅,*x*[0]) for different values of *x*[0].

*   
*   •  The *Laplacian* kernel is given by

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = exp (−*t*∥**x**−**y**∥),<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si131.png)

*   where *t* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si132.png) is a parameter. The dimensionality of the RKHS associated with the Laplacian kernel is infinite.
*   •  The *spline* kernels are defined as

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *B*[2*p* + 1](∥**x** − **y**∥²),<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si133.png)

*   where the *B*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si134.png) spline is defined via the *n* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si135.png) convolutions of the unit interval $\\lbrack - \\frac{1}{2},\\frac{1}{2}\\rbrack$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si136.png), that is,

$B\_{n}( \\cdot ): = \\bigotimes\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n + 1}\\chi\_{\\lbrack - \\frac{1}{2},\\frac{1}{2}\\rbrack}( \\cdot ),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">⨂</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si137.png)

*   and $\\chi\_{\\lbrack - \\frac{1}{2},\\frac{1}{2}\\rbrack}( \\cdot )$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si138.png) is the characteristic function on the respective interval.^([^(72)](#fn72))
*   •  The *sampling function* or *sinc* kernel is of particular interest from a signal processing point of view. This kernel function is defined as

${sinc}(x) = \\frac{\\sin(\\pi x)}{\\pi x}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si139.png)

*   Recall that we have met this function in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) while discussing sub-Nyquist sampling.
*   Let us now consider the set of all squared integrable functions, which are *bandlimited*, that is,

ℱ[*B*] = {*f*:∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)|*f*(*x*)|²*d**x*<+∞,  and |*F*(*ω*)|=0, |*ω*|>*π*},<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext> and </mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si140.png)

*   where *F*(*ω*)<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si141.png) is the respective Fourier transform

$F(\\omega) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\int\_{- \\infty}^{+ \\infty}f(x)e^{- j\\omega x}dx.$<mml:math><mml:mi>F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si142.png)

*   It turns out that ℱ[*B*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si143.png) is an RKHS whose reproducing kernel is the sinc function (e.g., \[51\]), that is,

*κ*(*x*, *y*) = *s**i**n**c*(*x* − *y*).<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si144.png)

*   This takes us back to the classical sampling theorem through the RKHS route. Without going into details, a by-product of this view is the Shannon sampling theorem; any bandlimited function can be written as^([^(73)](#fn73)) 
    
    $f(x) = \\sum\\limits\_{n}f(n){sinc}(x - n).$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si148.png)(11.14) 
    
    *   

#### Constructing kernels

Besides the previous examples, one can construct more kernels by applying the following properties (Problem [11.6](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#o0055), \[106\]): 

*   •  If

*κ*[1](**x**, **y**) : 𝒳 × 𝒳 ↦ ℝ, *κ*[2](**x**, **y**) : 𝒳 × 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:msub id="mmlbr0002"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si149.png)

*   are kernels, then

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *κ*[1](**x**, **y**) + *κ*[2](**x**, **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si150.png)

*   and

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *α**κ*[1](**x**, **y**), *α* > 0,<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si151.png)

*   and

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *κ*[1](**x**, **y**)*κ*[2](**x**, **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si152.png)

*   are also kernels.
*   •  Let

*f* : 𝒳 ↦ ℝ.<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si153.png)

*   Then

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *f*(**x**)*f*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si154.png)

*   is a kernel.
*   •  Let a function

*g* : 𝒳 ↦ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si155.png)

*   and a kernel function

*κ*[1](⋅, ⋅ ) : ℝ^(*l*) × ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si156.png)

*   Then

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *κ*[1](*g*(**x**),*g*(**y**))<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si157.png)

*   is also a kernel.
*   •  Let *A* be a positive definite *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si158.png) matrix. Then

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = **x**^(*T*)*A***y**<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si159.png)

*   is a kernel.
*   •  If

*κ*[1](**x**, **y**) : 𝒳 × 𝒳 ↦ ℝ,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si160.png)

*   then

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = exp (*κ*[1](**x**,**y**))<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si161.png)

*   is also a kernel, and if *p*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si162.png) is a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients,

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = *p*(*κ*[1](**x**,**y**))<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si163.png)

*   is also a kernel.

The interested reader will find more information concerning kernels and their construction in, for example, \[52,106,112\].

#### String kernels

So far, our discussion has been focused on input data that were vectors in a Euclidean space. However, as we have already pointed out, the input data need not necessarily be vectors, and they can be elements of more general sets.

Let us denote by 𝒮<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si164.png) an alphabet set; that is, a set with a finite number of elements, which we call *symbols*. For example, this can be the set of all capital letters in the Latin alphabet. Bypassing the path of formal definitions, a *string* is a finite sequence of any length of symbols from 𝒮<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si164.png). For example, two cases of strings are

*T*[1] = “MYNAMEISSERGIOS”,  *T*[2] = “HERNAMEISDESPOINA”.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>“MYNAMEISSERGIOS”</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>“HERNAMEISDESPOINA”</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si165.png)

In a number of applications, such as in text mining, spam filtering, text summarization, and bioinformatics, it is important to quantify how “similar” two strings are. However, kernels, by their definition, are similarity measures; they are constructed so as to express inner products in the high-dimensional feature space. An inner product is a similarity measure. Two vectors are most similar if they point to the same direction. Starting from this observation, there has been a lot of activity on defining kernels that measure similarity between strings. Without going into details, let us give such an example.

Let us denote by 𝒮^(\*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si166.png) the set of all possible strings that can be constructed using symbols from 𝒮<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si164.png). Also, a string *s* is said to be a *substring* of *x* if *x* = *b**s**a*<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si167.png), where *a* and *b* are other strings (possibly empty) from the symbols of 𝒮<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si164.png). Given two strings *x*, *y* ∈ 𝒮^(\*)<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si169.png), define

$\\kappa(x,y): = \\sum\\limits\_{s \\in \\mathcal{S} \\ast}w\_{s}\\phi\_{s}(x)\\phi\_{s}(y),$<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">S</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si170.png)(11.15) 

where *w*[*s*] ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si171.png), and *ϕ*[*s*](*x*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si172.png) is the number of times the substring *s* appears in *x*. It turns out that this is indeed a kernel, in the sense that it complies with the condition in [(11.10)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq31); such kernels constructed from strings are known as *string kernels*.

Obviously, a number of different variants of this kernel are available. The so-called *k*\-*spectrum* kernel considers common substrings only of length *k*. For example, for the two strings given before, the value of the 6-spectrum string kernel in Eq. [(11.15)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq61) is equal to one (one common substring of length 6 is identified and appears once in each one of the two strings: “NAMEIS”). The interested reader can obtain more on this topic from, for example, \[106\]. We will use the notion of the string kernel in the case study in Section [11.15](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0175).

## 11.6 Representer theorem

The theorem to be stated in this section is of major importance from a practical point of view. It allows us to perform *empirical* loss function optimization, based on a finite set of training samples, in a very efficient way even if the function to be estimated belongs to a very high (even infinite)-dimensional RKHS ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png).

Theorem 11.2

*Let*

*Ω* : \[0,  + ∞) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si173.png)

*be an arbitrary strictly monotonic increasing function. Let also*

Proof

The linear span, *A* :  = span{*κ*(⋅,**x**[1]), …, *κ*(⋅,**x**[*N*])}<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>span</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si180.png), forms a closed subspace. Then each *f* ∈ ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si175.png) can be decomposed into two parts (see Eq. [(8.20)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)), i.e.,

$f( \\cdot ) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{n}\\kappa( \\cdot ,\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) + f\_{\\bot},$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

where *f*[⊥]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si182.png) is the part of *f* that is orthogonal to *A*. From the reproducing property, we obtain

where we used the fact that ⟨*f*[⊥],*κ*(⋅,**x**[*n*])⟩ = 0, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">〈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">〉</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si184.png). In other words, the expansion in Eq. [(11.17)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq65) guarantees that at the training points, the value of *f* does not depend on *f*[⊥]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si182.png). Hence, the first term in Eq. [(11.16)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq64), corresponding to the empirical loss, does *not* depend on *f*[⊥]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si182.png). Thus, for *any* choice of *θ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si186.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si247.png), the cost function in Eq. [(11.16)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq64) is minimized for *f*[⊥] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊥</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si187.png). Thus, the claim is proved. □

The theorem was first shown in \[61\]. In \[2\], the conditions under which the theorem exists were investigated, and related sufficient and necessary conditions were derived. The importance of this theorem is that in order to optimize Eq. [(11.16)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq64) with respect to *f*, one uses the expansion in Eq. [(11.17)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq65) and minimization is carried out with respect to the *finite* set of parameters *θ*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si186.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si247.png).

Note that when working in high/infinite-dimensional spaces, the presence of a regularizer can hardly be avoided; otherwise, the obtained solution will suffer from overfitting, as only a finite number of data samples are used for training. The effect of regularization on the generalization performance and stability of the associated solution has been studied in a number of classical papers (for example, \[18,39,79\]).

Usually, a bias term is often added and it is assumed that the minimizing function admits the following representation:

*f̃* = *f* + *b*,<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si188.png)(11.18) 

$f( \\cdot ) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{n}\\kappa( \\cdot ,\\mathbf{x}\_{n}).$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si189.png)(11.19) 

In practice, the use of a bias term (which does not enter in the regularization) turns out to improve performance. First, it enlarges the class of functions in which the solution is searched and potentially leads to better performance. Moreover, due to the penalization imposed by the regularizing term, *Ω*(∥*f*∥²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si190.png), the minimizer pushes the values which the function takes at the training points to smaller values. The existence of *b* tries to “absorb” some of this action (see, for example, \[112\]).

Remarks 11.2

*   •  We will use the expansion in Eq. [(11.17)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq65) in a number of cases. However, it is interesting to apply this expansion to the RKHS of the bandlimited functions and see what comes out. Assume that the available samples from a function *f* are *f*(*n*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si191.png) (assuming the case of normalized sampling period *x*[*s*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si192.png)). Then according to the representer theorem, we can write the following approximation:

$f(x) \\approx \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{n}{sinc}(x - n).$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si193.png)(11.20) 

*   Taking into account the orthonormality of the *s**i**n**c*( ⋅  − *n*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sinc</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si194.png) functions, we get *θ*[*n*] = *f*(*n*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si195.png). However, note that in contrast to Eq. [(11.14)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq46), which is exact, Eq. [(11.20)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq71) is only an approximation. On the other hand, Eq. [(11.20)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq71) can be used even if the obtained samples are contaminated by noise.

### 11.6.1 Semiparametric representer theorem

The use of the bias term is also theoretically justified by the generalization of the representer theorem \[103\]. The essence of this theorem is to expand the solution into two parts, i.e., one that lies in an RKHS ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) and another that is given as a linear combination of a set of preselected functions. 

Theorem 11.3

*Let us assume that in addition to the assumptions adopted in* [Theorem 11.2](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#enun0050)*, we are given the set of real-valued functions*

*ψ*[*m*]: 𝒳 ↦ ℝ, *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si196.png)

*with the property that the* *N* × *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si197.png) *matrix with elements* *ψ*[*m*](**x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si198.png)*,* *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*, *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si199.png)*, has rank M. Then any*

*f̃* = *f* + *h*, *f* ∈ ℍ, *h* ∈ *span*{*ψ*[*m*], *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*},<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="italic">span</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si200.png)

*solving the minimization task*

$\\min\\limits\_{\\widetilde{f}}\\ J(\\widetilde{f}): = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}\\left( y\_{n},\\widetilde{f}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) \\right) + \\Omega({\\| f\\|}^{2})$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si201.png)(11.21) 

*admits the following representation:*

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx007.jpg)(11.22) 

Obviously, the use of a bias term is a special case of the expansion above. An example of successful application of this theorem was demonstrated in \[13\] in the context of image denoising. A set of nonlinear functions in place of *ψ*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si202.png) were used to account for the edges (nonsmooth jumps) in an image. The part of *f* lying in the RKHS accounted for the smooth parts in the image.

### 11.6.2 Nonparametric modeling: a discussion

Note that searching a model function in an RKHS space is a typical task of *nonparametric* modeling. In contrast to the parametric modeling in Eq. [(11.1)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq1), where the unknown function is *parameterized* in terms of a set of basis functions, the minimization in Eq [(11.16)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq64) or Eq. [(11.21)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq74) is performed with regard to functions that are *constrained to belong in a specific space*. In the more general case, minimization could be performed with regard to any (continuous) function, for example,

$\\min\\limits\_{f}\\ \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}\\left( y\_{n},f(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) \\right) + \\lambda\\phi(f),$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si203.png)

where ℒ(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si204.png) can be any loss function and *ϕ* an appropriately chosen regularizing functional.^([^(75)](#fn75))

$\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - f(x\_{n}) \\right)^{2} + \\lambda\\int{(f^{''}(x))}^{2}\\ dx,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>″</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si206.png)

then the solution is a cubic spline; that is, a piecewise cubic function with knots the points *x*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si207.png), and it is continuously differentiable to the second order. The choice of *λ* controls the degree of smoothness of the approximating function; the larger its value is, the smoother the minimizer becomes.

If, on the other hand, *f* is constrained to lie in an RKHS and the minimizing task is as in Eq. [(11.16)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq64), then the resulting function is of the form given in Eq. [(11.17)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq65), where a kernel function is placed at each input training point. It must be pointed out that the parametric form that now results was not in our original intentions. It came out as a by-product of the theory. However, it should be stressed that, in contrast to the parametric methods, now the number of parameters to be estimated is not fixed but it depends on the number of the training points. Recall that this is an important difference and it was carefully pointed out when parametric methods were introduced and defined in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml).

## 11.7 Kernel ridge regression

Ridge regression was introduced in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) and it has also been treated in more detail in Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml). Here, we will state the task in a general RKHS. The path to be followed is the typical one used to extend techniques which have been developed for linear models to the more general RKHS.

We assume that the generation mechanism of the data, represented by the training set (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]) ∈ ℝ × ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si208.png), is modeled via a nonlinear regression task

*y*[*n*] = *g*(**x**[*n*]) + *η*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si209.png)(11.23) 

Let us denote by *f* the estimate of the unknown *g*. Sometimes, *f* is called the *hypothesis* and the space ℍ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si112.png) in which *f* is searched is known as the *hypothesis space*. We will further assume that *f* lies in an RKHS, associated with a kernel

*κ* : ℝ^(*l*) × ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ.<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si210.png)

Motivated by the representer theorem, we adopt the following expansion:

$f(\\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{n}\\kappa(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si211.png)

According to the kernel ridge regression approach, the involved unknown parameters are estimated by the following task:

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}),J(\\mathbf{\\theta}): = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - \\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{m}\\kappa(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{m}) \\right)^{2} + C\\langle f,f\\rangle,$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true" id="mmlbr0005"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si212.png)(11.24) 

where *C* is the regularization parameter.^([^(76)](#fn76))

*J*(**θ**) = (**y** − 𝒦**θ**)^(*T*)(**y** − 𝒦**θ**) + *C***θ**^(*T*)𝒦^(*T*)**θ**,<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

**y** = \[*y*[1], …, *y*[*N*]\]^(*T*), **θ** = \[*θ*[1], …, *θ*[*N*]\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>
