### 11.10.3 Performance of SVMs and applications

A notable characteristic of the SVMs is that the complexity is independent of the dimensionality of the respective RKHS. This has an influence on the generalization performance; SVMs exhibit very good generalization performance in practice. Theoretically, such a claim is substantiated by their maximum margin interpretation, in the framework of the elegant *structural risk minimization theory* \[28,123,127\].

An extensive comparative study concerning the performance of SVMs against 16 other popular classifiers has been reported in \[77\]. The results verify that the SVM ranks at the very top among these classifiers, although there are cases for which other methods score better performance. Another comparative performance study is reported in \[25\]. However, it must be noted that these results are more of a historical value these days, since they were performed before the rise of the deep networks era.

It is hard to find a discipline related to machine learning/pattern recognition where SVMs and the concept of working in kernel spaces have not been applied. Early applications included data mining, spam categorization, object recognition, medical diagnosis, optical character recognition (OCR), and bioinformatics (see, for example, \[28\] for a review). More recent applications include cognitive radio (for example, \[35\]), spectrum cartography and network flow prediction \[9\], and image denoising \[13\].

In \[113\], the notion of *kernel embedding* of conditional probabilities is reviewed, as a means to address challenging problems in graphical models. The notion of kernelization has also been extended in the context of *tensor-based* models \[50,107,132\]. Kernel-based hypothesis testing is reviewed in \[49\]. In \[120\], the use of kernels in manifold learning is discussed in the framework of diffusion maps. The task of analyzing the performance of kernel techniques with regard to dimensionality, signal-to-noise ratio, and local error bars is reviewed in \[81\]. In \[119\], a collection of articles related to kernel-based methods and applications is provided.

### 11.10.4 Choice of hyperparameters

One of the main issues associated with SVM/SVRs is the choice of the parameter *C*, which controls the relative influence of the loss and the regularizing parameter in the cost function. Although some efforts have been made in developing theoretical tools for the respective optimization, the path that has survived in practice is that of cross-valuation techniques against a test data set. Different values of *C* are used to train the model, and the value that results in the best performance over the test set is selected.

The other main issue is the choice of the kernel function. Different kernels lead to different performance. Let us look carefully at the expansion in Eq. [(11.17)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq65). One can think of *κ*(**x**, **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si413.png) as a function that measures the *similarity* between ***x*** and **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si252.png); in other words, *κ*(**x**, **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si413.png) *matches* ***x*** to the training sample **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si252.png). A kernel is local if *κ*(**x**, **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si413.png) takes relatively large values in a small region around **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si252.png). For example, when the Gaussian kernel is used, the contribution of *κ*(**x**, **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si413.png) away from **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si252.png) decays exponentially fast, depending of the value of *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si415.png). Thus, the choice of *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si415.png) is very crucial. If the function to be approximated is smooth, then large values of *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si415.png) should be employed. On the contrary, if the function is highly varying in input space, the Gaussian kernel may not be the best choice. As a matter of fact, if for such cases the Gaussian kernel is employed, one must have access to a large number of training data, in order to fill in the input space densely enough, so as to be able to obtain a good enough approximation of such a function. This brings into the scene another critical factor in machine learning, related to the size of the training set. The latter is not only dictated by the dimensionality of the input space (curse of dimensionality) but it also depends on the type of variation that the unknown function undergoes (see, for example, \[12\]). In practice, in order to choose the right kernel function, one uses different kernels and after cross-validation selects the “best” one for the specific problem.

A line of research is to design kernels that match the data at hand, based either on some prior knowledge or via some optimization path (see, for example, \[29,65\]). In Section [11.13](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0165) we will discuss techniques which use multiple kernels in an effort to optimally combine their individual characteristics.

### 11.10.5 Multiclass generalizations

The SVM classification task has been introduced in the context of a two-class classification task. The more general *M*\-class case can be treated in various ways:

*   •  *One-against-all*: One solves *M* two-class problems. Each time, one of the classes is classified against all the others using a different SVM. Thus, *M* classifiers are estimated, that is,

*f*[*m*](**x**) = 0, *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si416.png)

*   which are trained so that *f*[*m*](**x**) > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si417.png) for **x** ∈ *ω*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si418.png) and *f*[*m*](**x**) < 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si419.png) if ***x*** otherwise. Classification is achieved via the rule

$\\text{assign~}\\mathbf{x}\\ \\text{in}\\ \\omega\_{k}:\\ \\text{~if~}k = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{m}f\_{m}(\\mathbf{x}).$<mml:math><mml:mtext>assign </mml:mtext><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>in</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext> if </mml:mtext><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si420.png)

*   According to this method, there may be regions in space where more than one of the discriminant functions score a positive value, e.g., \[123\]. Moreover, another disadvantage of this approach is the so-called *class imbalance* problem; this is caused by the fact that the number of training points in one of the classes (which comprises the data from *M* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si421.png) classes) can be much larger than the points in the other. Issues related to the class imbalance problem are discussed in, e.g., \[123\].
*   •  *One-against-one*. According to this method, one solves $\\frac{M(M - 1)}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si422.png) binary classification tasks by considering all classes in pairs. The final decision is taken on the basis of the majority rule.
*   •  In \[128\], the SVM rationale is extended in estimating simultaneously *M* hyperplanes. However, this technique ends up with a large number of parameters, equal to *N*(*M* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si423.png), which have to be estimated via a single minimization task; this turns out to be rather prohibitive for most practical problems.
*   •  In \[34\], the multiclass task is treated in the context of error correcting codes. Each class is associated with a binary code word. If the code words are properly chosen, an error resilience is “embedded” into the process (see also \[123\]). For a comparative study of multiclass classification schemes, see, for example, \[41\] and the references therein.
*   •  *Division and Clifford algebras*: The SVM framework has also been extended to treat complex and hypercomplex data, both for the regression and the classification cases, using either division algebras or Clifford algebras \[8\]. In \[124\], the case of quaternion RKH spaces is considered.
*   A more general method for the case of complex-valued data, which exploits the notion of *widely linear estimation* as well as *pure complex kernels*, has been presented in \[14\]. In that paper, it is shown that any complex SVM/SVR task is equivalent to solving two real SVM/SVR tasks exploiting a specific real kernel, which is generated by the chosen complex one. Moreover, in the classification case, it is shown that the proposed framework inherently splits the complex space into four parts. This leads naturally to solving the four-class task (quaternary classification), instead of the standard two-class scenario of the real SVM. This rationale can be used in a multiclass problem as a split-class scenario.

## 11.11 Computational considerations

Solving a quadratic programming task, in general, requires 𝒪(*N*³)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si424.png) operations and 𝒪(*N*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si425.png) memory space. To cope with such demands a number of decomposition techniques have been devised (for example, \[22,55\]), which “break” the task into a sequence of smaller ones. In \[59,88,89\], the *sequential minimal optimization* (SMO) algorithm breaks the task into a sequence of problems comprising two points, which can be solved analytically. Efficient implementation of such schemes leads to an empirical training time that scales between 𝒪(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si426.png) and 𝒪(*N*^(2.3))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2.3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si427.png).

The schemes derived in \[74,75\] treat the task as a minimum distance points search between reduced convex hulls and end up with an iterative scheme which projects the training points on hyperplanes. The scheme leads to even more efficient implementations compared to \[59,88\]; moreover, the minimum distance search algorithm has a built-in enhanced parallelism.

The issue of parallel implementation is also discussed in \[21\]. Issues concerning complexity and accuracy are reported in \[53\]. In the latter, polynomial time algorithms are derived that produce approximate solutions with a guaranteed accuracy for a class of QP problems including SVM classifiers.

Incremental versions for solving the SVM task which deal with sequentially arriving data have also appeared (for example, \[26,37,100\]). In the latter, at each iteration a new point is considered and the previously selected set of support vectors (active set) is updated accordingly by adding/removing samples.

Online versions that apply in the primal problem formulation have also been proposed. In \[84\], an iterative reweighted LS approach is followed that alternates weight optimization with cost constraint forcing. A structurally and computationally simple scheme, named *Primal Estimated sub-Gradient SOlver for SVM* (PEGASOS), has been proposed in \[105\]. The algorithm is of an iterative subgradient form applied on the regularized empirical hinge loss function in Eq. [(11.60)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq143) (see also Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)). The algorithm, for the case of linear kernels, exhibits very good convergence properties and it finds an *ϵ*\-accurate solution in $\\mathcal{O}\\left( \\frac{1}{\\epsilon} \\right)$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si428.png) iterations.

In \[43,56\] the classical technique of *cutting planes* for solving convex tasks has been employed in the context of SVMs in the primal domain. The resulting algorithm is very efficient and, in particular for the linear SVM case, the complexity becomes of order 𝒪(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si426.png).

In \[125\] the concept of the *core vector machine* (CVM) is introduced to lead to efficient solutions. The main concept behind this method is that of the minimum enclosing ball (MEB) in computational geometry. Then a subset of points is used, known as the *core set*, to achieve an approximation to the MEB, which is employed during the optimization.

In \[27\], a comparative study between solving the SVM tasks in the primal and dual domains is carried out. The findings of the paper point out that both paths are equally efficient, for the linear as well as for the nonlinear cases. Moreover, when the goal is to resort to approximate solutions, opting for the primal task can offer certain benefits. In addition, working in the primal also offers the advantage of tuning the hyperparameters by resorting to joint optimization. One of the main advantages of resorting to the dual domain was the luxury of casting the task in terms of inner products. However, this is also possible in the primal, by appropriate exploitation of the representer theorem. We will see such examples in Section [11.12.1](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0160).

More recently, a version of SVM for distributed processing has been presented in \[42\]. In \[99\], the SVM task is solved in a subspace using the method of random projections.

## 11.12 Random Fourier features

In Section [11.11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0150), a number of techniques were discussed in order to address and cope with the computational load and the way this scales with the number of training data points, *N*, in the context of SVMs. Furthermore, at the heart of a number of kernel-based methods, such as the kernel ridge regression (Section [11.7](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0070)) and the Gaussian processes (to be discussed in Section [13.12](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml)) lies the inversion of the kernel matrix, which has been defined in Section [11.5.1](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0035). The latter is of dimension *N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si429.png) and it is formed by all possible kernel evaluation pairs in the set of the training examples, i.e., *κ*(**x**[*i*], **x**[*j*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si430.png), *i*, *j* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si431.png). Inverting an *N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si429.png) matrix amounts, in general, to 𝒪(*N*³)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si424.png) algebraic operations, which gets out of hand as *N* increases. In this vein, a number of techniques have been suggested in an effort to reduce related computational costs. Some examples of such methods are given in \[1,45\], where random projections are employed to “throw away” individual elements or entire rows of the matrix in an effort to form related low-rank or sparse matrix approximations.

An alternative “look” at the computational load reduction task was presented in \[91\]. The essence of this approach is to bypass the implicit mapping to a higher (possibly infinite)-dimensional space via the kernel function, i.e., *ϕ*(**x**) = *κ*(⋅,**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si433.png), which comprises the spine of any kernel-based method (Section [11.5](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0030)). Instead, an explicit mapping to a *finite-dimensional* space, ℝ^(*D*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si434.png), is performed, i.e.,

**x** ∈ 𝒳 ⊆ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ **z**(**x**) ∈ ℝ^(*D*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si435.png)

However, the mapping is done in a “thoughtful” way so that the inner product between two vectors in this *D*\-dimensional space is approximately equal to the respective value of the kernel function, i.e.,

*κ*(**x**, **y**) = ⟨*ϕ*(**x**), *ϕ*(**y**)⟩ ≈ **z**(**x**)^(*T*)**z**(**y**), ∀**x**, **y** ∈ 𝒳.<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si436.png)

To establish such an approximation, Bochner's theorem from harmonic analysis was mobilized (e.g., \[96\]). To grasp the main rationale behind this theorem, without resorting to mathematical details, let us recall the notion of power spectral density (PSD) from Section [2.4.3](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml). The PSD of a stationary process is defined as the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation sequence, and there it was shown to be a real and nonnegative function. Furthermore, its integral is finite (Eq. [(2.125)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)). Although the proof given there followed a rather “practical” and conceptual path, a more mathematically rigorous proof reveals that this result is a direct by-product of the positive definite property of the autocorrelation sequence (Eq. [(2.116)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)).

In this line of thought, everything that was said above for the PSD is also valid for the Fourier transform of a shift-invariant kernel function. As is well known, a kernel function is a positive definite one (Section [11.5.1](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0035)). Also, the shift-invariant property, i.e., *κ*(**x**, **y**) = *κ*(**x** − **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si437.png), could be seen as the equivalent of the stationarity. Then one can show that the Fourier transform of a shift-invariant kernel is a nonnegative real function and that its integral is finite. After some normalization, we can always make the integral equal to one. Thus, the Fourier transform of a shift-invariant kernel function can be treated and interpreted as a PDF, that is, a real nonnegative function that integrates to one.

Let *κ*(**x** − **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si438.png) be a shift-invariant kernel and let *p*(**ω**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si439.png) be its (multidimensional) Fourier transform, i.e.,

$p(\\mathbf{\\omega}) = \\frac{1}{{(2\\pi)}^{l}}\\int\_{\\mathbb{R}^{l}}\\kappa(\\mathbf{r})e^{- j\\mathbf{\\omega}^{T}\\mathbf{r}}d\\mathbf{r}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si440.png)

Then, via the inverse Fourier transform, we have

*κ*(**x** − **y**) = ∫[ℝ^(*l*)]*p*(**ω**)*e*^(*j***ω**^(*T*)(**x** − **y**))*d***ω**.<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si441.png)(11.89) 

Having interpreted *p*(**ω**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si439.png) as a PDF, the right-hand side in Eq. [(11.89)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq200) is the respective expectation, i.e.,

*κ*(**x** − **y**) = 𝔼[**ω**]\[*e*^(*j***ω**^(*T*)**x**)*e*^( − *j***ω**^(*T*)**y**)\].<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si442.png)

One can get rid of the complex exponentials by mobilizing Euler's formula^([^(80)](#fn80))

$z\_{\\mathbf{\\omega},b}(\\mathbf{x}): = \\sqrt{2}\\cos(\\mathbf{\\omega}^{T}\\mathbf{x} + b),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si444.png)(11.90) 

where **ω** is a random vector that follows *p*(**ω**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si439.png) and b is a uniformly distributed random variable in \[0, 2*π*\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si446.png). Then it is easy to show that (Problem [11.12](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#o0085))

*κ*(**x** − **y**) = 𝔼[**ω**, *b*]\[*z*[**ω**, *b*](**x**)*z*[**ω**, *b*](**y**)\],<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si447.png)(11.91) 

where the expectation is taken with respect to *p*(**ω**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si439.png) and *p*(*b*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si448.png). The previous expectation can be approximated by

$\\kappa(\\mathbf{x} - \\mathbf{y}) \\approx \\frac{1}{D}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{D}z\_{\\mathbf{\\omega}\_{i},b\_{i}}(\\mathbf{x})z\_{\\mathbf{\\omega}\_{i},b\_{i}}(\\mathbf{y}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si449.png)

where (**ω**[*i*], *b*[*i*]), *i* = 1, 2, …, *D*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si450.png), are i.i.d. generated samples from the respective distributions.

We now have all the ingredients to define an appropriate mapping that builds upon the previous findings.

*   •  *Step 1*: Generate *D* i.i.d. samples **ω**[*i*] ∼ *p*(**ω**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si451.png) and *b*[*i*] ∼ 𝒰(0, 2*π*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si452.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *D*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si453.png).
*   •  *Step 2*: Perform the following mapping to ℝ^(*D*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si434.png):

$\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X}\\longmapsto\\mathbf{z}\_{\\Omega}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{2}{D}}\\left\\lbrack \\cos(\\mathbf{\\omega}\_{1}^{T}\\mathbf{x} + b\_{1}),\\ldots,\\cos(\\mathbf{\\omega}\_{D}^{T}\\mathbf{x} + b\_{D}) \\right\\rbrack^{T}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si454.png)

*   The above mapping defines an inner product approximation of the original kernel, i.e.,

*κ*(**x** − **y**) ≈ **z**[*Ω*](**x**)^(*T*)**z**[*Ω*](**y**),<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si455.png)

*   where, by definition,

$\\Omega: = \\begin{bmatrix} \\mathbf{\\omega}\_{1} & \\mathbf{\\omega}\_{2} & \\ldots & \\mathbf{\\omega}\_{D} \\\\ b\_{1} & b\_{2} & \\ldots & b\_{D} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si456.png)

*   Once this mapping has been performed, one can mobilize any linear modeling method to work in a finite-dimensional space. For example, instead of solving the kernel ridge regression problem, the ridge regression task in Section [3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) can be used. However, now, the involved matrix to be inverted is of dimensions *D* × *D*<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si457.png) instead of *N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si429.png), which can lead to significant gains for large enough values of *N*.
*   The choice of *D* is user-defined and problem dependent. In \[91\], related accuracy bounds have been derived. For within *ϵ* accuracy approximation to a shift-invariant kernel, one needs only $D = \\mathcal{O}(d\\epsilon^{- 2}\\ln\\frac{1}{\\epsilon^{2}})$<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si458.png) dimensions. In practice, values of *D* in the range of a few tens to a few thousands, depending on the data set, seem to suffice to obtain significant computational gains compared to some of the more classical methods.

Remarks 11.6

*   •  *Nyström approximation*: Another popular and well-known technique to obtain a low-rank approximation to the kernel matrix is known as the Nyström approximation.
*   Let 𝒦<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si107.png) be an *N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si429.png) kernel matrix. Then select randomly *q* < *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si459.png) points out of *N*. Various sampling scenarios can be used. It turns out that there exists an approximation matrix $\\widetilde{\\mathcal{K}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si460.png) of rank *q*, such that

$\\widetilde{\\mathcal{K}} = \\mathcal{K}\_{nq}\\mathcal{K}\_{q}^{- 1}\\mathcal{K}\_{nq}^{T},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si461.png)

*   where 𝒦[*q*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si462.png) is the respective invertible kernel matrix associated with the subset of the *q* points and 𝒦[*n**q*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si463.png) comprises the columns of 𝒦<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si107.png) associated with the previous *q* points \[130\]. Generalizations and related theoretical results can be found in \[36\]. If the approximate matrix, $\\widetilde{\\mathcal{K}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si460.png), is used in place of the original kernel matrix, 𝒦<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si107.png), the memory requirements are reduced to 𝒪(*N**q*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si465.png) from *N*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si466.png), and operations of the order of 𝒪(*N*³)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si424.png) can be reduced to 𝒪(*N**q*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si467.png).

### 11.12.1 Online and distributed learning in RKHS

One of the major drawbacks that one encounters when dealing with online algorithms in an RKHS is the growing memory problem. This is a direct consequence of the representer theorem (Section [11.6](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0055)), where the number of terms (kernels) in the expansion of the estimated function grows with *N*. Thus, in most of the online versions that have been proposed, the emphasis is on devising ad hoc techniques to reduce the number of terms in the expansion. Usually, these techniques build around the concept of a dictionary, where a subset of the points is judicially selected, according to a criterion, and subsequently used in the related expansion. In this vein, various kernel versions of the LMS (\[68,94\]), RLS (\[38,126\]), APSM and APA (\[108–112\]), and PEGASOS (Section [8.10.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml), \[62,105\]) algorithms have been suggested. A more extended treatment of this type of algorithms can be downloaded from the book's website, under the Additional Material part that is associated with the current chapter.

In contrast, one can bypass the growing memory problem if the random Fourier features (RFF) rationale is employed. The RFF framework offers a theoretically pleasing approach, without having to resort to techniques to limit the growing memory, which, in one way or another, have an ad hoc flavor. In the RFF approach, all one has to do is to generate randomly the *D* points for ***ω*** and *b* and then use the standard LMS, RLS, etc., algorithms. The power of the RFF framework becomes more evident when the online learning takes place in a distributed environment. In such a setting, all the dictionary-based methods that have been developed so far break down; this is because the dictionaries have to be exchanged among the nodes and, so far, no practically feasible method has been proposed.

The use of the RFF method in the context of online learning and in particular in a distributed environment has been presented in \[16,17\], where, also, related theoretical convergence issues are discussed. Simulation comparative results reported there reveal the power and performance gains that one can achieve. Values of *D* in the range of a few hundred seem to suffice and the performance is reported to be rather insensitive on the choice of its value, provided that this is not too small.

## 11.13 Multiple kernel learning

A major issue in all kernel-based algorithmic procedures is the selection of a suitable kernel as well as the computation of its defining parameters. Usually, this is carried out via cross-validation, where a number of different kernels are used on a validation set separate from the training data (see Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) for different methods concerning validation), and the one with the best performance is selected. It is obvious that this is not a universal approach; it is time consuming and definitely not theoretically appealing. The ideal would be to have a set of different kernels (this also includes the case of the same kernel with different parameters) and let the optimization procedure decide how to choose the proper kernel, or the proper combination of kernels. This is the scope of a research activity, which is usually called *multiple kernel learning* (MKL). To this end, a variety of MKL methods have been proposed to treat several kernel-based algorithmic schemes. A complete survey of the field is outside the scope of this book. Here, we will provide a brief overview of some of the major directions in MKL methods that relate to the content of this chapter. The interested reader is referred to \[48\] for a comparative study of various techniques.

One of the first attempts to develop an efficient MKL scheme is the one presented in \[65\], where the authors considered a linear combination of kernel matrices, that is, $K = \\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}a\_{m}K\_{m}$<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si468.png). Because we require the new kernel matrix to be positive definite, it is reasonable to impose in the optimization task some additional constraints. For example, one may adopt the general constraint *K* ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si469.png) (the inequality indicating semidefinite positiveness), or a stricter one, for example, *a*[*m*] > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si470.png), for all *m* = 1, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si471.png). Furthermore, one needs to bound the norm of the final kernel matrix. Hence, the MKL SVM task can be cast as

minimize with respect to *K* *ω*[*C*](*K*), subject to *K* ≥ 0, *t**r**a**c**e*{*K*} ≤ *c*,<mml:math><mml:mtext id="mmlbr0013">minimize with respect to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="1em" id="mmlbr0014"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0013" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">subject to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0014" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">trace</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si472.png)(11.92) 

where *ω*[*C*](*K*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si473.png) is the solution of the dual SVM task, given in Eqs. where each one of the functions, *f*[*m*], *m* = 1, 2, …*M*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si478.png), lives in a different RKHS, ℍ[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si479.png). The respective composite kernel matrix, associated with a set of training data, is given by $K = \\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}a\_{m}^{2}K\_{m}$<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si480.png), where *K*[1], …, *K*[*M*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si481.png) are the kernel matrices of the individual RKHSs. Hence, assuming a data set {(*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, …, *N*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si482.png), the MKL learning task can be formulated as follows:

$\\min\\limits\_{f}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}\\left( y\_{n},f(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) \\right) + \\lambda\\Omega(f),$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si483.png)(11.93) 

where ℒ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si484.png) represents a loss function and *Ω*(*f*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si485.png) the regularization term. There have been two major trends following this rationale. The first one gives priority toward a sparse solution, while the second aims at improving performance.

In the context of the first trend, the solution is constrained to be sparse, so that the kernel matrix is computed fast and the strong similarities between points in the data set are highlighted. Moreover, this rationale can be applied to the case where the type of kernel has been selected beforehand and the goal is to compute the optimal kernel parameters. One way (e.g., \[4,114\]) is to employ a regularization term of the form $\\Omega(f) = \\left( \\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}a\_{m}{\\| f\_{m}\\|}\_{\\mathbb{H}\_{m}} \\right)^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si486.png), which has been shown to promote sparsity among the set {*a*[1], …, *a*[*M*]}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si487.png), as it is associated to the group LASSO, when the squared error loss is employed in place of ℒ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si484.png) (see Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml)).

In contrast to the sparsity promoting criteria, another trend (e.g., \[30,63,92\]) revolves around the argument that, in some cases, the sparse MKL variants may not exhibit improved performance compared to the original learning task. Moreover, some data sets contain multiple similarities between individual data pairs that cannot be highlighted by a single type of kernel, but require a number of different kernels to improve learning. In this context, a regularization term of the form $\\Omega(f) = \\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}a\_{m}{\\| f\_{m}\\|}\_{\\mathbb{H}\_{m}}^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si488.png) is preferred. There are several variants of these methods that either employ additional constraints to the task (e.g., $\\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}a\_{m} = 1$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si489.png)) or define the summation of the spaces a little differently (e.g., $f( \\cdot ) = \\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}\\frac{1}{a\_{m}}f\_{m}( \\cdot )$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si490.png)). For example, in \[92\] the authors reformulate [(11.93)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq213) as follows:

$\\text{minimize\\ with\\ respect\\ to}\\ \\mathbf{a}\\quad J(\\mathbf{a}),\\ \\text{subject\\ to}\\ \\quad\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}a\_{m} = 1,\\quad a\_{m} \\geqslant 0,$<mml:math><mml:mtext id="mmlbr0016">minimize with respect to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="1em" id="mmlbr0017"/><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0016" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext mathvariant="normal">subject to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0017" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si491.png)(11.94) 

where

$J(\\mathbf{a}) = \\min\\limits\_{f\_{1:M},\\mathbf{\\xi},b}\\begin{Bmatrix} {\\frac{1}{2}\\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}\\frac{1}{a\_{m}}{\\| f\_{m}\\|}\_{\\mathbb{H}\_{m}}^{2} + C\\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}\\xi\_{n},} \\\\ {y\_{i}\\left( \\sum\_{m = 1}^{M}f\_{m}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) + b \\right) \\geqslant 1 - \\xi\_{n},} \\\\ {\\xi\_{n} \\geqslant 0.} \\\\ \\end{Bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo
