columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si492.png)

The optimization is cast in RKHSs; however, the problem is always formulated in such a way so that the kernel trick can be mobilized.

## 11.14 Nonparametric sparsity-aware learning: additive models

We have already pointed out that the representer theorem, as summarized by Eq. [(11.17)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq65), provides an approximation of a function, residing in an RKHS, in terms of the respective kernel centered at the points **x**[1], …, **x**[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si493.png). However, we know that the accuracy of any interpolation/approximation method depends on the number of points, *N*. Moreover, as discussed in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), how large or small *N* needs to be depends heavily on the dimensionality of the space, exhibiting an exponential dependence on it (curse of dimensionality); basically, one has to fill in the input space with “enough” data in order to be able to “learn” with good enough accuracy the associated function.^([^(81)](#fn81))

According to the additive models rationale, the unknown function is constrained within the family of *separable* functions, that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx012.jpg)(11.95) 

where **x** = \[*x*[1], …, *x*[*l*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si495.png). Recall that a special case of such expansions is the linear regression, where *f*(**x**) = **θ**^(*T*)**x**<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si496.png).

We will further assume that each one of the functions, *h*[*i*]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si497.png), belongs to an RKHS, ℍ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si498.png), defined by a respective kernel, *κ*[*i*](⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si499.png),

*κ*[*i*](⋅, ⋅ ) : ℝ × ℝ ↦ ℝ.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si500.png)

Let the corresponding norm be denoted as ∥ ⋅ ∥[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si501.png). For the regularized total squared error cost \[93\], the optimization task is now cast as

$\\text{minimize\\ with\\ respect\\ to}\\ f\\quad\\frac{1}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( y\_{n} - f(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) \\right)^{2} + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}{\\| h\_{i}\\|}\_{i},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>minimize with respect to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si502.png)(11.96) 

$\\text{s.t.}\\quad f(\\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}h\_{i}(x\_{i}).$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si503.png)(11.97) 

 Plugging Eq. [(11.97)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq220) into [(11.96)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq219) and following arguments similar to those used in Section [11.6](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0055), it is readily obtained that we can write

${\\widehat{h}}\_{i}( \\cdot ) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{i,n}\\kappa\_{i}( \\cdot ,x\_{i,n}),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si504.png)(11.98) 

where *x*[*i*, *n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si505.png) is the *i*th component of **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si252.png). Moving along the same path as that adopted in Section [11.7](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0070), the optimization can be rewritten in terms of

**θ**[*i*] = \[*θ*[*i*, 1], …, *θ*[*i*, *N*]\]^(*T*), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si506.png)

as

${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{l} = {arg\\, min}\_{{\\{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{l}}\\ J(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{l}),$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si507.png)

where

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{l}): = \\frac{1}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\mathcal{K}\_{i}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i} \\right\\|^{2} + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\sqrt{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{T}\\mathcal{K}\_{i}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si508.png)(11.99) 

and 𝒦[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si509.png), are the respective *N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si429.png) kernel matrices

stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si510.png)

Observe that Eq. [(11.99)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq224) is a (weighted) version of the *group* LASSO, defined in Section [10.3](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml). Thus, the optimization task enforces sparsity by pushing some of the vectors **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si511.png) to zero values. Any algorithm developed for the group LASSO can be employed here as well (see, for example, \[10,93\]).

Besides the squared error loss, other loss functions can also be employed. For example, in \[93\] the *logistic regression* model is also discussed. Moreover, if the separable model in Eq. [(11.95)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq217) cannot adequately capture the whole structure of *f*, models involving combination of components can be considered, such as the ANOVA model (e.g., \[67\]).

Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a method in statistics to analyze interactions among variables. According to this technique, a function *f*(**x**), **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *l* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si512.png), is decomposed into a number of terms; each term is given as a sum of functions involving a *subset* of the components of ***x***. From this point of view, separable functions of the form in Eq. [(11.95)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq217) are a special case of an ANOVA decomposition. A more general decomposition would be

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/fx013.jpg)(11.100) 

and this can be generalized to involve larger number of components. Comparing Eq. [(11.100)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq226) with Eq. [(11.2)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq2), the ANOVA decomposition can be considered as a generalization of the polynomial expansion. The same idea has already been used to decompose kernels, *κ*(**x**, **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si513.png), in terms of other kernels that are functions of a subset of the involved components of ***x*** and ***y***, giving rise to the so-called ANOVA kernels \[116\].

Techniques involving sparse additive kernel-based models have been used in a number of applications, such as matrix and tensor completion, completion of gene expression, kernel-based dictionary learning, network flow, and spectrum cartography (see \[10\] for a related review).

## 11.15 A case study: authorship identification

Text mining is the part of data mining that analyzes textual data to detect, extract, represent, and evaluate patterns that appear in texts and can be transformed into real-world knowledge. A few examples of text mining applications include spam e-mail detection, topic-based classification of texts, sentiment analysis in texts, text authorship identification, text indexing, and text summarization. In other words, the focus can be on detecting basic morphology idiosyncracies in a text that identify its author (authorship identification), on identifying complexly expressed emotions (sentiment analysis), or on condensing redundant information from multiple texts to a concise summary (summarization).

In this section, our focus will be on the case of authorship identification (for example, \[115\]), which is a special case of text classification. The task is to determine the author of a given text, given a set of training texts labeled with their corresponding author. To fulfill this task, one needs to represent and act upon textual data. Thus, the first decision related to text mining is how one represents the data.

It is very common to represent texts in a vector space, following the vector space model (VSM) \[97\]. According to the VSM, a text document, *T*, is represented by a set of terms *w*[*i*], 0 ≤ *i* ≤ *k*, *k* ∈ ℕ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si514.png), each mapped to a dimension of the vector **t** = \[*t*[1], *t*[2], …, *t*[*k*]\]^(*T*) ∈ ℝ^(*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si515.png). The elements, *t*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si516.png), in each dimension indicate the importance of the corresponding term *w*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si517.png) when describing the document. For example, each *w*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si517.png) can be one word in the vocabulary of a language. Thus, in practical applications, *k* can be very large, as large as the number of words that are considered sufficient for the specific task of interest. Typical examples of *k* are of the order of 10⁵.

Widely used approaches to assign values to *t*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si516.png) are the following:

*   •  *Bag-of-words, frequency approach*: The bag-of-words approach to text relies on the assumption that a text *T* is nothing more than a histogram of the words it contains. Thus, in the bag-of-words assumption, we do not care about the order of the words in the original text. What we care about is how many times the term *w*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si517.png) appears in the document. Thus, *t*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si516.png) is assigned the number of occurrences of *w*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si517.png) in *T*.
*   •  *Bag-of-words, Boolean approach*: The Boolean approach to the bag-of-words VSM model restricts the *t*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si516.png) values, such that *t*[*i*] ∈ {0, 1}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si518.png); *t*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si516.png) is assigned a value of 1 if *w*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si517.png) is found at least once in *T*, otherwise *t*[*i*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si519.png).

The bag-of-words approaches have proven efficient, for example, in early spam filtering applications, where individual words were clear indicators of whether an e-mail is spam. However, the spammers soon adapted and changed the texts they sent out by breaking words using spaces: the word “pills” would be replaced by “p i l l s.” The bag-of-words approach then needed to apply preprocessing to deal with such cases, or even to deal with changes in different word forms (via word stemming or lemmatization) or spelling mistakes (by using dictionaries to correct the errors).

An alternative representation, with high resilience to noise, is that of the *character n-grams*. This representation is based on character subsequences of a text of length *n* (also called the order of an *n*\-gram). To represent a text using *n*\-grams, we split the text *T* in (usually contiguous) groups of characters of length *n*, which are then mapped to dimensions in the vector space (bag-of-*n*\-grams). Below we give an example on how *n*\-grams can be extracted from a given text.

Example 11.5

Given the input text *T*\= *A\_ fine\_day\_today*, the character and word 2-grams (*n* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si520.png)) would be as follows:

*   •  *Unique* character 2-grams: *“A\_”, “\_ f”, “fi”, “in”, “ne”, “e\_”, “\_d”, “da”, “ay”, “y\_”, “\_t”, “to”, “od”.*
*   •  Unique word 2-grams: *“A\_ fine”, “fine\_day”, “day\_today”.*

Observe that “ay” and “da” appear twice in the phrase, yet only once in the sequence, since each *n*\-gram is uniquely represented. Even though this approach has proven very useful \[20\], the sequence of the *n*\-grams is still not exploited.

In the following, we describe a more complex representation, which takes into account the sequence of *n*\-grams, and at the same time allows for noise. The representation is termed *n-gram graph* \[46\]. An *n*\-gram graph is indicative on how *n*\-grams *cooccur* in a text.

Definition 11.4

If *S* = {*S*[1], *S*[2], …}, *S*[*k*] ≠ *S*[*l*],  for *k* ≠ *l*, *k*, *l* ∈ ℕ<mml:math><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mtext> for </mml:mtext><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si521.png) is the set of *distinct n*\-grams extracted from a text *T*, and *S*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si522.png) is the *i*th extracted *n*\-gram, then *G* = {*V*, *E*, *W*}<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si523.png) is a graph where *V* = *S*<mml:math><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si524.png) is the set of vertices *v*, *E* is the set of edges *e* of the form *e* = {*v*[1], *v*[2]}<mml:math><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si525.png), and *W* : *E* → ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si526.png) is a function assigning a weight *w*[*e*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si527.png) to every edge.

To generate an *n*\-gram graph, we first extract the unique *n*\-grams from a text, creating one vertex for each. Then, given a user-defined parameter distance *D*, we consider the *n*\-grams that are found *within* a distance *D* of each other in the text; these are considered *neighbors* and their respective vertices are connected with an edge. For each edge, a weight is assigned. The edge weighting function that is most commonly used in *n*\-gram graphs is the number of cooccurrences of the linked (in the graph) *n*\-grams in the text.

Two examples of 2-gram graphs, with directed neighborhood edges, with *D* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si528.png) are presented in [Figs. 11.19](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0100) and [11.20](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0105).

![Figure 11.19 The 2-gram graph (n = 2), with D = 2, of the string “A fine day.”](images/B9780443292385000172/gr019.jpg)

Figure 11.19 The 2-gram graph (*n* = 2), with *D* = 2, of the string “A fine day.”

![Figure 11.20 The 2-gram graph (n = 2), with D = 2, of the string “today.”](images/B9780443292385000172/gr020.jpg)

Figure 11.20 The 2-gram graph (*n* = 2), with *D* = 2, of the string “today.”

Between two *n*\-gram graphs, *G*^(*i*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si529.png) and *G*^(*j*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si530.png), there exists a symmetric, normalized similarity function called *value similarity* (VS). This measure quantifies the ratio of common edges between two graphs, taking into account the ratio of weights of common edges. In this measure, each matching edge *e*, having weights *w*[*e*]^(*i*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si531.png) and *w*[*e*]^(*j*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si532.png), in graphs *G*^(*i*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si529.png) and *G*^(*i*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si529.png), respectively, contributes to VS the amount $\\frac{\\text{VR}(e)}{\\text{max}(|G^{i}|,|G^{j}|)}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>VR</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si533.png), where | ⋅ |<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si534.png) indicates cardinality with respect to the number of edges and

$\\text{VR}(e): = \\frac{\\text{min}(w\_{e}^{i},w\_{e}^{j})}{\\text{max}(w\_{e}^{i},w\_{e}^{j})}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>VR</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si535.png)(11.101) 

Not matching edges have no contribution (consider that for an edge *e* ∉ *G*^(*i*)(*G*^(*j*))<mml:math><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si536.png), we define *w*[*e*]^(*i*) = 0 (*w*[*e*]^(*j*) = 0)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si537.png)). The equation indicates that the *Value ratio* (VR) takes values in \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si538.png), and it is symmetric. Thus, the full equation for the VS is

$\\text{VS}(G^{i},G^{j}) = \\frac{\\sum\_{e \\in G^{i}}\\frac{\\text{min}(w\_{e}^{i},w\_{e}^{j})}{\\text{max}(w\_{e}^{i},w\_{e}^{j})}}{\\text{max}(|G^{i}|,|G^{j}|)}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>VS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si539.png)(11.102) 

The VS takes a value close to 1 for graphs that share many edges with similar weights. A value of VS = 1<mml:math><mml:mtext>VS</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si540.png) indicates a perfect match between the compared graphs. For the two graphs shown in [Figs. 11.19](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0100) and [11.20](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#f0105), the calculation of the VS returns a value of VS = 0.067<mml:math><mml:mtext>VS</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.067</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si541.png) (verify it).

For our case study, the VS will be used to build an SVM kernel classifier, in order to assign (classify) texts to their authors. We should stress here that the VS function is a similarity function, but not a kernel. Fortunately, the VS on the specific data set is an (*ϵ*, *γ*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si542.png)\-good similarity function as defined in \[6, Theorem 3\], and hence this allows its use as a kernel function, in line with what we have already said about string kernels in Section [11.5.2](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0040).

It is interesting to note that given the VSM representation of a text, one can also employ any vector-based kernel on strings. Moreover, there have been several works that use *string kernels* \[69\] to avoid any loss of information in the transformation between the original string and its VSM equivalent. In this example, we demonstrate how one can combine even a complex representation with the SVM via an appropriate kernel function.

The data set we used to examine the effectiveness of this combination is a subset of the [Reuter\_50\_50 Data Set](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Reuter_50_50) from the UCI repository \[5\]. This data set contains 2500 training and 2500 test texts from 50 different authors (50 training and 50 test texts per author).

*   •  First, we used the [ngg2svm](https://github.com/ggianna/ngg2svm) command line tool^([^(82)](#fn82))
*   •  Given the kernel matrix, we can use the LibSVM software \[24\] to design a classifier, without caring about the original texts, but only relying on precomputed kernel values.

Then, a 10-fold cross-validation over the data was performed, using the “svmtrain” program in LibSVM. The achieved accuracy of the cross-validation in our example was 94%.

1.  11.14  Consider the regression problem described in [Example 11.2](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#enun0070). Read an audio file using MATLAB®'s wavread function and take 100 data samples (use *Blade Runner*, if possible, and take 100 samples starting from the 100, 000<mml:math><mml:mn>100</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si556.png)th sample). Then add white Gaussian noise at a 15 dB level and randomly “hit” 10 of the data samples with outliers (set the outlier values to 80% of the maximum value of the data samples). 
    1.  **(a)**  Find the reconstructed data samples using the unbiased kernel ridge regression method, that is, Eq. [(11.27)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#deq88). Employ the Gaussian kernel with *σ* = 0.004<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.004</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si222.png) and set *C* = 0.0001<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si557.png). Plot the fitted curve of the reconstructed samples together with the data used for training. 
    2.  **(b)**  Find the reconstructed data samples using the biased kernel ridge regression method (employ the same parameters as for the unbiased case). Plot the fitted curve of the reconstructed samples together with the data used for training.

For each point, compute

*y*[*n*] = 0.05*x*[*n*, 1]³ + 0.05*x*[*n*, 1]² + 0.05*x*[*n*, 1] + 0.05 + *η*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

Then, if *x*[*n*, 2] ≥ *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si409.png), assign it to *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si55.png), and if *x*[*n*, 2] < *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si565.png), assign it to class *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si56.png). 
    1.  **(a)**  Plot the points \[*x*[*n*, 1], *x*[*n*, 2]\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si566.png) using different colors for each class.
    2.  **(b)**  Obtain the SVM classifier using libsvm or any other related MATLAB® package. Use the Gaussian kernel with *σ* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si410.png) and set *C* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si412.png). Plot the classifier and the margin (for the latter you can employ MATLAB®'s contour function). Moreover, find the support vectors (i.e., the points with nonzero Lagrange multipliers that contribute to the expansion of the classifier) and plot them as circled points.
    3.  **(c)**  Repeat step 11.16b using *C* = 0.5, 0.1<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si567.png), and 0.05.
    4.  **(d)**  Repeat step 11.16b using *C* = 5, 10, 50<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>50</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000172/si568.png), and 100.
    5.  **(e)**  Comment on the results.
2.  11.17  Consider the authorship identification problem described in Section [11.15](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml#s0175). 
    1.  **(a)**  Using the training texts of the authors whose names start with “T” in the data set, perform 10-fold cross-validation using the *n*\-gram graph representation of the texts and the VS as a kernel function.
    2.  **(b)**  Using the same subset of the data set, create the vector space model representation of the texts and apply classification using a Gaussian kernel. Compare the results with the results of (a).
