## 12.1 Introduction

The Bayesian approach to parameter inference was introduced in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). Compared to other methods for parameter estimation we have covered, the Bayesian method adopts a radically different viewpoint. The unknown set of parameters is treated as random variables instead of as a set of fixed (yet unknown) values. This was a revolutionary idea at the time it was introduced by Bayes and later on by Laplace, as pointed out in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). Even now, after more than two centuries, it may seem strange to assume that a physical phenomenon/mechanism is controlled by a set of random parameters. However, there is a subtle point here. Treating the underlying set of parameters as random variables, **θ**, we do not really imply a random nature for them. The associated randomness, in terms of the prior distribution *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png), encapsulates our *uncertainty* about their values, prior to receiving any measurements/observations. Stated differently, the prior distribution represents our *belief* about the different possible values, although only one of them is actually true. From this perspective, probabilities are viewed in a more “open-minded” way, that is, as measures of uncertainty, as discussed in the beginning of Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml).

Recall that parameter learning from data is an inverse problem. Basically, all we do is deduce the “causes” (parameters) from the “effects” (observations). The Bayes theorem can be seen as an inversion procedure expressed in a probabilistic context. Indeed, given the set of observations, say, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png), which are controlled by the unknown set of parameters, we write

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathcal{X}) = \\frac{p(\\mathcal{X}|\\mathbf{\\theta})p(\\mathbf{\\theta})}{p(\\mathcal{X})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si3.png)

In other words, the posterior PDF, *p*(**θ**|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si4.png), which describes the “causes” given the “effects”, is expressed in terms of the conditional PDF, *p*(𝒳|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si5.png), that describes the “effects” given the “causes”. All that is needed for the above inversion is to have a guess about the prior PDF, *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png). This term has brought a lot of controversy in the statistical community for a number of years. However, once a reasonable guess of the prior is available, a number of advantages associated with the Bayesian approach emerge, compared to the alternative route. The latter embraces methods that view the parameters deterministically as constants of unknown values, and they are also referred to as *frequentist* techniques. The term comes from the more classical view of probabilities as frequencies of occurrence of repeatable events. A typical example of this family of methods is the maximum likelihood approach, which estimates the values of the parameters by maximizing *p*(𝒳; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si6.png); the value of the latter probability density function (PDF) is solely controlled by the obtained observations in a sequence of experiments.

This is the first of two chapters dedicated to Bayesian learning. We present the main concepts and philosophy behind Bayesian inference. We introduce the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and apply it in some typical machine learning parametric modeling tasks, such as regression, mixture modeling, and mixture of experts. Finally, the exponential family of distributions is introduced and the notion of conjugate priors is discussed.

## 12.2 Regression: a Bayesian perspective

The Bayesian inference treatment of the linear regression task was introduced in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). In the current chapter, we go beyond the basic definitions and reveal and exploit various possibilities that the Bayesian philosophy offers to the study of this important machine learning task. Let us first summarize the findings of Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) and then start building upon them.^([^(84)](#fn84))

Recall the (generalized) linear regression task, as it was introduced in previous chapters, that is,

$y = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\eta = \\theta\_{0} + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K - 1}\\theta\_{k}\\phi\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\eta,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si7.png)(12.1) 

where *y* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si8.png) is the output random variable, **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si434.png) is the input random vector, *η* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si10.png) is the noise disturbance, **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si11.png) is the unknown parameter vector, and

**ϕ**(**x**) :  = \[*ϕ*[1](**x**), …, *ϕ*[*K* − 1](**x**), 1\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si12.png)

where *ϕ*[*k*], *k* = 1, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si13.png), are some (fixed) basis functions. As we already know, typical examples of such functions can be the Gaussian function, splines, monomials, and others. We are given a set of *N* output–input training points, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si14.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si15.png). In our current setting, we assume that the respective (unobserved) noise values *η*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si16.png), are samples of jointly Gaussian distributed random variables of zero mean and with covariance matrix *Σ*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si17.png), that is,

$p(\\mathbf{\\eta}) = \\frac{1}{{(2\\pi)}^{N/2}|\\Sigma\_{\\eta}|^{1/2}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{\\eta}^{T}\\Sigma\_{\\eta}^{- 1}\\mathbf{\\eta} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si18.png)(12.2) 

where **η** = \[*η*[1], *η*[2], …, *η*[*N*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si19.png).

### 12.2.1 The maximum likelihood estimator

The maximum likelihood (ML) method was introduced in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). According to the method, the unknown set of parameters is treated as a deterministic vector variable, ***θ***, which parameterizes the PDF that describes the output vector of observations

**y** = *Φ***θ** + **η**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si20.png)(12.3) 

where

$\\Phi = \\begin{bmatrix} {\\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{x}\_{1})} \\\\ {\\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{x}\_{2})} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ {\\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{x}\_{N})} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋮</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si21.png)(12.4) 

and

**y** = \[*y*[1], *y*[2], …, *y*[*N*]\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si22.png)

A simple replacement of *X* with Φ in Eq. [(3.61)](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) changes the ML estimate to

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{ML} = \\left( \\Phi^{T}\\Sigma\_{\\eta}^{- 1}\\Phi \\right)^{- 1}\\Phi^{T}\\Sigma\_{\\eta}^{- 1}\\mathbf{y}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ML</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si23.png)(12.5) 

For the simple case of uncorrelated noise samples of equal variance *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si106.png) (*Σ*[*η*] = *σ*[*η*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si25.png)), Eq. [(12.5)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq8) becomes identical to the least-squares (LS) solution

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{ML} = \\left( \\Phi^{T}\\Phi \\right)^{- 1}\\Phi^{T}\\mathbf{y} = {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{LS}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ML</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">LS</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si26.png)(12.6) 

A major drawback of the ML approach is that it is vulnerable to overfitting, because no care is taken of complex models that try to “learn” the specificities of the particular training set, as already discussed in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml).

### 12.2.2 The MAP estimator

According to the maximum a posteriori probability (MAP) method, the unknown set of parameters is treated as a random vector **θ** and its posterior, for a given set of output observations, ***y***, is expressed as

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{y}) = \\frac{p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{\\theta})p(\\mathbf{\\theta})}{p(\\mathbf{y})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si27.png)(12.7) 

where *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png) is the associated prior PDF. We have eliminated from the notation the dependence on 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png), to make it look simpler. We emphasize that the input set, 𝒳 = {**x**[1], …, **x**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si28.png), is considered fixed, so all the randomness associated with the output random variables, **y**, is due to the noise source. Assuming both the prior and the conditional PDFs to be Gaussians,^([^(85)](#fn85))

*p*(**θ**) = 𝒩(**θ**|**θ**[0], *Σ*[*θ*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si30.png)(12.8) 

and

*p*(**y**|**θ**) = 𝒩(**y**|*Φ***θ**, *Σ*[*η*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si31.png)(12.9) 

where Eqs. [(12.2)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq4) and [(12.3)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq5) have been used, the posterior *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png) turns out also to be Gaussian with mean vector

**μ**[*θ*|*y*] :  = 𝔼\[**θ**|**y**\] = **θ**[0] + (*Σ*[*θ*]^( − 1)+*Φ*^(*T*)*Σ*[*η*]^( − 1)*Φ*)^( − 1)*Φ*^(*T*)*Σ*[*η*]^( − 1)(**y**−*Φ***θ**[0]).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si33.png)(12.10) 

Because the maximum of a Gaussian coincides with its mean, we have

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{MAP} = \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{y}\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si34.png)(12.11) 

In the present chapter's appendix, an analytical proof of Eq. [(12.10)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq13) is provided.^([^(86)](#fn86))

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{MAP} = \\left( \\lambda I + \\Phi^{T}\\Phi \\right)^{- 1}\\Phi^{T}\\mathbf{y},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si46.png)(12.12) 

where we have set $\\lambda: = \\frac{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}{\\sigma\_{\\theta}^{2}}$<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si47.png). We already know from Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) that the value of *λ* is critical to the performance of the estimator with respect to the mean-square error (MSE) performance. The main issue now becomes how to choose a good value for *λ*, or equivalently for *Σ*[*θ*], *Σ*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si48.png) in the more general case. In practice, the cross-validation method (Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)) is employed; different values of *λ* are tested and the one that leads to the best MSE (or some other criterion) is selected. However, this is a computationally costly procedure, especially for complex models, where a large number of parameters are involved. Moreover, such a procedure forces us to use only a fraction of the available data for training, to reserve the rest for testing. The reader may wonder why we do not use the training data to optimize with respect to both the unknown parameter vector ***θ*** and the regularization parameter. Let us consider as an example the simpler case of ridge regression, for centered data (*θ*[0] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si49.png)). The cost function comprises two terms, one that is data dependent and measures the misfit and one that depends only on the unknown parameters,

*J*(**θ**, *λ*) = ∥**y** − *Φ***θ**∥² + *λ*∥**θ**∥².<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si50.png)(12.13) 

It is obvious that the only value of *λ* that leads to the minimum squared error fit *over the training data set* (empirical loss) is *λ* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si51.png). Any other value of *λ* would result in an estimate of ***θ*** which scores larger values of the squared error term; this is natural, because for *λ* ≠ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si52.png) the optimization has to take care of the extra regularizing term, too. It is only when *test data sets* are employed, where values of *λ* ≠ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si52.png) lead to an overall decrease of the MSE (not the empirical one).

### 12.2.3 The Bayesian approach

The Bayesian approach to regression attempts to overcome the previously reported drawbacks, which are associated with the overfitting. All the involved parameters can be estimated on the training set. In this vein, the parameters will be treated as random variables. At the same time, because the main task now becomes that of inferring the PDF that describes the unknown set of parameters, instead of obtaining a single vector estimate, one has more information at her/his disposal. Having said that, it does not mean that Bayesian techniques are necessarily free from cross-validation; this will be needed to assess their overall performance. We will comment further on this in the Remarks at the end of Section [12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0035).

As we know, the starting point is the same as that for MAP, and in particular Eq. [(12.7)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq10). However, instead of taking just the maximum of the numerator in Eq. [(12.7)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq10), we will make use of *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png) as a whole. Most of the secrets here lie in the denominator *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si54.png), which is basically the normalizing constant,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx001.jpg)(12.14) 

As we will soon see, there is much more information hidden in *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si54.png) that goes beyond the need of just computing *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png). The difficulty with Eq. [(12.14)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq17) is that, in general, the evaluation of the integral cannot be performed analytically. In such cases, one has to resort to approximate techniques to obtain the required information. To this end, a number of approaches are available, and a large part of this book is dedicated to their study. More specifically, the following methods have been proposed and will be considered:

*   •  the Laplacian approximation method, presented in Section [12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0035);
*   •  the variational approximation method, presented in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml);
*   •  the variational bound approximation method, presented in Section [13.8](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml);
*   •  Monte Carlo techniques for the evaluation of the integral, which are discussed in Chapter [14](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml);
*   •  message passing algorithms, to be discussed in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml).

For the case under study in this section, where *p*(**y**|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si146.png) and *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png) are both assumed to be Gaussians, *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si54.png) can be evaluated analytically; it turns out that the joint distribution *p*(**y**, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si56.png) is also Gaussian and hence the marginal *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si54.png) is Gaussian as well. All these are shown in detail in the appendix of this chapter. Indeed, if we set in Eqs. (12.146) and (12.151) of the appendix **z** → **θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si36.png), **t** → **y**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si35.png), and *A* → *Φ*<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si37.png), it turns out that for the regression model of Eq. [(12.3)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq5) and the prior PDF in Eq. [(12.8)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq11) as well as the noise model of Eq. [(12.2)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq4), we obtain

*p*(**y**) = 𝒩(**y**|*Φ***θ**[0],*Σ*[*η*]+*Φ**Σ*[*θ*]*Φ*^(*T*)).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si59.png)(12.15) 

Moreover, the posterior *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png) is also Gaussian,

*p*(**θ**|**y**) = 𝒩(**θ**|**μ**[*θ*|*y*],*Σ*[*θ*|*y*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si60.png)(12.16) 

where **μ**[*θ*|*y*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si61.png) is given by Eq. [(12.10)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq13) and the covariance matrix results from Eq. (12.147), after the appropriate notational substitutions, that is,

*Σ*[*θ*|*y*] = (*Σ*[*θ*]^( − 1)+*Φ*^(*T*)*Σ*[*η*]^( − 1)*Φ*)^( − 1).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si62.png)(12.17) 

The posterior PDF in Eq. [(12.16)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq19) encapsulates our knowledge about **θ**, after the observations ***y*** have been obtained. Hence, our uncertainty about **θ** has been reduced, which is the main reason that Eq. [(12.16)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq19) is different from the prior PDF in Eq. [(12.8)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq11); the latter represents only our initial guess. The covariance matrix in Eq. [(12.17)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq20) provides the information about our uncertainty with respect to **θ**. If the Gaussian in Eq. [(12.16)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq19) is very broad around its mean **μ**[*θ*|*y*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si61.png), it indicates that in spite of the reception of the observations still much uncertainty about **θ** remains. This can be due (a) to the nature of the problem, for example, high noise variance, as this is conveyed by *Σ*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si17.png), (b) to the number of observations, *N*, which may not be enough, and/or (c) to modeling inaccuracies, as this is conveyed by Φ in Eq. [(12.17)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq20). The opposite comments are in order if the posterior PDF is sharply peaked around its mean.

As we have already stated in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), the Bayesian philosophy provides the means for a direct inference of the output variable, which in many applications is the quantity of interest; given the input vector, the task is to predict the output. In such cases, estimating a value for the unknown **θ** is only the means to an end. To formulate the prediction task directly, without involving **θ**, one has to integrate the contribution of **θ**. Having learned the posterior *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png), given a new input vector ***x***, for the regression model in Eq. [(12.1)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq2), the conditional PDF of the output variable, y, given the set of observations, is written as

*p*(*y*|**x**, **y**) = ∫*p*(*y*|**x**, **θ**)*p*(**θ**|**y**) *d***θ**.<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si63.png)(12.18) 

Note that we have used *p*(*y*|**x**, **y**, **θ**) = *p*(*y*|**x**, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si64.png) because y that corresponds to the new sample, ***x***, is conditionally independent of the observation variables, **y**, associated with the training set, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png), given the value of ***θ***. As already stated, strictly speaking, the posterior should have been denoted as *p*(**θ**|**y**; 𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si65.png) to indicate the dependence on the input training samples. However, the dependence on 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png) has been suppressed to unclutter notation.

In the sequel, and in order to simplify algebra and focus on the concepts, we assume that the noise model in Eq. [(12.2)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq4) is such that *Σ*[*η*] = *σ*[*η*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si25.png) and also *Σ*[*θ*] = *σ*[*θ*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si172.png) for the prior PDF in Eq. [(12.8)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq11). Then we have

*p*(*y*|**x**, **θ**) = 𝒩(*y*|**θ**^(*T*)**ϕ**(**x**),*σ*[*η*]²),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

Hence, given ***x*** one can predict the respective value of *y* using the most probable value, that is, *μ*[*y*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si75.png) in Eq. [(12.22)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq26). Note that the same prediction value would result via the MAP estimate in Eq. [(12.10)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq13) (or Eq. [(12.12)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq15), if **θ**[0] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si173.png), also obtained via the ridge regression task). Have we then gained anything extra by adopting the Bayesian approach? The answer is in the affirmative. *More information concerning the predicted value is now available, because* Eq. [(12.23)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq27) *quantifies the associated uncertainty*.

To investigate Eq. [(12.23)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq27) further, let us simplify it by adopting the following approximation:

$R\_{\\phi}: = \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x})\\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack \\approx \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n})\\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) = \\frac{1}{N}\\Phi^{T}\\Phi,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si77.png)

or

*Φ*^(*T*)*Φ* ≈ *N**R*[*ϕ*],<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si78.png)(12.24) 

where *R*[*ϕ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si79.png) is the autocorrelation matrix of the random vector **ϕ**(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si80.png). Employing Eq. [(12.24)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq29) into Eq. [(12.23)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq27) leads to

*σ*[*y*]² ≈ *σ*[*η*]²(1+*σ*[*θ*]²**ϕ**^(*T*)(**x**)(*σ*[*η*]²*I*+*N**σ*[*θ*]²*R*[*ϕ*])^( − 1)**ϕ**(**x**)),<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si81.png)(12.25) 

which for large enough *N* becomes

$\\sigma\_{y}^{2} \\approx \\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}\\left( 1 + \\frac{1}{N}\\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{x})R\_{\\phi}^{- 1}\\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si82.png)

Thus, for a large number of observations, *σ*[*y*]² → *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si83.png), and our uncertainty is contributed by the noise source, which cannot be reduced anymore. For smaller values of *N*, there is extra uncertainty associated with the parameter **θ**, measured by *σ*[*θ*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si174.png) in Eq. [(12.25)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq30).

So far in this section, we dealt with Gaussians, which led to tractable and analytically computed integrals. Are there ways to attack more general cases? Moreover, even in the case of Gaussian PDFs, we have assumed the covariance matrices *Σ*[*θ*], *Σ*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si48.png) to be known. In practice, they are not. Even if one assumes that *Σ*[*η*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si17.png) can be experimentally measured, there still remains *Σ*[*θ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si42.png). Can one select the related parameters via an optimization process? If the answer is yes, can this optimization be carried out on the training set, or one would necessarily run into problems similar to the ones we faced with the regularization approach? We will indulge in all these challenges in the sections to follow.

Remarks 12.1

*   •  The MAP estimator is sometimes referred to as *Type I* estimator, to be distinguished from the Type II estimation method, which will be discussed in [Remarks 12.2](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#enun0020), in the next section.
*   •  The posterior mean in Eq. [(12.10)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq13) can be met in different variants, which are obtained via the application of the matrix inversion lemmas given in Appendix A.1. In the chapter's appendix, it is shown that (Eq. (12.152))

**μ**[*θ*|*y*] = (*Σ*[*θ*]^( − 1)+*Φ*^(*T*)*Σ*[*η*]^( − 1)*Φ*)^( − 1)(*Φ*^(*T*)*Σ*[*η*]^( − 1)**y**+*Σ*[*θ*]^( − 1)**θ**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si86.png)(12.26) 

*   or (Eq. (12.148))

**μ**[*θ*|*y*] = **θ**[0] + *Σ*[*θ*]*Φ*^(*T*)(*Σ*[*η*]+*Φ**Σ*[*θ*]*Φ*^(*T*))^( − 1)(**y**−*Φ***θ**[0]).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si87.png)(12.27) 

*   
*   Also, using Woodbury's identity from Appendix A.1, we can readily see that

*Σ*[*θ*|*y*] = *Σ*[*θ*] − *Σ*[*θ*]*Φ*^(*T*)(*Σ*[*η*]+*Φ**Σ*[*θ*]*Φ*^(*T*))^( − 1)*Φ**Σ*[*θ*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si88.png)(12.28) 

*   
*   In practice, one uses the most computationally convenient form, depending on the dimensionality of the involved matrices to invert the one of lower dimension.

Example 12.1

This example demonstrates the prediction task summarized in Eqs. [(12.22)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq26) and [(12.23)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq27). Data are generated based on the following nonlinear model:

*y*[*n*] = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x*[*n*] + *θ*[2]*x*[*n*]² + *θ*[3]*x*[*n*]³ + *θ*[5]*x*[*n*]⁵ + *η*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" where *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si94.png) are i.i.d. noise samples drawn from a zero mean Gaussian with variance *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si106.png). Samples *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si95.png) are equidistant points in the interval \[0, 2\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si96.png). The goal of the task is to predict the value *y* given a measured value *x*, using Eq. [(12.22)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq26). The parameter values used to generate the data were equal to

*θ*[0] = 0.2, *θ*[1] =  − 1, *θ*[2] = 0.9, *θ*[3] = 0.7, *θ*[5] =  − 0.2.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>
