*y* = *θ*[0] + *θ*[1]*x* + *θ*[2]*x*² + *η*.<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>η</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si107.png)

1.  The used values were *σ*[*η*]² = 0.05<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si90.png), *N* = 500<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>500</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si102.png), and *σ*[*θ*]² = 2<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si103.png). Observe that once a wrong model has been adopted, one must not have “high expectations” for good prediction performance.

## 12.3 The evidence function and Occam's razor rule

In the previous section, we made a comment about the importance of the marginal PDF *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si54.png). This section is fully dedicated to this quantity. In the notation used in Eq. [(12.14)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq17), we did tacitly suppress the dependence on the adopted model. For example, the Gaussian assumption for the prior in Eq. [(12.8)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq11) and for the conditional in Eq. [(12.9)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq12) should have been reflected in the marginal as *p*(**y**; **ϕ**, *Σ*[*η*], *Σ*[*θ*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si108.png), because different Gaussians, different basis functions, and different orders *K* of the model can be used. Furthermore, non-Gaussian PDFs can also be adopted. In a more general setting, let us make the dependence on the model explicit as *p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si109.png). Assuming the choice of a model to be random, mobilizing the Bayes theorem once more, we have

$P(\\mathcal{M}\_{i}|\\mathbf{y}) = \\frac{P(\\mathcal{M}\_{i})p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i})}{p(\\mathbf{y})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si110.png)(12.29) 

where

$p(\\mathbf{y}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i}P(\\mathcal{M}\_{i})p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si111.png)(12.30) 

and *P*(ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si112.png) is the prior probability of ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png); *P*(ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si112.png) provides a measure of the subjective prior over all possible models, which expresses our guess on how plausible a model is with respect to alternative ones, prior to the data arrival. Because the denominator in Eq. [(12.29)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq39) is independent of the model, one can obtain the most probable model, after observing ***y***, by maximizing the numerator. If one assigns to all possible models equal probabilities, then detecting the most probable model under the given set of observations becomes a task of maximizing *p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si109.png) with respect to the model, ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png). This is the reason that this PDF is known as the *evidence function* for the model or simply as the *evidence*. In practice, we content ourselves with using the most probable model, although an orthodox Bayesian would suggest to average all obtained quantities over all possible models, as in Eq. [(12.30)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq40). In an ideal Bayesian setting, one does not choose among models; predictions are performed by summing over all possible models, each one weighted by the respective probability. However, in many practical problems we may have reasons to suggest that the evidence function is strongly peaked around a specific model; after all, such an assumption may simplify the task considerably.

From a mathematical formulation's point of view, each model is expressed in terms of a set of nonrandom (deterministic) parameters. To get the model that maximizes the evidence is equivalent to maximizing with respect to these parameters. For example, let us assume that in the regression task we adopt a Gaussian distribution for the noise and a Gaussian prior for the regression task random parameters, **θ**. Then this pair of Gaussians comprises our model and the parameters that describe it are the respective covariance matrices for the two Gaussians as well as the mean value of the prior. To distinguish from the random parameters, **θ**, which describe the original learning task (e.g., regression), these additional parameters are often called *hyperparameters*. Later on, in Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), we will see that the hyperparameters can also be treated as random variables. We now turn our attention to what is hidden behind the optimization of *p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si109.png) with respect to different models. Before we proceed, it is worth making a comment. A superficial first look may lead one to think whether this is any different from maximizing the likelihood *p*(**y**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si116.png), as done in Section [12.2.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0020). As a matter of fact, the two cases belong to two different worlds. ML maximizes with respect to a single (vector) parameter within an adopted model, and this is the weak point that makes ML vulnerable to overfitting. Maximizing the evidence is an optimization task with respect to the model itself, a wise alternative that guards us against overfitting, as we explain next.

From Eq. [(12.14)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq17) we have

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx003.jpg)(12.31) 

Let us assume for simplicity that *θ* is a scalar, *θ* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si119.png), and that the integrand in Eq. [(12.31)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq41), which according to the Bayes theorem is analogous to the posterior *p*(*θ*|**y**, ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si120.png), peaks around a value; this is obviously the value that would result as the MAP estimate, *θ̂*[*M**A**P*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si117.png). [Fig. 12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0020) illustrates the respective graphs. Thus, Eq. [(12.31)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq41) can be approximated by

*p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*]) ≈ *p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*], *θ̂*[*M**A**P*])*p*(*θ̂*[*M**A**P*]|ℳ[*i*])*Δ**θ*[*θ*|*y*].<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si122.png)(12.32) 

To get a better feeling for each one of the factors involved in Eq. [(12.32)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq42), let us also assume that the prior PDF is (almost) uniform with a width equal to Δ*θ*. Then Eq. [(12.32)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq42) is rewritten as

$p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i}) \\approx p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i},{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{MAP})\\frac{\\Delta\\theta\_{\\theta|y}}{\\Delta\\theta}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si123.png)(12.33) 

The first factor in the product on the right-hand side in Eq. [(12.33)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq43) coincides with the likelihood function at its optimal value, because for this case of uniform prior, *θ̂*[MAP] = *θ̂*[ML]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MAP</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>ML</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si124.png). In other words, this factor provides us with the best fit that model ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png) can achieve on the given set of observations. However, now, in contrast to the ML method, the evidence function also depends on the second factor, $\\frac{\\Delta\\theta\_{\\theta|y}}{\\Delta\\theta}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si125.png). As it has been pointed out in the insightful papers \[13,27,28\], this term accounts for the complexity of the model, and it is named the Occam factor for obvious reasons. Let us elaborate on this a bit more by following the reasoning given in \[28\].

![Figure 12.3 The posterior peaks around the value {\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{MAP}Equation and the posterior PDF can be approximated by p({\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{MAP}|\\mathbf{y};\\mathcal{M}\_{i})Equation over an interval of values equal to Δθθ|y.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#cf0430) The posterior peaks around the value *θ̂*[*M**A**P*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si117.png) and the posterior PDF can be approximated by *p*(*θ̂*[*M**A**P*]|**y**; ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si118.png) over an interval of values equal to Δ*θ*[*θ*|*y*].

The Occam factor penalizes those models which are finely tuned to the received observations. As an example, if two different models ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png) and ℳ[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si126.png) have a similar range of values for their prior PDFs, then if, say, *Δ**θ*[*θ*|*y*](ℳ[*i*]) ≪ *Δ**θ*[*θ*|*y*](ℳ[*j*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si127.png), then ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png) will be penalized more; only a small range of values for *θ* survive (i.e., correspond to high probability values) after the reception of ***y***. So, if this fine-tuned (to the data) model ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png) resulted in a large value of the ML term, it would not be certain that the evidence would be maximized for it, because the Occam factor would be small. Which model, between the two, finally wins it depends on the product of the two involved terms. Soon we will see that the Occam term is also related to the number of parameters, that is, to the complexity of the adopted model.

### Laplacian approximation and the evidence function

To investigate the evidence function for the general multiparameter case, we will employ the method of Laplacian approximation of a PDF. This is a general methodology that approximates any PDF *locally* in terms of a Gaussian one. To this end, define^([^(87)](#fn87))

*g*(**θ**) = ln (*p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*],**θ**)*p*(**θ**|ℳ[*i*])).<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si130.png)(12.34) 

Use Taylor's expansion around ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{MAP}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">MAP</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si131.png) and keep terms up to the second order,

and taking the logarithms we have

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx004.jpg)(12.38) 

The direct dependence of the Occam term on the complexity (number of basis functions) of the adopted model is now readily spotted. Moreover, the complexity-related Occam term depends on the prior PDF and the second derivatives (via *Σ*) of the conditional PDF, too; that is, it depends on how “sharp” the shape of the latter is in the *K*\-dimensional space. In other words, the covariance term controls the “error bar” information. Moreover, its determinant does depend on *K*, too. That is, the dependence on the complexity term *K* is more involved than what a naive look at Eq. [(12.38)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq49) suggests (see [Remarks 12.2](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#enun0020), concerning the BIC criterion). Hence, in a single equation, besides the number of parameters and the associated best-fit term, the evidence also takes into account information related to the associated variance; maximizing the evidence leads to the best tradeoff. [Fig. 12.4](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0025) illustrates the essence behind the evidence maximization for model selection. If the model is too complex, it can fit well a wide range of data sets, and because *p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si109.png) has to integrate to one, its value for any value of ***y*** is expected to be low. The opposite is true for models that are too simple; such models can model well some data sets but not a wide range of them, and consequently, the evidence function peaks sharply around a value in the space of observation sets. Thus, selecting a data set at random, it is rather unlikely that this has been generated by such a model. Having said that, it is important to emphasize, once more, the Occam term does not depend *solely* on the number of parameters; hence, complexity here should be interpreted in a more “open-minded” way. This robustness against overfitting, which is intrinsic in the Bayesian inference approach, is the consequence of integrating the parameters for any specific model in Eq. [(12.31)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq41); this integration penalizes models of high complexity because such models can model a large range of data.

![Figure 12.4 Too simple models can explain well a very small range of data. On the other hand, too complex models can explain a wide range of data; however, they do not provide any confidence because they assign low probability to all data sets. For the observation set, y, the evidence is maximized for the model with intermediate complexity.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 12.4](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#cf0485) Too simple models can explain well a very small range of data. On the other hand, too complex models can explain a wide range of data; however, they do not provide any confidence because they assign low probability to all data sets. For the observation set, ***y***, the evidence is maximized for the model with intermediate complexity.

Historically, the Occam's razor rule in its Bayesian interpretation was first demonstrated in \[13\] and later on in \[27,43\], although the foundations go back to the pioneering work of Sir Herald Jeffrey in the 1930s \[23\]. Two insightful reviews on the Bayesian inference approach that are well worth reading are given in \[22,26\].

Returning to Eq. [(12.14)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq17) and assuming for simplicity that

*p*(**y**|**θ**) = 𝒩(**y**|*Φ***θ**,*σ*[*η*]²*I*)   and  *p*(**θ**) = 𝒩(**θ**|**θ**[0],*σ*[*θ*]²*I*),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si137.png)(12.39) 

we can express the evidence as *p*(**y**; *σ*[*η*]², *σ*[*θ*]²)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si138.png), which, for this case, turns out to be Gaussian (appendix of this chapter); thus, it is available in closed form. Hence for this specific case, the model space is described via the hyperparameters *σ*[*η*]², *σ*[*θ*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si139.png) and maximization of the evidence with respect to these (unknown) model parameters can take place iteratively, for the given set of observations stacked in ***y*** (see, for example, \[27\]). However, in general we do not have the ability to express the evidence in closed form. The EM algorithm, which is described in Section [12.4](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0045), is a popular way and a powerful tool to this end. One could also resort to the Laplacian approximation to approximate the involved PDFs as Gaussians, but this approximation turns out not always to be a good choice; furthermore, in high-dimensional parameter spaces, the computations of the second-order derivatives and the determinant can become burdensome \[3\].

Finally, let us make a final comment concerning the Laplacian approximation. In the discussion above, our goal was to get an approximation of the integral (normalizing constant/evidence) of *p*(**y**|ℳ[*i*], **θ**)*p*(**θ**|ℳ[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si140.png). However, if our interest were to approximate the PDF itself, we should involve the normalizing constant, which by the nature of the Gaussian function leads to

$p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i},\\mathbf{\\theta})p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i}) \\approx \\frac{1}{{(2\\pi)}^{K/2}|\\Sigma|^{1/2}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}{(\\mathbf{\\theta} - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{MAP})}^{T}\\Sigma^{- 1}(\\mathbf{\\theta} - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{MAP}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi This is also the case for the Laplacian approximation for any PDF *p*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si142.png). 

Remarks 12.2

*   •  In the Bayesian approach, one makes all the modeling assumptions explicit, and it is then left to the rules of probability theory to provide the answers. One does not have to “worry” about the choice of an optimizing criterion, where different criteria lead to different estimators, and there is not an objective, systematic way to decide which criterion is best. On the other hand, in the Bayesian approach one has to make sure to select the prior that explains the data in the best possible way.
*   •  The choice of the prior PDF is very critical in the performance of Bayesian methods and must be carried out in such a way to encapsulate prior knowledge as fully as possible. In practice, different alternatives can be adopted \[3\]. 
    1.  –  *Subjective priors*. According to this path, we choose the prior *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png) to make the manipulation of the integration tractable, e.g., by employing conjugate priors (Section [3.11.1](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)) within the exponential family of PDFs. This family of PDFs will be presented in Section [12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0075).
    2.  –  *Hierarchical priors*. Each one of the components of *θ*[*k*], *k* = 0, 2, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si143.png), of **θ**, is controlled by a different hyperparameter; for example, all *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si144.png)s may be assumed to be independent Gaussian variables, each one with a different variance. In turn, variances are considered to be random variables that follow a statistical distribution controlled by another set of deterministic (not random) hyperparameters; thus, a hierarchy of priors is adopted. As we will see later on, hierarchical priors are often designed using conjugate pairs of PDFs.
    3.  –  *Noninformative or objective priors.* The choice of the prior is done in such a way to embed as little extra information as possible and to exploit knowledge that is conveyed only by the available data. One way to construct such priors is to resort to information theoretic arguments. For example, one can estimate *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png) by minimizing its Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png).
*   •  The fact that the Bayesian approach allows the recovery of all the required information from a single data set does not suggest that the method is “cross-validation-free.” Maximizing the evidence, which at the same time guards against overfitting, *does not* necessarily mean that the performance of the designed estimator is optimized. This is more true in practice where, as we are going to see very soon, most often a bound of the evidence is optimized instead to bypass computational obstacles. As is always the case in life, the proof of the cake is in the eating. Thus, the final verdict should only come from the generalization ability of the designed estimator, that is, its ability to make reliable predictions using before unseen data. Moreover, there is no reason to suggest that the evidence may be a reliable predictor of the generalization performance. This has been known and explicitly stated since the method's infancy stage (see, for example, \[27\]). The generalization performance depends heavily on whether the adopted prior matches the “true” distribution of the unknown parameters. This is nicely demonstrated with a toy example in \[17\]. It is shown that the Bayesian average is optimal only if the adopted prior coincides with the true one. The situation is less clear when this is not the case. A more theoretical treatment of the topic, when there is a mismatch between the true and the selected prior, can be found in \[18\]. Thus, to be able to assess the generalization performance of a model learned via Bayesian inference, cross-validation is required, unless an independent test set can be afforded (for example, \[44\]).
*   To avoid the need for cross-validation, an alternative way has been adopted by a number of authors. The cost function, to be minimized in Eq. [(12.13)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq16), is built to quantify the generalization performance of an estimator; optimization then takes place concurrently for the unknown model parameters as well as the regularization parameter (see, for example, \[15,32\]). In general, this leads to a nonconvex optimization task, and such techniques have not (yet) been widely embraced by the machine learning community.
*   •  The Laplacian approximation to the evidence function is closely related to the *Bayesian information criterion* (BIC) \[39\] for model selection, which is expressed as

$\\ln p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i}) \\approx \\ln p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathcal{M}\_{i},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{\\text{MAP}}) - \\frac{1}{2}K\\ln N.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>MAP</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si145.png)

*   The BIC is obtained as a large *N* approximation to Eq. [(12.38)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq49), assuming a broad enough Gaussian prior, and manipulating a bit the determinant involved in the last term. For a discussion including other related criteria, see \[3,41\].
*   •  The Bayesian framework is also closely related to the minimum description length (MDL) methods. The log-evidence is associated with the number of bits in the shortest message that encodes the data via model ℳ[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si113.png) (for example, \[45\]).
*   •  *Type II maximum likelihood*: Note that the evidence is the marginal likelihood function after integrating out the parameters **θ**. To distinguish it from the MAP method, when the evidence function is maximized with respect to a set of unknown parameters, it is usually referred to as *generalized maximum likelihood* or *Type II maximum likelihood* and sometimes as *empirical Bayes*. Recall from [Remarks 12.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#enun0010) that the MAP is named Type I estimator.

## 12.4 Latent variables and the EM algorithm

At the end of Section [12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0035), it was pointed out that if we assume that *p*(**y**|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si146.png) and *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png) are Gaussians of the form given in Eq. [(12.39)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq50), then the evidence function associated with the regression task in Eq. [(12.3)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq5) is also Gaussian parameterized via the (hyper)parameters *σ*[*η*]², *σ*[*θ*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si139.png). Let us denote this set of unknown nonrandom parameters as **ξ** = \[*σ*[*η*]², *σ*[*θ*]²\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si148.png), and we can write *p*(**y**; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si149.png). Maximizing the evidence with respect to ***ξ*** becomes a typical maximum likelihood one. However, in general, such closed form expressions for the evidence function are not possible, and the integration in Eq. [(12.14)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq17) is intractable. The main source of difficulty is the fact that our regression model is described via two sets of random variables, that is, **y** and **θ**, yet only one of them, **y**, can be directly observed. The other one, **θ**, cannot be observed, and this is the reason that the Bayesian philosophy tries to integrate it out of the joint PDF *p*(**y**, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si56.png). If **θ** could be observed, then the unknown set of parameters ***ξ*** could be obtained by maximizing the likelihood *p*(**y**, **θ**; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si150.png), given a set of (joint) observations of (**y**, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si151.png). Because they cannot be observed, the random variables in the vector **θ** are known as *hidden* variables.

Although we introduced the notion of hidden variables via our familiar regression task, unobserved variables (besides the noise) occur very often in a number of problems in probability and statistics. In a number of cases, from a larger set of jointly distributed random variables, only some can be observed and the rest remain hidden. Moreover, it is often useful to *build* hidden variables into a model by design. These variables are meant to represent latent causes that influence the observed variables, and their introduction may facilitate the analysis. Often, such models associate one extra variable for *each one* of the observations. We will refer to such unobserved variables as *latent* variables. Their difference with the hidden ones is that their number is equal to that of the observations and grows accordingly as more observations get available. In contrast, unobserved random variables that are associated with the model and not with each one of the observations, individually, will be referred to as hidden variables.

### 12.4.1 The expectation-maximization algorithm

The *expectation-maximization* (EM) algorithm is an elegant algorithmic tool to maximize the likelihood (evidence) function for problems with latent/hidden variables. We will state the problem in a general formulation, and then we will apply it to different tasks, including regression.

Let **x** be a random vector and let 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png) be the respective set of observations. Let 𝒳^(*l*) :  = {**x**[1]^(*l*), …, **x**[*N*]^(*l*)}<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si152.png) be the corresponding set of latent variables; these can be either of a discrete or of a continuous nature. Each observation in 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png) is associated with a latent vector **x**^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si153.png) in 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si154.png). These latent variables are also known as *local* ones and each one expresses the hidden structure associated with the corresponding observation. We will refer to the set {𝒳,𝒳^(*l*)}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si155.png) as the *complete* data set and to the set of observations, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png), as the *incomplete* one. Hidden random parameters, **θ**, can also be dealt with as latent variables; however, their number remains fixed (independent of *N*) and they are also known as *global* variables. In such cases, the complete data set is {𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*), **θ**}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si156.png). To unclutter notation, we will focus on the set 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si154.png); yet, everything to be said also applies to hidden/global as well as to a combination of local/latent and global/hidden variables. Furthermore, let the corresponding joint distribution be parameterized in terms of a set of unknown nonrandom (hyper)parameters, ***ξ***. We further assume that, although 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si154.png) cannot be observed, the posterior distribution *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si157.png) (*P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si158.png) for the discrete case) is fully specified, given the values in ***ξ*** and the observations in 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png). This is a critical assumption for the EM algorithm. If the posterior PDF is not known, then one has to resort to variants of the EM which attempt to approximate it. We will come to such schemes in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml).

If the complete log-likelihood *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*); **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si159.png) were available, then the problem would be a typical maximum likelihood one. However, because no observations for the latent variables are available, the EM algorithm considers the *expectation* of the complete log-likelihood with respect to the latent variables associated with 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si154.png); this operation is possible, because the posterior distribution *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si157.png) is assumed to be known, provided that ***ξ*** is known. It can be shown that maximizing this expectation is equivalent to maximizing the corresponding evidence function *p*(𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si161.png) (see Problem [12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#o0090) and Section [12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0070)). To this end, the EM algorithm builds on an iterative philosophy, initialized by an arbitrary value **ξ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si162.png). Then it proceeds along the following steps.

*The EM algorithm*

1.  **1.**  Expectation E-step: At the (*j* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si163.png)th iteration, compute *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳, **ξ**^((*j*)))<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si164.png) and

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx005.jpg)(12.40) 

1.  where the expectation is taken with respect to *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**^((*j*)))<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si165.png).
2.  **2.**  Maximization M-step: Determine **ξ**^((*j* + 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si166.png) so that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx006.jpg)(12.41) 

1.  
2.  **3.**  Check for convergence according to a criterion. If it is not satisfied go back to step 1.

A possible convergence criterion is to check whether ∥**ξ**^((*j* + 1)) − **ξ**^((*j*))∥ < *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si167.png), for some user-defined constant *ϵ*. The use of the EM algorithm presupposes that working with the joint PDF *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*); **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si159.png) is computationally tractable. This is, for example, the case when working within the exponential family of PDFs, where the E-step may require only the computation of a few statistics of the latent variables. The exponential family of distributions is a computationally convenient one and it is treated in more detail in Section [12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0075).

Remarks 12.3

*   •  The EM algorithm was proposed and given its name in the seminal 1977 paper by Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird, and Donald Rubin \[12\]. The paper generalized previously published results, as for example \[2,38\], and had a significant impact as a powerful tool in statistics. The complete convergence proof was given in \[47\]. See, for example, \[29\] for a related discussion.
*   •  It can be shown that the EM algorithm converges to an (in general, local) maximum of *p*(𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si161.png), which was our original goal. The likelihood never decreases. The convergence is slower than the quadratic convergence of Newton-type searching techniques, although near an optimal point a speedup may be possible. However, the convergence of the algorithm is smooth and its complexity more attractive to Newton-type schemes, with no matrix inversions involved. The keen reader may obtain more information in, for example, \[14,30,33,43\].
*   •  The EM algorithm can be modified to obtain the MAP estimate. To this end, the M-step is changed to (Problem [12.4](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#o0095))

$\\mathbf{\\xi}^{(j + 1)} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\xi}}\\left\\{ \\mathcal{Q}(\\mathbf{\\xi},\\mathbf{\\xi}^{(j)}) + \\ln p(\\mathbf{\\xi}) \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si169.png)(12.42) 

*   where *p*(**ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si170.png) is the prior PDF associated with ***ξ***, if it is considered to be a random vector.
*   •  The EM algorithm can be sensitive to the choice of the initial point **ξ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si162.png). In practice, one can run the algorithm a number of times, starting from different initial points, and keep the best of the results. Other initialization procedures have also been used, depending on the application.
*   •  *Missing data*: The EM algorithm can also be used to cope with cases where some of the values from the observed training data are missing. Missing values can be treated as hidden variables, and maximization of the likelihood can be done by marginalizing over them. Such a procedure makes sense only if data are *missing at random*; that is, the cause of missing data is a random event and does not depend on the values of the unobserved samples.

## 12.5 Linear regression and the EM algorithm

The Bayesian viewpoint to the regression task was considered in Section [12.2.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0030) via the Gaussian model assumption for *p*(**y**|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si146.png) and *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si1.png), given in Eqs. [(12.9)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq12) and [(12.8)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq11), which subsequently led to a Gaussian posterior for *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si32.png), given in Eq. [(12.16)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq19). In the current section, and for the sake of presentation simplicity, we will adopt the special case of diagonal covariance matrices, that is, *Σ*[*η*] = *σ*[*η*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si25.png), *Σ*[*θ*] = *σ*[*θ*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si172.png), and **θ**[0] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si173.png).

Our goal now becomes to consider *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si106.png) and *σ*[*θ*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si174.png) as (nonrandom) (hyper)parameters and to obtain their values by maximizing the corresponding evidence function in Eq. [(12.15)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq18). To this end, we will use the EM algorithm. Following the notation that we have adopted so far for the regression task, the observed variables are the outputs, ***y***, and the unobserved ones comprise the random parameters, **θ**, that define the regression model. Hence, in the current context, ***y*** will replace 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png) and **θ** will take the place of 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si154.png) in the general formulation of the EM algorithm in Section [12.4.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0050).

A prerequisite in order to apply the EM procedure is the knowledge of the posterior, which for this case is known, given the values of the parameters. We will work with the precision variables, and the parameter vector becomes

$\\mathbf{\\xi} = {\\lbrack\\alpha,\\beta\\rbrack}^{T},\\ \\alpha = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{\\theta}^{2}}\\quad{and}\\quad\\beta = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">and</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si176.png)

The EM algorithm is initialized with some arbitrary positive values *α*^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si177.png) and *β*^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si178.png). Then the algorithm at the (*j* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si163.png)th iteration step, where *α*^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si179.png) and *β*^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si180.png) are assumed known, proceeds as follows:

*   •  E-Step: Compute the posterior *p*(**θ**|**y**; **ξ**^((*j*)))<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si181.png), which according to Eq. [(12.16)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq19) and for **θ**[0] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si173.png) is fully specified if we compute its mean and covariance matrix, using Eqs. [(12.19)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq23) and [(12.20)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq24), that is,

![](images/B9780443292385000184/fx007.jpg)

*   Compute the expected value of the log-likelihood associated with the complete data set; this is given by

ln *p*(**y**, **θ**; **ξ**) :  = ln *p*(**y**, **θ**; *α*, *β*) = ln (*p*(**y**|**θ**;*β*)*p*(**θ**;*α*)),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si182.png)

*   or

$\\ln p(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{\\theta};\\alpha,\\beta) = \\ \\frac{N}{2}\\ln\\beta + \\frac{K}{2}\\ln\\alpha - \\frac{\\beta}{2}{\\|\\mathbf{y} - \\Phi\\mathbf{\\theta}\\|}^{2} - \\frac{\\alpha}{2}\\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{\\theta} - \\left( \\frac{N}{2} + \\frac{K}{2} \\right)\\ln(2\\pi).$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em" id="mmlbr0004"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi *   Treating the hidden parameters as random variables, the expected value of Eq. [(12.45)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq58), with respect to **θ**, is carried out via the Gaussian posterior defined by Eqs. (12.43) and (12.44). To this end, the following steps are adopted.
    
    1.  **1.**  To compute 𝔼 \[**θ**^(*T*)**θ**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si184.png), recall the definition of the respective covariance matrix,
    
    *Σ*[*θ*|*y*]^((*j*)) = 𝔼 \[(**θ**−**μ**[*θ*|*y*]^((*j*)))(**θ**−**μ**[*θ*|*y*]^((*j*)))^(*T*)\]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>
