### 12.6.1 Gaussian mixture modeling and clustering

Clustering belongs to the unsupervised learning family and it is an important part of machine learning that is not treated in this book. Extensive coverage of clustering is given in, for example, \[41\]. However, the mixture modeling task via the EM offers us a good excuse to say a few words. Without going into formal definitions, the task of clustering is to assign a number of points, **x**[1], …, **x**[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si247.png), into *K* groups or clusters. Points that are assigned to the same cluster must be more “similar” than points which are assigned to different clusters. Some clustering algorithms need the number of clusters, *K*, to be provided by the user as an input variable. Other schemes treat it as a free parameter to be recovered from the data by the algorithm. The other major issue in clustering is to quantify “similarity.” Different definitions end up with different clusterings. A clustering is a specific allocation of the points to clusters. In general, assigning points to clusters according to an optimality criterion is an NP-hard task (see, for example, \[41\]). Thus, in general, any clustering algorithm provides a suboptimal solution.

Gaussian mixture modeling is among the popular clustering algorithms. The main assumption is that the points which belong to the same cluster are distributed according to the same Gaussian distribution (this is how similarity is defined in this case) of unknown mean and covariance matrix. Each mixture component defines a different cluster. Thus, the goal is to run the EM algorithm over the available data points to provide, after convergence, the posterior probabilities *P*(*k*|**x**[*n*]), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si248.png), where each *k* corresponds to a cluster. Then, each point is assigned to cluster *k* according to the rule

$\\text{assign}\\ \\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\ \\text{to\\ cluster}\\ k = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{i}P(i|\\mathbf{x}\_{n}),\\ i = 1,2,\\ldots,K.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>assign</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>to cluster</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si249.png)

The EM algorithm for clustering can be considered to be a refined version of a more primitive scheme, known as the *k-means* or *isodata* algorithm. In the EM algorithm, the posterior probability of each point **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si216.png), with respect to each one of the clusters *k*, is computed recursively. Moreover, the mean value **μ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si250.png) of the points associated with cluster *k* is computed as a weighted average of *all* the training points Eq. (12.60). In contrast, in the *k*\-means algorithm, at each iteration the posterior probability gets a binary value in {1, 0}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si251.png); for each point **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si216.png), the Euclidean distance from all the currently available estimates of the mean values is computed, and the posterior probability is estimated according to the following rule:

$P(k|\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{lc} {1,\\ } & {\\text{if}\\ ||\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\mu}\_{k}||^{2} < ||\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{\\mu}\_{j}||^{2},\\ j \\neq k,} \\\\ {0,\\ } & \\text{otherwise.} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mtext>otherwise.</mml:mtext></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si252.png)

The *k*\-means algorithm is not concerned about covariance matrices. Despite its simplicity, it is not an exaggeration to say that it is the most well-known clustering algorithm, and a number of theoretical papers and improved versions have been proposed over the years (see, for example, \[41\]). Due to its popularity, we will take the liberty to state it in [Algorithm 12.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#enun0045).

Algorithm 12.1

**The** *k***\-means or isodata clustering algorithm**

*   •  Initialize 
    1.  –  Select the number of clusters *K*.
    2.  –  Set **μ**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si253.png), to arbitrary values.
*   •  **For** *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si15.png), **Do** 
    1.  –  Determine the closest cluster mean, say, **μ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si250.png), to **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si216.png).
    2.  –  Set *b*(*n*) = *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si255.png).
*   •  **End For**
*   •  **For** *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si256.png), **Do** 
    1.  –  Update **μ**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si253.png), as the mean of all the points with *b*(*n*) = *k*, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si257.png).
*   •  **End For**
*   •  Until no change in **μ**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si253.png), occurs between two successive iterations.

The *k*\-means algorithm can also be derived as a limiting case of the EM scheme (for example, \[34\]). Note that both the EM algorithm and the *k*\-means algorithm can only recover *compact clusters*. In other words, if the points are distributed in ring-shaped clusters, then this type of clustering algorithms is not appropriate.

[Fig. 12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0060)A shows the data points generated by two Gaussians: 200 points from each one. The points are shown by red and gray colors, depending on the Gaussian that generated them. Of course in clustering, the data points are given to the algorithm without the “color” (labeling). It is up to the algorithm to make the partition in clusters. For both the EM and the *k*\-means algorithm, the correct number of clusters (*K* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si258.png)) was given. The *k*\-means was initialized with zero mean values. [Fig. 12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0060)B shows the clusters formed by the *k*\-means and [Fig. 12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0060)D shows the clusters formed by the EM algorithm. [Fig. 12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0060)C shows the Gaussians that were used for the initialization of the EM.

![Figure 12.8 (A) The data points generated by two Gaussians (red and gray). (B) The recovered clusters by the k-means (red and gray). (C) The 80% probability curves for the initialization of the EM algorithm. (D) The final Gaussians obtained by the EM algorithm with the respective clusters.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr008.jpg)

Figure 12.8 (A) The data points generated by two Gaussians (red and gray). (B) The recovered clusters by the *k*\-means (red and gray). (C) The 80% probability curves for the initialization of the EM algorithm. (D) The final Gaussians obtained by the EM algorithm with the respective clusters.

[Fig. 12.9](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0065) shows the respective sequence of figures, which corresponds to points obtained by the same Gaussians; however, now, there is an imbalance in the number of the points, as only 20 points spring forth from the first one and 200 points from the second. Observe that the *k*\-means has a problem in recovering the true clustering structure; it attempts to make the two clusters more equally sized. A number of techniques and versions of the basic *k*\-means scheme have been proposed to overcome its drawbacks (see \[41\]). Finally, it must be stressed that both the EM and the *k*\-means algorithm will always recover as many clusters as the user-defined input variable *K* dictates. In the case of the EM algorithm, this drawback is overcome when the variational EM algorithm is used, as will be discussed in Section [13.4](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml).

![Figure 12.9 (A) The data points generated by two Gaussians (red and gray). One of the clusters consists of only 20 points and the other one of 200 points. (B) The recovered clusters by the k-means (red and gray). Observe that the algorithm has not identified the correct clusters, by assigning more points to the “smaller” one. (C) The 80% probability curves for the initialization of the EM algorithm. (D) The final Gaussians obtained by the EM algorithm, with the respective clusters.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr009.jpg)

Figure 12.9 (A) The data points generated by two Gaussians (red and gray). One of the clusters consists of only 20 points and the other one of 200 points. (B) The recovered clusters by the *k*\-means (red and gray). Observe that the algorithm has not identified the correct clusters, by assigning more points to the “smaller” one. (C) The 80% probability curves for the initialization of the EM algorithm. (D) The final Gaussians obtained by the EM algorithm, with the respective clusters.

## 12.7 The EM algorithm: a lower bound maximization view

In Section [12.4](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0045), the EM algorithm was introduced and it was stated that maximizing the expectation of the complete log-likelihood with respect to the set of parameters ***ξ*** is equivalent to maximizing the corresponding evidence function, i.e., *p*(𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si161.png). However, this was not explicitly shown. In this section, this connection will become clear. It will be shown that the EM algorithm basically maximizes a tight *lower bound* of the evidence. Furthermore, this interpretation of the EM will allow for generalizations to extend it to cases where the computations involving the posterior, *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si157.png), are not computationally tractable.

Let us consider the functional^([^(88)](#fn88))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx011.jpg)(12.63) 

where *q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si261.png) is any nonnegative function that integrates to one; that is, it is a PDF defined over the latent variables. The functional ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si262.png) depends on ***ξ*** and on *q*, and its definition bears a strong similarity to the notion of free energy, used in statistical physics. Indeed, Eq. [(12.63)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq83) can be written as

ℱ(*q*, **ξ**) = ∫*q*(𝒳^(*l*))ln *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*); **ξ**) *d*𝒳^(*l*) + *H*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si263.png)(12.64) 

where

*H* =  − ∫*q*(𝒳^(*l*))ln *q*(𝒳^(*l*)) *d*𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si264.png)

is the entropy associated with *q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si261.png). If one defines  − ln *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*); **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si265.png) as the *energy* of the system, (𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si266.png), then ℱ(*q*, **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si267.png) represents the negative of the so-called *free energy* \[34\]. Focusing on the first term on the right-hand side in Eq. [(12.64)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq84), this can be written as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx012.jpg)(12.65) 

In other words, the first term on the right-hand side is very similar to the 𝒬<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Q</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si268.png) term in Eq. [(12.40)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq53). The only difference is that the expectation here is taken with respect to *q*.

Taking into account Bayes' theorem, Eq. [(12.63)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq83) becomes

$\\mathcal{F}(q,\\mathbf{\\xi}) = \\int q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{p(\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi})p(\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})}d\\mathcal{X}^{l}, = \\int q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{p(\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})}d\\mathcal{X}^{l} + \\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi}),$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0009" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0009" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si269.png)(12.66) 

where the above equation results because ln *p*(𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si270.png) does not depend on *q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si261.png) and the latter integrates to one, being a probability distribution. The first term on the right-hand side is the negative of the so-called KL divergence (Eq. [(2.161)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)) between *q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si261.png) and *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si157.png), which we will denote as *K**L*(*q* ∥ *p*)<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">∥</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si271.png). Recall that the KL divergence measures how different two distributions are. If the two involved distributions are equal, then their KL divergence becomes zero. Thus, finally, we get

ln *p*(𝒳; **ξ**) = ℱ(*q*, **ξ**) + *K**L*(*q* ∥ *p*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">∥</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si272.png)(12.67) 

Because the KL divergence is a nonnegative quantity, i.e., *K**L*(*q* ∥ *p*) ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">∥</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si273.png) (Problem [12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#o0110)), it turns out that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx013.jpg)(12.68) 

In other words, the functional ℱ(*q*, **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si267.png) is a lower bound of the log-likelihood function. Also, the bound becomes tight if *K**L*(*q* ∥ *p*) = 0<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">∥</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si274.png), which is true *if and only if* *q*(𝒳^(*l*)) = *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si275.png). Moreover, the previous bound is valid for *all* distributions *q* and *all* parameters ***ξ***.

The previous findings pave the way of maximizing ln *p*(𝒳; *ξ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si276.png) by trying to maximize its lower bound. This is in line with a more general class of optimization algorithms, known as *minorize-maximization* (or mazorize-minimization) (MM) methods \[20\]. A surrogate function that minorizes the cost function (lower bound), which is easier to be maximized, is employed. Then maximizing this lower bound iteratively pushes the cost function to a local maximum. Note that in our case maximization of ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si262.png) involves two terms, namely, *q* and ***ξ***. We will adopt a widely used technique known as *alternating optimization*. Such an approach imposes an iterative procedure. Starting from some initial conditions, one “freezes” the value of one of the involved terms and maximizes with respect to the other. Then the value of the latter term is frozen and optimization is carried out with respect to the former. These alternating steps carry on until convergence. In our current context, starting from an arbitrary **ξ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si162.png), the (*j* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si163.png)th iteration comprises the following steps:

*   •  Step 1: Keeping **ξ**^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si277.png) fixed, optimize with respect to *q*. This step tightens the lower bound in [(12.68)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq89). This is achieved if *K**L*(*q* ∥ *p*) = 0<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">∥</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si274.png), and it can only happen if

*q*^((*j* + 1))(𝒳^(*l*)) = *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**^((*j*))),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si278.png)(12.69) 

*   that is, if we set *q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si261.png) equal to the posterior given 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png) and **ξ**^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si277.png); as Eq. [(12.67)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq88) suggests, this makes the bound tight, that is,

ln *p*(𝒳; **ξ**^((*j*))) = ℱ(*p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳;**ξ**^((*j*))),**ξ**^((*j*))).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si279.png)(12.70) 

*   
*   •  Step 2: Fixing *q*^((*j* + 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si280.png), insert it in the place of *q* in [(12.68)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq89), and because the bound holds for any *q*, maximize with respect to ***ξ***, that is,

$\\mathbf{\\xi}^{(j + 1)} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\xi}}\\mathcal{F}\\left( p\\left( \\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi}^{(j)} \\right),\\mathbf{\\xi} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si281.png)

*   

Hence, we have now obtained the following inequalities:

ln *p*(𝒳;**ξ**^(*j* + 1)) ≥ ℱ(*p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳;**ξ**^((*j*))),**ξ**^(*j* + 1)) ≥ ℱ(*p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳;**ξ**^((*j*))),**ξ**^(*j*)),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo
