### 12.8.1 The exponential family and the maximum entropy method

Besides the computational advantages associated with the exponential family, there is another reason that justifies its high popularity. Assume that we are given a set of observations, *x*[*n*] ∈ 𝒜[*x*] ⊆ ℝ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si361.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si15.png), drawn from a distribution whose functional form is unknown. Our goal is to estimate the unknown PDF; however, we require that it will respect certain empirical expectations, which are computed from the available observations, that is,

${\\widehat{\\mu}}\_{i}: = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}u\_{i}(x\_{n}),\\ i \\in \\mathcal{I},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si362.png)(12.89) 

where ℐ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si363.png) is an index set and *u*[*i*]: 𝒜[*x*] ↦ ℝ, *i* ∈ ℐ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si364.png) are specific functions. For example, if *u*[*i*](*x*) = *x*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si365.png), then *μ̂*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si366.png) is the sample mean. In such cases, it is not sensible to adopt a parametric functional form for the PDF and try to optimize with respect to the unknown parameters, for example, via the maximum likelihood method; in general, we cannot know if an adopted functional form can comply with the available empirical expectations.

The maximum entropy (ME) method (sometimes called principle) offers a possible way to estimate the unknown PDF, subject to the set of the available constraints \[21\]. According to this method, the cost function to be maximized is the *entropy* (Section [2.5.2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)) associated with the PDF, that is,

*H* :  =  − ∫[𝒜[*x*]]*p*(*x*)ln *p*(*x*) *d**x*.<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si367.png)(12.90) 

It is well known from Shannon's information theory that the entropy is a measure of uncertainty or randomness. Maximization of the entropy with respect to *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si368.png) results in the most random PDF, subject to the available constraints. Seen from another point of view, such a procedure guarantees that the estimation of an unknown PDF is carried out by adopting the lowest number of assumptions, that is, only the available set of constraints. For our case, the maximum entropy estimation method is cast as follows:

maximize with respect to *p*(*x*)  − ∫[𝒜[*x*]]*p*(*x*)ln *p*(*x*)*d**x*, subject to  𝔼\[*u*[*i*](*x*)\] = ∫[𝒜[*x*]]*p*(*x*)*u*[*i*](*x*)*d**x*, *i* ∈ ℐ.<mml:math><mml:mtext id="mmlbr0013">maximize</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>with respect to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0013" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>subject to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si369.png)(12.91) 

In addition to the previous set of constraints, one has to consider the obvious one that guarantees that *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si368.png) integrates to one, that is,

∫[𝒜[*x*]]*p*(*x*) *d**x* = 1.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si370.png)

In the case of discrete variables, the involved integrations are replaced by summations. Solving the optimization task in [(12.91)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq128), it turns out that (Problem [12.15](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#o0160))

$\\widehat{p}(x) = C\\exp\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i \\in \\mathcal{I}}\\theta\_{i}u\_{i}(x) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si371.png)(12.92) 

that is, the ME estimate is of an exponential form. The parameters *θ*[*i*], *i* ∈ ℐ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si372.png), are the Lagrange multipliers used in the optimization task and their values are determined via the constraints and are given in terms of the available empirical expectations, *μ̂*[*i*], *i* ∈ ℐ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si373.png). If no constraint is used other than the obvious (normalizing) one and 𝒜[*x*] = \[*a*, *b*\] ⊂ ℝ<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si374.png), then the resulting PDF is the uniform distribution, *p*(*x*) = *C*<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si375.png); indeed, this is the most random one, because it shows no preference for any specific interval of values. If two constraints are used such that *u*[1](*x*) = *x*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si376.png) and *u*[2](*x*) = *x*²<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si377.png) the resulting PDF is the Gaussian one, because the exponent is of a quadratic form (see chapter's appendix). In other words, the Gaussian is the most random PDF, subject to two constraints related to the mean and the variance. Note that although we focused on real-valued random variables, everything is trivially extended to vector-valued ones. An interesting discussion concerning the ME method and alternative views of the problem is provided in \[42\].

## 12.9 Combining learning models: a probabilistic point of view

The idea of combining different learners to boost the overall performance by exploiting their individual characteristics was introduced in Section [7.9](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml). We now return to this task via probabilistic arguments. The section is also useful from a pedagogical point of view, to familiarize the reader further with the use of the EM algorithm.

Our starting consideration is that the data are distributed in different regions of the input space. Thus, it seems reasonable to fit different learning models, one for each region. This idea reminds us of the decision trees treated in Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml). There, axis-aligned (linear) splits of the input space were performed. Here, the input space will be split via hyperplanes (generalizations to more general hypersurfaces are also possible) in a general position. Moreover, the main difference lies in the fact that in CARTS, the splits were of the hard-type decision rule. In the current setting, we adopt a more relaxed attitude and we are going to consider soft-type probabilistic splits, at the expense of some loss in interpretability.

The basic concept of the combining scheme of this section is illustrated in [Fig. 12.12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0080). It is common to refer to each one of the *K* learners as an *expert*. At the heart of our modeling approach lie the so-called *gating* functions, *g*[*k*](**x**), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si378.png), which control the importance of each expert towards the final decision. These are optimally tuned during the training phase, together with the set of parameters, **θ**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si379.png), which parameterize the experts, respectively. In the general case, the gating functions are functions of the input variables. We refer to this type of modeling as *mixture of experts*. In contrast, the special type of combination, where these are parameters and not functions, that is, *g*[*k*](**x**) = *g*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si380.png), will be referred to as *mixing of learners*. We will focus on the latter case and present the method in the context of the regression and classification tasks, using linear models.

![Figure 12.12 A block diagram of a mixture of experts. The output of each expert is weighted according to the outputs of the gating network. In the general case, these weights are considered functions of the input.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr012.jpg)

Figure 12.12 A block diagram of a mixture of experts. The output of each expert is weighted according to the outputs of the gating network. In the general case, these weights are considered functions of the input.

### 12.9.1 Mixing linear regression models

Our starting point is that each model is a linear regression model, **θ**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si379.png), where the dimensionality of the input space has been assumed to increase by one to account for the intercepts and the output variables are related to the input according to our familiar equation,

*y*[*k*] = **θ**[*k*]^(*T*)**x** + *η*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si382.png)(12.93) 

where η is a white Gaussian noise source with variance *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si106.png) and it is assumed to be common for all models; extension to more general cases can be obtained in a straightforward way. For generalized linear models, ***x*** can simply be replaced by the nonlinear mapping **ϕ**(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si383.png). We assume that the gating parameters are interpreted as probabilities, and they will be denoted as *g*[*k*] = *P*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si384.png).

Under the previous assumptions, the following mixing model is adopted:

$p(y;\\mathbf{\\Xi},\\mathbf{P}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}P\_{k}\\mathcal{N}\\left( y|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k}^{T}\\mathbf{x},\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si385.png)(12.94) 

where

**Ξ** :  = \[**θ**[1]^(*T*),…,**θ**[*K*]^(*T*),*σ*[*η*]²\]^(*T*),  **P** :  = \[*P*[1],…,*P*[*K*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si386.png)(12.95) 

are the vectors of the unknown parameters to be estimated during the training phase using the set of training points, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si387.png). Because each model is designed to be “in charge” of one region in space, the corresponding parameters should be trained using input samples that originate from the respective region; note, however, that the regions are not known and have to be learned during training as well. This is in analogy with the task of Gaussian mixture modeling; recall that during training, each observation was associated with a specific mixture component via the use of a hidden variable. In the current setting, each input sample will be associated with a specific learner. Thus, our current task is a close relative of the one treated in Section [12.6](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0060) and we could follow similar steps to derive our results. However, for the sake of variety, a slightly different route will be taken. This will also prove useful later on and at the same time fits slightly better with the jargon used for the current formulation. Instead of the indices *k*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si215.png), used in Gaussian mixture modeling, we will introduce a new set of *latent* variables, *z*[*n**k*] ∈ {0, 1}, *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si388.png). If *z*[*n**k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si389.png), then sample **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si216.png) is processed by expert *k*. At the same time, for each *n*, *z*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si390.png) becomes equal to one only for a single value of *k* and zero for the rest. We are now ready to write down the likelihood for the *complete* training data set,^([^(89)](#fn89))

$p(\\mathbf{y},Z;\\mathbf{\\Xi},\\mathbf{P}) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\left( P\_{k}\\mathcal{N}\\left( y\_{n}|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{k}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2} \\right) \\right)^{z\_{nk}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo Starting from some initial conditions, **Ξ**^((0)), **P**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si395.png), the (*j* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si396.png))th iteration is given by:

*γ*[*n**k*] :  = *P*(*k*|*y*[*n*];**Ξ**^((*j*)),**P**^((*j*))).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/fx015.jpg)(12.100)

#### Mixture of experts

In mixture of experts \[24\], the gating parameters are expressed in a parametric form, as functions of the input variables ***x***. A common choice is to assume that

$g\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}): = P\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{\\exp\\left( \\mathbf{w}\_{k}^{T}\\mathbf{x} \\right)}{\\sum\_{i = 1}^{K}\\exp\\left( \\mathbf{w}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{x} \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si409.png)(12.105) 

Referring to [Fig. 12.12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0080), the gating weights are the outputs of the gating network, which is also excited by the same inputs as the experts. In the neural networks context, as we will see in Chapter [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml), we can consider the gating network as a neural network, with activation function given by Eq. [(12.105)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq148), which is known as the *softmax* activation \[5\]. Note that Eq. [(12.105)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq148) is of exactly the same form as Eq. [(7.47)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml), used in the multiclass logistic regression. Under such a setting, *P*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si203.png) in Eq. [(12.99)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq138) is replaced by *P*[*k*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si410.png), and the respective M-step becomes equivalent to optimizing with respect to **w**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si411.png). ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si412.png)(12.106) 

Observe that Eq. [(12.106)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq149) is of the same form as Eq. [(7.49)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml), used for the multiclass logistic regression, and optimization follows similar steps (see also, for example, \[19\]).

A mixture of experts has been used in a number of applications with a typical one being that of inverse problems, where from the output, one has to deduce the input. However, in many cases, this is a one-to-many task and the mixture of experts is useful to model the choice among these “many” options. For example, in \[4\], mixture of experts is used for tracking people in video recordings, where the mapping from the image to pose is not unique, due to occlusion.

#### Hierarchical mixture of experts

A direct generalization of the mixture of experts concept is to add more levels of gating functions in a hierarchical fashion, giving rise to what is known as a *hierarchical mixture of experts* (HME). The idea is illustrated in the block diagram of [Fig. 12.13](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0085). This architecture resembles that of trees, having the experts as leaves, the gating networks as nonterminal nodes, and the output (summing) node as the root one. A hierarchical mixture of experts divides the space into a nested set of regions, with the information combined among the experts under the control of the hierarchically placed gating networks. This hierarchy conforms with the more general idea of *conquer and divide* strategies.

![Figure 12.13 A block diagram of a hierarchical mixture of experts with two levels of hierarchy.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 12.13](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#cf1170) A block diagram of a hierarchical mixture of experts with two levels of hierarchy.

Compared to decision trees, an HME evolves around soft decision rules, in contrast to the hard ones that are employed in CARTs. A hard decision, usually, leads to a loss of information. Once a decision is taken, it cannot change later on. In contrast, soft decision rules provide the luxury to the network to preserve information until a final decision is taken. For example, according to a hard decision rule, if a sample is located close to a decision surface, it will be labeled according to the label on which side it lies. However, in a soft decision rule, the information, related to the position of the point with respect to the decision surface, will be retained until the stage at which the final decision must be made, by taking into consideration more information that becomes available as the processing develops.

Note that training a mixture of experts can also be carried out via a different path, by optimizing a cost function without it being necessary to employ probabilistic arguments (see, for example, \[19\]).

### 12.9.2 Mixing logistic regression models

Following Section [12.9.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0090), the combination rationale can also be applied to classification tasks. To this end, we employ the two-class logistic regression model for each one of the experts, and the combination rule, given the input value ***x***, is now written as

$P(y;\\mathbf{\\Xi},\\mathbf{P}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}P\_{k}s\_{k}^{y}{(1 - s\_{k})}^{1 - y},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si413.png)(12.107) 

where the definition of logistic regression from Section [7.6](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml) has been used, the values of the label *y* ∈ {0, 1}<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si414.png) correspond to the two classes *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si415.png) and *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si416.png), respectively, and

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si422.png)(12.111) 

Note that in Eq. [(12.111)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq154), the notation *s*[*n**k*]^((*j*)), *s*[*n**i*]^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si423.png) should have been used, but we tried to unclutter it slightly.

In the M-step, maximization with respect to *P*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si203.png) is of the same form as it was for the regression task, and it leads to

$P\_{k}^{(j + 1)} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\gamma\_{nk}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si424.png)(12.112) 

To obtain the parameters for the experts, one has to resort to an iterative scheme. Observe that the only differences of Eq. [(12.110)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq153) with Eq. [(7.38)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml) are (a) the presence of the term involving *P*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si203.png), (b) the summation over *k*, and (c) the existence of the multiplicative factors *γ*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si425.png). The first two make no difference in the optimization with respect to a single **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si403.png) and the latter is just a constant. Hence the optimization is similar to the one used for the two-class logistic regression in Section [7.6](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml), with the gradient and the Hessian matrices being the same except for the multiplicative factors (and the sign, because there, the negative log-likelihood was considered). The extension to the multiclass case is straightforward and follows similar steps.

Example 12.7

This example demonstrates the application of a mixture of two linear regression models to a synthetic data set. The input and the output are scalars, *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si95.png) and *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si391.png). [Fig. 12.14](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0090)A shows the setup. The data reside in different parts of the input space, and in each region the input–output relation is of a different form. The goal is to estimate the two linear functions, *θ*[1, *k*]*x* + *θ*[0, *k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si427.png), *k* ∈ {1, 2}<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si428.png). The EM algorithm of Section [12.9.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#s0090) was initialized with the true value of the noise variance *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si106.png).

![Figure 12.14 The two fitted lines as estimated by the EM algorithm after (A) the first, (B) the seventh, and (C) the 15th iterations. Figures (D)–(F) show the corresponding posterior probabilities, for each one of the training points xn. The length of each segment is equal to the value of the respective probability.](images/B9780443292385000184/gr014.jpg)

Figure 12.14 The two fitted lines as estimated by the EM algorithm after (A) the first, (B) the seventh, and (C) the 15th iterations. Figures (D)–(F) show the corresponding posterior probabilities, for each one of the training points *x*[*n*]. The length of each segment is equal to the value of the respective probability.

[Fig. 12.14](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0090)A–C shows the resulting linear models after the first, the seventh, and finally the 15th iteration. [Fig. 12.14](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#f0090)D–F shows the resulting posteriors *P*(*k*|*y*[*n*], *x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si430.png) (measured by the length of the bar) associated with each learner as a function of *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si95.png). After convergence, they are of a bimodal nature, depending on where each sample resides in the input space. In this way, significant probability mass is assigned even to regions where data points do not exist. A smoother and more accurate, from a generalization point of view, estimate results if we let the gating parameters be functions of the input variables themselves.

2.  12.2  Let **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si434.png) be a random vector following the normal 𝒩(**x**|**μ**, *Σ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si342.png). Consider **x**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si207.png), to be i.i.d. observations. If the prior for ***μ*** follows 𝒩(**μ**|**μ**[0], *Σ*[0])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si437.png), show that the posterior *p*(**μ**|**x**[1], …, **x**[*N*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si438.png) is normal $\\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{\\mu}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}},\\widetilde{\\Sigma})$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si439.png) with

*Σ̃*^( − 1) = *Σ*[0]^( − 1) + *N**Σ*^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si440.png)

1.  and

$\\widetilde{\\mu} = \\widetilde{\\Sigma}(\\Sigma\_{0}^{- 1}\\mathbf{\\mu}\_{0} + N\\Sigma^{- 1}\\overline{\\mathbf{x}}),$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si441.png)

1.  where $\\overline{\\mathbf{x}} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si442.png).
2.  12.3  If 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si2.png) is the set of observed variables and 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si154.png) the set of the corresponding latent ones, show that

$\\frac{\\partial\\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\xi}} = \\mathbb{E}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\partial\\ln p(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\xi}} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si443.png)

1.  where 𝔼\[ ⋅ \]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si444.png) is with respect to *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si157.png) and ***ξ*** is an unknown vector parameter. Note that if one fixes the value of ***ξ*** in *p*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si157.png), then one has obtained the M-step of the EM algorithm.
2.  12.4  Show Eq. [(12.42)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml#deq55).
3.  12.5  Let **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si446.png), let **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si447.png), and let Φ be a matrix of appropriate dimensions. Derive the expected value of ∥**y** − *Φ***θ**∥²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si448.png) with respect to **θ**, given 𝔼\[**θ**\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si449.png) and the corresponding covariance matrix *Σ*[*θ*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si42.png).
4.  12.6  Derive the recursions in Eqs. (12.60)–(12.62).
5.  12.7  Show that the Kullback–Leibler divergence, *K**L*(*p* ∥ *q*)<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">∥</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si450.png), is a nonnegative quantity.
6.  *Hint*: Recall that ln ( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si451.png) is a concave function and use Jensen's inequality, i.e.,

*f*(∫*g*(**x**)*p*(**x**)*d***x**) ≤ ∫*f*(*g*(**x**))*p*(**x**)*d***x**,<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si452.png)

1.  where *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si128.png) is a PDF and *f* is a convex function.
2.  12.8  Prove that the binomial and beta distributions are conjugate pairs with respect to the mean value.
3.  12.9  Show that the normalizing constant *C* in the Dirichlet PDF

${Dir}(\\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{a}) = C\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}x\_{k}^{a\_{k} - 1},\\ \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}x\_{k} = 1$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Dir</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si453.png)

1.  is given by

$C = \\frac{\\Gamma(a\_{1} + a\_{2} + \\cdots + a\_{K})}{\\Gamma(a\_{1})\\Gamma(a\_{2})\\ldots\\Gamma(a\_{K})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋯</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si454.png)

1.

    2.  **(b)**  Note that due to the constraint $\\sum\_{k = 1}^{K}x\_{k} = 1$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si459.png), only *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si460.png) of the variables are independent. 3.  12.10  Show that 𝒩(**x**|**μ**, *Σ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si342.png) for known *Σ* is of an exponential form and that its conjugate prior is also Gaussian.
4.  12.11  Show that the conjugate prior of the multivariate Gaussian with respect to the precision matrix *Q* is a Wishart distribution.
5.  12.12  Show that the conjugate prior of the univariate Gaussian 𝒩(*x*|*μ*, *σ*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si463.png) with respect to the mean and the precision $\\beta = \\frac{1}{\\sigma^{2}}$<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000184/si311.png) is the Gaussian–gamma product

$p(\\mu,\\beta;\\lambda,\\mathbf{v}) = \\mathcal{N}\\left( \\mu \\middle| \\frac{v\_{2}}{\\lambda},{(\\lambda\\beta)}^{- 1} \\right){Gamma}\\left( \\beta \\middle| \\frac{\\lambda + 1}{2},\\frac{v\_{1}}{2} - \\frac{v\_{2}^{2}}{2\\lambda} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gamma</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>
