## 13.1 Introduction

This chapter is the second one dedicated to Bayesian learning. The emphasis here, compared to Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), is on more advanced topics, dealing with approximate inference methods. Such methods are employed when the involved integrations in computing the evidence function are no longer computationally tractable. Two paths for approximate inference, known as variational techniques, are discussed. One is based on the mean field approximation and the lower bound interpretation of the EM, and the other on convex duality and variational bounds. Regression and mixture modeling are discussed in this framework. Emphasis is given to sparse Bayesian modeling techniques and hierarchical Bayesian models. The relevance vector machine framework is presented. Expectation propagation is also discussed as an alternative to variational methods for approximate inference. At the end of the chapter, Bayesian learning in the context of nonparametric models is presented, including Dirichlet processes (DPs), the Chinese restaurant process (CRP), the Indian buffet process (IBP), and Gaussian processes. Finally, a case study concerning hyperspectral imaging is presented.

## 13.2 Variational approximation in Bayesian learning

Recall that in order to apply the EM algorithm, the functional form of the posterior of the latent/hidden variables, given the observations, must be known. However, analytic computations related to the posterior are not always tractable. In such cases, the EM algorithm, in its standard form as discussed in the previous chapter, is not applicable. In this section, we will describe an alternative path that builds upon the EM interpretation given in Section [12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml).

Once more, we will adopt a general notation, which can then be adapted to the needs of specific problems. Let 𝒳 = {**x**[1], …, **x**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si1.png) be the set of observed variables and 𝒳^(*l*) = {**x**[1]^(*l*), …, **x**[*N*]^(*l*)}<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si2.png) the set of the *N* corresponding (local) latent ones, as they have been defined in Section [12.4](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). Furthermore, in the current section, in addition to the latent variables, we will explicitly bring into the game a set of *K* (global) hidden random parameters, **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si3.png), whose number is fixed and which will be accompanied by a prior PDF. The complete likelihood function is now written *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*), **θ**; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si4.png), where ***ξ*** is the set of unknown nonrandom (hyper)parameters that have to be estimated. As is always the case in Bayesian learning, the goal is to infer the posterior probability distributions that describe the latent as well as the hidden random variables.

The functional in Eq. [(12.63)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) is now redefined as

$\\mathcal{F}(q,\\mathbf{\\xi}) = \\int q(\\mathcal{X}^{l},\\mathbf{\\theta})\\ln\\frac{p(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l},\\mathbf{\\theta};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{q(\\mathcal{X}^{l},\\mathbf{\\theta})}\\ d\\mathcal{X}^{l}\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si5.png)(13.1) 

The counterpart of Eq. [(12.66)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) becomes

$\\mathcal{F}(q,\\mathbf{\\xi}) = \\ln p(\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi}) + \\int q(\\mathcal{X}^{l},\\mathbf{\\theta})\\ln\\frac{p(\\mathcal{X}^{l},\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{q(\\mathcal{X}^{l},\\mathbf{\\theta})}\\ d\\mathcal{X}^{l}\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si6.png)(13.2) 

which leads to

ln *p*(𝒳; **ξ**) = ℱ(*q*, **ξ**) + KL(*q*(𝒳^(*l*),**θ**)||*p*(𝒳^(*l*),**θ**|𝒳;**ξ**)).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si7.png)

The difference with Eq. [(12.67)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) lies in the fact that in our current setting the posterior, *p*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si11.png), is *not* assumed to be known; thus, setting the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, *K**L*(*q*(𝒳^(*l*),**θ**)||*p*(𝒳^(*l*),**θ**|𝒳;**ξ**))<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">KL</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si9.png), to zero, in order to maximize the value of the functional, is no longer possible. The only alternative is to resort to computationally tractable approximations concerning the functional form of *q*, which will allow the optimization of the functional with respect to *q* (and with respect to the nonrandom parameters, ***ξ***).

Optimizing a functional with respect to a function is known in mathematics as *calculus of variations*. The simplest example of this problem is to compute the geodesic that connects two points on a surface. Two names whose contributions are considered significant breakthroughs that consolidated this field are the Swiss German mathematician Leonhard Euler (1707–1783) and the Italian-born mathematician and astronomer Joseph-Louis Lagrange (1736–1813). It is interesting to note that Lagrange succeeded Euler as director of mathematics in the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin.

In order to deal with the current problem, we will *constrain* *q*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si10.png) to lie within a specific family of functions. Note that in this case, if the unknown *p*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**|𝒳; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si11.png) does not belong to the selected family of functions, the KL divergence *cannot* become zero, and the lower bound, ℱ(*q*, **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si12.png), of the marginal log-likelihood *cannot* be made *tight*. This is the reason the method is called a variational approximation.

### The mean field approximation

This type of approximation results by constraining *q*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si10.png) to be factorized, that is,

*q*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**) = *q*[𝒳^(*l*)](𝒳^(*l*))*q*[**θ**](**θ**).<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si14.png)(13.3) 

This factorization can be, and usually is, extended to

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx001.jpg)(13.4) 

Furthermore, the hidden variables can be further factorized, i.e., $q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\_{i}^{K}q\_{\\theta\_{i}}(\\theta\_{i})$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∏</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si15.png). This type of factorized function approximation has been inspired from the field of statistical physics and is known as *mean field approximation* (e.g., \[17,47,62\]). No doubt, a number of combinations that group different variables together can also be used. To simplify the notation, without sacrificing generality, we will work with Eq. [(13.3)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq4), which involves only two factors.

Having adopted a factorized model as in Eq. [(13.3)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq4), Eq. [(13.1)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq1) becomes (Problem [13.1](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0105))

Note that Eqs. [(13.6)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq7) and [(13.7)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq8) are direct generalizations of Eq. [(12.65)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) in Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml).

The lower bound functional ℱ(*q*[𝒳^(*l*)], *q*[**θ**], **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si21.png) depends on three terms. Following the alternating optimization rationale, in every iteration step we will freeze two of them and maximization will be performed with respect to the remaining one, in an alternating fashion. Optimizing the lower bound functional with respect to a distribution will take place by setting to zero a corresponding and appropriately defined KL divergence. To this end, for example, let us rewrite Eq. [(13.6)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq7) in a slightly different and more convenient form. Define the quantity *p̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si22.png) as

𝔼[*q*[**θ**]] \[ln*p*(𝒳,𝒳^(*l*),**θ**;**ξ**)\] :  = ln *p̃*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*); **ξ**).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si23.png)(13.8) 

Then Eq. [(13.6)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq7) (or, equivalently, Eq. [(13.5)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq6)) is written as

$\\mathcal{F}(q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}},q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}};\\mathbf{\\xi}) = \\int q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{\\widetilde{p}(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l};\\mathbf{\\xi})}{q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}(\\mathcal{X}^{l})}d\\mathcal{X}^{l} + H\_{q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si24.png)(13.9) 

Observe that the first term on the right-hand side has the form of a KL divergence, where the hidden variables, **θ**, have been averaged out. Note, however, that by its definition, *p̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si22.png) is not necessarily a distribution. As we will soon see, in order to become a distribution, a normalizing constant is required.

We have by now all the ingredients to go ahead with the maximization of ℱ(*q*[𝒳^(*l*)], *q*[**θ**], **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si21.png). The optimization will take place by maximizing first with respect to *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si19.png), in the sequel with respect to *q*[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si20.png), and finally with respect to ***ξ***. The algorithm is initialized to some arbitrary values for **ξ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si28.png) as well as for *q*[**θ**]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si29.png). The latter is achieved by initializing parameters (statistics) related to *q*[**θ**]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si29.png) (this will become more clear while dealing with the examples). The (*j* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si31.png)th iteration comprises the following steps:

E-Step 1a: Holding **ξ**^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si32.png) and *q*[**θ**]^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si33.png) fixed, optimize Eq. [(13.9)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq10) with respect to *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si19.png); that is,

$q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}^{(j + 1)}(\\mathcal{X}^{l}) = \\text{arg}\\ \\text{max}\_{q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}}\\mathcal{F}\\left( q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}},q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{(j)},\\mathbf{\\xi}^{(j)} \\right) = \\text{arg}\\ \\text{max}\_{q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}}\\int q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{\\widetilde{p}\\left( \\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l};\\mathbf{\\xi}^{(j)} \\right)}{q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}(\\mathcal{X}^{l})}\\ d\\mathcal{X}^{l} + {constant},$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" where “constant” contains all the terms that do not depend on 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si35.png). The negative KL divergence in Eq. [(13.10)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq11) is maximized if we set

*q*[𝒳^(*l*)]^((*j* + 1))(𝒳^(*l*)) ∝ *p̃*(𝒳,𝒳^(*l*);**ξ**^((*j*))),<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si36.png)(13.11) 

where ∝ denotes proportionality. Combining Eqs. [(13.11)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq12) and [(13.8)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq9), we can now write

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx002.jpg)(13.12) 

where the proportionality constant has, necessarily, been replaced by the normalizing factor to guarantee that *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si19.png) is a distribution. For the specific form in Eq. [(13.12)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq13), the product rule, i.e., *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*), **θ**; **ξ**^((*j*))) = *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*)|**θ**; **ξ**^((*j*)))*p*(**θ**; **ξ**^((*j*)))<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si37.png), has been employed in both the numerator and the denominator.

E-Step 1b: In this step, **ξ**^((*j*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si32.png) and *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]^((*j* + 1))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si38.png) are frozen. Following similar steps as before (repeat the steps as an exercise), starting from the formulation in Eq. [(13.7)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq8) and maximizing with respect to *q*[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si20.png), we obtain

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx003.jpg)(13.13) 

Steps 1a and 1b comprise the E-step of the variational Bayesian EM.

M-Step 2: Freezing *q*[**θ**]^((*j* + 1))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si39.png) and *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]^((*j* + 1))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si38.png), maximize the lower bound with respect to ***ξ***, that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx004.jpg)(13.14) 

The counterpart of the EM illustration of [Fig. 12.10](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) is given in [Fig. 13.1](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0010). There are two observations to be made. Step 1 is now split into two parts, and more importantly, the KL divergence does *not* (in general) go to zero; hence the bound does not become tight. This comprises the E-step of the variational Bayesian EM.

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si46.png)

where for notational uniformity we have not differentiated between parameters and latent variables and the dependence on ***ξ*** has been suppressed. Then the general form of update becomes

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx005.jpg)(13.15) 

where the expectation is with respect to $\\prod\_{r = 1\_{r \\neq m}}^{M}q{}\_{r}(\\mathcal{X}\_{r}^{l})$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∏</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si47.png).

Remarks 13.1

*   •  Note that *q*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si10.png) is an estimate of the posterior *p*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si48.png) and each one of the factors is the respective posterior estimate given the observations 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si49.png), for example, *q*[**θ**](**θ**) ≈ *p*(**θ**|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si50.png).
*   •  Once *q*(𝒳^(*l*), **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si10.png) is factorized, *no additional assumptions on the functional form* of *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si19.png) and *q*[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si20.png) are made.
*   •  Note that factorization of a PDF implies independence. Thus, if this is not the case for the data at hand, the recovered approximations may not be faithful representations of the underlying data structure. Hence, choosing a specific factorization has to be carried out with care. In practice, one may have to use a number of alternatives and keep the best one. However, computational complexity is the other face of the coin, which one must consider in a tradeoff game. In general, the factorized variational approach tends to provide approximations to the posterior PDF that are more compact than the true ones (e.g., \[47\]).
*   •  Recall our discussion in Section [12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) related to model selection and Occam's rule. This was a kick-off point for our efforts to maximize the evidence with respect to different models, in order to achieve the complexity–accuracy tradeoff. However, having resorted to approximate solutions (even if we forget convergence to local maxima, which somehow can be bypassed by using different initializations) we do not maximize the evidence but a lower bound of it; the latter is not, in general, tight. How tight this is it depends on the KL divergence, which, unfortunately, cannot be trivially computed. Hence, if the lower bound is used for model selection, it has to be treated with caution \[7\].
*   •  The variational approximation to Bayesian inference was first proposed in \[25\] and later on used in a number of areas, ranging from machine learning to decoding (e.g., \[7,26,31–33,35\]).
*   •  *Online versions*: An online version of the variational Bayes algorithm was first proposed in \[73\]. There, the exponential family has been employed to show that parameter updating via the variational Bayes philosophy is equivalent to a natural gradient descent method (see Section [8.12](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml) for the natural gradient) with step size equal to one. This equivalence is further discussed in \[28\], where, similarly, a stochastic approximation algorithm is proposed in order to process chunks of data in parallel. An online variational Bayes algorithm for parameter estimation in the context of sparse linear regression modeling has also been proposed in \[86\].

### 13.2.1 The case of the exponential family of probability distributions

Looking carefully at Eqs. [(13.12)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq13) and [(13.13)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq14), it becomes clear that the practical application of the variational Bayesian EM depends on the computational tractability of the expected values of ln *p*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*)|**θ**; **ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si51.png). Let us now see the form that the iterative steps take when one adopts the PDF models from the exponential family.

Let us assume that the samples (**x**[*n*], **x**[*n*]^(*l*)), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si52.png), in the complete data set are i.i.d. Then

$p(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}|\\mathbf{\\theta}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si53.png)(13.16) 

We further assume *p*(**x**[*n*], **x**[*n*]^(*l*)|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si54.png) to lie within the exponential family (Section [12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)), that is,

*p*(**x**[*n*], **x**[*n*]^(*l*)|**θ**) = *g*(**θ**)*f*(**x**[*n*], **x**[*n*]^(*l*))exp (**ϕ**^(*T*)(**θ**)**u**(**x**[*n*],**x**[*n*]^(*l*))).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si55.png)(13.17) 

We also adopt a prior for ***θ*** to be of the respective conjugate form, that is,

*p*(**θ**|*λ*, **v**) = *h*(*λ*, **v**)(*g*(**θ**))^(*λ*)exp (**ϕ**^(*T*)(**θ**)**v**).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si56.png)(13.18) 

The parameters *λ*, **v**<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si57.png) constitute ***ξ***, which will be considered fixed, because our current emphasis is to follow up the specific functional forms that *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si19.png) and *q*[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si20.png) get as iterations progress. So we relax the notational dependence on these parameters.

E-Step 1a: We have from Eq. [(13.12)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq13)

$q\_{\\mathcal{X}^{l}}^{(j + 1)}(\\mathcal{X}^{l}) \\propto \\exp\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{(j)}}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\ln p(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack \\right) = \\exp\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{(j)}}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}|\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack \\right) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\exp\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{(j)}}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}|\\mathbf{\\theta}) $q\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}}^{(j + 1)}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}) = \\widetilde{g}f(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l})\\exp\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\phi}}}^{T}\\mathbf{u}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\phi}}}^{T} = \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{(j)}}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{\\phi}^{T}(\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="bold">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

This is very interesting indeed. Although no functional form was assumed for *q*[𝒳^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si19.png), it turns out to be a member of the exponential family!

Thus, the approximation *q*[**θ**]^((*j* + 1))(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si65.png) of the posterior *p*(**θ**|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si358.png) is of the same form as the conjugate prior with

$\\widetilde{\\lambda} = \\lambda + N,\\quad\\widetilde{v} = v + \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}}^{(j + 1)}}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{u}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{l}) \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si67.png)(13.21) 

Note that the equations in [(13.21)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq27) are of the same form as in [(12.77)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). We only have to average out the latent variables. This is a very elegant result, because nothing has been assumed about the functional form of *q*[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si20.png). In other words, once we adopt the functional form for the PDFs of the complete set as well as that of the prior of the parameters to be of the exponential type, then subsequent iterations become a “family business.”

## 13.3 A variational Bayesian approach to linear regression

Once more, let us consider our familiar regression task

**y** = *Φ***θ** + **η**, **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*), **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*K*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si68.png)

In Section [12.5](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), we treated the case where **η** was Gaussian and the prior *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si357.png) was also Gaussian. We used the EM in order to optimize the evidence *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si70.png) with respect to the hyperparameters that define the two adopted Gaussian PDFs; note that for this case, one could bypass the EM and resort to analytical computations in order to obtain the evidence and subsequently use an optimization technique to estimate the unknown hyperparameters.

In this section, we will adopt assumptions that do not allow for tractable analytic computations of the posterior, *p*(**θ**|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si105.png), which is a prerequisite both for the standard EM and for the analytic computations of the evidence *p*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si70.png). This approach is far from a pedagogic toy and has strong practical flavor. We will develop the task in some detail, and the reader is advised to go through the computations, because they are typical of what will be encountered in practice, once the variational Bayesian approach is selected for addressing a task.

Assume that

*p*(**y**|**θ**, *β*) = 𝒩(*Φ***θ**, *β*^( − 1)*I*).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si72.png)(13.22) 

That is, the noise is Gaussian and for simplicity we have considered it to be white, *Σ*[*η*] = *σ*[*η*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si73.png), and $\\beta = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}}$<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si74.png). In contrast to what we did in Section [12.5](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), now we will be more democratic and give the freedom to each one of the parameter components, *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si214.png), to have a different variance, $\\sigma\_{k}^{2}: = \\frac{1}{\\alpha\_{k}},\\ k = 0,1,\\ldots,K - 1$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si76.png). Moreover, we go one step further. The values of *β* and *α*[*k*], *k* = 0, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si228.png), will not be treated as deterministic variables. We will also treat them as random ones, (*β*, *α*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">β</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si78.png)), which will be assigned prior PDFs; these prior PDFs are in turn controlled by another set of hyperparameters. More specifically, our model, in addition to Eq. [(13.22)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq29), comprises \[8\]

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{\\alpha}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\\mathcal{N}(\\theta\_{k}|0,\\alpha\_{k}^{- 1}),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si79.png)(13.23) 

$p(\\mathbf{\\alpha}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}{Gamma}(\\alpha\_{k}|a,b),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gamma</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si80.png)(13.24) 

and

*p*(*β*) = *G**a**m**m**a*(*β*|*c*, *d*).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gamma</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si81.png)(13.25) 

Note that the previous choice of the priors indicates our will to “play” the game within the exponential family terrain. The prior *p*(**α**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si82.png) is the conjugate pair of Eq. [(13.23)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq30) (see Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)). Also, Eq. [(13.25)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq32) would be the conjugate of Eq. [(13.22)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq29), if we had considered ***θ*** fixed. [Fig. 13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0015) provides a graphical representation of the dependencies among the various variables involved in our model. Arrows indicate conditional dependencies. Graphical models will be considered in a formal way in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml). Note that such a model forms various levels of *hierarchy* in the dependency among the involved parameters.

![Figure 13.2 A graphical illustration of the dependencies among the various variables involved in the model of linear regression. The red circle indicates the random variable that is observed, gray circles indicate hidden random variables, and squares correspond to deterministic parameters. The direction of each arrow indicates the direction of the dependence between the connected variables. The red box indicates that the above dependencies hold for all N time instants.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr002.jpg)

[Figure 13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf0455) A graphical illustration of the dependencies among the various variables involved in the model of linear regression. The red circle indicates the random variable that is observed, gray circles indicate hidden random variables, and squares correspond to deterministic parameters. The direction of each arrow indicates the direction of the dependence between the connected variables. The red box indicates that the above dependencies hold for all *N* time instants.

This concept of hierarchy is at the heart of what we call *hierarchical Bayesian modeling*. Each one of the involved PDFs is expressed in terms of certain (hyper)parameters. Because the values of these parameters are unknown, they are also treated as random variables whose priors are expressed in terms of a new set of hyperparameters. Each one of them is in turn treated as a random variable associated with a new prior, known as *hyperprior*. This rationale can be extended in order to construct different levels of hierarchy. Often, at the higher level of hierarchy, the corresponding (unknown) hyperparameters are assigned values by the user, based on experience; for example, the overall model can be relatively insensitive to their specific values, which makes the corresponding choice a fairly easy job.

Our current task comprises hidden variables in the form of parameters grouped in **θ**, **α**, and β and it involves no other unobserved variables. The set of observations is now given by ***y***. Also, observe that the posterior *p*(**θ**, **α**, *β*|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si83.png) is not analytically tractable. We will resort to the variational Bayesian EM to obtain an estimate of the previous posterior PDF.

Using the mean field approximation, we assume that the approximation to the posterior (the dependence on ***y*** has been suppressed for notational convenience) factorizes as

*q*(**θ**, **α**, *β*) = *q*[**θ**](**θ**)*q*[**α**](**α**)*q*[*β*](*β*),<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">β</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si84.png)(13.26) 

where we have relaxed our notation, for simplicity, from the explicit dependence on *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*. We will bring them back into the game whenever needed. The variational EM consists of three substeps, one for each factor in Eq. [(13.26)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq33). Starting from some initial guesses, for 𝔼\[*β*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si147.png), 𝔼\[*α*[*k*]\], *k* = 0, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si86.png), (it will become clear soon why we need to start with those)^([^(90)](#fn90))

E-Step 1a: From the general update form of Eq. [(13.15)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq17), we have

ln *q*[**θ**]^((*j* + 1))(**θ**) = 𝔼[*q*[**α**]^((*j*))*q*[*β*]^((*j*))]\[ln*p*(**y**,**θ**,**α**,*β*)\] + constant,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>constant</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si88.png)(13.27) 

where now

ln *p*(**y**, **θ**, **α**, *β*) = ln (*p*(**y**|**θ**,**α**,*β*)*p*(**θ**,**α**,*β*)) = ln (*p*(**y**|**θ**,*β*)*p*(**θ**|**α**)*p*(**α**)*p*(*β*)),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0005" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" mathvariant="bold">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo
