For the EM algorithm, the initial mean values were generated randomly, using a Gaussian 𝒩(**μ**|0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si199.png) and the respective initial covariance matrices, *Σ*[*k*]^((0)), *k* = 1, 2, …, 25<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si200.png), with random elements, making sure that they are positive definite. One way to achieve this is to generate a matrix Φ with random elements from 𝒩(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si201.png) and then form *Φ*^(*T*)*Φ*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si202.png). Another possibility is to start with a diagonal matrix, for example, the identity one *I*.

For the variational EM algorithm, the following initial values were used: the mean values ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{k}^{(0)}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si203.png) and the initial covariance matrices *Σ̃*[*k*]^((0)), *k* = 1, 2, …, 25<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si204.png), were generated as before. Also, 𝔼[*q*[*Q*]^((0))]\[*Q*[*k*]\] = *I*, 𝔼[*q*[*Q*]^((0))] \[ln|*Q*[*k*]|\] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si205.png). In both cases, the initial probabilities were set to be equal.

Observe that the variational EM identifies the five clusters associated with the data; the rest of the mixtures correspond to zero probability weights. In contrast, the EM algorithm tries to identify all 25 mixtures and the result is not satisfactory.

## 13.5 When Bayesian inference meets sparsity

The Bayesian approach to sparsity-aware learning will soon become our major concern. However, we will use this section to “warm” us up. The close relationship between the use of a prior PDF and the regularization of a cost function has already been discussed in Section [12.2.2](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). There, the adoption of a Gaussian prior together with a Gaussian noise for the regression task led to the equivalence of MAP with the ridge regression. It will not take a minute to show that the use of a Gaussian model for the noise together with a Laplacian prior for each one of the weights, that is,

$p(\\theta\_{k}) = \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\exp\\left( - \\lambda|\\theta\_{k}| \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si206.png)

renders MAP equivalent to the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si207.png) norm regularization of the LS cost. For a Bayesian, however, who is not interested in cost functions, the secret that lies within the Laplacian prior is hidden in the heavy tails of this distribution. This is in contrast to a Gaussian PDF, which has very light tails. In other words, the probability that an observation of a Gaussian random variable can take values far from its mean decreases very fast. For example, the probability of observing variables that deviate from the mean by more than 2*σ*, 3*σ*, 4*σ*, and 5*σ* are 0.046, 0.003, 6 × 10^( − 5)<mml:math><mml:mn>6</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si208.png), and 6 × 10^( − 7)<mml:math><mml:mn>6</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si209.png), respectively. That is, if we provide a Gaussian prior, we basically inform the learning process to look for values “around” the mean; values away from the mean are heavily penalized. However, in sparsity-aware learning this would be the wrong information to pass over to our learning mechanism. Assuming the mean of the prior to be zero, although we expect most of the components of our parameters to be zero, still we want a few of them to be large. Hence, our prior information should be selected so as to assign small (but not too small) probabilities to large values. Hence, to a Bayesian, sparsity-aware learning becomes synonymous with imposing heavy-tail priors. Let us now turn back to our current task, and see how this brief introduction is related to our model. Our prior PDF, *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si357.png), according to the model of Eqs. [(13.23)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq30) and [(13.24)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq31), is obtained by marginalizing out the hyperparameters **α** (Problem [13.10](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0150)), that is,

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta};a,b) = \\int p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{\\alpha})p(\\mathbf{\\alpha})\\ d\\mathbf{\\alpha} = \\int\\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\\mathcal{N}\\left( \\theta\_{k}|0,\\alpha\_{k}^{- 1} \\right){Gamma}(\\alpha\_{k}|a,b)\\ d\\mathbf{\\alpha} = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}{st}\\left( \\theta\_{k}|0,\\frac{a}{b},2a \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0016" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0016" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" where *s**t*(*x*|*μ*, *λ*, *ν*)<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">st</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ν</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si211.png) is the Student's *t* PDF, defined by

${st}(x|\\mu,\\lambda,\\nu) = \\frac{\\Gamma(\\frac{\\nu + 1}{2})}{\\Gamma(\\frac{\\nu}{2})}\\left( \\frac{\\lambda}{\\pi\\nu} \\right)^{1/2}\\frac{1}{\\left( 1 + \\frac{\\lambda{(x - \\mu)}^{2}}{\\nu} \\right)^{\\frac{\\nu + 1}{2}}}.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">st</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si212.png)(13.53) 

The parameter *ν* is known as the number of degrees of freedom. [Fig. 13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0030) shows the graph of Student's *t* PDFs for different values of *ν*. For *ν* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>ν</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si213.png), the Student's *t* distribution tends to a Gaussian of the same mean and precision *λ*. Observe the heavy-tail feature of Student's *t* PDF, especially for low values of *ν*. Recall that in our case, where we have used uninformative hyperpriors, the hyperparameter, *a*, was given a small value. Thus, our treatment in this section favors sparse solutions for the regression model. It will push as many of the parameters *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si214.png) as possible toward zero. That is, it prunes the less relevant basis functions *ϕ*[*k*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si215.png) by setting the corresponding parameters to zero. This is also the reason for using different hyperparameters *α*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si118.png) for each one of the parameters *θ*[*k*], *k* = 0, 2, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si216.png), which provide more freedom to the learning procedure to adjust each one of them individually. In the earlier days, this approach was coined *automatic relevance determination* (ARD) \[48,53,55\]. An interesting discussion relating adaptive regularization and pruning is provided in \[24\].

![Figure 13.5 Observe that for low values of the degrees of freedom, ν, Student's t PDF has heavy tails. In contrast, the Gaussian PDF is a light-tailed PDF.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf0680) Observe that for low values of the degrees of freedom, *ν*, Student's *t* PDF has heavy tails. In contrast, the Gaussian PDF is a light-tailed PDF.

In \[42\], a unification of various sparsity promoting priors is presented. These originate from the starting integral in Eq. [(13.52)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq81) by plugging in different distributions for *p*(**a**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si217.png). Besides the Student's *t* PDF, one can obtain the Laplacian, the horseshoe, the generalized hyperbolic, and the Normal-Jeffreys distributions as special cases. This family of priors is referred to as the Gaussian scale mixture (GSM) priors.

[Fig. 13.6](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0035)A provides a clear demonstration of the sparsity imposing properties of the Student's *t* distribution. In the two-dimensional space, and as we move away from zero, probability mass is skewed toward the coordinate axes; that is, the PDF peaks around sparse solutions and *sparsity is now enforced probabilistically*. In contrast, the Gaussian does not give much chance to large values (see [Fig. 13.6](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0035)B).

![Figure 13.6 (A) The Student's t peaks sharply around zero and falls slowly along the axes; hence, sparse solutions are favored. (B) The Gaussian peaks around zero and decays very fast, along all directions.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr006.jpg)

Figure 13.6 (A) The Student's *t* peaks sharply around zero and falls slowly along the axes; hence, sparse solutions are favored. (B) The Gaussian peaks around zero and decays very fast, along all directions.

## 13.6 Sparse Bayesian learning

In Section [13.3](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0030), the prior for each one of the unknown parameters *θ*[*k*], *k* = 0, 1, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si218.png), was given the liberty to have their own variances, $\\sigma\_{k}^{2}: = \\frac{1}{\\alpha\_{k}}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si219.png). In turn, these variances were treated as hidden random variables and a prior was assigned to each one of them in terms of a number of hyperparameters.

In \[88,96\], the model was slightly modified. The concept of using different variances for the priors was retained, but the variances were treated as deterministic parameters and not as random ones.^([^(91)](#fn91))

*p*(**y**|**θ**; *β*) = 𝒩(**y**|*Φ***θ**, *β*^( − 1)*I*),<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si220.png)(13.54) 

*p*(**θ**; **α**) = 𝒩(**θ**|0, *A*^( − 1)),<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si221.png)(13.55) 

where

*A* :  = diag{*α*[0],…,*α*[*K* − 1]}.<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>diag</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si222.png)(13.56) 

The precision *β* is also treated as an unknown deterministic parameter. Our goal is (a) to obtain estimates for *β* and *α*[*k*], *k* = 0, 1, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si223.png), and (b) to compute the predictive distribution, *p*(*y*|**x**, **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si224.png), where ***y*** is the vector of observations.^([^(92)](#fn92))

In this section, we will adopt a different path, exploiting the Gaussian nature of the involved PDFs. A Type II maximum likelihood method will be employed, which was introduced in [Remarks 12.2](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). Type II likelihood is defined as the marginal one, after integrating out the parameters ***θ***. Following the discussion in Section [12.2](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and for our current needs, Eq. [(12.15)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) is written as

*p*(**y**; **α**, *β*) = 𝒩(**y**|0, *β*^( − 1)*I* + *Φ**A*^( − 1)*Φ*^(*T*)).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si225.png)(13.57) 

Also, for the sake of completeness, Eqs. [(12.16)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), [(12.17)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), and [(12.10)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) take the form

*p*(**θ**|**y**; **α**, *β*) = 𝒩(**θ**|**μ**, *Σ*; **α**, *β*),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si226.png)(13.58) 

with

**μ** = *β**Σ**Φ*^(*T*)**y**, *Σ* = (*A*+*β**Φ*^(*T*)*Φ*)^( − 1).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si227.png)(13.59) 

The objective now becomes to maximize with respect to *α*[*k*], *k* = 0, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si228.png), and *β* the following cost function

$L(\\mathbf{\\alpha},\\beta): = \\ln p(\\mathbf{y};\\mathbf{\\alpha},\\beta) = - \\frac{N}{2}\\ln(2\\pi) - \\frac{1}{2}\\ln|\\beta^{- 1}I + \\Phi A^{- 1}\\Phi^{T}|\\quad - \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbf{y}^{T}\\left( \\beta^{- 1}I + \\Phi A^{- 1}\\Phi^{T} \\right)^{- 1}\\mathbf{y}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0017" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0017" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false" linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0017" linebreakstyle="after">|</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si229.png)(13.60) 

Maximizing the above cost cannot be carried out analytically, and the following iterative scheme is derived (Problem [13.11](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0155), the proof is a bit tedious):

![](images/B9780443292385000196/fx006.jpg)

The iterative scheme is initialized by an arbitrary set of values and it is repeated until a convergence criterion is met; *Σ*[*k**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si230.png) is the respective diagonal element of the matrix *Σ*. Note that both *Σ* and ***μ*** depend on the values of *β* and *α*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si231.png). The main complexity per iteration step is due to the matrix inversion involved in the respective definition in [(13.59)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq88), which amounts to *O*(*K*³)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si232.png) operations. Moreover, because a matrix inversion is involved, one must take care of near singularities, due to numerical errors. This can be the case in practice, because some of the values of *α*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si231.png) may become very large. Thus, care must be taken so that once such values occur, one removes the corresponding columns in Φ and sets the respective values of *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si233.png) to zero. As a matter of fact, this is how sparsity is enforced by the method. Parameters with mean value equal to zero and a variance that becomes very small (precision very large) are set to zero. This behavior has empirically been observed in practice.

The alternative path to deal with the method is via the EM algorithm. This leads to an equivalent set of recursions \[88\], but practical experience has shown that the previously given set of updates converge faster.

Extensions of the SBL framework in the context of block sparsity and for the case of multiple measurement vectors (MMVs), when elements in each nonzero row of the solution matrix are temporally correlated, are reported in \[100,101\]. Moreover, in the latter one, a theoretical analysis is provided, which shows that the SBL cost function has the very desirable property that its global minimum coincides with the sparsest solution to the MMV problem.

Example 13.2

The goal of this example is to demonstrate the comparative performance, via a simulation example, of (a) the variational Bayesian method, (b) the maximum likelihood Eq. [(12.6)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), and (c) the EM algorithm of Section [12.5](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) in the context of linear regression and in particular in the sparse modeling framework. The SBL method gave results very similar to the variational approach, and it is not discussed any further. To this end, we generated the training data according to the following scenario.

The interval in the real axis \[ − 10, 10\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si234.png) was sampled at *N* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si235.png) equidistant points *x*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, 100<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si236.png). The training data comprise the pairs (*y*[*n*], *x*[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si237.png), where

$y\_{n} = \\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}\\frac{{(x\_{n} + 5.8)}^{2}}{0.1} \\right) + \\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}\\frac{{(x\_{n} - 2.6)}^{2}}{0.1} \\right) + \\eta\_{n},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>5.8</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.6</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si238.png)

where *η*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si239.png) are i.i.d. zero mean Gaussian noise samples of variance *σ*[*η*]² = 0.015<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.015</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si240.png). To fit the data, the following model was adopted:

$y = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{k}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}\\frac{{(x - x\_{k})}^{2}}{0.1} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si241.png)

Thus, the matrix Φ has the following elements:

${\\lbrack\\Phi\\rbrack}\_{nk} = \\exp\\left( - \\frac{1}{2}\\frac{{(x\_{n} - x\_{k})}^{2}}{0.1} \\right),\\quad n = 1,2,\\ldots,N,\\ \\ k = 1,2,\\ldots,N.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si242.png)

Note that we have as many parameters as the number of training points. This is in line with the relevance vector machine rationale, which will be discussed in Section [13.7](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0060). [Fig. 13.7](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0045) illustrates the results. The red full-line curve corresponds to the true function that generates the data. The gray full-line curve corresponds to the model, having plugged in as estimated values *θ̂*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si243.png) the respective posterior mean values from Eq. [(13.34)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq44) of the variational Bayesian approach. The curve almost coincides with the true one. The dotted red curve corresponds to the ML solution and the dotted gray curve to the EM, where the estimates correspond to the mean of the respective posterior (Eq. [(12.44)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)). The performance advantages of the variational approach are obvious, and observe how it has managed to cope with the overfitting and pushed most of the parameters to zero values.

![Figure 13.7 The figure corresponds to the setup of Example 13.2. Observe that the fitting curve obtained via the variational method is almost identical to the true one.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 13.7](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf0755) The figure corresponds to the setup of [Example 13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#enun0025). Observe that the fitting curve obtained via the variational method is almost identical to the true one.

### 13.6.1 The spike and slab method

This is an old technique for imposing sparsity \[43,51\]. Let us consider our familiar regression model,

*y* = **θ**^(*T*)**ϕ**(**x**) + *η*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si244.png)(13.64) 

A new set of auxiliary binary *indicator* variables are introduced, *s*[*k*] ∈ {0, 1}, *k* = 0, 1, …, *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si245.png). Let also the prior imposed on **θ** be a Gaussian, *p*(**θ**) = 𝒩(**θ**|0, *σ*²*I*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si246.png). As the name suggests, the indicator variables control the presence or absence of a parameter in the summation in Eq. [(13.64)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq93). For example, if *s*[*k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si247.png), then the corresponding parameter *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si214.png) is present, and if *s*[*k*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si248.png), then *θ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si214.png) is removed; this is the way sparsity is imposed onto the model. To this end, a joint Bernoulli prior distribution (Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)) is adopted for the indicator variables, i.e.,

$P(\\mathbf{s}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}p^{s\_{k}}{(1 - p)}^{1 - s\_{k}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si249.png)(13.65) 

where the parameter 0 ≤ *p* ≤ 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si250.png) specifies a prior level of sparsity. This turns out to be equivalent to adopting the following prior on the parameters:

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx007.jpg)(13.66) 

The latter is known as the *spike and slab* prior. The name comes from the fact that if *s*[*k*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si248.png), then a “spike” is imposed at the zero and the values *s*[*k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si247.png) impose a “slab,” because a Gaussian is a broad one (for large enough *σ*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si251.png)). The corresponding posterior is not Gaussian and its computation can be done by mobilizing approximate inference techniques, such as variational or Monte Carlo (see, e.g., \[29\] and the references therein).

Variants of the basic spike and slab scheme do also exist (see, e.g., \[80\]). In the latter reference, it is shown that one can obtain the classical ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si252.png)\-based sparsity enforcing constraint on the LS criterion (Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml)) as a limiting case of one of these variants. Such a path provides another connection between probabilistic and optimization-based techniques for sparsity. Another connection will be discussed in Section [13.9](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0075).

## 13.7 The relevance vector machine framework

An important aspect of the work in \[88\] was the introduction of *relevance vector machines* for regression as well as for classification. Inspired by the support vector regression (SVR), which was discussed in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), a specific regression model was considered, that is,

$y(\\mathbf{x}) = \\theta\_{0} + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{k}\\kappa(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{k}}) + \\eta.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si253.png)(13.67) 

In other words, the general regression model of Eq. [(12.1)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) is considered for *K* = *N* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si254.png), where *N* is the number of observations and

*ϕ*[*k*](**x**) = *κ*(**x**, **x**[*k*]),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si255.png)

where *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si256.png) is a kernel function, as defined in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), centered at the input observation points, **x**[*k*], *k* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si257.png). Thus, the number of parameters becomes equal (plus one) to the number of training points.

The task can be treated either via the SBL philosophy or via the employment of the variational approximation rationale, in order to impose sparsity. In \[88\], it is pointed out that the variational Bayesian approach is computationally more intensive and in practice it results in mean values for the hyperparameters, which are identical to the values obtained by using the SBL approach.

Inspired by the definition of the support vectors in the SVR, the surviving data points that contribute to Eq. [(13.67)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq96) are called *relevance vectors*. Also, the kernels to be used in the RVM framework need not be symmetric positive definite functions, because the modeling is not necessarily associated to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS).

### 13.7.1 Adopting the logistic regression model for classification

Besides the relevance vector regression, the relevance vector classification was also introduced in \[88\]. Recall that in the support vector machine (SVM) classification, a linear (in an RKHS) classifier was designed. The same model is also adopted for the RVM. Given the value of a feature vector, ***x***, classification is performed according to the sign of the discriminant function, namely,

$f(\\mathbf{x}): = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}): = \\theta\_{0} + \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{N}\\theta\_{k}\\phi\_{k}(\\mathbf{x}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si258.png)

The goal is to obtain an estimate of the parameters ***θ*** in the Bayesian framework; thus, somehow, we have to “embed” ***θ*** into a PDF that relates the input–output data. In this vein, a well-known and widely used technique is the *logistic regression* model, which was introduced in Section [7.6](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml).

According to this model and for a two-class (*ω*[1], *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si259.png)) classification task, the posterior probabilities, as required by the Bayesian classifier, are modeled as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx008.jpg)(13.68) 

and

*P*(*ω*[2]|**x**) = 1 − *P*(*ω*[1]|**x**).<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si260.png)(13.69) 

There is more than one reason that justifies such a choice (see, e.g., \[47\] and Problem [13.12](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0160)). Multiclass generalizations are also possible (e.g., \[87\] and Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml)).

For the sake of the less familiar reader, let us look at Eq. [(13.68)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq99) more closely. The graph of the function

$\\sigma(t) = \\frac{1}{1 + \\exp( - t)},$<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si261.png)(13.70) 

known as the *logistic sigmoid* function, is shown in [Fig. 13.8](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0050). For *t* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si262.png) (**θ**^(*T*)**ϕ**(**x**) > 0)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si263.png), $P(\\omega\_{1}|\\mathbf{x}) > \\frac{1}{2}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si264.png) and  the decision is in favor of *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si265.png). which is the counterpart of Eq. [(13.22)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq29) for the regression case. We also adopt a Gaussian prior for **θ**, as in Eqs. [(13.55)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq84) and [(13.56)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq85). As in the SBL approach, our goal is to maximize the Type II log-likelihood with respect to the unknown parameters, ***α***. However, *p*(**y**|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si272.png) is no longer Gaussian, and marginalizing out **θ** cannot be carried out analytically. In \[88\], the Laplacian approximation is employed and the following stepwise procedure is adopted:

1.  **1.**  Assuming ***α*** to be currently available, maximize with respect to ***θ*** the posterior, which by simple arguments is easily shown to be

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{\\alpha}) = \\frac{P(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{\\theta})p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{\\alpha})}{P(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{\\alpha})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

As pointed out in \[88\], although in general the Laplacian local approximation to a Gaussian may not be a good one, in the case of the current classification task, due to the specific nature of the adopted models, the approximation is expected to provide good accuracy.

Remarks 13.2

*   •  Compared to SVM (SVR), the RVM machinery presents advantages and disadvantages. The SVM approach has the mathematically elegant property of optimizing a convex cost function. This is not the case for the RVM framework, where the involved optimization steps refer to a nonconvex cost. It must be kept in mind that solving a nonconvex task, one may have to run the optimization algorithm a number of times, starting each time from different initial conditions, because a nonconvex problem can be trapped in a local minimum.
*   Concerning complexity, the algorithmic steps for the RVM involve the inversion of the Hessian matrix, which amounts to *O*(*N*³)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si289.png) complexity. As discussed in Section [11.11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), the complexity range of the efficient schemes for solving the SVM scales from linear to (approximately) quadratic. Also, the memory for the RVM exhibits an *O*(*N*²)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si290.png) dependence on the size of the training set, as opposed to a linear dependence for the SVM case. Besides complexity, inverting (big) matrices must be done with care in order to avoid numerical instabilities due to possible (near) singularity. Also, in general, RVMs need longer training times to converge, compared to SVMs, for similar error rates.
*   A fast RVM algorithm has been developed in \[89\] by analyzing the properties of the marginal likelihood. This enables a sequential addition and deletion of candidate basis functions (columns of Φ) to monotonically maximize the marginal likelihood. This iterative algorithm operates in a constructive manner, until all relevant basis functions (for which the associated weights are nonzero) have been included. If *M* denotes the number of relevant terms, the complexity amounts to *O*(*M*³)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si291.png), which for *M* <  < *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si292.png) is more efficient than the original RVM.
*   The main advantage of RVMs is that, in general, they result in sparser solutions compared to SVMs for similar levels of generalization errors. This makes the prediction step, after the training has been completed, more efficient compared to the prediction model resulting from SVM. Moreover, SVMs suffer from their dependence on the user dependent hyperparameter, *C* (*ϵ* for regression), and they are generally found by cross-validation, which involves multiple training for different values.
*   •  In \[8\], a different algorithmic approach has been adopted based on the *variational bound approximation* method, to be described next.

## 13.8 Convex duality and variational bounds

In the previous chapter, the Laplacian technique for the approximation of a general PDF by a Gaussian was introduced. The driving force behind such an approximation was to benefit from the computationally friendly nature of the Gaussian PDF. In this section, we will approach this task from a different perspective, involving maximization of a lower bound of the PDF at hand with respect to an extra parameter, which is introduced into the problem and on which the lower bound depends. Our theoretical framework is that of convex duality, a well-known and powerful tool in convex analysis.

Let a function *f* : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si293.png). The function

*f*^(\*) : ℝ^(*l*) ↦ ℝ,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si294.png)

defined as^([^(94)](#fn94))

$f^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\xi}) = \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\left\\{ \\mathbf{\\xi}^{T}\\mathbf{x} - f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si295.png)(13.78) 

is called the *conjugate* of *f*. The domain of the conjugate function consists of all **ξ** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si296.png) for which the maximum is finite. A notable property of the conjugate function is its *convexity*; this is true whether or not *f* is convex. The convexity is the outcome of the point-wise maximization of a family of (convex with respect to ***ξ***) affine functions \[12\].

Maximizing Eq. [(13.78)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq114) with respect to ***x*** results in a value of **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si297.png), such that

**x**[\*] : ∇*f*(**x**[\*]) = **ξ**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si298.png)(13.79) 

which leads to the value

*f*^(\*)(**ξ**) = **ξ**^(*T*)**x**[\*] − *f*(**x**[\*]).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si299.png)(13.80) 

Eqs. [(13.79)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq115) and [(13.80)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq116) provide the geometric interpretation of the conjugate function. The graph of the linear function **ξ**^(*T*)**x**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si300.png) defines a hyperplane whose direction is controlled by ***ξ***; the latter is now equal to ∇*f*(**x**[\*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si301.png), which defines the direction of the tangent hyperplane of the graph of *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si302.png) at **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si297.png). This tangent hyperplane is described by

*g*(**x**) = *f*(**x**[\*]) + (**x** − **x**[\*])^(*T*)∇*f*(**x**[\*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si303.png)

or using Eq. [(13.80)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq116),

*g*(**x**) = **ξ**^(*T*)**x** − *f*^(\*)(**ξ**).<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si304.png)(13.81) 

For **x** = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si305.png), Eq. [(13.81)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq118) becomes *g*(0) =  − *f*^(\*)(**ξ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si306.png). This is illustrated in [Fig. 13.10](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0060). Thus, *f*^(\*)(**ξ**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si307.png) corresponds to the displacement that the graph of **ξ**^(*T*)**x**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si300.png) has to undergo in order to “touch” that of *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si302.png). A by-product of all this turns out to be very useful for us. It can be shown (Problem [13.16](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0180)) that if *f* is a convex function, then (*f*^(\*))^(\*) = *f*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si308.png) and in this case we can write

$f(\\mathbf{x}) = \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\xi}}\\left\\{ \\mathbf{x}^{T}\\mathbf{\\xi} - f^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\xi}) \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si309.png)(13.82) 

Thus, once *f*^(\*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si310.png) is computed, a lower bound for *f* becomes readily available, that is,
