*f*(**x**) ≥ **x**^(*T*)**ξ** − *f*^(\*)(**ξ**),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si311.png)(13.83) 

where now ***ξ*** is interpreted as a parameter. To investigate this bound a bit further, we plug Eqs. [(13.79)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq115) and [(13.80)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq116) into Eq. [(13.83)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq120) to obtain^([^(95)](#fn95))

*f*(**x**) ≥ *f*(**x**[\*]) + (**x** − **x**[\*])^(*T*)∇*f*(**x**[\*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si312.png)

where the right-hand side is the linear function *g*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si313.png) describing the hyperplane tangent to *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si302.png) at **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si297.png). The bound becomes tight at **x** = **x**[\*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si314.png) (see [Fig. 13.10](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0060)). We will soon see how we can make this linear function a bound for a nonlinear one; it suffices to transform the argument of the function.

![Figure 13.10 The direction of the line y = ξx that crosses the origin is controlled by ξ (ξ = tanα). The (negative) value of the conjugate function f⁎ at ξ defines the point where the line y = g(x) cuts the vertical axis; g(x) is formed by translating ξx until it becomes tangent to f at x⁎.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr010.jpg)

Figure 13.10 The direction of the line *y* = *ξx* that crosses the origin is controlled by *ξ* (*ξ* = tan*α*). The (negative) value of the conjugate function *f*^⁎ at *ξ* defines the point where the line *y* = *g*(*x*) cuts the vertical axis; *g*(*x*) is formed by translating *ξx* until it becomes tangent to *f* at *x*[⁎].

All that has been said for convex functions applies to concave ones if we replace the max operation in Eqs. [(13.78)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq114) and [(13.82)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq119) with min operations. Note that following this definition, the conjugate function is *concave*, being the result of point-wise minimization of a set of concave functions (an affine function can be considered either convex or concave). Furthermore, if the involved function is neither convex nor concave, one can search for *invertible* transformations that render it convex or concave.

In our context, the purpose of resorting to the notion of the conjugate function is our expectation that such a function, which bounds a (PDF) function as in Eq. [(13.83)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq120), may lead to a functional form that lends itself to tractable computations of the involved integrations.

Example 13.3

Compute the conjugate of the logarithmic function *f*(*x*) = ln *x*, *x* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si315.png).

The logarithmic function is known to be concave. Hence

$f^{\\ast}(\\xi) = \\min\\limits\_{x > 0}\\left\\{ \\xi x - \\ln x \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si316.png)

or

$x\_{\\ast}:\\ \\frac{1}{x} = \\xi\\Rightarrow x\_{\\ast} = \\frac{1}{\\xi}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⇒</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si317.png)

Hence,

*f*^(\*)(*ξ*) = 1 + ln *ξ*.<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si318.png)

Therefore,

$\\ln x = \\min\\limits\_{\\xi > 0}\\left\\{ \\xi x - 1 - \\ln\\xi \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si319.png)

[Fig. 13.11](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0065) shows the respective graphs of the logarithmic function as well as the resulting *linear* function bound for different values of *ξ*.

![Figure 13.11 The linear functions g(x;\\xi) = \\xi x - 1 - \\ln\\xiEquation provide upper bounds to f(x) = \\ln xEquation. Each one of the lines is tangent to f(x) = \\ln xEquation at the point x\_{\\ast} = \\frac{1}{\\xi}Equation.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 13.11](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf0990) The linear functions *g*(*x*; *ξ*) = *ξ**x* − 1 − ln *ξ*<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si324.png) provide upper bounds to *f*(*x*) = ln *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si325.png). Each one of the lines is tangent to *f*(*x*) = ln *x*<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si325.png) at the point $x\_{\\ast} = \\frac{1}{\\xi}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si326.png).

Example 13.4

Consider the univariate Laplacian PDF, which we have already seen in Section [13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0045),

$p(\\theta) = \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\exp\\left( - \\lambda|\\theta| \\right),\\quad\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si320.png)(13.84) 

Our goal is to derive a lower bound in terms of its conjugate function. From Eq. [(13.84)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq126), we get

$\\ln p(\\theta) = \\ln\\frac{\\lambda}{2} - \\lambda|\\theta|.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si321.png)

Define

$f(x) = \\ln\\frac{\\lambda}{2} - \\lambda\\sqrt{x},\\quad x > 0.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si322.png)(13.85) 

Then

ln *p*(*θ*) = *f*(*θ*²).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si323.png)(13.86) 

Note that *f*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si327.png) is a convex function with respect to *x* (Problem [13.17](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0185)). The conjugate of *f*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si327.png) is obtained as^([^(96)](#fn96))

$f^{\\ast}(\\xi) = \\max\\limits\_{x}\\left\\{ - \\frac{\\xi}{2}x - f(x) \\right\\},\\ \\xi > 0.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si329.png)(13.87) 

The parameter *ξ* is constrained to positive values, because for *ξ* ≤ 0<mml:math><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si330.png) the maximum with respect to *x* becomes infinite, which violates the definition of the conjugate functions. Recalling Eq. [(13.85)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq128), maximization leads to

$x\_{\\ast}:\\lambda x^{- \\frac{1}{2}} = \\xi\\Rightarrow x\_{\\ast} = \\lambda^{2}\\xi^{- 2}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⇒</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si331.png)(13.88) 

Combining Eqs. [(13.87)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq130) and [(13.88)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq131) gives

$f^{\\ast}(\\xi) = \\frac{\\lambda^{2}}{2}\\xi^{- 1} - \\ln\\frac{\\lambda}{2}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si332.png)(13.89) 

Hence, we obtain the bound

$f(x) \\geqslant - \\frac{\\xi}{2}x - \\frac{\\lambda^{2}}{2}\\xi^{- 1} + \\ln\\frac{\\lambda}{2},$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si333.png)

or

$\\ln p(\\theta) \\geqslant - \\frac{\\xi}{2}\\theta^{2} - \\frac{\\lambda^{2}}{2}\\xi^{- 1} + \\ln\\frac{\\lambda}{2},\\quad\\xi > 0.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si334.png)

Because this is true ∀*ξ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si335.png), we can replace *ξ* with *ξ*^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si336.png), for notational convenience, which results in

$p(\\theta) \\geqslant \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{\\xi^{- 1}}{2}\\theta^{2} \\right)\\exp\\left( - \\frac{\\lambda^{2}}{2}\\xi \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si337.png)(13.90) 

which, after mobilizing the Gaussian notation and its integration property, can be rewritten as

*p*(*θ*) ≥ 𝒩(*θ*|0, *ξ*)*ϕ*(*ξ*), *ξ* > 0,<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si338.png)(13.91) 

with

$\\phi(\\xi) = \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\sqrt{2\\pi\\xi}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{\\lambda^{2}}{2}\\xi \\right),\\quad\\xi > 0.$<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si339.png)

This is very interesting indeed. The obtained lower bound has a functional dependence on *θ*, which is of a Gaussian nature; the Gaussian term is centered at zero with variance *ξ*. Maximizing with respect to *ξ*, we will obtain the required approximation. [Fig. 13.12](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0070) shows the obtained approximation for different values of *ξ*. Observe that introducing transformations in the involved variables can render the function in the obtained bound a *nonlinear* one.

![Figure 13.12 The Laplacian (red curves) and the approximating Gaussians for two different values of ξ.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr012.jpg)

Figure 13.12 The Laplacian (red curves) and the approximating Gaussians for two different values of *ξ*.

For a multivariate Laplacian and assuming a parameter vector with independent components, it can be trivially shown that

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}p(\\theta\_{k}) \\geqslant \\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{\\theta}|0,\\Xi)\\prod\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\\phi(\\xi\_{k}): = \\widehat{p}(\\mathbf{\\theta};\\mathbf{\\xi}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si340.png)(13.92) 

where **ξ** = \[*ξ*[0], …, *ξ*[*K* − 1]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si341.png) and

*Ξ* :  = *d**i**a**g*{*ξ*[0],*ξ*[1],…,*ξ*[*K* − 1]}.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">diag</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si342.png)

Remarks 13.3

*   •  The method of representing a convex function via the optimization of the lower bound in terms of its conjugate (dual form) is known as the *variational method*, and the associated parameters *ξ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si343.png) as *variational* parameters \[69\]. Its application in the context of machine learning was first reported in \[31\] (see also \[35\]), and its use subsequently proliferated and was adopted in different scenarios.
*   •  The method has been used to obtain variational approximations for a number of PDFs that are suitable for sparsity-aware learning, for example, Jeffreys', Student's *t*, generalized Gaussians (see, e.g., \[61\]), and the logistic regression model \[33\] (Problem [13.18](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#o0190)). Compared to the Laplacian approximation method, the variational approach provides the extra flexibility of optimizing with respect to the corresponding variational parameters (see \[33\] for a related discussion). The reader, however, has to keep in mind that both approximations need not always be good ones. This is readily observed from [Fig. 13.12](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0070). One may obtain a good approximation locally, but not everywhere. However, it turns out that in practice, in the context of Bayesian learning, a poor approximation of the prior (for which such approximations are used) does not necessarily lead to a poor approximation of the posterior. There is no guarantee of it, and it is only the performance in practice that has the final verdict.

## 13.9 Sparsity-aware regression: a variational bound Bayesian path

The goal of this section is to demonstrate the use of convex duality and the respective variational bounds in order to approximate the computation of the evidence function in cases where the corresponding integral is computationally intractable. We have chosen to describe the method in the framework of sparsity-aware learning; this can also help us establish bridges with Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml).

To comply with the assumptions made in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), and without loss of generality, let us assume that the involved data have zero mean values. If not, the training data can be centered by subtracting their respective sample means; thus, we set *θ*[0] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si344.png) and assume that the number of parameters is *K*. Then our regression model becomes

**y** = *Φ***θ** + **η**, **η**, **y** ∈ ℝ^(*N*),  **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*K*),  *K* > *N*,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si345.png)

where we are informed about the “secret” that most of the components of **θ** are (almost) zero. In Section [13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0045), we commented on the inadequacy of a Gaussian prior to provide a reasonable statistical description of a sparse random vector. A heavy-tailed distribution that enjoys popularity for sparse modeling is the Laplacian one. After all, adopting a Laplacian prior to **θ**, that is,

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}p(\\theta\_{k}) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\exp( - \\lambda|\\theta\_{k}|),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si346.png)

and a Gaussian conditional PDF, *p*(**y**|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si272.png), for the observations ***y*** as in Eq. [(13.22)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq29), makes the MAP estimation identical to our familiar LASSO task, discussed in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). In this vein, we will build this section around the Laplacian PDF. [Fig. 13.13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0075)A shows the Laplacian for different values of *λ*. In [13.13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0075)B the two-dimensional plot is provided, from which the respect that this PDF shows to sparse solutions is readily observed, by its slower decay along the two axes.

![Figure 13.13 (A) The one-dimensional Laplacian for different values of λ. (B) A plot of a two-dimensional Laplacian PDF.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr013.jpg)

Figure 13.13 (A) The one-dimensional Laplacian for different values of *λ*. (B) A plot of a two-dimensional Laplacian PDF.

The problem with the Laplacian PDF is that its presence in Eq. [(12.14)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) makes the computation of the integral computationally intractable. Also, recall from Section [12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) that the Laplacian PDF does not belong to the computationally attractive exponential family. To facilitate its treatment, we will employ the variational bound approximation method in order to approximate the Laplacian by a Gaussian, following Eqs. [(13.90)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq135) and [(13.92)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq138). The variational parameters will be determined by maximizing the respective evidence via the EM algorithm. This method in recovering sparse solutions was first introduced in \[21\] in the context of dictionary learning.

For simplicity, let the noise sequence in our regression model be white with variance $\\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2}: = \\frac{1}{\\beta}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si347.png). Then

*p*(**y**|**θ**; *β*) = 𝒩(**y**|*Φ***θ**, *β*^( − 1)*I*),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si220.png)

and using Eq. [(13.92)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq138), we can write

$p(\\mathbf{y};\\beta) = \\int\\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{y}|\\Phi\\mathbf{\\theta},\\beta^{- 1}I)p(\\mathbf{\\theta})\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta} \\geqslant \\left( \\int\\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{y}|\\Phi\\mathbf{\\theta},\\beta^{- 1}I)\\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{\\theta}|0,\\Xi)\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\phi(\\xi\_{k}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0020" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0020" linebreakstyle="before">⩾</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si349.png)

We know by now that the integral results in a new Gaussian function (recall Eq. [(12.15)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)), and hence

$p(\\mathbf{y};\\beta) \\geqslant \\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{y}|0,\\beta^{- 1}I + \\Phi\\Xi\\Phi^{T})\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\phi(\\xi\_{k}): = \\widehat{p}(\\mathbf{y};\\beta,\\Xi).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si350.png)(13.93) 

The unknown values of *β* and Ξ could be obtained by direct maximization of the previous bound. An alternative EM algorithm approach, similar to that of Section [12.5](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), is provided in the chapter's Additional Material part that can be downloaded from the website of the book.

Remarks 13.4

*   •  As we have already commented in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), sparsity-aware learning has been a field of intense research. Undoubtedly this is also the case for the Bayesian approach to sparsity promoting models. So far, we presented a hierarchical approach in Section [13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0045), where sparsity was indirectly imposed by associating a gamma PDF prior on each one of the precision variables individually; this led to an equivalent high-tail Student's *t* PDF description of the involved parameters **θ**. Sparse Bayesian learning was described in Section [13.6](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0050). In the current section, a Laplacian prior was imposed on **θ** in order to promote sparseness. These are not the only possibilities. We focused on them in order to demonstrate some possible paths to treat the evidence maximization whenever the resulting integral is computationally “awkward.”
*   •  In \[18\], sparsity in the Bayesian framework is attacked by imposing a Gaussian prior on the parameters, treating variance as latent variables with an exponential prior. Such modeling is equivalent to a Laplacian PDF, once variances are integrated out. The EM procedure is then used to compute the required estimates. Also in this paper, the use of Jeffreys' prior $(p(x) \\approx \\frac{1}{x})$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si351.png) is proposed as an alternative to the Laplacian one.
*   •  In \[5\], sparsity is imposed in a similar way as before, but in the hierarchical model, the parameter controlling the exponential prior of the precisions is also treated as a latent variable with a Jeffreys' prior. In \[6\], sparsity on the unknown parameters was imposed via a generalized Gaussian PDF, that is,

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\alpha) \\propto \\exp\\left( - \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}|\\theta\_{k}|^{p} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si352.png)(13.94) 

*   Combining this prior with a Gaussian PDF for the conditional, *p*(**y**|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si272.png) in Eq. [(13.22)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq29), would result in a MAP that corresponds to the LS regularized by a nonconvex ℓ[*p*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si353.png), *p* < 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si354.png), norm; we know that such norms are more aggressive, compared to the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si207.png) norm, in recovering sparse solutions. For *p* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si355.png), Eq. [(13.94)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq145) becomes the Laplacian prior. In \[6\], gamma priors are used in association with the hyperparameter *α* and the noise variance, and the variational Bayesian approach is used to obtain the solution.
*   •  In \[34\], the RVM framework is exploited to obtain sparse solutions and the information related to the variance of the obtained estimates is used to determine the number of measurements, which is sufficient for recovering the solution in the framework of compressed sensing. 

### Sparsity-aware learning: some concluding remarks

The task of sparsity-aware learning has been treated in a number of parts in this book. In Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), it was treated as an optimization problem of a regularized cost function. In Section [13.3](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0030) the automatic relevance determination (ARD) concept in Bayesian learning was discussed, and in Section [13.9](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0075), the variational bound technique was exploited to overcome the computational obstacle associated with the Laplacian prior.

In this vein, there are a number of questions that are naturally posed. The first one concerns the relationship between the Bayesian and the regularized cost function optimization approaches. How different are they? Are there any paths that establish connections among them? The second question addresses theoretical issues associated with the performance of the Bayesian techniques compared to their counterparts that were discussed in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). A first systematic attempt to address both questions was made in \[75,76,95,97,98\]. Furthermore, another important theoretical question addresses the task of *identifiability* concerning the sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) models \[66\].

A summary of results concerning the previous tasks can be downloaded from the book's website under the Additional Material part that is associated with the current chapter.

## 13.10 Expectation propagation

*Expectation propagation* is an alternative to the variational techniques for approximating posterior PDFs. The task of interest is the same as the one treated in the beginning of this chapter, in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0015). Assume that we are given a set of observations 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si49.png), which are distributed according to *p*(𝒳|**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si356.png), and a prior, *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si357.png), corresponding to the set of the unknown parameters **θ**.^([^(97)](#fn97))

Let us denote by *q*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si359.png) the estimate of the posterior. The starting point is to compute *q* by minimizing the KL divergence,

$\\text{KL}(p||q) = \\int p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathcal{X})\\ln\\frac{p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathcal{X})}{q(\\mathbf{\\theta})}\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si360.png)(13.95) 

Note that KL(*p*||*q*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si361.png) is different from the KL(*q*||*p*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si362.png) divergence, which is involved in the bound in Eq. [(13.2)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq2). Because the KL divergence is not symmetric, the two methods minimize a different cost. Before proceeding any further, it is important to highlight some implications associated with the two forms of the KL divergence.

*   •  *I-Projection*: The KL(*q*||*p*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si362.png) divergence is given by

$\\text{KL}(q||p) = \\int q(\\mathbf{\\theta})\\ln\\frac{q(\\mathbf{\\theta})}{p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathcal{X})}\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si363.png)(13.96) 

*   This is sometimes known as *I-projection* or *information projection*. Looking carefully at it, note that in regions of the parameter space where *p*(**θ**|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si358.png) assumes small values, KL(*q*||*p*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si362.png) gets large values and minimization pushes *q*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si359.png) to small values as well. Consider now the case that *p*(**θ**|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si358.png) is bimodal, while *q*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si359.png) is constrained to be unimodal. Then minimizing KL(*q*||*p*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si362.png) will force *q* to be placed close to either of the two peaks of *p* in order to get small values in the regions where *p* takes small values too.
*   •  *M-Projection*: We now turn our focus to KL(*p*||*q*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si361.png) divergence, defined in Eq. [(13.95)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq146). This is also known as *M-projection* or *moment projection*. For the case discussed before, in the regions where *p* assumes large values, KL(*p*||*q*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si361.png) gets large values and minimization estimates *q* in order to have large values in these regions too. Thus, the estimate *q* is placed in order for its mode to lie somewhere between the two modes of *p*, as a compromise between the two. Obviously, this is not a good result, because the estimate puts high-probability mass in regions where *p* assumes small values. This discussion points out some limitations on the performance that the expectation propagation method is expected to exhibit in practice, because it is based on KL(*p*||*q*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si361.png) minimization.

We now assume that *p*(𝒳, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si365.png) can be factorized, that is,

$p(\\mathcal{X},\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{j}f\_{j}(\\mathbf{\\theta}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si366.png)(13.97) 

For example, such a product can cover the case where

$p(\\mathcal{X},\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{n}p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}|\\mathbf{\\theta})p(\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si367.png)

where *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si357.png) is the corresponding prior. The more general formulation of the factorization used in Eq. [(13.97)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq148) can serve the needs for more general tasks, as for example graphical models to be treated in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml). Thus, we can now write

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx011.jpg)(13.98) 

where *p*(𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si368.png) is the evidence of the model. The estimate *q* will be chosen to be given in a factorized form, as in the variational approach in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0015), that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx012.jpg)(13.99) 

where *f̂*[*j*](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si369.png) corresponds to *f*[*j*](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si370.png) and *Z* is the normalizing constant. The next assumption is that *q*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si359.png) is constrained to lie within the exponential family of PDFs (Section [12.8](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)) and for our current needs it can be written as

*q*(**θ**) :  = *g*(**a**)*h*(**θ**)exp (**a**^(*T*)**u**(**θ**)),<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si371.png)(13.100) 

where ***a*** is the associated set of parameters.

### Minimizing the KL divergence

Plugging into Eq. [(13.95)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq146) the definition in Eq. [(13.100)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq152) and collecting all terms that are independent of ***a*** in a constant, we readily obtain 

KL(*p*||*q*) =  − ln *g*(**a**) − ∫*p*(**θ**|𝒳)(**a**^(*T*)**u**(**θ**)) *d***θ** + constants.<mml:math><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>constants</mml:mtext><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si372.png)(13.101) 

Taking the gradient with respect to ***a*** and equating to zero we get

$- \\frac{1}{g(\\mathbf{a})}\\nabla g(\\mathbf{a}) = \\mathbb{E}\_{p}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{u}(\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si373.png)(13.102) 

However, from Eq. [(13.100)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq152) we have

*g*(**a**)∫*h*(**θ**)exp (**a**^(*T*)**u**(**θ**)) *d***θ** = 1,<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si374.png)

and taking the gradient with respect to ***a*** results in

0 = ∇*g*(**a**)∫*h*(**θ**)exp (**a**^(*T*)**u**(**θ**)) *d***θ**  + *g*(**a**)∫*h*(**θ**)exp (**a**^(*T*)**u**(**θ**))**u**(**θ**) *d***θ**<mml:math><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo id="mmlbr0021" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mspace linebreak="newline"/><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si375.png)

or

$- \\frac{1}{g(\\mathbf{a})}\\nabla g(\\mathbf{a}) = \\mathbb{E}\_{q}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{u}(\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si376.png)

which combined with Eq. [(13.102)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq154) finally results in

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx013.jpg)(13.103) 

The latter is an elegant equation known as *moment matching*. It basically states that at the optimum, *q*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si359.png), the expectations of its sufficient statistics are equal to the expectations associated with the PDF to be learned. For example, if *q* is chosen to be a Gaussian, the sufficient statistics involves the mean and the covariance matrix. Thus, all one has to do is compute the mean and covariance with respect to *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si357.png) (assuming that they can be obtained) and use them to define the respective Gaussian.

### The expectation propagation algorithm

We will now make use of the moment matching result to obtain the factors, *f̂*[*j*](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si369.png), one at a time. The algorithm starts from some initial estimates, *f̂*[*j*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si377.png). Let us assume that we are currently seeking to update factor *f̂*[*k*](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si378.png). Let *q*^((*i*))(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si379.png) be the currently available estimate of *q*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si359.png), at the *i*th iteration.

1.  ***Step 1*:**  Remove *f̂*[*k*]^((*i*))(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si380.png) from *q*^((*i*))(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si379.png), and define

$q\_{/k}^{(i)}(\\mathbf{\\theta}): = \\frac{q^{(i)}(\\mathbf{\\theta})}{{\\widehat{f}}\_{k}^{(i)}(\\mathbf{\\theta})}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si381.png)(13.104) 

1.  
2.  ***Step 2*:**  Define the PDF
