*p*(**y**|**f**) = 𝒩(**y**|**f**, *σ*[*η*]²*I*).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si660.png)

Then, following exactly the same arguments as in Section [12.2](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), we obtain

*p*(**y**) = 𝒩(**y**|0, 𝒦 + *σ*[*η*]²*I*).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si661.png)(13.139) 

This is also obvious from the fact that the sum of two independent Gaussian variables is also Gaussian and the mean and covariance matrix can directly be obtained from Eq. [(13.138)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq225).

To obtain *p*(*y*|**x**, **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si224.png) we can use Eq. [(13.139)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq229) and apply it recursively. It will also be useful here to bring into the notation the number of available observations, *N*, explicitly and write

$\\mathbf{y}\_{N + 1}^{\\ } = \\begin{bmatrix} y \\\\ \\mathbf{y}\_{N} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},\\quad\\mathbf{y}\_{N}: = {\\lbrack y\_{1},\\ldots,y\_{N}\\rbrack}^{T}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si662.png)

From Eq. [(13.139)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq229), **y**[*N* + 1]^ <mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si663.png) follows a Gaussian distribution

*p*(**y**[*N* + 1]^ |0, *Σ*[*N* + 1]),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si664.png)

with

*Σ*[*N* + 1] :  = 𝒦[*N* + 1] + *σ*[*η*]²*I*[*N* + 1].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si665.png)

Then, from the product rule, we have

$p(y|\\mathbf{y}\_{N}) = \\frac{p(\\mathbf{y}\_{N + 1})}{p(\\mathbf{y}\_{N})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si666.png)(13.140) 

However, because the joint PDF is Gaussian, the conditional in Eq. [(13.140)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq233) is also Gaussian. The respective mean and variance are computed by partitioning the matrix *Σ*[*N* + 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si667.png) (see Appendix of Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), Eqs. (12.134) and (12.133))

$\\Sigma\_{N + 1} = \\begin{bmatrix} {\\kappa(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}) + \\sigma\_{\\eta}^{2},} & {\\mathbf{\\kappa}^{T}(\\mathbf{x})} \\\\ {\\mathbf{\\kappa}(\\mathbf{x}),} & \\Sigma\_{N} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},\\quad\\mathbf{\\kappa}(\\mathbf{x}): = {\\lbrack\\kappa(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}\_{1}),\\ldots,\\kappa(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}\_{N})\\rbrack}^{T},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si668.png)

i.e.,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/fx022.jpg)(13.141) 

Compare Eq. [(13.141)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq235) with Eq. [(11.27)](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml). Taking into account that *Σ*[*N*] = 𝒦[*N*] + *σ*[*η*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si669.png), *μ*[*y*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si670.png) is identical to *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si671.png) obtained by the kernel ridge regression, for appropriate choices of *C* and *σ*[*η*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si146.png). However, now we have also obtained information concerning the respective variance of the resulting estimate.

At this point, it is interesting to look back at the Bayesian regression task for parametric modeling in Section [12.2.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), and to remember that the obtained mean value in Eq. [(12.20)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) was the same (for a zero mean prior *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si357.png)) as that provided by the ridge regression, for an appropriate choice of *λ*.

Remarks 13.7

*   •  From the previous discussion it is apparent that solving the regression task by resorting to Gaussian processes is the Bayesian answer to solving a regression task in an RKHS. Both approaches share a common advantage. Although the underlying mapping to an RKHS (implied by the adopted kernel) may live in a high-dimensional space, the complexity for solving the task depends on the number of training points, *N*. The source of complexity associated with the Gaussian processes is the inversion of the matrix, which amounts to 𝒪(*N*³)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si672.png) operations.
*   •  Both equations in [(13.141)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq235) can be obtained from the corresponding equation derived for the linear case of Bayesian learning, covered in Section [12.2.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). Indeed, setting **θ**[0] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si673.png) in Eq. [(12.27)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and combining it with Eq. [(12.22)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), we obtain

*μ*[*y*](**x**) = *σ*[*θ*]²**x**^(*T*)*X*^(*T*)(*σ*[*η*]²*I*+*σ*[*θ*]²*X**X*^(*T*))^( − 1)**y**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>η</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si674.png)(13.142) 

*   where *X* has replaced Φ, because the linear case is treated. Applying now the kernel trick, as discussed in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), to replace *σ*[*θ*]²**x**[*i*]^(*T*)**x**[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si675.png) with a kernel *κ*(**x**[*i*], **x**[*j*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si676.png) operation, one readily obtains the corresponding equation in [(13.141)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq235).
*   In a similar way, one can obtain *σ*[*y*]²(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si677.png) in Eq. [(13.141)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq235) from Eq. [(12.23)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) by using Woodbury's formula for matrix inversion from Appendix A.1 to reformulate Eq. [(12.23)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) according to Eq. [(12.28)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) (try it).

#### Dealing with hyperparameters

As we have already stated, the kernel function can be given in terms of some parameters, say, ***θ***, which in turn have to be estimated from the data. There are various ways to deal with this task. The first that comes to mind is to optimize the resulting parameterized log-likelihood, ln *p*(**y**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si678.png), with respect to ***θ***, by taking the gradient and equating to zero. Another way is to assume a prior on the parameters and use Bayesian arguments to integrate them out. The integration is usually intractable and approximate techniques must be used, for example, Monte Carlo methods (Chapter [14](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml)). Needless to say, both techniques have their drawbacks. Optimizing the log-likelihood is a nonconvex task that cannot guarantee, in general, a global maximum. On the other hand, Monte Carlo techniques tend to be computationally intensive, requiring many iterations to converge. More on these issues can be found in \[68\].

#### Computational considerations

In order to reduce the 𝒪(*N*³)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si672.png) computational load associated with the inversion of *Σ*[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si679.png), a number of approximate techniques have been proposed. A possible path is the *sparse Gaussian processes*; in these methods, the full Gaussian process model is approximated by using an expansion in terms of a finite set of basis functions. For example, it is common to use as bases the set *κ*(**x**, **u**[*m*])<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si680.png), where **u**[*m*], *m* = 1, 2, …, *M* ≪ *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si681.png), is a subset of the input samples known as *active set*. Such techniques can lead to a reduced cost of the order of 𝒪(*M*²*N*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si682.png) (e.g., \[67\]). Other alternatives that do not require the active set to be a subset of the training samples have also been proposed (e.g., \[40,79\]). In \[90\], a variational sparse method is proposed that attempts to alleviate problems encountered when one increases the size of the active set.

A variation of the Gaussian processes approach is to equip it with the ability to forget past samples for time-varying environments; this method has been proposed in \[63,92\] as an alternative to the kernel RLS algorithm discussed in Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml). Other variants use transformations of the output variables to make Gaussian models applicable to a wider range of problems \[41,78\].

In \[72\], the connection between Gaussian processes and Kalman filtering is exploited and the solution is obtained via the involvement of stochastic differential equations, which makes the dependence of the complexity on time to be linear.

Finally, an extended review of related techniques is provided in \[44\].

### 13.12.3 Classification

In contrast to the regression task, under the Gaussian assumptions for the noise and the involved random process, the classification task gets more involved. In Section [13.7](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0060), the logistic regression in its parametric form, given in Eq. [(13.68)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq99), was employed. In the context of the Gaussian processes, the model becomes

$P(\\omega\_{1}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{1}{1 + \\exp\\left( - f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)} = \\sigma\\left( f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si683.png)

where now *f*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si302.png) will be treated in terms of a Gaussian random process, associated with a kernel function *κ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si256.png). Given a set of training samples, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*, *y*[*n*] ∈ {0, 1}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si684.png), and following the same arguments as in Section [13.7](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0060), we can now write

$P(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{f}) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\sigma{(f\_{n})}^{y\_{n}}{(1 - \\sigma(f\_{n}))}^{1 - y\_{n}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si685.png)

where *f*[*n*] :  = *f*(*x*[*n*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si686.png), and

*p*(**f**) = 𝒩(**f**|0, 𝒦).<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si658.png)

Note that *P*(**y**|**f**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si687.png) is no longer Gaussian and the involved integrations needed to obtain *P*(**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si688.png) and/or *P*(*y*|**x**, **y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si689.png) cannot be performed analytically. There are various ways to perform approximations. One path is to resort to the Laplacian approximation of *p*(*f*(*x*)|**y**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si690.png) (see Section [12.3](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)) \[93\]. Another is to use Monte Carlo techniques \[54\]. In \[20\], a variational approach has been used to obtain bounds on the logistic sigmoid and approximate the respective product with a product of Gaussians. The expectation propagation method has been used in \[58\].

For further reading on Gaussian processes, the interested reader may consult the classical reference \[68\].

Example 13.6

The goal of this example is to demonstrate the usage of Gaussian processes in regression. To this end, *N* = 20<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si691.png) points were randomly sampled from a realization of a Gaussian process, with zero mean and covariance function based on the Gaussian kernel with length scale *h* = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si692.png). The corresponding input points were drawn according to a normal distribution of zero mean and unit variance. In the sequel, Gaussian noise was added to these Gaussian process points, with variance 0.01, to form the set of observed data (shown as “+” in [Fig. 13.22](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0140)). Using these as the training data, predictions of the output variables, corresponding to *D* = 1000<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si693.png) equidistant input points in the interval \[ − 3, 4\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si694.png), were performed; for the prediction, the expressions for the posterior Gaussian process mean and variance in Eq. [(13.141)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq235) were used. The mean of the posterior Gaussian process is illustrated in [Fig. 13.22](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0140) as a solid red line. The shaded area surrounding the curve of the posterior mean corresponds to the error bars *μ*[*y*] ± 2*σ*[*y*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si695.png) of the posterior prediction. Note the increase of the posterior prediction variance in regions where observed data points are scarce.

![Figure 13.22 The red line corresponds to the mean of the posterior Gaussian process. The shaded area corresponds to ± twice the standard deviation.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr022.jpg)

## 13.13 A case study: hyperspectral image unmixing

*Hyperspectral image unmixing* (HSI) is a typical application of sparse regression modeling under a set of constraints. It is a good “excuse” for us to demonstrate the application of the hierarchical Bayesian modeling approach via a task of great practical importance.

In *hyperspectral remote sensing*, the electromagnetic solar energy emanating from the earth's surface is measured by sensitive scanners located aboard a satellite, an aircraft, or a space station. The scanners are sensitive to a number of wavelength bands of the electromagnetic radiation. Different properties of the earth's surface contribute to the reflection of the energy in the different bands. For example, in the visible–infrared range, properties such as the mineral and moisture contents of soils, the sedimentation of water, and the moisture content of vegetation are the main contributors to the reflected energy. In contrast, at the thermal end of the infrared, it is the thermal capacity and thermal properties of the surface that contribute to the reflection. Thus, each band measures different properties of the same patch of the earth's surface. In this way, images of the earth's surface corresponding to the spatial distribution of the reflected energy in each band can be created. The task now is to exploit this information in order to identify the various ground cover types, that is, built-up land, agricultural land, forest, fire burn, water, diseased crop, and so on.

[Fig. 13.23](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0145) illustrates the process of generating a pixel's spectral signature out of a hyperspectral image data cube (the cube consists of two spatial and one spectral dimension). Each image corresponds to a single wavelength (band) and each pixel to a specific patch of the earth's surface. The *spectral signature* of a pixel is simply a vector containing radiance values measured in the various spectral bands. Technological advances in recent years have allowed the implementation of imaging spectrometers, which have the ability to collect data in hundreds of adjacent spectral bands. The highly increased volume of data conveys spatial/spectral information that can be properly exploited to accurately determine the type and nature of the objects being imaged.

![Figure 13.23 Each image corresponds to a specific wavelength band and each pixel to a particular patch of the earth's surface. The signature of a pixel is a vector whose coefficients measure the radiance of the respective patch of the earth in the different bands (modified image taken from \[71\]).](images/B9780443292385000196/gr023.jpg)

[Figure 13.23](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf1815) Each image corresponds to a specific wavelength band and each pixel to a particular patch of the earth's surface. The signature of a pixel is a vector whose coefficients measure the radiance of the respective patch of the earth in the different bands (modified image taken from \[71\]).

An intimate limitation of hyperspectral remote sensing is that a single pixel often records a mixed spectral signature of different distinct materials, due to the low spatial resolution of the remote sensor. This raises the need for spectral unmixing (SU) \[37\], which is a very important step in hyperspectral image processing that has recently attracted strong scientific interest. SU is the procedure of decomposing the measured spectrum of an observed pixel into a collection of constituent spectral signatures (or *endmembers*) and their corresponding proportions (or *abundances*). A widely used model to perform SU is the linear mixing model.

Assume a remotely sensed hyperspectral image consisting of *M* spectral bands, and let **y** ∈ ℝ^(*M*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si696.png) be the vector containing the measured spectral signature (i.e., the radiance values in all spectral bands) of a single pixel (specific earth patch). Also let *X* = \[**x**[1],**x**[2],…,**x**[*l*]\]<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si697.png) stand for the *M* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si698.png) endmember signature matrix, where **x**[*i*] ∈ ℝ^(*M*), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si699.png), comprises the spectral signatures of the *i*th endmember, and *l* is the total number of (possible) distinct endmembers (earth surface/material types) present in the scene. Finally, let **θ** = \[*θ*[1],*θ*[2],…,*θ*[*l*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si700.png) be the *abundance vector* associated with ***y***, where *θ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si701.png) denotes the abundance fraction of **x**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si702.png) in ***y***. The linear mixing model assumes that there is a linear relationship between the spectra of the measured pixel and the endmembers, expressed as

**y** = *X***θ** + **η**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si703.png)(13.143) 

where ***η*** stands for the additive noise values, which are assumed to be samples of a zero mean Gaussian distributed random vector, with (i.i.d.) elements, that is, **η** ∼ 𝒩(**η**|0, *β*^( − 1)*I*[*M*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">η</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">η</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si704.png), where *β* denotes the inverse of the noise variance (precision), and *I*[*M*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si705.png) is the *M* × *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si706.png) identity matrix. Note that the model in Eq. [(13.143)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq240) is a typical regression model in its multivariate formulation, because now the output for each measurement is a vector and not a scalar (see also Section [4.9](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml) of Chapter [4](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml)). The output variables are measured and the matrix *X* is assumed known, and indeed there are methods to estimate its elements.

Treating such a model to recover the abundance coefficients would be a straightforward application of what has been said so far in the current and previous chapters of this book. However, there is a physical constraint that has to be considered and that makes the task more interesting. The abundance coefficients are nonnegative, that is,

*θ*[*i*] ≥ 0, *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si707.png)(13.144) 

Additionally, a valid assumption is that only a few of the endmembers present in the image will contribute to the spectrum of a single pixel ***y***. In other words, the abundance vector ***θ*** accepts a *sparse* representation in *X*.

Thus, our goal is to estimate ***θ*** subject to the nonnegativity as well as the sparsity constraints, given the spectral measurements, ***y***, and the endmember matrix, *X*. Obviously, there are different paths to achieve this goal. Because we are currently exploring the Bayesian world, we will employ the Bayesian framework. To this end, an appropriate prior model that expresses our prior belief on the parameters of interest will first be adopted, and we will then perform Bayesian inference using the variational Bayes methodology, as has been previously discussed.

### 13.13.1 Hierarchical Bayesian modeling

The presence of Gaussian noise in Eq. [(13.143)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq240) dictates that

$p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{\\theta},\\beta) = \\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{y}|X\\mathbf{\\theta},\\beta^{- 1}I\_{M}) = \\left( 2\\pi \\right)^{- \\frac{M}{2}}\\beta^{\\frac{M}{2}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{\\beta}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{y} - X\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right\\|^{2} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0024" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0024" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si708.png)(13.145) 

We now turn our attention to selecting suitable priors for the model parameters, which are treated as random variables, **θ**, *β*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">β</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si709.png). As a prior for the nonnegative noise precision β we adopt a Gamma distribution (Section [13.3](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0030), Eq. [(13.25)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq32)), expressed as

$p(\\beta) = {Gamma}(\\beta|c,d) = \\frac{d^{c}}{\\Gamma(c)}\\beta^{c - 1}\\exp\\left( - d\\beta \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gamma</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si710.png)(13.146) 

where *c* and *d* are the respective parameters (set equal to 10^( − 6)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si711.png) in the experiments).

For the abundance vector **θ**, we define a two-level hierarchical prior that is expressed in a conjugate form and imposes sparsity as well as nonnegativity on the abundance coefficients. Inspired by \[70\], a nonnegatively truncated Gaussian prior is selected, i.e.,

*p*(**θ**|**α**) = 𝒩[ℝ[+]^(*l*)](**θ**|0,*A*^( − 1)),<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si712.png)(13.147) 

where **α** :  = \[*α*[1], *α*[2], …, *α*[*l*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">α</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si713.png) is the precision parameter vector, *A* = diag{*α*[1], …, *α*[*l*]}<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>diag</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si714.png) is the corresponding diagonal matrix, and 𝒩[ℝ[+]^(*l*)]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si715.png) signifies the *l*\-variate normal distribution truncated at the nonnegative orthant of ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si716.png), denoted by ℝ[+]^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si717.png) \[84\]. In the second level of hierarchy, the precision parameters are also considered random variables, *α*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si718.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si719.png), that follow an inverse Gamma distribution, that is,

$p(\\alpha\_{i}) = {IGamma}\\ \\left( \\alpha\_{i}|1,\\frac{b\_{i}}{2} \\right) = \\frac{b\_{i}}{2}\\alpha\_{i}^{- 2}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{b\_{i}}{2}\\frac{1}{\\alpha\_{i}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">IGamma</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si720.png)(13.148) 

where *b*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si721.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si722.png), are scale hyperparameters. These two levels of hierarchy form a nonnegatively truncated multivariate Laplace prior over the abundance vector **θ**, which can be established by integrating out the precision **α** \[84\], that is,

$p(\\mathbf{\\theta}|\\mathbf{b},\\beta) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\sqrt{\\beta b\_{i}}\\exp\\left( - \\sqrt{\\beta b\_{i}}|\\theta\_{i}| \\right)I\_{\\mathbb{R}\_{+}^{l}}(\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si723.png)(13.149) 

where *I*[ℝ[+]^(*l*)](**θ**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si724.png) is the indicator function, with *I*[ℝ[+]^(*l*)](**θ**) = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si725.png) (resp. 0) if **θ** ∈ ℝ[+]^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si726.png) (resp. **θ** ∉ ℝ[+]^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si727.png)). In our formulation, the sparsity promoting scale hyperparameters in Eq. [(13.148)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq245) are also assumed to be random and are inferred from the data, by assuming the following Gamma prior distribution for each *b*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si728.png):

$p(b\_{i}) = {Gamma}(b\_{i}|\\kappa,\\nu) = \\frac{\\nu^{\\kappa}}{\\Gamma(\\kappa)}b\_{i}^{\\kappa - 1}\\exp\\left( - \\nu b\_{i} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Gamma</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ν</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ν</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>κ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>ν</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si729.png)(13.150) 

Hyperparameters *κ* and *ν* in Eq. [(13.150)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq247) are also set to small values (10^( − 6)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si711.png) in the experiments).

Having adopted the hierarchical Bayesian model, the variational EM algorithm discussed in Section [13.3](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#s0030) is applied with the goal of obtaining estimates, *q*(*θ*[*i*]), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si730.png), of the posteriors of the abundance parameters given the observations. In the experiments, the respective mean values of *q*(*θ*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si731.png) will be used as estimates of the unknown parameter values. Details on the derivation can be obtained from \[85\]. The alternative path to the variational EM algorithm is to employ Monte Carlo techniques (see, e.g., \[14\]).

### 13.13.2 Experimental results

The previously described model was applied to a real hyperspectral image, collected by the Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (AVIRIS) over a Cuprite mining district in Nevada in the summer of 1997.^([^(103)](#fn103))

![Figure 13.24 Composite of the AVIRIS Cuprite subimage using bands 183, 193, and 203 (from \[71\]). The full RGB color image is available from the website of this book.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr024.jpg)

[Figure 13.24](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf1890) Composite of the AVIRIS Cuprite subimage using bands 183, 193, and 203 (from \[71\]). The full RGB color image is available from the website of this book.

After removing some low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) bands and water vapor absorption bands, *M* = 188<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>188</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si733.png) spectral bands remain available for processing. As a preprocessing step, the vertex component analysis (VCA) algorithm^([^(104)](#fn104))

![Figure 13.25 Spectral signatures of 6 out of the 14 endmembers extracted from the Cuprite image using the VCA algorithm \[52\]. A figure showing all 14 signatures can be downloaded from the website of this book.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr025.jpg)

[Figure 13.25](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#cf1905) Spectral signatures of 6 out of the 14 endmembers extracted from the Cuprite image using the VCA algorithm \[52\]. A figure showing all 14 signatures can be downloaded from the website of this book.

[Fig. 13.26](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0160) shows the resulting abundance maps for six different endmembers, using the variational Bayes method. A dark (resp. light) pixel reveals a low (resp. high) proportional percentage for the respective endmember in that pixel. In other words, each image shows the distribution of values of a specific abundance coefficient, *θ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si701.png), over the sensed earth surface.

![Figure 13.26 Estimated abundance maps for the materials (A) muscovite, (B) alunite, (C) buddingtonite, (D) montmorillonite, (E) kaolinite 1, and (F) kaolinite 2. The full-color image is available from the website of this book.](images/B9780443292385000196/gr026.jpg)

Figure 13.26 Estimated abundance maps for the materials (A) muscovite, (B) alunite, (C) buddingtonite, (D) montmorillonite, (E) kaolinite 1, and (F) kaolinite 2. The full-color image is available from the website of this book.

More important, we are able to identify the presented endmembers in [Fig. 13.26](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0160) as muscovite, alunite, buddingtonite, montmorillonite, kaolinite 1, and kaolinite 2.

3.  13.12  Consider a two-class classification task and assume that the feature vectors in each one of the two classes, *ω*[1], *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si259.png), are distributed according to the Gaussian PDF. Prove that, given an observed feature vector, **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si750.png), the posterior probability for deciding in favor of one of the classes is given by the logistic function, i.e.,

$P(\\omega\_{2}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{1}{1 + \\exp\\left( - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{x} + \\theta\_{0} \\right)},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

$P(Z) = \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\frac{\\alpha}{K}\\frac{\\Gamma\\left( m\_{k} + \\frac{\\alpha}{K} \\right)\\Gamma\\left( N - m\_{k} + 1 \\right)}{\\Gamma\\left( N + 1 + \\frac{\\alpha}{K} \\right)}$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si763.png)

1.  and

$P(\\lbrack Z\\rbrack) = \\frac{K!}{\\prod\_{h = 0}^{2^{N} - 1}K\_{h}!}\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\frac{\\alpha}{K}\\frac{\\Gamma\\left( m\_{k} + \\frac{\\alpha}{K} \\right)\\Gamma\\left( N - m\_{k} + 1 \\right)}{\\Gamma\\left( N + 1 + \\frac{\\alpha}{K} \\right)},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo 2.  13.24  Show that the discarded pieces, *π*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si599.png), in the stick breaking construction of an IBP are equal to the sequence of probabilities produced in a DP stick breaking construction. 

### Computer exercises

1.  13.25  Generate *N* = 60<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>60</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si766.png) data points from each of the five Gaussian distributions given in [Example 13.1](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#enun0020). Implement the EM algorithm to obtain estimates of the parameters of the Gaussian mixture model (Exercise [12.18](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)). Run the EM algorithm on the generated data, assuming *K* = 25<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si198.png) clusters, using randomly chosen values for the initial mean values and the covariance matrices. Plot the initial and final estimates of the EM and the variational Bayes algorithm to reproduce the results of [Fig. 13.4](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0025). Play with different values of the parameters.

Compute *N* basis functions, each one located at a sampling point *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si767.png), of the form *ϕ*[*n*](*x*) = exp (−(*x* − *x*[*n*])²/2*σ*[*ϕ*]²)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si769.png), where *σ*[*ϕ*]² = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si770.png). [(12.43)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), [(12.44)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), [(12.51)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), and [(12.52)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), in order to fit a (generalized) linear regression model comprising the *N* basis functions to the generated data *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si771.png). 3.  13.27  Generate *N* = 150<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>150</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si772.png) two-dimensional data points **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si163.png), uniformly distributed in the region \[ − 5, 5\] × \[ − 5, 5\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si773.png). Assign a binary label to each **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si163.png), depending a) on which side of the graph of the function

*f*(*x*) = 0.05*x*³ + 0.05*x*² + 0.05*x* + 0.05<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn></mml:math>

1.  the point lies and b) on the value of a noise variable. To generate the training data, for each sample **x**[*n*] = \[*x*[*n*1], *x*[*n*2]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si775.png), compute
