Generate two-dimensional data from the Gaussian mixture model of [Example 13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#enun0060) and reproduce the results in [Fig. 13.17](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0105).
3.  13.29  Consider a one-dimensional Gaussian process with zero mean and Gaussian (kernel) covariance function, with length scale *h* = 0.5<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si692.png) 
    1.  **(a)**  Sample *D* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si783.png) equidistant input points in the interval \[ − 2, 2\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si784.png). Use these as input points to compute the covariance function of the Gaussian process and form the respective 100 × 100<mml:math><mml:mn>100</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si785.png) covariance matrix. Use the corresponding multivariate Gaussian to generate samples for five different realizations and plot the results, as in [Fig. 13.21](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0135). Repeat the same experiment with different values for the parameter *h*.
    2.  **(b)**  Now, sample *N* = 20<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si691.png) input points from a zero mean, unit-variance normal distribution. Based on these input points, evaluate the covariance function and the respective 20 × 20<mml:math><mml:mn>20</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>20</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si786.png) covariance matrix, as before. Then, generate noisy Gaussian process data, by first sampling *N* points from our Gaussian process, and then adding zero mean Gaussian noise with variance 0.1. Next, sample *D* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si783.png) points in the interval \[ − 3, 4\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000196/si694.png). Compute the corresponding mean and the variance of the predictive Gaussian process, as given in Eq. [(13.141)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#deq235). In a single figure, plot the observed data, the posterior mean, and the error bars of the predictive mean, as in [Fig. 13.22](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml#f0140).

## 14.1 Introduction

In Chapters [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), the Bayesian inference task was considered. A large part of the latter chapter was dedicated to dealing with approximation techniques, which offered escape routes when the involved PDFs were complex enough to render integral computations intractable. All these techniques were of a deterministic nature; that is, the goal was to approximate the mathematical expression of the corresponding PDF by another one that could ease the associated calculations. Such methods include the Laplacian approximation, as well as the variational methods based on the mean field theory or the convex duality concept. Deterministic approximation methods will also be used for approximate inference in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), to deal with graphical models.

In this chapter, we turn our attention to approximation methods with a much stronger statistical flavor, which are based on randomly generating samples using numerical techniques; these samples are typical of an underlying distribution, which may be of either continuous or discrete nature. This is an old field, with origins tracing back to the late 1940s and early 1950s in the pioneering work of Stanislav Ulam, John Von-Neumann, and Nicholas Metropolis in Los Alamos, when the term *Monte Carlo* was coined as an umbrella name of such techniques, inspired by the famous casino in Monaco (see, e.g., \[28\] for a historical note). The first application of such techniques, which coincided with the development of the first computers, was in the context of the Manhattan project for developing the hydrogen bomb; soon after, Monte Carlo methods were embraced by almost every scientific area where statistical computations are involved.

As is often the case with pioneering ideas, when they are looked at a posteriori, that is, once they have been stated, the basic idea seems simple. Our current task of interest is the computation of an integral, which involves a PDF; this can alternatively be interpreted as the computation of an “expectation.” Such a view provides the permit to approximate the integral as the sample mean of the involved quantities, given a sufficient number of samples and exploiting the law of large numbers.

To condense a field with a history of a number of decades in a single chapter is obviously impossible. Our goal is to present the basic concepts, definitions, and directions, with the aim of serving the needs associated with typical machine learning tasks rather than looking at it as an entity on its own.

We start with the more classical methods using transformations and then move on to the rejection and importance sampling techniques. In the sequel, the more powerful methods based on arguments from the theory of Markov chains are reviewed. The Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs sampling methods are presented and discussed. Finally, a case study concerning the change-point detection task is considered.

## 14.2 Monte Carlo methods: the main concept

Our starting point is the evaluation of integrals of the form

𝔼\[*f*(**x**)\] :  = ∫[ − ∞]^∞*f*(**x**)*p*(**x**) *d***x**,<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si1.png)(14.1) 

where **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si2.png) is a random vector and *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png) is the corresponding distribution.^([^(106)](#fn106))

Coming back to Eq. [(14.1)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq1), assume that one has at her/his disposal a number of i.i.d. samples, **x**[1], …, **x**[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si7.png), drawn from *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png). Then the approximation

$\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack \\approx \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}f(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}): = {\\overline{\\mathbb{E}}}\_{f,N}$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si8.png)(14.2) 

is justified by (a) the *law of large numbers* and (b) the *central limit theorem* \[32\]. Let us denote 𝔼\[*f*(**x**)\] = *μ*[*f*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si9.png) and the respective variance as *v**a**r*\[*f*(**x**)\] :  = 𝔼 \[(*f*(**x**)−𝔼\[*f*(**x**)\])²\] = *σ*[*f*]²<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">var</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si10.png). Then the previously referred two theorems guarantee that for large values of *N*

$\\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}{\\overline{\\mathbb{E}}}\_{f,N} = \\mu\_{f},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si11.png)(14.3) 

and

$p\\left( {\\overline{\\mathbb{E}}}\_{f,N} \\right) \\approx \\mathcal{N}\\left( {\\overline{\\mathbb{E}}}\_{f,N} \\middle| \\mu\_{f},\\ \\frac{\\sigma\_{f}^{2}}{N} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="5.2ex" minsize="5.2ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="5.2ex" minsize="5.2ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si12.png)(14.4) 

The limit in Eq. [(14.3)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq3) refers to the notion of *almost sure convergence*, that is,

${Prob}\\ \\left\\{ \\lim\\limits\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty} \\middle| {\\overline{\\mathbb{E}}}\_{f,N} - \\mu\_{f} \\middle| = 0 \\right\\} = 1.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Prob</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si13.png)

The approximate Gaussian distribution in Eq. [(14.4)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq4) guarantees that the variance (as one changes the set of *N* samples) of the obtained estimate ${\\overline{\\mathbb{E}}}\_{f,N}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si14.png) around the true value *μ*[*f*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si15.png) decreases with *N*.

Thus, if one generates the samples **x**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si16.png), from the distribution *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png), the use of Monte Carlo techniques offers the means for an approximation of the integral in Eq. [(14.1)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq1) with the following nice properties: (a) the approximation error is decreasing as $\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{N}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si17.png); (b) the obtained estimate using *N* samples is an unbiased estimate of the true value; and (c) the convergence rate is *independent* of the dimensionality *l*. The latter property is in contrast to methods based on the deterministic numerical integration, which, in general, have a convergence that slows down as the dimensionality increases. In Monte Carlo techniques, if one is not satisfied with the obtained accuracy, all he/she has to do is generate more samples.

The crucial point now becomes that of developing techniques to generate i.i.d. samples from *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png). This is not an easy task, especially for high-dimensional spaces. Note that achieving a certain accuracy for the estimator in Eq. [(14.2)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq2) is independent of the dimensionality, once i.i.d. samples drawn from *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png) are available. On the other hand, drawing i.i.d. samples typical of *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png) becomes harder as the dimensionality increases. We will return to this point soon. In the sequel, we will focus on some basic directions to achieve the aforementioned goal.

### 14.2.1 Random number generation

Random number generation can be achieved either as the result of an experiment or via the use of computers. For example, the tosses of a fair coin can generate a random sequence of 0s (heads) or 1s (tails). Another example is the sequence of numbers corresponding to the distance between radioactive emissions; such an experiment generates a sequence of exponentially distributed samples. However, such approaches are not of much practical value and the emphasis has been on techniques that generate samples via a computer, using a *pseudorandom number generator*. At the heart of such methods lie algorithms that guarantee the generation of a sequence of *integers*, *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si18.png), which approximately follow a *uniform distribution* in an interval in the real axis. In the sequel, the generation of random numbers/vectors, which follow an arbitrary distribution, is obtained *indirectly* via a variety of methods, each with its pros and cons. The path for generating integers in an interval (0, *M*<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si19.png)) follows the general recursion,

*z*[*i*] = *g*(*z*[*i* − 1], …, *z*[*i* − *m*])*m**o**d*  *M*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si20.png)

where *g* is a function depending on the *m* previously generated samples and mod denotes the modulus operation; that is, *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si18.png) is the remainder of the division of *g*(*z*[*i* − 1], …, *z*[*i* − *m*])<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si21.png) by *M*. The simpler form is the linear version,

*z*[*i*] = *α**z*[*i* − 1]*m**o**d*  *M*, *z*[0] = 1, *i* ≥ 1,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si22.png)(14.5) 

where *M* is a large prime number and *α* is an integer. Recursion [(14.5)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq7) generates a sequence of numbers between 1 and *M* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si23.png). The method is known as *linear congruential generator* or Lehmer's algorithm \[20\].

If *α* is properly selected, then the resulting sequence of numbers turns out to be periodic with period *M* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si23.png). This is the reason we call these generators pseudorandom, because a periodic sequence can never be claimed to be random. However, for large values of *M*, the obtained sequence can be sufficiently random with uniform distribution, provided, of course, that *N* ≤ *M* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si24.png). For example, a value of *M* of the order of 10⁹ is sufficient for most applications. Note that not all possible choices of the parameter *α* guarantee a good generator. In practice, a sequence is accepted as being random only if it meets a number of related tests of randomness and is subsequently used successfully in a variety of applications (see, e.g., \[32\]). A common choice of parameters that leads to a reasonably good uniformly distributed random sequence is *α* = 7⁵<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>7</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si25.png) and *M* = 2^(31) − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>31</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si26.png) (see, e.g., \[34\]). More on this topic can be found in Knuth's classical text and the references therein \[18\]. Once a sequence of integers is available, a sequence of uniformly distributed real random numbers is obtained as the ratio $x\_{i} = \\frac{z\_{i}}{M} \\in (0,1)$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si27.png) (as a matter of fact, this is the sequence on which the randomness tests are applied).

Remarks 14.1

*   •  Note that even the generation of a sequence of (pseudo)random numbers with uniform distribution in (0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si28.png) is not an easy task, in spite of the fact that the uniform distribution is an “easy” one; that is, all values are equally probable. Moreover, often in practice, a PDF is known up to its normalizing constant, i.e.,

$p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{\\phi(\\mathbf{x})}{Z},$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si29.png)

*   where

*Z* = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*ϕ*(**x**) *d***x**.<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si30.png)

*   However, if *ϕ*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si31.png) has a complicated form, the previous integration may be intractable. This is often met when computing posterior PDFs. The previous points make the process of sampling from a general *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png) much harder than for the case of a uniform one. The task becomes even harder in high dimensions, even if *Z* is available. The required number of points, in order to cover sufficiently a region in a high-dimensional space, exhibits an exponential dependence on the respective dimensionality (curse of dimensionality, Section [3.12](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)). Thus, a huge number of points is needed in order to get a good representation of *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png) in high-dimensional spaces. In practice, one would be more content to generate samples from the regions where *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png) gets relatively high values. However, the higher the dimensionality, the more difficult the task of locating the high-probability regions. Similar arguments hold for random variables of a discrete nature, where the number of states that the variable can take is very large. Ideally, in order to have a representative sequence of samples, all states have to be visited. 

## 14.3 Random sampling based on function transformation

In this section, we deal with some of the most basic techniques for drawing samples from a PDF, *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png).

*Function inversion*. Let x be a real random variable with a PDF, *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si32.png), and a corresponding cumulative distribution function

*F*[*x*](*x*) = ∫[ − ∞]^(*x*)*p*(*τ*) *d**τ*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si33.png)

It is known from probability theory that the random variable, u, defined as

*u* :  = *F*[*x*](*x*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si34.png)(14.6) 

is *uniformly* distributed in the interval 0 ≤ *u* ≤ 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si35.png) *irrespective of the nature* of *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si32.png) (see \[32\] and Problem [14.1](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#o0010)). If, in addition, we assume that the function *F*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si36.png) has an inverse, *F*[*x*]^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si37.png), then we can write

*x* = *F*[*x*]^( − 1)(*u*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si38.png)(14.7) 

Thus, following the reverse arguments, samples from *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si32.png) can be generated by first generating samples from the uniform distribution, 𝒰(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si39.png), and then applying on them the inverse function, *F*[*x*]^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si37.png) (Problem [14.2](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#o0015)).

This method works well provided that *F*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si36.png) has an inverse that can be easily computed. However, only a few PDFs can be “proud” of having inverses that can be expressed in an analytical form.

Example 14.1

Generate samples, *x*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si40.png), that follow the exponential distribution,

*p*(*x*) = *λ*exp ( − *λ**x*), *x* ≥ 0, *λ* > 0,<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si41.png)(14.8) 

using a pseudorandom generator that generates samples, *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si42.png), from the uniform distribution 𝒰(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si39.png).

We have

*F*[*x*](*x*) = ∫[0]^(*x*)*λ*exp ( − *λ**τ*) *d**τ* = 1 − exp ( − *λ**x*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si43.png)

By letting

*u* :  = *F*[*x*](*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si44.png)

and solving for *x*, we get

$x = - \\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\ln(1 - u): = F\_{x}^{- 1}(u).$<mml:math><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si45.png)

Hence, if *u*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si42.png) are samples drawn from a uniform distribution, the sequence

$x\_{n} = - \\frac{1}{\\lambda}\\ln(1 - u\_{n}),\\quad n = 1,2,\\ldots,N,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si46.png)

are samples drawn from the exponential PDF in Eq. [(14.8)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq13). [Fig. 14.1](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#f0010) shows the  histogram of the generated samples for *N* = 1000<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si47.png), alongside *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si32.png) for *λ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si48.png).

![Figure 14.1 The histogram of the samples generated from the uniform distribution, and using the inverse of Fx, which describes the exponential PDF, whose curve is shown in black. The length of the bin interval, Δx, was chosen equal to 0.02.](images/B9780443292385000202/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 14.1](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#cf0220) The histogram of the samples generated from the uniform distribution, and using the inverse of *F*[x], which describes the exponential PDF, whose curve is shown in black. The length of the bin interval, Δ*x*, was chosen equal to 0.02.

Example 14.2

*Generating samples from discrete distributions*. Here, an intuitive method for generating samples from discrete distributions is presented. We will use such distributions in Section [17.2](#Chp017_855-884_B9780443292385000238.xhtml).

Let *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*K*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si49.png) denote discrete random events occurring with probabilities *P*[1], *P*[2], …, *P*[*K*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si50.png), respectively, such that $\\sum\_{k = 1}^{K}P\_{k} = 1$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si51.png). Then the following simple algorithm draws samples from this distribution.

Algorithm 14.1

**Sampling discrete distributions**

*   •  Define $a\_{k} = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{k - 1}P\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si52.png), $b\_{k} = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{k}P\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si53.png), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si54.png), *a*[1] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si55.png).
*   •  **For** *i* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si56.png), **Do** 
    1.  –  *u*∼ 𝒰(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si57.png)
    2.  –  Select 
        1.  ⁎  *x*[*k*] if *u* ∈ \[*a*[*k*], *b*[*k*]), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si58.png)
*   •  **End For**

[Fig. 14.2](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#f0015) provides an illustration of the algorithm. Note that the probability jumps at the beginning of each interval and the corresponding cumulative distribution function (CDF) is constructed; the algorithm basically computes the inverse of *u*, according to this CDF (see, e.g., \[4\]).

![Figure 14.2 The CDF for a discrete distribution of K discrete random events. If P1 + P2 ⩽ u < P1 + P2 + P3, the event x3 is drawn. Note that the higher the probability of an event is, the larger the corresponding interval jump in the CDF becomes, hence the higher the probability of this event being drawn.](images/B9780443292385000202/gr002.jpg)

[Figure 14.2](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#cf0225) The CDF for a discrete distribution of *K* discrete random events. If *P*[1] + *P*[2] ⩽ *u* < *P*[1] + *P*[2] + *P*[3], the event *x*[3] is drawn. Note that the higher the probability of an event is, the larger the corresponding interval jump in the CDF becomes, hence the higher the probability of this event being drawn.

*Function transformation*. We will demonstrate the method via an example involving the transformation of two random variables, say, r and ϕ, to two new ones, x and y. Let

*x* = *g*[*x*](*r*, *ϕ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si59.png)

and

*y* = *g*[*y*](*r*, *ϕ*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si60.png)

Let us now assume that there is a unique solution for the inverses and that they can be expressed in an analytic form (which is not the case in general), that is,

*r* = *g*[*r*](*x*, *y*), *ϕ* = *g*[*ϕ*](*x*, *y*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal" id="mmlbr0001">r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0001" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si61.png)

We know from Section [2.2.5](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml) that if *p*[*r*, *ϕ*](*r*, *ϕ*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si62.png) is the joint distribution of r and ϕ, then the joint distribution of x and y is given by

$p\_{x,y}(x,y) = \\frac{p\_{r,\\phi}\\left( g\_{r}(x,y),g\_{\\phi}(x,y) \\right)}{\\left| \\text{det}\\left( J(x,y;r,\\phi) \\right) \\right|}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mtext>det</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si63.png)(14.9) 

where |det(*J*(*x*,*y*;*r*,*ϕ*))|<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mtext>det</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si64.png) is the absolute value of the determinant of the Jacobian matrix,

$J(x,y;r,\\phi) = \\left\\lbrack \\begin{array}{ll} {\\frac{\\partial g\_{x}}{\\partial r}\\ } & \\frac{\\partial g\_{x}}{\\partial\\phi} \\\\ {\\frac{\\partial g\_{y}}{\\partial r}\\ } & \\frac{\\partial g\_{y}}{\\partial\\phi} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si65.png)(14.10) 

and we have assumed, for simplicity, that to each value of (*r*, *ϕ*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si66.png) there corresponds one value of (*x*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si67.png). Let us now see how one can generate samples from a Gaussian *p*(*x*) = 𝒩(*x*|0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si68.png) by using samples drawn from a uniform and an exponential distribution, respectively, for ϕ and r; recall that in [Example 14.1](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#enun0015), we described a technique for generating samples from an exponential distribution.

*The Box–Muller method*. Let r be distributed according to an exponential distribution,

$p\_{r}(r) = \\frac{1}{2}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{r}{2} \\right),\\quad r \\geqslant 0,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si354.png)(14.11) 

and ϕ to a uniform distribution, 𝒰(0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si39.png),

$p\_{\\phi}(\\phi) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} {\\frac{1}{2\\pi},\\ } & {\\quad 0 \\leqslant \\phi \\leqslant 2\\pi,} \\\\ {0,\\ } & {\\quad\\text{otherwise},} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>otherwise</mml:mtext><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si70.png)(14.12) 

and also assume that they are independent, that is,

*p*[*r*, *ϕ*](*r*, *ϕ*) = *p*[*r*](*r*)*p*[*ϕ*](*ϕ*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si71.png)(14.13) 

Generate two new random variables as

$x = \\sqrt{r}\\cos\\phi,$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si72.png)(14.14) 

$y = \\sqrt{r}\\sin\\phi.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si73.png)(14.15) 

The physical interpretation of the previous transformation is that *x*, *y*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si74.png) correspond to the Cartesian coordinates of a point and *r*, *ϕ*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si75.png) are its polar ones ([Fig. 14.3](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#f0020)). From Eqs. [(14.14)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq26) and [(14.15)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq27), we can write

*r* = *x*² + *y*²,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si76.png)(14.16) 

$\\phi = \\arctan\\left( \\frac{y}{x} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arctan</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si77.png)(14.17) 

Adjusting Eq. [(14.9)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq21) to our current needs, using Eqs. [(14.11)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq23)–[(14.13)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq25), we obtain

$p\_{x,y}(x,y) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\frac{1}{2}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{x^{2} + y^{2}}{2} \\right)2 = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{x^{2}}{2} \\right)\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}}\\exp\\left( - \\frac{y^{2}}{2} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0002" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si78.png)(14.18) 

where we have used that (Problem [14.3](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#o0020))

$|J(x,y;r,\\phi)| = \\frac{1}{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si79.png)

Thus, we have shown that using the transformation given in Eqs. [(14.14)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq26) and [(14.15)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq27), we can generate samples from standard Gaussians.

![Figure 14.3 (A) Relation of the Cartesian (x,y) to the polar coordinates (r,ϕ). (B, C) If r and ϕ are random variables following an exponential and a uniform in \[0,2π\] distribution, respectively, then x and y are independent and they both follow the standard Gaussian, as shown in (D) for the x-variable.](images/B9780443292385000202/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 14.3](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#cf0240) (A) Relation of the Cartesian (*x*,*y*) to the polar coordinates (*r*,*ϕ*). (B, C) If r and ϕ are random variables following an exponential and a uniform in \[0,2*π*\] distribution, respectively, then x and y are independent and they both follow the standard Gaussian, as shown in (D) for the x-variable.

Once samples from a standard Gaussian, 𝒩(*x*|0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si80.png), are available, samples from a general Gaussian, 𝒩(*y*|*μ*, *σ*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si81.png), are obtained via the obvious transformation

*y* = *σ**x* + *μ*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si82.png)(14.19) 

The previous approach is also generalized to random vectors in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si83.png). One can first draw samples from **x** ∼ 𝒩(**x**|0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si84.png) by stacking together *l* i.i.d. samples drawn from the standard Gaussian, 𝒩(*x*|0, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si80.png), and then apply the transformation

**y** = *L***x** + **μ**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si85.png)

which is equivalent to drawing samples from

**y** ∼ 𝒩(**y**|**μ**, *Σ*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si86.png)(14.20) 

where *Σ* = *L**L*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si87.png) (Cholesky factorization, Problem [14.4](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#o0025)).

Example 14.3

Generate *N* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si88.png) samples, *r*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, 100<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si89.png), from the exponential distribution in Eq. [(14.11)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq23) (following [Example 14.1](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#enun0015)) and *N* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si88.png) samples, *ϕ*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, 100<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si90.png), from the uniform in Eq. [(14.12)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq24). Then use the transformations in Eqs. [(14.14)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq26), [(14.15)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq27), and [(14.19)](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#deq32) to obtain samples, *x*[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, 100<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si91.png), from *p*(*x*) = 𝒩(*x*|1, 0.5)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si92.png). The histogram of the obtained samples is shown in [Fig. 14.4](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#f0025).

[Figure 14.4](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#cf0320) The histogram of *N* = 100 points generated in [Example 14.3](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml#enun0030) together with the graph of *p*(*x*) = 𝒩(*x*|1, 0.5)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si92.png). The bin length was chosen to be equal to Δ*x* = 0.05.

## 14.4 Rejection sampling

Applying the previously reported techniques relies on having the involved transformation functions available in a convenient (analytic) form, which in general is the exception instead of the rule. From now on, we turn our attention to alternative methods.

*Rejection sampling* (e.g., \[7,37\]) is conceptually a simple technique; in order to generate independent samples from a desired PDF, *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si3.png), one draws samples from another one, say, *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si93.png), that is easier to handle, and then, instead of applying a transformation, some of the points are *rejected* according to an appropriate criterion.

Given two random variables, x and u, recall that the marginal, *p*(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si32.png), is obtained by integrating the joint PDF, *p*[*x*, *u*](*x*, *u*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si94.png), that is,

*p*(*x*) = ∫[ − ∞]^( + ∞)*p*[*x*, *u*](*x*, *u*) *d**u*.<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>u</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000202/si95.png)(14.21) 

Let us now consider the following identity:
