## 15.6 Moralization of directed graphs

At a number of points we have already made bridges between BNs and MRFs. In this section, we will formalize the bridge and see how one can convert a BN to an MRF and discuss the subsequent effects of such a conversion on the implied conditional independencies.

We can trust common sense to drive us to construct such a conversion. Because the conditional distributions will play the role of the potential functions (factors), one has to make sure that edges do exist among all the involved variables in each one of these factors. Because edges from the parents to children exist, we have to (a) retain these edges and make them undirected and (b) add edges between nodes that are parents of a common child. This is shown in [Fig. 15.20](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0110). In [Fig. 15.20](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0110)A, a DAG is shown, which is converted to the MRF of [Fig. 15.20](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0110)B by adding undirected edges between *x*[1], *x*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si217.png) (parents of *x*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si218.png)) and *x*[3], *x*[6]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si219.png) (parents of *x*[5]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si111.png)). The procedure is  known as *moralization* and the resulting undirected graph as a *moral graph*. The terminology stems from the fact that “parents are forced to be married.” This conversion will be very useful soon, when an inference algorithm will be stated that covers both BNs and MRFs in a unifying framework.

![Figure 15.20 (A) A DAG and (B) the resulting MRF after applying moralization on the DAG. Directed edges become undirected and new edges, shown in red, are added to “marry” parents with common child nodes.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr020.jpg)

Figure 15.20 (A) A DAG and (B) the resulting MRF after applying moralization on the DAG. Directed edges become undirected and new edges, shown in red, are added to “marry” parents with common child nodes.

The obvious question that is now raised is how moralization affects independencies. It turns out that if *H* is the resulting moral graph, then *I*(*H*) ⊆ *I*(*G*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si220.png) (Problem [15.11](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#o0095)). In other words, the moral graph can guarantee a smaller number of independencies compared to the original BN via its set of *d*\-separations. This is natural because one adds extra links. For example, in [Fig. 15.20](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0110)A, *x*[1], *x*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si217.png) in the converging node *x*[1] → *x*[3] ← *x*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">←</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si221.png) are marginally independent, not given *x*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="normal">3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si218.png). However, in the resulting moral graph in [15.20](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0110)B, this independence is lost. It can be shown that moralization adds the fewest extra links and hence retains the maximum number of independencies (see, for example, \[25\]).

## 15.7 Exact inference methods: message passing algorithms

This section deals with efficient techniques for inference on undirected graphical models. So, even if our starting point was a BN, we assume that it was converted to an undirected one prior to the inference task. We will begin with the simplest case of graphical models—graphs comprising a chain of nodes. This will help the reader to grasp the basic notions behind exact inference schemes. It is interesting to note that, in general, the inference task in graphical models is an NP-hard one \[10\]. Moreover, it has been shown that for general BNs, approximate inference to a desired number of digits of precision is also an NP-hard task \[11\]; that is, the time required has an exponential dependence on the number of digits of accuracy. However, as we will see in a number of cases that are commonly encountered in practice, the exponential growth in computational time can be bypassed by exploiting the underlying independencies and factorization properties of the associated distributions.

The inference tasks of interest are (a) computing the likelihood, (b) computing the marginals of the involved variables, (c) computing conditional probability distributions, and (d) finding modes of distributions.

### 15.7.1 Exact inference in chains

Let us consider the chain graph of [Fig. 15.21](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0115) and focus our interest on computing marginals. The naive approach, which overlooks factorization and independencies, would be to work directly on the joint distribution. Let us concentrate on discrete variables and assume that each one of them, *l* in total, has *K* states. Then, in order to compute the marginal of, say, *x*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si222.png), we have to obtain the sum

$P(x\_{j}): = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{1}}\\cdots\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{j - 1}}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{j + 1}}\\cdots\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{l}}P(x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{l}) = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{i}:i \\neq j}P(x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{l}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo Let us now bring factorization into the game and concentrate on computing *P*(*x*[1])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si89.png). ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si229.png)(15.38) 

*   •  Define

$\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{l}}\\psi\_{l - 1,l}(x\_{l - 1},x\_{l}): = \\mu\_{b}(x\_{l - 1}).$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si230.png)

*   Because the possible values of the pair (*x*[*l* − 1], *x*[*l*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si231.png) comprise a table with *K*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si232.png) elements, the summation involves *K*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si232.png) terms and *μ*[*b*](*x*[*l* − 1])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si233.png) consists of *K* possible values.
*   •  After marginalizing out *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si226.png), the only factor in the product that depends on *x*[*l* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si234.png) is

*ψ*[*l* − 2, *l* − 1](*x*[*l* − 2], *x*[*l* − 1])*μ*[*b*](*x*[*l* − 1]).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si235.png)

*   Then, in a similar way as before, we obtain

$P(x\_{1}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{i}:i \\neq 1,l - 1,l}\\ \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l - 3}\\psi\_{i,i + 1}(x\_{i},x\_{i + 1})\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{l - 1}}\\psi\_{l - 2,l - 1}(x\_{l - 2},x\_{l - 1})\\mu\_{b}(x\_{l - 1}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si236.png)

*   where this summation also involves *K*²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si232.png) terms. 

We are now ready to define the general recursion as

![](images/B9780443292385000214/fx006.jpg)

whose repeated application leads to

$\\mu\_{b}(x\_{1}) = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{2}}\\psi\_{1,2}(x\_{1},x\_{2})\\mu\_{b}(x\_{2}),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si237.png)

and finally

$P(x\_{1}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\mu\_{b}(x\_{1}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si238.png)(15.40) 

The series of recursions is illustrated in [Fig. 15.22](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0120).

![Figure 15.21 An undirected chain graph with l nodes. There are l − 1 cliques consisting of pairs of nodes.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr021.jpg)

[Figure 15.21](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#cf0720) An undirected chain graph with *l* nodes. There are *l* − 1 cliques consisting of pairs of nodes.

![Figure 15.22 To compute P(x1), starting from the last node, xl, each node (a) receives a message and (b) processes it locally via sum and product operations, which produces a new message; and (c) the latter is passed backward, to the node on its left. We have assumed that μb(xl)=1.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr022.jpg)

Figure 15.22 To compute *P*(*x*[1]), starting from the last node, x[*l*], each node (a) receives a message and (b) processes it locally via sum and product operations, which produces a new message; and (c) the latter is passed backward, to the node on its left. We have assumed that *μ*[*b*](*x*[*l*])=1.

We can think that every node, *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si34.png), (a) receives a message from its right, *μ*[*b*](*x*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si239.png), which for our case comprises *K* values, (b) performs locally sum-multiply operations and a new message *μ*[*b*](*x*[*i* − 1])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si240.png) is computed, which (c) is passed to its left, to node *x*[*i* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si241.png). The subscript “*b*” in *μ*[*b*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si242.png) denotes “backward” to remind us of the flow of the message passing activity from right to left.

If we wanted to compute *P*(*x*[*l*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si243.png), we would adopt the same reasoning but start summation from *x*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si54.png). In this case, message passing takes place forward (from left to right) and messages are defined as

![](images/B9780443292385000214/fx007.jpg)

where “*f*” has been used to denote “forward” flow. The procedure is shown in [Fig. 15.23](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0135).

![Figure 15.23 To compute P(xl), message passing takes place in the forward direction, from left to right. As opposed to Fig. 15.22, messages are denoted as μf, to remind us of the forward flow.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr023.jpg)

[Figure 15.23](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#cf0735) To compute *P*(*x*[*l*]), message passing takes place in the forward direction, from left to right. As opposed to [Fig. 15.22](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0120), messages are denoted as *μ*[*f*], to remind us of the forward flow.

The term *μ*[*b*](*x*[*j*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si244.png) is the result of summing the products over *x*[*j* + 1], *x*[*j* + 2], …, *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si245.png), and the term *μ*[*f*](*x*[*j*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si246.png) over *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*j* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si247.png). At each iteration step, one variable is *eliminated* by summing up over all its possible values. It can be easily shown, following similar arguments, that the marginal at any point, *x*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si57.png), 2 ≤ *j* ≤ *l* − 1<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>⩽</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si248.png), is obtained by (Problem [15.13](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#o0105))

$P(x\_{j}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\mu\_{f}(x\_{j})\\mu\_{b}(x\_{j}),\\quad j = 2,3,\\ldots,l - 1.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si249.png)(15.42) 

The idea is to perform one forward and one backward message passing operation, store the values, and then compute any one of the marginals of interest. The total cost will be 𝒪(2*K*²*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si250.png), instead of *K*^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si251.png) of the naive approach.

We still have to compute the normalizing constant *Z*. This is readily done by summing up both sides of Eq. [(15.42)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#deq60), which requires 𝒪(*K*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si252.png) operations,

$Z = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{j} = 1}^{K}\\mu\_{f}(x\_{j})\\mu\_{b}(x\_{j}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si253.png)(15.43) 

So far, we have considered the computation of marginal probabilities. Let us now turn our attention to their conditional counterparts. We start with the simplest case, for example, to compute *P*(*x*[*j*]|*x*[*k*] = *x̂*[*k*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si254.png), *k* ≠ *j*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si255.png). That is, we assume that variable *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si99.png) has been observed and its value is *x̂*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si256.png). The first step in computing the conditional is to recover the joint *P*(*x*[*j*], *x*[*k*] = *x̂*[*k*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si257.png). This is a normalized version of the respective conditional, which can then be obtained as

$P(x\_{j}|x\_{k} = {\\widehat{x}}\_{k}) = \\frac{P(x\_{j},x\_{k} = {\\widehat{x}}\_{k})}{P({\\widehat{x}}\_{k})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si258.png)(15.44) 

The only difference in computing *P*(*x*[*j*], *x*[*k*] = *x̂*[*k*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si257.png) compared to the previous computations of the marginals is that now, in order to obtain the messages, we *do not sum* with respect to *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si55.png). We just *clump* the respective potential function to its value *x̂*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si256.png). That is, the computations

$\\mu\_{b}(x\_{k - 1}) = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{k}}\\psi\_{k - 1,k}(x\_{k - 1},x\_{k})\\mu\_{b}(x\_{k}),\\mu\_{f}(x\_{k + 1}) = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{k}}\\psi\_{k,k + 1}(x\_{k},x\_{k + 1})\\mu\_{f}(x\_{k})$<mml:math><mml:msub id="mmlbr0012"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0012" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si259.png)

are replaced by

*μ*[*b*](*x*[*k* − 1]) = *ψ*[*k* − 1, *k*](*x*[*k* − 1], *x̂*[*k*])*μ*[*b*](*x̂*[*k*]), *μ*[*f*](*x*[*k* + 1]) = *ψ*[*k*, *k* + 1](*x̂*[*k*], *x*[*k* + 1])*μ*[*f*](*x̂*[*k*]).<mml:math><mml:msub ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si260.png)

In other words, *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si99.png) is considered a delta function at the *instantiated* value. Once *P*(*x*[*j*], *x*[*k*] = *x̂*[*k*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si257.png) has been obtained, normalization is straightforward and is locally performed at the *j*th node. The procedure can be generalized when more than one variable is observed.

### 15.7.2 Exact inference in trees

Having gained experience and learned the basic secrets in developing efficient inference algorithms for chains, we turn our attention to the more general case involving *tree-structured* undirected graphical models.

A tree is a graph in which there is a single chain/trail between any two nodes of the graph; thus, there are no cycles in the graph. [Figs. 15.24](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0140)A and B are two examples of trees. A tree can be directed or undirected. Note that in a directed tree, any node has only one parent and there is a single *root* node that has no parent. Furthermore, because in a directed one there are no children with two parents, the moralization step, which converts a directed graph to an undirected one, adds no extra links. The only change consists of making the edges undirected.

![Figure 15.24 Examples of (A) directed and (B) undirected trees. Note that in the directed one, any node has a single parent. In both cases, there is only a single chain that connects any two nodes. (C) The graph is not a tree because there is a cycle.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr024.jpg)

Figure 15.24 Examples of (A) directed and (B) undirected trees. Note that in the directed one, any node has a single parent. In both cases, there is only a single chain that connects any two nodes. (C) The graph is not a tree because there is a cycle.

There is an important property of the trees, which will prove very important for our current needs. Let us denote a tree graph as *T*, which is a collection of vertices/nodes *V* and edges *E*, which link the nodes, that is, *T* = {*V*, *E*}<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si261.png). Consider any node *x* ∈ *V*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si262.png) and consider the set of all its neighbors, that is, all nodes that share an edge with x. Denote this set as

𝒩(*x*) = {*y*∈*V*:(*x*,*y*)∈*E*}.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si263.png)

Looking at [Fig. 15.24](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0140)B, we have 𝒩(*x*) = {*y*, *u*, *z*, *v*}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si264.png). Then, for *each* element *r* ∈ 𝒩(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">r</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si265.png), define the subgraph *T*[*r*] = {*V*[*r*], *E*[*r*]}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si266.png) such that *any* node in this subgraph can be reached from r via paths that *do not pass* through x. In [Fig. 15.24](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0140)B, the respective subgraphs, each associated with one element in (*y*, *u*, *z*, *v*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si267.png)), are encircled by dotted lines. By the definition of a tree, it can easily be deduced that each one of these subgraphs is also a tree. Moreover, these subgraphs are *disjoint*. In other words, *each one* of the neighboring nodes of a node, for example, x, can be viewed as a *root* of a subtree, and these subtrees are mutually disjoint, having no common nodes. This property will allow us to break a large problem into a number of smaller ones. Moreover, each one of the smaller problems can be further divided in the same way, being itself a tree. We now have all the basic ingredients to derive an efficient scheme for inference on trees (recall that such a breaking of a large problem into a sequence of smaller ones was at the heart of the message passing algorithm for chains). However, let us first bring the notion of factor graphs into the scene. The reason is that using factor graphs allows us to deal with some more general graph structures, such as *polytrees*.

A directed polytree is a graph in which, although there are no cycles, a child may have more than one parent. [Fig. 15.25](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0145)A shows an example of a polytree. The unpleasant situation results after the moralization step because marrying the parents results in cycles, and we *cannot* derive *exact* inference algorithms in graphs with cycles, [Fig. 15.25](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0145)B. However, if one converts the original directed polytree into a factor graph, the resulting bipartite entity has a tree structure, with no cycles involved, [Fig. 15.25](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0145)C. Thus, everything we said before about tree structures applies to these factor graphs.

![Figure 15.25 (A) Although there are no cycles, one of the nodes has two parents, and hence the graph is a polytree. (B) The resulting structure after moralization has a cycle. (C) A factor graph for the polytree in (A).](images/B9780443292385000214/gr025.jpg)

Figure 15.25 (A) Although there are no cycles, one of the nodes has two parents, and hence the graph is a polytree. (B) The resulting structure after moralization has a cycle. (C) A factor graph for the polytree in (A).

### 15.7.3 The sum-product algorithm

We will develop the algorithm for exact inference in trees in a “bottom-up” approach, via the use of an example. Once the rationale is understood, the generalization can readily be obtained. Let us consider the factor tree of [Fig. 15.26](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0150). The factor nodes are denoted by capital letters and squares, and each one is associated with a potential function. The rest are variable nodes, denoted by circles. Assume that we want to compute the marginal *P*(*x*[1])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si89.png). Node *x*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si28.png), being a variable node, is connected to factor nodes only. We split the graph in as many (tree) subgraphs as the factor nodes connected to *x*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si28.png) (three in our case). In the figure, each one of these subgraphs is encircled, having as roots the nodes A, H, and G, respectively. Recall that the joint *P*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si268.png) is given as the product of all the potential functions, each one associated with one factor node, divided by the normalizing constant, *Z*. Focusing on the node of interest, *x*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si28.png), this product can be written as

$P(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\psi\_{A}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{A})\\psi\_{H}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{H})\\psi\_{G}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{G}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si269.png)(15.45) 

where **x**[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si270.png) denotes the vector corresponding to all the variables in *T*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si271.png); the vectors **x**[*H*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si272.png) and **x**[*G*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si273.png) are similarly defined. The function *ψ*[*A*](*x*[1], **x**[*A*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si274.png) is the product of all the potential functions associated with the factor nodes in *T*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si271.png), and *ψ*[*H*](*x*[1], **x**[*H*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si275.png) and *ψ*[*G*](*x*[1], **x**[*G*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si276.png) are defined in an analogous way. Then the marginal of interest is given by

$P(x\_{1}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{A} \\in V\_{A}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{H} \\in V\_{H}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{G} \\in V\_{G}}\\psi\_{A}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{A})\\psi\_{H}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{H})\\psi\_{G}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{G}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo We will concentrate on the subtree with root A, denoted as *T*[*A*] :  = {*V*[*A*], *E*[*A*]}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si278.png), where *V*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si279.png) stands for the nodes in *T*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si271.png) and *E*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si280.png) for the respective set of edges. Note that *x*[1] ∉ *V*[*A*] ∪ *V*[*H*] ∪ *V*[*G*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∉</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∪</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si282.png). Having reserved the symbol *ψ*[*A*](⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si283.png) to denote the product of all the potentials in the subtree *T*[*A*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si271.png) (and similarly for *T*[*H*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si284.png) and *T*[*G*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si285.png)), let us denote the individual potential functions, for each one of the factor nodes, via the symbol *f*, as shown in [Fig. 15.26](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0150). $\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{A} \\in V\_{A}}\\psi\_{A}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{A}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{A} \\in ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si288.png)

Observe that we were led to define two types of messages; one type is passed from variable nodes to factor nodes and the other type is passed from factor nodes to variable nodes.

*   •  Variable node to factor node messages ([Fig. 15.27](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0155)A):

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/fx008.jpg)(15.49) 

*   We use 𝒩(*x*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si289.png) to denote the set of the nodes with which a variable node x is connected; 𝒩(*x*) ∖ *f*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∖</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si290.png) refers to all nodes *excluding* the factor node *f*; note that all these nodes are factor nodes. In other words, the action of a variable node, as far as message passing is concerned, is to multiply incoming messages. Obviously, if it is connected only to one factor node (except *f*), then such a variable node passes what it receives, without any computation. This is, for example, the case with *μ*[*x*[2] → *f*[*a*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si293.png), as previously defined.

![Figure 15.26 The tree is subdivided into three subtrees, each one having as its root one of the factor nodes connected to x1. This is the node whose marginal is computed in the text. Messages are initiated from the leaf nodes toward x1. Once messages arrive at x1, a new propagation of messages starts, this time from x1 to the leaves.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr026.jpg)

Figure 15.26 The tree is subdivided into three subtrees, each one having as its root one of the factor nodes connected to x[1]. This is the node whose marginal is computed in the text. Messages are initiated from the leaf nodes toward x[1]. Once messages arrive at x[1], a new propagation of messages starts, this time from x[1] to the leaves.

![Figure 15.27 (A) Variable x is connected to S factor nodes, besides f; that is, \\mathcal{N}(x) \\smallsetminus f = \\{ f\_{1},f\_{2},\\ldots,f\_{S}\\}Equation. The output message from x to f is the product of the incoming messages. The arrows indicate directions of flow of the message propagation. (B) The factor node f is connected to S node variables, besides x; that is, \\mathcal{N}(f) \\smallsetminus x = \\{ x\_{1},x\_{2},\\ldots,x\_{S}\\}Equation.](images/B9780443292385000214/gr027.jpg)

Figure 15.27 (A) Variable x is connected to *S* factor nodes, besides *f*; that is, 𝒩(*x*) ∖ *f* = {*f*[1], *f*[2], …, *f*[*S*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∖</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si291.png). The output message from x to *f* is the product of the incoming messages. The arrows indicate directions of flow of the message propagation. (B) The factor node *f* is connected to *S* node variables, besides x; that is, 𝒩(*f*) ∖ *x* = {*x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*S*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si292.png).

*   
*   •  Factor node to variable node messages ([Fig. 15.27](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#f0155)B):

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/fx009.jpg)(15.50) 

*   where 𝒩(*f*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si294.png) denotes the set of the (variable) nodes connected to *f* and 𝒩(*f*) ∖ *x*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∖</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si295.png) the corresponding set if we exclude node x. The vector **x**^(*f*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si296.png) comprises all the variables involved as arguments in *f*, that is, all the variables/nodes in 𝒩(*f*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si294.png).

If a node is a leaf, we adopt the following convention. If it is a variable node, x, connected to a factor node, *f*, then

*μ*[*x* → *f*](*x*) = 1.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si297.png)(15.51) 

If it is a factor node, *f*, connected to variable node, x, then

*μ*[*f* → *x*](*x*) = *f*(*x*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000214/si298.png)(15.52) 

Adopting the previously stated definitions, Eq. [(15.48)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml#deq69) is now written as

$\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{A} \\in V\_{A}}\\psi\_{A}(x\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{A})\\quad = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{2}}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{3}}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{4}}f\_{a}(x\_{1},x\_{2},x\_{3},x\_{4})\\mu\_{x\_{2}\\rightarrow f\_{a}}(x\_{2})\\mu\_{x\_{3}\\rightarrow f\_{a}}(x\_{3})\\mu\_{x\_{4}\\rightarrow f\_{a}}(x\_{4})\\quad = \\mu\_{f\_{a}\\rightarrow x\_{1}}(x\_{1}).$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0016"><mml:mo
