### 16.2.2 Message passing in junction trees

By its definition, a junction tree is a join tree where we have associated a factor, say, *ψ*[*c*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si49.png), of a probability distribution, *p*, with each one of the cliques. Each factor may be the result of the product of all the potential functions, which are defined in terms of the variables associated with the nodes of the corresponding clique; hence, the domain of each one of these potential functions is a subset of the variables-nodes comprising the clique. Then, focusing on the discrete probability case, we can write

$P(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\prod\\limits\_{c}\\psi\_{c}(\\mathbf{x}\_{c}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si50.png)(16.3) 

where *c* runs over the cliques and **x**[*c*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si51.png) denotes the variables comprising the respective clique. Because a junction tree is a graph with a tree structure, exact inference can take place in the same way as we have already discussed in Section [15.7](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), via a message passing rationale. A two-way message passing is also required here. There are, however, some small differences. In the case of the factor graphs, which we have considered previously in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), the exchanged messages were functions of one variable. This is not necessarily the case here. Moreover, after the bidirectional flow of the messages has been completed, what is recovered from each node of the junction tree is the *joint probability of the variables associated with the clique,* *P*(**x**[*c*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si52.png). The computation of the marginal probabilities for individual variables requires extra summations in order to marginalize with respect to the rest.

Note that in the message passing, the following take place:

*   •  A separator receives messages and passes their product to one of its connected cliques, depending on the direction of the message passing flow, that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/fx001.jpg)(16.4) 

*   where 𝒩(*S*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si53.png) is the index set of the clique nodes connected to *S* and 𝒩(*S*)﹨*V*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>﹨</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si54.png) is this set excluding the index for clique node *V*. Note that the message is a function of the variables comprising the separator.
*   •  Each clique node performs marginalization and passes the message to each one of its connected separators, depending on the direction of the flow. Let *V* be a clique node and **x**[*V*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si55.png) the vector of the involved variables in it, and let *S* be a separator node connected to it. The message passed to *S* is given by

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/fx002.jpg)(16.5) 

*   

By **x**[*S*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si56.png) we denote the variables in the separator *S*. Obviously, **x**[*S*] ⊂ **x**[*V*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si57.png) and **x**[*V*]﹨**x**[*S*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>﹨</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si58.png) denotes all variables in **x**[*V*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si55.png) excluding those in **x**[*S*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si56.png); 𝒩(*V*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si59.png) is the index set of all separators connected to *V* and **x**[*s*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si60.png), the set of variables in the respective separator (**x**[*s*] ⊂ **x**[*V*], *s* ∈ 𝒩(*V*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si61.png)); 𝒩(*V*)﹨*S*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>﹨</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si62.png) denotes the index set of all separators connected to *V* excluding *S*. This is basically the counterpart of Eq. [(15.50)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml). [Fig. 16.9](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0050) shows the respective configuration.

![Figure 16.9 Clique node V “collects” all incoming messages from the separators it is connected with (except S); then it outputs a message to S, after the marginalization performed on the product of ψV(xV) with the incoming messages.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 16.9](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf0360) Clique node *V* “collects” all incoming messages from the separators it is connected with (except *S*); then it outputs a message to *S*, after the marginalization performed on the product of *ψ*[*V*](***x***[*V*]) with the incoming messages.

Once the two-way message passing has been completed, marginals in the clique as well as the separator nodes are computed as (Problem [16.3](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0055)):

*   •  Clique nodes:

$P(\\mathbf{x}\_{V}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\psi\_{V}(\\mathbf{x}\_{V})\\prod\\limits\_{s \\in \\mathcal{N}(V)}\\mu\_{s\\rightarrow V}(\\mathbf{x}\_{s}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si63.png)(16.6) 

*   
*   •  Separator nodes: Each separator is connected only to clique nodes. After the two-way message passing, every separator has received messages from both flow directions. Then it is shown that

$P(\\mathbf{x}\_{S}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\prod\\limits\_{v \\in \\mathcal{N}(S)}\\mu\_{v\\rightarrow S}(\\mathbf{x}\_{S}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si64.png)(16.7) 

*   

An important by-product of the previous message passing algorithm in junction trees concerns the joint distribution of all the involved variables, which turns out to be independent of *Z*, and it is given by (Problem [16.4](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0060))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/fx003.jpg)(16.8) 

where ∏[*v*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∏</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si65.png) and ∏[*s*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∏</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si66.png) run over the sets of clique nodes and separators, respectively, and *d*[*s*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si67.png) is the number of the cliques separator *S* is connected to.

Example 16.3

Let us consider the junction tree of [Fig. 16.8](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0045). Assume that *ψ*[1](*A*, *T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si68.png), *ψ*[2](*T*, *L*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si69.png), *ψ*[3](*S*, *L*, *B*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si70.png), *ψ*[4](*B*, *L*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si71.png), *ψ*[5](*X*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si72.png), and *ψ*[6](*B*, *D*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si73.png) are known. For example,

*ψ*[1](*A*, *T*) = *P*(*T*|*A*)*P*(*A*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si74.png)

and

*ψ*[3](*S*, *L*, *B*) = *P*(*L*|*S*)*P*(*B*|*S*)*P*(*S*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si75.png)

The message passing can start from the leaves, (*A*, *T*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si39.png) and (*X*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si76.png), toward (*S*, *L*, *B*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si77.png); once this message flow has been completed, message passing takes place in the reverse direction. Some examples of message computations are given below.

The message received by node (*T*, *L*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si42.png) is equal to

$\\mu\_{S\_{1}\\rightarrow V\_{2}}(T) = \\sum\\limits\_{A}\\psi\_{1}(A,T).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si78.png)

Also,

$\\mu\_{V\_{2}\\rightarrow S\_{2}}(L,E) = \\sum\\limits\_{T}\\psi\_{2}(T,L,E)\\mu\_{S\_{1}\\rightarrow V\_{2}}(T) = \\mu\_{S\_{2}\\rightarrow V\_{4}}(L,E),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si79.png)

and

$\\mu\_{V\_{4}\\rightarrow S\_{3}}(L,B) = \\sum\\limits\_{E}\\psi\_{4}(B,L,E)\\mu\_{S\_{2}\\rightarrow V\_{4}}(L,E)\\mu\_{S\_{4}\\rightarrow V\_{4}}(B,E).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si80.png)

The rest of the messages are computed in a similar way.

For the marginal probability *P*(*T*, *L*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si81.png) of the variables in clique node *V*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si82.png), we get

*P*(*T*, *L*, *E*) = *ψ*[*V*[2]](*T*, *L*, *E*)*μ*[*S*[2] → *V*[2]](*L*, *E*)*μ*[*S*[1] → *V*[2]](*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ψ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si83.png)

Observe that in this product, all other variables, besides *T*, *L*<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si84.png), and *E*, have been marginalized out. Also,

*P*(*L*, *E*) = *μ*[*V*[4] → *S*[2]](*L*, *E*)*μ*[*V*[2] → *S*[2]](*L*, *E*).<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>S</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si85.png)

Remarks 16.1

*   •  Note that a variable is part of more than one node in the tree. Hence, if one is interested in obtaining the marginal probability of an individual variable, this can be obtained by marginalizing over different variables in different nodes. The properties of the junction tree guarantee that all of them give the same result (Problem [16.5](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0065)).
*   •  We have already commented that there is not a unique way to triangulate a graph. A natural question is now raised: Are all the triangulated versions equivalent from a computational point of view? Unfortunately, the answer is no. Let us consider the simple case where all the variables have the same number of possible states, *k*. Then the number of probability values for each clique node depends on the number of variables involved in it, and we know that this dependence is of an exponential form. Thus, our goal while triangulating a graph should be to implement it in such a way that the resulting cliques are as small as possible with respect to the number of nodes-variables involved. Let us define the size of a clique, *V*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si32.png), as *s*[*i*] = *k*^(*n*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si86.png), where *n*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si87.png) denotes the number of nodes comprising the clique. Ideally, we should aim at obtaining a triangulated version (or equivalently an elimination sequence) so that the total size of the triangulated graph, ∑[*i*]*s*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si88.png), where *i* runs over all cliques, is minimum. Unfortunately, this is an NP-hard task \[1\]. One of the earliest algorithms proposed to obtain low-size triangulated graphs is given in \[71\]. A survey of related algorithms is provided in \[39\].

## 16.3 Approximate inference methods

So far, our focus has been on presenting efficient algorithms for exact inference in graphical models. Although such schemes form the basis of inference and have been applied in a number of applications, often one encounters tasks where exact inference is not practically possible. At the end of the previous section, we discussed the importance of small-sized cliques. However, in a number of cases, the graphical model may be so densely connected that it renders the task of obtaining cliques of a small size impossible. We will soon consider some examples.

In such cases, resorting to methods for tractable approximate inference is the only viable alternative. Obviously, there are various paths to approach this problem and a number of techniques have been proposed. Our goal in this section is to discuss the main directions that are currently popular. Our approach will be more on the descriptive side than that of rigorous mathematical proofs and theorems. The reader who is interested in delving deeper into this topic can refer to more specialized references, which are given in the following text.

### 16.3.1 Variational methods: local approximation

The current and the next subsections draw a lot of their theoretical basis on the variational approximation methods, which were introduced in Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml) and in particular in Sections [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml) and [13.8](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml).

The main goal in variational approximation methods is to replace probability distributions with computationally attractive bounds. The effect of such *deterministic* approximation methods is that it simplifies the computations; as we will soon see, this is equivalent to simplifying the graphical structure. Yet, these simplifications are carried out in the context of an associated optimization process. The functional form of these bounds is very much problem dependent, so we will demonstrate the methodology via some selected examples.

Two main directions are followed: the *sequential* one and the *block* one \[34\]. The former will be treated in this subsection and the latter in the next one.

In the sequential methods, the approximation is imposed on individual nodes in order to modify the functional form of the local probability distribution functions. This is the reason we called them *local methods*. One can impose the approximation on some of the nodes or to all of them. Usually, some of the nodes are selected, whose number is sufficient so that exact inference can take place with the remaining ones, within practically acceptable computational time and memory size. An alternative viewpoint is to look at the method as a sparsification procedure that removes nodes so as to transform the original graph to a “computationally” manageable one. There are different scenarios on how to select nodes. One way is to introduce approximation to one node at a time until a sufficiently simplified structure occurs. The other way is to introduce approximation to all the nodes and then reinstate the exact distributions one node at a time. The latter of the two has the advantage that the network is computationally tractable all the way (see, for example, \[30\]). Local approximations are inspired by the method of bounding convex/concave functions in terms of their conjugate ones, as discussed in Section [13.8](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml). Let us now unveil the secrets behind the method.

#### Multiple-cause networks and the noisy-OR model

In the beginning of Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) (Section [15.2](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml)) we presented a simplified case from the medical diagnosis field, concerning a set of diseases and findings. Adopting the so-called noisy-OR model, we arrived at Eqs. [(15.4)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) and [(15.5)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), which are repeated here for convenience. We have

$P(f\_{i} = 0|\\mathbf{d}) = \\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{j \\in \\text{Pa}\_{i}}\\theta\_{ij}d\_{j} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si89.png)(16.9) 

$P(f\_{i} = 1|\\mathbf{d}) = 1 - \\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{j \\in \\text{Pa}\_{i}}\\theta\_{ij}d\_{j} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

where we have exploited the experience we have gained so far and we have introduced in the notation the set of the parents Pa[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si91.png) of the *i*th finding. *f*^(\*)(*ξ*[*i*]) =  − *ξ*[*i*]ln (*ξ*[*i*]) + (*ξ*[*i*] + 1)ln (*ξ*[*i*] + 1), *ξ*[*i*] > 0.<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si100.png)

Note that usually, a constant *θ*[*i*0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si101.png) is also present in the linear terms (∑[*j* ∈ Pa[*i*]]*θ*[*i**j*]*d*[*j*] + *θ*[*i*0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si102.png)) and in this case the first exponent in the upper bound becomes exp ( − *f*^(\*)(*ξ*[*i*]) + *ξ*[*i*]*θ*[*i*0])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si103.png).

Let us now observe Eq. [(16.12)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq23). The first factor on the right-hand side is a constant, once *ξ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si97.png) is determined. Moreover, each one of the factors, exp (*ξ*[*i*]*θ*[*i**j*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si104.png), is also a constant raised in *d*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si105.png). Thus, substituting Eq. [(16.12)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq23) in the products in Eq. [(15.1)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), in order to compute, for example, Eq. [(15.3)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), each one of these constants can be absorbed by the respective *P*(*d*[*j*])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si106.png), that is,

*P̃*(*d*[*j*]) ∝ *P*(*d*[*j*])exp (*ξ*[*i*]*θ*[*i**j*]*d*[*j*]), *j* ∈ Pa[*i*].<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si107.png)

Basically, from a graphical point of view, we can equivalently consider that the *i*th node is delinked and its influence on any subsequent processing is via the modified factors associated with its parent nodes (see [Fig. 16.10](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0055)B). In other words, the variational approximation *decouples* the parent nodes. In contrast, for exact inference, during the moralization stage, all parents of node *i* are connected. This is the source of computational explosion (see [Fig. 16.10](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0055)C). The idea is to remove a sufficient number of nodes, so that the remaining network can be handled using exact inference methods.

There is still a main point to be addressed: how the various *ξ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si97.png)s are obtained. These are computed to make the bound as tight as possible, and any standard optimization technique can be used. Note that this minimization corresponds to a convex cost function (Problem [16.11](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0095)). Besides the upper bound, a lower bound can also be derived \[27\]. Experiments performed in \[30\] verify that reasonably good accuracies can be obtained in affordable computational times. The method was first proposed in \[27\].

#### The Boltzmann machine

The Boltzmann machine, which was introduced in Section [15.4.2](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), is another example where any attempt for exact inference is confronted with cliques of sizes that make the task computationally intractable \[28\].

We will demonstrate the use of the variational approximation in the context of the computation of the normalizing constant *Z*. Recall from Eq. [(15.23)](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) that

$Z = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{i}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{j > i}\\theta\_{ij}x\_{i}x\_{j} + \\theta\_{i0}x\_{i} \\right) \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}﹨x\_{k}}\\sum\\limits\_{x\_{k} = 0}^{1}\\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{i}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{j > i}\\theta\_{ij}x\_{i}x\_{j} + \\theta\_{i0}x\_{i} \\right) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo id="mmlbr0003" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si108.png)(16.13) 

where we chose node *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si109.png) to impose variational approximation. We split the summation into two, one with regard to *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si110.png) and one with regard to the rest of the variables; **x**﹨*x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>﹨</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si111.png) denotes summation over all variables excluding *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si110.png). Performing the inner sum in Eq. [(16.13)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq26) (terms different to *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si110.png) and *x*[*k*] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si112.png), *x*[*k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si113.png)), we get

\\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{i \\neq k}\\theta\_{ki}x\_{i} - \\theta\_{k0} \\right) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak"
