In other words, if from now on we replace *Z* with the bound, it is as if node *x*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si109.png) had been removed and the remaining network is a Boltzmann machine with one node less and the respective parameters modified, compared to the original ones. The value of *ξ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si121.png) can be obtained via optimization so as to make the bound as tight as possible.

[Fig. 16.11](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0060) illustrates the effect of applying variational approximation to node *x*[8]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si122.png). For the case of this figure, note that if *x*[5]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si123.png) is removed next (after *x*[8]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si122.png)) the remaining graphical structure becomes a chain and exact inference can be carried out.

![Figure 16.11 (A) An MRF corresponding to a Boltzmann machine. (B) The resulting MRF after removing x8 via variational approximation. Note that if x5 is removed next, then the remaining graphical model is a chain.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 16.11](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf0500) (A) An MRF corresponding to a Boltzmann machine. (B) The resulting MRF after removing x[8] via variational approximation. Note that if x[5] is removed next, then the remaining graphical model is a chain.

Following exactly similar arguments and employing the conjugate of the sigmoid function (Problem [13.18](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml)), one can apply the technique to the sigmoidal Bayesian networks, discussed in Section [15.3.4](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) (see also \[27\]).

### 16.3.2 Block methods for variational approximation

In contrast to the previous approach, where the approximation is introduced on selected nodes individually, here the approximation is imposed on a set of nodes. Once more, a derived bound of the involved probability distribution is optimized. In principle, the method is equivalent to imposing a specific graphical structure on the nodes, which can then be addressed by tractable exact inference techniques. In the sequel, the family of distributions, which can be factorized over this simplified substructure, is optimized with respect to a set of variational parameters. The method builds upon the same arguments as those used in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml). We will retain the same notation and we will provide the related formulas for the discrete variable case, to be used later on in our selected examples.

Let 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si124.png) be the set of observed and 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si125.png) the set of the latent random variables associated with the nodes of a graphical structure; in the graphical model terminology, we can refer to them as evidence and latent nodes, respectively. Define

$\\mathcal{F}(Q) = \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{P(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l})}{Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si126.png)(16.15) 

where *Q* is any probability function. Then, from Eq. [(16.15)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq32), we readily obtain

$\\mathcal{F}(Q) = \\ln P(\\mathcal{X}) + \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{P(\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X})}{Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si127.png)

or

$\\ln P(\\mathcal{X}) = \\mathcal{F}(Q) + \\sum\\limits\_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})\\ln\\frac{Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l})}{P(\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si128.png)(16.16) 

Note that the second term in Eq. [(16.16)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq34) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png) and *Q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si130.png). Because KL divergence is always nonnegative (Problem [12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)), we can write

ln *P*(𝒳) ≥ ℱ(*Q*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>⩾</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si131.png)

and the lower bound is maximized if we minimize the KL divergence. 

Let us now return to our goal, i.e., given the evidence, to perform inference on the graph associated with *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png). If this cannot be performed in a tractable way, the method adopts an approximation, *Q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si130.png), of *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png) and at the same time imposes a specific factorization on *Q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si130.png) (which equivalently induces a specific graphical structure) so that exact inference techniques can be employed. From the adopted family of distributions, we choose the one that minimizes the KL divergence between *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png) and *Q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si130.png). Such a choice guarantees the maximum lower bound for the log-evidence function. Among the different ways of factorization, the so-called *mean field* factorization is the simplest and, possibly, the most popular. The imposed structure on the graph has no edges, which leads to a complete factorization of *Q*(𝒳^(*l*))<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si130.png), that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/fx004.jpg)(16.17) 

#### The mean field approximation and the Boltzmann machine

As we already know, the joint probability for the Boltzmann machine is given by

$P(\\mathcal{X},\\mathcal{X}^{l}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{i}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{j > i}\\theta\_{ij}x\_{i}x\_{j} + \\theta\_{i0}x\_{i} \\right) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si134.png)

where some of *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si135.png) (*x*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si136.png)) belong to 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si124.png) and some to 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si125.png). Our first goal is to compute *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png) so as to use it in the KL divergence. Note that if both *x*[*i*], *x*[*j*] ∈ 𝒳<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si137.png), their contribution results to a constant, which is finally absorbed by the normalizing factor *Z*. If one is observed and the other one is latent, then the product contribution becomes linear with regard to the latent variable and it is absorbed by the respective linear term. Then we can write

$P(\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X}) = \\frac{1}{\\widetilde{Z}}\\exp\\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{i:x\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{j} \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}:j > i}\\theta\_{ij}x\_{i}x\_{j} + {\\widetilde{\\theta}}\_{i0}x\_{i} \\right) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si138.png)(16.18) 

We now turn our attention to the form of *Q*. Due to the (assumed) binary nature of the variables, a sensible completely factorized form of *Q* is \[34\]

$Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l};\\mathbf{\\mu}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i:x\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}\\mu\_{i}^{x\_{i}}{(1 - \\mu\_{i})}^{(1 - x\_{i})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si139.png)(16.19) 

where the dependence on the variational parameters, ***μ***, is explicitly shown. Also, due to the adopted Bernoulli distribution for each variable, 𝔼\[*x*[*i*]\] = *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si140.png) (Chapter [2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)). The goal now is to optimize the KL divergence with respect to the variational parameters. Plugging Eqs. [(16.18)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq38) and [(16.19)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq39) into

$KL(Q||P) = \\sum\\limits\_{x\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l};\\mathbf{\\mu})\\ln\\frac{Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l};\\mathbf{\\mu})}{P(\\mathcal{X}^{l}|\\mathcal{X})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si141.png)(16.20) 

we obtain (Problem [16.13](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0105), \[34\])

$KL(Q||P) = \\sum\\limits\_{i}\\left( \\mu\_{i}\\ln\\mu\_{i} + (1 - \\mu\_{i})\\ln(1 - \\mu\_{i}) + \\sum\\limits\_{j > i}\\theta\_{ij}\\mu\_{i}\\mu\_{j} + {\\widetilde{\\theta}}\_{i0}\\mu\_{i} \\right) + \\ln\\widetilde{Z},$<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si142.png)

where the indices *i* and *j* run over points in 𝒳^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si125.png). Minimizing the above with regard to *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si143.png) finally results in (Problem [16.13](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0105))

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/fx005.jpg)(16.21) 

where *σ*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si144.png) is the sigmoid link function; recall from the definition of the Ising model that *θ*[*i**j*] = *θ*[*j**i*] ≠ 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si145.png) if *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si146.png) and *x*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si147.png) are connected and zero otherwise. Plugging the values *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si143.png) into Eq. [(16.19)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq39), an approximation of *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png) in terms of *Q*(𝒳^(*l*); **μ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si148.png) has been obtained.

Eq. [(16.21)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq42) is equivalent to a set of coupled equations known as *mean field equations* and they are used in a recursive manner to compute a solution fixed point set, assuming that one exists. Eq. [(16.21)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq42) is quite interesting. Although we assumed independence among the latent nodes, imposing minimization of the KL divergence, information related to the (true) mutually dependent nature of the variables (as this is conveyed by *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si129.png)) is “embedded” into the mean values with respect to *Q*(𝒳^(*l*); **μ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si148.png); the mean values of the respective variables are *interrelated*. Eq. [(16.21)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq42) can also be viewed as a message passing algorithm (see [Fig. 16.12](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0065)). [Fig. 16.13](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0070) shows the graph associated with a Boltzmann machine prior to and after the application of the mean field approximation.

![Figure 16.12 Node k is connected to S nodes and receives messages from its neighbors, and then passes messages to its neighbors.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 16.12](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf0570) Node *k* is connected to *S* nodes and receives messages from its neighbors, and then passes messages to its neighbors.

![Figure 16.13 (A) The nodes of the graph representing a Boltzmann machine. (B) The mean field approximation results in a graph without edges. The dotted lines indicate the deterministic relation that is imposed among nodes, which were linked prior to the approximation with node x5.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 16.13](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf0575) (A) The nodes of the graph representing a Boltzmann machine. (B) The mean field approximation results in a graph without edges. The dotted lines indicate the deterministic relation that is imposed among nodes, which were linked prior to the approximation with node x[5].

Note that what we have said before is nothing but an instance of the variational EM algorithm, presented in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml); as a matter of fact, Eq. [(16.21)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq42) is the outcome of the E-step for each one of the factors of *Q*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si149.png), assuming the rest are fixed.

Thus far in the chapter, we have not mentioned the important task of how to obtain estimates of the parameters describing a graphical structure; in our current context, these are the parameters *θ*[*i**j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si150.png) and *θ*[*i*0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si101.png), comprising the set ***θ***. Although the parameter estimation task is discussed at the end of this chapter, there is no harm in saying a few words at this point. Let us give the dependence on ***θ*** explicitly and denote the involved probabilities as *Q*(𝒳^(*l*); **μ**, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si151.png), *P*(𝒳, 𝒳^(*l*); **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si152.png), and *P*(𝒳^(*l*)|𝒳; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si153.png). Treating ***θ*** as an unknown parameter vector, we know from the variational EM that this can be iteratively estimated by adding the M-step in the algorithm and optimizing the lower bound, ℱ(*Q*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si154.png), with regard to ***θ***, fixing the rest of the involved parameters (see, for example, \[29,69\]). In other words, treating the parameters ***θ*** deterministically, they take the place of the parameters ***ξ*** used in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml).

Remarks 16.2

*   •  The mean field approximation method has also been applied in the case of sigmoidal neural networks, defined in Section [15.3.4](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) (see, e.g., \[69\]).
*   •  The mean field approximation involving the completely factorized form of *Q* is the simplest and crudest approximation. More sophisticated attempts have also been suggested, where *Q* is allowed to have a richer structure while retaining its computational tractability (see, e.g., \[17,31,80\]).
*   •  In \[82\], the mean field approximation has been applied to a general Bayesian network, where, as we know, the joint probability distribution is given by the product of the conditionals across the nodes,

$p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i}p(x\_{i}|\\text{Pa}\_{i}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si155.png)

*   Unless the conditionals are given in a structurally simple form, exact message passing can become computationally tough. For such cases, the mean field approximation can be introduced in the latent variables, i.e.,

$Q(\\mathcal{X}^{l}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i:x\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{X}^{l}}Q\_{i}(x\_{i}),$<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si156.png)

*   which are then estimated so as to maximize the lower bound ℱ(*Q*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si154.png) in [(16.15)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq32). Following the arguments that were introduced in Section [13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), this is achieved iteratively starting from some initial estimates and at each iteration step optimization takes place with respect to a single factor, holding the rest fixed. At the (*j* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si158.png)th step, the *m*th factor is obtained as (Eq. [(13.15)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml))
