stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si292.png)(16.55) 

*Maximization step*: In this step, it suffices to obtain the derivatives/gradients with regard to *P*[*k*], *P*[*i**j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si293.png), and **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si275.png) and equate them to zero in order to obtain the new estimates, which will comprise *Θ*^((*t* + 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si295.png). Note that *P*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si272.png) and *P*[*i**j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si226.png) are probabilities; hence, their maximization should be constrained so that

$\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}P\_{k} = 1\\quad\\text{and}\\quad\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{K}P\_{ij} = 1,\\quad j = 1,2,\\ldots K.$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si296.png)

The resulting reestimation formulas are (Problem [16.18](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#o0130))

![](images/B9780443292385000226/fx010.jpg)

The reestimation of **θ**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si275.png) depends on the form of the corresponding distribution *p*(**y**[*n*]|*k*; **θ**[*k*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si297.png). For example, in the Gaussian scenario, the parameters are the mean values and the elements of the covariance matrix. In this case, we obtain exactly the same iterations as those resulting for the problem of Gaussian mixtures (see Eqs. [(12.60)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [(12.61)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)), if in place of the posterior we use *γ*.

In summary, training an HMM comprises the following steps:

1.  **1.**  Initialize the parameters in Θ.
2.  **2.**  Run the sum-product algorithm to obtain *γ*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si298.png) and *ξ*(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>ξ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si266.png), using the current set of parameter estimates.
3.  **3.**  Update the parameters as in Eqs. (16.56) and (16.57).

Iterations in steps 2 and 3 continue until a convergence criterion is met, such as in EM. This iterative scheme is also known as the *Baum–Welch* or *forward-backward* algorithm. Besides the forward-backward algorithm for training HMMs, the literature is rich in a number of alternatives with the goal of either simplifying computations or improving performance. For example, a simpler training algorithm can be derived tailored to the Viterbi scheme for computing the optimum path (e.g., \[63,72\]). Also, to further simplify the training algorithm, we can assume that our state observation variables, **y**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si193.png), are discretized (quantized) and can take values from a finite set of *L* possible ones, {1, 2, …, *L*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si299.png). This is often the case in practice. Furthermore, assume that the first state is also known. This is, for example, the case for left-to-right models like the one shown in [Fig. 16.17](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0090). In such a case, we need not compute estimates of the initial probabilities. Thus, the unknown parameters to be estimated are the transition probabilities and the probabilities *P*[**y**](*r*|*i*), *r* = 1, 2, …, *L*, *i* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si300.png), that is, the probability of emitting symbol *r* from state *i*.

*Viterbi reestimation*: The goal of the algorithm is to obtain the best path and compute the associated cost, say, *D*, along the path. In the speech literature, the algorithm is also known as the *segmental k-means training* algorithm \[63\].

Definitions:

*   •  *n*[*i*|*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si301.png):= number of transitions from state *j* to state *i*.
*   •  *n*[ ⋅ |*j*] : =<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si302.png) number of transitions originated from state *j*.
*   •  *n*[*i*|⋅] : =<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si303.png) number of transitions terminated at state *i*.
*   •  *n*(*r*|*i*) : =<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si304.png) number of times observation *r* ∈ {1, 2, …, *L*}<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si305.png) occurs jointly with state *i*.

Iterations:

*   •  Initial conditions: Assume the initial estimates of the unknown parameters.
*   •  Step 1: From the available best path, reestimate the new model parameters as

$\\begin{array}{rc} {P^{(\\text{new})}(i|j)\\ } & {= \\frac{n\_{i|j}}{n\_{\\cdot |j}},\\ } \\\\ {P\_{\\mathbf{y}}^{(\\text{new})}(r|i)\\ } & {= \\frac{n(r|i)}{n\_{i| \\cdot}}.\\ } \\\\ \\end{array}$<mml:math><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="right"><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si306.png)

*   
*   •  Step 2: For the new model parameters, obtain the best path and compute the corresponding overall cost *D*^((new))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si307.png). Compare it with the cost *D* of the previous iteration. If *D*^((new)) − *D* > *ϵ*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si308.png), set *D* = *D*^((new))<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si309.png) and go to step 1. Otherwise stop.

The Viterbi reestimation algorithm can be shown to converge to a proper characterization of the underlying observations \[14\].

Remarks 16.4

*   •  *Scaling*: The probabilities *α* and *β*, being less than one, as iterations progress can take very small values. In practice, the dynamic range of their computed values may exceed that of the computer. This phenomenon can be efficiently dealt with within an appropriate scaling. If this is done properly on both *α* and *β*, then the effect of scaling cancels out \[63\].
*   •  *Insufficient training data set*: Generally, a large amount of training data is necessary to learn the HMM parameters. The observation sequence must be sufficiently long with respect to the number of states of the HMM model. This will guarantee that all state transitions will appear a sufficient number of times, so that the reestimation algorithm learns their respective parameters. If this is not the case, a number of techniques have been devised to cope with the issue. For a more detailed treatment, the reader may consult \[8,63\] and the references therein.

### 16.5.3 Discriminative learning

*Discriminative learning* is another path that has attracted a lot of attention. Note that the EM algorithm optimizes the likelihood with respect to the unknown parameters of a *single* HMM in “isolation”; that is, without considering the rest of the HMMs, which model the other words (in the case of speech recognition) or other templates/prototypes that are stored in the data set. Such an approach is in line with what we defined as generative learning in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml). In contrast, the essence of discriminative learning is to optimize the set of parameters so that the models become optimally discriminated over the training sets (e.g., in terms of the error probability criterion). In other words, the parameters describing the different statistical models (HMMs) are optimized in a *combined* way, not individually. The goal is to make the different HMM models as distinct as possible, according to a criterion. This has been an intense line of research and a number of techniques have been developed around criteria that lead to either convex or nonconvex optimization methods (see, for example, \[33\] and the references therein).

Remarks 16.5

*   •  Besides the basic HMM scheme, which was described in this section, a number of variants have been proposed in order to overcome some of its shortcomings. For example, alternative modeling paths concern the first-order Markov property and propose models to extend correlations to longer times.
*   In the *autoregressive HMM* \[11\], links are added among the observation nodes of the basic HMM scheme in [Fig. 16.15](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0080); for example, **y**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si310.png) is not only linked to **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si178.png), but it shares direct links with, for example, **y**[*n* − 2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si311.png), **y**[*n* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si312.png), **y**[*n* + 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si313.png), and **y**[*n* + 2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si314.png), if the model extends correlations up to two time instants away.
*   A different concept has been introduced in \[56\] in the context of *segment modeling*. According to this model, each state is allowed to emit, say, *d* successive observations, which comprise a segment. The length of the segment, *d*, is itself a random variable and it is associated with a probability *P*(*d*|*k*), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si315.png). In this way, correlation is introduced via the joint distribution of the samples comprising the segment.
*   •  *Variable duration HMM*: A serious shortcoming of the HMMs, which is often observed in practice, is associated with the self-transition probabilities, *P*(*k*|*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si316.png), which are among the model parameters associated with an HMM. Note that the probability of the model being at state *k* for *d* successive instants (initial transition to the state and *d* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si317.png) self-transitions) is given by

*P*[*k*](*d*) = (*P*(*k*|*k*))^(*d* − 1)(1−*P*(*k*|*k*)),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si318.png)

*   where 1 − *P*(*k*|*k*)<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si319.png) is the probability of leaving the state. For many cases, this exponential state duration dependence is not realistic. In variable-duration HMMs, *P*[*k*](*d*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si320.png) is explicitly modeled. Different models for *P*[*k*](*d*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si320.png) can be employed (see, e.g., \[46,68,72\]).
*   •  Hidden Markov modeling is among the most powerful tools in machine learning and has been widely used in a large number of applications besides speech recognition. Some sampled references are \[9\] in bioinformatics, \[16,36\] in communications, \[4,73\] in optical character recognition (OCR), and \[40,61,62\] in music analysis/recognition, to name but a few. For a further discussion on HMMs, see, for example, \[8,64,72\].

## 16.6 Beyond HMMs: a discussion

In this section, some notable extensions of the hidden Markov models, which were previously discussed, are considered in order to meet requirements of applications where either the number of states is large or the homogeneity assumption is no more justified.

### 16.6.1 Factorial hidden Markov models

In the HMMs considered before, the system dynamics is described via the latent variables, whose graphical representation is a chain. However, such a model may turn out to be too simple for certain applications. A variant of the HMM involves *M* chains, instead of one chain, where each chain of latent variables unfolds in time independently of the others. Thus at time *n*, *M* latent variables are involved, denoted as **x**[*n*]^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si321.png), *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si322.png) \[17,34,81\]. The observations occur as a combined emission where all latent variables are involved. The respective graphical structure is shown in [Fig. 16.20](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0110) for *M* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si323.png). Each one of the chains develops on its own, as the graphical model suggests. Such models are known as *factorial HMMs* (FHMMs). One obvious question is, why not use a single chain of latent variables by increasing the number of possible states? It turns out that such a naive approach would blow up complexity. Take as an example the case of *M* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si323.png), where for each one of the latent variables, the number of states is equal to 10. The table of transition probabilities for each chain requires 10² entries, which amounts to a total number of 300, i.e., *P*[*i**j*]^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si324.png), *i*, *j* = 1, 2, …, 10<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si325.png), *m* = 1, 2, 3<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si326.png). Moreover, the total number of state combinations which can be realized is 10³ = 1000<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si327.png). To implement the same number of states via a single chain one would need a table of transition probabilities equal to (10³)² = 10⁶<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si328.png)!

![Figure 16.20 A factorial HMM with three chains of latent variables.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr020.jpg)

[Figure 16.20](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf1025) A factorial HMM with three chains of latent variables.

Let 𝕏[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si329.png) be the M-tuple (**x**[*n*]^((1)), …, **x**[*n*]^((*M*)))<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si330.png), where each **x**[*n*]^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si331.png) has only one of its elements equal to 1 (indicating a state) and the rest are zero. Then

$P(\\mathbb{X}\_{n}|\\mathbb{X}\_{n - 1}) = \\prod\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}P^{(m)}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{(m)}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}^{(m)} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si332.png)

In \[17\], the Gaussian distribution was employed for the observations, that is,

$p(\\mathbf{y}\_{n}|\\mathbb{X}\_{n}) = \\mathcal{N}\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{n} \\middle| \\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}\\mathcal{M}^{(m)}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{(m)},\\Sigma \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="5.2ex" minsize="5.2ex">|</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si333.png)(16.58) 

where

ℳ^((*m*)) = \[**μ**[1]^((*m*)),…,**μ**[*K*]^((*m*))\], *m* = 1, 2, …, *M*,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si334.png)(16.59) 

are the matrices comprising the mean vectors associated with each state and the covariance matrix is assumed to be known and the same for all. The joint probability distribution is given by

$p(\\mathbb{X}\_{1}\\ldots\\mathbb{X}\_{N},Y) = \\prod\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}\\left( P^{(m)}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{1}^{(m)} \\right)\\prod\\limits\_{n = 2}^{N}P^{(m)}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{(m)}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}^{(m)} \\right) \\right) \\times \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}p(\\mathbf{y}\_{n}|\\mathbb{X}\_{n}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si335.png)(16.60) 

The challenging task in factorial HMMs is complexity. This is illustrated in [Fig. 16.21](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0115), where the explosion in the size of cliques after performing the moralization and triangulation steps is readily deduced.

![Figure 16.21 The graph resulting from a factorial HMM with three chains of latent variables, after the moralization (linking variables in the same time instant) and triangulation (linking variables between neighboring time instants) steps.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr021.jpg)

[Figure 16.21](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf1035) The graph resulting from a factorial HMM with three chains of latent variables, after the moralization (linking variables in the same time instant) and triangulation (linking variables between neighboring time instants) steps.

In \[17\], the variational approximation method is adopted to simplify the structure. However, in contrast to the complete factorization scheme, which was adopted for the approximating distribution, *Q*, in Section [16.3.2](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#s0050) for the Boltzmann machine (corresponding to the removal of all edges in the graph), here the approximating graph will have a more complex structure. Only the edges connected to the output nodes are removed; this results in the graphical structure of [Fig. 16.22](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0120), for *M* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si323.png). Because this structure is tractable, there is no need for further simplifications. The approximate conditional distribution, *Q*, of the simplified structure is parameterized in terms of a set of variational parameters, *λ*[*n*]^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si336.png) (one for each delinked node), and it is written as

$Q(\\mathbb{X}\_{1}\\ldots\\mathbb{X}\_{N}|Y;\\mathbf{\\lambda}) = \\prod\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}\\left( {\\widetilde{P}}^{(m)}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{1}^{(m)} \\right)\\prod\\limits\_{n = 2}^{N}{\\widetilde{P}}^{(m)}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{(m)}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n - 1}^{(m)} \\right) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si339.png)

The variational parameters are estimated by minimizing the KL distance between Q and the conditional distribution associated with Eq. [(16.60)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq102). This compensates for some of the information loss caused by the removal of the observation nodes. The optimization process renders the variational parameters interdependent; this (deterministic) interdependence can be viewed as an approximation to the probabilistic dependence imposed by the exact structure prior to the approximation.

![Figure 16.22 The simplified graphical structure of an FHMM comprising three chains used in the framework of variational approximation. The nodes associated with the observed variables are delinked.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr022.jpg)

[Figure 16.22](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf1050) The simplified graphical structure of an FHMM comprising three chains used in the framework of variational approximation. The nodes associated with the observed variables are delinked.

### 16.6.2 Time-varying dynamic Bayesian networks

Hidden Markov as well as factorial hidden Markov models are homogeneous; hence, both the structure and the parameters are fixed throughout time. However, such an assumption is not satisfying for a number of applications where the underlying relationships as well as the structural pattern of a system undergoes changes as time evolves. For example, the gene interactions do not remain the same throughout life; the appearance of an object across multiple cameras is continuously changing. For systems that are described by parameters whose values are varying slowly in an interval, we have already discussed a number of alternatives in previous chapters. The theory of graphical models provides the tools to study systems with a mixed set of parameters (discrete and continuous); also, graphical models lend themselves to modeling of nonstationary environments, where step changes are also involved.

One path toward time-varying modeling is to consider graphical models of fixed structure but with time-varying parameters, known as *switching linear dynamic systems* (SLDSs). Such models serve the needs of systems in which a linear dynamic model jumps from one parameter setting to another; hence, the unobserved variables are both of discrete and of continuous nature. At time instant *n*, a switch discrete variable, *s*[*n*] ∈ {1, 2, …, *M*}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si340.png), selects a single LDS from an available set of *M* (sub)systems. The dynamics of *s*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si341.png) is also modeled to comply with the Markovian philosophy, and transitions from one LDS to another are governed by *P*(*s*[*n*]|*s*[*n* − 1])<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si342.png). This problem has a long history and its origins can be traced back to the time just after the publication of the seminal paper by Kalman \[35\]; see, for example, \[18\] and \[2,3\] for a more recent review of related techniques concerning the approximate inference task in such networks.

Another path is to consider that both the structure as well as the parameters change over time. One route is to adopt a quasistationary rationale, and assume that the data sequence is piece-wise stationary in time (for example, \[12,54,66\]). Nonstationarity is conceived as a cascade of stationary models, which have previously been learned by presegmented subintervals. The other route assumes that the structure and parameters are continuously changing (for example, \[42,79\]).  An example for the latter case is a Bayesian network where the parents of each node and the parameters, which define the conditional distributions, are time-varying. A separate variable is employed that defines the structure at each time instant; that is, the set of linking directed edges. The concept is illustrated in [Fig. 16.23](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0125). The method has been applied to the task of active camera tracking \[79\].

![Figure 16.23 The figure corresponds to a time-varying dynamic Bayesian network with two variables, x\_{n}^{1}Equation and x\_{n}^{2}Equation, n = 1,2,… . The parameters controlling the conditional distributions are considered as separate nodes, \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n}^{1}Equation and \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n}^{2}Equation, respectively, for the two variables. The structure variable, Gn, controls the values of the parameters as well as the structure of the network, which is continuously changing.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr023.jpg)

[Figure 16.23](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf1070) The figure corresponds to a time-varying dynamic Bayesian network with two variables, *x*[*n*]¹<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si343.png) and *x*[*n*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si344.png), *n* = 1,2,… . The parameters controlling the conditional distributions are considered as separate nodes, **θ**[*n*]¹<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si345.png) and **θ**[*n*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si346.png), respectively, for the two variables. The structure variable, *G*[*n*], controls the values of the parameters as well as the structure of the network, which is continuously changing.

## 16.7 Learning graphical models

Learning a graphical model consists of two parts. Given a number of observations, one has to specify both the graphical structure and the associated parameters.

### 16.7.1 Parameter estimation

Once a graphical model has been adopted, one has to estimate the unknown parameters. For example, in a Bayesian network involving discrete variables one has to estimate the values of the conditional probabilities. In Section [16.5](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#s0070), the case of learning the unknown parameters in the context of an HMM was presented. The key point was to maximize the joint PDF over the observed output variables. This is among the most popular criteria used for parameter estimation in different graphical structures. In the HMM case, some of the variables were unobserved, and hence the EM algorithm was mobilized. If all the variables of the graph can be observed, then the task of parameter learning becomes a typical maximum likelihood one. More specifically, consider a network with *l* nodes representing the variables *x*[1], …, *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si347.png), which are compactly written as a random vector **x**. Let also **x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si348.png) be a set of observations; then

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}} = {arg\\, max}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}\\ p(\\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{2},\\ldots,\\mathbf{x}\_{N};\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="bold">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg max</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si349.png)

where ***θ*** comprises all the parameters in the graph. If latent/hidden variables are involved, then one has to marginalize them out. Any of the parameter estimation techniques that were discussed in Chapters [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml) can be used. Moreover, one can take advantage of the special structure of the graph (i.e., the underlying independencies) to simplify computations. In the HMM case, its Bayesian network structure was exploited by bringing the sum-product algorithm into the game. Besides maximum likelihood, one can adopt any other method related to parameter estimation/inference. For example, one can impose a prior *p*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si350.png) on the unknown parameters and resort to a MAP estimation. Moreover, assuming the parameters to be random variables, the full Bayesian assumption can also be employed. Such a line presupposes that the unknown parameters have been included as extra nodes to the network, linked appropriately to those of the variables that they affect. As a matter of fact, this is what we did in [Fig. 13.2](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), although there, we had not talked about graphical models yet (see also [Fig. 16.24](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0130)). Note that in this case, in order to perform any inference on the variables of the network one should marginalize out the parameters. For example, assume that our *l* variables correspond to the nodes of a Bayesian network, where the local conditional distributions,

*p*(*x*[*i*]|Pa[*i*]; **θ**[*i*]), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*,<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si351.png)

depend on the parameters **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si352.png). Also, assume that the (random) parameters **θ**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si353.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si354.png), are mutually independent. Then the joint distribution over the variables is given by

$p(x\_{1},x\_{2},\\ldots,x\_{l}) = \\prod\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\int\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}}p(x\_{i}|\\text{Pa}\_{i};\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i})p(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i})\\ d\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>Pa</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si355.png)

Using convenient priors, e.g., conjugate priors, computations can be significantly facilitated; we have demonstrated such examples in Chapters [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml).

![Figure 16.24 An example of a Bayesian network, where new nodes associated with the parameters have been included in order to treat them as random variables, as required by the Bayesian parameter learning approach.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr024.jpg)

[Figure 16.24](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf1085) An example of a Bayesian network, where new nodes associated with the parameters have been included in order to treat them as random variables, as required by the Bayesian parameter learning approach.

Besides the previous techniques, which are offsprings of the generative modeling of the underlying processes, discriminative techniques have also been developed.

In a general setting, let us consider a pattern recognition task where the (output) label variable y and the (input) feature variables *x*[1], …, *x*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si347.png) are jointly distributed according to a distribution that can be factorized over a graph, which is parameterized in terms of a vector parameter ***θ***, i.e., *p*(*y*, *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x*[*l*]; **θ**) :  = *p*(*y*, **x**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si357.png) \[13\]. A typical example of such modeling is the naive Bayes classifier, which was discussed in Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml), whose graphical representation is given in [Fig. 16.25](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#f0135). For a given set of training data, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si358.png)), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si198.png), the log-likelihood function becomes

$L(Y,X;\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln p(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si359.png)(16.62) 

Estimating ***θ*** by maximizing *L*(⋅,⋅;**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si360.png), one would obtain an estimate that guarantees the best (according to the maximum likelihood criterion) fit of the corresponding distribution to the available training set. However, our ultimate goal is not to model the generation “mechanism” of the data. Our ultimate goal is to classify them correctly. Let us rewrite Eq. [(16.62)](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#deq109) as

$L(Y,X;\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln P(y\_{n}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}) + \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si361.png)

Getting biased toward the classification task, it is more sensible to obtain ***θ*** by maximizing the first of the two terms only, that is,

$L\_{c}(Y,X;\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln P(y\_{n}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left( \\ln p(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}) - \\ln\\sum\\limits\_{y\_{n}}p(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0015" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0015" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si362.png)(16.63) 

where the summation over *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si363.png) is over all possible values of *y*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si363.png) (classes). This is known as the *conditional log-likelihood* (see, for example \[19,20,67\]). The resulting estimate, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false" mathvariant="bold">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si364.png), guarantees that overall the posterior class probabilities, given the feature values, are maximized over the training data set; after all, Bayesian classification is based on selecting the class of ***x*** according to the maximum of the posterior probability. However, one has to be careful. The price one pays for such approaches is that the conditional log-likelihood is not decomposable, and more sophisticated optimization schemes have to be mobilized. Maximizing the conditional log-likelihood does not guarantee that the error probability is also minimized. This can only be guaranteed if one estimates ***θ*** so as to minimize the empirical error probability. However, such a criterion is hard to deal with, as it is not differentiable; attempts to deal with it by using approximate smoothing functions or hill climbing greedy techniques have been proposed (for example, \[58\] and the references therein). Note that the rationale behind the conditional log-likelihood is closely related to that behind conditional random fields, discussed in Section [15.4.3](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml).

![Figure 16.25 The Bayesian network associated with the naive Bayes classifier. The joint PDF factorizes as p(y,x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{l}) = p(y)\\prod\_{i = 1}^{l}p(x\_{i}|y)Equation.](images/B9780443292385000226/gr025.jpg)

[Figure 16.25](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml#cf1095) The Bayesian network associated with the naive Bayes classifier. The joint PDF factorizes as $p(y,x\_{1},\\ldots,x\_{l}) = p(y)\\prod\_{i = 1}^{l}p(x\_{i}|y)$<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∏</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000226/si356.png).

Another route in discriminative learning is to obtain the estimate of ***θ*** by *maximizing the margin*. The probabilistic class margin (for example, \[21,59\]) is defined as

$d\_{n} = \\min\\limits\_{y \\neq y\_{n}}\\frac{P(y\_{n}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta})}{P(y|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta})} = \\frac{P(y\_{n}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta})}{\\max\_{y \\neq y\_{n}}P(y|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta})} = \\frac{p(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta})}{\\max\_{y \\neq y\_{n}}p(y,\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta})}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo id="mmlbr0016" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi
