**θ**[\*]^(*T*)**x** > 0, if  **x** ∈ *ω*[1], **θ**[\*]^(*T*)**x** < 0, if  **x** ∈ *ω*[2].<mml:math><mml:msubsup id="mmlbr0001"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0001" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si6.png)

In other words, such a hyperplane classifies correctly *all* the points in the training set. For notational simplification, the bias term of the hyperplane has been absorbed in **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si578.png) after extending the dimensionality of the input space by one, as has been explained in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) and used in various parts of this book.

The goal now becomes that of developing an algorithm that iteratively computes a hyperplane that classifies correctly all the patterns from both classes. To this end, a cost function is adopted.

*The perceptron cost*: Let the available vector estimate at the current iteration step of the unknown parameters^([^(115)](#fn115))

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx001.jpg)(18.1) 

where

$y\_{n} = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} {+ 1,\\ } & {\\text{if}\\ \\mathbf{x} \\in \\omega\_{1},} \\\\ {- 1,\\ } & {\\text{if}\\ \\mathbf{x} \\in \\omega\_{2}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si9.png)(18.2) 

Observe that the cost function is nonnegative. Indeed, because the sum is over the misclassified points, if **x**[*n*] ∈ *ω*[1] (*ω*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si10.png), then **θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*] ≤ ( ≥ ) 0<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si11.png), rendering the product  − *y*[*n*]**θ**^(*T*)**x**[*n*] ≥ 0<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si12.png). A solution is achieved if there are no misclassified points, that is, 𝒴 = ⌀<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si13.png). By convention, we can say that in this case *J*(**θ**) = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si14.png).

The perceptron cost function is not differentiable at all points. It is a *continuous piece-wise linear* function. Indeed, let us write it in a slightly different way,

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\left( - \\sum\\limits\_{n:\\mathbf{x}\_{n} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}y\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T} \\right)\\mathbf{\\theta}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si15.png)

This is a linear function with respect to ***θ***, as long as the number of misclassified points remains the same. However, as one slowly changes the value of ***θ***, which corresponds to a change of the position of the respective hyperplane, there will be a point where the number of misclassified samples in 𝒴<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si8.png) suddenly changes; this is the time where a sample in the training set changes its relative position with respect to the (moving) hyperplane and as a consequence the set 𝒴<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si8.png) is modified. After this change, *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si16.png) will correspond to a new linear function.

*The perceptron algorithm*: It can be shown (for example, \[141,168\]) that, starting from an arbitrary point, **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si17.png), the following iterative update,

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx002.jpg)(18.3) 

converges after a *finite number of steps*. The parameter sequence *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si18.png) is judicially chosen to guarantee convergence. Note that this is the same algorithm as the one derived in Section [8.10.2](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml), for minimizing the hinge loss function via the notion of subgradient.

Besides the previous scheme, another version of the algorithm considers one sample per iteration in a cyclic fashion, until the algorithm converges. Let us denote by *y*[(*i*)], **x**[(*i*)], (*i*) ∈ {1, 2, …, *N*}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si19.png), the training pair that is presented in the algorithm at the *i*th iteration step.^([^(116)](#fn116))

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx003.jpg)(18.4) 

In other words, starting from an initial estimate, e.g., randomly initializing **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si17.png) with some small values, we test each one of the samples, **x**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si20.png). Every time a sample is misclassified, action is taken for a correction. Otherwise no action is required. Once all samples have been considered, we say that one *epoch* has been completed. If no convergence has been attained, all samples are reconsidered in a second epoch, and so on. This algorithmic version is known as a *pattern-by-pattern* scheme. Sometimes it is also referred to as *online* algorithm. However, note that the term “online” has been used in previous chapters in a different context, when data were received in a streaming/sequential fashion and their number was unbounded. In contrast, in the current context, the total number of data samples is fixed and the algorithm considers them in a *cyclic fashion*, epoch after epoch. To avoid confusion the former pattern-by-pattern term will be adopted.

After a successive *finite* number of epochs, the algorithm is guaranteed to converge. Note that for convergence, the sequence *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si18.png) must be appropriately chosen. This is pretty familiar to us by now. However, for the case of the perceptron algorithm, convergence is still guaranteed even if *μ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si18.png) is a positive constant, *μ*[*i*] = *μ* > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si21.png), usually taken to be equal to one (Problem [18.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#o0020)).

The formulation in Eq. [(18.4)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq7) brings the perceptron algorithm under the umbrella of the so-called *reward-punishment* philosophy of learning. If the current estimate succeeds in predicting the class of the respective pattern, no action is taken (reward). Otherwise, the algorithm is punished to perform an update.

[Fig. 18.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0010) provides a geometric interpretation of the perceptron rule. Assume that sample ***x*** is misclassified by the hyperplane, **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si22.png). As we know from geometry, **θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si22.png) corresponds to a vector that is perpendicular to the hyperplane which is defined by this vector (see also [Fig. 11.15](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml) in Section [11.10.1](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml)). Because ***x*** lies in the ( − )<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si23.png) side of the hyperplane and it is misclassified, it belongs to class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si24.png). Hence, assuming *μ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si25.png), the applied correction by the algorithm is

**θ**^((*i*)) = **θ**^((*i* − 1)) + **x**,<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si26.png)

and its effect is to turn the hyperplane to the direction toward ***x*** to place it in the ( + )<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si27.png) side of the new hyperplane, which is defined by the updated estimate **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si172.png).

![Figure 18.1 Pattern x is misclassified by the red line. The action of the perceptron rule is to turn the hyperplane toward the point x, in an attempt to include it in the correct side of the new hyperplane and classify it correctly. The new hyperplane is defined by θ(i) and it is shown by the black line.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 18.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf0375) Pattern ***x*** is misclassified by the red line. The action of the perceptron rule is to turn the hyperplane toward the point ***x***, in an attempt to include it in the correct side of the new hyperplane and classify it correctly. The new hyperplane is defined by ***θ***^((*i*)) and it is shown by the black line.

The perceptron algorithm in its pattern-by-pattern mode of operation is summarized in [Algorithm 18.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#enun0010). 

Algorithm 18.1

**The pattern-by-pattern perceptron algorithm**

*   •  Initialization 
    1.  –  Initialize **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si17.png); usually, randomly, to some small values.
    2.  –  Select *μ*; usually it is set equal to one.
    3.  –  *i* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si29.png).
*   •  **Repeat**; Each iteration corresponds to one epoch. 
    1.  –  counter = 0; Counts the number of updates per epoch.
    2.  –  **For** *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si30.png), **Do**; For each epoch, all samples are presented once. 
        1.  ⁎  **If** (*y*[*n*]**x**[*n*]^(*T*)**θ**^((*i* − 1)) ≤ 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si31.png)) **Then**
        2.  **θ**^((*i*)) = **θ**^((*i* − 1)) + *μ**y*[*n*]**x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si32.png)
        3.  *i* = *i* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si33.png)
        4.  counter=counter +1
    3.  –  **End For**
*   •  **Until** counter=0

Once the perceptron algorithm has run and converged, we have the weights, *θ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si34.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si35.png), of the synapses of the associated neuron/perceptron as well as the bias term *θ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si36.png). These can now be used to classify unknown patterns. [Fig. 18.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0015)A shows the corresponding architecture of the basic neuron element. The features *x*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si37.png), are applied to the input nodes. In turn, each feature is multiplied by the respective synapse (weight), and then the bias term is added on their linear combination. The outcome of this operation then goes through a nonlinear function, *f*, known as the *activation* function. Depending on the form of the nonlinearity, different types of neurons occur. In the more classical one, known as the McCulloch–Pitts neuron, the activation function is the Heaviside one, that is,

$f(z) = \\left\\{ \\begin{matrix} {1,\\ } & {\\text{if}\\ z > 0,} \\\\ {0,\\ } & {\\text{if}\\ z \\leq 0.} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo>&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si38.png)(18.5) 

Usually, the summation operation and the nonlinearity are merged to form a *node* in the respective graph and the architecture in [Fig. 18.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0015)B occurs. In the sequel, both terms, neuron and node, will be used interchangeably, the latter indicating a neuron within a larger network.

![Figure 18.2 (A) In the basic neuron/perceptron architecture the input features are applied to the input nodes and are weighted by the respective weights that define the synapses. The bias term is then added on their linear combination and the result is pushed through the nonlinearity. In the McCulloch–Pitts neuron, the output fires a 1 for patterns in class ω1 or a zero for class ω2. (B) The summation and nonlinear operation are merged together for graphical simplicity.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr002.jpg)

Figure 18.2 (A) In the basic neuron/perceptron architecture the input features are applied to the input nodes and are weighted by the respective weights that define the synapses. The bias term is then added on their linear combination and the result is pushed through the nonlinearity. In the McCulloch–Pitts neuron, the output fires a 1 for patterns in class *ω*[1] or a zero for class *ω*[2]. (B) The summation and nonlinear operation are merged together for graphical simplicity.

Thus, the basic model of an (artificial) neuron comprises the concatenation of (a) a linear combiner, (b) a threshold value (bias), and (c) a nonlinearity. Note that because of the existence of the nonlinearity, the output of the neuron indicates the class from which the input pattern originates. For the Heaviside nonlinearity, the output is 1 for patterns from class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si24.png) and 0 for those from class *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si39.png).

Remarks 18.1

*   •  *ADALINE*: Soon after Rosenblatt proposed the perceptron, Widrow and Hoff proposed the *adaptive line element* (ADALINE), which is a linear version of the perceptron \[218\]. That is, during training the nonlinearity of the activation function is not involved. The resulting scheme is the LMS algorithm, treated in detail in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). It is interesting to note that the LMS was readily adopted and widely used for online learning within the signal processing and communications communities.
*   •  A kernelized version of the perceptron algorithm has also been derived and the interested reader can obtain it via the book's site under the Additional Material part that is associated with the current chapter.

## 18.3 Feed-forward multilayer neural networks

A single neuron is associated with a hyperplane

*H*: *θ*[1]*x*[1] + *θ*[2]*x*[2] + … + *θ*[*l*]*x*[*l*] + *θ*[0] = 0,<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si40.png)

in the input (feature) space. Moreover, classification is performed via the nonlinearity, which fires a one or stays at zero, depending on which side of *H* a point lies. We will now show how to combine neurons, in a layer-wise fashion, to construct nonlinear classifiers. We will follow a simple constructive proof, which will unveil certain aspects of neural networks. These will be useful later on, when dealing with deep architectures.

As a starting point, we consider the case where the classes in the feature space are formed by unions of polyhedral regions. This is shown in [Fig. 18.3](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0020), for the case of the two-dimensional feature space. Polyhedral regions are formed as intersections of halfspaces, each one associated with a hyperplane. In [Fig. 18.3](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0020), there are three hyperplanes (straight lines in ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si41.png)), indicated as *H*[1], *H*[2], *H*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si42.png), giving rise to seven polyhedral regions. For each hyperplane, the ( + )<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si27.png) and ( − )<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si23.png) sides (halfspaces) are indicated. In the sequel, each one of the regions is labeled using a triplet of binary numbers, depending on which side it is located with respect to *H*[1], *H*[2], *H*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si42.png). For example, the region labeled as (101) lies in the (+) side of *H*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si43.png), the (–) side of *H*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si44.png), and the (+) side of *H*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si45.png).

![Figure 18.3 Classes are formed by unions of polyhedral regions. Regions are labeled according to the side on which they lie, with respect to the three lines, H1, H2, and H3. The number 1 indicates the (+) side and the 0 the (−) side. Class ω1 consists of the union of the (000) and (111) regions.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr003.jpg)

Figure 18.3 Classes are formed by unions of polyhedral regions. Regions are labeled according to the side on which they lie, with respect to the three lines, *H*[1], *H*[2], and *H*[3]. The number 1 indicates the (+) side and the 0 the (−) side. Class *ω*[1] consists of the union of the (000) and (111) regions.

[Fig. 18.4](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0025)A shows three neurons, realizing the three hyperplanes, *H*[1], *H*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si46.png), and *H*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si45.png), of [Fig. 18.3](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0020), respectively. The associated outputs, denoted as *y*[1], *y*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si47.png), and *y*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si48.png), form the label of the region in which the corresponding input pattern lies. Indeed, if the weights of the synapses have been appropriately set, then if a pattern originates from the region, say, (010), then the first neuron on the left will fire a zero (*y*[1] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si49.png)), the middle a one (*y*[2] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si50.png)), and the right-most a zero (*y*[3] = 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si51.png)).  In other words, combining the outputs of the three neurons together, we have achieved a *mapping* of the input feature space into the three-dimensional space. More specifically, the mapping is performed on the vertices of the *unit* cube in ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si52.png), as shown in [Fig. 18.5](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0030). Each region of the input space uniquely corresponds to one vertex of the cube. In the more general case, where *p* neurons are employed, the mapping will be on the vertices of the unit hypercube in ℝ^(*p*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si53.png). This layer of neurons comprises the first *hidden layer* of the network, which we are developing.

![Figure 18.4 (A) The neurons of the first hidden layer are excited by the feature values applied at the input nodes and form the polyhedral regions. (B) The neurons of the second layer have as inputs the outputs of the first layer, and they thereby form the classes. To simplify the figure, the bias terms for each neuron are not shown.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr004.jpg)

Figure 18.4 (A) The neurons of the first hidden layer are excited by the feature values applied at the input nodes and form the polyhedral regions. (B) The neurons of the second layer have as inputs the outputs of the first layer, and they thereby form the classes. To simplify the figure, the bias terms for each neuron are not shown.

![Figure 18.5 The neurons of the first hidden layer perform a mapping from the input feature space to the vertices of a unit hypercube. Each region is mapped to a vertex. Each vertex of the hypercube is now linearly separable from all the rest and it can be separated by a hyperplane realized by a neuron. The vertex 110, denoted as an unshaded circle, does not correspond to any region.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr005.jpg)

Figure 18.5 The neurons of the first hidden layer perform a mapping from the input feature space to the vertices of a unit hypercube. Each region is mapped to a vertex. Each vertex of the hypercube is now linearly separable from all the rest and it can be separated by a hyperplane realized by a neuron. The vertex 110, denoted as an unshaded circle, does not correspond to any region.

An alternative way to view this mapping is as a new *representation* of the input patterns in terms of code words. For three neurons/hyperplanes we can form 2³ binary code words, each corresponding to a vertex of the unit cube, which can represent 2³ − 1 = 7<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si54.png) regions (there is one remaining vertex, i.e., (110), which does not correspond to any region). Note, however, that this mapping encodes information concerning some *structure* of the input data; that is, information relating to how the input patterns are grouped together in the feature space in different regions.

We will now use this new representation, as it is provided by the outputs of the neurons of the first hidden layer, as input which feeds the neurons of a second hidden layer, which is constructed as follows. We choose all regions that belong to one class. For the sake of our example in [Fig. 18.3](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0020), we select the two regions that correspond to class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si24.png), that is, (000) and (111). Recall that all the points from these regions are mapped to the respective vertices of the unit cube in ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si52.png). However, in this new transformed space, each one of the vertices is *linearly separable* from the rest. This means that we can use a neuron/perceptron in the transformed space, which will place a single vertex in the (+) side and the rest in the (−) one of the associated hyperplane. This is shown in [Fig. 18.5](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0030), where two such planes are shown, which separate the respective vertices from the rest. Each of these planes is realized by a neuron, operating in ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si52.png), as shown in [Fig. 18.4](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0025)B, where a second layer of *hidden* neurons has been added.

Note that the output *z*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si56.png) of the left neuron will fire a 1 only if the input pattern originates from the region 000 and it will be at 0 for all other patterns. For the neuron on the right, the output *z*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si57.png) will be 1 for all the patterns coming from region (111) and zero for all the rest. Note that this second layer of neurons has performed a second mapping, this time to the vertices of the unit rectangle in ℝ²<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si41.png). This mapping provides a new representation of the input patterns, and this representation encodes information related to the classes of the regions. [Fig. 18.6](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0035) shows the mapping to the vertices of the unit rectangle in the (*z*[1], *z*[2])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si58.png) space.

![Figure 18.6 The patterns from class ω1 are mapped either to (01) or to (10) and patterns from class ω2 are all mapped to (00). Thus the classes have now become linearly separable and can be separated via a straight line realized by a neuron.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 18.6](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf0440) The patterns from class *ω*[1] are mapped either to (01) or to (10) and patterns from class *ω*[2] are all mapped to (00). Thus the classes have now become linearly separable and can be separated via a straight line realized by a neuron.

Note that all the points originating from class *ω*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si39.png) are mapped to (00) and the points from class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si24.png) are mapped either to (10) or to (01). This is very interesting; by successive mappings, we have transformed our originally nonlinearly separable task to one that is linearly separable. Indeed, the point (00) can be linearly separated from (01) and (10) and this can be realized by an extra neuron operating in the (*z*[1], *z*[2])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si58.png) space; it is known as the *output neuron*, because it provides the final classification decision. The final resulting network is shown in [Fig. 18.7](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0040). We call this network *feed-forward*, because information flows forward from the input to the output layer. It comprises the input layer, which is a nonprocessing one, two hidden layers (the term “hidden” is self-explained), and one output layer. We call such a neural network a three-layer network, without counting the input layer of nonprocessing nodes.

![Figure 18.7 A three-layer feed-forward neural network. It comprises the input (nonprocessing) layer, two hidden layers, and one output layer of neurons. Such a three-layer neural network can solve any classification task, where classes are formed by unions of polyhedral regions.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 18.7](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf0445) A three-layer feed-forward neural network. It comprises the input (nonprocessing) layer, two hidden layers, and one output layer of neurons. Such a three-layer neural network can solve *any* classification task, where classes are formed by unions of polyhedral regions.

We have constructively shown that a three-layer feed-forward neural network can, in principle, solve *any* classification task whose classes are formed by unions of polyhedral regions. Although we focused on the two-class case, the generalization to multiclass cases is straightforward, by employing more output neurons depending on the number of classes. Note that in some cases, one hidden layer of nodes may be sufficient. This depends on whether the vertices on which the regions are mapped are assigned to classes so that linear separability is possible. For example, this would be the case if class *ω*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si24.png) was the union of (000) and (100) regions. Then these two vertices could be separated from the rest via a single plane and a second hidden layer of neurons would not be required (check why). In any case, we will not take our discussion any further. The reason is that such a construction is important to demonstrate the power of building a multilayer neural network, in analogy to what is happening in our brain. However, from a practical point of view, such a construction has not much to offer. In practice, when the data live in high-dimensional spaces, there is no chance of determining the parameters that define the neurons analytically to realize the hyperplanes, which form the polyhedral regions. Furthermore, in real life, classes are not necessarily formed by the union of polyhedral regions and, usually, classes do overlap. Hence, one needs to devise a training procedure based on a cost function and a set of training data.

All that we have to keep from our previous discussion is the structure of the multilayer network; our focus will turn on seeking ways for estimating the unknown weights of the synapses and biases of the neurons. However, from a conceptual point of view, we have to remember that each layer performs a mapping into a new space, and each mapping provides a different, hopefully more informative, representation of the input data, until the last layer, where the task has been transformed into one that it is easy to solve.

### 18.3.1 Fully connected networks

The feed-forward networks that have been introduced before are also known as *fully connected networks*. This name is to stress that each one of the neurons/nodes in any layer is directly connected to *every* node of the previous layer. The nodes of the first hidden layer are *fully* connected to those of the input layer. In other words, *each* neuron is associated with a *vector* of parameters, whose dimension is equal to the number of nodes of the previous (input) layer. The algebraic operations which are performed are *inner products*.

To summarize in a more formal way the type of operations that take place in a fully connected network, let us focus on, say, the *r*th layer of a multilayer neural network and assume that it comprises *k*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si59.png) neurons. The input vector to this layer consists of the outputs at the nodes of the previous layer, denoted as **y**^(*r* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si60.png). Let **θ**[*j*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si101.png) be the vector of the synaptic weights, including the bias term, associated with the *j*th neuron of the *r*th layer, where *j* = 1, 2, …, *k*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si102.png) (see, also, [Fig. 18.11](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0065), Section [18.4](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0030)). The respective dimension is *k*[*r* − 1] + 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si63.png), where *k*[*r* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si64.png) is the number of the neurons of the previous, *r* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si65.png), layer and the increase by 1 accounts for the bias term. Then the performed operations, prior to the nonlinearity, are the inner products

*z*[*j*]^(*r*) = **θ**[*j*]^(*r**T*)**y**^(*r* − 1), *j* = 1, 2, …, *k*[*r*].<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si66.png)

Collecting all the output values into a vector, **z**^(*r*) = \[*z*[1]^(*r*), *z*[2]^(*r*), …, *z*[*k*[*r*]]^(*r*)\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si67.png), and stacking all the synaptic vectors as rows, one under the other, in a matrix Θ, we can write collectively

**z**^(*r*) = *Θ***y**^(*r* − 1), where *Θ* :  = \[**θ**[1]^(*r*),**θ**[2]^(*r*),…,**θ**[*k*[*r*]]^(*r*)\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>where</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si68.png)

The vector of the outputs of the *r*th hidden layer, after pushing each *z*[*i*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si69.png) through the nonlinearity *f*, is finally given by 

$\\mathbf{y}^{r} = \\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\\\ {f\\left( \\mathbf{z}^{r} \\right)} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix},$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si70.png)

where the notation above means that *f* acts on each one of the respective vector components, individually, and the extension of the vector by one is to account for the bias terms in the standard practice.

For large networks, with many layers and many nodes per layer, this type of connectivity turns out to be very costly in terms of the number of parameters (weights), which is of the order of *k*[*r*]*k*[*r* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si71.png). For example, if *k*[*r* − 1] = 1000<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si72.png) and *k*[*r*] = 1000<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si73.png), this amounts to an order of 1 million parameters. Note that this number is the contribution from the parameters of only one of the layers. However, a large number of parameters makes a network vulnerable to overfitting, when training is involved, as has already been discussed in Section [3.8](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml).

In contrast, one can employ the so-called *weight sharing* techniques (e.g., \[156,204\]), where a set of parameters is *shared* among a number of connections, via appropriately built-in constraints. The convolutional networks, to be discussed in Section [18.12](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0170), belong to this family of weight sharing networks. As we will see, in a convolutional network, convolutions replace the inner product operations, which allows for a significant weight sharing that leads to a substantial reduction in the required number of parameters.

Remarks 18.2

*   •  *Shallow and deep networks*: From now on, we will refer to the number of layers in a network as the *depth* of the network. Networks with up to three (two hidden) layers are known as *shallow*, whereas those with more than three layers are called *deep* networks.

## 18.4 The backpropagation algorithm

A feed-forward neural network consists of a number of layers of neurons, and each neuron is determined by the corresponding set of synaptic weights and its bias term. From this point of view, a neural network realizes a nonlinear parametric function, *ŷ* = *f*[**θ**](**x**)<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si74.png), where ***θ*** stands for all the weights/biases present in the network. Thus, training a neural network seems not to be any different from training any other parametric prediction model. All that is needed is (a) a set of training samples, (b) a loss function, ℒ(*y*, *ŷ*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si75.png), and (c) an iterative scheme, for example, gradient descent, to perform the optimization of the associated cost function (empirical loss; see Section [3.14](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml), Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)),

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}\\left( y\_{n},f\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si76.png)(18.6) 

The difficulty with training neural networks lies in their multilayer structure that complicates the computation of the gradients, which are involved in the optimization. Moreover, the McCulloch–Pitts neuron is based on the discontinuous Heaviside activation function, which is not differentiable. A first step in developing a practical algorithm for training a neural network is to replace the Heaviside activation function with a differentiable approximation of it.

*The logistic sigmoid neuron*: One possibility is to adopt the logistic sigmoid function, that is,

$f(z) = \\sigma(z): = \\frac{1}{1 + \\exp\\left( - az \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si77.png)(18.7) 

The graph of the function is shown in [Fig. 18.8](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0045). Note that the larger the value of the parameter *a* is, the closer the corresponding graph gets to that of the Heaviside function. Another possibility would be to use

$f(z) = a\\tanh\\left( \\frac{cz}{2} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">tanh</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si78.png)(18.8) 

where *c* and *a* are controlling parameters. The graph of this function is shown in [Fig. 18.9](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0050). Note that in contrast to the logistic sigmoid one, this is an antisymmetric function, that is, *f*( − *z*) =  − *f*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si79.png). Both are also known as *squashing* functions, because they limit the output to a finite range of values.

![Figure 18.8 The logistic sigmoid function for different values of the parameter a.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr008.jpg)

Figure 18.8 The logistic sigmoid function for different values of the parameter *a*.

![Figure 18.9 The hyperbolic tangent squashing function for a = 1.7 and c = 4/3.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 18.9](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf0470) The hyperbolic tangent squashing function for *a* = 1.7 and *c* = 4/3.

### Nonconvexity of the cost function

Optimization of cost functions has been a recurrent theme that runs across this book. In Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), the gradient descent optimization algorithm was introduced and some of its convergence properties were outlined. In the sequel, the stochastic approximation framework for optimizing expectations of loss functions in an online, sample after sample, mode of operation was discussed. The gradient descent scheme and the online optimization rationale comprise the spine for a number of optimization algorithms that have been proposed and used for training feed-forward neural networks. The reason that we need to discuss these algorithms specifically in the context of neural networks is that the *multilayer* structure of these networks poses difficulties that have to be understood, prior to applying an off-the-shelf optimization scheme.

A major difficulty when dealing with the minimization of a cost function, such as in Eq. [(18.6)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq14), in the framework of neural networks, is its *nonconvexity*. Convex functions were discussed in Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml). There, it was pointed out that for the case of a convex function, every local minimum is also a global one. Recall, for example, a typical graph of a convex function in [Fig. 8.3](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml). By the definition of a minimum of a function, we know that at this point the gradient (derivative in the simplest single-parameter space) becomes zero. Points where the gradient of a function becomes zero are known as *critical* or *stationary* points.

However, if the function is not convex, a stationary point can belong to one of the following three categories: to be (a) a local minimum (maximum), (b) a global minimum (maximum), or (c) a saddle point; see [Fig. 18.10](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0055) for the case of the one-dimensional space. All these stationary points are of importance in neural networks. A local minimum is the point where the value of the cost, *J*(*θ*[*l*])<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si80.png), becomes minimum within a region around *θ*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si81.png). The global minimum, *θ*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si82.png), is the point where *J*(*θ*[*g*]) ≤ *J*(*θ*)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si83.png), ∀*θ* ∈ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si84.png). A saddle point, *θ*[*s*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si85.png), is neither a minimum nor a maximum, yet the derivative (gradient in general) is equal to zero.

![Figure 18.10 A nonconvex function, besides the global, usually comprises a number of local minima and saddle points. To which minimum, out of the many, the algorithm will converge, depends on the point from which the algorithm was initialized. However, if the value of the cost at a local minimum, e.g., J(θl), is not much larger than that of the global minimum, i.e., J(θg), then θl can be a satisfactory solution in practice.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr010.jpg)

Figure 18.10 A nonconvex function, besides the global, usually comprises a number of local minima and saddle points. To which minimum, out of the many, the algorithm will converge, depends on the point from which the algorithm was initialized. However, if the value of the cost at a local minimum, e.g., *J*(*θ*[*l*]), is not much larger than that of the global minimum, i.e., *J*(*θ*[*g*]), then *θ*[*l*] can be a satisfactory solution in practice.

When adopting a gradient descent scheme to minimize a nonconvex cost function, the algorithm can converge to either a local or to a global minimum. Take, for example, the case of [Fig. 18.10](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0055). Recall from Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) that the update rule of the gradient descent algorithm, in its one-dimensional version, becomes

$\\theta(\\text{new}) = \\theta(\\text{old}) - \\mu\\frac{dJ}{d\\theta}|\_{\\theta(\\text{old})},$<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si86.png)

and the iterations start from an arbitrary initial point, *θ*^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si87.png). If at the current iteration the algorithm is, say, at the point *θ*(old) = *θ*[1]<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si88.png), then it will move toward the local minimum, *θ*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si81.png). This is because the derivative of the cost at *θ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si89.png) is equal to the tangent of *ϕ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si90.png), which is negative (the angle is obtuse) and the update, *θ*(new)<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si91.png), will move to the right toward the local minimum, *θ*[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si81.png). In contrast, if the algorithm had been initialized from a different point and the algorithm is currently at, say, *θ*(old) = *θ*[2]<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si92.png), the update will move toward the global minimum, *θ*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si82.png), since the derivative is now equal to the tangent of *ϕ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si93.png), which is positive (the angle is acute). As we know from Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), the choice of the step size, *μ*, is critical for the convergence of the algorithm.

In real problems in multidimensional spaces, the number of local minima can be large, so the algorithm can converge to a local one. However, this is not necessarily very bad news. If this local minimum is deep enough, that is, if the value of the cost function at this point, e.g., *J*(*θ*[*l*])<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si80.png), is not much larger than that achieved at the global minimum, i.e., *J*(*θ*[*g*])<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si94.png), convergence to such a local minimum can correspond to a good solution. In practice, one has to be careful with how to initialize an algorithm when dealing with nonconvex cost functions. We are going to discuss this issue later on. Also, the interplay between local, global, and saddle points, when the dimension of the parameter space becomes large, which is the case for deep networks, is discussed in Section [18.11.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0145).

### 18.4.1 The gradient descent backpropagation scheme

Having adopted a differentiable activation function, we are ready to proceed with developing the gradient descent iterative scheme for the minimization of the cost function. We will formulate the task in a general framework.

Let (**y**[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si95.png), be the set of training samples. Note that we have assumed multiple output variables, assembled as a vector. We assume that the network comprises *L* layers; *L* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si96.png) hidden layers and one output layer. Each layer consists of *k*[*r*], *r* = 1, 2, …, *L*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si97.png), neurons. Thus, the (target/desired) output vectors are

**y**[*n*] = \[*y*[*n*1],*y*[*n*2],…,*y*[*n**k*[*L*]]\]^(*T*) ∈ ℝ^(*k*[*L*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si98.png)

For the sake of the mathematical derivations, we also denote the number of input nodes as *k*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si99.png); that is, *k*[0] = *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si100.png), where *l* is the dimensionality of the input feature space.
