*   •  **Until** a stopping criterion is met.

The backpropagation algorithm can claim a number of fathers. The popularization of the algorithm is associated with the classical paper \[171\], where the derivation of the algorithm is provided. However, the algorithm had been derived much earlier in \[216\]. The idea of backpropagation also appears in \[23\] in the context of optimal control.

Remarks 18.3

*   •  A number of criteria have been suggested for terminating the backpropagation algorithm. One possibility is to track the value of the cost function, and stop the algorithm when this gets smaller than a preselected threshold. An alternative path is to check for the gradient values and stop when these become small; this means that the values of the weights do not change much from iteration to iteration (see, for example, \[106\]).
*   •  As is the case with all gradient descent schemes, the choice of the step size, *μ*, is very critical; it has to be small enough to guarantee convergence, but not too small; otherwise the convergence speed slows down. The choice depends a lot on the specific problem at hand. Adaptive values of *μ*, whose value depends on the iteration, are also popular alternatives and they will be discussed soon.
*   •  Due to the highly nonlinear nature of the neural network problem, the cost function in the parameter space has, in general, a complicated landscape and there are a number of local minima, where the algorithm can be trapped. If such a local minimum is deep enough, the associated solution can be acceptable. However, this may not be the case and the algorithm can be trapped in a shallow minimum resulting in a bad solution. Ideally, one should reinitialize randomly the weights a number of times and keep the best solution. Initialization has to be performed with care; we discuss this issue later on. A discussion concerning local and global minima in the context of deep networks is discussed in Section [18.11.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0145).

#### Pattern-by-pattern/online scheme

The scheme discussed in [Algorithm 18.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#enun0025) is of the *batch* type, where the parameters/weights are updated once per epoch, that is, after all *N* training samples have been presented to the algorithm. An alternative route is the *pattern-by-pattern* version; for this case, the weights are updated every time a new training sample appears in the input. Sometimes, such schemes are known as *online*. Yet, we will avoid using this term, because it usually refers to the case where streaming data are considered and observations are continuously coming in, instead of having a fixed sized training set where data points are considered repeatedly, epoch after epoch. Online algorithms have been considered in Chapters [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) and [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml). Another name that is more recently used to describe such algorithms is *stochastic* optimization. This is a reminiscent of the stochastic approximation method, introduced in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), where in order to minimize the expected loss, individual observations are sequentially used to update the estimates of the unknown parameters/weights. Of course, keep in mind that, in the true stochastic gradient descent, there is *no* data reuse (i.e., epoch after epoch) and data are assumed to arrive in a streaming way and convergence is achieved *asymptotically*.

Pattern-by-pattern versions exploit better the training set, when redundancies in the data are present or training samples are very similar. Averaging, as is done in the batch mode, wastes resources, because averaging the contribution to the gradient of similar patterns does not add much information. In contrast, in the pattern-by-pattern implementations, all examples are equally exploited, inasmuch as an update takes place for each one of the training samples.

The pattern-by-pattern mode leads to a less smooth convergence trajectory; however, such a randomness may have the advantage of helping the algorithm to escape from local minima.

#### Mini-batch schemes

An intermediate way, where the parameter updates are performed every *K* < *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si167.png) samples, has also been considered, which is referred to as a *mini-batch* or *stochastic mini-batch*. However, such schemes are commonly referred to as simply stochastic. The choice of the mini-batch size, *K*, is influenced by a number of factors and it depends on the application and the specific data as well as the available computing power.

For example, multicore architectures are underutilized if the batch size is very small. Also, when GPUs are used, employing mini-batch sizes of power of 2 can offer better run times. For such cases, some typical values are ranging from 16 to 256, depending on the size of the training set. On the other hand, the use of small mini-batch sizes can have a regularizing effect, due to the noise that is implicitly added in the computation of the gradients. However, in such cases, one has to use smaller values for the step size, for stability reasons, and this can increase the overall training time.

Batch and mini-batch schemes have an averaging effect on the computation of the gradients. In \[186\], it is advised to add a small white noise sequence to the training data, which may have a beneficial effect for the algorithm to escape from poor local minima.

To exploit randomness even further in the pattern-by-pattern/mini-batch schemes, it is advisable that prior to the pass of a new epoch, the sequence in which data are presented to the algorithm is randomized (see, for example, \[69\]). This has no meaning in the batch mode, because updates take place once all data have been considered. This random shuffling of the data “breaks” possible correlations that underlie successive samples, making successive gradient computations independent. Such correlations may be due to specific experimental protocols that have been followed for generating the data. Although it is advisable to shuffle the data for every epoch, this may not be practical when large data sets are used, e.g., of the order of a billion. In such cases, even a single data shuffling in the beginning is beneficial.

These days, in the context of deep learning with large data training sets, mini-batch schemes seem to be the ones that are favored for most applications.

A major problem in all gradient descent schemes and their stochastic variants is to select the step size or *learning rate*, *μ*. As we know from Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml), if its value is small the learning curves are smooth, but convergence can be slow. In contrast, if its value is relatively large, learning curves tend to be oscillatory but convergence can get faster, provided that the value does not become large enough for the algorithm to diverge. In practice, time-varying step sizes are more appropriate and they are in line with the stochastic gradient rationale. One can employ various strategies, yet these strategies are more an engineering “art” than the result of a theoretical analysis. It is advisable for a user to first look at what previous researchers/practitioners have done in similar situations and start with this experience.

A possible strategy is to start training with a linearly decreasing step size and then switch to a fixed one after a number of iterations. For example, one can proceed with a rule such as

*μ*[*i*] = (1 − *a*[*i*])*μ*[0] + *a*[*i*]*μ*[*I*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si168.png)

where *a*[*i*] = *i*/*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si169.png) for some fixed iteration *I*. After iteration *I*, the step size is fixed. The issue now is to set the parameters *μ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si170.png), *μ*[*I*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si171.png), and *I*. In practice, one has to monitor the learning curve for a number of iterations first and adjust the values of the parameters accordingly as a tradeoff between how fast or how slow the initial iterations move toward convergence and at the same time being cautious about instabilities.

### 18.4.2 Variants of the basic gradient descent scheme

The basic gradient descent scheme inherits all the advantages (low computational demands per iteration step) and all the disadvantages (slow convergence) of the gradient descent algorithmic family, as it was first presented in this book in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml). To speed up the convergence, a lot of research effort has been invested and a large number of variants of the basic gradient descent backpropagation scheme have been proposed. In this section, we provide some directions, which at the time the current edition is being compiled seem to be the trend in practice.

For simplicity, and having derived the backpropagation descent scheme, let us get rid of the indices *r* and *j* referring to the layer and the specific neuron in the respective layer. Instead, the parameter/weight vector ***θ*** will be used that comprises all the parameters of the network. Also, the corresponding estimate at the *i*th iteration of a learning algorithm will be denoted by **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si172.png).

Let ℒ(*y*, **x**, **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si173.png) be the adopted loss function. The latter measures the deviation between the true output, *y*, and the corresponding predicted value, *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si174.png), which depends on the respective input, ***x***, as well as the parameters that define the network, ***θ***. The cost function, over all the training points, is given by

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{L}(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{\\theta}).$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si175.png)

If batch processing is employed, then at each iteration the gradient of the above cost function is used for the update of the parameters, i.e., $\\frac{\\partial J(\\mathbf{\\theta})}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si176.png), which involves *all* the training points. That is, for every epoch, only one parameter vector update is performed. On the other extreme, if a pattern-by-pattern scheme is adopted, at each iteration the updates are estimated on the basis of the gradient of the loss function computed at the current input–output pair, i.e., $\\frac{\\partial\\mathcal{L}(y\_{n},\\mathbf{x}\_{n},\\mathbf{\\theta})}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si177.png). That is, in this case, *N* updates for the parameters are obtained for every epoch.

The mini-batch operation needs a bit more of elaboration. Let us assume that the data set is split in *M* mini-batches, each of size *K*. Obviously, *N* should be a multiple of *K*. Assuming that the data have been randomly shuffled, then at the current iteration epoch, the *N* input–output data pairs will appear in the algorithm in the following sequence:

$\\underset{1\\text{st\\ mini-batch}}{\\underset{︸}{(y\_{(1)},\\mathbf{x}\_{(1)}),\\ldots,(y\_{(K)},\\mathbf{x}\_{(K)})}}\\ldots\\underset{M\\text{th\\ mini-batch}}{\\underset{︸}{(y\_{((M - 1)K + 1)},\\mathbf{x}\_{((M - 1)K + 1)}),\\ldots,(y\_{(N)},\\mathbf{x}\_{(N)})}},$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mtext>st mini-batch</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mtext>th mini-batch</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si178.png)

where, as we have already pointed out in Section [18.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0015), the notation (*i*) ∈ {1, 2, …, *N*}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si179.png) is used, due to the data shuffling. Thus, during one epoch, *M* updates will be performed, each one involving the gradient of a different cost; this is because a different mini-batch will be considered each time, i.e.,

$\\frac{\\partial J^{(m)}(\\mathbf{\\theta})}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}},\\ m = 1,2,\\ldots,M,$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si180.png)(18.31) 

$J^{(m)}(\\mathbf{\\theta}): = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\mathcal{L}\\left( y\_{((m - 1)K + k)},\\mathbf{x}\_{((m - 1)K + k)},\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si181.png)(18.32) 

In the sequel, to simplify notations, we will use a common symbol, $\\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si182.png), to denote the gradient operation for all three possible cases discussed before. The true value of the function in the place of *J* will depend on (a) the specific scheme (i.e., batch, mini-batch, pattern-by-pattern) and (b) the current iteration step, as different samples are involved in each step (e.g., in the stochastic versions).

#### Gradient descent with a momentum term

One way to improve the convergence rate, while remaining within the gradient descent rationale, is to employ the so-called *momentum term* \[62,214\]. The correction term as well as the update recursion are now modified as

$\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = a\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu\\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}|\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)}},\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} + \\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal" id="mmlbr0003">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0003" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si183.png)(18.33) 

starting from an initial value for *Δ***θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si184.png), e.g., **0**. The gradient is computed via the backpropagation and *a* is the so-called *momentum factor*. In other words, the algorithm takes into account the correction used in the previous iteration step as well as the current gradient computations. Its effect is to increase the step size in regions where the cost function exhibits low curvature. The step size implicitly increases when a number of successive gradients point in exactly the same direction. Assuming that the gradient is approximately constant over, say, *I* successive iterations, it can be shown (Problem [18.3](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#o0030)) that using the momentum term, the corresponding correction becomes

$\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta} \\approx - \\frac{\\mu}{1 - a}\\mathbf{g},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si185.png)(18.34) 

where ***g*** is the gradient value over the *I* successive iteration steps. That is, the step size has been increased by the factor $\\frac{1}{1 - a}$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si186.png). Typical values of *a* are in the range of 0.5 to 0.9. In essence, the use of a momentum term helps to dampen the zig-zags of the convergence trajectory, as discussed in Chapter [5](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml) (see [Fig. 5.9](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)). It has been reported that the use of a momentum term can speed up the convergence with a factor of up to two \[187\]. Experience seems to suggest that the use of a momentum factor helps the batch mode of operation more compared to its stochastic counterparts.

*Iteration dependent step size*: A heuristic variant of the previous version results if the step size is left to vary as iterations progress. A rule is to change its value according to whether the cost function in the current iteration step is larger or smaller than the previous one. Let *J*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si187.png) be the computed cost value at the current iteration. Then if *J*^((*i*)) < *J*^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si188.png), the learning rate is increased by a factor of *r*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si189.png). If, on the other hand, the new value is larger than the previous one by a factor larger than *c*, then the learning rate is reduced by a factor of *r*[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si190.png). Otherwise, the learning rate remains unaltered. Typical values for the involved parameters are *r*[*i*] = 1.05<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.05</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si191.png), *r*[*d*] = 0.7<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si192.png), and *c* = 1.04<mml:math><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.04</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si193.png). For iteration steps where the value of the cost increases, it is advisable to set the momentum factor, *a*, equal to zero \[207\].

Such techniques, also known as *adaptive momentum*, are more appropriate for batch processing, because for online versions the values of the cost tend to oscillate from iteration to iteration.

*Using different step size for each weight*: It is beneficial for improving the convergence rate, to employ a *different step size* for each individual weight; this gives the freedom to the algorithm to exploit better the dependence of the cost function on each direction in the parameter space. In \[91\], it is suggested to increase the learning rate, associated with a weight, if the respective gradient value has the same sign for two successive iterations. Conversely, the learning rate is decreased if the sign changes, because this is indicative of possible oscillation.

In the sequel, more recent schemes that use iteration dependent as well as different for each weight step sizes will be discussed.

Example 18.1

In this toy example, the capability of a multilayer perceptron to classify nonlinearly separable classes is demonstrated in the two-dimensional space, where visualization is possible.  The classification task consists of two classes, each being modeled by a four-component Gaussian mixture model, where the covariance matrix for each component is *σ*²*I*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si194.png), with *σ*² = 0.08<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.08</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si195.png). The mean values are different for each of the Gaussians. Specifically, the samples of the class denoted by a red ∘ (see [Fig. 18.12](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0070)) are spread around the mean vectors

\[0.4, 0.9\]^(*T*), \[2.0, 1.8\]^(*T*), \[2.3, 2.3\]^(*T*), \[2.6, 1.8\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.4</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.8</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.6</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.8</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si196.png)

and those of the class denoted by a black + around the values

\[1.5, 1.0\]^(*T*), \[1.9, 1.0\]^(*T*), \[1.5, 3.0\]^(*T*), \[3.3, 2.6\]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.9</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3.0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>3.3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.6</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si197.png)

A total of 400 training vectors were generated, 50 from each distribution. A multilayer perceptron with three neurons in the first and two neurons in the second hidden layer were used, with a single output neuron. The activation function was the logistic one with *a* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si198.png) and the desired outputs 1 and 0, respectively, for the two classes. Two different algorithms were used for the training, namely, the momentum and the adaptive momentum. After some experimentation, the parameters employed were (a) for the momentum *μ* = 0.05<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si199.png), *α* = 0.85<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.85</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si200.png) and (b) for the adaptive momentum *μ* = 0.01<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si201.png), *α* = 0.85<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.85</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si200.png), *r*[*i*] = 1.05<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.05</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si191.png), *c* = 1.04<mml:math><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.04</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si193.png), *r*[*d*] = 0.7<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si192.png). The weights were initialized by a uniform pseudorandom distribution between 0 and 1. [Fig. 18.12](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0070)A shows the respective output error convergence curves for the two algorithms as a function of the number of epochs. The respective curves can be considered typical and the adaptive momentum algorithm leads to faster convergence. Both curves correspond to the batch mode of operation. [Fig. 18.12](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0070)B shows the graph of the decision line of the resulting classifier, using the parameters/weights that are estimated via the adaptive momentum training.

![Figure 18.12 (A) Error convergence curves for the adaptive momentum (red line) and the momentum algorithms, for Example 18.1. Note that the adaptive momentum leads to faster convergence. (B) The decision line implemented by the classifier that results from the adaptive momentum algorithm.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr012.jpg)

Figure 18.12 (A) Error convergence curves for the adaptive momentum (red line) and the momentum algorithms, for [Example 18.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#enun0035). Note that the adaptive momentum leads to faster convergence. (B) The decision line implemented by the classifier that results from the adaptive momentum algorithm.

#### Nesterov's momentum algorithm

A variant of the celebrated Nesterov algorithm \[143\] was suggested in \[197\]. The update rule for the correction term becomes

$\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = a\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} - \\mu\\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} + a\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}|\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si202.png)

The difference with the previous momentum update rule lies in that the gradient of the cost function is computed after pushing ***θ*** in the direction of the current correction term, *Δ***θ**^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si203.png). In words, the gradient is not computed at the currently available estimates of the parameters but at their approximate future values. As has been reported in \[197\], this can lead to substantial gains in convergence speed. The values for *a* are in the same range as in the case of the momentum algorithm.

#### The AdaGrad algorithm

The AdaGrad algorithm was introduced in its online form in the convex cost functions setting in Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml), Eq. [(8.71)](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml). Borrowing the main rationale behind the algorithm, in our current framework it can be rephrased as

**θ**^((*i*)) = **θ**^((*i* − 1)) − *μ**G*[*i* − 1]^( − 1/2)**g**^((*i* − 1)),<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si204.png)

where by definition

$\\mathbf{g}^{(i)}: = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}|\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)}}$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si205.png)

is the gradient computed at the respective estimate, **θ**^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si172.png), and the matrix *G*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si207.png) is the sum of the outer products of all the gradient vectors up to and including iteration *i*, that is,

$G\_{i}: = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{i}\\mathbf{g}^{(t)}\\mathbf{g}^{{(t)}^{T}}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si208.png)

In practice, matrix *G*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si207.png) is taken to be diagonal; hence the inverse of its root becomes computationally attractive. In such a case, if *D* is the total number of parameters of the network, the *D* × *D*<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si209.png) matrix *G*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si207.png) involves on its diagonal the squares of the respective gradients, i.e.,

$G\_{i}(d,d) = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{i}\\left( g\_{d}^{(t)} \\right)^{2},\\ d = 1,2,\\ldots,D,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si210.png)

where *g*[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si211.png) denotes the *d*th component of the respective gradient at iteration (*t*), i.e., $g\_{d}^{(t)} = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\theta\_{d}^{(t)}}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si212.png), and *θ*[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si213.png) is the *d*th element of **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*D*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si214.png). Usually, a small constant *ϵ* is used to avoid possible division by zero, and the corresponding updates for each one of the parameter vector components take the form

$\\theta\_{d}^{(i)} = \\theta\_{d}^{(i - 1)} - \\frac{\\mu}{\\sqrt{G\_{i - 1}(d,d)} + \\epsilon}g\_{d}^{(i - 1)},\\ d = 1,2,\\ldots,D.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si215.png)(18.35) 

The value of *ϵ* can be of the order of 10^( − 8)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si216.png) or so. In words, the step size in the AdaGrad is iteration dependent and also different for each component. The value of *μ* is usually set close to 0.01. The correction for each individual parameter is inversely proportional to the values of its gradients. Larger values lead to smaller step sizes. Thus, as iterations evolve, each dimension evens out over time. This can be beneficial when training deep networks, because the scale of the gradients can vary a lot in magnitude in different layers.

However, AdaGrad's main drawback is the accumulation of the squared gradients in the denominator, which can freeze the updates after a number of iterations.

#### The RMSProp with Nesterov momentum

In the RMSProp, the sum of the squares of the gradients used in AdaGrad is replaced by a recursively defined decaying average of all past squared gradients. In such a way, the remote past samples are exponentially discarded. At the same time, a Nesterov-type momentum rationale is employed. The main recursions are summarized as follows:

$\\mathbf{g} = \\frac{\\partial J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} + a\\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} \\right)}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}|\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)}},\\mathbf{v}^{(i)} = \\beta\\mathbf{v}^{(i - 1)} + (1 - \\beta)\\mathbf{g} \\circ \\mathbf{g},\\Delta\\theta\_{d}^{(i)} = a\\Delta\\theta\_{d}^{(i - 1)} - \\frac{\\mu}{\\sqrt{v\_{d}^{(i)}} + \\epsilon}g\_{d},\\ d = 1,2,\\ldots,D,\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)} + \\Delta\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i)},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic" id="mmlbr0004">g</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0004" mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si217.png)

where *β* is a user-defined parameter. The first of the recursions computes the gradient after the Nesterov-type correction. The second one updates the squares of the gradient values in the decaying average rationale. The “∘” operation denotes element-wise multiplication. The third recursion computes the correction term in the AdaGrad rationale and the fourth one provides the updates. The algorithm starts with initial conditions on **v**^((0)) = 0<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si218.png), *Δ***θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si184.png) and **θ**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si17.png). Some typical values for the hyperparameters are *ϵ* = 10^( − 8)<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si221.png), *β* = 0.9<mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si222.png), and *μ* = 0.001<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.001</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si223.png).

The RMSProp algorithm was proposed by Hinton et al. in a lecture.^([^(117)](#fn117))

#### The adaptive moment estimation algorithm (Adam)

The Adam algorithm proposed in \[103\] borrows the concept of forgetting past values of the squared gradients, yet it introduces and propagates the values of the gradients as well, in a similar way as the momentum algorithm does. Furthermore, it introduces some important normalization that takes care of bias that may be introduced. The major recursions around which the Adam algorithm evolves are

$\\mathbf{g} = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}}|\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}^{(i - 1)}},\\mathbf{m}^{(i)} = \\beta\_{1}\\mathbf{m}^{(i - 1)} + (1 - \\beta\_{1})\\mathbf{g},\\mathbf{v}^{(i)} = \\beta\_{2}\\mathbf{v}^{(i - 1)} + (1 - \\beta\_{2})\\mathbf{g} \\circ \\mathbf{g},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic" id="mmlbr0005">g</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0005" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi
