stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="left"><mml:mtext>if</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si264.png)(18.38) 

where

$a\_{ij}^{r}(\\text{new}) = \\min\\left\\{ \\frac{\\frac{\\partial J(\\text{new})}{\\partial\\theta\_{ij}^{r}}}{\\frac{\\partial J(\\text{old})}{\\partial\\theta\_{ij}^{r}} - \\frac{\\partial J(\\text{new})}{\\partial\\theta\_{ij}^{r}}},a\_{\\text{max}}^{r} \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si265.png)(18.39) 

with typical values of the parameters used being 0.01 ≤ *μ* ≤ 0.6<mml:math><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.6</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si266.png), and *a*[max]^(*r*) ≈ 1.75<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>max</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.75</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si267.png). An algorithm in similar spirit with the quickprop has been proposed in \[165\].

In practice, when large networks and data sets are involved, simpler methods, such as carefully tuned gradient descent schemes and their versions, as for example those previously discussed in Section [18.4.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0055), seem to work better and are currently the trend. The more complex second-order techniques can offer improvements in smaller networks, especially in the context of regression tasks.

## 18.5 Selecting a loss function

As we have already commented, feed-forward neural networks belong to the more general class of parametric models; thus, in principle, any loss function we have met so far in this book can be employed. Over the years, certain loss functions have gained in popularity in the context of regression and classification tasks. However, in the context of feed-forward multilayer networks, the choice of the loss function is tightly coupled to the type of the *output* nonlinearity that is used. A “wrong” *combination* can severely affect the speed at which the network learns during training. To understand this claim, let us consider the following combination.

Adopt as loss function the squared error one and as output nonlinearity the logistic sigmoid function, *σ*(*z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si268.png), given in Eq. [(18.7)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq15). For the sake of simplicity, let us assume that we only have a single output node and also suppress the index *n*, which relates to observations, and *r*, which relates to layers. Then, if *y* is the target value and *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si174.png) the estimated one, the contribution to the cost function will be

$J = \\frac{1}{2}\\left( y - \\widehat{y} \\right)^{2} = \\frac{1}{2}\\left( y - \\sigma(z) \\right)^{2},\\ z = \\mathbf{\\theta}^{T}\\mathbf{y},$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si269.png)(18.40) 

where ***y*** is the (extended) vector of the outputs of the last hidden layer and ***θ*** is the vector of synaptic weights connecting the nodes of the last hidden layer to the output one. The bias term has been absorbed in ***θ***, according to standard practice. Then the gradient of *J* with respect to ***θ***, using the chain rule for derivatives, is trivially seen to be

$\\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial z}\\frac{\\partial z}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} = \\delta\\mathbf{y},\\ \\delta: = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial z},$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si270.png)

where, after taking into account Eq. [(18.40)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq73), we get

$\\delta = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\widehat{y}}\\frac{\\partial\\widehat{y}}{\\partial z} = \\left( \\widehat{y} - y \\right)\\sigma^{\\prime}(z).$<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si271.png)

Thus,

$\\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}} = (\\widehat{y} - y)\\sigma^{\\prime}(z)\\mathbf{y}.$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si272.png)

In words, the above means that the gradient of the cost, with respect to the parameters leading to the output node, depends on the error, (*ŷ* − *y*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si273.png), and also on the derivative of the logistic sigmoid function. The dependence on the error is “healthy.” Indeed, this is what we want. The larger the error, the larger the gradient (in absolute value); this will make the correction term in Eq. (18.10) large to account for a large error or keep the update close to the current estimate when the error is small. However, the dependence on the derivative of the nonlinear function is not good news. Looking at the graph in [Fig. 18.8](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0045), for values of the argument that are not close to zero, the function quickly saturates and its derivative becomes very small. Hence, although the error can be large, the respective correction will be small. Also, recall that in the backpropagation, the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters of the last (output) layer, say, *L*, is passed to the previous one, layer *L* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si96.png), and is used to compute the respective gradients, and so on. If the values of the gradients of the last layer are small, this affects all the gradients in all layers and as a result convergence can significantly slow down.

In contrast, one can readily check that if the output node is a linear one, instead of being sigmoid, then the combination of the squared error loss function with a linear output unit is a good combination. The resulting gradient becomes proportional to the error, since now the derivative becomes a constant.

We will now focus on an alternative loss function that bypasses the previous drawback. Let us adopt, for a classification task, as targets the 0, 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si274.png) values. Then the true and predicted values, *y*[*n**m*], *ŷ*[*n**m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si275.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si30.png), *m* = 1, 2, …, *k*[*L*]<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si276.png), for *k*[*L*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si277.png) output nodes, can be interpreted as probabilities and a commonly used cost function in this setting is the *cross-entropy*, which is defined as

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx007.jpg)(18.41) 

Note that this is exactly the same cost used in Eq. [(7.49)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml) for the multiclass logistic regression treated in Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml). For the classification task, when the number of classes are equal to the output nodes, i.e., we have *k*[*L*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si277.png) classes, then the cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the observations. Indeed, for the 0, 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si274.png)\-class coding scheme for the observed label variables, *y*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si110.png), the corresponding target output vector, **y**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*k*[*L*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si278.png), will have a 1 at the position corresponding to the true class and the rest of the elements will be zero (one-hot vector). If we interpret *ŷ*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si279.png) as the respective posterior probability, i.e., *P*(*ω*[*k*]|**x**[*n*]; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si280.png), where ***θ*** denotes all the parameters that define the corresponding network, then the likelihood of the observations is given by

$P(\\mathbf{y}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{y}\_{N}|\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{k\_{L}}{({\\widehat{y}}\_{nk})}^{y\_{nk}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si281.png)(18.42) 

Taking the logarithm and changing the sign, Eq. [(18.41)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq77) is obtained.

A different formulation of the cross-entropy loss function, known as *relative entropy*, is sometimes used, i.e.,

$J = - \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{k\_{L}}y\_{nk}\\ln\\frac{{\\widehat{y}}\_{nk}}{y\_{nk}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si282.png)(18.43) 

This formulation brings up the affinity with the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (Section [2.5.2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)) that measures deviation between probabilities (distributions). In our context, it measures how different *y*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si110.png) is from *ŷ*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si279.png).

Besides the previously defined cross-entropy cost function, a variant of it is also used and it is given by

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx008.jpg)(18.44) 

whose minimum occurs when *y*[*n**k*] = *ŷ*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si283.png), which for binary target values is equal to zero. Comparing the above cost in Eq. [(18.44)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq80) with the cross-entropy in Eq. [(18.41)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq77), it is easily seen that the former, while trying to “push” *ŷ*[*n**k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si279.png) toward 1 for the correct class (*y*[*n**k*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si284.png)), at the same time it tries to “push” the corresponding values for the wrong classes toward 0, in order to minimize *J*. Note that the cost in Eq. [(18.44)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq80) can be seen as a generalization of the cross-entropy for the two-class case, using a single output neuron (see also Eq. [(7.38)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml)). Adopting the 0, 1<mml:math><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si274.png)\-class coding scheme and assuming, this time, that the *k*[*L*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si277.png) binary classes are not mutually exclusive and are independent, the counterpart of Eq. [(18.42)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq78) becomes

$P(\\mathbf{y}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{y}\_{N})|\\mathcal{X};\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\prod\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{k\_{L}}{({\\widehat{y}}\_{nk})}^{y\_{nk}}{(1 - {\\widehat{y}}\_{nk})}^{1 - y\_{nk}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si285.png)

which leads to Eq. [(18.44)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq80). Note, however, that this interpretation does not hold true if classes are mutually exclusive, which is the case in most classification tasks.

One can easily see that combining the above versions of the cross-entropy function with the logistic sigmoid nonlinearity “frees” the gradient of the cost, with respect to the synaptic weights of the *k*th output neuron, of the dependence on the derivative of the respective activation function. It can easily be shown that (Problem [18.7](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#o0050))

$\\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{j}^{L}} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\delta\_{nj}^{L}\\mathbf{y}\_{n}^{L - 1},\\ j = 1,2,\\ldots,k\_{L},$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si286.png)

where *δ*[*n**j*]^(*L*) = *y*[*n**j*](*ŷ*[*n**j*] − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si287.png) for the cross-entropy loss in Eq. [(18.41)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq77) and *δ*[*n**j*]^(*L*) = *ŷ*[*n**j*] − *y*[*n**j*]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si288.png) for the case of Eq. [(18.44)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq80). Note that **y**[*n*]^(*L* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si289.png) is the vector of the outputs of the last hidden layer, *L* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si96.png).

It can be shown (Problem [18.9](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#o0060)) that the cost functions in Eqs. [(18.41)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq77) and [(18.44)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq80) depend on the relative errors and not on the absolute errors, as is the case in the squared error loss; thus, small and large error values are equally weighted during the optimization. Furthermore, it can be shown that the cross-entropy belongs to the so-called well-formed loss functions, in the sense that if there is a solution that classifies correctly all the training data, the gradient descent scheme will find it \[1\]. In \[188\], it is pointed out that the cross-entropy loss function may lead to improved generalization and faster training for classification, compared to the squared error loss.

Having said all that, recall that we have interpreted the outputs of the network as probabilities; yet, there is no guarantee that these add to one. This can be enforced by selecting the activation function in the last layer of nodes to be

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx009.jpg)(18.45) 

which is known as the *softmax activation* function \[18\]. Recall that *z*[*n**k*]^(*L*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si290.png):=**θ**[*k*]^(*L*^(*T*))**y**[*n*]^(*L* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si291.png) is the value of the linear combiner (prior to the nonlinearity) associated with the *k*th output neuron (layer *r* = *L*<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si135.png), [Fig. 18.11](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0065)) that corresponds to the *n*th input training sample. For those familiar with logistic regression, discussed in Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml), compare Eq. [(18.45)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq83) with Eq. [(7.47)](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml); after all, the world is small!

As was the case with the sigmoid activation function, it is easy to show that combining the softmax activation with the cross-entropy loss function leads to gradients that are *independent* of derivatives of the nonlinearity (Problem [18.10](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#o0065)).

## 18.6 Vanishing and exploding gradients

We have already discussed the importance of trying to avoid involving nonlinearities in the output that promote small values of gradients, when they are combined with some loss functions. Let us now look at what is happening in the hidden layers. The secret lies in Eq. [(18.27)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq38) of the backpropagation algorithm. Let us investigate it a bit more. As we have seen in Section [18.4.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0040), at the heart of the computation of the gradients lie the quantities

$\\delta\_{j}^{r}: = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial z\_{j}^{r}},\\ j = 1,2,\\ldots,k\_{r},\\ r = 1,2,\\ldots,L,$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si292.png)

where the index *n* has been suppressed to unclutter notation, *r* is the index indicating the corresponding layer in an *L*\-layer network, and *j* is the index of a neuron at the *r*th layer that consists of *k*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si59.png) neurons. By definition, *z*[*j*]^(*r*) :  = **θ**[*j*]^(*r*^(*T*))**y**^(*r* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si293.png) is the linear output, prior to the nonlinearity *f*, of the *j*th neuron (associated with the parameter vector, **θ**[*j*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si101.png)) and **y**^(*r* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si60.png) is the vector of the output values of the (*r* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si65.png))th layer ([Fig. 18.11](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0065)). Then the propagation of the various *δ*\-derivatives follows the recursive rule (Eq. [(18.27)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq38)),

$\\delta\_{j}^{r - 1} = \\left( \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{k\_{r}}\\delta\_{k}^{r}\\theta\_{kj}^{r} \\right)f^{\\prime}(z\_{j}^{r - 1}),\\quad j = 1,2,\\ldots,k\_{r - 1}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si295.png)

In words, the *δ*\-derivatives for layer *r* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si65.png) depend on the respective *δ*\-derivatives of the layer above, *r*, and (a) on the respective weights and (b) on the *derivative* of the nonlinearity, both in a *multiplicative way*. For the sake of clarity, let us write the above formula for two successive steps,

$\\delta\_{j}^{r - 1} = \\left( \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{k\_{r}}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{k\_{r + 1}}\\delta\_{i}^{r + 1}\\theta\_{ik}^{r + 1} \\right)f^{\\prime}(z\_{k}^{r})\\theta\_{kj}^{r} \\right)f^{\\prime}(z\_{j}^{r - 1}),\\quad j = 1,2,\\ldots,k\_{r - 1}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si296.png)

All one has to keep in mind from the above is not its exact formulation, but the notion that as the backpropagation algorithm flows backwards, the *derivatives of the nonlinearities* as well as *the weights* are *multiplied* and the number of the involved products *grows*. The lower (closer to the input layer) in hierarchy *δ*[*j*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si297.png) is, the more products are involved for its computation. There are two extremes that may, and often do, occur in practice.

Taking into account that the derivatives of the activation function can be smaller than one (and in the case of the sigmoid-type nonlinearities can take very small values) if the estimated values of the parameters are not very large, the gradients of the cost, with respect to the parameters of the lower layers, can take vanishingly small values and this can make the training extremely slow (see, e.g., \[78,198\] for further discussion and insight). This phenomenon becomes more prominent when deep networks with many layers are involved.

On the other extreme, if the values of the parameters happen to get very large values, this can lead to an explosion of the gradient estimates. As a result, this can affect the learning by pushing the estimates of the parameters to the wrong region in the parameter space.

Another related problem is that the gradients along the various layers may take values of different scale. This means that some layers can learn faster than others. This is basically a form of instability.

All the above are some of the difficulties one encounters while training multilayer neural networks, especially when many layers are involved.

To cope with such problems, a number of modifications and tricks have been developed. Playing with different cost functions is one, playing with different optimization variants of the backpropagation algorithm is another (see, e.g., \[136\] for a discussion). In the subsection to follow, we will see how to cope with nonlinearities to be used in the hidden layers, which are not of the saturating type; hence, they can “guard” us from the small derivative values tendency.

### 18.6.1 The rectified linear unit

Besides the activation functions that we have considered so far, the *rectified linear unit* (ReLU), defined as

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx010.jpg)(18.46) 

has been proposed more recently (see [Fig. 18.13](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0075)).

![Figure 18.13 The graph of ReLU. Note that for z > 0 the derivative is equal to one and for z < 0 it is equal to zero.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 18.13](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf0930) The graph of ReLU. Note that for *z* > 0 the derivative is equal to one and for *z* < 0 it is equal to zero.

It has been reported that in the context of deep networks, the use of the ReLU nonlinearity in the hidden layers can significantly speed up the training time \[108\]. Such an activation function does not suffer from saturation and its derivative is equal to one when the neuron operates in its active region (*z* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si298.png)). Thus, it is desirable to set the biases of the neurons, during initialization, to some small positive value, e.g., *θ*[0] = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si299.png), in order to increase the probability that the input to the activation function is positive. For negative values, the derivative is zero. At *z* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si300.png) the derivative is not defined and if this happens during training, one can either choose 1 or 0; for those familiar with the notion of the subgradient (Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)) such a choice is fully justified.

Thus, selecting the ReLU as the activation function, one bypasses problems related to the slowing down when derivatives get small values. Recall that in the backpropagation algorithm, when gradients with respect to the parameters of hidden layers are computed, the derivative of the activation function enters in a multiplicative fashion.

A drawback of the ReLU is that training freezes when *z* < 0<mml:math><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si301.png). To overcome this problem, variants of the ReLU have been proposed. For example, one can employ

*f*(*z*) = max {0, *z*} + *α*min {0, *z*}.<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si302.png)

Depending on the value of *α*, different variants result. For *α* =  − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si303.png), the so-called *absolute value rectification* is obtained \[90\]. If *α* is assigned a fixed small value, e.g., 0.01, the resulting nonlinearity is known as the *leaky* ReLU \[126\]. In \[68\], *α* is left as a parameter to be learned during training. A further modification, known as the *max output* unit, a number of, say, *k* different linear units are employed, whose parameters are learned during the training, and, each time, the one that results in the maximum value is selected to activate the corresponding neuron \[52\]. The ReLU was first introduced in the context of dynamical networks in \[61\] and it was motivated by biological arguments.

The question that is now raised concerns the choice of the specific nonlinearity to be used in practice. There is no definite answer to that and the choice depends on the specific application. At the time this edition is compiled, it seems that the use of ReLU, in any one of its versions, is the more popular choice for the hidden layers. For classification tasks and for the output layer, the softmax nonlinearity, combined with the cross-entropy cost function, is most commonly used.

## 18.7 Regularizing the network

A crucial factor in training neural networks is to decide the size of the network. The size is directly related to the number of parameters to be estimated. Concerning feed-forward neural networks, two issues are involved. The first concerns the number of layers and the other the number of neurons per layer. As we will discuss in Section [18.11](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0140), a number of reasons support the use of more than two hidden layers. Such networks comprise a large number of parameters and can be vulnerable to overfitting, which affects the generalization performance of the learner. One path to cope with overfitting is via regularization. Over the years, various regularization approaches have been proposed. A brief presentation and some guidelines are given below. We will return to overfitting and generalization issues in the context of deep networks and from a different perspective in Section [18.11.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0145).

*Weight decay*: This path refers to a typical cost function regularization via the square Euclidean norm of the weights. Instead of minimizing a cost function, *J*(**θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si16.png), its regularized version is used, such that (e.g., \[71\])

*J*^′(**θ**) = *J*(**θ**) + *λ*||**θ**||².<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si304.png)(18.47) 

We have already discussed in Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml) in the context of ridge regression that involving the bias terms in the regularizing norm is not a good practice, because it affects the translation-invariant property of the estimator. A more sensible way to regularize is to remove the bias terms from the norm. Although this simple type of regularization helps in improving the generalization performance of the network, and it can be sufficient for some cases, in general it is not the most appropriate way to go.

Besides the square Euclidean norm, other norms can be used in Eq. [(18.47)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq89). For example, an alternative would be to employ the ℓ[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si305.png) norm. From Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), we know that the latter norm promotes sparsity. This is a welcome property when training a large network so that one can push less informative parameters to zero.

Over the years, various scenarios in applying the regularized cost function have been proposed. One scenario is to group all the parameters (excluding biases) for each layer together and apply Eq. [(18.47)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq89), involving different regularizing constants for each group. Another scenario is to deal with the parameters of each neuron separately. Another path is to look at regularization as being equivalent to constraining the norm to be less than a preselected value (Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)). This turns out to be equivalent to a projection step onto the respective ball associated with the norm, e.g., the ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si306.png) ball (see Chapter [8](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)), which leads to a normalization operation (see \[74\]).

*Weight elimination*: Instead of employing the norm of the weights, another approach involves more general functions for the regularization term, that is,

*J*^′(**θ**) = *J*(**θ**) + *λ**h*(**θ**).<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si307.png)(18.48) 

For example, in \[213\] the following is used:

$h(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\frac{\\theta\_{k}^{2}}{\\theta\_{h}^{2} + \\theta\_{k}^{2}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si308.png)(18.49) 

where *K* is the total number of the parameters involved and *θ*[*h*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si309.png) is a preselected threshold value. A careful look at this function reveals that if *θ*[*k*] < *θ*[*h*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si310.png), the penalty term goes to zero very fast. In contrast, for values *θ*[*k*] > *θ*[*h*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si311.png), the penalty term tends to unity. In this way, less significant weights are pushed toward zero. A number of variants of this method have also appeared (see, for example, \[173\]).

*Methods based on sensitivity analysis*: In \[112\], the so-called *optimal brain damage* technique is proposed. A perturbation analysis of the cost function in terms of the weights is performed, via the second-order Taylor expansion, that is,

$\\delta J = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{K}g\_{i}\\delta\\theta\_{i} + \\frac{1}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{K}h\_{ii}\\delta\\theta\_{i}^{2} + \\frac{1}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{K}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1,j \\neq i}^{K}h\_{ij}\\delta\\theta\_{i}\\delta\\theta\_{j},$<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si312.png)(18.50) 

where

$g\_{i}: = \\frac{\\partial J}{\\partial\\theta\_{i}},\\quad h\_{ij}: = \\frac{\\partial^{2}J}{\\partial\\theta\_{i}\\partial\\theta\_{j}}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∂</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si313.png)

Then, assuming the Hessian matrix to be diagonal and if the algorithm operates near the optimum (zero gradient), we can approximately set

$\\delta J \\approx \\frac{1}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{K}h\_{ii}\\delta\\theta\_{i}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>δ</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si314.png)(18.51) 

The method works as follows:

*   •  The network is trained using the backpropagation algorithm. After a few iteration steps, the training is frozen.
*   •  The so-called *saliencies*, defined as

$s\_{i} = \\frac{h\_{ii}\\theta\_{i}^{2}}{2},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si315.png)

*   are computed for each weight, and weights with a small saliency are removed. Basically, the saliency measures the effect on the cost function if one removes (sets equal to zero) the respective weight.
*   •  Training is continued and the process is repeated every few iterations, until a stopping criterion is satisfied.

In \[64\], the full Hessian matrix is computed, giving rise to the *optimal brain surgeon* method. Note that regularization techniques that remove connections are also known as *pruning* techniques.

*Early stopping*: An alternative, primitive in concept yet particularly useful in practice, technique to avoid overfitting is the so-called *early stopping*. The idea is to stop the training when the test error starts increasing. Training the network over many epochs can lead the training error to converge to small values. However, this is an indication of overfitting rather than indicative of a good solution. According to the early stopping method, training is performed for some iterations and then it is frozen. The network, using the currently available estimates of the weights/biases, is evaluated against a validation/test data set and the value of the cost function is computed. Then training is resumed, and after some iterations the previous process is repeated. When the value of the cost function, computed on the test set, starts increasing, then training is stopped.

Early stopping is also used in combination with other regularization strategies. Even when using regularization strategies that modify the objective function, the decision when to stop training cannot be based solely on focusing on the training error.

*Regularization via noise injection*: The regularization effect of the presence of noise during training has been well known since the early 1990s. There are various ways of adding extra noise to the input samples (e.g., \[16\]). This is equivalent to modifying the cost function by adding an extra term which acts as a regularizer.

The other alternative is to add noise to the parameters as they are being estimated during training (see, e.g., \[139\]). Looking at the noise as a small perturbation on the parameters and employing a first-order Taylor expansion of the output, one can show that this is equivalent to adding an extra regularizing term to the cost function. Large gradient values are penalized and this pushes the algorithm to converge to solutions in the parameter space, where they are relatively insensitive to small variations.

Besides the two previous possibilities, there are strategies that attempt to cope with noisy output labels. This is known as *label smoothing* (see, e.g., \[201\]).

*Regularizing via the artificial expansion of the data set*: As has already been discussed in various parts of the book (e.g., Chapter [3](#Chp003_65-117_B9780443292385000093.xhtml)), the cause of overfitting is the large size (capacity) of the number of unknown parameters of the model, with respect to the size of the training set. Keeping the model fixed, while increasing the number of the training data, acts beneficially on the overfitting problem. However, labeled data may not be always practical to have. In such cases and in certain applications, a way out is to generate artificially “fake” data and use them as part of the training set. For example, in tasks such as object recognition and OCR, one can generate many replicas of the objects or digits and letters by applying linear transformations, such as rotations, translations, and scaling, on existing images. In \[92\], data augmentation has also been applied to speech recognition. Later on, in Chapter [19](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml), we are going to discuss more recent techniques on how to artificially generate data.

Example 18.2

The goal of this example is to show the effect that regularization has on overfitting. [Fig. 18.14](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0080) shows the resulting decision lines that separate the samples of the two classes, denoted by black and red ∘, respectively. [Fig. 18.14](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0080)A corresponds to a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers and 20 neurons in each of them, amounting to a total of 480 weights. Training was performed via the batch gradient descent backpropagation algorithm. The overfitting nature of the resulting curve is readily observed. [Fig. 18.14](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0080)B corresponds to the same multilayer perceptron; however, this time a pruning algorithm was employed. Specifically, the method based on parameter sensitivity was used, testing the saliency values of the weights every 100 epochs and removing weights with saliency value below a chosen threshold. Finally, only 25 of the 480 weights survived and the curve is simplified to a straight line.

![Figure 18.14 Decision curve (A) before pruning and (B) after pruning.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr014.jpg)

Figure 18.14 Decision curve (A) before pruning and (B) after pruning.

### Dropout

This technique for regularizing deep networks follows a different concept from what we have already discussed. Its origin borrows ideas from the concept of combining learners, as has already been discussed in Sections [7.8](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml) and [7.9](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml), and in particular to the bagging rationale. However, dropout cleverly modifies the basic idea of bagging to make it more efficient and suitable to large networks.

The term “dropout” refers to dropping out units/nodes (in the hidden and input layers) in a neural network. At each iteration of the training algorithm, a number of nodes are removed (along with their incoming and outgoing associated connections). The parameters of the remaining nodes are updated according to the updating rule. In other words, at each iteration step only a *subset* of the parameters are updated while the rest (the ones associated with the removed nodes) are frozen to their currently available estimates from the previous iteration. The subset consisting of the remaining nodes defines a *subnetwork* of the original larger one. The procedure is illustrated in [Fig. 18.15](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0085). In [Fig. 18.15](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0085)A, the full network is shown. In [Fig. 18.15](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0085)B, the nodes to be removed are shown in red, together with all their incoming and outgoing connections. In [Fig. 18.15](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0085)C, the subnetwork to be updated in the current iteration involves only the gray nodes. The red ones have been removed and the estimates of their associated parameters are frozen to the values that have already been obtained in the previous iteration and which are *not updated* in the current step. In the figure, one of the removed nodes is an input one and the rest lie in hidden layers.

![Figure 18.15 (A) The full network. (B) The nodes to be removed are shown in red, together with all incoming and outgoing connections. (C) The red ones have been removed. The estimates of their associated parameters are frozen to the values obtained in the previous iteration and are not updated in the current iteration step.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr015.jpg)

Figure 18.15 (A) The full network. (B) The nodes to be removed are shown in red, together with all incoming and outgoing connections. (C) The red ones have been removed. The estimates of their associated parameters are frozen to the values obtained in the previous iteration and are not updated in the current iteration step.

The removal of nodes is carried out probabilistically. That is, each node is retained with probability *P*. Usually, the value of *P* is equal to 0.5 for the hidden layers and is set equal to 0.8 for the input layer nodes. For a network with, say, *K* nodes, the total number of possible subnetworks is 2^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si316.png). This is indeed a large number for large values of *K*, which is the case in practice. However, keep in mind that there is a high degree of parameter *sharing* among the various subnetworks and the total number of parameters to be learned is equal to the number of parameters that constitute the original network.

Once the training phase has been completed and the backpropagation algorithm has converged, the obtained estimates are multiplied by the respective probability, *P*. This corresponds to an averaging operation over all possible subnetworks that have been trained \[74\]. It can be shown that (e.g., \[55,74\]) for a network with one hidden layer and *K* nodes with a softmax output unit for computing the probabilities of the class labels, using the mean network is equivalent to taking the geometric mean of the probability distributions over labels predicted by all 2^(*K*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si316.png) possible networks. In \[212\], it is shown that applying the dropout rationale to a linear regression task is equivalent to an ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si306.png) regularization with different regularizing weights per model parameter. However, this equivalence does not carry to general deep networks.

A heuristic explanation on why dropout works is provided in \[74\]. Dropout reduces coadaptation of neurons, because in every iteration the parameters of different sets of neurons are updated. Thus the network is “forced” to learn more robust features. In other words, the network learns while, each time, parts of it are missing. A more theoretically pleasing explanation is given in \[221\], where it is shown that the dropout technique is equivalent to an approximate variational inference with specific priors in a deep Gaussian process.

At the time the current edition is compiled, the dropout technique seems to be the most popular method for regularization and has been applied to a wide range of applications (see, e.g., \[183\]). Also, using the dropout does not prevent combining it with other types of regularization \[74\]. Needless to say, the method is not a “panacea” and has its drawbacks. A major shortcoming is that typically one has to train much larger networks to account for the loss of capacity imposed by the regularization. Moreover, one needs more iterations for the training. A dropout network typically takes two to three times longer to train than a standard neural network of the same architecture. To this end, besides the previously reported scheme, computational efficient alternatives have also been proposed (see, e.g., \[208,210\]).

Example 18.3

[Fig. 18.16](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0090) illustrates the effect of the dropout regularization on the test error, in the context of an optical character recognition (OCR) classification task. A fully connected feed-forward network is used with 784 nodes in the input layer, 2000 nodes in each one of the two hidden layers, and 10 output nodes, one per class. The inputs to the network come from the MNIST data set for digit recognition. The input images are of 28 × 28 (784)<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>784</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si317.png) and the pixel values were normalized in the range \[0,1\]. For the training, 55000 images were used and 10000 were kept for the testing phase. The nonlinearity used in the hidden layers was the ReLU and for the output nodes the softmax one. The loss function was the cross-entropy one. The standard gradient descent algorithm was used with step size *μ* = 0.01<mml:math><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si201.png). The network was trained for 600 epochs and the mini-batch size was equal to 100. To obtain the curves, the error over the test set is computed using the estimates obtained during the training phase, every time an epoch iteration has been completed. Observe that the use of dropout has a significant effect on the obtained test error. Also, a combination of dropping out hidden as well as input nodes has a beneficial effect. One should notice that although the use of dropout is beneficial, even without regularization, the network is doing quite well. We will come back to that in Section [18.11.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0145).

This is verified by the test error measured by the number of errors committed in the test set. ## 18.8 Designing deep neural networks: a summary

So far in our discussion, we have touched upon a number of challenges that one has to address while building up a deep neural network for a specific application. No doubt, a practitioner has to make a number of critical decisions prior to running the code, using, usually, one of the off-the-self software packages.

Adopting the neural network architecture and selecting the related hyperparameters is still a task with a strong engineering flavor.
