In the more general setting, the convolution operation between two matrices, *H* ∈ ℝ^(*m* × *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si379.png) and *I* ∈ ℝ^(*l* × *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si380.png), is another matrix, defined as

$O(i,j) = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{m}\\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{m}h(t,r)I(i + t - 1,j + r - 1),$<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si381.png)(18.63) 

where for our case, *m* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si382.png). In words, *O*(*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si383.png) contains information in a window area of the input array. According to the definition in Eq. [(18.63)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq109), the element *I*(*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si384.png) is the top left element in this window area. The size of the window depends on the value of *m*. The size of the output matrix depends on the assumptions that one adopts on how to deal with the elements/pixels at the borders of *I*. We will come back to that soon. Strictly speaking, in the signal processing jargon, Eq. [(18.63)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq109) is known as the *cross-correlation* operation. For the convolution operation, as has already been defined in Eq. [(4.49)](#Chp004_119-175_B978044329238500010X.xhtml), a flipping of the indices has first to take place.^([^(119)](#fn119))

The previous discussion “forces” us to seize thinking of a hidden layer as a collection of nodes one next to the other. Instead, in a CNN, each hidden layer corresponds to a (or more than one, as we will soon see) matrix *H*. Furthermore, *H* is used to perform convolutions. From a signal processing point of view, this matrix is a *filter*, which acts upon the input to provide the output. In the machine learning jargon, it is also called the *kernel* matrix instead of a filter. The output matrix is usually referred to as the *feature map* array.

In summary, by performing convolutions, instead of inner product operations, we have achieved what was our original goal: (a) the parameters comprising the hidden layer are *shared* by all the input pixels and we do not have a dedicated set of parameters per input element (pixel), and (b) the outputs of the hidden layer encode local neighborhood correlation information from the various areas within the input image. Also, since the output of the hidden layer is also an image array, one can consider it as the input to a second hidden layer and in this way build a network with many layers, each one performing convolutions.

As a matter of fact, such filtering operations have traditionally been used in order to generate features from images. The difference was that the elements of the filter matrix were *preselected*. Take, as an example, the following matrix:

$H = \\begin{bmatrix} {- 1\\ } & {- 1\\ } & {- 1} \\\\ {- 1\\ } & {8\\ } & {- 1} \\\\ {- 1\\ } & {- 1\\ } & {- 1} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>8</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si385.png)(18.64) 

The above filter is known as *edge detector*. Convolving an image array, *I*, with the previous matrix, *H*, detects the edges in an image. [Fig. 18.19](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0105)A shows the boat image and [Fig. 18.19](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0105)B shows the output after filtering the image on the left with the filter matrix *H* above. Detecting edges is of major importance in image understanding. Moreover, by changing appropriately the values in *H*, one can detect edges in different orientations, e.g., diagonal, vertical, horizontal; in words, changing the values of *H* one can generate different types of features. We have come closer to the idea behind CNNs.

*   •  Instead of using a *fixed* filter/kernel matrix, as in the edge detector example, leave the computation of the values of the filter matrix, *H*, to the training phase. In other words, we make *H data-adaptive* and not preselected.
*   •  Instead of using a single filter matrix, employ more than one. Each of them will generate a different type of features. For example, one may generate diagonal edges, the other one horizontal, etc. Hence, each hidden layer will comprise more than one filter matrix. The values of the elements of each one of the filter matrices will be estimated/learned during the training phase, by optimizing some criterion. In other words, each hidden layer of a CNN generates a set of features *optimally*.

[Fig. 18.20](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0110) illustrates the input and the first hidden layer of a CNN. The input comprises an image array. The hidden layer consists of three filter matrices, namely, *H*[1], *H*[2], *H*[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si42.png). Observe that each feature map array is the result of sliding (convolving) a different filter matrix over the input image. The more filters are employed, the more feature maps are extracted and, in principle, the better the network should perform. However, the more filters we use, the more parameters have to be learned, raising computational as well as overfitting issues. Note that each pixel in an output feature map array encodes information within the window area that is defined by the corresponding position of the respective filter matrix.

![Figure 18.19 (A) The original image and (B) the image edges extracted after filtering the original image array with the filter matrix, H, in Eq. (18.64).](images/B978044329238500024X/gr019.jpg)

Figure 18.19 (A) The original image and (B) the image edges extracted after filtering the original image array with the filter matrix, *H*, in Eq. [(18.64)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq110).

![Figure 18.20 Each pixel in a feature map corresponds to a specific area in the input image, which is known as the receptive field of the corresponding pixel. In this figure, three filters/kernels are used. The number of filters is known as depth or sometimes we refer to it as the number of channels. Hence, in this case, the depth of the hidden layer is three.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr020.jpg)

Figure 18.20 Each pixel in a feature map corresponds to a specific area in the input image, which is known as the receptive field of the corresponding pixel. In this figure, three filters/kernels are used. The number of filters is known as depth or sometimes we refer to it as the number of channels. Hence, in this case, the depth of the hidden layer is three.

An important characteristic of a CNN is that *translation invariance* is naturally built into the network and it is a by-product of the involved convolutions. Indeed, the latter are performed by sliding the *same* filter matrix over the entire image. Thus, if an object, which is present in an image, is placed in another position, the only difference would be that the contribution of this object to the output will also move the same amount in the number of pixels.

It is interesting to note that there is strong evidence from the visual neuroscience field that similar computations are performed in the human brain (e.g., \[85,185\]). The notion of convolutions was first used in \[46\] in the context of unsupervised learning.

Below, we provide some jargon terms used in conjunction with CNNs.

*   •  *Depth*: The depth of a layer is the number of filter matrices that are employed in this layer. This is not to be confused with the depth of the network, which corresponds to the total number of hidden layers used. Sometimes, we refer to the number of filters as the number of *channels*.
*   •  *Receptive field*: Each pixel in an output feature map array results as a weighted average of the pixels within a specific area of the input (or of the output of the previous layer) image array. The specific area that corresponds to a pixel is known as its receptive field (see [Fig. 18.20](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0110)).
*   •  *Stride*: In practice, instead of sliding the filter/kernel matrix one pixel at a time, one can slide it by, say, *s* pixels. This value is known as the stride. For values of *s* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si386.png), feature map arrays that are smaller in size result. This is illustrated in [Figs. 18.21](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0115)A and B. The red crosses indicate the position of the 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si366.png) filter matrix on top of the 5 × 5<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si387.png) input array. For stride *s* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si388.png), there are nine possible positions and the output feature map is a 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si366.png) array. For stride *s* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si389.png), there are four possible positions and the output is a 2 × 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si368.png) array.

![Figure 18.21 The figure presents the case of an input matrix of size 5 × 5 and of a filter matrix 3 × 3. In (A), the stride is equal to s = 1 and in (B) it is equal to s = 2. In (A) the output is a matrix of size 3 × 3 and in (B) of size 2 × 2.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr021.jpg)

Figure 18.21 The figure presents the case of an input matrix of size 5 × 5 and of a filter matrix 3 × 3. In (A), the stride is equal to *s* = 1 and in (B) it is equal to *s* = 2. In (A) the output is a matrix of size 3 × 3 and in (B) of size 2 × 2.

*   
*   •  *Zero padding*: Sometimes, zeros are used to pad the input matrix around the border pixels. In this way, the dimension of the matrix increases. If the original matrix has dimensions *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si390.png), after expanding it with *p* columns and rows, the new dimensions become (*l* + 2*p*) × (*l* + 2*p*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si391.png). This is shown in [Fig. 18.22](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0120).

![Figure 18.22 An example where the original matrix is 5 × 5 and after padding with p = 2 rows and columns, its size becomes 9 × 9.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr022.jpg)

[Figure 18.22](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1440) An example where the original matrix is 5 × 5 and after padding with *p* = 2 rows and columns, its size becomes 9 × 9.

*   
*   •  *Bias term*: After each convolution operation that generates a feature map pixel, a bias term, *b*, is added. The value of this term is also computed during training. Note that a common bias term is used for all the pixels in the same feature map. This is in line with the weight sharing rationale; in the same way that all parameters of a filter matrix are shared by all the input image array pixels, the same bias term is used for all pixel locations.

One can adjust the size of an output feature map array by adjusting the value of the stride, *s*, and the number of extra zero columns and rows in the padding. In general, it can easily be checked that if *I* ∈ ℝ^(*l* × *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si380.png), *H* ∈ ℝ^(*m* × *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si379.png), *s* is the stride, and *p* is the number of extra rows and columns for padding, then the feature map has dimensions *k* × *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si392.png), where

$k = \\left\\lfloor \\frac{l + 2p - m}{s} + 1 \\right\\rfloor,$<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">⌊</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">⌋</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si393.png)(18.65) 

and ⌊ ⋅ ⌋<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">⌊</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">⌋</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si394.png) denotes the floor operation, i.e., ⌊3.7⌋ = 3<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">⌊</mml:mo><mml:mn>3.7</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">⌋</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si395.png). For example, if *l* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si396.png), *m* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si397.png), *p* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si398.png), and *s* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si388.png), then *k* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si399.png). On the other hand, if *l* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si396.png), *m* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si397.png), *p* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si398.png), and *s* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si389.png), then *k* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si400.png) (see [Figs. 18.21](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0115)A and B).

Note that if the values of *l*, *m*, *p*, and *s* are such that the filter matrix, as it slides over *I*, falls outside *I*, such operations are not performed. We only perform operations as long as the filter matrix is *contained* within *I*.

One may wonder why one has to pad with zeros. Note that by the way convolutions are performed, the size of the feature map is smaller than that of the input array. As we will soon see, in a deep network, the output feature map is used as input to the next layer. Thus, the size of the arrays would be decreasing as we move on deeper into the network. In contrast, after padding with zeros, as Eq. [(18.65)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq111) suggests, we can control the size of the involved arrays. For example, if *l* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si396.png), *m* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si397.png), *s* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si388.png), and *p* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si401.png), then the output will have the same size *k* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si402.png) as the input array. As a matter of fact, if *p* = (*m* − 1)/2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si403.png), for an odd value of *m*, *k* = *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si404.png). In such cases, we call the operation *same convolution*. The other reason that padding may be used is that the border pixels of the input image contribute less to the output, compared to the pixels that are located in the interior of the image. Take as an example [Fig. 18.18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0100). Pixel *I*(1, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si405.png) contributes only to *O*(1, 1)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si374.png). In contrast, pixel *I*(2, 2)<mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si406.png) contributes to all output elements, since it is contained within the window area, in all four positions. Using padding with zeros, we give the chance to the border elements to have a more equal “say” to the output values, when compared with the interior pixels.

#### The nonlinearity step

Once convolutions have been performed and the bias term has been added to all feature map values, the next step is to apply a nonlinearity (activation function) to each one of the pixels of every feature map array. Any one of the nonlinearities that have been previously discussed can be employed. Currently, the rectified linear activation function, ReLU, seems to be the most popular one.

[Fig. 18.23](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0125)A shows the image obtained after filtering the original boat image with the edge detector filter in Eq. [(18.64)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq110), and [Fig. 18.23](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0125)B shows the result that is obtained after the application of the ReLU nonlinearity on each individual pixel.

![Figure 18.23 (A) The image where the edges have been extracted and (B) the resulting image after applying the ReLU on each one of the pixels. Note that after filtering, the image array in (A) may involve negative values, which are set to zero after the ReLU activation.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr023.jpg)

Figure 18.23 (A) The image where the edges have been extracted and (B) the resulting image after applying the ReLU on each one of the pixels. Note that after filtering, the image array in (A) may involve negative values, which are set to zero after the ReLU activation.

#### The pooling step

The purpose of this step is to reduce the dimensionality of each feature map array. Sometimes, the step is also referred to as spatial pooling. To this end, one defines a window and slides it over the corresponding matrix. The sliding can be done by adopting a value for the respective stride parameter, *s*.

The pooling operation consists of choosing a *single* value to represent all the pixels that lie within the window. The most commonly used operation is the *max pooling*; that is, among all the pixels that lie within the window, the one with the maximum value is selected. Another possibility is the *average pooling*, where the average value of all the pixels is selected; sometimes, this is known as sum pooling. The pooling operation is illustrated in [Fig. 18.24](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0130). The original image array is 6 × 6<mml:math><mml:mn>6</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si407.png) and the window is of size 2 × 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si368.png). We have chosen the stride to be equal to *s* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si389.png). That is, every time the window slides two pixels to the right or to the bottom. Different colors have been used to indicate the various positions of the window. Within each window, the maximum value is selected. The resulting matrix is of size 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si366.png). The same formula as in Eq. [(18.65)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq111) can be used to compute the size of the resulting matrix in the general case. Thus, the effect of pooling is to reduce (via downsampling) the dimensionality and make the size of the arrays smaller. This is important because the output of each layer is presented as the input to the next one. Hence, controlling the size of the arrays is of paramount importance, in order to control the number of the involved parameters. Of course, the reduction in size should be done in such a way so that the loss of information is as small as possible.

![Figure 18.24 (A) The original matrix is of size 6 × 6. For pooling by a 2 × 2 window and stride s = 2, there are nine possible locations of the window. These locations are indicated by using different colors to show the elements that are grouped together in each one of the window locations. The maximum value per window location is indicated in bold. (B) The resulting 3 × 3 matrix after max-pooling.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr024.jpg)

[Figure 18.24](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1475) (A) The original matrix is of size 6 × 6. For pooling by a 2 × 2 window and stride *s* = 2, there are nine possible locations of the window. These locations are indicated by using different colors to show the elements that are grouped together in each one of the window locations. The maximum value per window location is indicated in bold. (B) The resulting 3 × 3 matrix after max-pooling.

[Fig. 18.25](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0135) shows the effect of applying pooling to the image shown on the left. No doubt, the edges become coarser, yet the information related to edges can still be extracted. Note that after pooling, the size of the image array is reduced.

![Figure 18.25 (A) The edges of the boat image after the application of the ReLU and (B) the resulting image after applying max-pooling using an 8 × 8 window. Although the resolution is lower, the basic edge information has not been lost.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr025.jpg)

[Figure 18.25](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1485) (A) The edges of the boat image after the application of the ReLU and (B) the resulting image after applying max-pooling using an 8 × 8 window. Although the resolution is lower, the basic edge information has not been lost.

Looking at pooling from a different view, it can be said that it summarizes the statistics within the pooling area. Pooling can be considered as a special type of filtering, where instead of convolution, the maximum (or average) value is selected. It turns out that pooling helps the representation to become approximately invariant to small translations of the input. This can be understood by the following simple argument. If a small translation does not bring in the window a new largest element and also does not remove the largest element by taking it outside the pooling window, then the maximum does not change.

### 18.12.2 Convolution over volumes

In [Fig. 18.20](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0110), the output of the first hidden layer comprises three image arrays. These will constitute the input to the next layer. Such an input setting that consists of multiple images is also the case when the input image is in color and its representation is given in terms of an RGB representation; that is, the input consists of three arrays, one per color. Another example is that of hyperspectral imaging, where the number of images is equal to that of the spectral bands (Section [13.13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml)). Thus, in general, the inputs to the various layers are not two-dimensional arrays but sets of two-dimensional arrays. In mathematics, such entities are known as *multilinear arrays*, or *three-dimensional arrays*, or *three-dimensional tensors*, or *volumes*. We will adhere to the latter term, because it is reminiscent of the associated geometry, in the same way that we think of an image as a two-dimensional square. The question now is to see how one can perform convolutions when volumes are involved.

By convention, the three dimensions of a volume will be represented as *h* for the height, *w* for the width, and *d* for the depth. Note that the depth *d* corresponds to the number of images involved. [Fig. 18.26](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0140) illustrates the geometry associated with the respective definitions for *h* = *w* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si408.png) and *d* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si409.png). So, if we have three 256 × 256<mml:math><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si358.png) images, then *h* = *w* = 256<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si410.png) and *d* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si409.png) and we will say that the volume is of size (dimension) 256 × 256 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si411.png).

![Figure 18.26 A number of d matrices each of size h × w are stacked together to form a volume of size h × w × d. In this case, h = w = 5 and d = 3.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr026.jpg)

[Figure 18.26](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1495) A number of *d* matrices each of size *h* × *w* are stacked together to form a volume of size *h* × *w* × *d*. In this case, *h* = *w* = 5 and *d* = 3.

Let the input to a layer be an *h* × *w* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si412.png) volume. When volumes are involved, hidden layers consist of filter/kernel volumes, too. However, there is a crucial point here. The filter volume associated with the hidden layer *must* be of the same depth as the input volume. The height and width dimensions can be (and in practice usually are) different. We are going to use bold capital letters to denote volumes. Assume that the input is the *l* × *l* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si413.png) volume ***I***. Obviously, this comprises *d* images, say, *I*[*r*], *r* = 1, 2, …, *d*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si414.png), each one of dimensions *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si390.png). Let the filter be the *m* × *m* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si415.png) volume ***H***. The latter comprises the set of *d* images, *H*[*r*], *r* = 1, 2, …, *d*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si416.png), each one of dimensions *m* × *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si417.png). Then the operation of convolution is defined via the following steps:

1)Convolve corresponding two-dimensional image arrays to generate *d* two-dimensional output arrays, i.e., *O*[*r*] = *I*[*r*] \* *H*[*r*], *r* = 1, 2, …, *d*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si418.png).

2)The convolution of the two volumes, ***I*** and ***H***, is defined as

$O = \\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{d}O\_{r}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si419.png)

In words, the convolution (denoted by ⁎) of two volumes is a *two-dimensional array*, i.e.,

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/fx011.jpg)

The operation is illustrated in [Fig. 18.27](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0145). Corresponding arrays (shown by different colors and types of lines) are convolved. The three (*d* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si409.png)) output arrays are subsequently added together to form the convolution of the two volumes. The dimension *k* of the output depends on the values of *l* and *m*, the stride *s*, and the padding *p*, if used, according to Eq. [(18.65)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq111).

![Figure 18.27 The figure illustrates the case of depth d = 3. Convolving the l × l × d input volume (I) with a filter volume (H) with dimensions m × m × d is equivalent to convolving the d (l × l) matrices which comprise the input volume with an equal number of d (m × m) filters. This operation results in d output (feature map) matrices, which are subsequently added together. The value of k is determined by the specific values of l, m, and the stride s. No padding is involved in the case of this figure.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr027.jpg)

[Figure 18.27](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1500) The figure illustrates the case of depth *d* = 3. Convolving the *l* × *l* × *d* input volume (***I***) with a filter volume (***H***) with dimensions *m* × *m* × *d* is equivalent to convolving the *d* (*l* × *l*) matrices which comprise the input volume with an equal number of *d* (*m* × *m*) filters. This operation results in *d* output (feature map) matrices, which are subsequently added together. The value of *k* is determined by the specific values of *l*, *m*, and the stride *s*. No padding is involved in the case of this figure.

In practice, each layer of a convolutional network comprises a number of such filter volumes. For example, if the input to a layer is an *l* × *l* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si413.png) volume, and there are, say, *c* kernel volumes, each one of dimensions *m* × *m* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si415.png), the output of the layer will be a *k* × *k* × *c*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si420.png) volume, where *k* is determined as explained before.

#### Network in network and 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution

The 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution \[118\] does not make sense when two-dimensional arrays are involved. Indeed, a 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) filter matrix is a scalar. Convolving an *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si390.png) matrix *I* with a scalar *a* is equivalent to sliding the scalar value over all the pixels and multiplying each one of them with *a*. The result is the trivial multiplication *aI*. However, when volumes are involved, the 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution makes sense. In this case, the corresponding filter, ***H***, is a volume of size 1 × 1 × *d*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si422.png). Geometrically, this is a “tube,” with *h* = *w* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si423.png) and *d* elements in depth, *h*(1, 1, *r*), *r* = 1, 2, …, *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si424.png), see [Fig. 18.28](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0150). Hence, the output of convolving an *l* × *l* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si413.png) volume ***I*** with a 1 × 1 × *d*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si422.png) volume ***H*** is the weighted average,

$O = \\mathbf{I} \\ast \\mathbf{H} = \\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{d}h(1,1,r)I\_{r},$<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si425.png)

where *I*[*r*], *r* = 1, 2, …, *d*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si414.png), are the *d* arrays, each of dimensions *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si390.png), that comprise ***I***. Now, one may wonder why we need such an operation in practice. The answer is related to the size of the involved volumes; via the use of 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolutions, one can control and change their sizes to fit the needs of the network.

![Figure 18.28 Illustration of the 1 × 1 convolution. There are c 1 × 1 × d tubes, where d is the depth of the input volume. The convolution of each one of the tubes with the input volume results in a two-dimensional array of the same dimensions as the input ones (5 × 5). The elements of the output arrays are weighted averages of the corresponding elements of the input arrays. For example, the red elements, at position (3,3) of the 5 × 5 output arrays, are the weighted averages of the red points at the (3,3) position of the input arrays. The weights used in the weighted average are the respective elements that define the corresponding tube. Since we have c tubes, the output volume will be of depth c.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr028.jpg)

Figure 18.28 Illustration of the 1 × 1 convolution. There are *c* 1 × 1 × *d* tubes, where *d* is the depth of the input volume. The convolution of each one of the tubes with the input volume results in a two-dimensional array of the same dimensions as the input ones (5 × 5). The elements of the output arrays are weighted averages of the corresponding elements of the input arrays. For example, the red elements, at position (3,3) of the 5 × 5 output arrays, are the weighted averages of the red points at the (3,3) position of the input arrays. The weights used in the weighted average are the respective elements that define the corresponding tube. Since we have *c* tubes, the output volume will be of depth *c*.

Let us assume that at one stage/layer of a deep network we have obtained a volume ***I*** of dimensions *k* × *k* × *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si427.png). To change the depth from *d* to *c*, while retaining the same size *k*, for the height and the width, we employ *c* volumes, **H**[*t*], *t* = 1, 2, …, *c*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si428.png), each of dimensions 1 × 1 × *d*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si422.png). Performing the *c* convolutions, we obtain

$O\_{t} = \\mathbf{I} \\ast \\mathbf{H}\_{t} = \\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{d}h\_{t}(1,1,r)I\_{r},\\ t = 1,2,\\ldots,c.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si429.png)(18.66) 

Stacking *O*[*t*], *t* = 1, 2…, *c*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si430.png), together, we obtain the volume ***O*** of dimension *k* × *k* × *c*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si420.png). The operation is illustrated in [Fig. 18.28](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0150).

For example, we can employ 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution to reduce the size, by selecting *c* < *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si431.png). In this way, although we reduce the depth, the elements of the new volume are weighted averages of the original ***I***. So, the original information is still retained within the new volume, in an averaging fashion. Often, once the new volume ***O*** is obtained, its elements are “pushed” through a nonlinearity, e.g., ReLU. Sometimes, the 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution followed by the nonlinearity is referred to as *network in network* operation and its purpose is to add an extra nonlinearity stage in the flow of operations through the network. Thus, in this context, if *c* < *d*<mml:math><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si431.png), the network in network operation can be thought of as a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique.

Looking at the 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution from a different viewpoint, it is nothing but a layer of a fully connected neural network, with *c* nodes. The weights connecting the *t*th node with the *d* input values are *h*[*t*](1, 1, *r*), *r* = 1, 2, …, *d*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si432.png). This is the reason that we also call the operation network in network, in the sense that we embed a fully connected neural network between two successive convolution layers in the network. In this way, one can add an extra nonlinearity in the flow of operations through the network. In practice, the parameters of the respective **H**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si433.png) tubes are learned during the training phase of the overall network.

Example 18.4

Let us consider the input to a layer to be a 28 × 28 × 192<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>192</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si434.png) volume, ***I***. The goal is to produce at the output of the layer a volume, ***O***, which is of dimension 28 × 28 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si435.png). To this end, employ 5 × 5<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si387.png) same convolutions. Compute the number of required operations.

a) *The direct way*: Since same convolutions are required, we should first pad all the arrays that are stacked in ***I*** with *p* zero columns and rows, where *p* = (5 − 1)/2 = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si436.png) (as has been explained in the text before, when “same convolutions” were defined). After padding, the height and width of each image become *h* = *w* = 32<mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si437.png). Using *s* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si388.png) for the stride, the total number of possible locations, as we slide the 5 × 5<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si387.png) window over a 32 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si438.png) image array, is 28² = 784<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>28</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>784</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si439.png). For each location of the window, we need to perform 5² = 25<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si440.png) multiplications and additions (MADS), or 784 × 25 = 19600<mml:math><mml:mn>784</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>19600</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si441.png) MADS operations per image. Since the volume involves 192 images, the total number of MADS operations needed is 19600 × 192 ≈ 3.7 × 10⁶<mml:math><mml:mn>19600</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>192</mml:mn><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>3.7</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si442.png). These operations are needed for each channel. Since the depth of the output should be 32, we need 32 such filter volumes (channels) and the total number of required MADS operations will be 3.7 × 10⁶ × 32 ≈ 120<mml:math><mml:mn>3.7</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>120</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si443.png) million.

b) *Via the use of* 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) *convolutions*: We will now produce a 28 × 28 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si435.png) output volume using a substantially lower number of operations. Our path will involve two stages. We will first employ 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolutions to generate an intermediate volume, **O**^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si444.png), of dimensions 28 × 28 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si445.png). To this end, we use 16 1 × 1 × 192<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>192</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si446.png) filter volumes and perform the respective convolutions, according to Eq. [(18.66)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#deq115). The corresponding number of MADS is 28² × 192 × 16 ≈ 2.4<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>28</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>192</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si447.png) million. In the sequel, we pad each one of the arrays contained in volume **O**^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si444.png) with *p* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si448.png) extra zero columns and rows (as before); then, we perform same convolutions with 32 filter volumes **H**[*t*], *t* = 1, 2, …32<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si449.png), each one of dimensions 5 × 5 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si450.png), to obtain the output volume, ***O***, of dimensions 28 × 28 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si435.png). The respective number of operations is 28² × 25 × 16 × 32 ≈ 10<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>28</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si451.png) million. Thus, now, the total number of operations, for both stages, amounts to approximately 12.4 million, which is substantially lower than the 120 million that were needed via the previous path (a).

Often, the intermediate volume, **O**^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">O</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si444.png), is known as the *bottleneck* layer; its role is to “shrink” the size of the input volume first, prior to obtaining the final output one. The overall layout is shown in [Fig. 18.29](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0155).

![Figure 18.29 The bottleneck layer. In the first step, c = 16 1 × 1 convolutions are performed and the output is a 28 × 28 × 16 volume. Then, we apply a same 5 × 5 × 32 convolution to obtain the final 28 × 28 × 32 volume.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr029.jpg)

[Figure 18.29](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1530) The bottleneck layer. In the first step, *c* = 16 1 × 1 convolutions are performed and the output is a 28 × 28 × 16 volume. Then, we apply a same 5 × 5 × 32 convolution to obtain the final 28 × 28 × 32 volume.

### 18.12.3 The full CNN architecture

The typical form of a full convolutional network consists of a sequence of convolutional layers, each comprising the three basic steps, namely, convolution, nonlinearity, and pooling, as described in the beginning of Section [18.12.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0175). Depending on the application, one can stack as many layers as required, where the output of one layer becomes the input to the next one. Inputs and outputs to each layer are volumes, as described before. The general architecture is illustrated in [Fig. 18.30](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0160). In the first layer, a number of filter volumes (channels) are employed to perform convolutions followed by the ReLU (usually) nonlinear operation. Then, the pooling stage takes over to reduce the height and width of each output volume, which is then used as input to the second layer, and so on. Finally, the output volume of the last layer is vectorized. Sometimes, this is also referred to as *flattening* operation. In words, all the elements of the output volume are stacked one under the other to form a vector. Vectorization can take place via various strategies. As a matter of fact, the obtained vector forms the *feature vector* that has finally been generated via the various *transformations* that the convolutions implement layer after layer. This feature vector will then be used as input to a learner, for example, to a fully connected neural network (lower part of the figure) or to any other predictor, such as a kernel machine.

![Figure 18.30 The full CNN comprises a series of layers. In the figure, two such layers are shown. Each layer consists of the convolution step, followed by the application of the nonlinearity, and then the pooling step, which reduces the height and width of the images that comprise the respective volume. The depth remains the same. As we move to higher layers, the tendency is to reduce the height and width and increase the depth of the volumes. The final output volume is vectorized and presented as input to a learner, usually a fully connected network.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr030.jpg)

Figure 18.30 The full CNN comprises a series of layers. In the figure, two such layers are shown. Each layer consists of the convolution step, followed by the application of the nonlinearity, and then the pooling step, which reduces the height and width of the images that comprise the respective volume. The depth remains the same. As we move to higher layers, the tendency is to reduce the height and width and increase the depth of the volumes. The final output volume is vectorized and presented as input to a learner, usually a fully connected network.

The general strategy is to keep reducing the height and width while increasing the depth of the volumes. Larger depth corresponds to more filters per stage, which translates to more features. Both the number of convolutional layers and the number of layers of the fully connected network depend heavily on the application and, up to now, there is not a formal method to determine automatically the number of layers as well as the number of filters or nodes per layer. The choice is a matter of “engineering” and evaluation of different combinations to select the best. A good practice is to select an existing architecture that has been used before in the related application and start from there. A more recent research path toward developing more systematic ways of learning the number of nodes/filters per layer is via Bayesian learning arguments (see, e.g., \[148\]).

Training of a convolutional network follows a similar rationale as that of backpropagation, which has been discussed in Section [18.4](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0030). However, certain modifications should be involved in order to take care of the constraints imposed by the weight sharing (see, e.g., \[51\] for details).

As a final remark, recall that the crucial point for training deep networks is, besides the available computational power, the existence of large data sets (e.g., \[172,227\]), which have made the training of such big networks possible.

#### What deep neural networks learn

It is by now well established that convolutional networks do work well and constitute powerful predictors in a large number of diverse applications. However, a critical question is: what type of features does a CNN learn? In other words, what is the information that is propagated from one layer to the other? This is crucial to the understanding of why they work so well. The answer to this question could facilitate their *interpretability*, which is of paramount importance in specific applications, such as in medical and financial fields. Also, such understanding could help to develop improved models.

To this end, visualization techniques have been mobilized to reveal the specific input stimuli that excite individual feature maps at any layer (e.g., \[226\]). In this paper, an experimental study has been conducted in the context of computer vision. The findings reveal a hierarchical nature of the features produced, as one moves from the input to the final output. For example, layer #2 seems to respond to the corners and other edge/color conjunctions associated with the objects present in the input image. Layer #3 has more complex invariances, capturing similar textures. Higher layers reveal more class-specific information, e.g., dog faces, bird lengths, etc. Such findings are in line with the discussion in Section [18.11.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#s0145).

Another interesting finding is that convergence in the lower layers, closer to the input, is rather fast. In contrast, the upper layers, closer to the output, develop after a considerable number of epochs. Furthermore, concerning feature invariance, with respect to translation and scaling, it seems that small transformations may have a dramatic effect in the first layers but a smaller impact on the top layers.

With the growing success of deep neural networks, the need of being able to *explain* the predictions is of paramount importance in building up confidence for their deployment in real-world applications. To this end, there are still a number of open questions and the topic is currently an ongoing research area. A more detailed coverage is beyond the scope of this chapter and the interested reader may obtain a good feeling of the current trends from, e.g., \[25\] and the references therein.

More recently (e.g., \[48\] and the references therein), the importance of *texture* in recognizing objects in images has been outlined. It is postulated that CNNs trained on ImageNet are strongly biased toward recognizing textures rather than shapes, which is in stark contrast to human behavioral evidence. It is pointed out that local textures may provide sufficient information about object classes. This seems to be in line with the results obtained in \[19\], where it is demonstrated that using small local patches, rather than integrating object parts for shape recognition, can achieve surprisingly high accuracies. Such findings may also facilitate the interpretability issue that has been previously discussed, since one can follow easier on how the evidence from smaller image patches is integrated to reach the final decision.

In a different direction, research has been focused on revealing various aspects associated with the multilayer structure of such networks in an effort to shed light from different viewpoints, which can help in their understanding. For example, in \[21,129\] deep architectures are implemented via a cascade of wavelet transform convolutions, combined with a nonlinear operation followed by an averaging operation, so as to build translation-invariant representations. Furthermore, such networks preserve high-frequency information related to classification. In \[22\], it is shown that the pooling step in deep CNNs results in shift invariance. In \[49\], it is shown that deep neural networks with random Gaussian weights perform a distance preserving embedding of the data. In this analysis, tools from the compressed sensing and dictionary learning tasks are employed, which establishes a bridge of deep learning with the topics treated in Chapters [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and [20](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml). A closely related dictionary learning approach is also followed in \[160\]. A multilayer convolutional sparse coding scheme is adopted and the similarity with deep convolutional networks is established. The ReLU nonlinearity is seen as a special type of a soft thresholding operation (Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), \[44\]).

In \[177,205\], information theoretic arguments are mobilized and deep networks are viewed as a succession of intermediate representations in a Markov chain; this is closely related to the successive refinement of information in rate distortion theory. Each layer in the network can now be characterized by the amount of information it retains from the input variables, on the target output variables, and on the predicted outputs of the network. In \[7\], a bridge between deep networks and approximation theory via spline functions is established. It is shown that a large class of deep networks can be written as a composition of max-affine spline operators.

Finally, another path is the one that establishes bridges between Gaussian processes and deep networks. This field is not new, and its origins can be traced back to the early 1990s \[142\]. Since then, it is well known that a single-layer fully connected neural network with an i.i.d. prior over its parameters is equivalent to a Gaussian process, in the limit of infinite network width. In more recent years, generalizations to more layers have been established and the topic seems to regain popularity (see, e.g., \[116\], \[3\], \[28\] and the references therein).

### 18.12.4 CNNs: the epilogue

What we have described in the last subsection are the basic steps that are used to design a CNN. There are a number of variants around the architecture given in [Fig. 18.30](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0160). Also, there are different tricks and algorithms that can be used to perform computations, e.g., for the efficient computation of the involved convolutions. Undoubtedly, there is a lot of “engineering” involved to make such big networks to learn the parameters and run efficiently in practical applications. Below we provide a brief description of some classical convolutional networks. The reader who wants to become familiar and get a deeper understanding of CNNs is advised to read the related papers. Although some of the implementation tricks adopted there may not be in use today, still these papers can help the reader to get further insight and understanding of CNNs.

*LeNet-5*: This is a typical example of the first generation of CNNs and it was built to recognize digits of numbers (see, e.g., \[114\]). For historical reasons, let us comment a bit on its architecture. The input of the network consists of grayscale images of size 32 × 32 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si452.png). The network employs two convolution layers. In the first layer, the output volume has size 28 × 28 × 6<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si453.png), which after pooling becomes 14 × 14 × 6<mml:math><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si454.png). The dimensions of the volume in the second layer were 10 × 10 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si455.png) and after pooling 5 × 5 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si450.png). The nonlinearity used at the time was of the sigmoid type. Observe that the height and the width of the volumes decrease and the depth increases, as pointed out before. The number of elements of the last volume is equal to 400. These elements are stacked into a vector and feed the corresponding input nodes of a fully connected network. The latter consists of two hidden layers with 120 nodes in the first and 84 nodes in the second. There are 10 output nodes, one per digit, using a softmax nonlinearity. The total number of the involved parameters is of the order of 60 thousand.

*AlexNet*: This network is also a historical one since it demonstrated that the crucial point for making big networks to work is the availability of large training sets \[108\]. The related paper is the one that really brought CNNs back into the scene and acted as a catalyst for their adoption much beyond the digit recognition task. The AlexNet is a development of LeNet-5, yet it is much bigger and involves approximately 60 million parameters. The inputs to the network are RGB images of size 227 × 227 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>227</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>227</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si456.png). It comprises five hidden layers and the final volume consists of 9216 elements that feed a fully connected network with two hidden layers of 4096 units each. The output consists of 1000 softmax nodes (one per class) to recognize images from the ImageNet data set for object recognition \[172\]. The ReLU has been used as the nonlinearity in the hidden layers.

*VGG-16*: This network \[189\] is much larger than AlexNet. It involves a total of approximately 140 million parameters. The main characteristic of this network is its regularity. It involves 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si366.png) filters to perform same convolutions using padding and stride *s* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si388.png) and 2 × 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si368.png) windows for maxpooling with stride *s* = 2<mml:math><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si389.png). Every time pooling is involved, the height and the width of the volumes are halved and every time the depth is increased by two. Starting with 224 × 224 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>224</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>224</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si457.png) input images and after 13 layers, the final volume has size 7 × 7 × 512<mml:math><mml:mn>7</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>512</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si458.png), a total of 25088 elements, which after its vectorization is fed to a fully connected network with 2 hidden layers, each comprising 4096 nodes. The 1000 output nodes are built around the softmax nonlinearity, and ReLU has been used for the hidden units throughout the network.

*GoogLeNet and the Inception network*: The architecture used in this network deviates from the “archetypal” one given in [Fig. 18.30](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0160). At the heart of this network lies the so-called inception module \[199\]. An inception module consists of filters of different sizes and depths as well as a different pooling path. There are a number of versions of the network. A typical architecture of an inception model that provides its rationale is shown in [Fig. 18.31](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#f0165).  Note that the output volume of the previous layer becomes the input to different paths. One involves a 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution that acts on the depth of the input volume. Another path performs pooling and then feeds a 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution. Two paths feed separately two different convolution stages, one based on a 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si366.png) filter and the other on a 5 × 5<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si387.png). Prior to the convolutions, a bottleneck layer, via 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si421.png) convolution, is employed to reduce the respective computational load ([Example 18.4](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#enun0070)). The output volumes of all these paths are then concatenated to form the final output of this stage. The idea behind the inception module is to leave the network, during the training phase, to “decide” what operations fit best for the different layers and inputs. For example, as we have already commented, features of higher abstraction are captured by layers closer to the output of the network. Hence, the spatial concentration of the respective information is expected to decrease. This suggests that the ratio of 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si366.png) and 5 × 5<mml:math><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B978044329238500024X/si387.png) convolutions should increase as we move to higher layers. The number of layers of the network was 22 and the total number of parameters reported in the paper was of the order of 6 million.

![Figure 18.31 The inception module concept. Each layer comprises different paths of convolutions. The intermediate outputs from all the paths are concatenated together, across the channel dimension, to build up the final output volume of the corresponding layer.](images/B978044329238500024X/gr031.jpg)

[Figure 18.31](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml#cf1665) The inception module concept. Each layer comprises different paths of convolutions. The intermediate outputs from all the paths are concatenated together, across the channel dimension, to build up the final output volume of the corresponding layer.

*Residual networks* (ResNets): The benefits of designing deep networks have already been discussed.
