## 19.1 Introduction

This is the second chapter related to neural networks and deep learning. The chapter deals with some of the more recent advances in machine learning, namely deep generative models, transformers and large language models (LLMs), and self-supervised learning. Generative networks have revolutionized the way we model and generate data. In an era of data-driven science, technology, industry and services, these techniques have escaped the terrain of research and have been diffused and used in a wide range of applications. In another front and after many years of reign of supervised and unsupervised learning, self-supervised techniques have risen to be key players in machine learning offering new vast potential in using and exploiting the abundance of unlabeled data that are available via the internet. Transformers and the large language models comprise a major breakthrough in language understanding, processing and text generation. Within only a couple of years from their appearance, these models have found their way in many areas beyond language processing tasks and they are becoming an indispensable tool for new scientific discoveries, new technological achievements and are transforming the way humans interact, entertain, and work. Although still early to forecast, it seems that all these machine learning advances will have a significant impact in all aspects of our lives, as persons and as social beings.

The chapter begins with refreshing the memory with some very basic notions from graphical models and then it presents deep belief networks. Besides their significant educational value, these networks have played a key role for the revival of the interest on neural networks, following the visionary work of G. Hinton and his co-workers in the early years of this century. In the sequel, generative adversarial networks (GANs) are discussed, followed by autoencoders and variational autoencoders (VAEs). Normalizing flows are briefly considered. A major focus of the chapter lies on the concept of attention and the transformer networks. The GPT and the BERT families of models are presented. The baton is then passed over to self-supervised learning, where its main categories are highlighted, such as masked prediction methods and contrastive techniques. The chapter concludes with an introduction to diffusion models, discussing the key concepts, the main modeling paths, algorithms and applications. Some hints on ethical issues related to the use of these technologies are, also, briefly touched.

## 19.2 Deep generative models

In Chapter [18](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml), our emphasis was on supervised learning via neural network architectures. The other main direction in machine learning is that of unsupervised learning, where one has to “learn” and unveil the underlying dependencies and structure that are hidden in the input data. Clustering, as introduced in Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) (see also \[181\] for an extensive coverage) is a major path of learning via unlabeled data. Another one is to learn explicit probabilistic dependencies with the final goal being that of estimating probability distributions, as was the focus in Chapters [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) and [16](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml).

Another direction, where the use of unlabeled samples is of importance, is that of learning an efficient representation of the input data. As a matter of fact, feature learning is a facet of data representation. The convolutional layers in a CNN, which precede the fully connected network part, are dedicated to this goal, that is, to obtain an efficient and information-rich representation of the input data. However, in the framework of CNNs, this takes place in the context of a specific learning task; that is, the output labels are also considered during training to reach an optimal representation that serves the needs of the task at hand.

In this section, the discussion setting is to learn representations that are independent of a specific target task; the goal is to extract such information using the input data only. The reason for such a focus is twofold. First, learning a model representation of the input data can be used subsequently in different tasks in order to facilitate the training. Sometimes, this is also known as *pretraining*, where parameters learned using unlabeled data can be used as initial estimates of the parameters for another supervised learning. This can be useful when the number of labeled examples is not large enough (see, e.g., \[125\] for a discussion). It is worth pointing out that such a pretraining rationale is of a historical importance, because it led to the revival of neural networks, as will be discussed soon \[80\].

Another path, which is currently of high interest, is to exploit such learned representations in order to *generate* new data; recall the discussion in Section [18.7](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml). Such techniques may *not* necessarily learn the underlying probability distribution *explicitly*, yet they acquire the necessary knowledge needed to be able to draw samples according to a distribution that “explains” the data.

### 19.2.1 Restricted Boltzmann machines

A *restricted Boltzmann machine* (RBM) is a special type of the more general class of Boltzmann machines, which were introduced in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) \[1,167\]. [Fig. 19.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0010) shows the probabilistic graphical model corresponding to an RBM. There are no connections among nodes of the same layer. Moreover, the upper level comprises nodes corresponding to hidden variables and the lower level consists of visible ones. That is, observations are applied to the nodes of the lower layer only. Deep RBMs can be constructed by stacking one on top of the other.

![Figure 19.1 An RBM is an undirected graphical model with no connections among nodes of the same layer. The lower level comprises visible nodes and the upper layer consists of hidden nodes only.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 19.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf0335) An RBM is an undirected graphical model with no connections among nodes of the same layer. The lower level comprises visible nodes and the upper layer consists of hidden nodes only.

Following the general definition of a Boltzmann machine, the joint distribution of the involved random variables is of the form

$P(v\_{1},\\ldots,v\_{J},h\_{1},\\ldots,h\_{I}) = \\frac{1}{Z}\\exp\\left( - E(\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si1.png)(19.1) 

where we have used different symbols for the *J* visible (*v*[*j*], *j* = 1, 2, …, *J*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si2.png)) and the *I* hidden (*h*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si3.png)) random variables. The *energy* is defined in terms of a set of unknown parameters,^([^(127)](#fn127))

$E(\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}) = - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{I}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}\\theta\_{ij}h\_{i}v\_{j} - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{I}b\_{i}h\_{i} - \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{J}c\_{j}v\_{j}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si4.png)(19.2) 

The normalizing constant is obtained as

$Z = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{v}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{h}}\\exp\\left( - E(\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}) \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si5.png)(19.3) 

We will focus on discrete variables; hence the involved distributions are probabilities. More specifically, we will focus on random variables of a binary nature, that is, *v*[*j*], *h*[*i*] ∈ {0, 1}, *j* = 1, …, *J*, *i* = 1, …, *I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si6.png). Observe from Eq. [(19.2)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq2) that, in contrast to a general Boltzmann machine, only products between hidden and visible variables are present in the energy term.

The goal in training an RBM is to learn the set of unknown parameters, *θ*[*i**j*], *b*[*i*], *c*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si7.png), which will be collectively denoted as Θ, ***b***, and ***c***, respectively. A major path to this end is to maximize the log-likelihood, using *N* observations of the visible variables, denoted as **v**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si8.png), where

**v**[*n*] :  = \[*v*[1*n*], …, *v*[*J**n*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si9.png)

is the vector of the corresponding observations at time *n*. We will say that the visible nodes are *clamped* on the respective observations. The corresponding (average) log-likelihood is given by

$L(\\Theta,\\mathbf{b},\\mathbf{c}) = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln P(\\mathbf{v}\_{n};\\Theta,\\mathbf{b},\\mathbf{c}) = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln\\left( \\frac{1}{Z}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{h}}\\exp\\left( - E(\\mathbf{v}\_{n},\\mathbf{h};\\Theta,\\mathbf{b},\\mathbf{c}) \\right) \\right) = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{h}}\\exp\\left( - E(\\mathbf{v}\_{n},\\mathbf{h};\\Theta,\\mathbf{b},\\mathbf{c}) \\right) \\right) - \\ln\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{v}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{h}}\\exp\\left( - E(\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0001" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac id="mmlbr0002"><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi where the index *n* in the energy refers to the respective observations onto which the visible nodes have been clamped, and *Θ*, **b**, **c**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si11.png) have explicitly been brought into the notation.

Taking the derivative of *L*(*Θ*, **b**, **c**)<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si12.png) with respect to *θ*[*i**j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si13.png) (similar is the case of the derivatives with respect to *b*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si14.png) and *c*[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si15.png)) and applying standard properties of derivatives, it is not difficult to show ([Problem 19.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0045)) that

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/fx001.jpg)(19.4) 

where the following has been used:

$P(\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{v}) = \\frac{P(\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h})}{\\sum\_{\\mathbf{h}^{\\prime}}P(\\mathbf{v},\\mathbf{h}^{\\prime})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si16.png)

The gradient in [(19.4)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq6) involves two terms. The first one can be computed once *P*(**h**|**v**)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si17.png) is available. Basically, this term is the mean *firing rate* or *correlation* when the RBM is operating in its clamped phase; often, we refer to it as the *positive* phase, and the term is denoted as  < *h*[*i*]*v*[*j*]\>^+<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si18.png). The second term is the corresponding correlation when the RBM is working in its so-called *free running* or *negative* phase, and it is denoted as  < *h*[*i*]*v*[*j*]\>^−<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si19.png). Thus, a gradient ascent scheme for maximizing the log-likelihood will be of the form

*θ*[*i**j*](new) = *θ*[*i**j*](old) + *μ*(<*h*[*i*]*v*[*j*]\>^+−<*h*[*i*]*v*[*j*]\>^−).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si20.png)

Let us take a minute to justify why we have named the two phases of operation as positive and negative, respectively. These terms appear in the seminal papers on Boltzmann machines by Hinton and Sejnowski \[77,78\]. The first one, corresponding to the clamped condition, can be thought of as a form of a *Hebbian* learning rule. Hebb was a neurobiologist and stated the first ever (to the best of my knowledge) learning rule \[74\]: “If two neurons on either side of a synapse are activated simultaneously, the strength of this synapse is selectively increased.” Note that this is exactly the effect of the positive phase correlation in the parameter's update recursion. On the contrary, the effect of the negative phase correlation term is the opposite. Thus, the latter term can be thought of as a *forgetting* or *unlearning* contribution; it can be considered as a control condition of a purely “internal” nature (note that it does not depend on the observations), compared to the “external” information received from the environment (observations).

Details concerning the optimization of the log-likelihood as well as the finally derived algorithm can be obtained from the site of the book under the Additional Material part that is associated with the current chapter.

### 19.2.2 Pretraining deep feed-forward networks

This subsection presents the rationale of employing RBMs to pretrain a deep forward neural network. This concept was first presented in \[80\]. Although this type of pretraining is no more widely used, it can still offer advantages in cases where labeled data are not enough to train a big neural network.

[Fig. 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0015) presents a block diagram of a neural network with three hidden layers. The vector of the input random variables is denoted as **x** and those associated with the hidden ones as **h**^(*i*), *i* = 1, 2, 3<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si21.png). The vector of the output nodes is denoted as **y**. Pretraining evolves in a sequential fashion, starting from the weights connecting the input nodes to the nodes of the first hidden layer. This can be achieved by maximizing the likelihood of the observed samples of the input observations, ***x***, and treating the variables associated with the first layer as hidden ones. Once the weights corresponding to the first layer have been computed, the respective nodes are allowed to fire an output value and a vector of values, **h**¹<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si22.png), is formed. This is the reason that a generative model for the unsupervised pretraining is adopted (such as the RBM), to be able to generate *in a probabilistic way* outputs at the hidden nodes. These values are in turn used as observations for the pretraining of the next hidden layer, and so on.

![Figure 19.2 Block diagram of a neural network architecture, with three hidden layers and one output layer. The vector of the input random variables at the input layer is denoted as x. The vector of the variables associated with the nodes of the ith hidden layer is denoted as hi, i = 1,2,3. The output variables are denoted as y. At each phase of the pretraining, the weights associated with one hidden layer are computed, one at a time. For the network of the figure, comprising three hidden layers, pretraining consists of three stages of unsupervised learning. Once pretraining of the hidden units has been completed, the weights associated with the output nodes are pretrained via a supervised learning algorithm. During the final fine-tuning, all the parameters are estimated via a supervised learning rule, such as the backpropagation scheme, using as initial values those obtained during pretraining.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr002.jpg)

Figure 19.2 Block diagram of a neural network architecture, with three hidden layers and one output layer. The vector of the input random variables at the input layer is denoted as **x**. The vector of the variables associated with the nodes of the *i*th hidden layer is denoted as **h**^(*i*), *i* = 1,2,3. The output variables are denoted as **y**. At each phase of the pretraining, the weights associated with one hidden layer are computed, one at a time. For the network of the figure, comprising three hidden layers, pretraining consists of three stages of unsupervised learning. Once pretraining of the hidden units has been completed, the weights associated with the output nodes are pretrained via a supervised learning algorithm. During the final fine-tuning, all the parameters are estimated via a supervised learning rule, such as the backpropagation scheme, using as initial values those obtained during pretraining.

Once pretraining has been completed, a supervised learning rule, such as backpropagation, is then employed to obtain the values of weights leading to the output nodes, as well as to fine-tune the weights associated with the hidden layers, using as initial weight values those obtained during the pretraining phase.

As already said before, unsupervised learning is a way to discover and unveil information hidden in the data, by learning the underlying regularities and the statistical structure of the data. In this way, pretraining can be thought of as a data-dependent *regularizer* that pushes the unknown parameters to regions where good solutions exist, by exploiting the extra information acquired by the unsupervised learning (see, for example, \[47\]).

[Fig. 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0015) illustrates a multilayer perceptron with three hidden layers. As is always the case with any supervised learning task, the kick-off point is a set of training examples, (*y*[*n*], **x**[*n*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si23.png). Training a deep multilayer perceptron, employing what we have said before, involves two major phases: (a) pretraining and (b) supervised fine-tuning. Pretraining the weights associated with hidden nodes involves unsupervised learning via the RBM rationale. Assuming *K* hidden layers, **h**^(*k*), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si24.png), we look at them in pairs, that is, (**h**^(*k* − 1), **h**^(*k*)), *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si25.png), with **h**⁰ :  = **x**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si26.png) being the input layer. Each pair will be treated as an RBM, in a hierarchical manner, with the outputs of the previous one becoming the inputs to the next. It can be shown (for example, \[80\]) that adding a new layer each time increases a variational lower bound on the log-probability of the training data.

Pretraining of the weights leading to the output nodes is performed via a supervised learning algorithm. The last hidden layer together with the output layer is not treated as an RBM, but as a one-layer feed-forward network. In other words, the input to this *supervised* learning task comprises the features formed in the last hidden layer.

Finally, fine-tuning involves retraining in a typical backpropagation algorithm rationale, using the values obtained during pretraining for initialization. This is very important for getting a better feeling and understanding of how learning works. The label information is used in the hidden layers *only* at the fine-tuning stage. During pretraining, the feature values in each layer grasp information related to the input distribution and the underlying regularities. The label information does not participate in the process of discovering the features. Most of this part is left to the unsupervised phase, during pretraining. Note that this type of learning can also work even if some of the data are unlabeled. Unlabeled information is useful, because it provides valuable extra information concerning the input data. As a matter of fact, this is at the heart of semisupervised learning (see, e.g., \[181\]).

More details on RBM-based pretraining can be found on the site of the book under the Additional Material part associated with the current chapter (see also \[82\]).

### 19.2.3 Deep belief networks

The emphasis given in the previous chapter was on discussing feed-forward architectures. Our focus was on the information flow in the feed-forward or bottom-up direction. However, this is only part of the whole story. The other part concerns training *generative* models. The goal of such learning tasks is to “teach” the model to generate data. One way to achieve this is via learning probabilistic models that relate a set of variables, which can be observed, with another set of hidden ones. RBMs are just an instance of such models. Moreover, it has to be emphasized that RBMs can represent any discrete distribution if enough hidden units are used \[54,112\].

In our discussion up to now in this section, we viewed a deep network as a mechanism forming layer-by-layer features of features, that is, more and more higher-level representations of the input data. The issue now becomes whether one can start from the last layer, corresponding to the highest level representation, and follow a *top-down* path with the new goal of generating data. Besides the need in some practical applications, there is an additional reason to look at this reverse direction of information flow.

Some studies suggest that such top-down connections exist in our visual system to generate lower-level features of images starting from higher-level representations. Such a mechanism can explain the creation of vivid imagery during dreaming, as well as the disambiguating effect on the interpretation of local image regions by providing contextual prior information from previous frames (for example, \[110,111,136\]).

A popular way to represent statistical generative models is via the use of probabilistic graphical models, which were treated in Chapters [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml) and [16](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml). A typical example of a generative model is that of sigmoidal networks, introduced in Section [15.3.4](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), which belong to the family of parametric Bayesian (belief) networks. A sigmoidal network is illustrated in [Fig. 19.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0020)A, where a directed acyclic graph (Bayesian) is shown. Following the theory developed in Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml), the joint probability of the observed (***x***) and hidden variables, distributed in *K* layers, is given by

$P\\left( \\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{h}^{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{h}^{K} \\right) = P\\left( \\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{h}^{1} \\right)\\left( \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K - 1}P\\left( \\mathbf{h}^{k}|\\mathbf{h}^{k + 1} \\right) \\right)P\\left( \\mathbf{h}^{K} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si27.png)

where the conditionals for each one of the *I*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si28.png) nodes of the *k*th layer are defined as

It is a mixture of directed and undirected edges connecting nodes. The top layer involves undirected connections and it corresponds to an RBM.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr003.jpg)

Figure 19.3 (A) A graphical model corresponding to a sigmoidal belief (Bayesian) network. (B) A graphical model corresponding to a deep belief network. It is a mixture of directed and undirected edges connecting nodes. The top layer involves undirected connections and it corresponds to an RBM.

A variant of the sigmoidal network was proposed in \[80\], which has become known as *deep belief network*. The difference with a sigmoidal one is that the top two layers comprise an RBM. Thus, it is a mixed type of network consisting of both directed and undirected edges. The corresponding graphical model is shown in [Fig. 19.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0020)B. The respective joint probability of all the involved variables is given by

$P\\left( \\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{h}^{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{h}^{K} \\right) = P\\left( \\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{h}^{1} \\right)\\left( \\prod\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K - 2}P\\left( \\mathbf{h}^{k}|\\mathbf{h}^{k + 1} \\right) \\right)P\\left( \\mathbf{h}^{K - 1},\\mathbf{h}^{K} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∏</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si30.png)(19.5) 

It is known that learning Bayesian networks of relatively large size is intractable, because of the presence of converging edges (see Section [15.3.3](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml)). To this end, variational approximation methods can be mobilized to bypass this obstacle (see Section [16.3](#Chp016_805-853_B9780443292385000226.xhtml)).

In \[80\], an alternative path was proposed following a scheme similar to that used before for pretraining neural networks. In other words, all hidden layers, starting from the input one, are treated as RBMs, and a greedy layer-by-layer pretraining bottom-up philosophy is adopted. It should be emphasized that the conditionals, which are recovered by such a scheme, can only be thought of as approximations of the true ones. After all, the original graph is a directed one and not undirected, as the RBM assumption imposes. The only exception lies at the top level, where the RBM assumption is a valid one.

Once the bottom-up pass has been completed, the estimated values of the unknown parameters are used for initializing another fine-tuning training algorithm; such a scheme has been developed in \[79\] for training sigmoidal networks and is known as *wake-sleep* algorithm. The objective behind the wake-sleep scheme is to adjust the weights during the top-down pass, so as to maximize the probability of the network to generate the observed data. The scheme has a variational approximation flavor, and if initialized randomly takes a long time to converge. However, using the values obtained from the pretraining for initialization, the process can significantly be sped up \[83\].

Once training of the weights has been completed, data generation is achieved by the scheme summarized in [Algorithm 19.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0010).

Algorithm 19.1

**Generating samples via a DBN**

*   •  Obtain samples **h**^(*K* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si31.png), for the nodes at level *K* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si32.png). This can be done via running a Gibbs chain, by alternating samples, **h**^(*K*) ∼ *P*(**h**|**h**^(*K* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si33.png) and **h**^(*K* − 1) ∼ *P*(**h**|**h**^(*K*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si34.png). This can be carried out in analogy to the technique used to train RBMs (see the Additional Material for the current chapter on the book's site), as the top two layers comprise an RBM. The convergence of the Gibbs chain can be sped up by initializing the chain with a feature vector formed at the (*K* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si32.png))th layer by one of the input patterns; this can be done by following a bottom-up pass to generate features in the hidden layers, as the one used during pretraining.
*   •  **For** *k* = *K* − 1, …, 1<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si35.png), **Do**; Top-down pass. 
    1.  –  **For** *i* = 1, 2, …, *I*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si36.png), **Do** 
        1.  ⁎  *h*[*i*]^(*k* − 1) ∼ *P*(*h*[*i*]|**h**^(*k*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si37.png); Sample for each one of the nodes. 
    2.  –  **End For**
*   •  **End For**
*   •  **x** = **h**⁰<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si38.png); Generated pattern.

### 19.2.4 Autoencoders

*Autoencoders* have been proposed in \[12,159\] as methods for dimensionality reduction. An autoencoder consists of two parts, the *encoder* and the *decoder*. The output of the encoder is the reduced representation of the input pattern, and it is defined in terms of a vector function,

**f** : **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*) ↦ **h** ∈ ℝ^(*m*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si39.png)(19.6) 

where

*h*[*i*] :  = *f*[*i*](**x**) = *ϕ*[*e*](**θ**[*i*]^(*T*)**x**+*b*[*i*]), *i* = 1, 2, …, *m*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si40.png)(19.7) 

with *ϕ*[*e*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si41.png) being the activation function; the latter is usually taken to be the logistic sigmoid function, *ϕ*[*e*]( ⋅ ) = *σ*( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si42.png). In other words, the encoder is a single hidden layer feed-forward neural network.

The decoder is another function ***g***,

$\\mathbf{g}:\\mathbf{h} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m}\\longmapsto\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si43.png)(19.8) 

where

*x̂*[*j*] = *g*[*j*](**h**) = *ϕ*[*d*](**θ**[*j*]^(′ *T*)**h**+*b*[*j*]^′), *j* = 1, 2, …, *l*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si44.png)(19.9) 

The activation *ϕ*[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si45.png) is, usually, taken to be either the identity (linear reconstruction) or the logistic sigmoid one. The task of training is to estimate the parameters

*Θ* :  = \[**θ**[1],…,**θ**[*m*]\], **b**, *Θ*^′ :  = \[**θ**[1]^′,…,**θ**[*l*]^′\], **b**^′.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si46.png)

It is common to assume that *Θ*^′ = *Θ*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si47.png). The parameters are estimated so the reconstruction error, $\\mathbf{e} = \\mathbf{x} - \\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si48.png), over the available input samples is minimum in some sense. Usually, the squared error cost is employed, but other choices are also possible. Regularized versions, involving a norm of the parameters, are also a possibility (for example, \[155\]). If the activation *ϕ*[*e*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si41.png) is chosen to be the identity (linear representation) and *m* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si49.png) (to avoid triviality), the autoencoder is equivalent to the PCA technique \[12\]. PCA is treated in more detail in Chapter [20](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml).

Another version of autoencoders results if during training one adds noise to the input \[191,192\]. This is a stochastic counterpart, known as the *denoising autoencoder*. For reconstruction, the uncorrupted input is employed. The idea behind this version is that by trying to undo the effect of noise, one captures statistical dependencies between inputs. More specifically, in \[191\], the corruption process randomly sets some of the inputs (as many as half of them) to zero. Hence, the denoising autoencoder is forced to predict the missing values from the nonmissing ones, for randomly selected subsets of missing patterns.

Autoencoders have also been used for pretraining deep networks, in place of the RBMs discussed before (see, e.g., \[81\]). In the latter, autoencoders with many layers, instead of a single one, have been employed.

### 19.2.5 Generative adversarial networks

In Sections [19.2.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0020) and [19.2.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0030), we considered generative probabilistic graphical models for probability distribution estimation as well as for data generation. The major drawback of such models comes from the computational intractability when maximizing the associated likelihood function and related costs in order to compute the unknown parameters that define the graphical model.

An alternative path for designing generative models was first described in \[61\]. The breakthrough concept was to abandon the idea of modeling the probability distribution *directly*; instead, a game theoretic scenario was adopted, where the generator network was left to *compete* against an *adversary*.^([^(128)](#fn128))

![Figure 19.4 One class comprises the real images and the other the fake ones. The latter are produced by the generator, which is excited by noise. The output of the discriminator represents the probability of an input pattern to originate from the real data class. If the classes were perfectly separable, the discriminator's output, y, would be equal to 1 for real images and 0 for the fake ones. The goal of training a GAN is to “confuse” the discriminator so that its output becomes 1/2 both for the real and for the fake ones.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 19.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf0475) One class comprises the real images and the other the fake ones. The latter are produced by the generator, which is excited by noise. The output of the discriminator represents the probability of an input pattern to originate from the real data class. If the classes were perfectly separable, the discriminator's output, *y*, would be equal to 1 for real images and 0 for the fake ones. The goal of training a GAN is to “confuse” the discriminator so that its output becomes 1/2 both for the real and for the fake ones.

The generator is fed to its input with noise samples, according to a probability distribution *p*[**z**](**z**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si50.png), which is typically a uniform or a Gaussian PDF. The generator transforms the input noise vector,^([^(129)](#fn129))

The discriminator is a *binary* classifier that is implemented as a deep neural network. Its input is fed with samples ***x*** and it outputs a corresponding probability value, *y* = *D*(**x**; **θ**[*d*])<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow/><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si55.png). The parameter vector **θ**[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si56.png) comprises all the parameters that define the associated neural network and are learned during training. The output value, *y*, represents the probability that the corresponding input pattern, ***x***, originates from the observations rather than from the generator. In other words, *D*(**x**; **θ**[*d*])<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si57.png) is the probability of ***x*** being real, and 1 − *D*(**x**; **θ**[*d*])<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si58.png) is the probability of ***x*** being fake. If the discriminator were designed to make perfect decisions, then the output should be 1 for the real data and 0 for the fake ones.

During training, the parameter vectors are optimally estimated so that the discriminator *confuses* the real with the fake data points. To this end in \[61\], the following two-player minmax game value (cost) is adopted:

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{g}}\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{d}}\\ J(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{g},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{d}),$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si59.png)(19.10) 

where

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/fx002.jpg)(19.11) 

and *p*[*r*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si60.png) denotes the probability distribution associated with the real data (subscript *r* reminds us of *real*).

In words, if **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) is kept fixed, then the discriminator is trained, via **θ**[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si56.png), so that its output is maximized both for real (*D*(**x**; **θ**[*d*])<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si57.png)) and for fake (1 − *D*(*G*(**z**; **θ**[*g*]); **θ**[*d*])<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si61.png)) examples. Furthermore, keeping **θ**[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si56.png) fixed, *G* is *simultaneously* trained through **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) to minimize 1 − *D*(*G*(**z**; **θ**[*g*]); **θ**[*d*])<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si61.png), in order to confuse the discriminator.

[Algorithm 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0015) summarizes the main concept, adopting a mini-batch (of size *K*) optimization rationale.

Algorithm 19.2

**The GAN algorithm**

*   •  Initialize **θ**[*d*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si63.png) and **θ**[*g*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si64.png).
*   •  Set the mini-batch size equal to *K*.
*   •  Set the number of iterations, *m*, for the discriminator; the simplest case is *m* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si65.png), and it is used in the original paper.
*   •  **While** **θ**[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si56.png) and **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) have not converged, **Do** 
    1.  –  **For** *t* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si66.png), **Do**
        
        1.  ⁎  Sample **z**^((*i*)), *i* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si67.png), from *p*[**z**](**z**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si50.png)

Remarks 19.1

*   •  In \[61\], it is pointed out that rather than training *G* to minimize ln (1 − *D*(*G*(**z**)))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si75.png), it is better to train *G* to maximize ln (*D*(*G*(**z**)))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si76.png). This turned out to deal better with the involved gradients. Further theoretical justification for this modification, together with comparative experimental results, can be found in \[51\].

#### On the optimality of the solution

The first question that is now raised concerns the optimal solution associated with the minmax optimization task in Eq. (19.11). Note that the generator *G implicitly* defines a probability distribution, *p*[*g*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si77.png), of the samples **x** = *G*(**z**; **θ**[*g*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si51.png) that are generated if **z** ∼ *p*[**z**](**z**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si78.png).

For our analysis, we will free ourselves from the parametric modeling of the involved functions via **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) and **θ**[*d*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si56.png), and we will study the optimal solution in terms of functions *D*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si80.png) and *G*(**z**)<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si81.png), considered in a *general* nonparametric formulation. Under such a scenario, Eq. (19.11) is rephrased as

$\\min\\limits\_{G}\\max\\limits\_{D}J(G,D): = \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack \\ln D(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack + \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{\\mathbf{z}}(\\mathbf{z})}\\left\\lbrack \\ln\\left( 1 - D(G(\\mathbf{z})) \\right) \\right\\rbrack.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi By the definition of the expectation we can write

*J*(*G*, *D*) = ∫[**x**]*p*[*r*](**x**)ln (*D*(**x**))*d***x** + ∫[**z**]*p*[**z**](**z**)ln (1−*D*(*G*(**z**)))*d***z** = ∫[**x**](*p*[*r*](**x**)ln(*D*(**x**))+*p*[*g*](**x**)ln(1−*D*(**x**)))*d***x**,<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo where the subscript *g* stands for the distribution associated with the *generator* output. Fixing function *G* (equivalently, fixing the probability distribution function *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png)), the optimal value of the discriminator's output probability function *D* is easily derived by taking the derivative of the integrand with respect to the function *D* and setting it equal to zero ([Problem 19.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0055)). It is easily shown that

$D^{\\ast} = \\frac{p\_{r}}{p\_{r} + p\_{g}}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si85.png)(19.13) 

Thus, plugging the above optimal value in Eq. [(19.12)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq23), the cost with respect to *G* of the minimax game is reformulated as

$C(G): = \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x})}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\ln\\frac{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x})}{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x}) + p\_{g}(\\mathbf{x})} \\right\\rbrack + \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{g}(\\mathbf{x})}\\ \\left\\lbrack \\ln\\frac{p\_{g}(\\mathbf{x})}{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x}) + p\_{g}(\\mathbf{x})} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi
