mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si86.png)(19.14) 

where the above is a function of *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png). Recalling the definition of the KL divergence (Sections [2.5.2](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml) and [12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)), Eq. [(19.14)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq26) is compactly rewritten as

*C*(*G*) = KL(*p*[*r*]||*p*[*r*] + *p*[*g*]) + KL(*p*[*g*]||*p*[*r*] + *p*[*g*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si87.png)

where, as we know, the KL divergence is *not* symmetric with respect to its arguments. Normalizing by 2, and taking into account the definition of the KL divergence, the above is easily rewritten as

$C(G) = - \\ln 4 + \\text{KL}\\left( p\_{r}||\\frac{p\_{r} + p\_{g}}{2} \\right) + \\text{KL}\\left( p\_{g}||\\frac{p\_{r} + p\_{g}}{2} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si88.png)

or

*C*(*G*) =  − ln 4 + 2JS(*p*[*r*]||*p*[*g*]),<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mtext>JS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si89.png)(19.15) 

where JS denotes the *Jensen–Shannon divergence* between *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) and *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png), defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/fx003.jpg)

Thus, as Eq. [(19.15)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq29) suggests, the cost *C*(*G*)<mml:math><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si91.png) associated with the generator depends on the JS divergence between the *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) of the real data and the *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png) that the generator implements. It can easily be checked that the JS divergence, in contrast to KL divergence, is a symmetric one. As conjectured in \[180\], it is exactly the use of this divergence, compared to the KL one, that gave GANs the advantage over more traditional maximum likelihood-based approaches.

It can easily be seen that the JS divergence is nonnegative and the minimum value is achieved if and only if *p*[*r*] = *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si92.png). Hence, the solution of the minmax task defined in [(19.12)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq23) is obtained when *D* is given by Eq. [(19.13)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq25) and when *G* minimizes Eq. [(19.15)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq29), leading to

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/fx004.jpg)

In other words, optimality of the game is achieved when the generator learns the distribution of the true data and the discriminator *D* is “confused” and becomes unable to discriminate between the true and the fake data.

#### Problems in training GANs

In the previous part of the subsection, the optimality of the GANs has been established. Yet, the task is far from solved. The main reason is that the optimality analysis was carried out in the probability function space. However, in practice, we use parametric models to achieve an approximation to the above, and this is where problems arise. As a matter of fact, as [Algorithm 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0015) suggests, in practice, optimization is carried out via parameter optimization and the involved gradients are computed via the backpropagation rationale and updates follow one of the available gradient-based optimization schemes. However, updating the parameters of the generator and the discriminator concurrently, to solve a nonconvex optimization task, does not necessarily mean that the scheme converges to the optimal game solution.

Looking at Eq. [(19.15)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq29) and following the arguments on how we reached it, one would expect that training the discriminator close to its optimality (so that the cost function on **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) is a good approximation of Eq. [(19.15)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq29)) and then applying the gradient steps on **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) is the way to proceed. However, in practice, this is not the case. As the discriminator improves, the updates of the generator get worse. An explanation of this phenomenon is provided in \[6\]. At the heart of this “strange” behavior lies the fact that *parameterized* approximations of *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) and *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png) lie in low-dimensional manifolds and this makes it very difficult to share common supports (regions in the input space where both functions share nonzero values). This is illustrated in [Fig. 19.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0030). As a consequence, it can be shown that the trained discriminator, instead of achieving a cost according to Eq. [(19.15)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq29), achieves a zero error, meaning that it can easily recognize perfectly the fake from the true data. This leads the cost to zero and the gradients with respect to **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) to vanishingly small values that makes the training of GANs, via the JS cost, difficult. While training, one has to decide how much to train the discriminator. In other words, there is a tradeoff between inaccuracy and vanishing gradients for training.

![Figure 19.5 In the three-dimensional space, the two straight lines are low-dimensional (linear) manifolds. It is highly unlikely that they share a common intersection. So if, say, pr is confined to one and pg to the other of the two lines, it is highly improbable for the two distributions to share a nonnegligible support.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 19.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf0565) In the three-dimensional space, the two straight lines are low-dimensional (linear) manifolds. It is highly unlikely that they share a common intersection. So if, say, *p*[*r*] is confined to one and *p*[*g*] to the other of the two lines, it is highly improbable for the two distributions to share a nonnegligible support.

Another problem associated with training GANs is the so-called *mode collapse*. This means that although the generator may “fool” the discriminator, the generator produces “same” outputs. It seems that the generator gets stuck in a “small” region, which leads to outputs of low variability. This may be due to the fact that the generator cannot learn sufficiently well the data distribution, and it focuses on some parts of it, while ignoring other parts.

In order to bypass the aforementioned drawbacks, a number of tricks and techniques have been proposed (see, e.g., \[108,163,203\]). In \[146\], convolutional generative networks are introduced. In \[128\], least-squares arguments are adopted for the design of GANs. In \[98\], the discriminator estimates the probability that a real example is more realistic than a generated one rather than the probability that it is a real one. In \[118\], the concept of combining models is employed based on a competitive training procedure that splits the data distribution into components, which are approximated well by independent generative models.

#### The Wasserstein GAN

In \[7\], the task of matching *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) and *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png) in low-dimensional manifolds is systematically tackled via the so-called *Wasserstein distance* between distributions. It is first shown that when learning distributions in low-dimensional manifolds, the divergence that measures the difference between distributions must have certain properties. Both JS and KL divergences do not have these properties. In contrast, the Wasserstein distance is a proper one in this context.

The Wasserstein distance, or *earth moving distance* (EMD), between two distributions *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) and *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png), is defined as

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/fx005.jpg)(19.16) 

Although the previous definition may look a bit complicated to the unfamiliar reader, it makes a lot of sense; *Π*(*p*[*r*], *p*[*g*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si94.png) is the set of *all* joint distributions between the random vectors, whose marginals are equal to *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) and *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png), respectively. Intuitively, the expectation indicates how much probability mass has to be transferred from **x** to **y** in order to transform *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) to *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png). Their distance corresponds to the “minimum” value among all possible joint distributions.^([^(130)](#fn130))

In practice, Eq. [(19.16)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq32) cannot easily be implemented. An alternative way is via its dual formulation, known as the Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality (e.g., \[190\]), given by

$W(p\_{r},p\_{g}) = \\sup\\limits\_{||f||\_{L} < 1}\\left\\{ \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{g}(\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack f(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack \\right\\},$<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sup</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si95.png)(19.17) 

where ||*f*||[*L*] < 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si96.png) denotes all the 1-Lipschitz functions (see also Section [8.10.2](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)), *f* : 𝒳 ↦ ℝ<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">↦</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si97.png), i.e.,

|*f*(**x**[1]) − *f*(**x**[2])| < ||**x**[1] − **x**[2]||, ∀**x**[1], **x**[2] ∈ 𝒳.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>∀</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si98.png)

Thus, the Wasserstein probability distance between two distributions, in the form of Eq. [(19.17)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq33), is given by the “maximum” in the difference of the mean values, over all possible 1-Lipschitz functions, with respect to the two distributions.

Designing a GAN according to Eq. [(19.17)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq33) makes the setting different from the one that evolved around the cost in Eq. (19.11). The goal is no more to design a binary classifier (discriminator) to distinguish real from fake data, but a Lipschitz function, *f*. The latter is parameterized via a deep neural network, in terms of a set of parameters, **θ**[*f*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si99.png), i.e., *f*(**x**; **θ**[*f*])<mml:math><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si100.png). The respective parameters are estimated by solving the task

$\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{f}}\\left\\{ \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{r}(\\mathbf{x})}\\ \\left\\lbrack f(\\mathbf{x};\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{f}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\_{p\_{\\mathbf{z}}(\\mathbf{z})}\\ \\left\\lbrack f(G(\\mathbf{z};\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{g});\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{f}) \\right\\rbrack \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si101.png)

Fixing the parameters **θ**[*f*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si99.png), the parameters **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) that define the generator are estimated by minimizing the difference in the bracket above. Note that this gradient depends only on the second term, the first being independent of **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png). As the loss function decreases during the training, the Wasserstein distance gets smaller and the output of the generator gets closer to the real data distribution. The Wasserstein GAN scheme is outlined in [Algorithm 19.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0025).

Algorithm 19.3

**The Wasserstein GAN algorithm**

*   •  Initialize **θ**[*f*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si103.png) and **θ**[*g*]^((0))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si64.png).
*   •  Set the mini-batch size equal to *K*.
*   •  Set the number of iterations, *m*, for the function parameters **θ**[*f*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si99.png).
*   •  Set the clipping parameter *c*; this parameter takes care of the Lipschitz condition. Typically, *c* = 0.01<mml:math><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si104.png).
*   •  **While** **θ**[*f*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si99.png) and **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) have not converged, **Do** 
    1.  –  **For** *t* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si66.png), **Do**

Remarks 19.2

*   •  Note that since [Algorithm 19.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0025) does not train a discriminator, the better the estimate of the function *f* is, the higher the quality of the gradient with respect to **θ**[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si102.png) is expected to be. Hence, *m* can be given a fairly large value, without having to worry about balancing the discriminator and generator, as was the case with [Algorithm 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0015).
*   •  In \[7\], it is reported that the Wasserstein GAN leads to improved stability and robustness compared to previously developed schemes.
*   •  However, as everything in life, nothing is perfect. For example, clipping is a rather “crude” way to enforce the Lipschitz condition. Improvements of the basic scheme have been proposed in, e.g., \[196\] and \[68\]. 

#### Which algorithm then

So far, in our discussion on GANs, we focused on two possible algorithms and we also provided references to a number of other alternatives. The Wasserstein GAN helped us to outline some important issues that underlie the task of learning distributions (implicitly or explicitly) where, most often, the learning process takes place in lower-dimensional manifolds. The reader and any practitioner may wonder which algorithm is “best” or more suitable to be used in a practical application.

One of the major problems associated with data generation is to be able to test the performance of the generator by assessing the quality of the generated patterns. The main issue in evaluating the performance stems from the fact that one cannot explicitly compute the distribution *p*[*g*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si77.png). Thus, classical costs such as the likelihood function cannot be employed. Attempts to approximate it in high-dimensional spaces seem to be problematic in the current context (e.g., \[92\]). To this end, related metrics have been suggested.

The so-called *inception score* (IS) builds upon the concept that a good model should generate samples for which, when evaluated by an independent pretrained classifier (usually an inception network, Section [18.12.4](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml)), the class distribution has low entropy. In other words, given a generated image, this should look like one and only one among the available classes in the training set. Thus, the class probability that is predicted by the classifier should be sharply peaked at the correct class. At the same time, the generated samples should exhibit large variation \[163\] and they should be distributed to all classes with equal probability.

The *Fréchet inception distance* (FID) focuses on a metric that quantifies the difference between true and fake data samples, after a specific embedding in a feature space via an inception network, \[76\]. Assuming that the embedded data follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution, the distance between the two distributions is quantified by the Fréchet distance between the corresponding Gaussians, \[46\].

A comparative experimental study on various GANs has been presented in \[121\]. The findings there, using a number of metrics, including the previously stated quality measuring ones, do not seem to favor any one of the proposed GANs against the others. It is reported that most models can achieve similar scores after careful hyperparameter tuning in optimization, higher computational budget, and random restarts. A review of various methods, algorithms, and applications is given in, e.g., \[67\].

Remarks 19.3

*   •  *Conditional GANs*: Conditional GANs were introduced in \[134\]. The main idea is that one may impose certain constraints/conditions on the generating samples. For example, we may want to generate samples from a specific class, e.g., images of the digit “1” or images containing only, say, “cats.” Also, we may want to select, e.g., the color of the hair when we generate faces. One way to achieve this is to *condition* both the generator and the discriminator on the desired extra information, say, ***c***. The latter is a vector that encodes the conditioning information. For example, it may be the vector that encodes the classes, in case the conditioning refers to class-related information. In practice, this can be implemented by appropriately augmenting the inputs (e.g., concatenation with the input vector ***z*** of the standard GAN) of the generator and the discriminator by the vector ***c*** (or a transformed version of it, if the inputs are required to be images). There are cases where the conditioning information is provided to an intermediate layer of the discriminator. The goal of the discriminator is to discriminate whether the input is a generated sample augmented with the target ***c*** or a real sample augmented with the true ***c***.
*   From a theoretical perspective, training conditional models relies on the conditional counterpart objective of the unconditional one in Eq. (19.11), i.e.,

*J*[**c**](**θ**[*g*], **θ**[*d*]) = 𝔼[*p*[*r*](**x**)]\[ln*D*(**x**|**c**;**θ**[*d*])\] + 𝔼[*p*[**z**](**z**)]\[ln(1−*D*(*G*(**z**|**c**;**θ**[*g*]);**θ**[*d*]))\].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si109.png)

*   
*   In \[137\] the notion of the *auxiliary classifier* GANs (AC-GANs) was proposed. The class-conditioning encoding vector, ***c***, augments the input of the generator. The discriminator takes as input the real/fake samples and it provides two types of predictions. It predicts whether an input is real or fake and, also, it provides an estimate of the corresponding class probability. In other words, for an *M*\-class task, the discriminator has *M* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si110.png) outputs: one for the real/fake prediction, and *M* for the respective class probabilities. It is claimed that in this way, adding more structure to the GAN latent space results in higher quality samples.
*   •  In \[33\], the notion of *information maximizing* GANs (InfoGAN) was proposed. In contrast to the conditional GANs and the AC-GANs that rely on a predetermined conditioning information, ***c***, the input to the InfoGAN generator comprises two vectors: one for the random noise, **z**, and one for random attributes, **c**. The discriminator accepts as input the real/fake samples and it provides two types of outputs. Its goal is to a) predict whether a sample is real or fake and, also, b) to estimate the input conditioning attribute samples, ***c***. In this way, InfoGAN attempts to identify and disentangle important attributes in a fully unsupervised manner. For example, it is claimed that InfoGAN successfully disentangles writing styles from digit shapes on the MNIST data set, and pose from lighting of 3D rendered images, see, \[33\].
*   •  In \[100\], the StyleGAN was proposed. The main rationale behind StyleGAN is to learn to separate high-level attributes (e.g., pose and identity of a face) from low-level/stochastic variation ones (e.g., hair, freckles) in a fully unsupervised way. To achieve this, it employs two sets of (latent) random vectors, one for noise (e.g., **z**) and one for style (e.g., **w**). Moreover, this information is not presented to the input but it is injected to intermediate layers (different scales) of the generator. In this way, the generator adjusts the “style” of the image at each convolutional layer by adjusting the various image features at different scales. The input of the generator starts from a learned constant. Note that the style random variables, **w**, are created at the output of a separate fully connected neural network, whose input is excited by another set of random variables. The rationale behind this nonlinear mapping is to allow the network to learn to decorrelate aspects of style so that each dimension of the style variables refer to an independent real-world attribute, e.g., head pose or lighting.
*   It is interesting to note that a number of the previously discussed novelties have been adopted in the context of diffusion models, treated in Section [19.7](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0235).
*   •  Besides generating images, GANs have been used as generative models for other modalities such as audio, video, EEG, molecular graphs, see, e.g., \[67\].

Example 19.1

The purpose of this example is to describe a basic experiment on GANs to generate images of hand-written characters. To this end, the generator as well as the discriminator networks have to be designed.

*   •  The generator network has 100 input nodes that are excited by i.i.d. Gaussian noise samples of zero mean and unit variance. The network comprises three hidden layers, with 256, 512, and 1024 neurons, respectively. The nonlinearity used for the neurons of the hidden layers was the leaky ReLU (Section [18.6.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml)), with *α* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si111.png). There are 784 output units and the output nonlinearity was the tanh function. The number of output units is chosen to be equal to the dimension of the vectorized images in the MNIST image data set,^([^(131)](#fn131))
*   •  The discriminator has 784 input nodes, to match the 1 × 784<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>784</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si112.png) size vector associated with the 28 × 28<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si113.png) MNIST images. The discriminator consists of three hidden layers, of 1024, 512, and 256 neurons, respectively. The leaky ReLU unit, with *α* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si111.png), was used as the activation function for the hidden layer neurons. The output is a single binary sigmoidal node and the cost function was the two-class cross-entropy function (Eq. [(18.44)](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml)). For the training, the dropout method was used with the probability of discarding hidden neurons being equal to 0.3. The Adam optimizer was employed for training ([Problem 19.9](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0085)). The input images were normalized in the range \[ − 1, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si114.png). The number of images used for training was 60000 and the size of the mini-batches equal to 100.

[Fig. 19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0035) shows examples of generated images by the generator after 1, 20, and 400 epochs of training. Observe how the quality of the fake images improves as the training algorithm converges.

![Figure 19.6 Fake images produced at the output of the generator network after training for (A) 1, (B) 20, and (C) 400 epochs, respectively.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf0730) Fake images produced at the output of the generator network after training for (A) 1, (B) 20, and (C) 400 epochs, respectively.

### 19.2.6 Variational autoencoders

At the heart of GANs lies the concept of generating samples, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png), *n* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si115.png), of a random vector, **x**, by exciting the generator network with corresponding samples, **z**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si116.png), of a random noise vector, **z**. Moreover, recall that GANs do not involve any explicit probabilistic arguments. In contrast, *variational autoencoders* (VAEs) are probabilistic generative models. Furthermore, the generator, known as the decoder in this case, is excited by random variables whose posterior PDF has been *learned* from the data. The training builds upon Bayesian learning arguments; see Chapters [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml). Variational autoencoders were proposed in \[103\], \[154\].

The basic assumption behind VAEs is that we are given a set of observations, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si117.png), which are samples of a random vector, **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si118.png). Moreover, the latter is the result of another process that involves a set of *latent* random variables, **z** ∈ ℝ^(*m*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si119.png), where usually *m* ≪ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si120.png). That is, VAEs fall under the more general umbrella of schemes for which the underlying generation mechanism evolves along the following steps:

*   •  A sample, **z**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si116.png), is generated according to some PDF, *p*(**z**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si121.png), where ***θ*** is a set of unknown parameters.
*   •  A sample, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png), is generated from a conditional PDF, *p*(**x**|**z**[*n*]; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si122.png).

As we know from the Bayesian related chapters, a way to estimate a set of parameters, ***θ***, in the presence of latent (unobserved) variables, is via the EM algorithm. A prerequisite for its application is to know the posterior, *p*(**z**|**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si123.png); this is needed for averaging out the (unknown) latent variables. In general, this posterior is not available (or the required by the EM computations may not be computationally tractable) and one has to resort to approximations. In Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), a factorized form was adopted in the framework of the mean field approximation. In contrast, according to the VAEs, the approximation, *q*(**z**|**x**; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si124.png), of the posterior is implemented via the use of a neural network; the vector ***ϕ*** denotes the set of the unknown parameters that have to be learned together with ***θ***.

In the VAE jargon, *q*(**z**|**x**; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si124.png) is known as the probabilistic *encoder*; indeed, given an observation, ***x***, it produces a distribution (e.g., a Gaussian) over the possible values of **z**, which is also known as the *code*. On the other hand, *p*(**x**|**z**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si125.png) is referred to as the probabilistic *decoder*; given a code ***z***, it produces a distribution over the possible corresponding values of **x**. The major difference with the autoencoders considered before in Section [19.2.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0035) is that, in the variational autoencoder context, the encoder is not designed to output a *single value* for each input variable; in contrast, it is designed to provide a corresponding *probability distribution*. This is also true for the decoder.

The concept behind VAEs should be clear by now. Once we learn the parameters associated with the approximate models of the posterior and the conditional distributions, ***ϕ*** and ***θ***, then we can generate new samples: Generate samples, **z**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si116.png), of the latent variables and in the sequel use these samples to generate samples by sampling the learned conditional, *p*(**x**|**z**[*n*]; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si122.png). All that remains for us now is a) to adopt the explicit parametric models for the conditional, *p*(**x**|**z**; **θ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si125.png), and for the approximation to the posterior, *q*(**z**|**x**; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si124.png) and b) to establish the method for estimating the unknown parameters.

*The parametric models*: In \[103\], the following model is proposed:

*   •  For the prior, the standard multivariate Gaussian is adopted, i.e., *p*(**z**) = 𝒩(**z**|0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si126.png). Thus, according to such a choice, the prior does not depend on any parameters.
*   •  For the posterior approximation, *q*(**z**|**x**; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si124.png), the multivariate Gaussian is also selected, with diagonal covariance matrix (*Σ*[*n*] = diag{*σ*[*n**i*]²}[*i* = 1]^(*m*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>diag</mml:mtext><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si127.png)), i.e.,

*q*(**z**|**x**[*n*]; **ϕ**) = 𝒩(**z**|**μ**[*n*], *Σ*[*n*]).<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si128.png)

*   The crucial point here is that the above mean values and variances are provided as outputs of the encoding network; in the simplest case, a network of a single hidden layer is employed (deeper networks and other variants can also be considered). More specifically,

**h**[*n*] = tanh (*W*[1]**x**[*n*]+**b**[1]),<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">tanh</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si129.png)(19.18) 

*   

**μ**[*n*] = *W*[2]**h**[*n*] + **b**[2],<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si130.png)(19.19) 

*   

ln **σ**[*n*]² = *W*[3]**h**[*n*] + **b**[3],<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si131.png)(19.20) 

*    where ln **σ**[*n*]²<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si132.png) in the last equation denotes an element-wise action on the vector comprising the variances. Thus, the parameters ***ϕ*** comprise the set of all the parameters that define the network, i.e., *W*[1], *W*[2], *W*[3], **b**[1], **b**[2], **b**[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si133.png), which are matrices and bias vectors of appropriate dimensions, respectively. Note that, in order to guarantee nonnegative values for the variance, we model its logarithm. Then, its value can be obtained via the exponent operation.
*   •  For the conditional PDF, if it is also Gaussian, a similar model as the one above is used, where the role of ***x*** and ***z*** are swapped and ***θ*** comprises the parameters of the associated decoder network. If on the other hand, the observations are of a discrete nature, a different model should be used. For example, for binary images, a Bernoulli distribution can be employed to implement the decoder network, e.g., \[103\].

[Fig. 19.7](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0040) illustrates the VAEs architecture. For each observation, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png), the encoder's network outputs the corresponding mean values and variances, which define the specific posterior multivariate Gaussian pdf of the respective latent variables, **z**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si116.png). Sampling from the posterior pdf, one can generate samples, according to the conditional, at the output of the decoder network that match the original input.

![Figure 19.7 The encoder network outputs the mean values and variances of the multivariate Gaussian posterior that describes the latent variables, which correspond to the current input. The decoder network is excited by samples of the latent variables, drawn according to their posterior estimate, to generate samples similar to the original input.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 19.7](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf0760) The encoder network outputs the mean values and variances of the multivariate Gaussian posterior that describes the latent variables, which correspond to the current input. The decoder network is excited by samples of the latent variables, drawn according to their posterior estimate, to generate samples similar to the original input.

*The cost function*: Following the arguments in Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), ideally one should maximize the likelihood of the observations with respect to the unknown parameters. However, the computation of the likelihood is not tractable for this case. Instead, we will maximize a related *lower bound* of it, i.e., Eqs. [(13.1)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml) and [(13.2)](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml). Assuming the observations to be i.i.d., and adjusting to the current notational context, this lower bound, ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si134.png), becomes,

$\\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{2},\\ldots,\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\geq \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi};\\mathbf{x}\_{n}),$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si135.png)

where

ℱ(**θ**, **ϕ**; **x**[*n*]) :  = 𝔼[*q*]\[ln*p*(**x**[*n*],**z**;**θ**)−ln*q*(**z**|**x**[*n*];**ϕ**)\].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si136.png)(19.21) 

Note that in the previous equation, we explicitly introduce the notation for the posterior *q*(**z**|**x**[*n*]; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si137.png), in contrast to the definition of the lower bound defined in Eq. [(12.63)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), where the definition of the bound is given in terms of any distribution of the latent functions. After applying the Bayes theorem on the joint distribution term and recalling the definition of the KL divergence (see Eq. [(2.161)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)), Eq. [(19.21)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq46) can be rewritten as,

$\\mathcal{F}(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi};\\mathbf{x}\_{n}) = \\underset{\\text{reconstruction\\ term}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q}\\left\\lbrack \\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}|\\mathbf{z};\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack}} - \\underset{\\text{prior\\ matching\\ term}}{\\underset{︸}{\\text{KL}\\left( q(\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\phi})||p(\\mathbf{z}) \\right)}},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>reconstruction term</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>prior matching term</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si138.png)(19.22) 

where we have assumed that the prior does not depend on any parameters. The lower bound involves two terms. The first term on the right hand side is the expected value over the latent variables. To maximize the bound, this term should be maximized for the respective observations, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png); this encourages the decoder to learn to *reconstruct* the data. The second term is non-positive (the KL divergence is a non-negative quantity, see [Problem 12.7](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)). To maximize the bound, the KL should be minimized; thus, the corresponding posterior will remain close to the prior; the latter has been chosen to be the standard multivariate Gaussian, 𝒩(**z**|0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si139.png). Hence, the prior acts as a regularizer that “pushes” the network's latent variables to match the standard Gaussian distribution as closely as possible.

The existence of the prior is very important. The regularizer “forces” the posterior distribution of the latent variables to be broad enough. We do not want, for example, two different images/samples from the same class to be mapped to two different and far away located regions in the latent space; i.e., we do not want their corresponding PDFs to be very narrow, with small variance, placed at mean values that are very different. Our desire is to map/code every input sample of the same class via latent variables that lie “close” enough within a small region in the latent space. Our desire is to construct a latent space that is smooth enough on a local scale for similar samples. As a matter of fact, our goal should be to construct encodings which are all as close as possible (dense packing) while still being distinct for different classes (cluster formation). This would facilitate smooth interpolation between different classes when generating new samples. Moreover, such a dense encoding packing, which is promoted by the KL term, would be highly helpful to sample the latent variables according to the standard Gaussian (𝒩(0, *I*))<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si140.png) prior and the decoder to be able to decode and generate samples successfully.

Once the parametric forms of the involved distributions have been adopted, all one has to do is to maximize ℱ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">F</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si134.png) with respect to the unknown parameters. Taking into account that the adopted models are feedforward neural networks, the necessary gradients for the optimization task are computed in the backpropagation rationale. To this end, the following “trick” comes into the game, see, e.g., \[103\].

*The reparameterization trick*: The backpropagation algorithm requires the computation of the gradient of the loss function in Eq. [(19.22)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq47). As we will soon see, the KL divergence term pauses no computational issues. In contrast, the first term on the right hand side requires more attention. The computation of the respective gradient, in every step of the backpropagation algorithm, demands an averaging operation with respect to the current estimate of the posterior PDF, *q*. However, it turns out that following standard arguments (e.g., \[20\]) in order to obtain estimates of the respective mean gradient values, via sampling from *q*, lead to estimates with high variances that render the method rather impractical, e.g., \[103\].

The previous difficulty is bypassed by the so-called reparameterization trick. The idea is to view each one of the latent variables as a function in terms of a) the parameters that define the respective distribution (Gaussian in this case) and b) of an independent auxiliary random variable that takes care of the associated randomness. For example, in the case of Gaussians, the defining parameters are the mean values and variances (covariance matrix). The auxiliary random variable can follow a simple PDF (e.g., Gaussian or uniform). It suffices for the function to be *differentiable*. In the current context, the implied transformation is a linear one and the involved random latent variables are expressed as

*z*[*i*] = *μ*[*i*] + *σ*[*i*]*ϵ*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *m*,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si141.png)

where *ϵ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si142.png) are the respective auxiliary random variables with zero mean and unit variance. Stacking together *ϵ*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si143.png), into the random vector **ϵ** ∈ ℝ^(*m*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si144.png), the corresponding to **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png) latent random vector can be written as

**z**[*n*] = **μ**[*n*] + **σ**[*n*] ⊙ **ϵ**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si145.png)

where **σ**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si146.png) is the vector formed by the respective *m* variances, and ⊙ denotes the element-wise multiplication. To draw samples of the latent variables, i.e., **z**[*n*]^((*k*)), *k* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si147.png), it suffices to draw corresponding samples, **ϵ**^((*k*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si148.png), of the auxiliary variable. Thus, the first term in the loss function in Eq. [(19.22)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq47) can be approximated by the respective sample mean, after drawing *K* successive samples, i.e.,

$A\_{n}: = \\mathbb{E}\_{q}\\left\\lbrack \\ln p(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}|\\mathbf{z};\\mathbf{\\theta}) \\right\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{K}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\ln p\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{n}|\\mathbf{z}\_{n}^{(k)};\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si149.png)(19.23) 

where

**z**[*n*]^((*k*)) = **μ**[*n*] + **σ**[*n*] ⊙ **ϵ**^((*k*)).<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si150.png)
