Recall that the conditional, *p*, is Gaussian and the respective logarithm is trivially computed. The term *A*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si151.png) is a function of both ***θ*** and ***ϕ*** (via **μ**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si152.png) and **σ**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si146.png)). Using the reparameterization trick, it turns out that the variance of the associated estimator is substantially reduced. Thus, *K* need not take large values. In practice, drawing just one sample, i.e., *K* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si153.png), seems to be sufficient for most of the cases.

The second term on right hand side of Eq. [(19.22)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq47) is analytically computed for Gaussian pdfs. Taking into account that the prior, *p*(**z**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si154.png), is the standard Gaussian of zero mean and unit variance, it can be shown, after preforming the involved algebra,^([^(132)](#fn132))

$B\_{n}: = - \\text{KL}\\left( q(\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{x}\_{n};\\mathbf{\\phi})||p(\\mathbf{z}) \\right) = \\frac{1}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}\\left( 1 + \\ln(\\sigma\_{ni}^{2}) - \\mu\_{ni}^{2} - \\sigma\_{ni}^{2} \\right).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mtext>KL</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si155.png)(19.24) 

The term *B*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si156.png) is a function of ***ϕ***, through the involved mean values and variances. The cost function is formed by summing over all the input samples, i.e.,

$\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbf{\\phi},\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}(A\_{n} + B\_{n}),$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si157.png)

which is minimized w.r. to ***ϕ*** and ***θ*** via the backpropagation algorithm. Usually, mini-batch algorithmic variants are employed.

Once training has been completed, sampling for generating samples can be carried out in various ways. One can sample from the standard Gaussian prior, *p*(**z**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si154.png), and then pass the generated latent variable vector through the encoder to generate a sample by sampling the conditional. Sometimes, instead of sampling the conditional one can set the generated sample equal to the corresponding mean of the conditional distribution, as this is the predicted output of the neural network that implements the decoder (Eq. [(19.19)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq43)). However, sampling from the prior, *p*(**z**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si154.png), usually results in rather low quality samples. Another alternative is to sample the latent variables from the distribution that results by averaging out the learned posteriors, *q*(**z**|**x**[*n*]; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si158.png) over all input samples, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png). This is no more Gaussian, it is a mixture of Gaussians and can be more representative of the true distribution in the latent space. If, on the other hand, one wants to generate samples from a single class, e.g., the digit “3” from the MNIST data set, sampling in the latent space can be performed by drawing samples from the corresponding learned posterior, *q*(**z**|**x**[*n*]; **ϕ**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si158.png).

Although VAEs are easier to train compared to GANs, experimental evidence indicates that when VAEs are used for generating images, the obtained images tend to be more blurred compared to the ones that are produced via GANs. In \[185\], the Wasserstein distance is used to replace the KL divergence in the cost function for training VAEs, and it is reported that this has a beneficial effect on the obtained performance. Another line of research that has been pursued is along the convergence of GANs and VAEs, in an effort to combine the benefits of both; see, e.g., \[126\], \[129\]. Another path that has been followed is to construct VAEs with a hierarchy of latent variables. In this vein, latent variables are interpreted as generated from other higher-level ones, see, e.g., \[104\]. Conditional VAEs have been proposed in \[170\].

Remarks 19.4

*   •  We have already dealt with a number of different generative networks. In Section [19.7](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0235), we are going to discuss the family of diffusion models. The *normalizing flows* are, also, members of this family of methods. They are probabilistic models that try to *fit* a probability distribution to the input data. Thus, similarly to VAEs, normalizing flows evolve around the likelihood objective concept to obtain estimates of the associated model-defining parameters.
*   At the heart of the normalizing flows modeling lies a base distribution, e.g., *p*[**z**](**z**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si50.png) which can be easily sampled, e.g., the standard Gaussian. Furthermore, it is assumed that the input data samples, ***x***, are generated via a parameterized *invertible* (vector-valued) function/transformation that acts upon samples, ***z***, drawn from *p*(**z**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si154.png), i.e.,

**x** = **f**(**z**; **θ**) and **z** = **f**^( − 1)(**x**; **θ**).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si159.png)

*   As we know from Chapter [2.2.5](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml), Eq. [(2.45)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml), the respective PDFs are related as

$p\_{\\mathbf{x}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{p\_{\\mathbf{z}}(\\mathbf{z})}{|\\text{det}(J(\\mathbf{x};\\mathbf{z}))|}|\_{\\mathbf{z} = \\mathbf{f}^{- 1}(\\mathbf{x})},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mtext>det</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si160.png)(19.25) 

*   where *J*(⋅; ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si161.png) is the respective Jacobian matrix. For example, for scalar random variables the previous equation becomes

$p\_{x}(x) = \\frac{p\_{z}(z)}{\\left| \\frac{dx}{dz} \\right|}|\_{z = f^{- 1}(x)}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si162.png)

*   The challenge now is to obtain such an invertible transformation. To this end, a multilayer network may be mobilized and the associated defining parameters, ***θ***, are learned during training. The cost function is the likelihood one computed via Eq. [(19.25)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq55) on a set of observed examples, **x**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si163.png).
*   Invertibility is imposed by judiciously selecting the layers (flows) of the network. Each one of the layers, *k* = 1, 2, …, *K*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si164.png), implements a corresponding *invertible* transformation **f**[*k*](⋅;**θ**[*k*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si165.png). The overall functions, ***f*** and **f**^( − 1)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si166.png), result as the composition of the individual ones, i.e.,

**f** = **f**[*K*](**f**[*K* − 1](…**f**[2](**f**[1]).…)), and **f**^( − 1) = **f**[1]^( − 1)(**f**[2]^( − 1)(…**f**[*K* − 1]^( − 1)(**f**[*K*]^( − 1))…)),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si167.png)

*   and **θ** :  = \[**θ**[1]^(*T*), …, **θ**[*K*]^(*T*)\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si168.png). In other words, once learning of the parameters is completed, the approximation of the input distribution, *p*[**x**](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si169.png), is achieved in a *step-wise* layer after layer fashion starting from, say, the standard Gaussian pdf. The critical point in designing normalizing flows is to model and select these invertible functions. To this end, various methods and techniques have been proposed. For more details see, e.g., \[139\] and the references therein.

## 19.3 Transformers

So far, our discussion has evolved around three modeling concepts as the basic tools to build deep networks: the fully connected feed-forward neural networks, the convolutional networks, and the recurrent neural networks. Now, we turn our attention to the most recent trend known as *transformers*. The main rationale behind the so-called transformer networks is the attention mechanism, which has already been introduced and used before in Section [18.13.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml). At the time the current edition is being compiled, transformers constitute the state-of-the art in deep learning. To present the underlying basic idea and the related architectures for implementing such networks, we will follow a historical path, starting from the natural language processing (NLP) applications domain.

### 19.3.1 Natural language processing: a primer

The goal of this subsection is very humble and its purpose is to provide some very basic definitions and concepts related to the *natural language processing* (NLP) discipline that are needed for introducing transformers. After all, a more extended treatment of the NLP field would require a dedicated book, see, e.g., \[58\].

Natural language processing is broadly defined as the scientific area whose goal is the automatic manipulation (process, analyze, and synthesize) of natural languages, such as speech and text, via the use of computers. In Section [11.15](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml), a case study on the closely related topic of authorship identification was discussed. There, a number of terms such as bag-of-words and n-grams were defined and used in the context of SVM classification.

For our current needs, the starting point refers to the representation of the words that comprise a vocabulary in a computer. We will assume that each word is represented by a single vector. For example, in the so-called *one-hot* representation/encoding, each word corresponds to a specific one-hot vector. The dimension, *l*, of these vectors is equal to the number of the words in the vocabulary, which is used in the respective NLP task. Currently, a typical vocabulary size that is employed for training the so-called large language models (LLMs) (see Section [19.5.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0185)) can be of the order of 30000 words.

By convention, each one of the, say, 30000 words (including punctuation and special symbols) is assigned a specific number/index between 1 and 30000 and is represented by a corresponding one-hot vector. The latter comprizes *l* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si170.png) elements which are equal to 0, and the only nonzero element is equal to 1. The 1 is placed at the vector dimension that is equal to the index of the corresponding word in the vocabulary. For example, if the vocabulary index of the, say, *n*th word, *n* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si171.png), in the vocabulary is denoted by *l*[*n*] ∈ {1, 2, …, *l*}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si172.png), the corresponding one-hot representation is of the following form,

$\\mathbf{x}\_{n} = \\overset{l}{\\overset{︷}{\\left\\lbrack 0,\\ldots,0,\\underset{l\_{n}}{\\underset{︸}{1}},0,\\ldots,0 \\right\\rbrack^{T}}} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{l},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,l,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover><mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︷</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si173.png)

with the 1 being at the *l*[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si174.png) dimension of the vector. Note that the number of existing words in a language vocabulary can be much larger than the, say, 30000 that are used for practical purposes. For example, in the Greek language, being an ancient one, it is estimated that there are, approximately, 100000 words and 300000 meanings.

The stage of our discussion will be the *neural machine translation* (NMT) task, which is a subtopic of the natural language processing discipline. Let us consider, as an example, the French phrase “Je suis étudiant,” whose English translation is “I am a student.” The phrase in French consists of three words, each one represented by a one-hot vector, i.e., **x**[1], **x**[2], **x**[3]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si175.png), respectively. The breaking of a phrase into individual words is often referred to as *tokenization* and the individual words/vectors as *tokens*.^([^(133)](#fn133))

⟨SOS⟩, **x**[1], **x**[2], **x**[3], ⟨EOS⟩.<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si179.png)

In a similar way, the output sequence, which is the translated phrase into English, is represented as

⟨SOS⟩, **y**[1], **y**[2], **y**[3], **y**[4], ⟨EOS⟩,<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si180.png)

where the one-hot vector representation has, also, been employed for the output sequence. Note that the dimensionality of the vectors/tokens in the input and output sequences may not be the same, since the two vocabularies (e.g., French and English) are, in general, of different sizes.

In practice, most often, the so-called *embeddings* are employed, instead of the one-hot vectors. That is, each one-hot vector is projected into a lower dimensional space via its multiplication with an *embedding matrix*, i.e., **x**[*n*]^′ = *E***x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si181.png), where *E* is of appropriate dimensions and its elements are learned during training. Similar embeddings are used for the output sequence. Besides the reduction in the respective dimensions, which leads to a substantial reduction of the involved network parameters, such an embedding can also exploit further semantic relations that exist among different words, see, e.g., \[19\].

### 19.3.2 RNNs, transformers and the notion of context

In any NLP task, the input data comprise a *sequence* of tokens/vectors As it is always the case with sequential data (see Section [18.13](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml)), the specific order in which the input tokens appear in the sequence is of major importance. Looking at it from a slightly different view, given a phrase, the *position* of each word (of each token after the tokenization of the phrase) is important for deciphering the meaning of the phrase. Furthermore, the specific meaning of each word in a phrase is, most often, in *context*; that is, the meaning depends on which words are present in the phrase and, also, in which *relative position* they appear. Let us give two examples to make this more clear, because what we call “context” will play a major role in our discussion in the following sections. “The *animal* did not eat the food because *it* was not hungry.” In the above phrase, the word “it” refers to the word “animal.” “The animal did not eat the *food* because *it* was rotten.” In the above phrase, the word “it” refers to the word “food.” Thus, depending on the context, the word “it” obtains a different meaning, since it refers to different entities.^([^(134)](#fn134))

Another example is the following: “I arrived at the *bank* after crossing the *river*.” “I arrived at the *bank* after crossing the *road*.” Thus, the word “bank” has a different meaning that depends on the context.^([^(135)](#fn135))

Until around 2017, the trend in NLP tasks was to use RNNs due to their power to deal with sequential data; see Section [18.13](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml).^([^(136)](#fn136))

![Figure 19.8 A bidirectional RNN is used as an encoder. For each stage, t, t = 1,2,…,N, of the encoder, two state vectors are computed. The forward vector, ({\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}Equation), that is propagated from left to right, and the backward one, ({\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}Equation), which is propagated from right to left. At the decoder, each stage, n, is fed with a corresponding context vector, cn. The latter is a linear combination, over all time instants/stages of the encoder, of the combined state vectors (concatenation of {\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}Equation and {\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}Equation). The coefficients, αnt, t = 1,…,N, are learned during training. The figure focuses on the nth stage of the decoder, to unclutter the illustration, and assumes N′ stages in total.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr008.jpg)

Figure 19.8 A bidirectional RNN is used as an encoder. For each stage, *t*, *t* = 1,2,…,*N*, of the encoder, two state vectors are computed. The forward vector, (${\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si182.png)), that is propagated from left to right, and the backward one, (${\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">←</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si183.png)), which is propagated from right to left. At the decoder, each stage, *n*, is fed with a corresponding context vector, ***c***[*n*]. The latter is a linear combination, over all time instants/stages of the encoder, of the combined state vectors (concatenation of ${\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si182.png) and ${\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">←</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si183.png)). The coefficients, *α*[*nt*], *t* = 1,…,*N*, are learned during training. The figure focuses on the *n*th stage of the decoder, to unclutter the illustration, and assumes *N*′ stages in total.

The stage/time dependent context vector, **c**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si186.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*^′<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si188.png), is defined as

$\\mathbf{c}\_{n} = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{N}\\alpha\_{nt}\\mathbf{h}\_{t},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si189.png)(19.26) 

and the weighting coefficients are given by

$\\alpha\_{nt} = \\frac{\\exp(e\_{nt})}{\\sum\_{k = 1}^{N}\\exp(e\_{nk})},\\ \\text{with}\\ e\_{nt} = \\phi(\\mathbf{h}\_{t}^{T}\\mathbf{h}\_{n - 1}^{\\prime}),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>with</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si190.png)(19.27) 

where *ϕ* is a nonlinearity that is implemented via a neural network, whose parameters are “learned” during training. The output state vector at the *t*th stage of the encoder, **h**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si191.png), is formed as the concatenation of the respective forward (${\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si182.png)) and backward (${\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\mathbf{h}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">←</mml:mo></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si183.png)) state vectors. The variable *e*[*n**t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si192.png) is known as the *alignment* model and accounts on how well the state vectors of the encoder, at time *t*, and the decoder, at time *n* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si193.png), match, i.e., how similar they are. Note that similarity is measured through the inner product of the respective vectors.

The context vectors are passed over to a decoder RNN that outputs the sequence of predictions, i.e., ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si194.png), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*^′<mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si188.png). Note that, in general, the size of the output sequence at the decoder, *N*^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si195.png), is different from that of the input sequence at the encoder, *N*. The encoder-decoder network is trained with the goal the decoder to act as a *predictor*. In other words, the decoder is trained to predict at stage *n* (${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si194.png)), the corresponding target word (**y**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si196.png)), given the input encodings, i.e., **c**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si186.png), as well as the previous target words, i.e., **y**[1], **y**[2], …, **y**[*n* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si197.png). A detailed description of the RNN network in the context of the translation task can be downloaded from the book's website under the Additional Material part that is associated with the current chapter.

Using an RNN encoder, the context-related information is unveiled by two mechanisms. One is through the hidden states. However, recall that the states are processed sequentially. Thus, disambiguating the word, e.g., “bank,” has to be delayed until the last word “river” (or “road”) has been processed. The second mechanism is by applying attention with the aim to extract more information by assigning weights to the sequentially formed states. These weights are trained to quantify *similarity* between the state vectors of the decoder and those of the encoder (see the Additional Material from the book's website for more details). Furthermore, this information has to be *aligned* with the sequentially formed states in the decoder. As long as the phrases are short, RNNs can work well.

However, problems arise when long phrases are considered. For example, it is very common in NLP tasks for a set of multiple related phrases to be involved. These phrases are *contextually* related and they feed the input of the encoder sequentially, one after the other. As it has already been discussed in Section [18.13.1](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml), for such long sequences, RNNs are seriously challenged by the vanishing gradient phenomenon.

In addition to the above drawback, looking more closely at the concept of the state, around which a typical RNN evolves, it may be too much to “ask” from a network to encode the whole history in a single vector state! As a matter of fact, the use of attention tries to exploit the memory of the system in a complimentary fashion, via a weighted combination of the state vectors. Moreover, via such a weighting one can model *dependencies* without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences.

Besides the previous drawbacks, there are computational issues involved. The recurrent/sequential nature of a typical RNN, as discussed in Section [18.13](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml), poses serious obstacles in parallelizing the involved computations.

In a breakthrough paper, \[189\], the authors came up with the idea of abolishing recurrence and retain only the attention mechanism in order to compute input and output representations. As they state in the title of the paper “Attention is all you need.”

### 19.3.3 The transformer network

A (full) transformer network comprises two parts, namely the encoder and the decoder. A corresponding block diagram is shown in [Fig. 19.9](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0050). Both the encoder as well as the decoder consist of a stack of structurally identical blocks. In general, the number of the involved blocks in the encoder, say *L*, may not be the same as the number of blocks in the decoder, say *L*^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si198.png). As it is always the case, the role of the encoder is to output an information-rich representation/coding of its input sequence. This information is then passed on to the decoder blocks, as it is shown in the figure. Before we proceed to the more detailed description of the encoder and decoder blocks, let us make a few comments related to the input and output sequences in the encoder and the decoder, respectively.

![Figure 19.9 A (full) transformer consists of two parts: the encoder and the decoder. The input to the encoder consists of the tokens/embeddings of the input phrase. The information-rich outputs of the encoder are passed on to the decoder. During training, the input to the decoder is the target output associated with the input to the encoder. For example, in a translation task, the decoder is fed with the sequence of tokens associated with the translation of the input phrase. The decoder outputs vectors of probabilities. Both the encoder and the decoder comprise a stack of building blocks.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr009.jpg)

Figure 19.9 A (full) transformer consists of two parts: the encoder and the decoder. The input to the encoder consists of the tokens/embeddings of the input phrase. The information-rich outputs of the encoder are passed on to the decoder. During training, the input to the decoder is the target output associated with the input to the encoder. For example, in a translation task, the decoder is fed with the sequence of tokens associated with the translation of the input phrase. The decoder outputs vectors of probabilities. Both the encoder and the decoder comprise a stack of building blocks.

In Section [19.3.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0075), we discussed that the first step in representing words by vectors is to assign an id number to each word of the vocabulary and then employ *l*\-dimensional one-hot vector encodings, where *l* is the size of the vocabulary of the language corpus. In the sequel, each one of these vectors is projected to a lower dimensional space of appropriate dimensions, say *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png), via the use of the so-called embedding matrix. We will refer to the resulting vectors as embedding vectors, tokens, or simply embeddings. We will soon discuss how embeddings are implemented in the context of transformers.

Note that in [Fig. 19.9](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0050), the outputs of the top block of the decoder, block #*L*^′<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">#</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si200.png), are first linearly transformed and then passed through a softmax nonlinearity. The purpose of the linear transform is to project the output vectors of the top block of the decoder, of dimension *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png), back to the vocabulary dimension *l*, and the goal of the softmax nonlinearity is to normalize the values of the elements of the resulting *l*\-dimensional vectors so that they can be interpreted as probabilities. In other words, the elements of the output vectors in the decoder correspond to probabilities. What is the nature of these probabilities and how they are used in order to reach decisions will be explained soon.

### 19.3.4 Encoder: the input sequence

In the RNN-based encoder, the input was provided sequentially, token after token. In contrast, in the encoder of a transformer all tokens that form the input sequence are presented simultaneously. Let us focus on a simple example of translating the phrase “Je suis étudiant” from French to English, i.e., “I am a student.” Then, the input to the encoder will be ⟨SOS⟩, **x**[1], **x**[2], **x**[3], ⟨EOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si201.png), where the ⟨SOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si177.png) and ⟨EOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si176.png) are the special tokens that indicate the start and the end of a sequence, respectively (see, also, Section [19.3.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0075)). In our current discussion, we will assume that **x**[1]( → Je)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>Je</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si202.png), **x**[2]( → suis)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>suis</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si203.png), **x**[3]( → étudiant)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>étudiant</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si204.png) are the vectors that result after embedding the original one-hot vectors to a lower dimensional space of dimension *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png), i.e., **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*d*[*m*]), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si205.png), where *N* is the length of the input sequence, and in this case *N* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si206.png). By convention, we will denote as **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png) the ⟨SOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si177.png) embedding and as **x**[*N* + 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si208.png) the ⟨EOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si176.png), unless stated otherwise. The symbol *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png) has been reserved for the dimensionality of the embedding space and the subscript “*m*” is used to remind us of the word “model.” This is because all the vectors/tokens/embeddings that propagate through the different blocks of the encoder and decoder are of the same dimension, i.e., *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png), which is a user-defined model parameter.

However, the choice of the embeddings needs special attention. Note that since the input sequence appears to the input of the transformer as a whole, and not sequentially, one needs to assist the network and provide extra information concerning the position of each word/token relative to the others. In other words, to provide information that indicates which token is first, which is second, and so on. We refer to this process as *positional embedding*.

The embedding of the original vocabulary words into input tokens involves two steps:

*   •  *Vocabulary word embeddings*: For our current notational needs, let us denote as **x**[*n*]^(*o**h*) ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si209.png) the one-hot vectors that result after tokenizing the input sequence of words.^([^(137)](#fn137)) 
    
    **x**[*n*]^′ ∈ ℝ^(*d*[*m*]) = *E***x**[*n*]^(*o**h*), *n* = 0, 1, …, *N* + 1,<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>o</mml:mi><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si210.png)
    
    *   where *E* is the respective embedding matrix of appropriate dimensions. The elements of this matrix are *learned* during training. The dimensionality of the embedding space, *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png), is preselected. For example, in \[189\], *d*[*m*] = 512<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>512</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si211.png).
    *   •  *Positional embeddings*: Various techniques have been proposed over the years. In the original paper, \[189\], a sinusoidal positional encoding was used.
    *   For the token at the *k*th position in the input phrase, and for each vector dimension, *i*, of the respective vector/token, the following equations are employed:
    
    $\\text{PE}\_{(k,2i)} = \\sin\\left( \\frac{k}{b^{\\frac{2i}{d\_{m}}}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si212.png)(19.28) 
    
    *   
    
    $\\text{PE}\_{(k,2i + 1)} = \\cos\\left( \\frac{k}{b^{\\frac{2i}{d\_{m}}}} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si213.png)(19.29) 
    
    *    where $i = 0,1\\ldots,\\frac{d\_{m}}{2} - 1$<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si214.png), and, for simplicity, we assume that *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png) is an even number. In \[189\], *b* = 10000<mml:math><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10000</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si215.png). Thus for each position, *k*, even dimensions of the vector are coded according to the sine function and odd dimensions via the cosine one, for all positions, starting counting from *k* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si216.png). Hence, the positional embedding depends on two indices and it equivalently defines a matrix.

Example 19.2

Assume that the input sequence is of length *N* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si206.png), e.g., Je suis étudiant, and for simplicity we ignore the start and end of sequence tokens, i.e., ⟨SOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si177.png) and ⟨EOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si176.png). Also, assume that *d*[*m*] = 4<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si217.png) and *b* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>b</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si218.png). To obtain the corresponding *N* × *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si219.png) positional embedding matrix, the following computations are in order:

| Je || suis || étudiant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *k* = 0 || *k* = 1 || *k* = 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |

(*k*, *i*) = (0, 0) → PE[(0, 0)] = sin (0) = 0, PE[(0, 1)] = cos (0) = 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si220.png)

(*k*, *i*) = (0, 1) → PE[(0, 2)] = sin (0) = 0, PE[(0, 3)] = cos (0) = 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si221.png)

(*k*, *i*) = (1, 0) → PE[(1, 0)] = sin (1) = 0.84, PE[(1, 1)] = cos (1) = 0.54<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.84</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.54</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si222.png)

(*k*, *i*) = (1, 1) → PE[(1, 2)] = sin (0.1) = 0.1, PE[(1, 3)] = cos (0.1) ≈ 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si223.png)

(*k*, *i*) = (2, 0) → PE[(2, 0)] = sin (2) = 0.91, PE[(2, 1)] = cos (2) =  − 0.42<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.91</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.42</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si224.png)

(*k*, *i*) = (2, 1) → PE[(2, 2)] = sin (0.2) = 0.2, PE[(2, 3)] = cos (0.2) = 0.98<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.98</mml:mn></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si225.png)

The embedding matrix becomes

$\\text{PE} = \\begin{bmatrix} {0\\ } & {1\\ } & {0\\ } & 1 \\\\ {0.84\\ } & {0.54\\ } & {0.1\\ } & 1 \\\\ {0.91\\ } & {- 0.42\\ } & {0.2\\ } & 0.98 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>PE</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable columnspacing="0em"><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.84</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.54</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.91</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>−</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.42</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mn>0.98</mml:mn></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si226.png)

One may wonder why not to use, for example, the position index, *k*, as positional embedding. In practice, however, this number can become quite large and it can lead to large biases for the tokens at the end of the sequence. On the other hand, straightforward normalization, in the range \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si227.png), can lead to problems when variable length sequences are involved, especially when they are normalized within the same interval of values. No doubt, alternatives to Eqs. [(19.28)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq64) and [(19.29)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq65) have been proposed over the years, including learnable ones, which are learned during training, see, e.g., \[57\], \[114\]. In \[176\], the *rotary position embedding* (RoPE) is proposed that encodes the position information via a rotation matrix that incorporates the relative position dependency among the tokens. It turns out that RoPE shares some welcome properties such as flexibility with respect to the sequence length, and decaying inter-token dependency with increasing relative distances.

For each token, the final embedding vector, which is provided as input to the first block of the encoder of the transformer, is computed as the summation,

**x**[*n*] = **x**[*n*]^′ + **p**[*n*], *n* = 0, 1, …, *N* + 1,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si228.png)(19.30) 

where **x**[*n*]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si229.png) is the corresponding vocabulary word embedding, and **p**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si230.png) is the positional embedding, which is the row vector of the embedding matrix that corresponds to the *n*th word.
