| *n* = 1: ***y***[0],***y***[1] || ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{0},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1}\\rightarrow\\text{am}\\rightarrow\\mathbf{y}\_{2}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>am</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si366.png) |
| *n* = 2: ***y***[0],***y***[1],***y***[2] || ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{0},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{2}\\rightarrow\\text{a}\\rightarrow\\mathbf{y}\_{3}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>a</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si367.png) |
| *n* = 3: ***y***[0],***y***[1],***y***[2],***y***[3] || ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{0},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{2},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{3}\\rightarrow\\text{student}\\rightarrow\\mathbf{y}\_{4}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>student</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si368.png) |
| *n* = 4: ***y***[0],***y***[1],***y***[2],***y***[3],***y***[4] || ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{0},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{2},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{3},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{4}\\rightarrow\\langle\\text{EOS}\\rangle\\rightarrow\\text{STOP}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mtext>STOP</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si369.png) |

The previous algorithm is suboptimal. This is because, at each step, we optimize w.r. to a single quantity (dimension of the maximum value of a single vector), while keeping the previous decisions fixed. More elaborate schemes have been proposed and used in practice. For example, in the *beam search* algorithm, e.g., \[177\], more than one (conditional) probability values, e.g., the largest *K*, with *K* = 5<mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si372.png) being a typical value, are selected at each stage and propagated through time. Although such an algorithm is still suboptimal, in this way, the final decision is based on information that relies on successive symbol combinations and not on each stage individually.

Remarks 19.6

*   •  The original transformer network presented in \[189\] was trained on the WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French data sets and exhibited significant performance improvements compared to previous state-of-the art results at the time of publication. In that paper, two models were used: the base one, which comprised 65 million parameters, and the big one with 213 million parameters. More details on the adopted user-defined parameters can be found in the paper.
*   •  *Mamba and xLSTM*: Very recently, the interest in the state space models has been revived via a fresh look in their structure and training that overcomes the complexity issues that are associated with the transformers. At the same time, based on the performed experiments, it is claimed that they can result in competitive performance to that of the transformers, see. e.g., \[42\], \[17\] and the references therein. So, soon, another edition of the book may be needed!

## 19.4 GPT: generative pretrained transformers

The publication of the transformer network in \[189\] ignited a new wave of research, both in theory as well as in the applications front, and a number of variants that spring from the underlying basic idea have been proposed. Among the very first attempts, in the framework of NLP tasks, were the GPT, \[147\], and the BERT, \[43\], models. Besides translation, which was treated before, these networks have been used in a wide range of other NLP tasks, such as textual entailment, question-answering, semantics similarity assessment, sentiment analysis, document classification, and text generation.

The first *generative pretrained transformer*, known as GPT-1, builds upon a fairly old idea, e.g., Section [19.2.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0025). First, one uses unlabeled data to pretrain a network. Once the pretraining phase has been completed, the learned parameters that describe the network are used as initial estimates for the next phase of supervised learning. During the latter, labeled data are used for the so-called fine-tuning to a specific task. Depending on the type of pretraining, different methods result. We will come to such techniques in more detail in Section [19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0190).

In GPT, during pretraining, a transformer network is trained to learn to predict/generate the next word of an input text sequence of tokenized words, say, 𝒰 = {**u**[1], **u**[2], …, **u**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si373.png), where in our current discussion *N* accounts for all tokens, including those of the special symbols. In contrast to the original transformer network, which involves two parts, i.e., the encoder and the decoder, in GPT only one stack of transformer blocks is employed. Each block comprises a) a masked self-attention layer, b) a residual “Add & Normalize” layer, c) a feed-forward fully connected network, and d) a final residual “Add & Normalize” layer, see [Fig. 19.14](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0075). In other words, the structure is similar to that of the decoder block of the full transformer network of [Fig. 19.13](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0070), by ignoring the encoder-decoder attention layer and the “Add & Normalize” layer above it. The goal in this section is to present the general idea behind GPT and not delving into details, which can be found in the related reference.

![Figure 19.14 Each block of the GPT architecture consists of four layers. The outputs of each layer become the inputs to the layer above. The input sequence embeddings, un, n = 1,2,…,N, feed the first in the hierarchy block.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr014.jpg)

[Figure 19.14](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf1320) Each block of the GPT architecture consists of four layers. The outputs of each layer become the inputs to the layer above. The input sequence embeddings, ***u***[*n*], *n* = 1,2,…,*N*, feed the first in the hierarchy block.

### 

#### Pretraining

Similar to the concept of Eq. [(19.44)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq99), during pretraining, the cost is built upon the conditional probabilities, i.e.,

$J\_{1}(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathcal{U}}\\sum\\limits\_{n}\\ln P(\\mathbf{u}\_{n}|\\mathbf{u}\_{n - 1},\\mathbf{u}\_{n - 2},\\ldots,\\mathbf{u}\_{n - k};\\mathbf{\\theta}),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>;</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si374.png)(19.50) 

where ***θ*** is the set of all the parameters involved in the network. In GPT, *k* is the size of the so-called *context window*. In other words, *k* determines the window of the past information that is involved in the conditional probabilities. Of course, since GPT does not involve a separate encoder, the conditional probabilities depend only on past input tokens. The first summation is over all possible text sequences in the corpus. In other words, GPT is pretrained to perform as a non-linear predictor.

Note that for the next word prediction, an extra network on top of the last block of the transformer is used, that first linearly transforms the outputs back to the dimensionality of the vocabulary, followed by the softmax nonlinearity layer. This is exactly the same technique as the one used in the decoder in [Fig. 19.9](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0050). Thus in GPT, the single stack of transformer blocks could be seen as acting both as the encoder as well as the decoder.

The main idea associated with pretraining is that by forcing the network to learn to predict, using a large corpus of unlabeled data, it equivalently learns basic structural and contextual information that resides in the associated type of data. Digging in this information, the network can encode, at the output of the top block, a *universal representation* that can subsequently be transferred, with little adaptation, to a wide range of tasks. This rationale draws inspiration directly from the transfer learning discussed in Section [18.16](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml) and it will be the main theme in Section [19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0190).

#### Supervised fine-tuning

Once pretraining is over, one can use the trained transformer to perform supervised learning NLP tasks, such as those mentioned in the beginning of this section. For example, in a sentiment analysis or document classification task, given a sequence of say, *M*, tokens, i.e., 𝒳 = {**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*M*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si375.png) with a corresponding class label, *y*, the goal is to maximize the conditional probability *P*(*y*|𝒳)<mml:math><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si376.png).

During fine-tuning, an extra network, parameterized in terms of a new set of parameters, ***w***, is added on top of the last block of the pretrained transformer network. This is different from the extra network (that transformed vectors to word probabilities) used during pretraining. For example, for the case of classification tasks, the aim of the extra network that is employed during fine-tuning is to transform the outputs of the last transformer block into *class* probabilities. This is achieved by first applying a) a linear transformation to bring the corresponding outputs into the right dimensionality, as dictated by the specific task (e.g., number of classes), followed b) by a softmax nonlinearity that transforms the final outputs into class probabilities. The weights of this extra network are learned by maximizing, with respect to ***w***, the cost function,

$J\_{2}(\\mathbf{w}) = \\sum\\limits\_{(y,\\mathcal{X})}\\ln P(y|\\mathcal{X}).$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si377.png)(19.51) 

During fine-tuning, one can also employ a combination of Eqs. [(19.51)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq116) and [(19.50)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq115) and optimize with respect to both ***θ*** and ***w***. In other words, instead of keeping the parameters of the pretrained transformer fixed to the optimal values, which were obtained during pretraining, one can use them as initial estimates and obtain updated estimates during fine-tuning for the specific supervised learning task. Note, however, that this alternative may not be useful in practice, due to the very large size of today's models.

Remarks 19.7

*   •  In the machine learning jargon, the pretraining phase is often referred to as the *pretext* task and the supervised learning fine-tuning, associated with a specific supervised learning case, as the *downstream* task.
*   •  At the time of the publication of \[147\], the reported results showed impressive performance improvements in a number of NLP tasks, compared to previous state-of-the art techniques.

### 19.4.1 GPT: few-shot learners

The original GPT architecture employed fine-tuning for the downstream tasks. However, in language processing, this may still require data sets of a few to many thousands of learning examples, see, e.g., \[27\]. This is in contrast to humans, who can perform a new language task by generalizing from few examples or simple instructions. To close this gap, later versions of GPT substituted the fine-tuning step, which was required for each specific downstream task, by employing a *meta-learning* rationale.^([^(139)](#fn139))

As it is pointed out in \[27\], during pretraining, the language model develops a *broad set of skills* and *pattern recognition abilities*, which are, somehow, encoded in the learned parameters. This “knowledge” can subsequently be used at the *inference* phase to adapt to or recognize a specific task, e.g., translation, question-answering, etc. Furthermore, it turns out that such “in context” learning capabilities can significantly be improved with scale. To this end, later versions to GPT-1, e.g., GPT-2 (\[148\]) and GPT-3 (\[27\]), are of much larger size compared to GPT-1. [Table 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#t0015) summarizes the related numbers.

[Table 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf1385)

 Values of the model parameters in the GPT family. 

 
| Model  || GPT-1 || GPT-2 || GPT-3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Size |
| Numbers of parameters || 117 millions || 1.5 billions || 175 billions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number of blocks || 12 || 48 || 96 |
| Context window || 512 || 1024 || 2048 |
| Embedding dimensions || 768 || 1600 || 12288 |
| Number of attention heads || 12 || 25 || 96 |

![Table 19.2](images/B9780443292385000251/t0015.png)

All versions build upon the basic architecture of GPT-1 with some variations that can be found in the related papers. The model capacity of GPT-3 allowed the use of in-context learning abilities to recognize, at inference phase, the specific task to be performed with a few examples and/or description of what the network is expected to do. In other words, these large language models, having been pretrained on massive unlabeled data, have acquired the capacity to “match” the pattern of the given examples with what they have learned during pretraining on similar data sets and use this “knowledge” to perform a specific task. Moreover, as it has already been stated, this ability seems to increase with increasing the number of model parameters. There are three types of related schemes that are currently popular in NLP:

*Few-shot setting*: The trained model is given a task description and a few example demonstrations of the specific task at inference time. These act as constraints that *condition* (drive) the output toward a specific task. Each example consists of a) a “context” and b) a “completion.” In the few-shot setting, *K* such examples are provided with typical values of *K* being in the range of 10–100, depending on how many they can fit, given the context window size. Following these examples, a final example is given that comprises the “context” only. The model is expected to output the “completion.” Below we provide a typical case, in the framework of the translation task from French to English.

*   •  Task description: “Translate French to English”
*   •  Example #1: “Bon jour” ⟨EOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si176.png) “Good morning”
*   •  Example #2: “Belle journée” ⟨EOS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>EOS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si176.png) “Nice day”
*   •  Prompt (context): “Je suis étudiant”

The model is expected to predict (completion): “I am a student.”

*One-shot setting*: This is a special case of the previous one, where only one example is provided.

*Zero-shot setting*: In this setting, only the task description is given without any examples.

Remarks 19.8

*   •  GPT-3 was trained on a mix of five corpora, namely the Common Crawl, the WebText2, Books1, Books2, and Wikipedia. A weighting procedure was used so that high-quality data sets were sampled more often.
*   •  Later versions, such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, \[63\], are much larger models and they have also incorporated reinforcement learning techniques. The GPT-4 version consists of 170 trillion parameters. Furthermore, GPT-4 is a multimodal model that, besides text, is capable of dealing with other modalities, such as images.

## 19.5 BERT: bidirectional encoder representation from transformers

The GPT family builds upon a single stack of transformer blocks, and the masked self-attention philosophy is adopted. In other words, GPTs are *unidirectional* language models and each token can only attend on previous tokens of the sequence.

In BERT, \[43\], a single stack of transformer blocks is, also, used. However, in contrast to GPT, the blocks are similar in structure to the encoder ones of the full encoder-decoder transformer of Section [19.3.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0085). That is, (full) self-attention is employed in the respective layers in the blocks. This, obviously, makes BERT models *bidirectional* and each token attends to past as well as to future ones. This can be beneficial, for example, when applying fine-tuning to token-level tasks, such as question-answering, where it is crucial to incorporate context from both directions, see, e.g., \[43\].

The goal of this section is to present the general rationale behind BERT, and a more detailed description can be obtained from the related reference. [Fig. 19.15](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0080) shows a simplified block diagram that focuses on the input-output variables. The internal structure of BERT consists of a number of blocks similar to the encoder ones of [Fig. 19.10](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0055).

![Figure 19.15 The first input token is the special classification token, 〈CLS〉, and the corresponding output is denoted as c. For some applications, more than two sentences are used, e.g., sentence A and sentence B, separated by the special token 〈SEP〉.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr015.jpg)

Figure 19.15 The first input token is the special classification token, 〈CLS〉, and the corresponding output is denoted as ***c***. For some applications, more than two sentences are used, e.g., sentence A and sentence B, separated by the special token 〈SEP〉.

However, BERT employs some novel features. More specifically:

*   •  It introduces a special classification token, ⟨CLS⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>CLS</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si378.png), which is added at the beginning of every input sequence of tokens; see [Fig. 19.15](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0080). The final (output of the last block) state/embedding/representation vector that corresponds to this special token, denoted as ***c*** in [Fig. 19.15](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0080), is used as the *aggregate class* representation of the whole sequence, for the case of classification tasks.
*   •  BERT, also, uses another special token, ⟨SEP⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SEP</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si379.png), to separate parts of the input sequence. For certain applications, the input consists of a pair of sentences, such as in question-answering tasks. In [Fig. 19.15](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0080), one sentence, denoted as “A,” consists of *N* tokens, **x**[*n*]^(*A*), *n* = 1, 2…, *N*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si380.png). The other sentence, denoted as “B,” comprises *M* tokens, **x**[*m*]^(*B*), *m* = 1, 2…, *M*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si381.png). Note that **x**[*n*]^(*A*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si382.png) and **x**[*m*]^(*B*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si383.png) are the embedding vectors that are presented as inputs to the network.
*   •  In BERT, besides the vocabulary and positional embeddings, a third embedding is used to provide sentence information. This embedding is, also, learned during pretraining. Thus, in BERT, the sentence-related information is provided by a) the ⟨SEP⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>SEP</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si379.png) symbol, which separates the two sentences, and b) the sentence embedding. Hence, for each token, the final input embedding results as the summation of three terms, in contrast to Eq. [(19.30)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq73) that involves two terms. The sentence embedding vector is the same for all the tokens in sentence “A” (“B”), i.e., **s**[*A*] (**s**[*B*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si385.png).

### 19.5.1 Pretraining

Recall from Section [19.3.10](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0120), that during pretraining, the goal of the decoder was to predict the next word in the sequence, given the current and the previous ones. Prediction was used because all future (for a specific position) tokens were *masked*. However, in BERT, the whole sequence is available simultaneously and the attention scores involve all, past as well as future, positions. To overcome this, in BERT, a very old technique is employed, known as the *cloze task*; see \[179\]. A number of input tokens are randomly selected and masked, e.g., they are replaced by a special token ⟨MASK⟩<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">〈</mml:mo><mml:mtext>MASK</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">〉</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si386.png). The goal of the training becomes that of *predicting* the true words in the original vocabulary (one-hot representations) that correspond to the masked embeddings *only*. Borrowing the philosophy used for the decoder in [Fig. 19.9](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0050), the output vectors of the last block, which correspond to the masked input embeddings, go through an extra network that comprises a linear transformation followed by the softmax nonlinearity. Thus, the outputs that correspond to the masked words are transformed to *l*\-dimensional (vocabulary size) vectors of probabilities, and during training they are optimally “pushed” to predict the id of the corresponding original word. The cost function is formed by following a similar rationale as that leading to Eq. [(19.45)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq101). Thus, the single stack of transformer blocks that comprise BERT acts both as the encoder as well as the decoder. Training via random masking is further discussed in Section [19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0190).

Besides masking, BERT also employs another path to pretraining coined as *next sentence prediction* (NSP). As it is pointed out in \[43\], a number of NLP tasks, such as question-answering, are based on understanding the *relationship* between two sentences, which is not easy to be directly captured by predictive language modeling. To facilitate relationship learning, the output embedding vector ***c*** is mobilized in the context of a *binary* classification “next sentence prediction” task. To this end, a number of training example pairs of sentences, say “A” and “B,” which are extracted from a corpus, are provided to the input. For 50% of these examples, sentence “B” is the next sentence (label *ISNEXT* or, say, 1) and for the rest 50%, sentence “B” is randomly selected from the corpus (label *ISNOTNEXT*, or 0). For the training, ***c*** is first linearly transformed to a two-dimensional vector and then the softmax nonlinearity transforms each one of the two elements to probabilities. The network is trained to optimally solve this binary classification task.

### 19.5.2 Fine-tuning

During fine-tuning, the output vectors of the last (top) transformer block are used to feed, as input, an extra network that is described in terms of a new set of parameters, ***w***. Training in the framework of a specific downstream task is performed by optimizing the network *end-to-end*, i.e., with respect to the extra parameters, ***w***, as well as with respect to the parameters ***θ*** that define the BERT transformer. The optimal set of parameters, e.g., **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png), learned during pretraining are used as the respective initial estimates for the back-propagation algorithm, during the fine-tuning. Note that the input tokens are not masked during the fine-tuning phase.

The way the output BERT embeddings are utilized during the fine-tuning depends on the nature of the corresponding task. For example, for classification-related tasks, such as entailment or sentiment analysis, the output **c** ∈ ℝ^(*d*[*m*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si388.png) is utilized. Assuming that *K* classes are involved in the downstream task, the extra network that builds on top of ***c*** consists of a) a transformation matrix, say *W* ∈ ℝ^(*K* × *d*[*m*])<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si389.png) that outputs a *K*\-dimensional vector (*W***c**<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si390.png)), which is followed by b) a softmax nonlinearity that acts on the elements of this vector (Softmax(*W***c**)<mml:math><mml:mtext>Softmax</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si391.png)) and transforms them into class probabilities.

On the other hand, for the question-answering task, the output vectors, which correspond to the embeddings that comprise sentence “B,” are utilized. The goal of this task is to extract that specific part from the sentence “B,” which, with high probability, is the answer to the question that comprises sentence “A.” For more details, see \[43\].

Remarks 19.9

*   •  BERT was pretrained using the bookcorpus data set and the English Wikipedia. Two models of different size were trained: a small one that comprised 110 million parameters (12 blocks, *d*[*m*] = 768<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>768</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si392.png), and 12 attention heads) and a large one that comprised 340 million parameters (24 blocks, *d*[*m*] = 1024<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1024</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si393.png), and 16 attention heads). At the time of publication, the reported results showed significant performance improvements for a number of tasks, compared to previous state-of-the-art models; see \[43\].
*   •  In \[39\], an analysis of the BERT network is preformed in an effort to better understand what aspects and features of language these models learn. The related analysis indicates that specific heads tend to specialize to particular relations. For example, there are heads that detect objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of propositions and objects of possessive pronouns with relatively high accuracy. A summary of related results can be found in, e.g., \[156\].
*   •  Among the very first attempts to modify and apply transformers to the computer vision terrain are the ViT and the Swin networks. The *visual transformer* (ViT), proposed in \[45\], follows closely the BERT rationale. The image is split into a number of patches, which are subsequently vectorized to form the input tokens to the transformer. ViT employed patches of 16 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si394.png) pixels in size. In ViT, the supervised mode of pretraining resulted in better performance compared to the masked self-supervision.
*   The *shifted windows* (Swin) transformer, \[116\], is a variant of ViT and it uses different sizes of patches, starting from 4 × 4<mml:math><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si395.png) to larger ones 16 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si394.png), as one moves upwards to the higher level blocks. This hierarchical architecture has the flexibility to model at various scales. The proposed changes in the Swin transformer aim at coping with a major difference between language and vision, namely the large variations in the scale of visual entities and the high resolution of pixels in images compared to words in texts.

### 19.5.3 Transformers: some concluding remarks

Following the success of BERT and the GPT family of what is known as *large language models* (LLMs), a number of models and software packages appeared with similar capabilities, e.g., \[150\], \[38\], \[187\]. All these models have shown “admirable” state-of-the art performance in a wide range of applications, such as question-answering, translation, word unscrambling, performing arithmetic operations and some basic reasoning, generation of program coding, article learning, text generation in a prose that often is indistinguishable from that produced by an “average” person, e.g., \[147\], \[90\], \[94\].

Besides NLP, transformers have been used in a wide range of applications including, but not limited to, computer vision, e.g., \[99\], speech/audio processing and learning, e.g., \[109\], biology, e.g., \[64\], music generation, e.g., \[205\], health, e.g., \[113\], weather forecast, e.g., \[21\], and human life event prediction, e.g., \[165\]. In all these areas, their use has led to significant performance improvements compared to previous state-of-the-art techniques. Their learning power has ignited a new wave of applying and using such machine learning models in almost all aspects of human activity, ranging from science to technology, from services to industry, from gaming to education and human networking.

An interesting and important question is to understand and explain the reasons why these models exhibit such impressive learning and performance capabilities. This is an ongoing challenging research topic with many open questions to be answered. A rather detailed report on applying LLMs in various applications pointing out capabilities as well as limitations and possible future research directions is given in, e.g., \[28\].

On the other hand, due to the previously reported capabilities, besides the advantages that these models can offer, they also pose a number of *social and ethical* threats, which are related to their misuse by malicious actors. Also, potentially, the generated text can propagate stereotypes and prejudice content related to gender, race, religion, political ideas, as well as human values. Moreover, such models can produce content that is not reliable and the text they generate may contain wrong information. In other words, they suffer from “hallucinations,” see, e.g., \[63\]. Many related articles, statements, and discussions, often with opposing views, by prominent experts have been published in the news and social media, concerning the potential dangers as well as the possible measures to be taken in order to minimize these threats. Such measures could come from the technology itself and/or via an appropriate legal framework that regulates the use of the related platforms. A summary of opinions, from world-renowned experts, on such issues can be found in, e.g., \[175\]. An interesting poetic-like view compiled by two leading AI experts is given in \[25\].

## 19.6 Self-supervised learning

In the previous sections, the focus was on transformers and the discussion evolved around the natural language processing (NLP) tasks. We have already pointed out that during pretraining, also known as the pretext task, via the use of unlabeled data, a transformer network can produce an updated efficient contextualized representation of its input. Subsequently, the pretrained transformer can be used in a supervised learning framework for a wide range of specialized tasks, known as downstream tasks.

Learning during pretraining was achieved either via next word prediction or via masking some of the input word embeddings. In the latter case, the involved parameters were optimized for the network to predict the masked words. This type of training, via unlabeled data, is also known as self-supervised learning, for reasons that we will soon discuss.

The question that is now raised is whether such techniques can be used with other modalities other than text, e.g., images, speech, audio, video, etc. In NLP tasks, the involved word embeddings/tokens are sequential and of a discrete nature. This is not the case, for example, in images in computer vision tasks or in speech signals, as well as for many other types of signal modalities. Pixels in images take values in continuous intervals and they are not sequential. Audio signals are of a sequential nature but their amplitude varies within continuous intervals.

Due to the different nature of the involved data modalities, different techniques have been developed for self-supervised learning over the years, which may or may not use transformers. Before we entail in reviewing some basic directions for this type of learning tasks, let us first define what we mean by self-supervision. So far, we used the term in a rather loose way.

### 19.6.1 Unsupervised versus self-supervised learning

Pretraining during the pretext task is preformed via the use of unlabeled data. So far in the book, the term unsupervised learning has been used for such tasks, see, e.g., Section [12.6](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml). In which aspects is self-supervised learning different from unsupervised tasks to “deserve” a different name? As we have already discussed in Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-17_B978044329238500007X.xhtml), typical unsupervised tasks are clustering, manifold learning, probability distribution learning. The goal that is shared by all these tasks is to learn the structure, e.g., hidden regularities and statistical dependencies that underlie the associated input data. Learning of unsupervised tasks is different from supervised learning. In the latter, for *each input example* there exists a corresponding *target* value and the training objective is to optimize the network parameters such that the predicted outputs are close, in some sense, to the corresponding targets.

In *self-supervised learning* (SSL), no labeled data are available but, instead, target values are *constructed* from the available unlabeled examples. Different techniques follow different paths for obtaining targets/labels. For example, recall that in BERT the targets are the true word one-hot vector encodings, which correspond to the masked tokens in the input sequence. Thus, one could consider self-supervised learning as a category of learning methods that lies between supervised and unsupervised ones.

The power on training via a vast amount of unlabeled data, compared to supervised learning, springs from the fact that SSL extracts *generic representations* of the available data, which can subsequently be useful *across many tasks*. This is in contrast to supervised learning that tries to focus on the needs of a specific task. For example, in \[138\], a study is carried out in an effort to relate SSL with the way children acquire basic visual categories, through generic learning mechanisms without substantive inductive bias. Although, at the time the current edition of this book is being compiled, it is still rather early to fully grasp the how's and why's behind SSL, findings point out that the representations of the input data that are learned via SSL tend to be more robust to adversarial examples, label corruption and input perturbations, e.g., \[75\], \[62\]. Finally, note that a major drawback of supervised learning is the requirement of annotated data, which is a particularly high cost process, especially when massive data sets are used.

Self-supervised learning is not new in machine learning. Our aim here is not to review all the techniques and paths that have been proposed over the years but to focus on some basic directions of SSL, which seem to be more popular at the time of the current edition. Recent related reviews on SSL methods are provided in, e.g., \[13\], \[49\], \[96\], \[117\].

### 19.6.2 The pretext task

The first phase in self-supervised learning is the pretext task, whose aim is the training of an *encoder* via unlabeled examples (pretraining) in order to generate an informative encoding/representation of the input data. The goal of this section is to describe a generic scheme that covers most of the methods that have been suggested. Of course, as it is always the case, there may be specific methods that deviate from this general rationale, see, for example, [Remarks 19.11](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0085).

A major part in any self-supervised technique is to *create* the output targets/labels from the unlabeled samples. Often, we refer to these constructed targets as *pseudo labels*. In a more formal way, let us assume that the input comprises a set of *N* unlabeled vectors, 𝒳 = {**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si396.png). For example, in an NLP task these may be the *N* token vectors corresponding to the input sequence of words. In a computer vision problem, they may correspond to the *N* vectorized successive patches that comprise an image. In a speech processing task, these may be the vectors of the time samples in a sequence of *N* successive windows, which result after the segmentation of the corresponding speech signal. When the input data are treated individually as single entities, e.g., each example is a single vector to feed the input of a multilayer perceptron or an image array to feed the input of a convolutional network, then *N* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si397.png) and the input set, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png), is a singleton. Thus, the stage of our discussion covers the more general modeling, where the encoder can be, e.g., a transformer (*N* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si399.png)) or a convolutional neural network or a fully connected feed-forward network. 

The main steps in the pretext task are:

1.  **1.**  Select an encoder (also called the backbone), to map the inputs, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si52.png), to a corresponding set of encoder output vectors, **h**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si403.png), i.e.,

**x**[*n*] ↦ **h**[*n*] = *f*[**θ**](**x**[*n*]).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si404.png)

1.  Note that the equivalent (vector) mapping function, which the encoder implements, is parameterized in terms of a set of parameters, ***θ***. It is very common that the input vectors first undergo another transformation prior to the presentation to the encoder. For example, recall that in BERT some of the input tokens are masked, which is a type of transformation. Thus, in a more general setting, we can write

$\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\longmapsto{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n}\\longmapsto\\mathbf{h}\_{n} = f\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n}),\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si405.png)

1.  Collecting all the transformed inputs together in a set, $\\widetilde{\\mathcal{X}} = \\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{1},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{2},\\ldots,{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{N}\\}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si406.png), we can compactly write

$\\mathcal{H} = f\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\widetilde{\\mathcal{X}}),$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si407.png)

1.  where ℋ = {**h**[1], **h**[2], …, **h**[*N*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si408.png). This action is schematically illustrated in the upper branch of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085).

![Figure 19.16 Generic scheme for pretext tasks: The upper branch feeds the encoder, fθ(⋅), and the projector/predictor, gϕ(⋅), generates predictions to predict the targets/pseudo labels. The latter are generated in the lower branch. Dotted boxes are optional. During training, via backpropagation, the involved parameters are adjusted to minimize the cost function that quantifies deviation between the targets, \\mathcal{T}Equation, and their corresponding predictions, \\widehat{\\mathcal{T}}Equation. When g\_{\\mathbf{\\xi}}^{\\prime}( \\cdot )Equation is employed, the updating of the corresponding parameters may need special attention. In some cases, gϕ(⋅) and g\_{\\mathbf{\\xi}}^{\\prime}( \\cdot )Equation may be implemented as a serial connection of two sub-networks.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr016.jpg)

Figure 19.16 Generic scheme for pretext tasks: The upper branch feeds the encoder, *f*[***θ***](⋅), and the projector/predictor, *g*[***ϕ***](⋅), generates predictions to predict the targets/pseudo labels. The latter are generated in the lower branch. Dotted boxes are optional. During training, via backpropagation, the involved parameters are adjusted to minimize the cost function that quantifies deviation between the targets, 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png), and their corresponding predictions, $\\widehat{\\mathcal{T}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si401.png). When *g*[**ξ**]^′( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si402.png) is employed, the updating of the corresponding parameters may need special attention. In some cases, *g*[***ϕ***](⋅) and *g*[**ξ**]^′( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si402.png) may be implemented as a serial connection of two sub-networks.

1.  
2.  **2.**  Generate a corresponding set of target values (pseudo labels), 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png), from the set 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png), via a transformation process, *P*, i.e.,

𝒯 = *P*(𝒳).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>P</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si409.png)

1.  For example, 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png) could comprise the one-hot vector representations of the masked tokens in BERT. In the case of GPT, 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png) would consist of the one-hot vector representations of the next word to be predicted at each time instant. Let us assume that, in general, 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png) comprises *m* vectors/targets, i.e., 𝒯 = {**t**[1], **t**[2], …, **t**[*m*]}<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si410.png). Needless to say that *m* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si65.png) is a special case that is commonly encountered in practice. The action of *P* on the input data, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png), is schematically shown by the lower branch in [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085), and it corresponds to the box “Transform #2.” Note that in the figure a second (nonlinear) network, denoted by *g*[**ξ**]^′( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si402.png), parameterized in terms of another set of parameters, ***ξ***, may be optionally used (for reasons that we see later on) to provide the final targets, 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png).
2.  **3.**  A decoder, often referred to as the predictor, the predictor head, or the projector is selected (e.g., a feed-forward neural network) that maps the *N* encoded outputs of the encoder, ℋ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si411.png), into *m* target estimates, $\\widehat{\\mathcal{T}} = \\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{t}}}\_{1},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{t}}}\_{2},\\ldots,{\\widehat{\\mathbf{t}}}\_{m}\\}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si412.png), i.e.,

$\\widehat{\\mathcal{T}} = g\_{\\mathbf{\\phi}}(\\mathcal{H}),$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si413.png)

1.  where ***ϕ*** is the set of parameters that define the projector/predictor network. For example, in the case of GPT and BERT, the predictor comprises the extra networks on top of the last transformer block, which converts the outputs to probability vectors.
2.  **4.**  A loss function, ℒ(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si414.png), is selected to quantify the deviation between the predicted targets in $\\widehat{\\mathcal{T}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si401.png) and the targets/pseudo labels in 𝒯<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si400.png). The corresponding cost function is minimized with respect to the unknown parameters, ***θ*** and ***ϕ***, i.e.,

$(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast},\\mathbf{\\phi}\_{\\ast}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathcal{X} \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathcal{L}(\\mathcal{T},\\widehat{\\mathcal{T}}),$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si415.png)

1.  where 𝒟<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">D</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si327.png) is the corpus of the available unlabeled data.^([^(140)](#fn140)) 
    
    $\\mathcal{L}(\\mathcal{T},\\widehat{\\mathcal{T}}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}||\\mathbf{t}\_{i} - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{t}}}\_{i}||\_{2}^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>
    
    ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si417.png)(19.52) 
    
    1.  where || ⋅ ||[2]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si418.png) is the Euclidean norm of the corresponding vector argument. In the case of BERT and GPT in the context of NLP tasks, the loss function was the cross-entropy one. Training, as usually, follows the backpropagation rationale.

### 19.6.3 The downstream task

Once the pretext task is completed and the optimal set of parameters, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png), has been obtained, the trained encoder is used in the context of a specific downstream task. As a matter of fact, the encoder is the *only* module from the pretext task of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085) that is utilized in the downstream task! Its role is to provide information-rich encodings, ℋ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si411.png), of an associated input, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png). In other words, the encoder acts as a *feature generator* for the downstream task.

More formally, we are given a set of input-output pairs, i.e., (𝒳[*i*], *y*[*i*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si419.png), *i* = 1, 2, …, *N*^′<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si420.png), where 𝒳[*i*] = {**x**[*i*1], **x**[*i*2], …, **x**[*i**N*]}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si421.png) and *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si422.png) denotes the corresponding label. For example, 𝒳[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si423.png) could be the sequence of tokens associated with a phrase, and *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si422.png) the corresponding label of a sentiment category in a sentiment classification task. In computer vision, 𝒳[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si423.png) could be the set of patches comprising an image and *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si422.png) the category label, e.g., the label corresponding to the class “cat.” We assume that we have *N*^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si195.png) of such labeled input patterns.

For each set of *N* input vectors, 𝒳[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si423.png), the corresponding set of *N* encoder output vectors is produced, i.e., ℋ[*i*] = *f*[**θ**](𝒳[*i*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si426.png). See the first block in the lower branch in [Fig. 19.17](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0090). Note that, in general, the input data are directly fed to the encoder. Recall, for example, that in BERT, during the downstream task, no masking of the input tokens is performed. The outputs of the encoder are fed to a (nonlinear) predictor, e.g., a feed-forward neural network, *g*[**ϕ**]^(*d*)( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si427.png) (superscript *d* refers to the downstream task), whose goal is to output an estimate, *ŷ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si425.png), of the corresponding target/label, i.e., *y*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si422.png), see [Fig. 19.17](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0090).

![Figure 19.17 The downstream supervised learning task. \\mathcal{X}\_{i}Equation is the input set and yi the corresponding label. The predictor, g\_{\\mathbf{\\phi}}^{d}Equation provides an estimate, {\\widehat{y}}\_{i}Equation, of the label. During fine-tuning, there are two scenarios to optimize the cost function: a) Optimization with respect to ϕ and the knob in the feedback dotted line remains open with the values of the parameters in the encoder fixed to θ⁎, which were obtained during the pretext task. b) Optimization w.r. to both (θ,ϕ) and the knob closes. In the latter case, in the backpropagation algorithm, θ⁎ is used as the corresponding vector of initial values.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr017.jpg)

Figure 19.17 The downstream supervised learning task. 𝒳[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si423.png) is the input set and *y*[*i*] the corresponding label. The predictor, *g*[**ϕ**]^(*d*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si424.png) provides an estimate, *ŷ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si425.png), of the label. During fine-tuning, there are two scenarios to optimize the cost function: a) Optimization with respect to ***ϕ*** and the knob in the feedback dotted line remains open with the values of the parameters in the encoder fixed to ***θ***[⁎], which were obtained during the pretext task. b) Optimization w.r. to both (***θ***,***ϕ***) and the knob closes. In the latter case, in the backpropagation algorithm, ***θ***[⁎] is used as the corresponding vector of initial values.

For the supervised training of the downstream task (fine-tuning), a loss function, ℒ(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si414.png) is selected. There are two paths for the fine-tuning. According to the first, the encoder parameters are fixed to the optimal values, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png), obtained during the pretext task, and training takes place only with respect to ***ϕ***. The other alternative is to use **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png) as initial estimates in the backpropagation algorithm and optimize with respect to both, ***θ***, to obtain an updated set of optimal parameters **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png), and ***ϕ***, i.e.,
