$(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast},\\mathbf{\\phi}\_{\\ast}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi}}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N^{\\prime}}\\mathcal{L}(y\_{i},{\\widehat{y}}\_{i}).$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si428.png)

Once fine-tuning is completed, during inference, the resulting from the above minimization optimal networks, *f*[**θ**[\*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si429.png) and *g*[**ϕ**[\*]]^(*d*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si430.png), are used to predict the label *ŷ*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si431.png) that corresponds to a given input set, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png).

### 19.6.4 Masked prediction methods

The basic idea of the masked prediction rationale has already been presented in the discussion regarding BERT, Section [19.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0170). The idea of degrading parts of the input and then trying to undo this degradation is not new. For example, in Section [19.2.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0035), the concept of denoising autoencoders was mentioned. There, degradation of the input data was performed via the addition of noise to the input. In the process of denoising, the network learns and captures statistical dependencies in the input data.

In \[142\], a computer vision task was considered and the so-called *context encoders* were proposed. Whole patches of the input to the encoder image were masked, turned into white, and the goal of the decoder was to produce a possible hypothesis of the missing parts. It turned out that the encoder learned a representation that while predicting the missing regions of the image could capture not just appearance but also the *semantics* of the visual structures. In order to train the encoder-decoder pair, the output target values had to be selected from the unlabeled images and these were the original image patches that were masked at the input of the encoder.

[Fig. 19.18](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0095) illustrates the case of an image masking process. In [19.18](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0095)A three images are shown. The left one is the original image partitioned in *N* = 9<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si432.png) patches. In the center one, three of the patches have been masked. The image on the right shows the original patches that correspond to the masked ones. [Fig. 19.18](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0095)B illustrates the previous versions of the images in their vectorized form.^([^(141)](#fn141))

![Figure 19.18 (A) The original image partitioned in N = 9 patches (left). Three patches in the original image have been masked (center). The original patches that correspond to the masked ones (right). (B) As in (A) where patches have been vectorized and they are represented via their corresponding vectors.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr018.jpg)

Figure 19.18 (A) The original image partitioned in *N* = 9 patches (left). Three patches in the original image have been masked (center). The original patches that correspond to the masked ones (right). (B) As in (A) where patches have been vectorized and they are represented via their corresponding vectors.

There are various ways in dealing with masked image patches in self-supervised learning. A straightforward path is to feed the encoder with the masked sequence of vectors, i.e., [Fig. 19.18](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0095)B (center). The outputs of the encoder are fed to a predictor that is trained to provide estimates of the masked patches, i.e., ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{1}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si435.png), ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{6}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si436.png), ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{8}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si437.png). These steps are in line with the upper branch of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085). The action of “Transform #1” is to mask the patches, according to some protocol. For example, a preselected percentage of patches can be randomly masked. The action of the “Transform # 2” is to retain the original vectors of the masked patches, i.e., **x**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si438.png), **x**[6]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si439.png), **x**[8]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si440.png), which act as the targets in the cost function. A possible choice for the loss function can be the square Euclidean norm of the difference between pixel values in the original patches that were masked and the predicted ones, e.g., Eq. [(19.52)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq123). Other norms can also be used or a combination of loss functions, see, e.g., \[142\].

In the *BERT pretraining of image transformers* (BEiT), \[14\], prior to the pretraining, an autoencoder is first used to encode image patches as *discrete* tokens. In other words, each one of the patches of an image is associated with a number in a discrete vocabulary. Subsequently, a BERT-like structure is trained so that the outputs that are associated with the masked patches to predict the corresponding id number in the associated discrete vocabulary. Although the reported results indicate performance improvements with respect to previously published methods, the training, due to the tokenization step, poses certain challenges.

The idea of predicting the pixel values of masked patches has been adopted to audio tasks in \[59\] (SSAST: Self-supervised audio spectrogram transformer). The inputs to the encoding transformer are the spectrograms that are computed from the input audio sequence. In \[87\] (HuBERT: Hidden-Unit BERT), the raw audio data are first coded via a CNN network to produce a sequence of coded frames that are fed as inputs to the transformer. After randomly masking some of the frames, the goal of the training during the pretext task is to predict the *cluster* indices of the masked frames. To this end, a clustering of the input frames is first performed, e.g., via the *k*\-means algorithm. In other words, in this case, the pseudo labels consist of cluster indices.

In \[73\], the so-called *masked autoencoder* was introduced. The proposed architecture follows the general rationale shown in [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085). However, in this case, the input to the encoder transformer, *f*[**θ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si441.png), is fed with the *unmasked* patches *only*. The masked patches are simply removed and they are *not* replaced by a mask symbol. Thus, the input consists of, say, *M* < *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si442.png) vectorized patches, where *N* is the total number of patches that result from the original image splitting. The input to the predictor module, *g*[**ϕ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si443.png), consists of the output of the encoder, augmented with the masked symbols placed at the positions that correspond to the removed patches in the input. That is, the decoder accepts as inputs *N* tokens. The network is trained to reconstruct/predict the image patches. In \[73\], the cost function involves only the masked patches, similar to the BERT rationale. Up to 75% of the input patches can be masked, which also leads to substantial computational savings. The predictor *g*[**ϕ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si443.png) is also a transformer network, and the outputs of its last block are linearly transformed to match the dimensions of the image patches.

The idea of masked autoencoders has been applied to spectrograms of audio signals in \[91\]. This idea is further enhanced in \[199\], where the multi-head-multi-window transformer is proposed. Each head in the decoder computes attention over windows of different sizes. The reason is that, in this way, one can cope better with the issue of local versus global information. It is known that in audio signals, some audio events are more localized than others, and this applies both to time as well as to the frequency domains.

### 19.6.5 Contrastive techniques

The rationale that underlies the so-called *contrastive* techniques is to *encourage* similarity between versions of semantic preserving transformations of an input. The main idea behind such methods can be traced back to \[18\] and \[26\]. In the former, the goal was to replace the external “teacher”/target used in a supervised learning task by internally derived “signals.” Such signals can be generated by assuming that different parts of the perceptual input have common causes in the external world. Such a view changes the concept of training. Instead of “pushing” an output to “match” a corresponding externally provided target, the goal becomes that of “pushing” the outputs of two networks, whose inputs are fed with different views of the same input sample, to agree with each other. For example, the different views may be different modalities (e.g., vision and touch), or they can originate from the same modality at different times, or could be spatially adjacent parts of the same image.

In \[26\], the notion of *contrastive loss* was introduced. Two networks were, also, employed and they were constrained to share all the parameters. The goal of the task was to recognize genuine from fake signatures. During training, the parameters were adjusted to “push” the outputs of the two networks to be “close,” when both modules were provided with genuine signatures. Otherwise, in the case of a forged signature, the respective outputs were “pushed” to be “far” (according to a distance measure).

In the context of self-supervised learning, since only unlabeled data are involved, to identify similar inputs we often form variants of a single input using known semantic preserving transformations. This process is also known as *data augmentation*, and we often refer to it as *joint-embedding self-supervised learning* (JESSL). The variants that originate from the *same* input sample are called *positive* pairs or examples. It is for such pairs that we wish to make the corresponding outputs of the two networks look “similar.” Transformed versions that originate from *different* input samples are called *negatives*, and we wish to make the corresponding outputs “dissimilar.” Note that contrastive techniques fall under the general scheme of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085), where each one of the branches corresponds to different variants of the same input sample.

To unveil the main rationale behind these techniques, let us pick and discuss one typical method known as *simple framework for contrastive learning* (SimCLR), presented in \[35\]. [Fig. 19.19](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0100) illustrates schematically the idea, where we have assumed that the input comprises single vectors. For every input ***x***, two variants are generated by randomly applying the same semantic preserving transformation family. The variants are denoted as ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si444.png) for one of the two branches and ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si445.png) for the other. Examples of such semantic preserving transformation for images are random cropping followed by resizing, crop resize and flip, rotate, cut out, adding noise; see [Fig. 19.20](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0105). In audio signals, such transformations could be the altering of the order of some of the frames in the sequence, or masking some of them.

![Figure 19.19 For every input sample, x, two correlated transformed versions are generated, via the same family of data augmentation operations, e.g., t ∼ T, and t′ ∼ T. The two branches consist of the encoder network, fθ and the projector head, gϕ. Both branches share the same parameters. The contrastive loss function is such as a) to maximize agreement between samples of positive pairs and b) to minimize agreement between negative examples.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr019.jpg)

Figure 19.19 For every input sample, ***x***, two correlated transformed versions are generated, via the same family of data augmentation operations, e.g., *t* ∼ *T*, and *t*′ ∼ *T*. The two branches consist of the encoder network, *f*[***θ***] and the projector head, *g*[***ϕ***]. Both branches share the same parameters. The contrastive loss function is such as a) to maximize agreement between samples of positive pairs and b) to minimize agreement between negative examples.

![Figure 19.20 Examples of possible data augmentation transformations that are used in contrastive learning in computer vision applications.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr020.jpg)

[Figure 19.20](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf1780) Examples of possible data augmentation transformations that are used in contrastive learning in computer vision applications.

In SimCLR, the two branches are identical and the two versions of the input sample feed the encoder, *f*[**θ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si441.png), which, in the sequel, feeds the input of a nonlinear network, *g*[**ϕ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si443.png). Going back to the generic scheme of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085), the nonlinear module, *g*[**ξ**]^′( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si402.png), results as a serial concatenation of the *f* and *g* networks, whose parameters are constrained to be the same as those of the other branch.

The encoders' outputs **h**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si446.png) and **h**[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si447.png) feed the modules, *g*[**ϕ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si443.png). Since the goal in this type of learning is to enforce similarity (or dissimilarity) one may wonder why this extra module is needed. One could train only with respect to the parameters ***θ*** of the encoder, based on **h**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si446.png) and **h**[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si447.png). However, it turns out that introducing *g*[**ϕ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si443.png) further improves the learned representations. This extra network is also known as the *projector* head that maps, non-linearly, the set **h**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si446.png) and **h**[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si447.png) to a new set of vectors, i.e., **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si448.png) and **z**[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si449.png) that, in general, lie in a different subspace from that of **h**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si446.png), **h**[*j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si447.png).

In \[35\], the ResNet-50 network (\[71\]) was used in place of the encoder network, and a 2-layer MLP projection head to project the representations to a 128-dimensional latent space. Referring to the generic scheme in Section [19.6.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0200), note that in this case the input and output sets, 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png) and ℋ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si411.png), respectively, are singletons, i.e., *N* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si397.png). The inputs to the encoder consist of images (not patches) and the corresponding outputs at the encoder of 2048-dimensional vectors.

Let us now consider two different input samples, e.g., images represented as vectors, ***x*** and **x**^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si450.png). Each one of them generates a corresponding pair of transformed versions, i.e., (${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si451.png)) and (${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i}^{\\prime},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}^{\\prime}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si452.png)). According to the previously given definitions, (${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si451.png)) and (${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i}^{\\prime},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}^{\\prime}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo form positive pairs/samples, while pairs such as (${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}^{\\prime})$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si453.png) or (${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{i}^{\\prime},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{j}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si454.png)) correspond to negative pairs/samples, since they originate from different images.

For the current notational needs, let us reserve *N*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si455.png) to denote the number of the available training samples. After the data augmentation step, there will be 2*N*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si456.png) samples. Also, for every positive pair of samples, there will be 2(*N*[*t*] − 1)<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si457.png) negative ones.

The goal of training is to obtain estimates of the involved parameters, ***θ***, ***ϕ***, so that the outputs that correspond to positive pairs to be “pulled” together and those associated with negative ones to be “pushed” apart. In \[35\], the following criterion, coined *normalized temperature-scaled cross entropy* (NT-Xent), is used,

$(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast},\\mathbf{\\phi}\_{\\ast}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi}}\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi})\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbf{\\theta},\\mathbf{\\phi}) = - \\sum\\limits\_{(i,j) \\in P^{+}}\\ln\\frac{\\exp\\left( \\text{sim}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i},\\mathbf{z}\_{j})/\\tau \\right)}{\\sum\_{k = 1,k \\neq i}^{2N\_{t}}\\exp\\left( \\text{sim}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i},\\mathbf{z}\_{k})/\\tau \\right)}.$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false" id="mmlbr0007">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false" linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo mathvariant="normal">exp</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>sim</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si458.png)(19.53) 

The summation is over all positive pairs (*P*^+<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si459.png)), considered twice, i.e., as (*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si460.png) and (*j*, *i*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si461.png). sim(⋅, ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:mtext>sim</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si462.png) is a similarity measure, which in \[35\] is taken to be the normalized inner product, i.e.,

$\\text{sim}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i},\\mathbf{z}\_{j}) = \\frac{\\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{z}\_{j}}{||\\mathbf{z}\_{i}||||\\mathbf{z}\_{j}||}.$<mml:math><mml:mtext>sim</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si463.png)

No doubt, different similarity functions can and have been proposed and used. The so-called temperature parameter, *τ*, is a user-defined parameter. Note that in Eq. [(19.53)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq125), the more similar the samples of positive pairs in the numerator are, the larger (closer to 1) the corresponding value of the similarity function is. In contrast, the less similar the samples of the negative pairs in the denominator are, the smaller the value of the corresponding similarity function (close to 0) is.

Hence, by minimizing the previous cost function, the encoder is trained to “learn” what are the semantic features that make two patterns similar and what dissimilar. Put it differently and in a jargon popular in the SSL literature, the model learns *invariances*. Data augmentation is employed to leverage the unveiling of such invariances. For example, using cropping combined with different views of a given image, the SSL model is trained to produce a representation that is *invariant* to the different crops.

As it is always the case with self-supervised learning, during the downstream task training, only the encoder is employed, in line with what has already been stated in Section [19.6.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0205).

The loss function involved in Eq. [(19.53)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq125) is very similar to the so-called infoNCE, (*noise-contrastive estimation*) loss function that was introduced in \[188\], which was derived via information theoretic arguments. Noise contrastive estimation methods were first introduced in \[69\]. The basic idea is to estimate the involved unknown parameters that describe a model by learning to discriminate between the input data and some artificially generated noise. Thus, parameter estimation relies on noise with which the data is contrasted.

Another path in contrastive learning criteria is to involve a margin parameter, *m*, that imposes the distance between examples from different classes (e.g., positive and negative ones) to be larger than *m* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si464.png). The *triplet cost*, \[195\], is a typical example of this family. Three samples are involved in the cost; the query or anchor point, a positive example and a negative one. The triplet loss requires the difference between the two distances, i.e., the one between the query point and a positive example and the (same) query point from a negative example, to be larger than the margin, *m*. In a more formal way, the triplet cost function is expressed as

$\\mathcal{L} = \\sum\\limits\_{(i,j) \\in P^{+}}\\sum\\limits\_{(i,k) \\in P^{-}}\\left\\lbrack ||\\mathbf{z}\_{i} - \\mathbf{z}\_{j}||\_{2} - ||\\mathbf{z}\_{i} - \\mathbf{z}\_{k}||\_{2} + m \\right\\rbrack\_{+},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si465.png)

where *P*^−<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si466.png) is the index set of all the negative pairs and \[ ⋅ \][+]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si467.png) is the hinge loss function (i.e., max {0,  ⋅ }<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">max</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si468.png), see also Section [11.10](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml)). The cost function penalizes those pairs for which the distance of a negative sample from the query point is smaller than *m*, compared to the corresponding distance of a positive example.

Over the years, various contrastive loss functions have been proposed and used, see, e.g., \[13\] for a related review. In \[183\], a unification of various contrastive losses is presented. Also, contrastive learning has been used in the context of masked self-supervision, in order to match the output to the correct masked patch as contrasted to the incorrect ones, see, e.g., \[183\], \[9\]. In the *momentum contrast* (MoCo) scheme, \[72\], contrastive learning is seen as a process of matching an encoded query vector, ***q***, produced in one of the two branches, to a dictionary of encoded keys, **k**[0], **k**[1], …<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si469.png), produced in the other branch, using a contrastive loss. The dictionary keys are defined on-the-fly via a set of data samples.

In \[186\], a theoretical analysis on contrastive self-supervised learning points out that the learned representations are nearly optimal on downstream prediction tasks, whenever the two views provide a *redundant information* about the labels.

Remarks 19.10

*   •  The nonlinear projector, *g*[**ϕ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si470.png), is usually a feed-forward neural network with two to three layers employing the ReLU nonlinearity. As it is pointed out in \[35\], the use of this projector network acts beneficially on what the encoder learns. Note that contrastive loss implies a loss of information, since the network is trained so that **z** = *g*[**ϕ**](**h**)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si471.png) to be invariant in transformations. Hence, *g*[**ϕ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si470.png) can remove information that may be important to downstream tasks, such as color or orientation. By leveraging *g*[**ϕ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si470.png), more information can be formed and retained in ***h***, which is the input representation used in the downstream tasks.
*   •  A theoretical analysis of contrastive learning is provided in \[194\]. The paper introduces two properties, namely *alignment* and *uniformity*. Alignment favors encoders that assign similar features to similar samples. Uniformity promotes a feature distribution that preserves maximal information. It is shown that the contrastive loss directly optimizes for these two properties in the limit of infinite negative samples. This is in line with the spirit of contrastive learning, i.e., the representations to be invariant to unnecessary details, and at the same time to preserve as much information as possible, e.g., \[188\]. 
*   •  Contrastive techniques are closely related to a family of algorithms known as *deep metric learning* techniques (DML); see, e.g., \[13\] for related comments.

### 19.6.6 Self-distillation techniques

Knowledge distillation has been used as a method for transfer learning. The main idea is to transfer/“distill” knowledge that has been acquired, after training, by a large network (e.g., a neural network with many layers and parameters) to a smaller one. As it is most often the case, this is, also, an old idea and was first used in \[166\] to compress a hierarchy of RNNs into a single RNN. The idea was later used for model compression in \[29\], \[84\].

In the context of transfer learning, the rationale of the method is to first train a large/complex model, known as the *teacher*, via a large set of *labeled* data. In the sequel, a smaller network, known as the *student*, is trained via a set of training data that consist, mainly, of *unlabeled* samples. The latter training set is, also, known as the *transfer* set. The targets/pseudo labels used for the training of the student network are the corresponding outputs of the teacher network. For example, in \[84\], while training the student, both networks are fed with the same input samples and the pseudo labels used for the student are the corresponding *soft* class probabilities at the output of the teacher. As it is pointed out in \[84\], it turns out that by appropriately distilling knowledge from a large to a small network, the latter inherits generalization properties from the former.

The idea of employing two different networks that share knowledge has been adopted in the framework of self-supervision. To this end, two different views of an input sample feed the inputs of two *different* encoders, respectively. One of the branches is trained as the teacher, which generates the targets/pseudo labels, i.e., it operates as the target network. The other one acts as the student and it is sometimes called the *online* branch, which is trained to predict the corresponding targets/pseudo labels. Recall that such a rationale falls, also, under the generic idea of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085). Training the teacher and the student network takes place *simultaneously* on a set of unlabeled data and the goal is to drive the respective outputs of the two network branches to match as much as possible.

However, one has to be careful with the previous setup. There is always the danger of what we call *training collapse*, which corresponds to an undesired trivial solution. In other words, the outputs of both branches to collapse to a constant. To bypass this drawback, a line of research has emerged and various techniques have been proposed.

*BYOL*: In \[66\], the *bootstrap your own latent* (BYOL) algorithm was proposed. The corresponding architecture is shown in [Fig. 19.21](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0110). Two different augmented views of the input are produced by drawing from two distributions, *t* ∼ *T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si472.png) and *t*^′ ∼ *T*^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si473.png). In the current setup, we also assume, as in Section [19.6.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0215), that the input-output sets of the generic scheme, i.e., 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si398.png), ℋ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">H</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si411.png), to be singletons (*N* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si397.png)). The student (online) part comprises three networks: a) the representation (encoder) network, *f*[**θ**[1]]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si474.png), b) the projection network, *g*[**θ**[2]]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si475.png), and c) the predictor network, *q*[**θ**[3]]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si476.png). In the teacher branch, the same (structurally) models for the representation and the projection networks are used, which, however, are parameterized via a different set of parameters, i.e., *f*[**ξ**[1]]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si477.png) and *g*[**ξ**[2]]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si478.png).
