At the *t*\-th iteration step, the parameters of the teacher branch are updated via the so-called *exponential moving average* (EMA) (momentum) rationale, i.e.,

**ξ**[*i*]^((*t*)) = *α***ξ**[*i*]^((*t* − 1)) + (1 − *α*)**θ**[*i*]^((*t*)), *i* = 1, 2,<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si486.png)

where *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si487.png) is a user-defined momentum term. Since the parameters ***ξ*** are not updated via the backpropagation scheme, the computed gradients at each iteration step are propagated only in the student branch. This is denoted by the “sg” symbol that indicates a “stop gradient” propagation operation. It turns out, empirically, that using this training strategy, BYOL avoids collapsed solutions.

In \[66\], different convolutional residual networks were used to implement the encoders. For the case of ResNet-50 with width multiplier 1 (\[71\]), the encoded output, ***h***, was a 2048-dimensional vector. The representation vectors were then projected to a lower dimensional space by the projection networks, *g*. The latter was implemented as a multilayer perceptron consisting of a linear layer with 4096 nodes, followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation functions, and the last layer was a linear one with 256 output nodes. The network *q* had the same architecture as *g*.

Note that BYOL introduces two types of *asymmetry* between the two branches. One is the architectural asymmetry between the online and the target branches, due to the presence of the predictor in the upper branch. The other comes from the different parameter updating mechanisms that are used in each one of the branches. These asymmetries contribute to overcoming collapsed solutions.

The previous rationale for avoiding collapsed solutions has given birth to a number of variants that employ different loss objectives and/or different architectures, e.g., the so-called *data2vec* scheme proposed in \[10\]. In \[145\], a study of EMA is performed and the findings point out that the algorithm enjoys certain stability properties. Moreover, in this paper, a number of methods that evolve around the EMA scheme are investigated and compared.

*SimSIAM*: In \[34\], the so-called *simple siamese* (SimSIAM) network is proposed. It retains the main idea of the two branches as in BYOL, but instead of adopting the EMA algorithm to update the target branch, it forces both branches to share parameters. However, at each iteration of the backpropagation algorithm a stop gradient operation is employed to freeze the adaptation of the parameters in one of the branches and the corresponding output is treated as a constant. This simple modification turns out to contribute to the robustness against the collapsing phenomenon.

In \[182\], an attempt was made to understand the dynamics of BYOL and SimSIAM schemes with respect to their robustness against collapsing.

*DINO*: The *distillation with no label* (DINO) algorithm was proposed in \[32\] and it is a variant of BYOL. The EMA scheme is retained. The difference lies in that the output of each branch is *discretized* to a, say, *K*\-dimensional vector and the outputs of both branches are transformed to *K* probabilities via the use of our familiar softmax operation. Then, similarity between the two branches is quantified via the cross-entropy loss function.

The DINO scheme is the evolution of a line of research in this topic, see, e.g., \[30\], \[31\]. The underlying idea is to discretize the generated output representations and then resort to clustering arguments. For example, in \[31\], the *swapping assignments between multiple views* (SwAV) scheme is proposed. The outputs of the two branches are discretized, forming a code book with, say, *K* prototypes, and then a clustering operation is performed *in parallel* with the parameters' learning. Similarity between the two branches is achieved by encouraging the cluster assignments in both branches to be similar. Collapse is discouraged by employing appropriate regularization that promotes the formed clusters to be populated as uniformly as possible.

### 19.6.7 Correlation-based techniques

The main idea in all the techniques that we have treated so far is that of enforcing similarity/dissimilarity, in one way or another (depending on the specific method), among data that originate in two different branches. In the last category of this subsection the notion of correlation is mobilized as a measure of similarity. This leads to slightly different task formulation needs, and we treat such schemes as a different category.

The stage of our discussion is that of the canonical correlation method (CCA), which is treated in more detail in Section [20.4](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml). The main idea that underpins CCA is that if two sets of random variables (two random vectors) are involved, the value of their correlation depends on the coordinate system in which the random vectors are represented. The goal behind CCA is to seek a pair of linear transformations, one for each set of variables, such that after the transformation, the resulting transformed variables are maximally correlated. The main idea of CCA has been generalized to involve nonlinear transforms. For example, in \[5\], the objective becomes that of *jointly* learning the parameters of two networks such as their outputs are maximally correlated.

*Barlow twins*: This is a typical example of this family of schemes. The *Barlow twins* architecture, \[202\], follows the philosophy of the two identical (parameter sharing) branches, as that of [Fig. 19.19](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0100). However, instead of a contrastive loss, a similarity enforcing loss is employed based on correlations. As we will see, such a loss function has an “in-built” property to avoid collapse.

To simplify notation, let us denote as ***z*** and **z**^′<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si483.png) the outputs of the two branches, respectively. To form the loss function to be minimized with respect to the shared set of parameters, i.e., ***θ***, ***ϕ***, one sums over a mini-batch of input samples, to compute the elements of the corresponding normalized cross-correlation matrix, i.e.,

$C\_{i,j} = \\frac{\\sum\_{n}z\_{ni}z\_{nj}^{\\prime}}{\\sqrt{\\sum\_{n}z\_{ni}^{2}}\\sqrt{\\sum\_{n}z\_{nj}^{\\prime 2}}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si488.png)

where, for simplicity, we have assumed that **z**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si116.png) and **z**[*n*]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si257.png) have been centered to zero mean values. The loss function for optimizing with respect to the involved parameters is selected so that the normalized cross-correlation matrix, *C*, is as close as possible to the identity matrix, *I*. In other words, the diagonal elements, *C*[*i**i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si489.png), to be as close as possible to one, and the off-diagonal elements, *C*[*i**j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si490.png) for *i* ≠ *j*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si491.png), to be as close as possible to zero. Such a loss function can be formulated as

$\\mathcal{L}: = \\underset{\\text{invariance}}{\\underset{︸}{\\sum\\limits\_{i}\\left( 1 - C\_{ii} \\right)^{2}}} + \\lambda\\underset{\\text{redundancy}}{\\underset{︸}{\\sum\\limits\_{i}\\sum\\limits\_{j,j \\neq i}C\_{ij}^{2}}}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>invariance</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>redundancy</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si492.png)(19.54) 

Minimizing ℒ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si493.png) forces the diagonal elements to be close to 1 and at the same time the off-diagonal ones to be close to 0, and *λ* is a user-defined regularization parameter that weighs the relative importance of the two terms. As it is pointed out in \[202\], trying to equate all the diagonal elements in the *invariance* term to 1 is equivalent to increasing the correlation between all elements, *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si494.png) and *z*[*i*]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si495.png) in the same (*i*th) dimension of the two vectors. In other words, the minimization task forces, via this invariance term, to make the final output embeddings of the two branches invariant to the distortions applied by the input transformations. At the same time, the *redundancy reduction* term, by trying to zero the off-diagonal elements of the cross-correlation matrix, decorrelates the vector components at different vector dimensions. As a consequence, the output units contain non-redundant information about the input sample. The redundancy term could be seen as playing a similar role as the denominator in the contrastive loss function, Eq. [(19.53)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq125), that tries to increase dissimilarity among negative pairs. In \[202\], it is shown that the loss function in Eq. [(19.54)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq132) is an instantiation of the information bottleneck objective \[184\].

In \[202\], the encoder networks were implemented via the ResNet-50 convolutional network, giving rise to 2048-dimensional vector representations. For the projector networks, multilayer neural networks were used with three linear layers, each of 8192 nodes width. The first two layers were followed by batch normalization and then ReLU activations.

The name Barlow twins honors the great neuroscientist H. Barlow, who stated that the goal of the sensory system in our brains is to *encode* highly redundant inputs to a code that comprises statistically independent components, \[16\].

The techniques known as *whitening MSE* (W-MSE), \[53\], and *variance-invariance-covariance regularization* (VICReg), \[15\], are in the same line as the Barlow twins but they employ alternative loss functions. In the latter one, a comparative performance study of a number of self-supervised techniques within the framework of computer vision is provided.

Remarks 19.11

*   •  So far in our discussion, we focused on SSL techniques that are based on a single modality. However, multi-modal approaches have also been proposed. For example, in the *contrastive language-image pretraining* (CLIP), \[149\], and *a large-scale image and noisy-text embedding* (ALIGN), \[95\], methods, image-caption pairs are used to learn a joint embedding space for images and captions. Images and corresponding captions feed separate encoders that encode each modality into a fixed-length embedding vector. The embeddings of the image-caption pairs are aligned, whereas other combinations are repelled. Thus, it is no longer required to generate multiple augmented views. Following the contrastive learning rationale, semantically meaningful representations are learned by observing similar captions that re-occur with similar images. CLIP slightly deviates from the generic scheme of [Fig. 19.16](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0085). The upper branch involves only the encoder *f*[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si496.png) and does not use a predictor network, *g*[**ϕ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si470.png). The network *g*[**ξ**]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si497.png) plays the role of an encoder in the lower branch. We will return to the CLIP model in Section [19.7.7](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0290).
*   •  In \[13\], a number of practical implementation recipes for self-supervised learning are discussed, such as hyperparameter tuning, choice of architectures, optimizers and batch sizes, practical tips and pitfalls, as well as performance evaluation techniques.
*   •  Note that some of the generative techniques that have been discussed in Section [19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0015) can also be considered as special cases of self-supervised learning. For example, the autoencoders/VAEs are trained so that the output of the decoder is to reconstruct the input of the encoder. In the GAN networks, a discriminator is trained to recognize fake from real samples, via the use of unlabeled data, see also, \[117\].

### 19.6.8 Self-supervised learning: some concluding remarks

In the previous subsections, the focus was on the main directions that are currently popular in self-supervised learning. The emphasis was on some typical methods for each category with the aim to shed light on the main idea and principles that underpin each one of the categories.

At the time the current edition of the book is written, self-supervised learning is a hot area of research and a large number of papers are published every year, concerning novel methods and algorithms, comparative performance results in various applications as well as tools for theoretical analysis of the respective methods. Despite the fast-moving research, the breadth of SSL methods and their notable successes, there are still many open problems and questions to be answered.

For example, one of the challenges concerns the data augmentation phase. It is not a surprise to say that what is learned by the SSL methods is determined by the choice of the type of data augmentation. Because the pretext task differs from the downstream tasks, there is an inherent *misalignment or pretraining bias*. As it is pointed out in \[23\], the use of the projector network can mitigate some of the effects of this bias, but only to some degree. The role of the projector is further analyzed in \[24\]. In \[35\], it is stated that no single transformation type, e.g., random cropping or random color distortion, suffices to learn good representations, even though the model can almost perfectly identify the positive pairs in the contrastive task.

In \[50\], it is shown that different augmentations lead to learning different type of invariances. Moreover, it turns out that some of them are better on some downstream tasks than others. In \[48\], an extensive comparative experimental study is carried out in the context of computer vision, using over 40 downstream tasks and 13 SSL models. The findings in the paper point out that no single self-supervised method dominates overall, suggesting that universal pretraining is still unsolved. Another interesting finding from this study is that self-supervised methods can match and, even, outperform supervised representation learning across most tasks considered.

Besides data augmentation, the size of the involved networks is also a challenge. Currently, this is also a line of research. How large or how small the dimensionality of the encoder and the projector networks should be? Are they interrelated? This interplay and how this influences the performance for some SSL models is studied in, e.g., \[23\].

In spite of the rapid developments of self-supervised learning and the continual emergence of novel methods, there is still a lack of widely accepted principled guidelines for evaluating the “goodness” of the obtained representations, at the output of the encoder, across a wide range of potential tasks. This is a drawback that may hinder their practical deployment. The reason is that for most of the methods, during the pretext training phase, there is no loss function to account for the input reconstruction, which could indicate successful or unsuccessful training. Masked methods are the exception, because they are forced to reproduce the missing parts. To this end, a number of techniques have been proposed.

One path for the quality assessment of the obtained representation at the output of the encoder is based on the performance of the downstream task. To this end, one popular protocol is to add a linear classifier (linear probe) on top of the encoder, which is trained via the corresponding labeled examples, e.g., \[135\]. The advantage of using a linear classifier is that its performance heavily relies on the quality of the representation since its discriminative power is low and, also, it is computationally cheap. Extensions to employ non-linear classifiers, such as feed-forward neural networks that comprise two or three layers or *k*\-NN classifiers, have also been used, e.g., \[197\]. However, relying only on downstream tasks can limit our understanding of what information is retained in the representation of a given input.

Another path is to move away from labeled training. For example, in \[22\] a feature inversion technique is proposed for visualizing, in the input data space, the learned representations/features, for computer vision applications. However, such an approach suffers from the bias, introduced by the specific inversion method that is used, and it is not clear how these methods would perform on different data modalities other than computer vision.

In \[56\], the rank of the output representation matrix is used as a performance evaluation index. At the heart of this method lies Cover's theorem, \[40\] (see, also, Chapter [11](#Chp011_519-582_B9780443292385000172.xhtml)), which relates the training accuracy of a given embedding in linear regression or classification with the corresponding data matrix rank. The training accuracy increases with increasing rank. The rank criterion, called RankMe, is tightly related to what is known as *dimensional collapse* (e.g., \[89\], \[97\]). This phenomenon is different to what we called before as training collapse and it refers to learning rank-deficient (dimensional collapsed) embeddings. In other words, the information encoded across different dimensions of the representation at the output of the encoder is redundant. The RankMe criterion links dimensional collapse with the quality of the obtained representation.

In \[2\], the eigenspectrum of the empirical output representation covariance matrix is employed. It is demonstrated that the eigenspectrum decay can serve as a measure of representation quality.

In a nutshell, self-supervised learning is a highly promising and powerful learning method that, at the time the current edition of this book is being compiled, is dynamically evolving.

## 19.7 Diffusion models

The most recent family of generative networks is that of *diffusion models*. Strictly speaking, these models should have been discussed as part of Section [19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0015). The reason they are presented separately is that their treatment requires some concepts and terms which have been introduced in Sections [19.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0070) and [19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0190).

Diffusion models are *probabilistic* models that are closely related to the notion of Markov chains, which have been introduced in Chapter [14](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml). The basic idea that underpins these networks was proposed in \[169\] and it is inspired from the field of statistical physics. The main rationale is that in order to learn a generative model, a two-stage procedure is followed. One starts by systematically and slowly destroying structure in a data distribution via an iterative process. This is known as the *forward or diffusion process*. In the sequel, during the second stage, one *learns* a *reverse process* which *restores* structure in the data. In practice, in the forward process the input data, e.g. an image array, is gradually perturbed by adding Gaussian noise in a step-wise fashion. In the reverse path, the task is to recover the original input data from the generated noisy (diffused) versions, by reversing the process in a corresponding step-wise rationale.

There are three main directions in implementing diffusion models, namely: a) the denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), b) the noise conditional score networks (NCSNs), and c) modeling the forward and reverse processes via stochastic differential equations (SDEs). Our emphasis will be on the first path that was historically the first to be proposed in \[169\]. Furthermore, the underlying theoretical notions are easier to be grasped by the newcomer, and the related mathematical tools have already been treated in previous chapters in the book.

### 19.7.1 Denoising diffusion probabilistic models

At the heart of *denoising probabilistic models* (DDPMs) lies a set of latent random (vector) variables (see, Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)), **x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si498.png), where the subscripts, *t* = 1, 2, …, *T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si499.png), denote the corresponding time/steps in an iterative Markov chain process.^([^(142)](#fn142))

*p*[**θ**](**x**[0]) = ∫*p*[**θ**](**x**[0 : *T*])*d***x**[1 : *T*],<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∫</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si505.png)(19.55) 

where the joint distribution *p*[**θ**](**x**[0], **x**[1], …, **x**[*T*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si506.png) is denoted as *p*[**θ**](**x**[0 : *T*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si507.png) and *d***x**[1 : *T*]<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si508.png) is the shorthand of *d***x**[1]*d***x**[2]…*d***x**[*T*]<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si509.png).

*Forward process*: Given an observation (vector), **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), the goal of the forward/diffusion process is to generate a corresponding sequence of diffused (latent) random variables/vectors, **x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si498.png). The diffusion process adds noise according to the following *predetermined* and *fixed* Markov chain,

![](images/B9780443292385000251/fx013.jpg)

where *β*[*t*] ∈ \[0, 1)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si510.png) is a sequence of process variances. Although this sequence could be learned, in a typical model it is fixed according to a user-defined schedule, see, e.g., \[169\]. For example, in \[85\], *β*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si511.png) is set equal to 10^( − 4)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si512.png) and it increases linearly up to the value of *β*[*T*] = 0.02<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.02</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si513.png), where *T* is set equal to 1000. In other words, the conditional/transition distribution (see Chapter [14](#Chp014_717-754_B9780443292385000202.xhtml)) at time *t* is Gaussian with the mean value being a scaled version of **x**[*t* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si514.png) and covariance matrix equal to *β*[*t*]*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si515.png), where *I* is the identity matrix.

Due to the Gaussian nature of the conditionals, it is not difficult to show ([Problem 19.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0060)) that the diffused version at time *t*, conditioned on the input observation, is described by,

$q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}|\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) = \\mathcal{N}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{t}|\\sqrt{{\\overline{a}}\_{t}}\\mathbf{x}\_{0},(1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t})I \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si516.png)(19.56) 

where, *a*[*t*] :  = 1 − *β*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si517.png) and ${\\overline{a}}\_{t}: = \\prod\_{k = 1}^{t}a\_{k}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∏</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si518.png). Alternatively, given an observation, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), and using the reparameterization trick, discussed in Section [19.2.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0065), we can write

$\\mathbf{x}\_{t} = \\sqrt{{\\overline{a}}\_{t}}\\mathbf{x}\_{0} + \\sqrt{1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t}}\\mathbf{\\epsilon},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si519.png)(19.57) 

which is used for sampling and **ϵ** ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si520.png). Note that if *β*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si521.png) is selected so that ${\\overline{a}}\_{T} \\approx 0$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si522.png), then the latent random vector at time *T*, **x**[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si523.png), follows the standard Gaussian, i.e., **x**[*T*] ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si524.png).

*Reverse process*: This is defined as a Markov chain with *learned* Gaussians (transitions), starting from *p*[**θ**](**x**[*T*]) :  = *p*(**x**[*T*]) = 𝒩(**x**[*T*]|0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si525.png), according to the following rule,

![](images/B9780443292385000251/fx014.jpg)

where **μ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si526.png) and *Σ*[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si527.png) are learned during training. As we will soon see, the parameters, ***θ***, which are estimated during training, define a neural network that is used for learning the mean values as well as the covariance matrices. Note the explicit dependence on the time step, *t*.

Recall that our final goal is to be able to *sample* from *p*[**θ**](**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si504.png), given by Eq. [(19.55)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq133). The rationale behind diffusion methods is that for small values of *β*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si521.png), *t* = 1, 2, …<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si528.png), the reversal of a diffusion process is of an *identical* functional form as the forward one, \[169\], \[52\]. Thus, since the conditionals in the forward process are Gaussians, the conditionals in the reverse process should also be Gaussians. Hence, the goal of training is to optimize with respect to the involved parameters, ***θ***, so that *p*[**θ**](**x**[0], **x**[1], …, **x**[*T*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si506.png) to be as close as possible to *q*(**x**[0], **x**[1], …, **x**[*T*])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si529.png). We will come to this soon.

[Figs. 19.22A and 19.22B](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0125) illustrate the forward and the reverse processes, respectively. Looking at it from a slightly different view point, the forward process could be considered as an *encoder* and the reverse one as the *decoder*. However, a notable characteristic of the diffusion models is that the coding, through the sequence of the generated latent variables, is not the result of a learning process, but, instead, the forward process follows a *fixed* Markov chain deployment that gradually adds noise to the data. In contrast, for example, in the variational autoencoders (Section [19.2.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0065)), the latent variables in the encoder are learned from the data.

![Figure 19.22 (A) In the forward/diffusion process, one gradually adds noise to the observed data, x0, sampled from an unknown distribution, q(x0), till the final stage, T, where xT is approximately described by (Gaussian) random noise. Diffusion is performed on the basis of a pre-selected and fixed Markov process, q(xt|xt−1). (B) The reverse process acts as a denoising scheme, that starts from a random noise sample, xT, and its goal is to produce a sample from the original (unknown) distribution. The reverse process follows a learned backward Markov chain, pθ(xt−1|xt), that tries to “match” the diffusion steps of the forward path.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr022.jpg)

[Figure 19.22](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf2225) (A) In the forward/diffusion process, one gradually adds noise to the observed data, ***x***[0], sampled from an unknown distribution, *q*(***x***[0]), till the final stage, *T*, where ***x***[*T*] is approximately described by (Gaussian) random noise. Diffusion is performed on the basis of a pre-selected and *fixed* Markov process, *q*(***x***[*t*]|***x***[*t*−1]). (B) The reverse process acts as a denoising scheme, that starts from a random noise sample, ***x***[*T*], and its goal is to produce a sample from the original (unknown) distribution. The reverse process follows a *learned* backward Markov chain, *p*[***θ***](***x***[*t*−1]|***x***[*t*]), that tries to “match” the diffusion steps of the forward path.

One could also look at the reverse path as a denoising process, whose aim is to remove the noise that was gradually added during the forward process. From this point of view, the underlying action resembles that of the denoising autoencoders (Section [19.2.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0035)).

#### Training

The goal of training is to obtain estimates of the parameters ***θ***. Note that these parameters implicitly define the mean values and the variances of the involved conditionals in the reverse path. The loss function to be optimized is the usual “suspect,” i.e., the likelihood function, *p*[**θ**](**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si504.png). In other words, the objective is to select ***θ*** such that the probability *p*[**θ**](**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si504.png), assigned to **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), is as large as possible. To this end, the variational approximation method, which has been introduced and discussed in Chapters [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml), will be mobilized.

Following the definition of the bound in Eqs. [(12.63)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [(12.68)](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml), tailored for our current needs, the following inequality holds (see, also, [Problem 19.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0065)),

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/fx015.jpg)(19.58) 

Note that the expectation is with respect to *q*(**x**[1 : *T*]|**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si530.png), i.e., the joint distribution of the latent variables conditioned on the observation, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), in the forward process. The numerator, *p*[**θ**](**x**[0 : *T*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si507.png), is the joint (model) distribution of the observations and the latent variables. Taking the negative of Eq. (19.62), we obtain

$- \\ln p\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) \\leq \\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{1:T}|\\mathbf{x}\_{0})}\\left\\lbrack \\ln\\frac{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{1:T}|\\mathbf{x}\_{0})}{p\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{0:T})} \\right\\rbrack: = L\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{0}}.$<mml:math><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" According to the variational approximation method, instead of minimizing the negative log-likelihood, which cannot be obtained in a computationally tractable form, we are going to minimize its upper bound, denoted as *L*[**x**[0]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si533.png).

minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mtext>denoising matching</mml:mtext><mml:mspace linebreak="newline"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi ![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si534.png)(19.60) 

The bound involves three components:

*   •  *L*[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si535.png): The first component is a constant independent of ***θ***. Recall that *p*(**x**[*T*])<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si536.png) is the standard Gaussian. Also, the conditional Gaussian of the forward process does not depend on ***θ***. This term encourages the final noisified conditional distribution to be as close as possible to the standard Gaussian one, in the Kullback–Leibler divergence sense. 
*   •  *L*[*t* − 1], *t* = 2, 3, …, *T*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si537.png): The second component is the most interesting one and it comprises the sum of Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergences (see the definition in Eq. [(2.161)](#Chp002_19-64_B9780443292385000081.xhtml)). Taking into account that the KL divergence is a non-negative quantity, minimizing the bound forces the desired denoising conditional, *p*[**θ**](**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si538.png), in the reverse process, to be as close as possible to *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], **x**[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si539.png), see [Fig. 19.23](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0130). Note that *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], **x**[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si539.png) defines the step of denoising **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) having access to the ground-truth original noiseless example, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png). Thus, each one of the terms in the summation contributes to the step-wise denoising process.

![Figure 19.23 During training, the model parameters, θ, in the reverse process are adjusted so that the reverse model conditionals, pθ(xt−1|xt), t = 2,3,…,T, to be as close as possible to the true reverse posteriors conditioned on the observations, x0.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr023.jpg)

[Figure 19.23](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf2250) During training, the model parameters, ***θ***, in the reverse process are adjusted so that the reverse model conditionals, *p*[***θ***](***x***[*t*−1]|***x***[*t*]), *t* = 2,3,…,*T*, to be as close as possible to the true reverse posteriors *conditioned* on the observations, ***x***[0].

*   This is because the minimum of each term is achieved when the numerator and the denominator become equal and the KL divergence becomes zero. Moreover, each one of the *T* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si541.png) KL divergence terms in the sum can be computed in a closed form, since the involved pdfs are Gaussians. Indeed, *p*[**θ**](**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si538.png) is Gaussian by its definition in Eq. (19.61) with mean value **μ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si526.png) and covariance matrix *Σ*[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si527.png). The other pdf in the numerator, *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], **x**[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si539.png), is not defined directly and it pops up in the derivation of the bound, by exploiting the Markov property of the forward process, i.e., *q*(**x**[*t*]|**x**[*t* − 1]) = *q*(**x**[*t*]|**x**[*t* − 1], **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si542.png)) ([Problem 19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0070)). Note that the true posterior, *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si543.png), is not computationally tractable, since one has to integrate out the dependence on **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), and the respective distribution is unknown. However, conditioning it on **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png) renders it to a Gaussian (\[85\] and [Problem 19.7](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0075)), i.e.,

$q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t - 1}|\\mathbf{x}\_{t},\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) = \\mathcal{N}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{t - 1}|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},\\mathbf{x}\_{0}),{\\widetilde{\\beta}}\_{t}I \\right),$<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

*   where,

${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) = \\frac{\\sqrt{{\\overline{a}}\_{t - 1}}\\beta\_{t}}{1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t}}\\mathbf{x}\_{0} + \\frac{\\sqrt{a\_{t}}(1 - mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si560.png). In other words, the task of training becomes equivalent to a nonlinear regression one. Similar arguments hold if the covariance matrix is not fixed but parameterized, \[169\].
    *   •  *L*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si561.png): This term can be interpreted as a reconstruction term that predicts the log-probability of the original data samples given the first-step latent variables. The term plays the same role as the corresponding one in the VAE in Eq. [(19.22)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq47). Due to the Gaussian nature of the conditionals, this component can also be computed in closed form. For the case of Eq. [(19.69)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq143), it is straightforward to see that minimizing *L*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si561.png) is equivalent with forcing **μ**[**θ**](**x**[1], 1)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si562.png) to be close, in the Euclidean norm sense, to **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png).

The cost function results by averaging over all the observations, i.e., 𝔼[**x**[0] ∼ *q*(**x**[0])]\[*L*[**x**[0]]\]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si563.png), which in practice is obtained by taking the sample mean over all the observed input examples.

#### A simplified model

The model simplification that was introduced before, i.e., *Σ*[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*) = *σ*[*t*]²*I*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si564.png), was further exploited in \[85\]. There are different possible choices for the sequence *σ*[*t*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si565.png). One possibility is to set *σ*[*t*]² = *β*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si566.png) that makes the covariance matrices involved in the reverse path to be equal to those involved in the forward process. This assumption leads to Eq. [(19.70)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq144), and the training is simplified to adjust the output of the neural network at time step *t*, **μ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si526.png), to predict ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},\\mathbf{x}\_{0})$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si560.png). Let us now elaborate a bit more on Eq. [(19.70)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq144).

Combining Eqs. [(19.59)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq135) and [(19.66)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq140) and after a bit of algebra ([Problem 19.8](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#o0080)), one obtains that

${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{a\_{t}}}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{t} - \\frac{\\beta\_{t}}{\\sqrt{1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t}}}\\mathbf{\\epsilon} \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si567.png)(19.67) 

where ***ϵ*** is the vector of noise samples drawn from the standard Gaussian to obtain **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) (Eq. [(19.59)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq135)). Recall that the goal of training is to estimate **μ**[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si557.png) to optimally predict the corresponding ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{t}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si558.png) in Eq. [(19.71)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq145), given the samples **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) as input to the involved neural network. Thus, in \[85\], it is suggested to use the reparameterization,

$\\mathbf{\\mu}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t) = \\frac{1}{{\\sqrt{a}}\_{t}}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{t} - \\frac{\\beta\_{t}}{\\sqrt{1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t}}}\\mathbf{\\epsilon}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si568.png)(19.68) 

where **ϵ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si569.png) is a function approximator (implemented via a neural network) intended to predict ***ϵ***, in Eq. [(19.71)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq145), from **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png). Plugging Eqs. [(19.71)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq145) and [(19.72)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq146) into Eq. [(19.70)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq144), the following is obtained

$L\_{t - 1} = \\lambda\_{t}||\\mathbf{\\epsilon} - \\mathbf{\\epsilon}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t)||^{2},\\ \\ \\ \\lambda\_{t}: = \\frac{\\beta\_{t}^{2}}{2\\sigma\_{t}^{2}a\_{t}(1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t})},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak"
