where **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) is sampled according to Eq. [(19.59)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq135) and *λ*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si571.png) is a weighting sequence.

Note that although *λ*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si571.png) guarantees optimality, in practice it can get relatively large values for some time steps *t* (recall that *σ*[*t*]² = *β*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si566.png)). In \[85\], it is pointed out that setting *λ*[*t*] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si573.png) results in good performance. Other, more “fancy,” choices for the weighting sequence have also been proposed, see, e.g., \[37\].

The cost function to be minimized results from the bound in Eq. [(19.64)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq138), after taking the expectation over all observations, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png). Moreover, note that the involved conditional expectation with respect to *q*(**x**[*t*]|**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si574.png) is equivalent with taking the expectation with respect to *p*(**ϵ**) = 𝒩(**ϵ**|0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si575.png), from Eq. [(19.59)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq135). Hence, for the case of the simplified model, the contribution to the cost of the second component becomes

$\\sum\\limits\_{t = 2}^{T}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{0} \\sim q(\\mathbf{x}\_{0})}\\ \\mathbb{E}\_{\\epsilon \\sim \\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\\left\\lbrack \\lambda\_{t}||\\mathbf{\\epsilon} - \\mathbf{\\epsilon}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t)||^{2} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si576.png)(19.70) 

where **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) is given in terms of ***ϵ*** in Eq. [(19.59)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq135). In practice, expectations are replaced by sample means. In \[85\], it is suggested that instead of summing up the terms over time t, one can randomly select a time index in \[1, *T*\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si577.png) using uniform sampling and perform parameter updating based on the corresponding term. The second expectation with respect to noise is approximated by a singe sample. [Algorithm 19.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0090) summarizes the training steps. The term *f*[**θ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si441.png) denotes the output of the parameterized neural network.

Algorithm 19.4

**Training the DDP model**

*   •  **Repeat** 
    1.  –  **x**[0] ∼ *q*(**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si503.png); New input observation.
    2.  –  *t* ∼ 𝒰\[1, *T*\]<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si578.png); Uniform discrete distribution.
    3.  –  **ϵ** ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si520.png); Sample from the standard Gaussian.
    4.  –  $\\mathbf{x}\_{t} = {\\sqrt{\\overline{a}}}\_{t}\\mathbf{x}\_{0} + \\sqrt{1 - {\\overline{a}}\_{t}}\\mathbf{\\epsilon}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si580.png); Noisy sample at time *t* (Eq. [(19.59)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq135)).
    5.  –  **ϵ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*) = *f*[**θ**](**x**[*t*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si581.png); Output of the neural network.
    6.  –  *Δ***θ** = ∇[**θ**]||**ϵ** − **ϵ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)||²<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si582.png); Compute gradient.
    7.  –  **θ**(new) = **θ**(old) − *μ**Δ***θ**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>new</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mtext>old</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si583.png); Update parameters.
*   •  **Until** Convergence

Training is performed via any backpropagation-type algorithm. Once training has been completed and the optimal parameters, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png), have been obtained, one is ready to generate samples via the reverse process. The heart of sampling in the reverse path beats around Eq. (19.61) and its respective reparameterization that leads to,

**x**[*t* − 1] = **μ**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*) + *σ*[*t*]**z**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si584.png)(19.71) 

where **z** ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si585.png), and **μ**[**θ**[\*]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si586.png) is given in Eq. [(19.72)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq146). However, now, the samples **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) are generated via sampling in the reverse process. For step *t* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si587.png), we set the sample **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png) equal to **μ**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[1], 1)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si588.png); see related discussion in \[85\] and, also, recall that **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png) was the target value of the latter mean value during training, (term *L*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si561.png) in Eq. [(19.64)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq138)). [Algorithm 19.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0095) summarizes the steps.

Algorithm 19.5

**Sampling of the DDPM reverse process**

*   •  **x**[*T*] ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si524.png); Sample from the standard Gaussian.

Remarks 19.12

*   •  As it is pointed out in \[85\], setting in Eq. [(19.73)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq147) *λ*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si571.png) equal to 1, is equivalent with optimizing a *weighted* variational approximation bound, which downweighs the contribution of terms that are associated with small values of *t*. These terms are contributed from diffused input samples that contain small amounts of noise. Thus, putting relatively less emphasis on them helps the optimization algorithm to focus on the more noisy versions that correspond to larger vales of *t*.
*   •  Taking the gradient of the logarithm of the Gaussian in Eq. [(19.58)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq134), it is not difficult to see that

We will come back to this in Section [19.7.3](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0260).

### 19.7.2 The neural network implementation

The goal of training is to learn the parameters of a neural network, denoted as *f*[**θ**]( ⋅ )<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si441.png). The inputs to the network are samples, **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png), *t* = 1, 2…, *T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si596.png), of the corresponding latent (diffused) variables that are generated during the forward process. The network is trained so that, at each time step, the corresponding output to predict the associated target. For example, for *t* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si597.png), the output-target pairs are $(\\mathbf{\\mu}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t),{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\mu}}}\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},\\mathbf{x}\_{0}))$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si598.png) or (**ϵ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*), **ϵ**)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si599.png).

The parameters, ***θ***, that define the neural network are *shared* by all time steps. In principle, any neural network whose input and output are of the same dimensions could be used. However, one of the most popular architectures that has been used in practice is the U-Net, \[158\], or variants of it. A block diagram illustration of the U-Net, in the context of diffusion networks, is shown in [Fig. 19.24](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0135). Each block in the figure indicates a stage of the network. The U-Net is a convolutional network (Section [18.12](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml)) that employs a contractive path followed by an expansive one that reminds us of the U-shape. In other words, the output feature maps for each stage of the network become smaller and smaller in size via downsampling, up to some minimum value. Then, upsampling takes place in a symmetric way, compared to the downsampling. A key feature of the U-Net is the existence of the skip connections (dotted lines in [Fig. 19.24](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0135)), that pass information from the downsampling stages to the corresponding upsampling ones. One could consider the contractive path as an encoder. The minimum size feature maps, block #5 in the middle of the figure, encode/learn information that “resides” in the input data, and it is important to the associated prediction task, see, e.g., \[168\]. Input and output of the U-Net are of the same dimensions.

![Figure 19.24 A typical variant of the U-Net used in diffusion networks: U-Net accepts as input the noisy images, xt (e.g., of dimensions 128 × 128), and outputs predictions, ϵθ(xt,t), of the same dimensions (e.g., 128 × 128). The U-Net consists of a contracting path of residual convolutional layers followed by an expansive one (U-shape). As the size of the feature maps keeps decreasing (increasing) the number of channels keeps increasing (decreasing). Feature maps from the contractive path are copied and concatenated with feature maps in the expansive path (dotted lines). The bottom line indicates the time positional vector embedding, which is passed to the convolutional layers after appropriate projections to match the dimensions of the corresponding computed feature maps.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr024.jpg)

Figure 19.24 A typical variant of the U-Net used in diffusion networks: U-Net accepts as input the noisy images, ***x***[*t*] (e.g., of dimensions 128 × 128), and outputs predictions, ***ϵ***[***θ***](***x***[*t*],*t*), of the same dimensions (e.g., 128 × 128). The U-Net consists of a contracting path of residual convolutional layers followed by an expansive one (U-shape). As the size of the feature maps keeps decreasing (increasing) the number of channels keeps increasing (decreasing). Feature maps from the contractive path are copied and concatenated with feature maps in the expansive path (dotted lines). The bottom line indicates the time positional vector embedding, which is passed to the convolutional layers after appropriate projections to match the dimensions of the corresponding computed feature maps.

Each block in the contractive path consists of two successive residual convolutional layers (e.g., 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si600.png) convolutions) followed by an ReLU activation function and a downsampling operation. The latter is preformed via a pooling operation (2 × 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si601.png) max pooling). At each downsampling step, the size of each dimension of the computed feature maps is halved and we double the number of the feature channels. Thus, for the case of the figure, assume a 128 × 128<mml:math><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si602.png) input image, and that block #1 computes 16 feature maps (channels) of size 128 × 128<mml:math><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si602.png). After downsampling, these are reduced in size to 64 × 64<mml:math><mml:mn>64</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>64</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si603.png) and are provided as input to block #2. Block #2 computes 32 feature maps of size 64 × 64<mml:math><mml:mn>64</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>64</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si603.png), which after downsampling are reduced to size 32 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si604.png) and become the input to block #3. Following this rationale, block #3 computes 64 maps of size 32 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si604.png), block #4 128 maps of size 16 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si394.png), and the one in the middle, block #5, outputs 256 feature maps of size 8 × 8<mml:math><mml:mn>8</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si605.png).

In the expansive path, a reverse operation takes place. The number of channels decreases and the size of the feature maps increases in symmetry to the contractive path. To achieve this, each one of the blocks #6 to #9 comprises an upsampling operation by 2, followed by a 2 × 2<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si601.png) convolution operation that halves the number of channels. The feature maps computed in the contractive path are copied and concatenated with the corresponding feature maps in the expansive path followed by two cascaded residual convolutional layers (e.g., 3 × 3<mml:math><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si600.png) convolutions). Thus, block #6 computes 128 channels of size 16 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si394.png), and so on, until the last block that computes 16 channels of 128 × 128<mml:math><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si602.png). The output 128 × 128<mml:math><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si602.png) image is formed via an extra 1 × 1<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si606.png) convolution (Section [18.12.2](#Chp018_885-995_B978044329238500024X.xhtml)) that computes a weighted average over the 16 128 × 128<mml:math><mml:mn>128</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>128</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si602.png) feature maps.

When the U-Net is used in the context of diffusion models, some extra information is required that is related to time. The parameters, ***θ***, describing the U-Net are shared by all time steps in the reverse process. However, as we have already discussed before in various places, the outputs of the network (e.g., **ϵ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*))<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si607.png) depend explicitly on time, *t*. In diffusion models, time carries important information that is related to the amount of noise degradation of the input. Thus, time information should be provided explicitly to the network. The method of positional embedding, which has been discussed in the context of transformers (Section [19.3.4](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0090)), is adopted to implement this goal. To this end, time is encoded into a vector of a user-defined dimension, and this information is passed to each one of the U-Net stages. Furthermore, for each block, an extra projection via a linear network is needed to match the time vector embedding dimensions to those of the corresponding U-Net layers. Time information is exploited in an additive way to the corresponding feature maps.

Furthermore, in most diffusion model implementations, an extra attention layer (Section [19.3.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0095)) is employed between two successive residual blocks. For example, in \[85\], this layer is added after the 16 × 16<mml:math><mml:mn>16</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>16</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si394.png) feature map resolution of the corresponding U-Net implementation.^([^(144)](#fn144))

### 19.7.3 Noise conditional score networks

Besides the previously treated DDPMs, other approaches for building diffusion models have also been developed. The *noise conditional score network* (NCSN) proposed in \[172\] has its roots in \[93\]. In a general setting, given a probability distribution, *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si608.png), its Stein *score function* is defined as ∇[**x**]ln *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si609.png). Note that the gradient is a vector that points to the direction along which the pdf, *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si608.png), has its largest growth (see, e.g., Section [5.2](#Chp005_177-248_B9780443292385000111.xhtml)). Thus, if the goal is to sample from this distribution, it is reasonable to exploit this information so that to move from a randomly drawn sample, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), toward samples in regions of high density. This process can take place iteratively, via what is known in physics as the *Langevin dynamics*, described as,

$\\mathbf{x}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{x}^{(i - 1)} + \\frac{\\gamma}{2}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\ln q(\\mathbf{x}^{(i - 1)}) + \\sqrt{\\gamma}\\mathbf{\\epsilon}\_{i},\\ i = 1,2,\\ldots,N,$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si610.png)(19.72) 

where **ϵ**[*i*] ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si611.png). The starting point **x**^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si612.png) is sampled from a prior distribution and *γ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si613.png) is a control variable that adjusts the relative magnitude of the involved terms. It can be shown that as *N* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si614.png) and *γ* → 0<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">→</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si615.png), the distribution of **x**^((*N*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si616.png) equals that of *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si608.png). Thus, **x**^((*N*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si616.png) becomes an exact sample from *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si608.png) under some general regularity conditions, \[172\].

However, since *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si608.png) is not known, one has to resort to approximations. In the context of diffusion models, *q*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si608.png) refers to the pdf associated with the observed input samples. Following the rationale that underlies such models, the required approximation is achieved by gradually disturbing a given observation point, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), via a number of steps that add noise, according to a sequence of variances, *σ*[1]² < *σ*[2]² < … < *σ*[*T*]²<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si617.png). A typical model follows conditionals, *q*(**x**[*t*]|**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si574.png), of the Gaussian form, 𝒩(**x**[*t*]|**x**[0], *σ*[*t*]²*I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si618.png), *t* = 1, 2, …, *T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si499.png). For sampling purposes, the previous Gaussian assumption is expressed as

**x**[*t*] = **x**[0] + *σ*[*t*]**ϵ**, **ϵ** ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si619.png)(19.73) 

A noise conditional score network is a deep neural network, which is trained to *estimate* the score function ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *q*(**x**[*t*]|**x**[0])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si620.png). Ideally, one would like to obtain estimates of ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *q*(**x**[*t*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si621.png), but this is not, in general, computationally tractable. So we rest on the corresponding conditionals, as we did with the DDP models. Due to the Gaussian assumption, i.e., 𝒩(**x**[*t*]|**x**[0], *σ*[*t*]²*I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si618.png), it is trivial to show that

$\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{t}}\\ln q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}|\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) = - \\frac{\\mathbf{x}\_{t} - \\mathbf{x}\_{0}}{\\sigma\_{t}^{2}},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si622.png)

and taking into account Eq. [(19.77)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq152), we get

$\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{t}}\\ln q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}|\\mathbf{x}\_{0}) = - \\frac{1}{\\sigma\_{t}}\\mathbf{\\epsilon},\\ t = 1,2,\\ldots,T.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si623.png)

Denoting the output of the neural network (e.g., U-Net) at step *t*, **s**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si624.png), the network is trained to minimize the cost function,

$J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\frac{1}{T}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{T}\\lambda\_{t}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{0} \\sim q(\\mathbf{x}\_{0})}\\ \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{\\epsilon} \\sim \\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\\ \\left\\lbrack ||\\mathbf{\\epsilon} + \\sigma\_{t}\\mathbf{s}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t)||^{2} \\right\\rbrack,$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si625.png)(19.74) 

where *λ*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si571.png) is a weighting sequence (which has absorbed *σ*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si626.png) in Eq. [(19.78)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq155)), and **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) is given via Eq. [(19.77)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq152). Note that this is the counterpart of Eq. [(19.74)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq148), which also establishes a bridge between the two approaches; see, also, [Remarks 19.12](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0100).

After training, the optimal values of the parameters, **θ**[\*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si387.png), are obtained. When, at step *t*, a sample, **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png), is applied to the input of the neural network, the output of the network, **s**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si627.png), provides a corresponding estimate of ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *q*(**x**[*t*])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si621.png).

Sampling is performed according to [Algorithm 19.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0105).

Algorithm 19.6

**Sampling of the NSCN reverse process**

*   •  **Input** 
    1.  –  *N*; Number of Langevin iterations.
    2.  –  *γ*[1], *γ*[2], …, *γ*[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si628.png); Sequence of control variables in Langevin equation.
*   •  **x**[*T*]^((0)) ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si629.png); Draw the first sample at *t* = *T*<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si630.png).
*   •  **For** *t* = *T*, *T* − 1, …, 1<mml:math><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si631.png), **Do** 
    1.  –  **For** *i* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si632.png), **Do**; Generate *N* samples for each step *t*. 
        1.  ⁎  **ϵ** ∼ 𝒩(0, *I*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∼</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si520.png)
        2.  ⁎  $\\mathbf{x}\_{t}^{(i)} = \\mathbf{x}\_{t}^{(i - 1)} + \\frac{\\gamma\_{t}}{2}\\mathbf{s}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}^{(i - 1)},t) + \\sqrt{\\gamma\_{t}}\\mathbf{\\epsilon}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" In \[172\], the involved parameters are set as *T* = 10<mml:math><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si639.png), *N* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si640.png), and the sequence of increasing standard deviations follows a geometric progression starting from *σ*[1] = 0.1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si641.png) to *σ*[10] = 10<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si642.png).

### 19.7.4 Generative modeling via stochastic differential equations

In the two previously discussed approaches for constructing diffusion models, the perturbation of the input data was performed via a *finite* number of noise distributions. An alternative approach was proposed in \[173\], where a *continuum* of distributions is employed, which evolve over time according to a diffusion process. The method builds upon a stochastic differential equation (SDE) that progressively diffuses a data point to random noise. Moreover, the corresponding SDE is not trainable and does not depend on data. It turns out that this process can be reversed, via a reverse-time SDE that molds noise back to data for sample generation.

Without resorting to strict definitions related to stochastic differential equations, differentials of random variables, Wiener processes, and Brownian motion (see, e.g., \[140\]) and following \[173\], the (forward) diffusion SDE is written as

*d***x** = **f**(**x**, *t*)*d**t* + *g*(*t*)*d***w**,<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">w</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si643.png)(19.75) 

where **w** is a standard Wiener process, i.e., a Brownian motion, and **f**(⋅,*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si644.png) is a vector function that determines the drift and *g*(*t*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si645.png) a function that determines the diffusion of the SDE. In \[173\], it is shown that DDPM and NCSN result as different discretizations of this SDE. It has been shown (\[4\]) that there exists a reverse SDE^([^(145)](#fn145))

$d\\mathbf{x} = \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{x},t) - g{(t)}^{2}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\ln q\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack dt + g(t)d\\widetilde{\\mathbf{w}},$<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si646.png)(19.76) 

where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{w}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">w</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si647.png) is a standard Wiener process with time flowing backwards from *T* to 0, *dt* is an infinitesimal negative time step, and *q*[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si648.png) denotes the distribution of **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si649.png) in the forward process. The main issue with Eq. [(19.80)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq157) is to learn the score of the involved distribution, ∇[**x**]ln *q*[*t*](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si650.png). In \[173\], it is shown that there exists a deterministic counterpart of Eq. [(19.80)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq157), given by the following ordinary differential equation (ODE),

$d\\mathbf{x} = \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{x},t) - \\frac{1}{2}g^{2}(t)\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\ln q\_{t}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack dt,$<mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si652.png)(19.77) 

which can be determined from Eq. [(19.80)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq157), once the scores are known. The ODE in Eq. [(19.81)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq159) is coined the *probability flow* ODE, and its trajectories have the same marginal pdfs as the reverse-time SDE in Eq. [(19.80)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq157). Once the score function is estimated, sampling is performed after solving the involved SDE or ODE via any appropriate numerical method.

### 19.7.5 Beyond the basic models: a discussion

At the time the current edition of the book is being prepared, there is a “happening” in the research and applications front of diffusion models. Our aim is not to exhaustively review the related literature, but to present some basic directions, where research and applications are currently focusing on. For a more extensive literature review, one may consult, e.g., \[41\], \[200\], \[115\].

A major drawback associated with the previous three basic diffusion models is their slow sampling, which, in practice, requires many steps. In \[198\], it is pointed out that generative models struggle to simultaneously meet three requirements: a) sample quality, b) mode coverage,^([^(146)](#fn146))

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) (Section [19.2.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0040)) generate high-quality samples fast, but exhibit a rather low mode coverage. This could be due to the fact that their adversarial learning procedure does not easily scale to modeling complex, multimodal distributions. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Section [19.2.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0065)) exhibit a rather broad mode coverage and fast sampling, but often suffer from low sample quality. Diffusion models, being likelihood-based models, do not exhibit mode-collapse and can generate surprisingly high quality samples and they have a broad mode coverage. Yet, their sampling speed is low, requiring thousands of network evaluations. For example, it takes 20 hours to sample 50K images of size 32 × 32<mml:math><mml:mn>32</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>32</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si604.png) from DDPM, but less than a minute to do the same task using a GAN on Nvidia 2080 Ti GPU. When images of size 256 × 256<mml:math><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si653.png) are involved, 1000 hours are needed on the same GPU, when diffusion models are employed; see \[174\]. A further discussion related to the comparative performance of different families of generative models can be found in \[44\].

A major effort in research on diffusion models focuses on dealing with the sampling speed drawback. For example, in \[198\], it is argued that the slow sampling in diffusion networks is fundamentally attributed to the Gaussian assumption in the denoising step, which is justified only for small steps. To overcome this, it is proposed to employ a more complex multimodal distribution. This is implemented via the use of a GAN. It is claimed that much faster sampling rates are achieved without sacrificing sample quality and diversity.

In \[105\], instead of keeping the forward (diffusion) process fixed, it is suggested to parameterize and optimize it jointly with the rest of the model. Such a rationale brings diffusion models closer to VAEs. It is claimed that in this way, learning the noise schedule improves likelihood and can lead to fewer diffusion steps. In \[174\], the notion of *denoising diffusion implicit models* (DDIM) is introduced, where the Markovian assumption used in DDPMs is removed. Adopting a non-Markovian modeling can correspond to a *deterministic* generative process, which, in turn, can lead to much faster high-quality sampling.

In \[164\], the distillation concept (Section [19.6.6](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0220)) is combined with the previous DDIM. An algorithm is used to iteratively halve the number of the required sampling steps by distilling a slow teacher diffusion model to a faster student one. In \[131\], it is proposed to parameterize the variances in the reverse path, instead of keeping them fixed as in DDPM, and learn the parameters during training. Also, a cosine noise schedule is used, instead of the linear one employed in DDPM. It is claimed that these simple modifications lead to improved likelihoods that favor faster sampling.

In \[157\], to enable training on limited computational resources, while retaining high sample quality, diffusion models are applied in a latent space of pretrained autoencoders. The autoencoder provides a lower dimensional representation space, which is perceptually equivalent to the data space.

Another direction for speeding up sampling is via the so-called *consistency models*, e.g., \[171\], \[122\]. These models build upon the probability flow ODE rationale and they learn to map any point at any time to the trajectory's starting point. In other words, given a probability flow ODE, any point on the respective trajectory (e.g., points **x**[*t*[1]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si654.png), **x**[*t*[2]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si655.png), **x**[*t*[3]]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si656.png)) is mapped directly, that is in a single-step, to the origin, **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png). The “consistency” name comes from the imposed constraint that the models are trained so that their outputs are consistent on points on the same trajectory. It is claimed that this leads to significant computational savings without sacrificing the advantages of iterative sampling.

In \[124\], it is suggested to stop the diffusion process early and to start the reverse denoising from a non-Gaussian distribution. Sampling from the latter can be done via a pretrained GAN or VAE. In this way, the number of the required denoising steps is significantly reduced.

The task of speeding up sampling is treated in the context of efficient ODE solvers in, e.g., \[119\], \[120\]. In \[101\], a number of samplers are compared in light of some related theoretical findings.

### 19.7.6 Conditional diffusion models

The emphasis, so far, has been on what is known as the *unconditional* sample generation. In other words, the model was *unconstrained* and free to explore all learned modes from the input data. For example, an unconditional model trained to generate digits will generate digits randomly from all classes. However, one may wish to condition the model to generate samples from, say, one class only. In the so-called *conditional models*, one can control the class or other properties of the generated samples. For example, in computer vision, conditional models are used to manipulate the image synthesis process. The goal of this subsection is to summarize some basic directions that are currently popular in designing conditional diffusion models.

More formally, the task now becomes to construct an approximation *p*[**θ**](**x**[0]|**c**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si657.png) of the unknown input pdf conditioned on ***c***, i.e., *q*(**x**[0]|**c**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si658.png), where ***c*** denotes a constraint. The main issue now becomes how to implement this in diffusion models. To this end, a number of techniques have been proposed. Let us first focus on class-conditional models, where the constraint, ***c***, refers to the class labels, *y*. Other types of constraints will be discussed later on.

For class-conditional models, one straightforward way that comes into mind is to obtain class-related vector embeddings. That is, class information is encoded as a vector and projected to appropriate dimensions that feed the various layers of the U-Net, together with the time embeddings. One can think of various ways of combining class information with the feature maps computed in the layers of the U-Net, e.g., \[44\]. Under these modifications, the U-Net returns class-conditioned estimates, i.e., **μ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si659.png) or **ϵ**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si660.png).

A drawback of the previous vanilla formulation is that the learned models may downplay the related conditioning information on which they have been trained on. To this end, guidance models have been proposed that offer the capability of more explicitly controlling the available conditioning-related information.

#### Classifier guidance

In \[44\], it is proposed to train a classifier, *p*[**ϕ**](*y*|**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si661.png), on noisy samples, **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png), where *y* denotes the class label variable. Having trained the classifier, the gradients ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *p*[**ϕ**](*y*|**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si662.png) are employed to *guide* the reverse process to sample from an arbitrary class, *y*. During sampling, one replaces **μ**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si663.png) in Eq.
