*γ*∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *p*[**ϕ**[\*]](*y*|**x**[*t*], *t*) = ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln (*p*[**ϕ**[\*]](*y*|**x**[*t*],*t*))^(*γ*).<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si666.png)

For *γ* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si667.png), the distribution (*p*[**ϕ**[\*]](*y*|**x**[*t*],*t*))^(*γ*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si668.png) becomes sharper than the optimally trained classifier, *p*[**ϕ**[\*]](*y*|**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si669.png), since larger values are amplified by the exponent. Hence, using a larger scaling factor, *γ*, the focus turns more on the modes of the classifier, which is potentially desirable for producing higher fidelity, albeit less diverse, samples, \[44\].

The classifier is trained on samples that result from the same noising distribution as the corresponding diffusion model. After training, the classifier is incorporated into the sampling process of the diffusion model according to Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160).

It is interesting to shed more light into Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160), not for the sake of mathematics but for the sake of understanding the rationale behind the method. The starting point for satisfying the conditional sampling constraint is to express the (true) conditional reverse process as *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], *y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si670.png). Mobilizing the Bayes theorem and after a bit of algebra (see, \[44\] for details), it turns out that for the class-conditional reverse transition pdfs, the following holds true:

*q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], *y*) ∝ *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*])*q*(*y*|**x**[*t* − 1]),<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si671.png)

where ∝ denotes proportionality within a normalizing factor that does not depend on **x**[*t* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si514.png). Thus, it is reasonable to assume that the model to adopt in the reverse path to approximate *q*(**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], *y*)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si670.png) should be of the form

*p*[**θ**, **ϕ**](**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*], *y*) ∝ *p*[**θ**](**x**[*t* − 1]|**x**[*t*])*p*[**ϕ**](*y*|**x**[*t* − 1], *t* − 1),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si672.png)

where *p*[**ϕ**](*y*|**x**[*t* − 1], *t* − 1)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si673.png) is a classifier that predicts the label *y* given **x**[*t* − 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si514.png). In \[44\], it is proposed to take a) the logarithm of the previous equation and b) to perform a first order Taylor approximation of ln *p*[**ϕ**](*y*|**x**[*t* − 1], *t* − 1)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si674.png) around the mean value **μ**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si663.png). Recall that the Taylor expansion involves the gradient of the logarithmic function, which justifies the presence of the corresponding gradient term in Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160). Under certain smoothness assumptions, it turns out that the conditional distribution can be approximated by a Gaussian similar to the unconditional transition pdf, but with its mean shifted by a term proportional to the product of the covariance matrix with the gradient vector, as in Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160).

Similar arguments hold true if, instead of the unconditional model, the classifier guidance rationale is imposed on the class-conditional diffusion model. This can further improve the sample quality compared to that obtained by the class-conditional model alone. In this case, the involved mean values and covariance matrix in Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160) should be replaced by their conditional counterparts, i.e., **μ**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si675.png) and *Σ*[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si676.png).

If one starts with the score-based formulation of the diffusion models, and ignoring the notational dependence on **x**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si207.png), the starting point is the conditional distribution,

$q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}|y) = \\frac{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t})q(y|\\mathbf{x}\_{t})}{q(y)}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si677.png)

Taking the gradient of the logarithm of both sides in the previous equation, we get

∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *q*(**x**[*t*]|*y*) = ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *q*(**x**[*t*]) + ∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *q*(*y*|**x**[*t*]),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si678.png)(19.79) 

where the gradient of ln *q*(*y*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si679.png) with respect to **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png) is zero. Thus, the conditional score function is given in terms of the unconditional one plus a term that depends on the class distribution of the noisy samples, **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png). Thus, employing the respective models of the quantities involved in Eq. [(19.83)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq165), we can write

*s*[**θ**[\*], **ϕ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*) = *s*[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*) + *γ*∇[**x**[*t*]]ln *p*[**ϕ**[\*]](*y*|**x**[*t*], *t*),<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si680.png)(19.80) 

where *γ* has been introduced to adjust for the relevant importance of the two terms, in analogy to Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160).

#### Classifier-free guidance

A major problem with the previous method is the training of a separate classifier. In \[86\], the need for a separate classifier is bypassed by jointly training conditional and unconditional diffusion models.

Let us denote as **s**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si681.png) the class-conditioned estimate of the score function and as **s**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si624.png) the unconditional one. During training, a single neural network is used to parameterize both models. This is achieved via a simple trick. An input token, ∅, that corresponds to the unconditional model is used to feed the class-embedding vector in place of the associated class label *y*. That is

**s**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*) = **s**[**θ**](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y* = ⌀).<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si682.png)

The conditional and unconditional models are jointly trained by randomly selecting between conditional (*y* ≠ ⌀<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si683.png)) and unconditional (*y* = ⌀<mml:math><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si684.png)) inputs according to a pre-selected user-defined probability, *p*[⌀]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si685.png).

To perform sampling for the class-conditional model, the required estimate of the score function is obtained via the following linear combination:

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{s}}}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t,y) = \\mathbf{s}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t,\\varnothing) + \\gamma\\left( \\mathbf{s}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t,y) - \\mathbf{s}\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t},t,\\varnothing) \\right),$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si686.png)(19.81) 

where *γ* > 0<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si613.png) is a guidance scale constant. In words, the output of the neural network is extrapolated further to the direction of **s**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*, *y*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si687.png) and away from **s**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*, ⌀)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>∅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si688.png). If one takes the negative of both sides and multiply with the associated, for the time step, standard deviation, then Eq. [(19.85)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq168) can be equivalently expressed in terms of the corresponding **ϵ**[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si689.png) estimates in place of the **s**[**θ**]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si690.png)'s. Observe that if *γ* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si691.png) Eq. [(19.85)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq168) reduces to the unconditional model, and if *γ* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si692.png) it aligns with the vanilla class-conditional one.

The interpretation of Eq. [(19.85)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq168) relies on Eq. [(19.83)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq165). Eq. [(19.85)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq168) involves the approximate gradients of their true counterparts in Eq. [(19.83)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq165), if in the place of the classifier we use an *implicit* one,

$q^{(i)}(y|\\mathbf{x}\_{t}) \\propto \\left( \\frac{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}|y)}{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t})} \\right)^{\\gamma}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si693.png)

Note that according to the Bayes rule,

$q(y|\\mathbf{x}\_{t}) \\propto \\frac{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}|y)}{q(\\mathbf{x}\_{t})}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si694.png)

In words, in the implicit classifier, we raise the previous ratio to the power of *γ*. Selecting the value of *γ*, in practice, is the outcome of a trade-off between sample variability and sample quality. While generating images, increasing *γ* decreases variability and increases sample fidelity, e.g., \[86\]. This is shown in [Fig. 19.25](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0140). The figure to the left corresponds to the unconditional model, *γ* = 0<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si691.png) (high variability-low fidelity), the one in the middle to *γ* = 1.5<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si695.png), and the one to the right to *γ* = 3<mml:math><mml:mi>γ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si696.png) (low variability-high fidelity).^([^(147)](#fn147))

![Figure 19.25 (Left) The unconditional model (γ = 0) exhibits high variability and low image fidelity. (Center) It corresponds to γ = 1.5. (Right) It corresponds to γ = 3 and it exhibits low variability and high image fidelity.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr025.jpg)

[Figure 19.25](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf2870) (Left) The unconditional model (*γ* = 0) exhibits high variability and low image fidelity. (Center) It corresponds to *γ* = 1.5. (Right) It corresponds to *γ* = 3 and it exhibits low variability and high image fidelity.

As we will soon see, conditional models based on classifier or classifier-free guidance have been extended and used in cases where the models are constrained not on class labels but on more general constrains, such as text captions.

### 19.7.7 Applications

Diffusion models have been applied to a wide range of applications and, currently, there is a fast growing trend to embrace such modeling in more and more disciplines.

In computer vision, they have been used for, e.g., image super-resolution, editing, impainting, restoration, and segmentation, besides image and video generation. In time series analysis, they have been applied to tasks such as imputation, forecasting, waveform generation. In NLP tasks, they have been used for sequence-to-sequence generation, e.g., \[60\]. For a related extensive literature review see, e.g., \[41\], \[200\], \[115\].

One of the most “trendy” and well-known applications (well beyond the scientific community) is the text-to-image generation, which is highlighted next.

#### Text-to-image generation

Text-to-image generation can be seen as an image generation task conditioned on a corresponding text description. The topic of text-to-image generation traces its origins back to \[127\], where the DRAW (\[65\]) generative model was extended to condition on image captions to generate novel visual scenes. Following this work, in \[153\], a GAN was employed that improved the generated image quality and could generate objects with recognizable properties. In \[151\], the text-to-image generation was performed based on a transformer that autoregressively modeled the text and image tokens as a single stream of data.^([^(148)](#fn148))

*CLIP*: Following the general rationale behind self-supervision, CLIP uses two branches to jointly train two encoders. See [Fig. 19.26](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0145) for a simplified block diagram. The input to the encoder of the upper branch is fed with the text description (caption) that describes an image, which feeds the input of the encoder in the lower branch. For example, if the image contains a dog that wears a hat (as in the figure), the corresponding description could be something like “dog wearing a hat.” The text in the caption is encoded into a corresponding vector representation, after an appropriate embedding (see, e.g., Section [19.3.1](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0075)).

![Figure 19.26 CLIP consists of two branches. In the upper one, a text description/caption is prompted, which is then mapped into a vector embedding, t. The lower branch is fed with an image, x, that relates to the text description. In the sequel, t and x are provided as inputs to two parameterized encoders, gϕ and fξ, respectively. The corresponding encoded outputs, zt = gϕ(t) and zi = fξ(x), are used in the contrastive loss function \\mathcal{L}Equation. The parameters, ϕ and ξ, of the two encoders are jointly optimized to make the respective encoded outputs, zt and zi, more similar (dissimilar) if the text description and the content of the corresponding image match (do not match).](images/B9780443292385000251/gr026.jpg)

[Figure 19.26](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf2945) CLIP consists of two branches. In the upper one, a text description/caption is prompted, which is then mapped into a vector embedding, ***t***. The lower branch is fed with an image, ***x***, that relates to the text description. In the sequel, ***t*** and ***x*** are provided as inputs to two parameterized encoders, *g*[***ϕ***] and *f*[***ξ***], respectively. The corresponding encoded outputs, ***z***[*t*] = *g*[***ϕ***](***t***) and ***z***[*i*] = *f*[***ξ***](***x***), are used in the contrastive loss function ℒ<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">L</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si493.png). The parameters, ***ϕ*** and ***ξ***, of the two encoders are jointly optimized to make the respective encoded outputs, ***z***[*t*] and ***z***[*i*], more similar (dissimilar) if the text description and the content of the corresponding image match (do not match).

Let ***t*** and ***x*** be the text and image representations, respectively, that feed the corresponding encoders. The outputs of the two encoders, denoted as **z**[*t*] = *g*[**ϕ**](**t**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ϕ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si698.png) and **z**[*i*] = *f*[**ξ**](**x**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ξ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si699.png), are of the same dimensions. The parameters ***ϕ*** and ***ξ*** which parameterize the two encoders, respectively, are jointly optimized according to the contrastive loss rationale, which has already been discussed in Section [19.6.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0215). In other words, during training, the encoded output vectors of the two encoders are made more similar if the description in the caption matches the content of the image, and more dissimilar if there is no matching, according to a contrastive loss function. Similarity is quantified via the normalized inner product function. For example, assume that an image contains a cat and it is encoded as **z**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si448.png). For the description of the image content, we are given two captions. One, say, “A cat sitting” (encoded as **z**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si700.png)) and another one, say, “A dog running” (encoded as **z**[*t*]^′<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si701.png)). Then, we expect that after training,

$\\frac{\\mathbf{z}\_{t}^{T}}{||\\mathbf{z}\_{t}||}\\frac{\\mathbf{z}\_{i}}{||\\mathbf{z}\_{i}||} > \\frac{{\\mathbf{z}\_{t}^{\\prime}}^{T}}{||\\mathbf{z}\_{t}^{\\prime}||}\\frac{\\mathbf{z}\_{i}}{||\\mathbf{z}\_{i}||},$<mml:math><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi where || ⋅ ||<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si556.png) denotes the Euclidean norm. Details of the two encoder networks are provided in \[149\].

At inference stage, each image in the data set is treated as a *separate class*. Given a text description/caption, this is encoded and the resulting vector representation is compared to the encoded representations of the images in the data set. An image is selected according to the largest value of the similarity measure (normalized inner product). In computer vision, this type of classification, where examples are treated as separate classes, is known as one-shot classification.^([^(149)](#fn149))

*GLIDE*: In the model called *guided language to image diffusion for generation and editing*, proposed in \[132\], the CLIP plays the role of the classifier to guide the reverse process in a diffusion model. CLIP is separately trained on *noisy* images, **x**[*t*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si540.png). During sampling in the reverse process of the diffusion model, the conditional model mean values, **μ**[**θ**[\*]](**x**[*t*], *t*, **t**)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⁎</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si703.png), conditioned on the text caption, ***t***, are perturbed as,

In words, the gradient of the log-probability in Eq. [(19.82)](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq160) is replaced by the gradient of the respective inner product of the two encoders' output embeddings.

Besides the CLIP-based guidance, GLIDE, also, used the classifier-free guidance concept of Section [19.84](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#deq166), where the label *y* is replaced by the associated captions ***t*** and ∅ corresponds to an empty text sequence. It is reported that classifier-free guidance yields higher quality images.

GLIDE was trained to generate images *conditioned* on the text caption encodings, produced at the output of a text transformer-based encoder; see \[132\] for more on implementation details.

*unCLIP*: In \[152\], a three step approach is used in the text-to-image generation task.

*   •  A CLIP network is first trained to learn a joint representation of text and images in a latent space, via the two encoders' output embeddings.
*   •  A so-called *prior* diffusion model is trained to generate *CLIP image embeddings*, which are *conditioned* on the respective encoded text captions and, optionally, on the corresponding CLIP text embeddings. To improve sample quality, the classifier-free guidance approach was also employed by randomly dropping text conditioning information 10% of the time during training.
*   •  A diffusion model, called the decoder, is employed which is trained to generate images *conditioned* on *CLIP image embeddings* that are generated from the prior diffusion model. Optionally, conditioning on encoded text captions may be employed. The classifier-free guidance was, also, used in the decoder, by randomly setting the CLIP embeddings to zero 10% of the time, and randomly dropping the text caption encodings 50% of the time during training. The decoder also involves two super-resolution diffusion upsampler models.

While the decoder could work with direct CLIP image embeddings, the prior can *generate* image embeddings conditioned on the caption inputs. The name unCLIP indicates that images are generated by inverting the CLIP image encoder. Furthermore, this setup facilitates image manipulations in the latent (CLIP embedding) space, such as interpolation, editing, etc.

[Fig. 19.27](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#f0150) illustrates a simplified block diagram of the unCLIP network.^([^(150)](#fn150))

![Figure 19.27 During sampling, the prior diffusion model generates samples in the CLIP image (encoded) embedding space, zi, conditioned on the input text description embeddings, t, and (optionally) on the corresponding CLIP text embeddings, zt. The decoder generates images in the input image space, conditioned on the generated, from the prior network, CLIP image embeddings, zi, and (optionally) on the input text embeddings, t.](images/B9780443292385000251/gr027.jpg)

[Figure 19.27](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#cf3000) During sampling, the prior diffusion model generates samples in the CLIP image (encoded) embedding space, ***z***[*i*], conditioned on the input text description embeddings, ***t***, and (optionally) on the corresponding CLIP text embeddings, ***z***[*t*]. The decoder generates images in the input image space, conditioned on the generated, from the prior network, CLIP image embeddings, ***z***[*i*], and (optionally) on the input text embeddings, ***t***.

More details on the specific architectures used in the prior as well as the decoder can be found in the related paper. Also, in the paper, some other options for implementing the prior are discussed. 

*Latent Diffusion Models*: These models^([^(151)](#fn151))

*Imagen*: This model was proposed in \[161\], and it consists of an encoder for the caption text sequence combined with a *cascade* of diffusion models for generating high-resolution images. The diffusion models are conditioned on the text embeddings that are produced by a large language model (LLM). The cascade of diffusion models involves an image generator diffusion model followed by two super-resolution upsampling diffusion networks. In Imagen, the classifier-free guidance approach is employed but no latent space is involved. As it is pointed out in the paper, Imagen^([^(152)](#fn152))

#### Text-to-image generation: a brief discussion

The previously discussed state-of-the-art text-to-image generators turn out to be very powerful to combine unrelated concepts such as objects, textures, color, to generate sampling examples with unprecedented degree of photorealism. This provides them with significant potential for their deployment and use to various applications. However, due to their powerful capabilities, a number of ethical issues are raised.

For example, such models can become powerful tools for malicious actors to generate harmful content and deepfakes^([^(153)](#fn153))

Spreading of disinformation is not only harmful to individuals, e.g., bullying or sexual abuse. It goes much beyond and poses threats that undermine basic core functions and norms related to our social and political structure as human beings. As social beings, we need to participate in collective actions based on well-informed decision-making. The potential of large-scale disinformation that spreads fast can seriously harm this social activity that is unique to human beings, and it comprises one of the basic forces that drives progress and civilization, e.g., \[143\].

Furthermore, the related platforms pose a big threat for artists and graphic designers. To this direction, some of the latest versions of such platforms are designed to decline requests to generate images in the style of living artists.

Remarks 19.13

*   •  *Performance measures*: We have already discussed in Section [19.7.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0270) that a major goal in designing a generative network is the generated samples to be of good quality and exhibit wide coverage. In other words, the generated samples should be “faithful” to the real examples used for training and, also, to be as diverse as possible and their variation should match that in the training set. At the end of Section [19.2.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0040), the inception score (IS) and the Fréchet inception distance (FID) were discussed as related measures. These are also used for evaluating performance in diffusion models. However, these metrics, from their definition, attempt to measure the previous concepts via a single index.
*   More recently, e.g., in \[162\], \[106\], it is proposed that quality and diversity could be measured via two separate metrics. The *precision* measures the average sample quality and the *recall* quantifies the coverage of the sample distribution. In a more “technical” jargon, let *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) and *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png) be the distributions for the real and generated samples, respectively. *Precision* is the probability that a randomly generated sample from *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png) falls within the support of *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png). *Recall* is the probability that a randomly drawn sample from *p*[*r*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si90.png) falls within the support of *p*[*g*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si84.png).
*   •  *Super-resolution*: In the applications section, the emphasis was on text-to-image generation. However, many of the concepts that were discussed there can be “borrowed” and used in many other applications. Take, as an example, a related area in computer vision, that of super-resolution (SR). The task in SR is to generate a high-resolution image, **y** ∈ ℝ^(*h**w*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si707.png) (vectorized form of an image array *Y* ∈ ℝ^(*h* × *w*)<mml:math><mml:mi>Y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>w</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si708.png)), given a low-resolution version of it, $\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{\\overline{h}\\overline{w}}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi *   From the diffusion models perspective, the goal is to sample from the unknown conditional distribution, *q*(**y**|**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si713.png). In \[160\], the task is tackled via the use of a conditional diffusion model that is conditioned on the low-resolution image, ***x***. The forward process is gradually diffused in *T* steps, starting from a high-resolution observation, **y**[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si320.png), to noise, **y**[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si714.png). The reverse process is trained to sample high-resolution images, starting from **y**[*T*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si714.png), conditioned on the corresponding low-dimensional image, ***x***. Sampling is performed following the reverse conditional model rationale, where conditioning is on ***x***. For a related literature survey, see e.g., \[130\].

### Computer exercises

1.  19.9  This exercise focuses on the original generative adversarial network (GAN) network, which is trained on the MNIST data set to learn to generate fake hand-written characters.
2.  To implement and train the network use the PyTorch framework. 
    1.  **(a)**  Load the data set of 60000 to be used for training. Normalize image values so that all values are in the \[ − 1, 1\]<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si114.png) interval.
    2.  **(b)**  The generator is fed to its input with a noise vector and outputs an image. The dimension of the input noise vector is 100, and its elements are i.i.d. sampled from a normal distribution of zero mean and unit variance. The generator consists of three fully connected layers with 256, 512, 1024 neurons, respectively. The activation function used for the neurons in the hidden layers is the leaky ReLU with parameter *α* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si111.png). The output layer comprises 784 nodes and the tanh is employed as the respective activation function.
    3.  **(c)**  The discriminator takes as input a 1 × 784<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>784</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si112.png) vector, corresponding to the vectorized form of the 28 × 28<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si113.png) MNIST images. The discriminator consists of three fully connected layers with 1024, 512, 256 neurons, respectively. The leaky ReLU activation function is also employed, with *α* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si111.png). During training, use the dropout regularization method, with probability of discarding nodes equal to 0.3. The output layer consists of a single node with a sigmoid activation function.
    4.  **(d)**  To train the implemented network, use the two-class (binary) cross-entropy loss function. Adopt the Adam optimizer with step size (learning rate) equal to 2 ⋅ 10^( − 3)<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>⋅</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si718.png),  *β*[1] = 0.5<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si719.png) and *β*[2] = 0.999<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.999</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si720.png) as parameters for the optimizer. The recommended batch size is 100. Train the network for 400 epochs as follows: For each training loop: a) generate a random set of input noise and images, b) generate fake images via the generator, c) train only the discriminator, and d) then, train only the generator, according to [Algorithm 19.2](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#enun0015). Play with the number of iterations, associated with the discriminator training.
    5.  **(e)**  During training and every 20 epochs, visualize the generated images created by the generator and comment on the evolution of the learning process.
    6.  **(f)**  Play with all the various parameters that have been suggested above and see the effect on the training.
3.  19.10  This exercise helps to familiarize with transformer architectures and explore the impact of positional encoding. The focus is on the language translation NLP task, and more specifically on German-to-English translation, following the PyTorch tutorial: [https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/translation\_transformer.html](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/translation_transformer.html).
4.  In the tutorial, the setup of the data sets, the transformer and the training procedure are described in detail. A simple qualitative evaluation is provided at the end by translating the German sentence “Eine Gruppe von Menschen steht vor einem Iglu,” which in English means “A group of people stands in front of an igloo.” 
    1.  **(a)**  Experiment with various transformer hyperparameters, namely: 
        *   •  EMB\_SIZE (dimensionality of the embedding space, *d*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si199.png)). Start with EMB\_SIZE= 512.
        *   •  NHEAD (number of heads). Start with NHEAD=8.
        *   •  FFN\_HID\_DIM (hidden layer dimensionality of the two-layer FCN module). Start with FFN\_HID\_DIM=512.
        *   •  NUM\_ENCODER\_LAYERS (number of encoder blocks). Start with NUM\_ENCODER\_LAYERS=3.
        *   •  NUM\_DECODER\_LAYERS (number of decoder blocks). Start with NUM\_DECODER\_LAYERS=3.How much one can compress the architecture (i.e., reduce the aforementioned values) without sacrificing performance?
    2.  **(b)**  Tweak the *PositionalEncoding* class in order to remove the effect of the positional encoding. You can add an argument that controls whether positional encoding is added to the token embedding or not. Specifically, you can modify the *PositionalEncoding* class to have an extra argument *use\_pos\_encoding*.
    3.  Note that dropout of this *PositionalEncoding* layer may affect performance, so for this experiment set the dropout value to zero. Note that this *Seq2SeqTransformer* definition has a dropout argument, where you can set *dropout=0*. Evaluate the performance of the transformer without positional embedding on the previous German sentence. Comment on the obtained results with respect to the functionality of positional encoding.
5.  19.11  This exercise serves as an introduction to self-supervised methods, focusing on implementing SimCLR, Section [19.6.5](#Chp019_997-1102_B9780443292385000251.xhtml#s0215), on the MNIST data set. SimCLR applies contrastive learning during pretraining, while it involves various implementation details and hyperparameters that affect downstream performance during fine-tuning.  
    1.  **(a)**  *Implementation details* 
        *   •  Augmentations: Create a dataloader providing two augmented versions for each image. Use the following sequence of transformations: *RandomHorizontalFlip()*, *RandomResizedCrop(size=28, scale=(0.2, 1.))*, *ToTensor()*, *Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))*
        *   •  Encoder: Design a sequence of three convolutional layers with output channels: 32, 64, and 128 respectively. Use *kernel size* 3, *stride* 1, and *padding* 1. Apply batch normalization, ReLU activation, and max pooling after each convolutional layer. Use *kernel size* 2 and *stride* 2 for *max pooling*, with *padding* 1 for the last operation.
        *   •  Projector: A projector head should be applied on the output of the encoder. Use a linear layer that maps the output dimension of the encoder to an 128-dimensional feature space.
    2.  **(b)**  *Pretrain*: Implement the InfoNCE loss function by using the cross-entropy loss function from PyTorch. Think of InfoNCE as a binary cross entropy loss over the feature similarities. Train the encoder and its projection head for 100 epochs with a temperature of 0.07 and a batch size of 64. Use the Adam optimizer with a *learning rate* of 0.003 and *weight decay* of 0.003.
    3.  **(c)**  *Downstream performance*: In order to evaluate your network, use your encoder (not the projector) to extract for all train and test images the corresponding feature vectors. Use these vectors as a new data set and train three different classifiers (i) a linear layer, (ii) logistic regression, and (iii) a *k*\-NN to evaluate downstream performance.
    4.  **(d)**  *Role of the batch size*: Try different batch sizes for the pretraining stage. How does the performance change as the batch sizes grow larger? Comment on the results.
    5.  **(e)**  *Role of the temperature*: Pretrain with different *temperature values*, namely 0.07, 0.2, 0.5<mml:math><mml:mn>0.07</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si721.png) and 1. How does temperature affect downstream performance?
    6.  **(f)**  *Role of the projection head*: A projector head should be applied at the output of the encoder. Use a linear layer that maps the output dimension of the encoder to an 128-dimensional feature space. ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si722.png) normalization should be applied on the output features. Investigate the impact on downstream performance of pretraining (i) without the projection head and (ii) using a two-layer MLP with one ReLU activation as the projector. Assess the importance of the projector.
    7.  **(g)**  *Role of the number of epochs*: Explore the impact of extending pretraining duration (e.g., 200, 300, 400<mml:math><mml:mn>200</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>300</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>400</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000251/si723.png) epochs) on downstream performance metrics.
6.  19.12  The focus of this exercise is on diffusion models, using DDPMs based on the *Diffusers* package from *HuggingFace*, which is written in PyTorch. The source code is here: [*https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers*](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers). The exercise comprises the following steps: 
    1.  **(a)**  Load a pretrained Stable Diffusion model from the *HuggingFace* model hub, namely *Stable Diffusion v2*. In PyTorch, this can be done by using the *stable-diffusion-2* pretrained model from the *StableDiffusionPipeline* module of the *diffusers* package.
    2.  **(b)**  Remove few self-attention and cross-attention layers, and generate images after each modification to analyze their impact on image coherence and relevance. This can be done by applying the function *param.fill\_(0)* to the parameters of any attention layer of the U-Net backbone. 
    3.  **(c)**  Vary the number of diffusion steps (e.g., reducing by half, doubling) and observe changes in image quality and generation time. Use the DPM-Solver++ scheduler (*DPMSolverMultistepScheduler* module of the *diffusers* package).
    4.  **(d)**  In working with classifier-free guidance, examine how the model performs when we tune the model toward stronger or weaker prompt-conditioning. Tune the *guidance\_scale* model's parameter; *guidance\_scale = 1* corresponds to no guidance.
    5.  **(e)**  Modify the noise schedule used in the diffusion process. Evaluate its impact on the smoothness and realism of the generated images. Tune the *DPMSolverMultistepScheduler* module's parameters *beta\_start* and *beta\_end*, which are the starting and final beta value of inference, and define *beta\_schedule* either as linear or *scaled\_linear*.
