## 20.1 Introduction

In many practical applications, although the data reside in a high-dimensional space, the true dimensionality, known as *intrinsic dimensionality*, can be of a much lower value. We have met such cases in the context of sparse modeling in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml). There, although the data lie in a high-dimensional space, a number of the components were known to be zero. The task was to learn the locations of the zeros; this is equivalent to learning the specific subspace, which is determined by the locations of the nonzero components. In this chapter, the goal is to treat the task in a more general setting and assume that the data can lie in any possible subspace (not only the ones formed by the removal of coordinate axes) or manifold. For example, in a three-dimensional space, the data may cluster around a straight line, or around the circumference of a circle or the graph of a parabola, arbitrarily placed in ℝ³<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si1.png). In all previous cases, the intrinsic dimensionality of the data is equal to one, as any of these curves can equivalently be described in terms of a single parameter. [Fig. 20.1](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0010) illustrates the three cases. Learning the lower-dimensional structure associated with a given set of data is of great importance in the context of *big data* processing and analysis. Some typical examples are the disciplines of computer vision, robotics, medical imaging, and computational neuroscience.

![Figure 20.1 The data reside close to (A) a straight line, (B) the circumference of a circle, and (C) the graph of a parabola in the three-dimensional space. In all three cases, the intrinsic dimensionality of the data is equal to one. In (A) the data are clustered around a (translated/affine) linear subspace and in (B) and (C) around one-dimensional manifolds.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr001.jpg)

Figure 20.1 The data reside close to (A) a straight line, (B) the circumference of a circle, and (C) the graph of a parabola in the three-dimensional space. In all three cases, the intrinsic dimensionality of the data is equal to one. In (A) the data are clustered around a (translated/affine) linear subspace and in (B) and (C) around one-dimensional manifolds.

The goal of this chapter is to introduce the reader to the main directions, which are followed in this topic, starting from more classical techniques, such as the principal component analysis (PCA) and the factor analysis methods, both in their standard as well as in their probabilistic formulations. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA), independent component analysis (ICA), nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), and dictionary learning techniques are also discussed; in the latter case, data are represented via an expansion in terms of overcomplete dictionaries, and sparsity-related arguments are mobilized to detect the most relevant atoms in the dictionary. Finally, nonlinear techniques for learning (nonlinear) manifolds are presented such as the kernel PCA, the local linear embedding (LLE), and the isometric mapping (ISOMAP) techniques. More recent trends including matrix completion, low-rank matrix factorization, and the robust PCA methods are introduced and two related application examples are discussed. At the end of the chapter, a case study in the context of fMRI data analysis is described.

## 20.2 Intrinsic dimensionality

A data set 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si2.png) is said to have *intrinsic dimensionality* *m* ≤ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si3.png) if 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si4.png) can be (approximately) described in terms of *m* free parameters. Take as an example the case where the vectors in 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si4.png) are generated as functions in terms of *m* random variables, that is, **x** = **g**(*u*[1], …, *u*[*m*])<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si5.png), *u*[*i*] ∈ ℝ, *i* = 1, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si6.png). The corresponding geometric interpretation is that the respective observation vectors will lie along a manifold, whose form depends on the vector-valued function **g** : ℝ^(*m*) ↦ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟼</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si7.png). Let us consider the case where

**x** = \[*r*cos *θ*, *r*sin *θ*\]^(*T*),<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si8.png)

where *r* is a constant and the random variable *θ* ∈ \[0, 2*π*\]<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si9.png). The data lie along the circumference of a circle of radius *r* and a single free parameter suffices to describe the data. If now a small amount of noise is added, then the data will be clustered close to the circumference, as for example in [Fig. 20.1](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0010)B, and the intrinsic dimensionality is equal to one. From a statistical point of view, it means that the components of the random vectors are highly correlated. Sometimes, we say that the “effective” dimensionality is lower than the apparent one of the “ambient” space, in which the lower-dimensional manifold lies.

In a more general setting, the data may lie in groups of manifolds or even in groups of clusters or they may follow a special spatial or temporal structure. For example, in the wavelet domain most of the coefficients of an image are close to zero and can be neglected, yet the larger (nonzero) ones have a particular structure that is characteristic of natural images. Such a structured sparsity has been exploited in the JPEG2000 coding scheme. Structured sparsity representations are often met in many big data applications (see, for example, \[42\]). In this chapter, we will only focus on identifying manifold structures, linear (subspaces/affine subspaces) in the beginning and nonlinear ones later on.

Learning the manifold in which a data set resides can be used to provide a compact low-dimensional encoding of a high-dimensional data set, which can subsequently be exploited for performing processing and learning tasks in a much more efficient way. Also, dimensionality reduction can be used for data visualization.

## 20.3 Principal component analysis

*Principal component analysis* (PCA) or *Karhunen–Loève transform* is among the oldest and most widely used methods for dimensionality reduction \[105\]. The assumption underlying PCA, as well as any dimensionality reduction technique, is that the observed data are generated by a system or process that is driven by a (relatively) small number of *latent* (not directly observed) variables. The goal is to learn this latent structure.

Given a set of observations, **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si10.png), of a random vector **x**, which will be assumed to be of zero mean (otherwise the mean/sample mean is subtracted), PCA determines a *subspace* of dimension *m* ≤ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si3.png), such that after projection on this subspace, the statistical variation of the data is optimally retained. This subspace is defined in terms of *m mutually orthogonal axes*, known as *principal axes* or *principal directions*, which are computed so that the variance of the data, after projection on the subspace, is maximized \[95\].

We will derive the principal axes in a step-wise fashion. First, assume that *m* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si11.png) and the goal is to find a single direction in ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si12.png) so that the variance of the corresponding projections of the data points is maximized. Let **u**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si13.png) denote the principal axis. The variance of the projections (having assumed centered data) is given by

$J(\\mathbf{u}\_{1}) = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}{(\\mathbf{u}\_{1}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{n})}^{2} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}(\\mathbf{u}\_{1}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{n})(\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}\\mathbf{u}\_{1}) = \\mathbf{u}\_{1}^{T}\\widehat{\\Sigma}\\mathbf{u}\_{1},$<mml:math><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo id="mmlbr0001" linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0001" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si14.png)

where

$\\widehat{\\Sigma}: = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}^{T}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si15.png)(20.1) 

is the sample covariance matrix of the data. For large values of *N* or if the statistics can be computed, the covariance (instead of the sample covariance) matrix can be used. The task now becomes that of maximizing the variance. However, because we are only interested in directions, the principal axis will be represented by the respective unit norm vector. Thus, the optimization task is cast as

![](images/B9780443292385000263/fx001.jpg)

This is a constrained optimization problem and the corresponding Lagrangian is given by

*L*(**u**, *λ*) = **u**^(*T*)*Σ̂***u** − *λ*(**u**^(*T*)**u** − 1).<mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si16.png)(20.4) 

Taking the gradient and setting it equal to zero we get

*Σ̂***u** = *λ***u**.<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si17.png)(20.5) 

In other words, the principal direction is an eigenvector of the sample covariance matrix. Plugging Eq. [(20.5)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq5) into Eq. (20.2) and taking into account (20.3), we obtain

**u**^(*T*)*Σ̂***u** = *λ*.<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si18.png)(20.6) 

Hence, the variance is maximized if **u**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si13.png) is the eigenvector that corresponds to the maximum eigenvalue, *λ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si19.png). Recall that because the (sample) covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, all the eigenvalues are real and nonnegative. Assuming *Σ̂*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si137.png) to be invertible (hence, necessarily, *N* > *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si21.png)), the eigenvalues are all positive, that is, *λ*[1] > *λ*[2] > …*λ*[*l*] > 0<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si22.png), and we also assume they are distinct, in order to simplify the discussion.

The second principal component is selected so that it (a) is orthogonal to **u**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si13.png) and (b) maximizes the variance after projecting the data onto this direction. Following similar arguments as before, a similar optimization task results with an extra constraint, **u**^(*T*)**u**[1] = 0<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si23.png). It can easily be shown ([Problem 20.1](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#o0075)) that the second principal axis is the eigenvector corresponding to the second-largest eigenvalue, *λ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si24.png). The process continues until *m* principal axes have been obtained; they are the eigenvectors corresponding to the *m* largest eigenvalues.

### PCA, SVD, and low-rank matrix factorization

The SVD decomposition of a matrix was discussed in Section [6.4](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml). Given a matrix *X* ∈ ℝ^(*l* × *N*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si25.png), we can write

*X* = *U**D**V*^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si26.png)(20.7) 

For an *r*\-rank matrix *X*, *U* is the *l* × *r*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si27.png) matrix having as columns the eigenvectors corresponding to the *r* nonzero eigenvalues of *X**X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si28.png), and *V* is the *N* × *r*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si29.png) matrix having as columns the respective eigenvectors of *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si30.png); *D* is a square *r* × *r*<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si31.png) diagonal matrix comprising the singular values^([^(154)](#fn154))

$X = \\underset{l \\times l}{\\underset{︸}{\\lbrack\\mathbf{u}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{u}\_{l}\\rbrack}}\\underset{l \\times N}{\\underset{︸}{\\begin{bmatrix} {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{1}\\mathbf{v}\_{1}^{T}} \\\\ \\vdots \\\\ {\\sqrt{\\lambda\_{l}}\\mathbf{v}\_{l}^{T}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}}} = \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{u}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{u}\_{l} \\right\\rbrack\\begin{bmatrix} {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{1}v\_{11}\\ } & {\\ldots\\ } & {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{1}v\_{1n}\\ } & {\\ldots\\ } & {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{1}v\_{1N}} \\\\ {\\vdots \\ } & {\\vdots \\ } & {\\vdots \\ } & {\\vdots \\ } & \\vdots \\\\ {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{l}v\_{l1}\\ } & {\\ldots\\ } & {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{l}v\_{ln}\\ } & {\\ldots\\ } & {{\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{l}v\_{lN}} \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}.$<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mo 1}^{l}z\_{ni}\\mathbf{u}\_{i},$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si37.png)(20.9) 

where **z**[*n*]^(*T*) :  = \[*z*[*n*1], …, *z*[*n**l*]\]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si38.png) is the *n*th column of the *l* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si39.png) matrix on the right-hand side in Eq. [(20.8)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq8). That is, by definition, $z\_{n1} = {\\sqrt{\\lambda}}\_{1}v\_{1n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si40.png) and so on. The sum in Eq. [(20.9)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq9) has been split into two terms, where *m* can be any value 1 ≤ *m* ≤ *l*<mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si41.png). Note that, due to the orthonormality of the **u**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si42.png)s,

*z*[*n**i*] = **u**[*i*]^(*T*)**x**[*n*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*, *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si43.png)
