[Figure 20.2](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#cf0305) The projection of ***x***[*n*] on the principal axis ***u***[1] is given by ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n} = z\_{n1}\\mathbf{u}\_{1}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si52.png), where *z*[*n*1] = **u**[1]^(*T*)**x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si53.png).

The previous arguments establish a bridge between PCA and SVD. In other words, the principal axes can be obtained via the SVD decomposition of *X*. Moreover, the columns of the best *m*\-rank matrix approximation, *X̂*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si47.png), of *X* are the projections of the observation vectors **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si466.png) on the (optimally) reduced in dimension subspace, spanned by the principal axes. 

Looking at Eq. [(20.10)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq11), PCA can also be seen as a *low-rank matrix factorization* method. Matrix factorization will be a recurrent theme in this chapter. Given a matrix *X*, there is not a unique way to factorize it, in terms of two matrices. PCA provides an *m*\-rank matrix factorization of *X*, by imposing *orthogonality* on the structure of the involved factors. Later on, we are going to discuss other approaches.

Finally, it is important to emphasize that the bridge between PCA and SVD establishes a connection between the low-rank factorization of a matrix *X* and the intrinsic dimensionality of the subspace in which its column vectors reside, since this is the subspace where maximum variance of the data is guaranteed.

### Minimum error interpretation

Having established the bridge between PCA and SVD, another interpretation of the PCA method becomes readily available. Because *X̂*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si47.png) is the best *m*\-rank matrix approximation of *X* in the Frobenius sense, the quantity

$||\\widehat{X} - X||\_{F}^{2}: = \\sum\\limits\_{i}\\sum\\limits\_{j}|\\widehat{X}(i,j) - X(i,j)|^{2} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}||{\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n} - \\mathbf{x}\_{n}||^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si55.png)

is minimum; that is, obtaining any other *m*\-dimensional approximation (say, ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si56.png)) of **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si466.png), by choosing to project onto another *m*\-dimensional subspace, would result in higher squared error norm approximation, compared to that resulting from PCA. This is also a strong result that establishes a notable merit of the PCA method as a dimensionality reduction technique. This interpretation goes back to Pearson \[146\].

### PCA and information retrieval

The previous minimum error interpretation paves the way to build around PCA an efficient searching procedure in identifying similar patterns in large databases. Assume that a number *N* of prototypes are represented in terms of *l* features, giving rise to feature vectors, **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si10.png), which are stored in a database. Given an unknown object, which is represented by a feature vector ***x***, the task is to identify to which one among the prototypes this pattern is most similar. Similarity is measured in terms of the Euclidean distance ||**x** − **x**[*n*]||²<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si58.png). If *N* and *l* are large, searching for the minimum Euclidean distance can be computationally very expensive. The idea is to keep in the database the components **z**[*n*]^((*m*)) :  = \[*z*[*n*1], …, *z*[*n**m*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si59.png) (see Eq. [(20.12)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq13)) that describe the projections of the *N* prototypes in span{**u**[1], …, **u**[*m*]}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si60.png), instead of the original *l*\-dimensional feature vectors. Assuming that *m* is large enough to capture most of the variability of the original data (i.e., the intrinsic dimensionality of the data is *m* to a good approximation), then **z**[*n*]^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si61.png) is a good feature vector description because we know that in this case ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n} \\approx \\mathbf{x}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si62.png). Given now an unknown pattern, ***x***, we first project it onto span{**u**[1], …, **u**[*m*]}<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si60.png), resulting in

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}(\\mathbf{u}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{x})\\mathbf{u}\_{i}: = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}z\_{i}\\mathbf{u}\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si63.png)(20.13) 

Then we have

$||\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\mathbf{x}||^{2} \\approx ||{\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}}\_{n} - \\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}||^{2} = \\left\\| \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}z\_{ni}\\mathbf{u}\_{i} - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}z\_{i}\\mathbf{u}\_{i} \\right\\|^{2} = ||\\mathbf{z}\_{n}^{(m)} - \\mathbf{z}||^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo id="mmlbr0002">≈</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0002" linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si64.png)

where **z** :  = \[*z*[1], …, *z*[*m*]\]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si65.png). In other words, Euclidean distances are computed in the lower-dimensional subspace, which leads to substantial computational gains (see, for example, \[22,63,160\] and the references therein). This method is also known as *latent semantics indexing*.

### Orthogonalizing properties of PCA and feature generation

We will now shed light on PCA from a different angle. We have just discussed, in the context of the information retrieval application, that PCA can also be seen as a feature generation method that generates a set of new feature vectors, ***z***, whose components describe a pattern in terms of the principal axes. Let us now assume (to make life easier) that *N* is large enough and the sample covariance matrix is a good approximation of the (full rank) covariance matrix *Σ* = 𝔼\[**x****x**^(*T*)\]<mml:math><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si66.png). We know that any vector **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si67.png) can be described in terms of **u**[1], …, **u**[*l*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si68.png), that is,

$\\mathbf{x} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}z\_{i}\\mathbf{u}\_{i} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}(\\mathbf{u}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{x})\\mathbf{u}\_{i}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si69.png)

Our focus now turns to the covariance matrix of the random vectors, **z**, as **x** changes randomly. Taking into account that

*z*[*i*] = **u**[*i*]^(*T*)**x**,<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si70.png)(20.14) 

and the definition of *U* in Eqs. [(20.7)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq7) and [(20.8)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq8), we can write **z** = *U*^(*T*)**x**<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si71.png), and hence

𝔼\[**z****z**^(*T*)\] = 𝔼 \[*U*^(*T*)**x****x**^(*T*)*U*\] = *U*^(*T*)*Σ**U*.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.2em"/><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">\[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si72.png)

However, we know from linear algebra (Appendix A.2) that *U* is the matrix that diagonalizes *Σ*; hence,

𝔼\[**z****z**^(*T*)\] = diag{*λ*[1],…,*λ*[*l*]}.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext>diag</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si73.png)(20.15) 

In other words, the new features are *uncorrelated*, that is,

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/fx002.jpg)(20.16) 

Furthermore, note that the variances of *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si209.png) are equal to the eigenvalues *λ*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si75.png), respectively. Hence, by selecting as features the ones that correspond to the dominant eigenvalues, one has maximally retained the total variance associated with the original features, *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si76.png); indeed, the corresponding total variance is given by the trace of the covariance matrix, which in turn is equal to the sum of the eigenvalues, as we know from linear algebra. In other words, the new set of features, *z*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si77.png), represent the patterns in a more compact way, as they are *mutually uncorrelated* and most of the variance is retained. It is common in practice, when the goal is that of feature generation, for each one of the *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si209.png)s to be normalized to unit variance.

Later on, we will see that a more recent method, known as ICA, imposes the constraint that after a linear transformation (a projection is a linear transformation, after all) the obtained latent variables (components) are statistically independent, which is a much stronger condition than being uncorrelated.

### Latent variables

The random components *z*[*i*], *i* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si77.png), are known as *principal components*. Sometimes, their observed values, *z*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si79.png), are known as *principal scores*. As a matter of fact, the principal components comprise the *latent* variables, which we mentioned at the beginning of this section.

According to the general (linear) latent variable modeling approach, we assume that our *l* variables comprising **x** are modeled as

**x** ≈ *A***z**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si80.png)(20.17) 

where *A* is an *l* × *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si81.png) matrix and **z** ∈ ℝ^(*m*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si337.png) is the corresponding set of latent variables. Adopting the PCA model, we have shown that

*A* = \[**u**[1], …, **u**[*m*]\] :  = *U*[*m*],<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si83.png)

and the model implies that each one of the *l* components of **x** is (approximately) generated in terms of these mutually uncorrelated *m* latent random variables, that is,

*x*[*i*] ≈ *u*[*i*1]*z*[1] + … + *u*[*i**m*]*z*[*m*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si84.png)(20.18) 

Alternatively, in linear latent variable modeling, we can assume that the latent variables can also be recovered by a linear model from the original random variables, as for example,

**z** = *W***x**.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si353.png)(20.19) 

In the case of the PCA approach, we have already seen that

*W* = *U*[*m*]^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si86.png)

Eqs. [(20.17)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq22) and [(20.19)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq25) constitute the backbone of this chapter, and different methods provide different solutions for computing *A* or *W*.

Let us now collect all the principal score vectors, **z**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si269.png), as the columns of the *m* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si88.png) score matrix *Z*, that is,

*Z* :  = \[**z**[1], …, **z**[*N*]\].<mml:math><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si89.png)(20.20) 

Then Eq. [(20.10)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq11) can be rewritten in terms of the score matrix

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/fx003.jpg)(20.21) 

Moreover, taking into account the definition of the principal components in Eq. [(20.14)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq18), we can also write

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/fx004.jpg)(20.22) 

Remarks 20.1

*   •  A major issue in practice is to select the *m* dominant eigenvalues. One way is to rank them in descending order, and determine *m* so that the gap between *λ*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si90.png) and *λ*[*m* + 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si91.png) is “large.” The interested reader can obtain more on this issue in \[55,104\].
*   •  The treatment so far involved centered quantities. In case we want to approximate the original observation vectors by taking into consideration the respective mean value of the data set, Eq. [(20.13)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq15) is rephrased as

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} = \\overline{\\mathbf{x}} + \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}\\mathbf{u}\_{i}^{T}(\\mathbf{x} - \\overline{\\mathbf{x}})\\mathbf{u}\_{i},$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">ˆ</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si92.png)(20.23) 

*   where $\\overline{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si93.png) is the sample mean (mean if it is known)

$\\overline{\\mathbf{x}} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\mathbf{x}\_{n}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si94.png)

*   and ***x*** denotes the original (not centered) vector.
*   •  PCA builds upon *global* information spread over *all* the data observations in the set 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si4.png). Indeed, the main source of information is the sample covariance matrix (*X**X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si28.png)). Thus, PCA is effective if the covariance matrix provides a sufficiently rich description of the data at hand. For example, this is the case for Gaussian-like distributions. In \[41\], modifications of the standard approach are suggested in order to deal with data having a clustered nature. Soon, we are going to discuss techniques alternative to PCA in order to overcome this drawback.
*   •  Computing the SVD of large matrices can be computationally costly and a number of efficient techniques have been proposed (see, e.g., \[1,83,194\]). In a number of cases in practice, it turns out that *l* > *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si95.png). Of course, in this case, the sample covariance is not invertible and some of the eigenvalues are zero. In such scenarios, it is preferable to work with an *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si30.png) (*N* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si96.png)) instead of an *X**X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si28.png) (*l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si596.png)) matrix. To this end, the relationships given in Section [6.4](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml), in order to obtain **u**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si42.png) from **v**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si98.png), can be employed.
*   •  The treatment of PCA bears a similarity with the Fisher linear discriminant (FLD) method (Chapter [7](#Chp007_293-342_B9780443292385000135.xhtml)). They both rely on the eigenstructure of matrices that, in one way or another, encode (co)variance information. However, note that PCA is an *unsupervised* method, in contrast to FLD, which is a *supervised* one. As a consequence, PCA performs dimensionality reduction so as to preserve data variability (variance) while FLD class separability. [Fig. 20.3](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0025) demonstrates the difference in the resulting (hyper)planes.

![Figure 20.3 The case of a two-class task in the two-dimensional space. PCA computes the direction along which the variance is maximally retained after the projections of the data on it. In contrast, FLD computes the line so that the class separability is maximized.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 20.3](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#cf0365) The case of a two-class task in the two-dimensional space. PCA computes the direction along which the variance is maximally retained after the projections of the data on it. In contrast, FLD computes the line so that the class separability is maximized.

*   
*   •  *Multidimensional scaling* (MDS) is another linear technique used to project in a lower-dimensional space, while respecting certain constraints. Given the set 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊂</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si2.png), the goal is to project onto a lower-dimensional space, so that inner products are optimally preserved; that is, the cost

$E = \\sum\\limits\_{i}\\sum\\limits\_{j}\\left( \\mathbf{x}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{x}\_{j} - \\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{z}\_{j} \\right)^{2}$<mml:math><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">(</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si100.png)

*   is minimized, where $\\textit{\\textbf{z}}\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si101.png) is the image of $\\textit{\\textbf{x}}\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si102.png) and the sum runs over all the training points in 𝒳<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si4.png). The problem is similar to PCA and it can be shown that the solution is given by the eigendecomposition of the Gram matrix,^([^(156)](#fn156))
*   More on these issues can be found in \[29,60\]. As we will soon see in Section [20.9](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#s0145), the main idea behind MDS of preserving the distances is used, in one way or another, in a number of more recently developed nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques.
*   •  In a variant of the basic PCA, known as *supervised PCA* \[16,195\], the output variables in regression or in classification (depending on the problem at hand) are used together with the input ones, in order to determine the principal directions.

Example 20.1

This example demonstrates the power of PCA as a method to represent data in a lower-dimensional space. Each pattern in a data set, described in terms of a feature vector, **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si104.png), will be represented by a corresponding vector of a reduced dimensionality, **z**[*n*]^((*m*)) ∈ ℝ^(*m*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si105.png). In this example, each feature vector comprises the pixels of a 168 × 168<mml:math><mml:mn>168</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>168</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si106.png) face image. These face images are members of the software-based aligned version \[191\] of the *Labeled Faces in the Wild* (LFW) data set \[102\]. In particular, among the over 13,000 face images of this data set, *N* = 1924<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1924</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si107.png) have been selected with criteria such as the quality of the image and the face angle (portraits were of preference). Moreover, the images are zoomed in order to omit most of the background. Examples of the face images used are depicted in [Fig. 20.4](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0030) and the full collection of all the 1924 images can be found in the companion site of this book.

![Figure 20.4 Indicative examples of the face images used.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr004.jpg)

Figure 20.4 Indicative examples of the face images used.

The images are first vectorized (in ℝ^(*l*), *l* = 168 × 168 = 28, 224<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>168</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>168</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>224</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si108.png)) and in the sequel are concatenated in the columns of the 28, 224 × 1924<mml:math><mml:mn>28</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>224</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1924</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si109.png) matrix *X*. Moreover, the mean value across each one of the rows is computed and then subtracted from the corresponding element of each column.

In this case, where *l* > *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si95.png), it is convenient to compute the eigenvectors of *X*^(*T*)*X*<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si30.png), denoted by **v**[*i*], *i* = 1, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si110.png), and then the principal axes directions, that is, the eigenvectors of *X**X*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>X</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si28.png) are computed by **u**[*i*] ∝ *X***v**[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si111.png) (Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml), Eq. [(6.18)](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)). These eigenvectors can be rearranged in a matrix form to give 168 × 168<mml:math><mml:mn>168</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>168</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si106.png) images, known as *eigenimages*, which in the particular case of face images are referred to as *eigenfaces*. [Fig. 20.5](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0035) shows examples of eigenfaces resulting from the PCA of matrix *X* and specifically those corresponding, from top left to bottom right, to the 1st, 2nd, 6th, 7th, 8th, 10th, 11th, and 17th largest eigenvalues.

![Figure 20.5 Examples of eigenfaces.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 20.5](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#cf0395) Examples of eigenfaces.

Next, the quality of reconstruction of an original image, in terms of its lower-dimensional representation, is examined according to Eq. [(20.13)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq15) for different values of *m*. As an example, the images depicting Marilyn Monroe and Andy Warhol, shown in [Fig. 20.4](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0030), are chosen.  The results are illustrated in [Fig. 20.6](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0040). It is observed that for *m* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si112.png), or even better, for *m* = 600<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>600</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si113.png), the resulting approximation is very close to the original images. Note that exact reconstruction will be achieved when the full set of the 1924 eigenfaces is used.

![Figure 20.6 Image reconstruction based on the first m eigenvectors.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 20.6](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#cf0410) Image reconstruction based on the first *m* eigenvectors.

To put our previous findings in an information retrieval context, assume that one has available an image and wants to know what person is depicted in it. Assuming that the image of this person is in the data set, the procedure would be (a) to vectorize the image, (b) to project it onto the subspace spanned by the, say, *m* = 100<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si112.png) eigenfaces, and (c) to search in this lower-dimensional space to identify the vectorized image in the data set that is closest in the Euclidean norm sense. Usually, it is preferable to identify the, say, 5 or 10 most similar images and rank them according to the Euclidean distance (or any other distance) similarity. In the sequel, one can retrieve the name and all the associated information that is kept in the data set/database.

In information retrieval, each one of the images in the data set can be stored in terms of the corresponding vector of the principal scores.

Example 20.2

In this example, the use of PCA for image compression is demonstrated. In the previous example, PCA was performed across the different images of a database. Here, the focus will be on a single image.

The pixel values of the image are stored in an *l* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si39.png) matrix *X* and the columns of this matrix are considered to be the observation vectors **x**[*n*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*), *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si10.png). Note that *X* needs to be zero mean along the rows so the mean vector, $\\overline{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si93.png), is computed and subtracted from each column. Then the eigenvectors corresponding to the *m*, 1 ≤ *m* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si115.png), largest eigenvalues are obtained either via the sample covariance matrix or directly through SVD. Exploiting the matrix factorization formulation of PCA in Eq. [(20.22)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq29), a compressed representation of *X*, comprising *m* instead of *l* rows, is given by

$Z^{(m)} = \\underset{m \\times l}{\\underset{︸}{{\\lbrack\\mathbf{u}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{u}\_{m}\\rbrack}^{T}}}X,$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow><mml:mo>︸</mml:mo></mml:munder><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si116.png)(20.24) 

where the dimensionality *m* has been explicitly brought into the notation. Thus, only *Z*^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si117.png) and **u**[1], …, **u**[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si118.png) are needed to get an estimate of the, mean-subtracted, *X* via Eq. [(20.21)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq28). Finally, in order to reconstruct the image, the mean vector $\\overline{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si93.png) needs to be added back to each column (see Eq. [(20.23)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq30)).

The effectiveness of the PCA-based image compression will be demonstrated with the aid of the top-left image depicted in [Fig. 20.7](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0045). This image is square, having *l* = *N* = 400<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>400</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si119.png). For any *m* chosen, the compression ratio is easily computed considering that instead of 400 × 400<mml:math><mml:mn>400</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>400</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si120.png) values of the original image, after compression the storage of 2 × *m* × 400<mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>400</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si121.png) values for the matrix *Z*^((*m*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si117.png) and the eigenvectors, **u**[1], …, **u**[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si118.png), plus 400 values for the mean vector $\\overline{\\mathbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si93.png) is needed. This amounts to a compression ratio of 400 : (2*m* + 1)<mml:math><mml:mn>400</mml:mn><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si123.png). The reconstructed images together with the corresponding MSE between the original and the reconstructed image for different compression rates are shown in [Fig. 20.7](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0045).

![Figure 20.7 PCA-based image compression. The image is from the Greek island Andros.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr007.jpg)

Figure 20.7 PCA-based image compression. The image is from the Greek island Andros.

Remarks 20.2

*   •  *Subspace tracking*: Online subspace tracking is another old area with a revived interest recently. A well-known algorithm of relative low complexity, for tracking the signal subspace, is the so-called projection approximation subspace tracking (PAST), proposed in \[197\]. In PAST, the recursive least-squares (RLS) technique is employed for subspace estimation. Alternative algorithms in this line of philosophy have been presented in, for example, \[69,115,170,179\].
*   More recently, the work in \[25,50,137\] tackles the problem of subspace tracking with missing/unobserved data. The methodology presented in \[25\] is based on gradient descent iterations on the Grassmannian manifold. Furthermore, the algorithms of \[50,137\] attempt to estimate the unknown subspace by minimizing properly constructed loss functions.
*   Finally, \[51,52,92,132,162\] attack the subspace tracking problem in environments where observations are contaminated by outlier noise. 

## 20.4 Canonical correlation analysis

PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique focusing on a *single* data set. However, in a number of cases, one has to deal with multiple data sets which, although they may originate from different sources, are closely related. For example, many problems in medical imaging fall under this umbrella. A typical case occurs in the study of brain activity where one can use different modalities, for example, electroencephalogram (EEG), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), or structural MRI. Each one of these modalities can grasp a different type of information and it is beneficial to exploit all of them in a complementary fashion. Thus, the respective experimental data can appropriately be fused in order to get a better description concerning the brain activity that gives birth to the data. Another scenario where multiple data sets are of interest is when a single modality is used but different data are available measured on different subjects; thus, jointly analyzing the results can be beneficial for the finally reached conclusions (see, e.g., \[56\]).

*Canonical correlation analysis* (CCA) is an old technique developed in \[96\] to process two data sets jointly. Our starting point is the fact that when two sets of random variables (two random vectors) are involved, the value of their correlation *does depend* on the coordinate system in which the random vectors are represented. The goal behind CCA is to seek a pair of linear transformations, one for each set of variables, such that after the transformation, the resulting transformed variables are *maximally correlated*.

Let us assume that we are given two sets of random variables comprising the components of two random vectors, **x** ∈ ℝ^(*p*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si124.png) and **y** ∈ ℝ^(*q*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si125.png), and let the corresponding sets of observations be **x**[*n*], **y**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si126.png), respectively. Following a step-wise procedure, as we did for PCA, we will first compute a single pair of directions, namely, **u**[*x*, 1], **u**[*y*, 1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si127.png), so that the correlation between the projections onto these directions is maximized. Let *z*[*x*, 1] :  = **u**[*x*, 1]^(*T*)**x**<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si128.png) and *z*[*y*, 1] :  = **u**[*y*, 1]^(*T*)**y**<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>y</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">y</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si129.png) be the (zero mean) random variables after the linear transformation (projection). Note that these variables are the counterparts of what we called principal components in PCA. The corresponding correlation coefficient (normalized covariance) is defined as

$\\rho: = \\frac{\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack z\_{x,1}z\_{y,1}\\rbrack}{\\sqrt{\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack z\_{x,1}^{2} \\right\\rbrack\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack z\_{y,1}^{2} \\right\\rbrack}} = \\frac{\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack (\\mathbf{u}\_{x,1}^{T}\\mathbf{x})(\\mathbf{y}^{T}\\mathbf{u}\_{y,1}) \\right\\rbrack}{\\sqrt{\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack {(\\mathbf{u}\_{x,1}^{T}\\mathbf{x})}^{2} \\right\\rbrack\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack {(\\mathbf{u}\_{y,1}^{T}\\mathbf{y})}^{2} \\right\\rbrack}}$<mml:math><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak"
