$\\min\\limits\_{Z}\\quad||X - AZ||\_{F}^{2},\\text{s.t.}\\quad||\\mathbf{z}\_{n}||\_{0} \\leq T\_{0},\\quad n = 1,2,\\ldots,N,$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0006"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0006" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si270.png)

which, due to the definition of the Frobenius norm, is equivalent to solving *N* distinct optimization tasks,

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{z}\_{n}}\\quad||\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - A\\mathbf{z}\_{n}||^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si271.png)(20.66) 

s.t. ||**z**[*n*]||[0] ≤ *T*[0], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si272.png)(20.67) 

A similar objective is met if the following optimization tasks are considered instead:

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{z}\_{n}}\\quad||\\mathbf{z}\_{n}||\_{0},\\text{s.t.}\\quad||\\mathbf{x}\_{n} - A\\mathbf{z}\_{n}||^{2} < \\epsilon,\\quad n = 1,2,\\ldots,N,$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0007"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0007" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si273.png)

where *ϵ* is a constant acting as an upper bound of the error.

The task in [(20.66)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq96) and [(20.67)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq97) can be solved by any one of the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si268.png) minimization solvers, which have been considered in Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml), for example, the OMP. This stage is known as *sparse coding*.

*Stage 2*: This stage is known as the *codebook update*. Having obtained **z**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si269.png) (for fixed *A*), from Stage 1, the goal now is to optimize with respect to the columns of *A*. This is achieved on a *column-by-column* basis. Assume that we currently consider the update of **a**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si275.png); this is carried out so as to minimize the (squared) Frobenius norm, ||*X* − *A**Z*||[*F*]²<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si276.png). To this end, we can write the product *AZ* as a sum of rank-one matrices, that is,

$AZ = \\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{a}\_{1},\\ldots,\\mathbf{a}\_{m} \\right\\rbrack\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{z}\_{1}^{r},\\ldots,\\mathbf{z}\_{m}^{r} \\right\\rbrack^{T} = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}\\mathbf{a}\_{i}\\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{rT},$<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si277.png)(20.68) 

where **z**[*i*]^(*r**T*), *i* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si278.png), are the *rows* of *Z*. Note that in the above sum, the vectors for indices *i* = 1, 2, …, *k* − 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si279.png) are fixed to their recently updated values during this second stage of the current iteration step, while the vectors corresponding to *i* = *k* + 1, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si280.png) are fixed to the values that are available from the previous iteration step. This strategy allows for the use of the most recent updated information. We will now minimize with respect to the rank one outer product matrix, **a**[*k*]**z**[*k*]^(*r**T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si281.png). Observe that this product, besides the *k*th column of *A*, also involves the *k*th row of *Z*; both of them will be updated. The rank one matrix is estimated so as to minimize

||*E*[*k*]−**a**[*k*]**z**[*k*]^(*r**T*)||[*F*]²,<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si282.png)(20.69) 

where

$E\_{k}: = X - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1,i \\neq k}^{m}\\mathbf{a}\_{i}\\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{rT}.$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si283.png)

In other words, we seek to find the best, in the Frobenius sense, rank-one approximation of *E*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si284.png). Recall from Chapter [6](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml) (Section [6.4](#Chp006_249-291_B9780443292385000123.xhtml)) that the solution is given via the SVD of *E*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si284.png). However, if we do that, there is no guarantee that whatever sparse structure has been embedded in **z**[*k*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si285.png), from the update in Stage 1, will be retained. According to the *k*\-SVD, this is bypassed by focusing on the active set, that is, involving only the nonzero of its coefficients. Thus, we first search for the locations of the nonzero coefficients in **z**[*k*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si285.png) and let

*ω*[*k*] :  = {*j*[*k*],1≤*j*[*k*]≤*N*: *z*[*k*]^(*r*)(*j*[*k*])≠0}.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≠</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="3.8ex" minsize="3.8ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si286.png)

Then, we form the reduced vector ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{z}}}\_{k}^{r} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{|\\omega\_{k}|}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si287.png), where |*ω*[*k*]|<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si288.png) denotes the cardinality of *ω*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si289.png), which contains only the nonzero elements of **z**[*k*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si285.png). A little thought reveals that, when writing *X* = *A**Z*<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si290.png), the column of current interest, **a**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si275.png), contributes (as part of the corresponding linear combination) only to the columns **x**[*j*[*k*]], *j*[*k*] ∈ *ω*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si291.png), of *X*. We then collect the corresponding columns of *E*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si284.png) to construct a reduced-order matrix, *Ẽ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si292.png), which comprises the columns that are associated with the locations of the nonzero elements of **z**[*k*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si285.png), and select $\\mathbf{a}\_{k}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{z}}}\_{k}^{rT}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si293.png) so as to minimize

$\\left| \\left| {\\widetilde{E}}\_{k} - \\mathbf{a}\_{k}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{z}}}\_{k}^{rT} \\right| \\right|\_{F}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si294.png)(20.70) 

Performing SVD, *Ẽ*[*k*] = *U**D**V*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si295.png), **a**[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si275.png) is set equal to **u**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si13.png) corresponding to the largest of the singular values and ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{z}}}\_{k}^{r} = D(1,1)\\mathbf{v}\_{1}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si296.png). Thus, the atoms of the dictionary are obtained in *normalized* form (recall from the theory of SVD that ||**u**[1]|| = 1<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si297.png)). In the sequel, the updated values obtained for ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{z}}}\_{k}^{r}$<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si298.png) are placed in the corresponding locations in **z**[*k*]^(*r*)<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si285.png). The latter now has at least as many zeros as it had before, as some of the elements in **v**[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si299.png) may be zeros. Simple arguments ([Problem 20.3](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#o0085)) show that at each iteration the error decreases and the algorithm converges to a local minimum. The success of the algorithm depends on the ability of the greedy algorithm to provide a sparse solution during the first stage. As we know from Chapter [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml), greedy algorithms work well for sparsity levels, *T*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si266.png), small enough compared to *l*.

In summary, each iteration step of the *k*\-SVD algorithm comprises the following computation steps.

*   •  Initialize *A*^((0))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si300.png) with columns normalized to unit ℓ[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si301.png) norm.
*   •  Set *i* = 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si302.png).
*   •  *Stage 1*: Solve the optimization task in [(20.66)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq96) and [(20.67)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq97) to obtain the sparse coding representation vectors, **z**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si269.png); use any algorithm developed for this task.
*   •  *Stage 2*: For any column, *k* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si303.png), in *A*^((*i* − 1))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si304.png), update it according to the following: 
    1.  –  Identify the locations of the nonzero elements in the *k*th row of the computed, from Stage 1, matrix *Z*.
    2.  –  Select the columns in *E*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si284.png), which correspond to the locations of the nonzero elements of the *k*th row of *Z* and form a reduced-order error matrix, *Ẽ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si292.png).
    3.  –  Perform SVD on *Ẽ*[*k*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si292.png): *Ẽ*[*k*] = *U**D**V*^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si295.png).
    4.  –  Update the *k*th column of *A*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si305.png) to be the eigenvector corresponding to the largest singular value, **a**[*k*]^((*i*)) = **u**[1]<mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si306.png).
    5.  –  Update *Z*, by embedding in the nonzero locations of its *k*th row the values *D*(1, 1)**v**[1]^(*T*)<mml:math><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si307.png).
*   •  Stop if a convergence criterion is met.
*   •  If not, *i* = *i* + 1<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si308.png), and continue. 

### Why the name *k*\-SVD?

The SVD part of the name is pretty obvious. However, the reader may wonder about the presence of “*k*” in front. As stated in \[4\], the algorithm can be considered a generalization of the *k*\-means algorithm, introduced in Chapter [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) ([Algorithm 12.1](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml)). There, we can consider the mean values, which represent each cluster, as the code words (atoms) of a dictionary. During the first stage of the *k*\-means learning, given the representatives of each cluster, a sparse coding scheme is performed; that is, each input vector is assigned to a single cluster. Thus, we can think of the *k*\-means clustering as a sparse coding scheme that associates a latent vector with each one of the observations. Note that each of the latent vectors has only one nonzero element, pointing to the cluster where the respective input vector is assigned, according to the smallest Euclidean distance from all cluster representatives. This is a major difference with the *k*\-SVD dictionary learning, during which each observation vector can be associated with more than one atom; hence, the sparsity level of the corresponding latent vector can be larger than one. Furthermore, based on the assignment of the input vectors to the clusters, in the second stage of the *k*\-means algorithm, an update of the cluster representatives is performed, and for each representative only the input vectors assigned to it are used. This is also similar in spirit to what happens in the second stage of *k*\-SVD. The difference is that each input observation may be associated with more than one atom. As pointed out in \[4\], if one sets *T*[0] = 1<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si309.png), the *k*\-means algorithm can result from *k*\-SVD.

### Dictionary learning and dictionary identifiability

Dictionary learning was introduced via the ℓ[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ℓ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si268.png) norm in (20.64)–(20.65). In a more general setting, the dictionary learning task is cast as follows:

minimize with respect to *A* ∈ 𝒜 and *Z*    {||*X*−*A**Z*||[*F*]²+*λ**g*(*Z*)},<mml:math><mml:mtext>minimize with respect to</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si310.png)(20.71) 

where *g*(*Z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si311.png) is a sparsity promoting function of the elements of matrix *Z*. For example,

$g(Z) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}|Z(i,j)|,$<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si312.png)(20.72) 

and *λ* is a regularization parameter. The set 𝒜 ⊆ ℝ^(*l* × *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊆</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si313.png) is a compact constraint set. For example, often we assume that the columns of *A* have unit norm. This guarantees *scale invariance*. Indeed, assuming *A*, *Z*<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si314.png) is a solution, if we do not use any constraint, the set $A^{\\prime} = (cA),\\ Z^{\\prime} = (\\frac{1}{c}Z)$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>′</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si315.png) would also be a solution, for any value of *c*. Other constraints can also be used to account for extra a priori knowledge concerning the available data (see, e.g., \[85\]).

In practice, the solution involves two stages, as with *k*\-SVD. Assuming that *A*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si305.png) is known at the iteration step *i*, minimization with respect to the code vectors first takes place, i.e.,

*Stage 1*:

$Z^{(i)} = \\min\\limits\_{Z}\\ \\left\\{ ||X - A^{(i)}Z||\_{F}^{2} + \\lambda g(Z) \\right\\}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">{</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">}</mml:mo><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si316.png)(20.73) 

Then, fixing *Z*^((*i*))<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si317.png), the code book update results as

*Stage 2*:

$A^{(i + 1)} = \\min\\limits\_{A \\in \\mathcal{A}}\\ ||X - AZ^{(i)}||\_{F}^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="script">A</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si318.png)(20.74) 

In the last equation, the sparsity promoting term is not involved, since it is independent of *A*. Assuming that *g*(*Z*)<mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si311.png) is a convex function, at each stage a convex optimization task is solved. Such problems are known as *biconvex*, in the sense that by fixing one of the arguments in the cost function the optimization problem becomes a convex one with respect to the other. The solution of the optimization task can be obtained via different paths; for example, via majorize-minimize (MM) techniques or the ADMM scheme (Section [8.14](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml)); see, e.g., \[80,140,196\] for some application cases under various constraints.

Solving the dictionary learning task is a nonconvex optimization problem. An important related issue is that of the characterization of the associated local minima. This task is another face of what we call *identifiability*. In other words, assuming that there exists a dictionary that generates the data, can this be recovered? To know the answer to this question is of major importance in a number of applications. For example, in a source localization task, the atoms of the dictionary relate to the directions of the arrival of the involved signals. Also, in fMRI (see Section [20.11](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#s0205)) the atoms of the dictionary provide information related to the time responses of the neurons associated with the activated regions in the brain. In \[86\], it is shown that, under certain assumptions related to sparsity, the minimized cost function in the dictionary learning task has a *guaranteed* local minimum around the dictionary that generates the data, with high probability. Moreover, the bound on the number of samples that are sufficient for the existence of such a minimum is also derived.

Remarks 20.5

*   •  Alternative paths to *k*\-SVD to dictionary learning have also been suggested. For example, in \[73\] a dictionary learning technique referred to as method of optimal directions (MOD) was proposed, which differs from *k*\-SVD in the dictionary update step. In particular, the full dictionary is updated via direct minimization of the Frobenius norm. In \[126,143\] probabilistic arguments are employed, using a Laplacian prior to enforce sparsity. We know from Chapter [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml) (Section [13.5](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml)) that in this case, the involved integrations are not analytically tractable and approximations are used to bypass this obstacle. In the former, the maximum value of the integrand is used and in the latter a Gaussian approximation of the posterior is adopted in order to handle the integration. In \[82\], variational bound techniques are mobilized (see Section [13.9](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml)).
*   •  The method proposed in \[125\] bears some similarities to *k*\-SVD, because it also revolves around SVD, but the dictionary is constrained to be a union of orthonormal bases. This can lead to some computational advantages; on the other hand, *k*\-SVD puts no constraints on the atoms of the dictionary, which gives more freedom in modeling the input. Another difference lies in the column-by-column update introduced in *k*\-SVD.
*   •  A more detailed comparative study of *k*\-SVD with other methods is given in \[4\].
*   •  Dictionary learning is essentially a matrix factorization problem where a certain type of constraint is imposed on the matrix factor to the right. This approach can be considered to be just a manifestation of a wider class of constrained matrix factorization methods that allow several types of constraints to hold. Such techniques include the regularized PCA, where functional and/or sparsity constraints are imposed on the left and on the right factors \[12,190,200\], as well as the structured sparse matrix factorization in \[14\].
*   •  Besides the previously reported algorithms, a number of *online* and *distributed* dictionary learning schemes have been proposed. In \[127\], a distributed version of the *k*\-SVD algorithm is developed. A cloud-based version of *k*\-SVD is proposed in \[149\] with an emphasis on big data applications. A dictionary learning algorithm employing arguments inspired by the EXTRA optimization scheme, which is briefly discussed in Section [8.15](#Chp008_343-416_B9780443292385000147.xhtml), is described in \[182\]. In \[49\], the various agents/nodes learn different parts of the dictionary. Such an approach is also suited for big data applications. An online algorithm for dictionary learning has been presented in \[139\] and an online version for a distributed setting, with provable convergence to a stationary point, has been proposed in \[53\]. In \[62\], the decentralized case over time-varying digraphs is considered that involves a general set of constraints, where a number of matrix factorization schemes result as special cases.

Example 20.5

The goal of this example is to show the performance of the dictionary learning technique in the context of the image denoising task. In the case study of Section [9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), image denoising, based on a predetermined and fixed DCT dictionary, was considered. Here, *k*\-SVD will be employed in order to learn the dictionary using information of the image *itself*. The two (256 × 256)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si319.png) images, without and with noise corresponding to PSNR = 22, are shown in [Figs. 20.12](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0085)A and B, respectively. The noisy image is divided in overlapping patches of size 12 × 12 (144)<mml:math><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>144</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si320.png), resulting in (256 − 12 + 1)² = 60, 025<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>256</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>60</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>025</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si321.png) patches in total; these will constitute the training data set used for the learning of the dictionary. Specifically, the patches are sequentially extracted from the noisy image, vectorized in lexicographic order, and used as columns, one after the other, to define the (144 × 60, 025)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mn>144</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>60</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>025</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si322.png) matrix *X*. Then, *k*\-SVD is mobilized to train an overcomplete dictionary of size 144 × 196<mml:math><mml:mn>144</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>196</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si323.png). The resulting atoms, reshaped in order to form 12 × 12<mml:math><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si324.png) pixel patches, are shown in [Fig. 20.13](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0090). Compare the atoms of this dictionary with atoms of the fixed DCT dictionary of [Fig. 9.14](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml).

![Figure 20.12 Image denoising based on dictionary learning.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr012.jpg)

Figure 20.12 Image denoising based on dictionary learning.

![Figure 20.13 Dictionary resulting from k-SVD.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 20.13](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#cf0955) Dictionary resulting from *k*\-SVD.

Next, we follow the same procedure as in Section [9.10](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), by replacing the DCT dictionary with the one obtained by the *k*\-SVD method. The resulting denoised image is shown in [Fig. 20.12](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0085)C. Note that although the dictionary was trained based on *the noisy data*, it led to about 2 dB PSNR improvement over the fixed-dictionary case. As a matter of fact, because the number of patches is large and each one of them carries a different noise realization, the noise, during the dictionary learning stage, is averaged out, leading to nearly noise-free dictionary atoms. More advanced use of dictionary learning techniques to further improve performance in tasks such as denoising and inpainting can be found in \[71,72,138\]. 

## 20.7 Nonnegative matrix factorization

The strong connection between dimensionality reduction and low-rank matrix factorization has already been stressed while discussing PCA. ICA can also be considered as a low-rank matrix factorization, if a smaller number, compared to the *l* observed random variables, of independent components is retained (e.g., selecting the *m* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si325.png) least Gaussian ones).

An alternative to the previously discussed low-rank matrix factorization schemes was suggested in \[144,145\], which guarantees the *nonnegativity* of the elements of the resulting matrix factors. Such a constraint is enforced in certain applications because negative elements contradict physical reality. For example, in image analysis, the intensity values of the pixels cannot be negative. Also, probability values cannot be negative. The resulting factorization is known as *nonnegative matrix factorization* (NMF) and it has been used successfully in a number of applications, including document clustering \[192\], molecular pattern discovery \[28\], image analysis \[122\], clustering \[171\], music transcription, music instrument classification \[20,166\], and face verification \[198\].

Given an *l* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si39.png) matrix *X*, the task of NMF consists of finding an approximate factorization of *X*, that is,

*X* ≈ *A**Z*,<mml:math><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si326.png)(20.75) 

where *A* and *Z* are *l* × *m*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si81.png) and *m* × *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si88.png) matrices, respectively, *m* ≤ min(*N*, *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mtext>min</mml:mtext><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si327.png), and all the matrix elements are nonnegative, that is, *A*(*i*, *k*) ≥ 0, *Z*(*k*, *j*) ≥ 0, *i* = 1, 2, …, *l*, *k* = 1, 2, …, *m*, *j* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si328.png). Clearly, if matrices *A* and *Z* are of low rank, their product is also a low-rank, at most *m*, approximation of *X*. The significance of the above is that every column vector in *X* is represented by the expansion

$\\mathbf{x}\_{i} \\approx \\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{m}Z(k,i)\\mathbf{a}\_{k},\\ i = 1,2,\\ldots,N,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si329.png)

where $\\textit{\\textbf{a}}\_{k},\\ k = 1,2,\\ldots,m$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si330.png), are the column vectors of *A* and constitute the basis of the expansion. The number of vectors in the basis is smaller than the dimensionality of the vector itself. Hence, NMF can also be seen as a method for *dimensionality reduction*.

To get a good approximation in Eq. [(20.75)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq108) one can adopt different costs. The most common cost is the Frobenius norm of the error matrix. In such a setting, the NMF task is cast as follows:

$\\min\\limits\_{A,Z}||X - AZ||\_{F}^{2}: = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{l}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}\\left( X(i,j) - \\lbrack AZ\\rbrack(i,j) \\right)^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">|</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>X</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si331.png)(20.76) 

s.t.*A*(*i*, *k*) ≥ 0, *Z*(*k*, *j*) ≥ 0,<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>≥</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si332.png)(20.77) 

where \[*A**Z*\](*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>Z</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si333.png) is the (*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si334.png) element of matrix *AZ*, and *i*, *j*, *k*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si335.png) run over all possible values. Besides the Frobenius norm, other costs have also been suggested (see, e.g., \[168\]).

Once the problem has been formulated, the major issue rests at the solution of the optimization task. To this end, a number of algorithms have been proposed, for example, Newton-type or gradient descent-type algorithms. Such algorithmic issues, as well as a number of related theoretic ones, are beyond the scope of this book, and the interested reader may consult, for example, \[54,67,178\]. More recently, regularized versions, including sparsity promoting regularizers, have been proposed (see, for example, \[55\]).

## 20.8 Learning low-dimensional models: a probabilistic perspective

In this section, the emphasis is on looking at the dimensionality reduction task from a Bayesian perspective. Our focus will be more on presenting the main ideas and less on algorithmic procedures; the latter depend on the specific model and can be dug out from the palette of algorithms that have already been presented in Chapters [12](#Chp012_583-634_B9780443292385000184.xhtml) and [13](#Chp013_635-716_B9780443292385000196.xhtml). Our path to low-dimensional modeling traces its origin to the so-called *factor analysis*.

### 20.8.1 Factor analysis

Factor analysis was originally proposed in the work of Charles Spearman \[169\]. Charles Spearman (1863–1945) was an English psychologist who has made important contributions to statistics. Spearman was interested in human intelligence and developed the method in 1904 for analyzing multiple measures of cognitive performance. He argued that there exists a general intelligence factor (the so-called g-factor) that can be extracted by applying the factor analysis method on intelligence test data. However, this notion has also been disputed, as intelligence comprises a multiplicity of components (see, e.g., \[84\]).

Let **x** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si336.png). The factor analysis model assumes that there are *m* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si325.png) underlying (latent) zero mean variables or *factors* **z** ∈ ℝ^(*m*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si337.png) so that

$x\_{i} - \\mu\_{i} = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}a\_{ij}z\_{j} + \\epsilon\_{i},\\quad i = 1,2,\\ldots,l,$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si338.png)(20.78) 

or compactly written using the vector notation,

**x** − **μ** = *A***z** + **ϵ**,<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si339.png)(20.79) 

where ***μ*** is the mean of **x** and *A* ∈ ℝ^(*l* × *m*)<mml:math><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si340.png) is formed by the weights *a*[*i**j*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si179.png) known as *factor loadings*. The variables *z*[*j*], *j* = 1, 2, …, *m*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si341.png), are sometimes called *common factors*, because they contribute to all observed variables, *x*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si76.png), and *ϵ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si342.png) are the *unique* or *specific factors*. As we have already done so far and without loss of generality, we will assume our data are centered, that is, **μ** = 0<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">μ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si343.png). In factor analysis, we assume *ϵ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si342.png) to be of zero mean and mutually uncorrelated, that is, *Σ*[*ϵ*] = 𝔼\[**ϵ****ϵ**^(*T*)\] :  = *d**i**a**g*{*σ*[1]², *σ*[2]², …, *σ*[*l*]²}<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϵ</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">diag</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si344.png). We also assume that **z** and **ϵ** are independent. The *m* ( < *l*)<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si345.png) columns of *A* form a lower-dimensional subspace, and **ϵ** is that part of **x** not contained in this subspace. The first question that is now raised is whether the model in Eq. [(20.79)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq113) is any different from our familiar regression task. The answer is in the affirmative. Note that here the matrix *A* is not known. All that we are given is the set of observations, **x**[*n*], *n* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si34.png), and we have to obtain the subspace described by *A*. It is basically the same linear model that we have considered so far in this chapter, with the difference that now we have introduced the noise term. Once *A* is known, **z**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si265.png) can be obtained for each **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si466.png).

From Eq. [(20.79)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq113), it is readily seen that

*Σ*[*x*] = 𝔼\[**x****x**^(*T*)\] = *A*𝔼\[**z****z**^(*T*)\]*A*^(*T*) + *Σ*[*ϵ*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si346.png)

We will further assume that 𝔼\[**z****z**^(*T*)\] = *I*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si347.png); hence, we can write

*Σ*[*x*] = *A**A*^(*T*) + *Σ*[*ϵ*].<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si348.png)(20.80) 

Hence, *A* results as a factor of (*Σ*[*x*] − *Σ*[*ϵ*])<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si349.png). However, such a factorization, if it exists, is not unique. This can be easily checked if we consider $\\overline{A} = AU$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:mi>U</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si350.png), where *U* is an orthonormal matrix. Then $\\overline{A}{\\overline{A}}^{T} = AA^{T}$<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">¯</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>A</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si351.png). This has brought a lot of controversy around the factor analysis method when it comes to interpreting individual factors (see, for example, \[44\] for a discussion). To remedy this drawback, a number of authors have suggested methods and criteria that deal with the rotation (orthogonal or oblique) in order to gain improved interpretation of the factors \[157\]. However, from our perspective, where the goal is to express our problem in a lower-dimensional space, this is not a problem. Any orthonormal matrix imposes a rotation within the subspace spanned by the columns of *A*, but we do not care about the exact choice of the coordinates, that is, the common factors.

There are different methods to obtain *A* (see, e.g., \[64\]). A popular one is to assume *p*(**x**)<mml:math><mml:mi>p</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si191.png) to be Gaussian and employ the maximum likelihood method to optimize with respect to the unknown parameters that define *Σ*[*x*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si352.png) in Eq. [(20.80)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq115). Once *A* becomes available, one way to estimate the factors is to further assume that these can be expressed as linear combinations of the observations, that is,

**z** = *W***x**.<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si353.png)

Postmultiplying by **x**, taking expectations, and recalling Eq. [(20.79)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq113) and that 𝔼\[**z****z**^(*T*)\] = *I*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si347.png), we get

𝔼\[**z****x**^(*T*)\] = 𝔼\[**z****z**^(*T*)*A*^(*T*)\] + 𝔼\[**z****ϵ**^(*T*)\] = *A*^(*T*).<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">ϵ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si355.png)(20.81) 

Also,

𝔼\[**z****x**^(*T*)\] = *W*𝔼\[**x****x**^(*T*)\] = *W**Σ*[*x*].<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">z</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\[</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">\]</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si356.png)(20.82) 

Hence,
