linebreakstyle="before">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si493.png)(20.109) 

where

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/fx011.jpg)(20.110) 

and $\\textit{\\textbf{z}}^{T} = \\lbrack z\_{1},z\_{2},\\ldots,z\_{N}\\rbrack$<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si494.png). The Laplacian matrix, *L*, is symmetric and positive semidefinite. The latter is readily seen from the definition in Eq. [(20.109)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq167), where *E*[*L*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si495.png) is always a nonnegative scalar. Note that the larger the value of *D*[*i**i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si496.png) is, the more “important” is the sample $\\textit{\\textbf{x}}\_{i}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si102.png). This is because it implies large values for *W*(*i*, *j*), *j* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si498.png), and plays a dominant role in the minimization process. Obviously, the minimum of *E*[*L*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si495.png) is achieved by the trivial solution *z*[*i*] = 0, *i* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si499.png). To avoid this, as is common in such cases, we constrain the solution to a prespecified norm. Hence, our problem now becomes

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{z}}\\mathbf{z}^{T}L\\mathbf{z},\\text{s.t.}\\mathbf{z}^{T}D\\mathbf{z} = 1.$<mml:math><mml:munder id="mmlbr0013"><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="newline" indentalign="id" indenttarget="mmlbr0013" linebreakstyle="after">,</mml:mo><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si500.png)

Although we can work directly on the previous task, we will slightly reshape it in order to use tools that are more familiar to us. Define

**y** = *D*^(1/2)**z**,<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si501.png)(20.111) 

and

*L̃* = *D*^( − 1/2)*L**D*^( − 1/2),<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si502.png)(20.112) 

which is known as the *normalized graph Laplacian* matrix. It is now readily seen that our optimization problem becomes

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y}}\\mathbf{y}^{T}\\widetilde{L}\\mathbf{y},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si503.png)(20.113) 

s.t.**y**^(*T*)**y** = 1.<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mtext>s.t.</mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si504.png)(20.114) 

Using Lagrange multipliers and equating the gradient of the Lagrangian to zero, it turns out that the solution is given by

*L̃***y** = *λ***y**.<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si505.png)(20.115) 

In other words, computing the solution becomes equivalent to solving an eigenvalue-eigenvector problem. Substituting Eq. [(20.115)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq174) into the cost function in [(20.113)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq172) and taking into account the constraint in [(20.114)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq173), it turns out that the value of the cost associated with the optimal ***y*** is equal to *λ*. Hence, the solution is the eigenvector corresponding to the minimum eigenvalue. However, the minimum eigenvalue of *L̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si506.png) is zero and the corresponding eigenvector corresponds to a trivial solution. Indeed, observe that

*L̃**D*^(1/2)1 = *D*^( − 1/2)*L**D*^( − 1/2)*D*^(1/2)1 = *D*^( − 1/2)(*D* − *W*)1 = 0,<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mn mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si507.png)

where **1** is the vector having all its elements equal to 1. In words, $\\textit{\\textbf{y}} = D^{1/2}\\textbf{1}$<mml:math><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si508.png) is an eigenvector corresponding to the zero eigenvalue and it results in the trivial solution, *z*[*i*] = 1, *i* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si509.png). That is, all the points are mapped onto the same point in the real line. To exclude this undesired solution, recall that *L̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si506.png) is a positive semidefinite matrix and, hence, 0 is its smallest eigenvalue. In addition, if the graph is assumed to be connected, that is, there is at least one path (see Chapter [15](#Chp015_755-803_B9780443292385000214.xhtml)) that connects any pair of vertices, *D*^(1/2)**1**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si510.png) is the only eigenvector associated with the zero eigenvalue, *λ*[0]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si511.png) \[19\]. Also, as *L̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si506.png) is a symmetric matrix, we know (Appendix A.2) that its eigenvectors are orthogonal to each other. In the sequel, we impose an extra constraint and we now require the solution to be *orthogonal* to *D*^(1/2)**1**<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>D</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo stretchy="false">/</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si510.png). Constraining the solution to be orthogonal to the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest (zero) eigenvalue drives the solution to the next eigenvector corresponding to the next smallest (nonzero) eigenvalue *λ*[1]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si19.png). Note that the eigendecomposition of *L̃*<mml:math><mml:mover accent="true"><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">˜</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si506.png) is equivalent to what we called generalized eigendecomposition of *L* in Step 3 before.

For the more general case of *m* > 1<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&gt;</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si512.png), we have to compute the *m* eigenvectors associated with *λ*[1] ≤ … ≤ *λ*[*m*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>≤</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si513.png). As a matter of fact, for this case, the constraints prevent us from mapping onto a subspace of dimension less than the desired *m*. For example, we do not want to project in a three-dimensional space and the points to lie on a two-dimensional plane or on a one-dimensional line. For more details, the interested reader is referred to the insightful paper \[19\].

#### Local linear embedding (LLE)

As was the case with the Laplacian eigenmap method, *local linear embedding* (LLE) assumes that the data points rest on a smooth enough manifold of dimension *m*, which is embedded in the ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si12.png) space, with *m* < *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">&lt;</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si325.png) \[155\]. The smoothness assumption allows us to further assume that, provided there are sufficient data and the manifold is “well” sampled, nearby points lie on (or close to) a “locally” *linear* patch of the manifold (see, also, related comments in Section [20.8.3](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#s0140)). The algorithm in its simplest form is summarized in the following three steps:

Step 1: For each point, $\\textit{\\textbf{x}}\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si34.png), search for its nearest neighbors.

Step 2: Compute the weights *W*(*n*, *j*), *j* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si514.png), that best reconstruct each point, **x**[*n*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si466.png), from its nearest neighbors, so as to minimize the cost

$\\arg\\min\\limits\_{W}\\ \\ E\_{W} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left\\| \\mathbf{x}\_{n} - \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}W(n,j)\\mathbf{x}\_{n\_{j}} \\right\\|^{2},$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:munder><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munder><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>W</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si515.png)(20.116) 

where $\\textit{\\textbf{x}}\_{n\_{j}}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si516.png) denotes the *j*th neighbor of the *n*th point. (a) The weights are constrained to be zero for points which are not neighbors and (b) the rows of the weight matrix add to one, that is, 

$\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}W(n,j) = 1,\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N.$<mml:math><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si517.png)(20.117) 

That is, the sum of the weights, over all neighbors, must be equal to one.

Step 3: Once the weights have been computed from the previous step, use them to obtain the corresponding points $\\textit{\\textbf{z}}\_{n} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si518.png), so as to minimize the cost with respect to the unknown set of points $\\mathcal{Z} = \\{\\textit{\\textbf{z}}\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N\\}$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Z</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">{</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">}</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si519.png),

$\\arg\\min\_{\\mathbf{z}\_{n}:\\ n = 1,\\ldots,N}\\ \\ E\_{\\mathcal{Z}} = \\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\left\\| \\mathbf{z}\_{n} - \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{N}W(n,j)\\mathbf{z}\_{j} \\right\\|^{2}.$<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>:</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="script">Z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>j</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="true" maxsize="2.4ex" minsize="2.4ex">‖</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si520.png)(20.118) 

The above minimization takes place subject to two constraints, to avoid degenerate solutions: (a) the outputs are centered, $\\sum\_{n}\\textit{\\textbf{z}}\_{n} = \\textbf{0}$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo>∑</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold">0</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si521.png), and (b) the outputs have unit covariance matrix \[159\]. Nearest points, in Step 1, are searched in the same way as for the Laplacian eigenmap method. Once again, the use of the Euclidean distance is justified by the smoothness of the manifold, as long as the search is limited “locally” among neighboring points. For the second step, the method exploits the local linearity of a smooth manifold and tries to predict *linearly* each point by its neighbors using the least-squares method. Minimizing the cost subject to the constraint given in Eq. [(20.117)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq177) results in a solution that satisfies the following three properties:

1.  **1.**  rotation invariance,
2.  **2.**  scale invariance,
3.  **3.**  translation invariance.

The first two can easily be verified by the form of the cost function and the third one is the consequence of the imposed constraints. The implication of this is that the computed weights encode information about the intrinsic characteristics of each neighborhood and they do not depend on the particular point.

The resulting weights, *W*(*i*, *j*)<mml:math><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si473.png), reflect the intrinsic properties of the local geometry underlying the data, and because our goal is to retain the local information after the mapping, these weights are used to reconstruct each point in the ℝ^(*m*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si522.png) subspace by its neighbors. As is nicely stated in \[159\], it is as if we take a pair of scissors to cut small linear patches of the manifold and place them in the low-dimensional subspace.

It turns out that solving [(20.118)](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#deq178) for the unknown points, $\\textit{\\textbf{z}}\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si269.png), is equivalent to:

*   •  performing an eigendecomposition of the matrix (*I* − *W*)^(*T*)(*I* − *W*)<mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mml:mo><mml:mi>W</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si524.png),
*   •  discarding the eigenvector that corresponds to the smallest eigenvalue,
*   •  taking the eigenvectors that correspond to the next (smaller) eigenvalues. These yield the low-dimensional latent variable scores, $\\textit{\\textbf{z}}\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si269.png).

Once again, the involved matrix *W* is sparse, and if this is taken into account, the eigenvalue problem scales relatively well to large data sets with complexity subquadratic in *N*. The complexity for Step 2 scales as *O*(*N**k*³)<mml:math><mml:mi>O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>k</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si525.png), and it is contributed by the solver of the linear set of equations with *k* unknowns for each point. The method needs two parameters to be provided by the user, the number of nearest neighbors, *k* (or *ϵ*) and the dimensionality *m*. The interested reader can find more on the LLE method in \[159\].

#### Isometric mapping (ISOMAP)

In contrast to the two previous methods, which unravel the geometry of the manifold on a local basis, the ISOMAP algorithm adopts the view that only the geodesic distances between all pairs of the data points can reflect the true structure of the manifold. Euclidean distances between points in a manifold cannot represent it properly, because points that lie far apart, as measured by their geodesic distance, may be close when measured in terms of their Euclidean distance (see [Fig. 20.17](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0110)). ISOMAP is basically a variant of the multidimensional scaling (MDS) algorithm, in which the Euclidean distances are substituted by the respective geodesic distances along the manifold. The essence of the method is to estimate geodesic distances between points that lie far apart. To this end, a two-step procedure is adopted.

![Figure 20.17 The point denoted by a “star” is deceptively closer to the point denoted by a “dot” than to the point denoted by a “box” if distance is measured in terms of the Euclidean distance. However, if one is constrained to travel along the spiral, the geodesic distance is the one that determines closeness and it is the “box” point that is closer to the “star.”](images/B9780443292385000263/gr017.jpg)

[Figure 20.17](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#cf1395) The point denoted by a “star” is deceptively closer to the point denoted by a “dot” than to the point denoted by a “box” if distance is measured in terms of the Euclidean distance. However, if one is constrained to travel along the spiral, the geodesic distance is the one that determines closeness and it is the “box” point that is closer to the “star.”

Step 1: For each point, $\\textit{\\textbf{x}}\_{n},\\ n = 1,2,\\ldots,N$<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mtext></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si34.png), compute the nearest neighbors and construct a graph *G*(*V*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si477.png) whose vertices represent the data points and the edges connect nearest neighbors. (Nearest neighbors are computed with either of the two alternatives used for the Laplacian eigenmap method. The parameters *k* or *ϵ* are user-defined parameters.) The edges are assigned weights based on the respective Euclidean distance (for nearest neighbors, this is a good approximation of the respective geodesic distance).

Step 2: Compute the pair-wise geodesic distances among all pairs (*i*, *j*), *i*, *j* = 1, 2, …, *N*<mml:math><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>j</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si526.png), along shortest paths through the graph. The key assumption is that the geodesic between any two points on the manifold can be approximated by the *shortest path* connecting the two points along the graph *G*(*V*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si477.png). To this end, efficient algorithms can be used to achieve it with complexity 𝒪(*N*²ln *N* + *N*²*k*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>k</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si527.png) (e.g., Dijkstar's algorithm, \[59\]). This cost can be prohibitive for large values of *N*.

Having estimated the geodesics between all pairs of points, the MDS method is mobilized. Thus, the problem becomes equivalent to performing the eigendecomposition of the respective Gram matrix and selecting the *m* most dominant eigenvectors to represent the low-dimensional space. After the mapping, Euclidean distances between points in the low-dimensional subspace match the respective geodesic distances on the manifold in the original high-dimensional space. As is the case in PCA and MDS, *m* is estimated by the number of significant eigenvalues. It can be shown that ISOMAP is guaranteed asymptotically (*N* → ∞<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">⟶</mml:mo><mml:mo>∞</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si528.png)) to recover the true dimensionality of a class of nonlinear manifolds \[66,173\].

All three graph-based methods share a common step for computing nearest neighbors in a graph. This is a problem of complexity 𝒪(*N*²)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="script">O</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si529.png), but more efficient search techniques can be used by employing a special type of data structures (for example, \[23\]). A notable difference between the ISOMAP on the one side and the Laplacian eigenmap and LLE methods on the other is that the latter two approaches rely on the eigendecomposition of sparse matrices as opposed to the ISOMAP that relies on the eigendecomposition of the dense Gram matrix. This gives a computational advantage to the Laplacian eigenmap and LLE techniques. Moreover, the calculation of the shortest paths in the ISOMAP is another computationally demanding task. Finally, it is of interest to note that the three graph-based techniques perform the task of dimensionality reduction while trying to unravel, in one way or another, the geometric properties of the manifold on which the data (approximately) lie. In contrast, this is not the case with the kernel PCA, which shows no interest in any manifold learning. However, as the world is very small, in \[88\] it is pointed out that the graph-based techniques can be seen as special cases of kernel PCA! This becomes possible if data-dependent kernels, derived from graphs encoding neighborhood information, are used in place of predefined kernel functions.

The goal of this section was to present some of the most basic directions that have been suggested for nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Besides the previous basic schemes, a number of variants have been proposed in the literature (e.g., \[21,70,163\]). In \[150\] and \[118\] (*diffusion maps*), the low-dimensional embedding is achieved so as to preserve certain measures that reflect the connectivity of the graph *G*(*V*, *E*)<mml:math><mml:mi>G</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si477.png). In \[30,101\], the idea of preserving the local information in the manifold has been used to define linear transforms of the form $\\textit{\\textbf{z}} = A^{T}\\textit{\\textbf{x}}$<mml:math><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mml:mtext><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>A</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mml:mtext></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si530.png), and the optimization is now carried out with respect to the elements of *A*. The task of incremental manifold learning for dimensionality reduction was more recently considered in \[121\]. In \[172,184\], the *maximum variance unfolding* method is introduced. The variance of the outputs is maximized under the constraint that (local) distances and angles are preserved among neighbors in the graph. Like the ISOMAP, it turns out that the top eigenvectors of a Gram matrix have to be computed, albeit avoiding the computationally demanding step of estimating geodesic distances, as is required by the ISOMAP. In \[164\], a general framework, called *graph embedding*, is presented that offers a unified view for understanding and explaining a number of known (including PCA and nonlinear PCA) dimensionality reduction techniques, and it also offers a platform for developing new ones. For a more detailed and insightful treatment of the topic, the interested reader is referred to \[29\]. A review of nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques can be found in, for example, \[32,123\].

Example 20.7

Let a data set consisting of 30 points be in the two-dimensional space. The points result from sampling the spiral of Archimedes (see [Fig. 20.18](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0115)A), described by

*x*[1] = *a**θ*cos *θ*, *x*[2] = *a**θ*sin *θ*.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">cos</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si531.png)

The points of the data set correspond to the values *θ* = 0.5*π*, 0.7*π*, 0.9*π*, …, 2.05*π*<mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace width="0.25em"/><mml:mn>0.9</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mo>…</mml:mo><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.05</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si532.png) (*θ* is expressed in radians), and *a* = 0.1<mml:math><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.1</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si533.png). For illustration purposes and in order to keep track of the “neighboring” information, we have used a sequence of six symbols, “x,” “+,” “⋆,” “□,” “⋄,” and “∘” with black color, followed by the same sequence of symbols in red color, repeatedly.

![Figure 20.18 (A) A spiral of Archimedes in the two-dimensional space. (B) The previous spiral together with the projections of the sampled points on the direction of the first principal component, resulting from PCA. It is readily seen that neighboring information is lost after the projection and points corresponding to different parts of the spiral overlap. (C) The one-dimensional map of the spiral using the Laplacian method. In this case, the neighboring information is retained after the nonlinear projection and the spiral nicely unfolds to a one-dimensional line.](images/B9780443292385000263/gr018.jpg)

Figure 20.18 (A) A spiral of Archimedes in the two-dimensional space. (B) The previous spiral together with the projections of the sampled points on the direction of the first principal component, resulting from PCA. It is readily seen that neighboring information is lost after the projection and points corresponding to different parts of the spiral overlap. (C) The one-dimensional map of the spiral using the Laplacian method. In this case, the neighboring information is retained after the nonlinear projection and the spiral nicely unfolds to a one-dimensional line.

To study the performance of PCA for this case, where data lie on a nonlinear manifold, we first performed the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix, estimated from the data set. The resulting eigenvalues are

*λ*[2] = 0.089 and *λ*[1] = 0.049.<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.089</mml:mn><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:mtext>and</mml:mtext><mml:mspace width="1em"/><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.049</mml:mn><mml:mo>.</mml:mo></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si534.png)

Observe that the eigenvalues are comparable in size. Thus, if one would trust the “verdict” coming from PCA, the answer concerning the dimensionality of the data would be that it is equal to 2. Moreover, after projecting along the direction of the principal component (the straight line in [Fig. 20.18](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0115)B), corresponding to *λ*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>λ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si24.png), neighboring information is lost because points from different locations are mixed together.

In the sequel, the Laplacian eigenmap technique for dimensionality reduction is employed, with *ϵ* = 0.2<mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si535.png) and $\\sigma = \\sqrt{0.5}$<mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:msqrt><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msqrt></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si536.png). The obtained results are shown in [Fig. 20.18](#Chp020_1103-1179_B9780443292385000263.xhtml#f0115)C. Looking from right to left, we see that the Laplacian method nicely “unfolds” the spiral in a one-dimensional straight line. Furthermore, neighboring information is retained in this one-dimensional representation of the data. Black and red areas are succeeding each other in the right order, and also, observing the symbols, one can see that neighbors are mapped to neighbors.

## 20.10 Low-rank matrix factorization: a sparse modeling path

The low-rank matrix factorization task has already been discussed from different perspectives. In this section, the task will be considered in a specific context; that of missing entries and/or in the presence of outliers. Such a focus is dictated by a number of more recent applications, especially in the framework of big data problems. To this end, sparsity promoting arguments will be mobilized to offer a fresh look at this old problem. We are not going to delve into many details, and our purpose is to highlight the main directions and methods which have been considered.

### 20.10.1 Matrix completion

To recapitulate some of the main findings in Chapters [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml) and [10](#Chp010_463-518_B9780443292385000160.xhtml), let us consider a signal vector **s** ∈ ℝ^(*l*)<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mml:mi><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si543.png), where only *N* of its components are observed and the rest are unknown. This is equivalent to sensing ***s*** via a sensing matrix having its *N* rows picked uniformly at random from the standard (canonical) basis *Φ* = *I*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si544.png), where *I* is the *l* × *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si596.png) identity matrix. The question that was posed there was whether it is possible to recover ***s*** exactly based on these *N* components. From the theory presented in Chapter [9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml), we know that one can recover all the components of ***s***, provided that ***s*** is sparse in some basis or dictionary, Ψ, which exhibits low mutual coherence with *Φ* = *I*<mml:math><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>I</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si544.png), and *N* is large enough, as has been pointed out in Section [9.9](#Chp009_417-462_B9780443292385000159.xhtml).

Inspired by the theoretical advances in compressed sensing, a question similar in flavor and with a prominent impact regarding practical applications was posed in \[33\]. Given an *l*[1] × *l*[2]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si545.png) matrix *M*, assume that only *N* ≪ *l*[1]*l*[2]<mml:math><mml:mi>N</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si546.png) among its entries are known. Concerning notation, we refer to a general matrix *M*, irrespective of how this matrix was formed. For example, it may correspond to an image array. The question now is whether one is able to recover the exact full matrix. This problem is widely known as *matrix completion* \[33\]. The answer, although it might come as a surprise, is “yes” with high probability, provided that (a) the matrix is *well structured* and complies with certain assumptions, (b) it has a *low rank*, *r* ≪ *l*<mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi><mml:mo>≪</mml:mo><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si547.png), where *l* = min (*l*[1], *l*[2])<mml:math><mml:mi>l</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">min</mml:mi><mml:mo>⁡</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si548.png), and (c) *N* is large enough. Intuitively, this is plausible because a low-rank matrix is fully described in terms of a number of parameters (degrees of freedom), which is much smaller than its total number of entries. These parameters are revealed via its SVD

$M = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{r}\\sigma\_{i}\\mathbf{u}\_{i}\\mathbf{v}\_{i}^{T} = U\\begin{bmatrix} \\sigma\_{1} & & O & \\\\ & \\ddots & & \\\\ O & & \\sigma\_{r} & \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}V^{T},$<mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:munderover><mml:mo movablelimits="false">∑</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="badbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:munderover><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>\[</mml:mo><mml:mtable><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>O</mml:mi></mml:mtd></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mo>⋱</mml:mo></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/></mml:mtr><mml:mtr><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:mi>O</mml:mi></mml:mtd><mml:mtd columnalign="center"/><mml:mtd columnalign="center"><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mtd></mml:mtr></mml:mtable><mml:mo>\]</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>V</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>,</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math>

![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si549.png)(20.119) 

where *r* is the rank of the matrix, **u**[*i*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*[1])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>∈</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>l</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si550.png) and **v**[*i*] ∈ ℝ^(*l*[2])<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi *i* = 1, 2, …, *r*<mml:math><mml:mi>i</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mspace orthonormal singular vectors, spanning the column and row spaces of *M*, respectively, *σ*[*i*]<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>i</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si553.png), the corresponding singular values, and *U* = \[**u**[1], **u**[2], ⋯, **u**[*r*]\]<mml:math><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo stretchy="false">\]</mml:mo></mml:math>![Equation](images/B9780443292385000263/si555.png), *V* = \[**v**[1], **v**[2], ⋯, **v**[*r*]\]<mml:math><mml:mi>V</mml:mi><mml:mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">\[</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi
